en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Great Division of the Long Discourses.
1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta:
Explanation of the Discourse Concerning Former Existences 1.
It was covered by groves of *kareri* trees, which, with their thick foliage, branches, and shoots, formed canopies like pavilions.
The term *padesa* (place) is intended here as the "Kareri pavilion. Regarding the word "at the door" (*dvāre*), it means in the vicinity of the door.
The phrase beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) was stated to show that there is a conventional designation for other places as well, based on the trees standing at the door.

But how is it that the Blessed One, instead of staying in the Great Fragrant Chamber (*mahāgandhakuṭī*), dwelt at that time in the Kareri hut? That too was a fragrant chamber used by the Buddha, the Blessed One, for his residence.
Showing this, he said, “In the Jeta Grove,” and so forth. “A salaḷa-house” means a dwelling made of *devadāru* (deodar) trees.
“After the regular meal” means after the usual time for the monks’ meal; the meaning is, subsequent to the midday hour.
“Of those who have returned from the alms round” means of those who have finished eating the alms-food. Therefore he said, “the duty of the meal,” and so forth.
A sitting hall constructed in the shape of a mandala by way of a pillared pavilion is intended here as a “maṇḍalamāḷa”; thus he said, “of the sitting hall.

Regarding the phrase “connected with past lives” (*pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā*): here the word *pubba* (past) has the past as its object, while the word *nivāsa* (dwelling/life) is used in the sense of an action noun (*kamma-sādhana*).
Furthermore, there is no phenomenon that dwells apart from the aggregates (*khandha*), and the aggregates exist only by way of a continuum (*santāna*).
"They occur" means: "by means of past abodes, which are designated as the continuity of aggregates in which one previously dwelt.
"Having joined" means having joined them by way of being objects. "Occurred" means spoken of. Because they are associated with the Dhamma, they do not depart from the Dhamma;
thus they are "connected with the Dhamma. Therefore he said: "conjoined with the Dhamma."
"Udapādi" (it arose) is the extraction of the word; its connection is with "uppannā jātā" (arisen, born). That mode of its arising, however, has been shown in the text only in brief;
in order to show it in detail, the passage beginning with "Aho acchariyam" (Oh, how wonderful!
was commenced. Therein, regarding the two phrases "Who recollects? and "Who does not recollect?", first of all, [the answer is] the serpent-creeping [of the mind], and not...
The word "others" refers to those same individuals as demonstrated by way of their classification as persons, the division of time, the mode of recollection, and through similes;
thus it was said: "the sectarians (titthiyā) recollect," and so forth.

Those who profess that action has reached its summit are those who maintain that action has reached its pinnacle—namely, the ascetics and wanderers who stand firm in the knowledge of the ownership of action, thinking: "there is action, there is the result of action."
"They recollect exactly forty eons" is stated by the Blessed One in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and other discourses, having thus delimited it;
"they do not recollect beyond that" is likewise stated because the knowledge of those who are established in views is exceedingly weak.
"The disciples" refers to the Great Disciples, for their prior aspiration (*pubbābhinīhāra*) extended over a hundred thousand eons; as for ordinary disciples, however, it was less than that.

They recollect only less than that. Because the application of merit and knowledge, as well as the accumulation of the perfections for the sake of disciple-enlightenment (sāvakabodhi) and paccekabodhi, have respectively these magnitudes in terms of time—namely, "one asaṅkhyeyya plus one million aeons" and "two asaṅkhyeyyas"—therefore it is said: "The two chief disciples... [and so on] ...and one hundred thousand aeons."

If the range of the noble ones' knowledge of direct higher powers (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) were limited by the time it took them to accumulate the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), then it would follow that even the Buddhas have such a limitation; with reference to this objection, he says:
"But for the Buddhas there is no such limit as 'only this much'; they recollect as much as they wish, to whatever extent. "To whatever extent... [the text continues].
This is because of the statement: "It is to be understood; such is the extent of that knowledge.

For just as with omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), there is no limit to the Buddhas' direct knowledges (*abhiññāñāṇa*) within their own respective domains; therefore, whatever they wish to know, they certainly know it.

Alternatively, even though there is a limitation by time, due to the preeminence of the requisites for Great Enlightenment—such as being encompassed by compassion and skillful means—there is no such limitation.

There is no limit to the manifestation of the power of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramitā), so how could there be any limit to the super-knowledge knowledges (abhiññā-ñāṇa) that are caused by it?
Thus it is said: "For the Buddhas... [there is] none.

"In the sequence of the aggregates" means according to the succession of the aggregates as they proceed in order, each arising in dependence upon its respective condition. "The occurrence of the aggregates" refers to the process of their arising.
The occurrence of the aggregates beginning with feeling. For their grasping of the modes of experiencing and so forth is preeminent;

having grasped those in various places within the existence of perception by way of recollection, they go on, but not finding them in the one-aggregate existence, they are said to "not see," like birds fallen into a net or like fish—this is the intended meaning. "As if blunted" means sluggish.
"Like the lame" means like those who crawl on their bellies (pīṭhasappino). "They grasp a view" means they grasp the view of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannika-diṭṭhi).
"Movement by means of the tip of a staff" refers to movement caused by the tip of a staff, because one does not let go of the succession of the aggregates (khandha-paṭipāṭi).
"Even though this is so" means that although it is true that even the disciples of the Buddha do not perceive the occurrence of aggregates in the non-percipient realm (asañña-bhava), even so...
Even though those disciples of the Buddha have transcended the state of non-perception (*asaññabhava*), they still recollect what lies beyond it.
The passage beginning with “In the cycle of existence” (*vaṭṭe*) and so forth demonstrates the manner in which they recollect it. “Standing by the method given by the Buddhas” means:

standing by this teaching taught by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, namely, “That wherein there is only the occurrence of form for five hundred eons, but no occurrence of the formless—that is the state of non-perception.”
"Standing upon the guide of the Dhamma. For it is by not seeing the intermediate states of death and rebirth-linking in this way that they recollect the future, just as the Venerable Sobhita did.

It is said that having attained mastery over his former abodes, as he recollected his own places of birth in successive order, he saw as far back as his mindless rebirth-linking in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*).
After that, for a period measuring five hundred kappas, he did not see any instances of death and rebirth;
finally, seeing a death at the very end and reflecting, "What indeed is this?", he reached the conclusion through his methodical reasoning that "it will be a state of non-perception" (*asaññabhava*).
Then the Blessed One, taking that circumstance as the occasion for a teaching, placed him in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives.
He established [this]. The phrase "having observed the death and rebirth-linking" is a demonstration of the transition of their knowledge by way of death and rebirth-linking;
it shows that they are unable to go without having touched upon existence (*bhava*) in every respect.
"They see only that very thing" means, for example, as when at the time of midday during the autumn season, standing on a four-cubit platform...
It is a matter established in the world that for a man with eyes, visible forms are indeed very clearly manifest;

yet it may be that those forms—distinguished as subtle, concealed, and so forth—are not within his range. But there is no such thing as the knowable (ñeyya) being outside the range of the Buddhas when they desire to know it;
rather, that [knowable] is illuminated by the light of their knowledge like an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of the hand.
It becomes as clearly manifest and distinct as if it were right before one's eyes, because the cognitive obscurations (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*) have been thoroughly abandoned. Therefore he said:
"But the Buddhas [know] what has been seen or done by themselves or by others, like the radiance of the solar disk," and so forth.
Likewise for the disciples (*sāvaka*) and the paccekabuddhas. Here, by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is implied that they know only what has been seen, done, or heard by themselves.

By concluding with the words, “recalling thus,” he demonstrates that their recollection is indeed partial (*sappadesa*) and not complete (*nippadesa*), because the power of their knowledge is exceedingly slight, like the light of a glowworm.
Here, for the ordinary disciples (*pakatisāvaka*), it is like the light of an ordinary lamp;
for the Great Disciples (*mahāsāvaka*), it is like the light of a great lamp. Thus it was said in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Resembling the radiance of a torch”: resembling the radiance of the medicinal-star (osadhitāraka).
It is like the light of that star which has acquired the name “osadhī” because it possesses abundant radiance, or because it provides auxiliary support to medicinal herbs.
It is like the radiance of the autumnal solar orb because it completely dispels darkness. “Stumbling” is the state of instability in grasping the object, caused by a lack of clarity.
Resistance is the non-comprehension of an object caused by dullness. "Dependent solely upon adverting" means it is contingent merely upon the act of adverting;
the meaning is that it penetrates whatever is desired as soon as it has been adverted to. This same principle applies to the other two phrases as well.
The Blessed One’s knowledge, proceeding without attachment and unimpeded, is exactly the same whether the object is very light or very heavy.
To demonstrate this, two similes beginning with “in a weak leaf-cup” were stated.

Because it pertains to the qualities of the Blessed One’s Dhamma-body, it is said that [this discourse] “arose with reference to the Blessed One himself. “All of that” refers to all the aforementioned talk concerning past lives.
The recollection of past lives by both the non-Buddhists (titthiyas) and the disciples (sāvakas)—
This was spoken here by way of showing an inferior example of the Blessed One’s recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussaraṇa*).
For in this way, the greatness of the Blessed One is especially made manifest. "In brief" (*saṅkhepato*) means concisely.
Whatever variety of the occurrence of the knowledge of the recollection of past lives falls within the range of his own knowledge—all that, at that time—
Having condensed what was said by you, those monks said, "It is thus" (*itipi*). Because it possesses many aspects, there is a reduplicated expression;

the word *pi* has the sense of inclusion. Showing that the word *iti* has the sense of "aspect"—as in such passages as "Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear"—he stated its meaning as "it is even so" (*evampi*).
2–3. Regarding the phrase "Vuttameva" (already stated): here, what is intended by "already stated" is that which is common to this reading and is already expressed by that [previous] text;
it does not refer to what is uncommon, since that would require an additional commentary on new words. Demonstrating this, he says, "For this indeed is the distinction," and so forth.
The word "assosi" (heard) is used in the sense of the accomplishment of the act of hearing by way of the apprehension of sound.
Because the understanding of that meaning has been established. In that context, however, it is stated in the Pāḷi: “Having understood this summarized Dhamma. The construction is:
“These bhikkhus are praising my qualities; how so? By means of my knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa). “Nipphatti” means the accomplishment of the task;
the sense is: the completion of the duty to be performed. “No” is a particle used for questioning.
The particle *nu* has the same meaning as this [particle]; thus it is said, “*iccheyyātha nū*. *Naṃ* refers to the Blessed One.
In the phrase “*yaṃ bhagavā*,” the word *yaṃ*, which functions to refer back to the action, points to what was stated as “*dhammiṃ kathaṃ katheyyā*.
He says that the meaning of the word “*etassa*” is the performance of the discourse on the Dhamma (*dhammikathākaraṇa*), which is what is being referred to.
“...of delivering a discourse on the Dhamma. However, it is stated twice out of a sense of reverence. 4.
Regarding the word *suṇātha* (“listen”), the particle *iti* here has the sense of “beginning” or “manner”; by this, it includes the phrase “attend to it” (*manasi karotha*).
*Sotāvadhānaṃ* means the fixing of the ear; the meaning is “desire to hear” (*sussūsā*). *Chinnaṃ upacchinnaṃ vaṭumaṃ* means a path that is cut off or interrupted.
The cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*) has been cut off for these; they are the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddhā*) and other [noble ones] whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsavā*).
Here, however, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones are intended. For the complete recollection of them is not within the scope of others. Therefore he said, "unshared by others.
The word *yaṃ* is seen in the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) because it indicates the agentive sense; [it is also used] in the accusative case (*upayogavacana*).
The word *yaṃ* is seen [in this context] because it indicates the object of the act of questioning.

And *taṃ* is indeed the accusative case, since the verb *pucchati* (he asks) takes two objects. He says, "It is seen in the instrumental case," meaning that here the sense of *yaṃ* is "by which reason.
It should be understood as being in the locative case (*bhummē*), for the word *yaṃ* is not found only in the nominative and accusative cases.
Thus, while it is seen as an instrumental suffix (*karaṇe*), here it should be understood as a locative (*bhummē*).

"The ten-thousandfold world-system" refers to the ten-thousandfold cycle of world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*) that constitutes the field of his birth. He arose "proclaiming aloud" because the appearance of a Buddha is adorned by the manifestation of many wonders.
The "excellence of the time" refers to the abundance of virtues among the beings there; and the supreme abundance of virtue is the appearance of a Buddha.

Because of the abundance of virtues in this aeon, it is called a "fortunate aeon" (*bhaddakappa*); thus he said, "because it is adorned by the arising of five Buddhas, it is a beautiful aeon" (*sundarakappa*).
Likewise, by way of its essential qualities, it is called a "substantial aeon" (*sārakappa*).
Having stated, "Praising this aeon, he spoke thus," he said "from which time onwards," etc., in order to show that the manner in which this aeon is to be praised is not shared by any other.

In that context, "from which time onwards" means from the moment the aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) was made—that is, when the aspiration endowed with the eight factors such as being born as a human being was set in motion.
Since *saṃsāra* is beginningless, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who arose prior to this Blessed One’s aspiration were infinite and immeasurable;
thus, in order to exclude the eons (*kappa*) that had already passed since their appearance, [the text says] "in this..."

He said, "In the interval. Granted that this Blessed One made his formal resolve (abhinīhāra) during the arising of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, yet the birth of that Blessed One was even earlier than this resolve; thus it is said, "Our... [etc.]... were born.
"At the conclusion of incalculable eons" means at the end of incalculable great eons (mahākappa). This same method applies to those that follow as well.
By the phrase "more than thirty thousand aeons from now," it is shown that between the Blessed One Padumuttara and the Blessed One Sumedha,
there were sixty-nine thousand aeons devoid of Buddhas. By the phrase "more than eighteen thousand aeons from now," [it is shown that between] the Blessed One Sujāta and the Blessed One Atthadassi...
This shows that between the time of the Blessed One [Kassapa] and [the present], there were twelve thousand aeons minus one that were devoid of Buddhas.
By the phrase "ninety-four aeons from now," it shows that between the Blessed One Dhammadassi and the Blessed One Siddhattha,
there were seventeen thousand aeons plus ninety-six that were devoid of Buddhas.
By the phrase "In thirty-one aeons," it is shown that between the Blessed One Vipassi and the Blessed One Sikhī,

sixty aeons were devoid of Buddhas. All of these, when combined with the aeons beginning from Sumedha and others prior to the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, amount to one hundred thousand aeons, during which—
The great disciples and others accumulated wholesome roots conducive to the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Even when the world is empty of a Buddha, Paccekabuddhas arise and become conditions for the increase of the overflowing merit of those distinguished persons.
With the words "In this way," etc., he states the aforementioned meaning by way of conclusion.
“What is this? and so forth was begun for the purpose of explaining the preliminary signs (*pubbanimitta*). Therein, “this” refers to the arising of Buddhas.
“At the time of the formation of an eon” means at the time when the eon of evolution (*vivaṭṭakappa*) is being established.

“One incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*)” is said with reference to the period of dissolution and subsistence (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyi*). “Remaining as a single level” means that mountains, trees, shrubs, and so forth, as well as clouds and so forth, [remain thus].

The courtyard having become open due to the absence [of clouds], it stands [there]. "In the world-habitat" (*lokasannivāse*) means in the place where one is to dwell together with the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*).
Twenty *yaṭṭhis* make one *usabha*. The word *matta* (measure/extent) should be applied individually in such phrases as "one *usabha*-measure," "two *usabha*-measures," and so forth.
"Having become a thousand *yojanas* in measure" means that the falling stream of water [occupies] a space in the sky measuring a thousand *yojanas*.
Having pervaded [the world], it extends for a mere thousand yojanas in its movement.
"As far as the non-perishing Brahmā-world" means as far as the Ābhassara Brahmā-world, as far as the Subhakiṇha Brahmā-world, and as far as the Vehapphala Brahmā-world—this is the meaning.
"By way of the wind" refers to the supporting wind-circle, which is nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas in height.
By way of [this] sequence. "The Great Enlightenment Throne" refers to the specific location of the Great Enlightenment Throne.
Its subsequent destruction and its initial formation should be understood as occurring by way of natural law (*dhammatā*). "Therein" means in that location.
"Having become a precursor" means having become a precursor to the arising of a Buddha; for the grove, being dependent on that precursor, is designated by the name of what it supports.
Thus it was said. Therefore he says, “of that,” and so forth. “Having become bound by a central hub (kaṇṇikā)” means having become like those with attached hubs.
The construction is: “The Brahmās of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), joyful... go. By including the Subhakiṇha realm within the Vehapphala realm, they are called the “nine Brahma-worlds.
For indeed, they belong to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) alone. “As they were departing” means:

Regarding those who have gone forth in the Great Renunciation: here, "birth" (*abhijāti*) is included specifically as the descent into the womb, by virtue of its commonality with the state of being born.
A "sign" (*nimitta*) is that by which a result is inferred or measured; it is a cause.
For even when a cause is seen as an indicator, one grasps the result as already established through its invariable concomitance, just as the seer Asita did.
Having seen the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisa) belonging to his noble birth, he accepted them after establishing that the qualities of a Buddha were necessarily concomitant with them.
When it is accepted in this way, the fruit caused by those marks is spoken of as if it were established by their power, because [the fruit] exists when they exist.
Therefore he said: "By the power of those marks," and so forth. Likewise:
And the Blessed One said: "Endowed with that mark... [and so on]... what does he obtain when he is a king, and what does he obtain when he is a Buddha?
and so forth. "This matter" means they knew, according to reality, this matter: that five Buddhas will arise in this kappa.
Commentary on the Analysis of Births (Jātiparicchedādivaṇṇanā) 5–7.

"By way of the analysis of eons" means by way of delimiting and fully understanding each respective eon in which those various Buddhas appeared, as expressed in passages such as, "In the ninety-first eon from now... and so forth.
“Pariccheda” (delimitation) is the act of delimiting—that is, knowing by way of defining and circumscribing with the thought, “This is for you.
“Paritta” means limited. “Lahuka” means very light; since “life-span” is intended here, it is said to be “short. Therefore he said:
“Both of these are synonyms for ‘little’ (appaka).”
“‘A little more’ is an expression used without specific qualification;

having established it according to what is obtained by way of an unrestricted sense—as ‘twenty or thirty,’ and so on—he said, ‘But one with such a long life is exceedingly rare,’ showing that this method is not uncommon.
Then, demonstrating that very specific determination by including it among individuals, he said, ‘In this regard, Visākhā... and so forth.”
"If this is so, why did our Blessed One not live for such a long time?
Is it not the case that Great Bodhisattvas, in their final existence, take rebirth through an exceedingly sublime volitional formation of merit? "That is true.
To show the reason for this, the passage beginning with "But Vipassī and the others... was stated. In that context, because of his birth, he was an object of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the preliminary stage for the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*). For the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) is specifically concordant with that.

Its specific association with joy (*somanassasahagata*) should be understood as being due primarily to its dependence on thoughts of safety (*khemavitakka*); its association with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) is due to its dependence on a specific excellence of knowledge that is not shared by others and is free from instruction by another;
and its unprompted nature (*asaṅkhārikatā*) is likewise to be understood. Furthermore, its lifespan is incalculable due to the excellence of its basis and the excellence of its support.
The immeasurable power of the cause is due to its removal of opposing factors and its specific mode of manifestation.

In this regard, the state of being a distinguished basis consists in the fact that the mental continuum has been cultivated by the perfections for a very long time. The state of being a distinguished support consists in the perfection of the underlying disposition, such as the inclination toward non-greed.
The removal of opposing factors consists in the suppression of unwholesome states such as gain and stinginess. [This applies] to all beings...
The accumulation [of karma] for the sake of escaping all the suffering of saṃsāra should be understood as a specific mode of manifestation.
And since this method is common to the accumulation of karmic effort that brings about the final existence of all Great Bodhisattvas, it must also be identical in its result;
thus he said, "Therefore, all Buddhas have an incalculable lifespan."
The meaning is that their lifespan lasts for an incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*). There exists accumulated karma capable of bringing about an incalculable lifespan;

however, the Buddhas pass away into *parinibbāna* after remaining for only as long as corresponds to the maximum human lifespan at that time, because there is no further purpose to be accomplished by remaining beyond that point.
Alternatively, this should be understood as a natural law (*dhammatāvesa*). Thus it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, regarding what follows, the reason given for the impossibility [of such things] is "due to the failure of climate and food.
It cannot be said that this does not apply to the Tathāgatas, who are born and awakened in the world, for they too certainly experience illness, fatigue, and so forth.
"By way of climate and food" means by way of both deficient and excellent climate and food.
According to the sequence, life-span both decreases and increases. And by "life-span" (*āyu*), the maximum life-span (*paramāyu*) is intended.
Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and other texts.
Now, in order to demonstrate that matter starting from its origin, the passage beginning with “Therein, when... was spoken. Regarding the phenomena (*dhamme*):
Those who are engaged [in such acts] are righteous; those who are not righteous are unrighteous, being devoted to violence and other unrighteous deeds.

It becomes unrighteous through following the lead of powerful persons and by falling into conformity with the views of others. "Hot-cloud deities" refers to sons of gods who cause the arising of masses of clouds that serve as the condition for the hot season.
Indeed, it is said that for them, [the result occurs] simultaneously with the arising of such a thought.
A garland of clouds, spreading heat to wherever it is desired, not too thick, spreads out and covers the sky here and there.
This same method applies to cold-clouds and rain-clouds. However, cloud-deities (*abbhavalāhakā*) should be understood as those who produce only a mass of clouds, without the cold, heat, or rain.
In the phrase "tāsanti," the word "mittā" (friends) is [to be supplied].

Having brought [the meaning] into connection (*yojanā*). Granted that the sevenfold classes of deities mentioned below are indeed those belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*), yet having described them according to their respective specific distinctions, [the author] now speaks of "the Cātumahārājikas" in order to include, in a general sense, the other sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) deities of the first plane.

Regarding the phrase "due to their unrighteousness": this refers to the lineage of unrighteousness beginning with the subordinate kings and so forth, which is rooted in the unrighteous nature of the kings themselves.
Because of the unrighteousness of those deities. "The moon and sun move unevenly" means that,
being oppressed by the wind blowing unevenly through the power of common evil karma—
characterized as the aforementioned unrighteousness and serving as the supporting condition for undesirable results such as frequent illness— the moon and sun, while encircling Sineru, move unevenly.

“They revolve contrary to their proper course; they do not proceed as they should. To show that the irregular occurrence of seasons, rains, and so forth—just as the irregular revolution of the moon and sun is caused by the agitation of irregular winds—is stated: “The wind does not blow according to its proper course,” and so on.
“Of the deities” refers to the deities such as the cloud-deities of cold and heat. Therefore he said: “The distinction between cold and heat...”

"Regarding the phrase beginning with *utū* (the seasons): 'When that [season] does not succeed' means when that aforementioned season, which serves as the seed for the rains, does not attain its proper fulfillment at the appropriate time.
Expanding upon the meaning briefly stated as 'the rain does not fall properly,' he says 'sometimes,' and so forth. Therein..."
"Sometimes it rains" means that it rains at a time when it ought not to rain. "Sometimes it does not rain" means that it does not rain at a time when it ought to rain.
"It rains in some places, it does not rain in others" refers to specific locations. The passage beginning with "Even while raining" and so forth is an explanation of the meaning of the two phrases:
"sometimes it rains" and "sometimes it does not rain. "Devoid of fragrance, color, taste, and so forth" [is the description of the rain].
By the word "etc.," the state of being seedless is included. "In one place" means on one side of the vessel for cooking the rice.

"With the husks removed" means the rice that has been stripped of its husks during the cooking process. "In three ways" refers to these three modes: entirely undigested, partially digested, and improperly digested.
It is "cooked" when it reaches the receptacle of digested food (the *pakvāśaya*). Regarding the term "short-lived": here—

“‘And they are ill-favored’—this too should be stated. Thus, through the influence of the season and food, life-span diminishes because the condition becomes exceedingly weak even though the cause has not yet been exhausted.
‘But when,’ etc., the meaning of the bright fortnight should be understood by reversing what was said [for the dark fortnight].”

It should be understood that [the Buddhas] have passed away after having increased [their lifespans] again and again. Why? Because many Buddhas do not arise in a single intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*);
rather, only one arises. Now, in order to demonstrate this matter in detail, the passage beginning with "How" was stated.
"Having stood for four [aeons]" is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). "In whichever respective measures of lifespan... [and so forth].
"In whatever measure of maximum lifespan"—that is, for those Buddhas as well, their lifespan is exactly that same measure;
the reason for this has already been stated below.
The commentary on the delimitation of birth and so forth is concluded.
Commentary on the Chapter on Awakening (Bodhipariccheda): 8.
Regarding "at the root" (*mūle*): it means in the vicinity of the root part. Since that [vicinity] is the area directly below it, he says, "beneath the *pāṭali* tree.
"On that day" (*taṃdivasaṃ*) refers either to the day he himself was born, or alternatively, to the day the Blessed One attained full awakening (*abhisambodhi*).
It is said that the Bodhi tree, like a *sāla-kalyāṇī* flower, grew first within the earth itself;
then, on the day of his full enlightenment, it burst forth from the ground and stood filling the sky, a hundred cubits high and as wide, remaining just so.
This too, it is said, was its distinction from others, just as there is a difference in its nature as a tree.

With flowers whose stalks and stems were thick and firm, as if bound together by a central core (*kaṇṇika*), they formed a single covering due to the density of the blossoms. Here and there they were fastened...

[as before] ...and they shone brightly with flower garlands hanging here and there, with clusters of garlands scattered about, and with various pearl-like flowers strewn hither and thither upon their stems.
And it was truly radiant. "Endowed with mutual splendor" means they were possessed of each other’s glory and beauty.
"The splendor of the majesty of the Buddha’s qualities" refers to the radiance of the abundant excellence of those qualities that must be realized by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

"Penetrating" means attaining. "The white-fruit *amba* tree" is a mango tree with white-colored fruit. "That very same" means the same measurement as that stated for the *pāṭali* tree. "On one side" means on one flank. "Surasāni" means having an exceedingly sweet flavor.
"Only one throne" means only one location for a throne. Each such tree is called "Bodhi," based on the derivation that they are "awakened" (*bujjhanti*) therein.
Regarding the commentary on the section concerning the disciples:
"In the section concerning the disciples" refers to the section concerning the pairs of disciples. "Khaṇḍa-Tissa"—both are taken together as a single unit.
He said, "Khaṇḍa and Tissa," because it was stated by way of their unity.

Since there was no uterine brother or even a half-brother who was an elder brother to the Buddhas, it is said, "the younger half-brother from the same father. [This refers to him] among the remaining sons.

Having stated, "he reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī)," the passage beginning with "by the Blessed One Sikhī" was spoken in order to show his specific excellence of qualities that had reached that pinnacle.

“Uttara” means the highest. Again, “Uttara” is said by name to address the Elder. “Pāraṃ” means the ultimate limit or summit. “Paññāvisaye” means in the context of wisdom; for he speaks of its occurrence by way of the place where it occurs.
Commentary on the Section on the Assembly of Disciples (10):
“Uposatha” refers to the *Āṇāpātimokkha* (the Patimokkha as a formal command). “In the second and third” means in the second and third assemblies of disciples.
"The same method" refers by extension to its fourfold nature. Having explained the basis starting from the initial aspiration, the going-forth should be illustrated;
however, since that has been set forth in detail in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, it should be understood according to the method stated therein.
Commentary on the Section on Attendants (Upaṭṭhākaparicchedavaṇṇanā):
“Fixed state of being an attendant” means the state of being a constant attendant from the commencement [of his ministry] until his final nibbāna.
However, there were many attendants to the Blessed One during his first awakening who were not fixed in that role. Therefore he said, “Of the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Now, in order to show the reason why the Elder Ānanda became the Buddha’s permanent attendant, and how he came to that position, the passage beginning with “There on one occasion” was spoken.
[Ānanda] said, “I am going by this path,” being urged on by karma that leads to ruin and disaster. Then the Blessed One, without yet revealing the matter to him—
Referring to the secure path, he said, "Come, bhikkhu, let us go by this way. But why did the Blessed One not explain the matter to him?
Even if it were explained, he would not accept it because he would not believe it; for that [explanation] would lead to his harm and suffering for a long time.
"Tena" means "by that going," or alternatively, the reading is "tam" (meaning "that").
*Anvāsatta* means followed or afflicted. *Dhammasaṃvega* is the agitation based on reverence for the Dhamma, thinking:
"While we ourselves are present, such a thing has happened even to the Blessed One. When the Dhamma-Senāpati says, "I shall attend upon you," he is speaking in this very sense;
thus it was said: "Venerable sir, I [shall attend upon] you," and so forth. That [abode] of mine is indeed not empty...
"That direction" means that very direction of mine is indeed not empty. He states the reason for this: "Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas.
"He will not allow [me] to dwell" means the intention is that he will not grant me residence in the single Perfumed Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*).
"Even of the Dhamma taught in his absence" is said with reference to the teaching of the Suttantas; however, as for his teaching of the Abhidhamma...
It occurs even without being spoken in the presence [of the Buddha], let alone through formal request. Even the path of its recitation originated from the Elder Sāriputta.
Why? Because it belongs to the same category as the mass of Dhamma received by the Elder from the Bhikkhu, just like the analytical knowledge of exposition (niddesa-paṭisambhidā).
Others, however, say: "The Dhamma-warden, having been granted daily leave by the Blessed One for the sequential sets of three and two [factors],..."
He asked questions, and the Blessed One answered each question of his by way of providing guidance and instruction. Thus they say:
"Even though the Abhidhamma was taught by the Teacher in his absence, it was as if it were received directly from him by the Elder.
All of this should be accepted after careful investigation.
“Chief attendant” means an attendant who is foremost in his diligent performance of service.

For from the time he obtained the position of attendant, the Elder served the Blessed One with these and other duties: the two kinds of water, the three kinds of tooth-sticks, foot-massage, sweeping the Gandhakuṭi and its courtyard, and so forth—serving at such-and-such a time.
Thinking, "It is fitting for me to obtain such-and-such from the Teacher; it is fitting for me to perform such-and-such," he would produce each of those things.
Taking a large staff-lamp, he would walk nine times around the Gandhakuṭi courtyard during a single night.
For this was his thought: "If sloth and torpor should overcome me, when the Blessed One calls out to me, I shall give my reply."
“I would not be able to give it,” thinking thus, he does not let go of the staff-lamp from his hand throughout the entire night.
Therefore it is said, “the foremost attendant.
12. The definition of the city born of father and mother is called the “definition of the father” because it comes through the mouth of the father.

"He entered the vihāra" means he entered the Gandhakuṭī. "Having spoken this much" means having delivered the teaching up to this point—adorned with nine sections beginning with the delimitation of the *kappa*—concerning the previous births of the seven Buddhas beginning with Vipassī.
But why did the Blessed One here speak of the previous births of only these seven Buddhas beginning with Vipassī?
Is it not the case that, as in the *Buddhavaṃsa* exposition, there are twenty-five Buddhas, or even more than that?
No, because there is no relevant subject matter and because there would be no purpose [for such an enumeration]. For in the *Buddhavaṃsa* exposition, it is asked:
“Of what nature was your resolve, O Great Hero, O Supreme among Men?”
"At what time, O Hero, was the supreme enlightenment sought by you?"—
taking such a question as it arose, as its subject matter, and as its occasion,
[the text begins] with the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, at whose feet he made his great aspiration, and proceeds through the twenty-four [Buddhas].
Having received the prophecy regarding his enlightenment from the Buddhas, he fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) here and there;
thus, his past lives consisting of those practices were recounted, as was his own practice.
However, in this case, there is no such qualification by which one could recount past lives concerning the Buddhas starting from Dīpaṅkara or even prior to him.
He would have spoken. Therefore, the previous births are not detailed here as they are in the *Buddhavaṃsa* teaching.

Furthermore, because the teaching of the Buddhas is according to the power of knowledge of the individuals who are the vessels for that teaching, and not according to the power of their own knowledge, [it is therefore] there [in the *Buddhavaṃsa*] that the chief disciples, the great disciples, and similar deities and brahmās...

The teaching was expanded according to those [instances]. Here, however, while recounting his own past lives (pubbenivāsa) for the sake of ordinary disciples and similar deities, he recounted the past lives of only seven Buddhas.
For the Blessed One, in order to inspire and encourage them, did not bring the teaching to its conclusion with the discourse on the snake-venom (sappapañcatā).
He entered the Fragrant Chamber. And likewise, following this very teaching, the recitation of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta and others came to pass.

Furthermore, in order to include within his own subsequent teaching that elucidates his journey to the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), the Blessed One recounted the previous births of the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones, beginning with Vipassī. For it was their disciples who, at that time, [performed...]
And at present they abide in the Suddhāvāsa realm because others have attained final nibbāna.
It is said that the disciples of the Buddhas Siddhattha, Tissa, and Phussa were reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realms;
immediately upon their rebirth, like Upaka and others in this current dispensation, they attained arahantship and passed away into final nibbāna before long, rather than remaining here and there.

They say, "He remained for the full span of his life. Likewise, while praising those Perfectly Enlightened Ones whose teaching of realization (*paṭivedhasāsana*) has not yet been definitively determined as having ceased even today—meaning it has not vanished—it was on account of the inclinations of those to be trained that he spoke in this sutta specifically of the previous births of the Blessed Ones beginning with Vipassī. As for the rule regarding "neither first nor last," however:

It should be understood that this is not contradicted by the statement that [the Buddha] "wished for [beings] in a single world-system" because he intended to cause them to transmigrate from one state to another according to their dwelling as sentient beings.

"Having brought it to the ultimate point without interval" means having brought it to its peak and summit, starting from the [Buddha’s] birth up until the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and as long as the fulfillment of the Buddha’s duties continues. The construction is: "it was not yet spoken."

"Dhammatanti" means the "lineage of the Dhamma," which is to say the "scripture" (pariyatti). A "section on many" (sambahulavāra) is a section that proceeds by way of illustrating numerous meanings, such as those concerning a son, a mother of a son, a vehicle, a dwelling, wealth, a donor, and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the section on many:
although this is not found in the canonical text (pāḷi), since it is found in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), it should be brought forward and explained; thus, explaining it:
He said, “For all Bodhisattvas,” and so forth. *Kulavaṃsa* means the lineage of a family; *paveṇī* means succession.
Having asked, “Why?”—inquiring about the cause for the birth of a son—he replied with the words, “For all omniscient Bodhisattvas,” and so forth.
Therefore, their birthplace and so on must necessarily be made known for the purpose of recognizing their human nature.

He shows that otherwise the accomplishment of the intended Buddha-activities would simply not occur; for it is because the manifestation of Great Beings takes place only in the human world during their final existence, and not elsewhere.
Commentary on the Numerous Sections.
He is called Rāhu because he seizes and causes the moon and other luminaries to lose their distinctive beauty; thus he is the planet Rāhu.
Furthermore, here he is called Rāhu because he is like Rāhu. The term "bondage" (bandhana) is stated with reference to being a source for the arising of misfortune.
Having taken that very word spoken by the Great Being, they gave the prince the name "Rāhula. The word *atha* is a mere particle. *Rocinī* means one whose nature is to shine.
The meaning is "of radiant form. *Rucaggatī* means "having come to radiance" (*rucaṃ pabhātaṃ āgatibhūtā*); this is stated by adding the letter *ga*.
She is called *Bimbā* because, due to her status as the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratanabhāvato*), she was like a concealed image for all women in the human world.
*Jhānā vuṭṭhāyā* means "having emerged from the foundational jhāna."
"Eight finger-breadths high" means having a thickness measuring eight finger-breadths.
"Covering with the small part" means covering the entire area of the monastery by way of placing it across the horizontal dimension.
"With golden rods as ploughshares" means with golden rods the size of ploughshares. "Golden elephant feet" means pieces of gold the size of the feet of an ordinary elephant.

“By the same method as stated” means by the same method as the *Cūḷa-senāsana*. “With golden pegs” means with pieces of gold. “Of those possessing the marks” means of those endowed with the [thirty-two] marks, having thousand-spoked wheels.

“The Bodhi throne” (bodhipallaṅka) is the place where one sits at the time of attaining full enlightenment. “Not abandoned” means that because the Buddhas’ sitting in that manner leads to no other state, it is not relinquished.
Therefore he said: “It remains in exactly one place. “The first knot of words” (paṭhamapadagaṇṭhikā).
The place where the right foot was set down while it was being placed upon the lowest step of the staircase.
Because that spot was firm, stable, and indestructible by anyone, it is called the "Foot-Node" (*padagaṇṭhī*).
On that portion of ground where the Great Monastery of Jetavana now stands, at the very spot where [the feet of] all the previous Buddhas...
The beds were prepared; and because the bed for our Blessed One was prepared in that very same place, it is said:
"the four positions of the bed’s feet remained exactly where they were.
However, whether the area for preparing the beds is large or small is not the measure; rather, by the power of the Buddha, that place—
It should be understood that it is said, "the four places for the bed-legs remain unseparated," because [the bed] always remains of one and the same measure.
The same principle applies here to the phrase "the dwelling (vihāra) also is not left behind";
for the meaning is that one does not abandon the previous location of the dwelling.

*Visiṭṭhā mattā* means distinguished measure; *vimattā* means varied; *vemattaṃ* is simply variety, the meaning being dissimilarity. *Pamāṇaṃ* refers to stature. *Padhānaṃ* refers to the practice of austerities.

*Rasmī* refers to the radiance of the body. They say: "A middle-sized man is six cubits by the ordinary human hand-span; the Blessed One’s bodily stature is three times that, thus the Blessed One is eighteen cubits tall.
Others, however, say: "By the ordinary human hand-span..."

"A middle-sized man is four cubits tall; the Blessed One’s bodily measure is three times that. Thus, in terms of his conditioned material form (*upādinnakarūpadhamma*), the Blessed One is twelve cubits tall.
Furthermore, since the fathom-wide radiance (*byāmappabhā*) extends all around him, it rises six cubits above [his head];
together with this denser radiance, he is eighteen cubits in height.
"Enduring" means for a long period of time.

"Dependent on aspiration" means that at the time of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, it becomes vast and even more vast, being dependent on the aspiration that has arisen accordingly and conforming to the corresponding yearning;
this meaning is stated according to the method explained in the *Cariyāpiṭaka-vaṇṇanā*.
It should be understood. And here, because the physical stature, the exertion, and the bodily radiance of the Buddhas are unique, they are not mentioned in this textual passage;
therefore, by way of their commonality in diversity with those [other qualities], the lineages of birth (*āyukula*) have also been brought forward and explained here.

"In regard to the qualities realized" means in regard to the qualities of omniscience that have been attained. But is it not the case that [this applies] to the requisites for enlightenment and the number of persons to be trained?

And is there no difference between them? It is true that there is none; however, since both of these are already included by the mention of the "grasping of the Buddha-qualities," they were not specifically singled out.

For, to the extent that there is no difference among all Buddhas regarding their Buddha-qualities, to that same extent there is no difference among them regarding the requisites for enlightenment (*sambodhisambhāra*). Why? Because the fruit is necessarily in accordance with its cause.
The diversity regarding the measure of individuals to be converted has been elucidated. For those individuals to be converted,
who have accumulated the necessary conditions and whose faculties have reached maturity during the causal stage of the Great Bodhisattvas, are awakened by the touch of the Tathāgata’s majestic power—
just as clusters of lotuses are awakened by the contact with the rays of the sun— through the attainment of Arahantship in their final existence.
The masters of the commentaries have declared that [beings] "approach.

By the term "treasure-pot," he speaks with reference to the four great treasures. Regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and was born" (*jāto ca*): it should be understood that by this particle, the meaning "and having made the great resolution" (*katamahābhinīhāro ca*) is also included. For this has been stated in the *Buddhavamsa*:
"The clusters of stars shine, the constellations in the circle of the sky;"
“Visākhā is joined with the moon; surely the Buddha will appear. And they say: “By this very fact, for all Buddhas, the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) occurs during the Visākhā constellation. 13.
“This is the course” means this process of occurrence and the manner of its proceeding; others who recollect past lives [do so] by way of this mode.

The meaning is "recalling. This is because, from the moment of death until rebirth-linking, the act of recalling—consisting of the ascent of knowledge toward past lives designated as the past, further past, and most distant past—is considered its forward progression.
Therefore, from the moment of rebirth-linking until death, the act of recalling is the descent into past lives.
"Knowledge proceeds by way of being directed toward [the object]"—thus he said, "having sent forth knowledge backward.

"That which is to be gone to by death" means that the destination to be reached by the course of knowledge at the moment of death is what is understood; this is the meaning. "Heavy" means burdensome and difficult to perform.
Therefore he said, "as if showing a footprint in the sky. "Another reason" refers to the recollection of the path already traversed (*chinnavaṭumānussaraṇa*).
The dispatching of knowledge toward the rear (pacchāmukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ) is another cause for wonder and amazement. In the phrase "yatrā," *yat* is used in the sense of the locative case;
*nāma* is a particle used in the sense of "wonderful"; and the word *hi* is devoid of meaning [here]. Therefore he said, "the Tathāgata who is indeed such.
And by doing so, the separate inclusion of the word *yatra* as a particle is justified. They proliferate (*papañcenti*).
They are called *papañca* because they extend the continuum of beings within saṃsāra.

It is said that the "round of kamma" is included by the mention of *papañca* as the round of defilements, since the round of result is already included by the mention of suffering. In the phrase "when the rounds are exhausted," this means when the rounds have been completely worn away.
Having stated "by the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit," it follows that this virtue of the path and fruit is preceded by mundane virtue.

To show that even the mundane virtue (*lokiyasīla*) of the Buddhas is unique and not shared by others—just like their supramundane virtue (*lokuttarasīla*)—it is said: "by means of mundane and supramundane virtue.

The same principle applies to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*paññā*). Regarding the term *samādhipakkhā*: it refers to both concentration itself and the factors conducive to concentration (*samādhipakkhā*);
this should be understood as an elliptical compound (*ekadesasarūpekaseso*). Therefore, he says: "by means of path-concentration," and so forth; [this is] the dwelling (*vihāro*).
And [the phrase] "or grasped. The factors on the side of concentration (*samādhipakkha*) are energy, mindfulness, and so forth.

"They lie down by themselves" means they are overcome by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth—that is, by the hindrances themselves, by those evil states associated with them, and by applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the rest.
By the statement, "Because of being liberated, they receive the designation 'liberation' (*vimutti*)," the word *vimutti* is shown to have the sense of an object (*kamma-sādhana*).

He said: "Because its object is the eight attainments and so forth. And regarding the phrase "because of being liberated," it should be construed as "because of being liberated by way of suppression" (*vikkhambhanavasena*), and so on.

"Of this or that" refers to the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and the rest. "By way of the factors of opposition" means by way of the factors that are the counteragents to what is to be abandoned.
"Because of arising at the stage of subsiding" (*paṭippassaddhante*): the subsiding of the defilements is "subsidence" (*paṭippassaddha*); that very [state]...
The meaning is: because it is the ultimate end; because it is produced when that [goal] is to be accomplished;
and because it proceeds by way of the subsiding of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path.
As for the statement "because it stands far away," he says this because Nibbāna is free from defilements and is secluded from them.
16. "The element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*) means the intrinsic nature of phenomena; in terms of meaning, it refers to the Four Noble Truths.
"Thoroughly penetrated" (*suppaṭividdha*) means well-penetrated by virtue of abandoning all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).

For in this way, all the qualities of a Buddha—such as omniscience (*sabbaññutā*), the ten powers (*dasabala*), and the various knowledges—were attained by the Blessed One. Some maintain that the "element of phenomena" is *arahantship*; others say it is "omniscient knowledge" (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
"Others. "By two phrases" means by two sentences. "Bound" (*ābaddha*) means connected, because the subsequent teaching is rooted in that.

"The clamor of the journey to the deva-world" (*devacārikakolāhala*): he will examine this at the conclusion of the Sutta, showing the manifestation of the Suddhāvāsa devas' curiosity during his own journey to the deva-world;
the construction is that he will clarify its meaning. "This teaching" (*ayaṃ desanā*).

With the words beginning “From this, monks,” he speaks of the teaching as it was set forth in detail. With the words beginning “In the Nidānakhaṇḍa,” he speaks of the teaching given by way of summary at the outset;
for that was spoken thus because it serves as the introductory basis (nidāna) for this present teaching.
This concludes the commentary on the nature of the Bodhisatta.
17. Having stated, “‘Vipassī’ is his name,” the passage beginning with “And that indeed... was spoken in order to show the etymological appropriateness (*anvatthatā*) of that name.
It refers to "various meanings" (*vividhe atthe*): in various objects such as those concealed, those situated at a distance, and so forth, as well as blue and other colors;

and to other things within the range of the sense faculties (*indriya-gocara*), both as they are actually encountered and as they are determined through conventional expression (*vohāra-vinicchaya*). "By skill in seeing" (*passana-kusalatāya*) means in regard to vision.
By way of skillfulness (*nipuṇabhāvena*). It is called *bodhi* because one awakens (*bujjhati*) to the knowable (*ñeyya*) exactly as it is;

and because that very [awakening] is associated with a being (*satta*), he is called a *bodhisatta*. Thus he said, "a being who is wise (*paṇḍita*), a being who is an awakener (*bujjanaka*). However, regarding his state of wisdom through well-considered reflection and so forth, there is simply nothing further to be said.
And from the time he made the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), because of his absolute inclination toward Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*), [he is a bodhisatta].
He says, "bound for enlightenment, a bodhisatta," in the passage beginning with "in those things reckoned as enlightenment.

For omniscient knowledge has the knowledge of the path as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the path has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause; this is what is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).

By the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending," he shows that [the Bodhisatta] entered the fourth mode of descent into the womb. For there are four modes of descent into the womb here; someone [enters]...
Regarding the descent into the mother’s womb, the stay therein, and the emergence—these are the three stages at which one may be lacking in clear comprehension (*asampajañña*).
One person is clearly comprehending at the first stage but not at the others; another is clearly comprehending at both the first and second stages but not at the third;
and another is clearly comprehending at all three stages. Among these, the first type of descent into the womb belongs to the ordinary worldling (*lokiyamahājana*).

The first [statement] was spoken with reference to the general case; the second, with reference to the eighty great disciples; and the third, with reference to the two chief disciples and the paccekabuddhas.

It is said that they, as if cast head-first and feet-upward into a precipice hundreds of fathoms deep by the winds born of karma, experience great suffering as they emerge through the narrow birth canal, like an elephant passing through the hole of a palm-leaf.
Because they do not reach [full consciousness], they lack the clear comprehension [to think], "We are departing. The fourth [category] is by way of the omniscient Bodhisattvas.
For even when they take rebirth in the mother’s womb, they understand; while dwelling there, they understand;
and at the time of departure, they also understand. Indeed, the kamma-born winds cannot cast them out with their feet upward and heads downward.
They are able; they emerge while still standing with both hands extended and eyes wide open. "Having delimited by knowledge" means:

having delimited and known by means of the five kinds of great reviewing-knowledge (pañcamahāvilokana-ñāṇa) in the prior stage, as well as the knowledge that delimits the death-moment by thinking "I am now passing away," and in the subsequent stage, the knowledge that delimits the rebirth-linking by thinking "Rebirth-linking has been taken here by me."

Although the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*) and the conduct for the benefit of relatives (*ñātatthacariyā*), etc., are included within the perfections (*pāramī*), they are mentioned separately in order to show their status as specific requisites (*sambhāra*). Among these, the five great renunciations are:
the renunciation of limbs, the renunciation of eyes, the renunciation of oneself, the renunciation of the kingdom, and the renunciation of wife and children. Furthermore, therein—

Granted that even the sacrifice of limbs and so forth are indeed the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), nevertheless, the great sacrifices are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing a specific kind of relinquishment and for the purpose of showing their extreme difficulty.

For this very reason, the sacrifice of eyes is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of limbs; and although there is a commonality in the nature of relinquishment, the sacrifice of kingdom and the sacrifice of wife and children are also mentioned separately.
It is said: "Beneficial conduct toward relatives" (*ñātatthacariyā*) means acting for the welfare of one's kin, and that indeed by way of compassion.

Likewise, "beneficial conduct toward the world" (*lokatthacariyā*) means acting for the benefit of the world of beings with respect to their welfare in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. This is done by way of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, by way of blameless spheres of action, spheres of craft, and branches of science, by way of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, and by way of the investigation of the three characteristics and so on.

And the range of knowledge through the establishment of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) therein, both for oneself and for others, is the conduct of a Buddha (*buddhacariyā*). This, however, in its actual meaning, is simply the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*);

it is mentioned separately, though, in order to show the distinction of the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*). By the use of the plural form "of the conducts of a Buddha," one should understand that this includes previous application (*pubbayoga*), previous conduct (*pubbacariyā*), the proclamation of the Dhamma, and so forth.
In that regard, [it refers to] that which is designated as the practice of going and returning...
The accomplishment of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) together with the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) is the "prior application" (*pubbayoga*).
An especially distinguished practice in giving and so forth is the "prior conduct" (*pubbacariyā*). Some say:

"The 'prior application' is the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) as included in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, while the 'prior conduct' is solitary wandering by means of physical seclusion and so forth. [This refers to] giving and so forth, as well as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth.

The proclamation of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhāna*) is discourse that proceeds by way of elucidating the dangers and benefits of *saṃsāra* and *nibbāna*, and by way of establishing and maturing sentient beings for the three types of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
"Having reached the limit" means having attained the ultimate boundary, the supreme excellence.
"The seven great gifts" refers to the aspiration made at the age of eight, thinking, "I shall give even my heart-flesh and so forth to supplicants."
Having given these seven great gifts: the gift bestowed after making a resolve, the gift of the auspicious elephant,

the great gift of seven times seven bestowed at the time of departure, the gift of the horse bestowed while traveling on the road, the gift of the chariot, the gift of the son, and the gift of the wife.
“May my death occur right now”—resolving thus and passing away is "death through resolve" (*adhimuttikāla-kiriya*); this belongs only to Bodhisattvas, not to others.

It is said that when Bodhisattvas, remaining in the long-lived divine worlds, think, "While staying here, it is impossible for me to accumulate the requisites for enlightenment," they become weary of dwelling there;
at that time, having entered their celestial palaces (*vimāna*), [they pass away].
Closing their eyes and resolving their minds with the thought, "May my life not continue beyond this point," they sit;

immediately upon that mental resolve, death occurs. For, due to the supreme manifestation of the perfections (*pāramī-dhamma*), their mental continuum has been distinguished by supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in each respective existence, and thus their attachment to self (*attasineha*) has become attenuated.

And because of the sublime nature of their resolve toward beings through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and because that resolve attains a state of sharpness and clarity, the intentions of Bodhisattvas are fulfilled.
They possess mastery over both their minds and their karmic actions;
therefore, wherever they are reborn, the perfections (*pāramitā*) flourish perfectly for them. Having passed away according to the manner described, they are reborn there. Likewise...
Indeed, our Great Being, having passed away from various births within this very kappa without falling away from his jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma-world.
After staying there for only a short time, he passed away from there and was reborn in the human world, becoming intent upon fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs).
Therefore it is said: "Of the Bodhisattas alone, and not of others. "Within the interval of one single existence..."
By the phrase "because all the perfections (pāramīs) were completely fulfilled," he shows that there was no death while remaining in that state due to a lack of purpose.
Furthermore, just as in his final existence (carimabhava) there arose a great prosperity— resembling divine fortune and preceded by the emergence of many great treasures—
so too, for one who has become a Buddha, [there arises a similar attainment] by way of incomparable giving and so forth.

And it should be understood that this occurs by way of the accumulation of merit, which has generated such enthusiasm as to think, "Beyond this, there is no further experience of divine excellence for the Great Being," just like the arising of gains not shared with others. This is indeed the natural law (dhammatā) here;
it is according to the calculation of human beings, not the calculation of deities. "Omens" (pubbanimittāni) means omens preceding death.

Regarding the phrase "without fading" (*amilāyitvā*): it should be understood that by the very mention of "not withered," the non-destruction of those garlands' excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of beauty is also demonstrated.
Because there is an absence of even a coating of external or internal dust and dirt, the garments on the bodies of the devas remain at all times perfectly pure and radiant.

He said, "It remains," and added, "the same principle applies to clothing as well. That which is neither cold nor hot is such that it is not a coldness requiring the application of excessive heat for its remedy, nor is it a heat that, becoming harsher by itself, overcomes [the body] and produces perspiration;
such is what is neither cold nor hot. "At that time" refers to the aforementioned time when death is imminent.
"Drop by drop" means that they fall drop by drop, like pearls falling from a string of pearls whose thread has been cut.

"Sweat" means that streams of sweat are released. "Brokenness of the teeth" (*khaṇḍicca*) is the state of the teeth being broken. "Graying of the hair" (*pālicca*) is the state of the hair becoming white.
By the word "etcetera," the wrinkling of the skin is included. The personal existence (*attabhāva*) is of a weary form.
The intention is that [the body] remains intact, but there is no brokenness, baldness, and so forth. "Discontented" means lacking delight.
That [discontent] does not exist because increasingly magnificent and especially difficult-to-perceive riches continue to arise for them.
"Sighing" means sighing out heat. "Yawning" means performing a yawn due to a lack of delight.
"Only the wise" means only those deities endowed with intelligence. Just as deities born into a state of excellence reflect, "By what kind of meritorious deed were we reborn here?

and know, "We were reborn here by this specific meritorious deed," so too these beings of great merit know the meritorious deeds they themselves performed in a past existence, or even certain other meritorious deeds performed at other times.
He said, “Those of great merit,” and so forth.

They do not appear because of the extreme length of their supreme lifespan. It is called “not leading to liberation” because it does not bring about the transcendence [of suffering] for beings, owing to their lack of fitness as vessels.
Beings are said not to possess a supreme lifespan because of the prevalence of evil; thus he said, “For at that time, beings...”
"...their defilements become excessive. Here it may be asked: Why do the Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise only in the human world and not in the worlds of the devas or the Brahmās?

First of all, they do not arise in the deva-world because there is no opportunity for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*), and likewise because [the attainment of enlightenment] would not be extraordinary (*anacchariya*) there.
For the Blessed Buddhas possess wondrous qualities (*acchariyadhamma*); such is their nature of wondrous qualities.
It is not manifest to those established in a divine state as it is to those who have become human;
for when the Perfectly Enlightened One is seen in his divine form, the world perceives the Buddha’s majesty through the power of the gods rather than through the power of the Buddha himself.
This being so, one does not resolve upon him as "the Perfectly Enlightened One," nor does one find confidence in him; one does not relinquish the grasping at him as a protector or a guardian.

And because they maintain their divine state for a long duration, they are not liberated from the doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*). The same principle applies here as well regarding the statement that they do not arise in the Brahma-world.

For it is precisely in the human happy destiny (*manussasugati*) that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise in order to liberate beings from such grasping, and not in the divine happy destiny (*devasugati*). Even when arising in the human happy destiny, [they do so...]
They are not of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), because if they were of spontaneous birth, they could not avoid the faults already mentioned;
and because, just as it is desired to establish the Dhamma for those to be trained by the Dhamma, so too it is necessary to establish the relics for those to be trained by the relics.
Indeed, after the final Nibbāna of those of spontaneous birth, no bodily relics remain. Even when they arise in the human world...

However, in their final existence as human beings, the great Bodhisattvas, in order to manifest their human state, take wives and remain in the midst of household life until they see the face of a son; even when their perfections such as virtue, renunciation, and wisdom have reached full maturity, they do not yet go forth.
What is the use of investigating the reason for this? It is because this has been the established practice followed by all Buddhas.
That is to say, awakening occurs only for those who have become human, not for those who have become devas. This is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in this regard.
For likewise, even the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) for that purpose succeeds only for those who have become human, not for those who have become devas.
But why do the Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise only in Jambudvīpa and not in the other continents? On this point, some say:

“Because it is on the earth of Jambudvīpa alone that the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍa exists—unconquered by the earth, endowed with the majesty of the Buddhas, and being an immovable place—therefore they arise only in Jambudvīpa”;

likewise, “because for others as well, those places not abandoned [by previous Buddhas] are found only there. This, however, is our own preference here: because of the former Buddhas and the Great Bodhisattvas...

The aspiration for the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*) by disciple-bodhisattvas, as well as the accumulation and maturation of the perfections (*pāramī*) for the sake of becoming a *paccekabuddha*, are successful only here in Jambudvīpa within this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), which serves as the field of a Buddha, and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, the purpose of a Buddha’s appearance is the training of those to be trained (*veneyya*); thus, it depends upon specific individuals to be trained, such as the chief disciples and great disciples.
It is precisely in this Jambudīpa that Buddhas are born, and not in other continents. And this principle has been the established custom of all Buddhas.
It should be understood that the arising of those Supreme Persons occurs in that very place because, like the wheels of prosperity, they proceed from one to another through mutual dependence;
it is for this very reason that this world-system is made the center along with this [continent].

The fact that the field [of activity] consists of exactly ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) is indicated because no other place for the arising of Buddhas besides this is found in the Buddha-word of the Tipiṭaka.
Therefore he said: "Buddhas do not arise in the three continents; they arise only in Jambudīpa—thus, see the continent.
In this same manner, one should state the reason by drawing it out even regarding the restriction of the region.

And now, the khattiya clan was esteemed by the world because it is worthy of honor even by the brahmins. He saw that the family would be designated by way of the father, thinking, "The king shall be my father.
He saw that [the birth would occur] "ten months and seven days" later; thereby he knew there would be no obstacle for himself, as well as her enjoyment of divine splendor in the Tusita realm.
"Those deities" refers to the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system. But how did those deities [know] of the Bodhisatta at that time?
How do they know his state of having fulfilled the perfections and his state of Buddhahood? It is by means of the deities of great power;

for the majority of those deities are partakers of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Indeed, on many occasions during the Blessed One’s distribution of the gift of Dhamma, there was an assembly of deities from ten thousand world-systems.
“I am falling away”: one knows this because the state of being present at death is clearly recognized by the death-proximate impulsions accompanied by knowledge.
One does not know the death-consciousness itself because of its momentary nature. For that reason, it is also not within the range of the knowledge of death and rebirth.
The same principle applies to the rebirth-linking consciousness as well. “The sequence of adverting” means the order of adverting. Because...
It is not possible to determine the object by merely adverting to it once; therefore, one determines it after adverting to that same object a second and a third time.
Here, the term "adverting" includes the entire process up to the impulsion phase (*javana*). Thus he said:
"One will know [it] only during the second and third mental moments. From several mental moments prior to death, one thinks: "My death is near."

Because it knows [the process], it is said: "Even at the moment of death, one knows, 'I am dying. However, because it has never existed before, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not know the rebirth-linking [consciousness itself].
Following the arising of attachment (*nikanti*), one knows: "Rebirth was taken by me in such-and-such a place.
"At that time" means at the time of taking rebirth. "The ten-thousandfold world-system shakes" means...
The cause for this trembling has already been explained below in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

As for what needs to be said regarding the meaning here, that will follow later in the commentary on the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*. Since the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who possess great compassion, are predominantly joyful because they are intent upon providing welfare and happiness to sentient beings, [this occurred] with their first great resultant consciousness (*mahāvipākacitta*).

The taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, the Elder Mahāsīva says that although the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who possess great compassion, are intent upon providing welfare and happiness for beings, they nevertheless have a disposition for seclusion, are inclined toward the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*), and are frequently characterized by equanimity toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
thus, he asserts that rebirth-linking occurs through the fifth great resultant consciousness (*pañcama-mahāvipākacitta*).
“From the seventh day before the full moon” means from the seventh day prior to the full moon;
the meaning is that it begins from the ninth day of the waxing fortnight. “On the seventh day” means on the seventh day from the ninth, namely, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha.
“This dream” refers to the manner that will now be described. However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: “Having led him to Lake Anotatta...”
They stood to one side. Then their queens came, bathed them in order to remove human impurities,” so it is said.
In that context, "their queens" refers to the queens of the Great Kings. "Having wandered" means having wandered for the sake of grazing.
"Smeared with green" means having been plastered with fresh cow dung. "And yet, that was a male fetus... [and so on].
“A woman’s womb; you will have a son”—this much the brahmins told him according to their own system of dream-interpretation.
But the passage beginning with “If he shall dwell at home,” etc., they proclaimed that matter as it truly is through the intervention of a deity. Regarding the term *dhammatā*:
here the word *dhamma* has the sense of “nature” (or “intrinsic character”), as in such passages as “O monks, for beings who are subject to birth (*jātidhammānaṃ*),” and so forth.
"Dhamma itself is the nature (dhammatā), just as a deity is the divinity," he said, "this is the inherent nature (sabhāva)"; the meaning is that this is the original constitution (pakati).
This inherent nature, in its actual sense, is the state of being thus determined; therefore he said, "this is what is meant by 'the fixed course' (niyāma).
Since the fixed course is of many kinds, having extracted all of them by way of enumerating their meanings, he now shows specifically the fixed course intended here.

“‘And what is called determination (niyāma),’ etc., was said. Therein, the determination of kamma is *kammaniyāma*. The same method applies to the three others: the determination of seasons (*utuniyāma*), and so forth.
But the other is the phenomenon itself as determination, *dhammaniyāma*, which is the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
Of wholesome kamma. ‘Setting it,’ meaning making it sharp.”
Because specific differences in climate are observed due to the distinctions between the various regions of the formless realm and other planes,
the mention of the flowers, fruits, and so forth of trees and other plants— which are produced by those specific climates— is stated with the qualification "in those respective countries.
"At that respective time" means at that respective season, such as springtime and so on.
The construction is: "from a sweet seed, from a bitter seed. 18.
Regarding the statement "he enters," it is said that what is near the present may be expressed as if it were actually present;
thus he says, "the meaning is simply 'he has entered. "Thus there is" means that there is his clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) in the manner just described. Not while entering...
Because the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is difficult to discern; as it is said: "The rebirth-linking consciousness does not know.
Or, it is immeasurable because it extends over ten thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa). It is sublime (uḷāra) due to its state of extreme radiance.
