"The majesty of the devas" (devānubhāva) refers to the power and splendor of the devas. For that light outshines the radiance of the devas, but it does not surpass their sovereignty.
Therefore he said, “of one whose clothes are wrapped,” and so forth.
The interval or gap between worlds—that is, between world-systems—is *lokantara*; that very term is expressed as *lokantarikā* by way of the feminine gender.
Because they are not struck by anything such as trees or shrubs, they are *agha*, meaning unobstructed. Therefore he said, “perpetually open.”
“Uncovered” (*asaṃvutā*) means not closed by anything below or above. Therefore it is said, “without a foundation even below.

Therein, by the word “even” (*pi*), it is shown that just as the intermediate space between worlds (*lokantarika*) is uncovered because there is no earth to cover the water below, so too it is uncovered and without a foundation above, due to the absence of celestial mansions (*devavimāna*) as there are in the world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

It is called "darkness" (*andhakāra*) because darkness exists therein. Visual consciousness does not arise there due to the absence of light, not because of the eye. For it is said: "By that radiance, they recognize one another.
At the time of midday for those staying in Jambudīpa, half of the solar disk appears to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha as it is setting, and to the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna...
By way of its rising, he said, "It becomes manifest simultaneously in three continents," referring likewise to the remaining continents.
Otherwise, however, it becomes manifest simultaneously in only two continents.
The dispelling of darkness over nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction should also be understood by this same method. Regarding the radiance:
“Are not sufficient” means they are unable to illuminate by their own radiance.
Because they move through space as vast as the Yugandhara mountain, it is said that “they move through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
“Vāvaṭā” means those who attempt to seize [the food] for the purpose of eating. “Viparivattitvā” means having turned over. “Chijjitvā” means having been cut.
Having been released from the place where it was situated due to its state of coagulation, or having broken apart through the cutting off of its limbs and members. Regarding "extremely salty":
this "extreme salinity" may be stated with reference to an extreme coldness resulting from the absence of the heat of the sun;
for that water which establishes the eon, poured down by the great rain-clouds of prosperity and supporting the earth, does not destroy the eon.
It ought to become alkaline like water. For if that were the case, even the earth would dissolve;

or rather, by the power of their evil karma, just as the saliva of those *petas* turns water into spittle, so too does that water then turn into an alkaline substance—thus it is said, "in extremely alkaline water."

"Even for the duration of drinking a single measure of gruel" means even for the time it takes to drink a measure of gruel contained in a bowl or other vessel after taking it up with the tip of the tongue or similar means. "On all sides" means from every part, in all six directions.
"By way of the four Great Kings" means by way of the common status of being one of the four Great Kings, such as Vessavaṇa and the others.
"To their respective abodes" means to each of their own individual dwellings.
20. *Pakatiyā* means by her own nature alone. Therefore he said, "by her very essence.
Without receiving it from another, she was endowed with virtue (*sīlasampannā*) by her own nature alone, having made a resolve for herself.
*Bodhisattamātāpīti* means our Bodhisattva’s mother also. *Kāladevilassāti*: just as she would receive [the embryo] from Kāladevila at other times, so too when the Bodhisatta—
However... [as before] ...the intention is that the mother of the Vipassī Bodhisatta likewise took up the precepts herself.
21. The phrase "among humans" is stated according to their natural conduct; it means that "in a human woman, a mind with the intention toward a human male would arise.
But in the case of the Bodhisatta’s mother, such a mind [arose] even among the devas.

It does not arise at all. Just as, through the power of the Bodhisatta, no thought of sexual desire arises in the mind of the Bodhisatta’s mother, so too, by his very power, she cannot be overcome by any man; thus it is said:
"Her feet do not move; they are bound as if by a divine chain."

22. Previously it was stated that “a mind associated with the strands of sensual pleasure does not arise,” yet later it was also stated that “she sports, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
How is this not mutually contradictory? To this he says, “Previously,” and so forth.
“The negation of the basis” means the prohibition of the basis for unchaste conduct. Therefore he said, “by way of the man’s intention.”
“Acquisition of an object” means the acquisition of the objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure, such as visible forms and so forth.
23. “Fatigue” means exhaustion; at that time, even the body’s heaviness, rigidity, and other such states do not exist for her.
It is said, “She sees what has passed beyond her womb. From what point onward does she see? To this he says: “Having passed the stage of the *kalala* and so forth,” and so on.
He himself states the purpose for seeing. Due to its absence, one does not see during the stages of the *kalala* and so forth.
Together with a young son, one who is weak and lying on his back. The passage beginning with “That which [is seen] by the mother” is stated by way of natural behavior (*pakaticāritta*).
For even compared to the womb of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), the womb of a Bodhisatta receives more distinguished treatment due to the equipment of merit (*puññasambhāra*).
Because of her exceptional nature, the Bodhisatta’s mother maintains an extremely suitable diet and conduct and carefully tends to him.
"For the sake of a comfortable dwelling" means for the sake of the Bodhisatta’s comfortable residence. "Facing eastward" means facing the front part of his mother's body.
Now, in order to show both the internal and external reasons for the Bodhisatta being visible while remaining within the womb, [the text says] "previously..."
The words “*kata-kamma*” and so forth were spoken. “*Assā*” means of the queen. “*Vatthuṃ*” means the womb.

Because there is no obstruction of light—due to the subtle nature of the Bodhisattva’s body within the mother’s womb, like a crystal or a layer of clouds—the Bodhisattva’s mother sees the Bodhisattva as he has entered her womb;
but does the Bodhisattva likewise see his mother and others standing before him?
He sees what belongs to the form-aggregate; thus he says, "But the Bodhisatta," and so forth.
Why, however, does he not see when there is both the eye and light? He says: "For visual consciousness does not arise within the womb.
Indeed, just like inhalation and exhalation, visual consciousness does not arise there due to the absence of the corresponding mental application (*samannāhāra*).

24. Just as other women die, being overcome by such diseases due to the occasion of childbirth, no disease whatsoever arose in the mother of the Bodhisatta when the Bodhisatta had entered her womb for the purpose of his birth;
she passed away solely through the exhaustion of her lifespan, as this matter has already been explained above. "By the Bodhisatta..."
"Because it was his dwelling place," and so forth, is the statement of the reason for that. "Not to be used by others" means it should not be utilized by others;
the sense is that it is unfit for their use. This being the case, there ought to have been another chief queen for the Bodhisatta’s father;
nevertheless, as it would have been inappropriate while the Bodhisatta’s mother was still pregnant, he said, "And it was not possible," and so forth. "Having removed" means...
Having removed [the woman] from the position of chief queen. By means of desire and lust for himself alone, he seeks an external object;
thus, showing that lust for sense objects is the powerful cause for beings' attachment to sense objects, he said:
"Beings' desire and lust for their own personal existence (attabhāva) is powerful. He is unable to protect [her] means he is unable to provide proper care for the pregnancy.

She does not apply herself [to her duties]. Because of that, the pregnancy becomes fraught with many ailments. "The physical basis (*vatthu*) is clear" means the womb-locus (*gabbhāsayo*) is purified.

The descent of the Bodhisatta into the womb during the third stage of the mother’s middle age is also included within the very act of her surveying the limit of her lifespan, because it avoids the transformations that arise due to the influence of age. The transformation arising from the nature of womanhood—
However, it is pacified by the very power of the Bodhisatta. 25.
"Born seven months" means born in the seventh month from the moment of conception. Because of his extreme delicacy, he is not able to endure cold or heat.
One born eight months is certainly superior in intelligence and age to one born seven months; however, some...
The sections of skin, as they grow, cannot withstand friction; therefore, he does not live by that [means].
They say, "But for one seven months old, those [sections] have not yet fully developed.
27. "The devas receive him first" means: "We ourselves shall first receive the Great Man, the Lord of the World."
The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, whose taints are exhausted, having conceived reverence and great esteem, receive [the embryo] from the beginning while proclaiming their own joy.
"Sūtivessantī" means wearing the guise of a woman in labor. "Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri. "Like the eye of a fish" is said by way of the complexion of the skin.
She stood; she neither sat nor lay down. Therefore it is said: "The mother of the Bodhisatta remained standing."
"She gives birth. She gives birth while remaining in a state free from suffering.
For because of the intensity of pain, other women, unable to endure that suffering, give birth while sitting or lying down.

"On a couch of antelope skin" means on a couch made by sewing together antelope hides. "Of great majesty" means of great power. "Of great renown" means having a large retinue and a wide-spread reputation for fame.
29. "Broken and shattered" (*bhaggavibhaggā*): because they have been dispersed by emerging from the narrow passage, they are "broken" (*bhaggā*);
and because they have become as if shattered (*vibhaggā*), this shows their very lack of solidity. "Without clinging" (*alaggo hutvā*):
having become unattached and unfettered at any point within the womb-abode or the birth canal; hence it is said that "it is like water flowing out from a water-pot."
"By water" means by the water contained within the womb. He emerges entirely unstained, because there is no such thing as water, mucus, or other such substances to smear him there.

Indeed, due to the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, from the moment of conception that place remains pure even before birth, and it stands emitting the fragrance of sandalwood like a supreme, most fragrant perfumed chamber.
“Water-whirlpools” means masses of water.
“A newborn for a moment” means having been born for a moment, being only a moment old. “Being carried along” means being led in a favorable direction.
“Just as they came” means having merely arrived at that place. “With many branches” means a diamond [jewel] with hundreds of facets made of various gems.
“Sahassamaṇḍala” means a diamond set with many thousands of facets standing above them. “Marū” refers to the gods.
However, it should not be viewed as if he were taking a step; rather, this is because he had already performed the surveying of the directions. Therefore he said, “The Great Being,” and so forth.
“Ekaṅgaṇāni” means that, by virtue of being open, they resembled a single courtyard, like the courtyards of a monastery or the courtyards of a dwelling cell.
“There were none equal to you. Regarding this vision of yours, they said, “There is not even anyone here who is equal to you;
how much less one who is superior? *Aggō* means preeminent (*padhāna*). To the question, “By what is its preeminence? he replied, “By qualities (*guṇehī*).
Here, the word *paṭhama* is a synonym for preeminence. As for the preeminence of the Bodhisatta—
He said "the very first" (*sabbapaṭhamo*) because it is not shared by others; the meaning is "the most preeminent. "Of this very one" means of the word *agga* (foremost) itself.
And here, while the gods of great power speak thus, how do the others speak? By seeing the majesty of the Great Being (*Mahāsatta*) and so forth.
For even among the gods of great power, there is a majesty similar to that of the Great Being.
"The majestic power was directly perceived," they said; as for the others, having heard their words, they spoke thus out of faith and inference.
Urged by the natural law (*dhammatā*) perfected by previously matured causes, he explained this... [etc.
...The standing postures and other signs of the Bodhisatta immediately upon his birth were the precursors of those specific attainments.
Having extracted these points, he says “And here,” etc., in order to demonstrate them.

Therein, “firm standing” is a premonitory sign for the acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), because through the bases of psychic power there is the successful attainment of being well-established in supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*). “Facing northward” is a premonitory sign for the act of going by way of crossing over the world.
For it was by means of that [direction] that the Blessed One [crossed over] the world together with its devas.
He was victorious, unconquered by anyone. Therefore it is said: "It was the omen for his departure, having overwhelmed and surpassed the great multitude.
Likewise, the taking of seven steps is the omen for the journey upon the Noble Path endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment.
The holding of the perfectly pure white parasol is the omen for the holding of the perfectly pure parasol of liberation. The acquisition of the five royal insignia...
It is the possession of the fivefold qualities of liberation. It is the surveying of all directions without obstruction due to the state of unobstructed knowledge.
It is the speaking of words without trepidation, such as "I am the foremost," because it cannot be hindered by anyone. It is the turning of the Wheel of the True Dhamma which does not cease.

It is the proclamation that there will be no further birth in the future, saying, "This is my last birth"; this should be understood as the omen of the attainment of *anupādisesa* (nirvana without remainder).
Because each respective sign is unfailing for the specific distinction to be attained in the future.
"Has not come" means it has not been mentioned in this sutta, nor in the sequence that will be explained elsewhere.
"Having brought forward" means it should be illustrated by bringing it forward according to the method found in those respective suttas and commentaries.
The statement, “The ten-thousandfold world-system trembled,” is said here to show that, although this is included in the text, it is the root of the wonders that will be described;
other similar cases should be understood in the same way. The mention of lutes bound with strings and drums bound with leather is merely an illustration of the fivefold musical ensemble;
or, by the word “and” (ca), the inclusion of other instruments should also be understood.

They say: "Just as leather straps and the like, having been cut at that very moment, become as they were before, so too the eyes, ears, and other faculties of those born blind and others arise at that very moment due to such kamma-conditions and vanish immediately.
*Chijjiṃsu* means they were severed at the places where the feet were bound. *Vigacchiṃsu* means they subsided.

The "space-dwelling jewels" refers to the gems and precious stones located within their respective celestial mansions (*vimānas*). "Illuminated by their own splendor" means they were made radiant by their exceedingly brilliant inherent light. "There was no movement" means there was no gathering together.
"No wind blew" means the harsh wind did not blow; however, a soft and pleasant wind, bringing happiness to sentient beings, did blow. They came to rest upon the earth in elevated places.

Unable to remain still. "Endowed with the proper season" means endowed with the season characterized by neither excessive heat nor cold. "Clapping" refers to the sound produced by the striking together of the arms and hands;
in terms of its actual meaning, it is the making of a sound by clapping the hand with the right broad palm while placing the left hand upon the chest.
"Whistling with the mouth" is the emission of a sound through the mouth, known as *seḷana*.
There was a single garland of banners that became a continuous mass through the convergence of many such garlands.

And not only these things occurred; moreover, other wonders appeared: a rain of variegated flowers and fragrant blossoms fell like a shower from the sky; while the sun was still visible, the stars shone;
clear and limpid water welled up from the earth; and wild animals dwelling in their burrows...
They emerged from their abodes; lust, hatred, and delusion became attenuated; dust subsided upon the earth;
foul odors vanished and divine fragrances wafted; the visible deities appeared before humans in their own forms;
and there was no passing away or rebirth among beings—these and other such thirty-two portents that arose at the time of the Great Resolve.
"At that time, those [signs] occurred without exception.
Regarding the phrase "there too," it should be understood that this status as a prior sign applies to those very phenomena such as the earthquake;
the intention is that it is not only in the places where the Buddha was born, stood, and so forth. It is the prior sign for the attainment of omniscient knowledge regarding all that is to be known.

And because it shakes the doctrine of the heretics. The gathering together in this very world-system of those who have not been urged by anyone is a precursor to the simultaneous gathering and receiving of the Dhamma by those who have likewise not been urged by anyone.
First, the acceptance by the deities is a sign of their attainment of divine abodes; afterwards, that of humans.
The receiving [of the sound] right there is a premonitory sign of attaining the imperturbable abiding (*āneñjavihāra*), because that state is by nature immovable.
The lutes’ sounding of themselves, without instruction from another, is a premonitory sign of attaining the successive abidings (*anupubbavihāra*) spontaneously.
The sounding of the drums is a premonitory sign of the Dharma-drum capable of proclaiming itself to an assembly as vast as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The sounding of the proclamation is the precursor to the sound of the drum of the Deathless. The cutting of the fetters and so forth is the precursor to the breaking of the bonds of conceit.
The healing of the great multitude’s disease is the precursor to the attainment of Truth, which constitutes the cessation of the entire disease of suffering within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The phrase “of the great multitude” [refers] to the great multitude’s attainment of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
In various places, this should be connected by bringing forward such passages as, "for the great multitude’s attainment of the divine ear-element," and so forth.
Regarding the accomplishment of the excellence of the speed of knowledge through the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), it is said:

"The attainment of speed by those who were cripples is a precursor to the acquisition of the four bases of psychic power. Reaching a good landing place is [a sign] of the realization of the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
It is a foretoken because it is the state of correctly practicing toward the goal and so forth, in accordance with the goal and so forth.
It is a foretoken of the fact that the jewels will illuminate the world with the light of the Dhamma by means of their own inherent radiance.
It is a foretoken of the attainment of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) because they completely pacify all enmity. [It is a foretoken] of the extinguishing of the eleven fires...
It is a "foretoken" (*pubbanimitta*) because it is the precursor to the state of *nibbāna*, which is difficult to extinguish.

It is a foretoken for the seeing of the light of knowledge because it is the seeing of light where there was no light. "By the flavor of *nibbāna*" means by the flavor of the extinguishing of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Of the single-flavored nature" refers to the single-flavored nature of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) everywhere; and that indeed is by bringing about a state of absolute sweetness in a world that is not sweet.
The breaking of the sixty-two types of views is preceded by the complete removal of the winds of those views.

Just as birds leave the sky and other unstable, uneven, and shifting places to go to the earth, so too is the going for refuge to the Triple Gem with one’s life the precursor to the abandonment of such false graspings by sentient beings. This is because it is beloved by the many people.

It is like the moon, due to its being beloved by many people. It is a premonitory sign for the sun’s attainment of physical and mental happiness free from feverish distress, characterized by a season devoid of excessive heat or cold.

The gods’ play of clapping hands and so forth is a premonitory sign for the manifestation of joy through the departure into existence and the awakening to the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), which occurs by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
"By the force of the rain of Dhamma" means by the power of the knowledge of teaching.

It is the omen of the raining down of the nectar of the Dhamma. Having made the jhāna obtained by means of mindfulness directed to the body the foundation, the experience of the bliss of the path and fruit produced thereby is the acquisition of the nectar of mindfulness directed to the body;
and because that body also brings about a bliss that is not satiating, the absence of oppression by hunger and thirst is called its omen. Furthermore, in the Commentary...

This was said after having broken through hunger and thirst. In that context, the breaking of the omens should be understood by way of the distinction between the specific and the general, and according to the maxim of the "cow and the ox.
The word "by itself" (*sayameva*) should also be brought over and connected here with the phrase "of the opening of the door of the Eightfold Path.
"Of the state of being filled" means of the state of being complete. "Adorned with the garland of the noble banner" means...

Some say it is because he possesses a garland of the saffron-colored banner; however, it is the omen for his becoming garlanded with the banners and garlands of the Noble Path and the Factors of Enlightenment for the world including its devas. Whatever has not been explicitly mentioned here is easily understood.
"Here" refers to this section introduced by the words "Just born," etc. It has already been answered; therefore, we [shall explain] it here...
The intention is that there is nothing new to be said. At that time, even though the Great Being was walking upon the earth, he appeared to the great multitude as if he were walking through the sky;

this is here described as "the fixed order of things," "the natural law of Bodhisattvas," and "their inherent nature" according to the doctrine of determinism (*niyativāda*). Previously, in former births, such a kamma consisting of the accumulation of merit...
"Because it was performed and accumulated by the great multitude, it appeared in such a way"—this is a statement made according to the doctrine of past-deeds (pubbekata-kamma).
Because of its nature of presiding over these beings, one's own respective karma alone is called the "Lord" (issara);
its "creation" (nimmāna) is the production of its own fruit, [a power] by which even a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) is able to overcome the world together with its devas.
"Produced by a sublime meritorious deed, he is therefore called 'created by a Lord' (*issaranimmāna*);
and this specific quality of his creation is his great majesty (*mahānubhāvatā*), by which he appeared thus to the multitude"—this is the explanation according to the doctrine of creation by a Lord.
Having thus spoken extensively of various such [theories], [the Buddha asks]: "What is the use of this figurative discourse? and at the end, [he speaks] directly.
He explained: "Immediately after being born, how could he walk upon the earth with his feet?
So great was his majesty that, as if imagining he were traveling through the sky, he appeared as though he were moving through the air.
Yet, because he took seven strides so rapidly, although his form was visible, he seemed as if invisible to the multitude. His state of nakedness..."

It should be understood that his small stature was not suited to such a manner of deportment; therefore, by way of the miracle produced through the power of his karma, he appeared to the great multitude as if adorned and prepared for a festival, as if sixteen years of age.
This appearance at that time was merely due to the power of the Great Being’s merit. Afterwards, he remained just like a young child.

"He was not such [a being]. Because the power of the Bodhisatta, which is worthy of the state of Buddhahood, has been explained exactly as it is, the assembly became as delighted by his declaration as if by the Buddha himself... [etc. ...

"The nature of all things" (sabbadhammatā) should be understood as referring to all sixteen kinds of natural laws mentioned above, which belong to all Bodhisattas; for they are identical in this regard through their accumulation of merit and knowledge.
Commentary on the Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man (Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā) 33.
Regarding "a pillow of fine linen" (*dukūlacumbaṭaka*): this refers to fine linen (*dukūla*) woven together so as to be suitable for a young person to lie upon.
"A khattiya, a brahmin," and so forth, is *jāti* (birth). "A Koṇḍañña, a Gotama," and so forth, is *gotta* (clan). "Poṇikā, cikkhallikā... [and so forth].
“Sākiyas, Koḷiyas,” and so forth—this refers to lineage and station. By the word “and so forth” (ādi), all forms of excellence, such as physical beauty, sovereignty, and retinue, are included.

“Of the great” means of the vast or sublime; this is the meaning. “Accomplishments” (nipphattiyo) means successes. Regarding the phrase “destinies to be gone to,” he indicates that the word *gati* functions as the object (*kamma-sādhana*).
For it is by way of rebirth (*upapajjana*) that one goes to those states through good and bad conduct.
*Gatiyo*: specific states of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). It is called a *gati* because one goes (*gacchati*) or proceeds according to one’s inclination;

it is thus a disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). *Paṭisaraṇe*: in the sense of a refuge, a resort, or a support. For the Arahant, who is dissociated from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*), Nibbāna alone is his refuge. *Tyāhaṃ*: "those [I].
He is called *dhammika* because he is devoted to the tenfold wholesome qualities (*kusala-dhamma*) and to the blameless duties of a king (*rājadhamma*). And by that Dhamma...

He is a *dhammarāja* because he delights the entire world. Since a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī*) attains sovereignty through the Dhamma and by way of justice, not through what is contrary to the Dhamma, it is therefore said: "He is a *dhammarāja* because he has obtained the kingdom through the Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase "the four quarters": because it extends to the edge of the ocean in the four directions, it is called "four-cornered";
thus he said: "In the east... [and so on]... the great earth upon each of those islands."

"Lord. "The Victor" (Vijitāvī) means one who has conquered that which is to be conquered; he is a conqueror of the internal host of enemies such as desire, anger, and so forth, as well as the external host of enemy kings.
The meaning is that he stands having conquered. Granted, a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) has no actual battle with anyone;
however, because the success of his victory—which is to be accomplished through battle—is established, he is called "one who has won the battle" (Vijitasaṅgāmo).
It is said: the country itself, being endowed with the fourfold wonderful qualities and so forth, attained a firm state of devotion that was unshakable by anyone while this king reigned;

or else, having attained a stable state through its own righteous conduct, it is called "one that has attained stability in the country" (*janapadatthāvariyappatta*). Having placed a weapon upon the chests of men...
They are *sāhasika* (reckless) because they commit acts of violence against others by seizing their desired wealth and so forth.

In the sense of producing delight (*ratijananaṭṭhena*), it means by generating intense joy and gladness. Etymologically, however, it is called a *ratana* (jewel) because it causes one to rejoice (*rameti*).
It is "highly esteemed" (*cittīkata*) because it is to be held in high regard in the mind with the thought, "Oh, how captivating! And this high esteem exists because of its worthiness of worship.
"Cittīkata" means "worthy of worship"—this is the meaning they say. It is "mahaggha" because it is worth a great, vast, and immeasurable price.
It is "atula" because there is no scale or comparison for it; it is peerless. Because it arises only occasionally and is difficult to obtain, it is "dullabhadassana" (rare to behold).
Because it is to be enjoyed only by beings possessing extraordinary and sublime qualities, it is "anomasattaparibhoga" (the enjoyment of extraordinary beings).
Now, having shown how these qualities— such as being honored and so forth— are obtained specifically by the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*),
the passage beginning with “And of the Wheel-Treasure” is commenced in order to extend [these qualities] to the other [treasures] as well. There is no other place for a deity,
because it is the cause for the king’s attainment of sovereignty and other perfections not shared by others, and because it is the cause for sentient beings’ attainment of whatever aims they desire.
There is no price for it because it is composed of the seven extremely sublime and radiant gems, and because of its wonderful, marvelous, and great majesty.
To the extent that it is of great value, to that same extent it is incomparable.

Just as the time that is free from the stain of evil in beings due to their loathing of sin, and which is like a crest-ornament due to their devotion to merit—such a time is worthy of the arising of a Buddha; even for a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), it is only at such a time [that he appears].
He says, “And because,” and so forth, to explain their occurrence. This has been stated by way of a simile;

however, there is no absolute similarity between the simile and that which is illustrated by it. Therefore, while universal monarchs (cakkavatti) do not arise as frequently as Buddhas do, they are nevertheless indeed rare in their appearance, both because of the fact that they arise only at certain times and because the fulfillment of the duties of a universal monarch is also difficult to accomplish.
It should be understood that by this commonality of being difficult to arise, their difficulty of being seen is stated.
Granted, the benefit accomplished through the power of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) is shared with the retinue of the universal monarch (cakkavatti);
nevertheless, because it arises for that specific purpose, it is appropriate to say that "only the universal monarch enjoys it as his own master through his sovereign power."
Showing this, he said, "This very thing," and so forth. Since the five or six aforementioned meanings are also found among the other jewels, it was said, "In the same way, the rest as well.
He is endowed with the elephant, horse, and counselor jewels through their conquest of the unconquered; with the wheel jewel by way of being its retinue;
and with the remaining ones by way of being articles of enjoyment. [He is endowed] with the elephant, horse, gem, and woman jewels...
The construction is as follows: [he is superior] by way of being the objects of enjoyment and requisites for the remaining [beings], and by way of being their retinue.
"The glory and wealth of the four great continents" refers to both the attainment of splendor and the attainment of enjoyments obtained therein.
"Just like that" means precisely the same majestic power as described in the passage beginning with "before the meal. By pervading a region measuring one *yojana*...
A darkness measuring one *yojana*. Free from the six kinds of defects, such as being too long.
"Brave" (*sūra*) means possessing power; the meaning is "fearless," which is why he said "courageous" (*abhīruka*). "Factor" (*aṅga*) means a cause.
That cause by which they might be called "heroes" (*vīra*) is the "hero-factor" (*vīraṅga*). Therefore he said, "This is the name for energy. As far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains.
Because it revolves like a wheel, it is said to be "bounded by the ocean, having made the Cakkavāḷa mountain its limit.

By the phrase "without punishment," the non-infliction of both monetary fines and corporal punishment is indicated. By the phrase "without weapons," the non-engagement of an army in combat is indicated;
thus, in order to show both of these, the passage beginning with "those who have committed offenses" was stated.
"Of the kind described" means extending as far as the ocean.
"Lust (rāga) in the sense of coloring; craving (taṇhā) in the sense of stretching"—thus greed itself is stated in two ways according to the distinction in its modes of manifestation.
For in both cases, its meaning of "concealing" is absolute. As it is said: "Then there is blinding darkness..."
"Whom passion overcomes, O man," and "covered by the veil of craving"—by this method, the meaning of "veiling" for hatred and the other defilements should also be explained.
By the mention of "defilements" (kilesa), the remaining defilements such as doubt and so forth are included.
Because all those evil states, upon arising, remain having covered and enveloped the continuum of a being, they obstruct the occurrence of the wholesome.
Therefore, they are called "coverings" (*chadanā*) and "covers" (*chadā*). And the term "one whose cover is peeled away" (*vivaṭṭacchada*) is a designation formed by changing the vowel *o* to *ā*.
35. "Tāsanti" refers to the manifestation of both [types of] results. "Serving as signs" means serving as indicative causes. For it is thus:

they are "marks" (*lakkhaṇāni*) because by means of them the state of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) is characterized (*lakkhīyati*). On the ground, in standing, walking, and so forth, [the feet] are perfectly level.
"Suppatiṭṭhitapādo" means one whose feet are well-settled. To clarify this quality of having well-settled feet by way of contrast, the passage beginning with "yathā" (just as) was stated.
Therein, "aggatalaṃ" refers to the surface of the forefoot. "Paṇhī" refers to the surface of the heel.
"Passaṃ" refers to each of the two sides of the sole of the foot, or both edges together. "Assa... [The remainder of the sentence follows].
The passage beginning with “panā” and so forth is an analytical exposition of the meaning by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). It is placed straight, like the sole of a golden sandal.
“All at once” means in a single moment. The construction is as follows: “the entire sole of the foot touches the ground when set down;
all at once, the entire sole of the foot rises from the ground. Therefore, this is the conclusion: “he has well-placed feet.”
As for the wonderful and marvelous outflow-fruit that should be mentioned here regarding its gradual progression,
that will be made clear later in the commentary on the *Lakkhaṇa-sutta*.
"The navel is seen" means that the navel of the wheel of marks is seen as being perfectly circular in shape and clearly defined.
The intended meaning is "it is obtained. "Not delimited by the nave" means situated within that nave, established by way of its boundaries.
"A binding band around the face of the nave" refers to the binding band that must be placed on the face of the nave for the purpose of protecting it from being struck by the axle-pin;
what is intended here is that which is covered by such a band. "The jewels on the rim" refers to [the jewels] on the rim.
A "jewel-line" (*maṇikālekha*) is a line of jewels arranged in the form of a row. A "multitude of turns" (*sambahulavāra*) refers to a section that manifests various types of decorative patterns.
A "dart" (*satti*) is a weapon-dart. A "śrīvatsa" (*sirivaccha*) is a mark of glory. A "nandyāvarta" (*nandi*) is a clockwise spiral.

A "sovatthika" (*sovattika*) is a *sovatthika* motif. A "wreath" (*vaṭaṃsaka*) is a garland. A "vaddhamānaka" (*vaḍḍhamānaka*) is a lamp-base among the frontal [ornaments] and so forth. A "peacock-feather fan" (*morahatthaka*) is a bundle of peacock feathers.
A specific type of fan bound with peacock feathers; a *vāḷabījanī* is the tail of a yak (*cāmarī*). Full jars and full bowls containing white mustard seeds and other auspicious items.
Having stated "the world-system" (*cakkavāḷa*), the passage "Himavā, Sineru... [and so on]... thousands" is spoken in order to show its principal components.
The phrase "with reference to the retinue of a wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāya*) demonstrates that the elephant-treasure and the other treasures are also found therein.
It should be understood that the specific characteristics of the limbs already mentioned, beginning with the sevenfold strength, are the adjuncts to the mark of the wheels themselves.
Regarding the phrase "long heels," this was said with reference to the length of others' heels;

however, it is not [meant] to be excessively long, as indicated by the term "full heels. Furthermore, as to how the characteristic of the heels is called "complete," that shall be explained by way of contrast.
The phrase beginning with “Just as” (*yathā hi*) was stated in order to demonstrate this. “With the tip” (*āraggena*) means with the point of the circle.
“Having rounded it” (*vaṭṭetvā*) means having rounded it so that it becomes well-rounded. “Resembling a ball made of red wool” (*rattakambalageṇḍukasadisā*) means resembling a ball made of red wool.
“Just like a monkey’s” (*makkaṭasseva*) is said with reference to its length and its evenness. “With resin-oil” (*niyyāsatelena*) refers to oil mixed with resins such as *chattirita* and others.

With oil—that which they also call "fragrant extract" (*surabhiniyyāsa*). And here, the mention of "extract-oil" is for the purpose of showing the thick and glossy nature of the *haritāla-vaṭṭī* (the fragrant resin).

Just as a cotton wick beaten a hundred times becomes exceedingly soft when dipped in the cream of clarified butter (*sappimaṇḍa*), so too are the hands and feet of the Great Man; thus he said "in the cream of clarified butter," etc., demonstrating this. "Taluṇā" means delicate.
"Skin" means the skin covering the space between the fingers. "With the spaces between the fingers joined" means that the spaces between the fingers are not connected on one side.
"Of equal measure" means they are of the same length. "The barley-mark" refers to the barley-shaped mark situated on the joints of the fingers from the inside.
"Having pierced through" [refers to] because of the common location of the respective joints, even when the fingers are extended.
They stand touching one another as if pierced together.
*Saṅkha* refers to the ankles; those which have their ankles above are *ussaṅkha*, namely the feet. *Piṭṭhipāde* means near the back of the foot. The construction is:
"by that" means they are bound by way of being situated at the ankle on the back of the foot. This word "by that" (*tena*)—
This should also be applied to the two subsequent lines: “Because they are bound by that [tendon], they cannot turn over at will;
because they cannot turn over at will, the soles of the feet of those walking are not visible.
“Above” means two finger-breadths above the back of the foot; some also say it is four finger-breadths. And they are hidden, not...
Appearing as if belonging to others. "By that" means by virtue of being established above the ankles. "Of him" refers to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Although there is movement to other places, the mention of the navel is for the purpose of showing that he is motionless [there].
"Only the lower body moves"—this is a statement of the reason for the preceding phrase. Because only the lower body moves, therefore from the navel... [he is] motionless.
[The word] “there is. However, the statement “the feet turn over with ease” is the explanatory reason for both what precedes and what follows.
Because the feet turn over with ease, therefore only the lower part of the body moves; because the feet turn over with ease, therefore [one moves] forward... and so on... and backward.
Because the legs of the eṇi deer become gradually thicker upwards with flesh that is uniform on all sides, so too it is with the Great Man;
therefore it is said, "having legs like those of the eṇi deer. "Full legs" means having legs full of flesh on all sides. Hence he said, "not on one side," and so forth.
"By this" means by the statement beginning with "not shrinking," the sense being that it demonstrates the state of having well-formed knees.

"The rest of people" refers to those individuals who lack these characteristics; they may be hunchbacked due to the upper body being shorter than the lower body, or they may be dwarfish due to the lower body being shorter than the upper body.
By this, [it is shown that] with the exception of the Perfectly Enlightened One, [no one else possesses such limbs].
This shows that while the wheel-turning monarchs and other beings belong to the category of the hunchbacked and the dwarfed, the lotus pericarp (*padumakaṇṇikā*) is indeed golden in color throughout;

however, because the golden lotus pericarp (*kañcanapadumakaṇṇikā*) is exceptionally radiant, he says, "resembling the pericarp of a golden lotus. *Ohitaṃ* means placed within, contained within, or included within.
But because that which has become thus is concealed by it, he said "concealed" (*paṭicchanna*).
Regarding "golden-colored," the meaning here is "possessing the color of gold"; thus he said "with natural vermilion," and so forth.
This meaning should also be understood according to the principle of ellipsis (*āvutti-ñāya*). The intention is that the word "color" (*vaṇṇa*) here is a synonym for the body.

Having stated the first alternative, the second alternative was stated by taking the word *vaṇṇa* in the sense of the "element of color" (*vaṇṇadhātu*) alone, while bearing in mind the absence of such a conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).
Therefore, even with both phrases, what is meant is that the color of the skin is like well-polished gold. *Raja* means fine dust. *Jalla* is a collection of dust that brings about a state of filth;
hence he said, "or dirt. If it is peeled away, how can there be bathing and so forth? To this he replied, "hand-washing and so forth," etc.
"At the conclusion of the turning" means at the end of the turning that occurs by way of circumambulation from left to right.
Because the body of Brahmā rises straight up without leaning forward or backward, it is said:

"He is straight-limbed like Brahmā. Furthermore, this quality of being straight-limbed is to be understood as having reached its full development in the individual parts [of the body], not during infancy.
It is said: “He will have a tall and long body. Regarding the phrase “in the others,” the connection is made by supplying the words “bending forward”;
that is, bending in these two places—the shoulders and the knees. “Crooked on one side” means crooked either toward the right side or the left side.
“Like a stake” means like the foot of a stake set in place when making a figure out of cloth.
"He has seven protuberances" (*sattussada*) means that his seven bodily parts, such as the backs of the hands and so forth, are prominent and possess thick flesh.
The construction is: "the ends of the bones are discernible. Regarding the phrase "with hidden veins and lines," this is a technical term for a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*);

by this, it is effectively stated that "the ends of the bones are hidden. In the expression "by the backs of the hands and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the tops of the shoulders and the nape of the neck.
Having established that, he shows it by way of a single part, saying: "Having turned... with the shoulder.
Or rather, it should be understood that by the phrase "like a statue of stone," etc., the hiddenness of the shoulder-joints is indeed already made manifest.
"Sīhapubbaddha" means the forepart of a lion; because all its parts are complete, the entire [body] is like the forepart of a lion.
“His body is like that” means his body is like the forepart of a lion’s body. Therefore it was said: “The entire body is complete, just like the forepart of a lion’s body.
“Like that of a lion” means like that of a lion. “It is not ill-proportioned or misshapen” means it is not poorly proportioned, nor is it deformed in its shape;
for the configuration of its various parts has not reached a state of being ill-fitted or unsightly.
The meaning is "it does not exist. "They settle" means they become established. "By the long" refers to the fingers, the nose, and so forth. "By the short" refers to the neck and so forth.

"By the thick" refers to the thighs, the arms, and so forth. "By the thin" refers to the hair of the head, the body hair, the middle [of the body], and so forth. "By the broad" refers to the eyes, the palms of the hands, and so forth.
"By the rounded" refers to the shanks, the forearms, and so forth.
Because it possesses the hundred marks of merit (*satapuññalakkhaṇatā*), it has been fashioned and brought to the state of being formed by various meritorious thoughts;
it was prepared and constructed through the ten perfections (*pāramī*), [with the thought]: "Only such a thing is fit to be the basis for the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas.
Alternatively, the reading is "by a mind of giving, by a meritorious mind," which means by a meritorious mind proceeding by way of giving, virtue (*sīla*), and so forth.
"Between the two shoulders" means the middle of the two upper arms, the upper portion of the back.
"Full and rounded" means full because it is not sunken, and rounded because the two shoulders are level with one another. "Rising up" means having risen;
the intention is that it is not sunken but level. Therefore he said, "like a golden plate."
“Round like a banyan tree” means he is round like a banyan tree that is itself round;
although one would have to say “round-round-banyan-tree,” the word *parimaṇḍala* has been elided once, and thus it is said “round-banyan-tree.
Therefore he says, “a banyan tree with symmetrical trunk and branches,” and so forth. For not every banyan tree is round; [this is understood] by virtue of the proximity of the word *parimaṇḍala*.
“Or, ‘like a banyan tree, it is rounded’—even without the elision of one word *parimaṇḍala*, this meaning is obtained;
thus he said, ‘rounded like a banyan tree. *Yāvatako assa*: having substituted the letter *v* for the *o*-vowel of *yāvataka*.

“With a trunk that is even and well-rounded”: with a trunk that is equally well-rounded. The construction is: “with a long neck like a crane, a crooked neck like a heron, and a broad neck like a boar. “Resembling a golden *āliṅga*”: resembling a small golden drum (*mudiṅga*).
*Rasaggasaggī*: They are "rasaggasā" because they swallow (*gasanti*) and draw inward (*pavesanti*) tastes such as sweet and so forth;

those that are the best (*agga*) among the *rasaggasā* are "rasaggasaggā. One who possesses these is "rasaggasaggī. By that—namely, by the non-pervasion of nutritive essence (*ojā*)—they have inferior constituents (*dhātu*) and thus become subject to much affliction (*bahvābādha*).
“Hanu” is a designation for the jaw-bone that serves as a support; this belongs to the Blessed One, who is like a lion, and therefore the Blessed One is “Sīhahanu” (Lion-Jawed).

Therein, because there can only be inferior similes for the physical body and the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas—there is no equal simile, much less a superior one—it is said “Therein,” etc., in order to show that this too is an inferior simile.
It has been said. Because the upper part of the Great Man’s body is established in accordance with the lower part, it is said that "both are complete";
yet this is not due to being perfectly circular in every respect, but rather because they are circular except for a remaining third part.
Therefore, he says: "They resemble the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight. "Having observed" means according to his own manual of characteristics (*lakkhaṇasattha*).
Having examined them. The unevenness of the teeth is to be understood by way of their inner and outer surfaces as well, not solely by way of their tips.
Therefore he said: "Like a section of a conch shell cut with an iron band. "Iron band" refers here to a saw. They will be even, not uneven;
the meaning is that they will have a uniform shape.

"Pabhūtā" means that his physical elements have become abundant, having attained qualities such as being exceedingly soft, long, and broad; by changing the letter *bha* to *ha*, it becomes "pahūta-jivho," meaning one who has a large tongue.

They are called "chinnassara" (broken-voiced) because their resonance proceeds in a broken or interrupted manner. They are called "bhinnassara" (split-voiced) because of their manifold modes of sound.
They are called "kākassara" (crow-voiced) because their resonance is as unpleasant as that of a crow. "Apalibuddhattā" means because the basis [of the voice] is unobstructed.
"Subject matter" (*vatthu*) should be understood as the locus where the syllables arise. Regarding the phrase "endowed with eight factors," the factors themselves will be explained later.
"Mañjughosa" means having a sweet voice.
"Abhinīlanetta" means having intensely blue eyes; and this intensity should be understood as being due to an exceeding degree of blueness, not...
Because the quality of being blue-black is predominant [in the eyes], he said, "not entirely blue-black eyes," and so forth.

The yellow and red colors are to be understood by way of the streaks located within the white circles (the sclera). However, the blue, white, and black colors are to be understood according to their respective circles.
Some say, "The 'eye-ornament' (*cakkhubhaṇḍa*) is the eyelid" (*akkhidala*). Others say, "It is the socket of the eyelid" (*akkhidala-vaṭuma*). But by means of the eyelids...
It should be understood as being together with the eye-socket (*akkhibimba*). For in this way, even the description of the light-rays as "emerging" is appropriate.
By the word "intended" (*adhippetam*), he shows that the intended meaning here is by way of characterizing the whole through a part (*ekadesena samudāyupalakkhaṇa-nayena*).

Since the word *pakhuma* is conventionally established in the world for the eyelashes (*akkhidala-loma*), for that very reason he says: "the eyes are covered with soft, glossy, dark, and fine eyelashes."
Although the word *uṇṇā* (wool) is used in the world generally as a synonym for body hair (*loma*), here it refers to a specific kind of hair;
thus he says, "the wool-hair" (*uṇṇā loma*). "Born in the middle of the forehead" means born having reached the center of the forehead.

This is a comparison by way of its whiteness, not its softness; for the wool-hair is even more exceedingly soft than that. Therefore he says, "like clarified butter scum," and so forth. "A silver bubble" means...
He speaks of the silver-like star.

Regarding the phrase "it was said with two purposes in mind": because Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are called "those with uṣṇīṣa heads" due to their full foreheads and full cranial domes, it was for those two purposes that it was said.
“With a turban-like head” (uṇhīsasīso) was thus stated. Now, to show that these two qualities are well-established in the Great Man, it is said: “Of the Great Man,” and so forth.

Because of its extreme softness, golden color, radiant luster, and fullness, it shines like the turban-band of a king’s kinsman. “Monkey-heads” (kapisīsā) refers to heads split in two. “Fruit-heads” (phalasīsā) refers to shaven heads.
"Bone-heads" (aṭṭhisīsā) refers to those whose heads are excessively bony due to the absence of flesh, or whose heads consist of nothing but bone covered with skin because the flesh has fallen away.

"Gourd-heads" (tumbasīsā) refers to those whose heads resemble a gourd (lābu). "Overhanging-heads" (pabbhārasīsā) refers to those whose heads hang down over the back portion [of the neck]. "By the former method" means by way of having a full forehead.
"Like a head wrapped in a turban" (uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viya) refers to a region of the head that is wrapped with a turban-band (uṇhīsapaṭṭa).
"Like a turban" means like a turban-circle fashioned by a skilled craftsman.
37. "The detailed account of his" refers to the detailed account of the fortune-tellers' gratification upon examining his physical marks.
The detailed explanation. Regarding the appearance in the womb, it has already been stated in the section on the gratification of the dream-interpreters who served as the sign.
"Faultless" means free from defects such as being overly salty (*khārikaloṇika*). "Nurses" (*dhātiyo*) refers to nurses who suckle with breast milk;

for they nourish (*dhāpenti*) and give milk to drink (*pāyanti*), thus they are called *dhātiyo*. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he connects it with the term "sixty"; [this implies] "the rest also."
There are three kinds: the *nhāpikā* (bather), the *dhārikā* (nurse), and the *parihārikā* (attendant).
They are called "nurses" (*dhātiyo*) because they bathe, they warm, they wash, and they carry. Among these, "carrying" means supporting for a long time on the chest, the thighs, or the hands.
"Attending" means taking from the lap of another to one's own lap, or from the arms of another to one's own.
"Carrying away by those extending their arms" means bringing about abduction.
38. "Melodious-voiced" means having a soft voice. For that which is soft is not harsh; thus he says, "not harsh-voiced.
"Sweet-voiced" means having a charming voice; and because its charm arises from cleverness and the application of merit, he says, "clever and refined-voiced."
"Madhurassara" means a voice pleasant to the ear; because its quality of being pleasant to the ear is exceedingly desirable, he said "sātassara.
"Pemanīyassara" means a voice that should be loved; because its quality of being lovable arises in those who hear it by producing devotion toward oneself, he said "pemajanakassara.
Regarding "karavīkassara": the word *karavīka* refers to those beings whose range of hearing...
He approaches them, and by means of the excellence of his own voice, causing them to abandon their natural state, he brings them under his control and makes them act according to his will.
Showing that it is thus sweet, he said, "In this regard," and so forth. Therein, "the karavīka bird" and so on is a description of its essential nature.
*Lalita* is a graceful play arising from the force of joy. *Chaḍḍetvā* means "having abandoned," [even] the act of arranging...
Having removed the grass that "creates an obstacle to hearing sweet sounds," he [proceeded]. "Without setting down" means without placing them on the ground, but keeping them suspended in the air.

"The deer followed by predatory beasts" refers to those pursued by wild animals; having abandoned the fear of death from them, they remain standing without falling, having spread their wings as wide as possible.
He released the golden cage because it moved through the sky at a distance of one *yojana* by his own command. Therefore he said, "By that king’s command," and so forth.
"They sported" means they began to engage in playful movements. "That joy" refers to that joy which has the Buddha’s qualities as its object;
without abandoning that joy which arose repeatedly in that same manner, the Elder monks suppressed their defilements.

Because he possessed the perfection of the supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti) conducive to hearing the Dhamma in the presence [of the elders] and because his wisdom was fully matured, he established himself through the seven [stages].

It is said, "together with seven hundred legged ones," because he approached the elders on foot together with a retinue of about seven hundred women of the harem. "From that" means from the sound of the karavīka bird. "By a hundredth part... etc.

It should be understood [as such] because it possesses the perfection of its physical basis (*vatthusampatti*), which has arisen from a store of merit accumulated over many hundreds of millions of eons. 39. "Born of the ripening of karma" (*kammavipākaja*) means: produced by exceptionally wholesome karma; unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth;
capable of receiving even a distant object; co-nascent with the ripening of karma; or, by way of being the result of karma.
The eye of clarity has arisen. For the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) is twofold: consisting of kamma and consisting of meditation (bhāvanāmaya).
Here, he says "not consisting of meditation" to indicate that this [eye] consists of kamma. However, that which consists of meditation will arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
This recognition of "that" occurs through mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa), yet it is by way of visual consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) because it has been clearly manifested as such.
"Because mental consciousness proceeds there in such a manner," he said: "by which the sign... [etc. ...he is able. 40.
"The meaning of the word" (*vacanattha*) refers to the lexical meaning. "Closing" (*nimīlana*) is not the seeing of closing;
likewise, the eyes are not actually closed because the seeing of closing is not a state of purity. By contrast, however, the seeing is pure.

And he said "vivaṭañca" (and opened) with the words "antarantarā" (from time to time), and so forth. Taking the root *nī* in the sense of knowing, he said "panayati jānāti" (he leads away; he knows). For it is said:
"The signless ones do not lead [others]," and "The knowers [know] what is to be known by the Best of Men. But taking *nī* in the sense of causing to proceed, [he takes] the root...
Having taken [it], he "leads it" and "carries it out. He was diligent in those various duties and tasks. 42.

*Vassāvāsa* (the rainy-season residence) is [called] *vassa* by the elision of the latter member of the compound; therefore, because it is worthy of being a comfortable place of residence during the *vassa*, it is called *vassika*, as in "the *vassika* palace.
However, the months are called *vassikā* because they exist during the *vassa* season. Regarding the others: *hemantika*.
"Gimhika" means "among these. "The same method applies" refers by extension to the analysis [of the term] through the elision of the latter member of the compound.
"Neither too tall nor too short" means it is not as tall as one suited for the summer (*gimhika*) nor as short as one suited for the winter (*hemantika*);
rather, because it possesses the characteristic of being intermediate between those two, it is neither too tall nor too short. "Of" (*assa*) refers to the palace. "Not too many" means...
"Not too many" means not as numerous as those of the summer; "not too few" means not as small as those of the winter, nor with such extremely fine meshes.
"Mixed" means that they are neither exclusively for heat like those of the winter, nor exclusively for cold like those of the summer, but rather a mixture of both.
"Thin" means not broad. "For the purpose of entering the heat" means for the sake of entering the sun's scorching heat.
"Bhittiniyūhāni" means niches on the walls on the right side. "Siniddha" means oily; by the very mention of "oily," its heaviness is also implied.
"Kaṭukasannissita" means mixed with pungent substances such as the three spices (tikaṭuka) and so forth.
"Udakayantāni" means those from which streams of water flow. Just as there are water-emitting [machines], so too there are snow-emitting ones there.
They indeed do so. Therefore, it should be understood that it is as if snow were falling even during the winter.

"All places" means all locations for rejecting [food], eating, sporting, wandering about, and so forth, not merely dwelling places. Hence he said, "The gatekeepers too," and so on. Regarding this, he states the reason: "The king, it is said," and so forth.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Old Man (Jiṇṇapurisa): 44.
"Crooked like a rafter" means like a crooked rafter. Indeed, in order to illustrate the state of being crooked in those things that are crooked, even a straight rafter is included.
"Archedly crooked" refers to the state of having a body that is curved, rising upward from the very beginning.

[Vaṅkaṃ]. Therefore he said, "the aggregates" (khandhe), and so forth. It is called *daṇḍaparāyanaṃ* because its way (*ayana*) or movement is dependent upon the staff (*daṇḍa*), meaning it is intent on grasping the staff;
or, the staff is its supreme way, its cause of movement, thus it is *daṇḍaparāyanaṃ*.
It is called *daṇḍagatikaṃ* because the staff is its course, its support, since it cannot function without it; it is that by which one goes.
"Or *gati* means 'course'; that which has a staff as its course—that is, its cause for going—is called *daṇḍagatika*.
The same method applies here to the term *daṇḍapaṭisaraṇa* (having a staff as one's refuge). "Afflicted by old age (*jarātura*)" means exhausted by old age and lacking self-control.
"When the chariot is in front" means when the two roads have met and the army is moving forward, he has mounted upon a certain formation and is proceeding in the middle.
When the chariot mounted by the Bodhisatta is moving toward another formation and is ahead, and the body of troops is behind, then the entire body of troops is behind.
"In such a place" means in such a section of the road as has been described.
"That man" refers to that old man. "Suddhāvāsas" refers to the three Perfectly Enlightened Ones, beginning with Siddhattha.
"Brahmas reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm after having practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) within the Teaching; for they remain there at that time.
"But what is the meaning of this term 'one who is old' (jiṇṇa) as it is being used by you?
Explain that to me after determining its specific nature," he shows [this]. For, because its specific form has not been determined, the Bodhisatta refers to himself by means of the gendered pronoun.
When asking "What? while referring to that, he says: "In what way has it been born for you? For in the world, two things are mostly born: either a woman or a man.
Nevertheless, that [gender] is expressed by a general term for gender (*liṅga-sabbānāma*); it should be understood that this case is exactly like that.
The phrase "What is meant? and so forth clarifies precisely its undetermined nature.

“‘Tena hi,’ etc., is an exposition of the manner in which the Great Being was moved by the thought: ‘And since this state of old age is common to all, it will surely come upon me as well. A *sārathi* is one who drives a chariot (*ratha*).

An *uyyāna* is that to which people go or approach when they have set out for the purpose of sporting and recreation. *Alaṃ* is a word of refusal or prohibition. *Nāma* is a particle used in the sense of censure.”
As in the passage beginning with “How indeed could it be so? and others, [the root of birth] is like the uprooting of its foundation for the purpose of seeing the danger in birth;
and because that [foundation] has been firmly established, he said, “He sat down digging up the root of birth.
For when the cause is accomplished, the fruit is necessarily accomplished as well. Having produced affliction by way of piercing within, first of all, the heart—
The construction is: "He sat down as if pierced in the heart by the first arrow because he remained [there] without having entered [the city].
47. Commentary on the Sick Man:

"In the manner previously stated" means by the very method previously stated in the passage beginning with "It is said that the Suddhāvāsa [deities...]. "Afflicted" (*ābādhika*) means possessing an ailment. "Pained" (*dukkhita*) means one in whom suffering has arisen. "Unborn" (*ajāta*) refers to the state of being unborn, or alternatively, to Nibbāna.
50. Regarding the description of the man of blackened face:
because it must be obtained by making various parts such as the eyeballs and eyelids askew, it is called *vilāta* (a disfigured corpse); thus he says, "A *vilāta* is a palanquin (*sivika*).
Because he had previously seen a palanquin, the Great Being [referred to] the lattice-work of the funeral pyre as a "palanquin."
He said: "Departed from here" means departed from this existence. "At the time of death" means at the conclusion of the period of life. Therefore he said, "as much as," and so forth.
53. Commentary on Renunciation:

One who practices the Dhamma is a "dhammacaraṇa"; the state of such a person is the "state of practicing the Dhamma" (*dhammacaraṇabhāva*), which is simply the practice of the Dhamma (*dhammacariyā*).

He speaks thus: "In this way, for each individual term"—just as the construction is "gone forth for the sake of good practice of the Dhamma," so too should the construction for each individual term be understood through such phrases as "gone forth for the sake of good conduct" and so on.

"All" refers to all the terms—*dhamma*, *sama*, *kusala*, and *puñña*—that appear in the passage beginning with "good practice of the Dhamma. They are synonyms for the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).
The terms "generosity" and so forth refer to the categories of the ten wholesome states.
Regarding the commentary on the Bodhisatta’s going forth (54):
the connection is with the phrase "having heard a discourse on the Dhamma after he had gone forth. Furthermore, there is another portion not included in the Saṅgīti [Pariyāya]. By that...
The construction is: "then [he delivered] a discourse on the Dhamma. By the three words beginning with "vaṃso," he shows that this is the natural order of things (*dhammatā*).
They see him after long intervals because of their long life-span; for it has been said: "after the passing of many years... [etc.]".
"By that very fact" means by the very fact of having seen him not long ago. An action belonging to a prior time occurs within a very short interval of time.

Demonstrating this, he said, “Having seen an old man... and having seen one who has gone forth, therefore I have gone forth, O King,” just as one might say, “Having bathed, put on clothes, anointed with perfume, adorned with garlands, and eaten.
—Commentary on the Great Multitude’s Going Forth.

55. By the words beginning with “But why, in this case...,” [the author] shows that those eighty-four thousand beings possessed great devotion toward the Mahāsatta and were filled with a profound sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);

for it was precisely while standing at the place where they had heard [his teaching], and without taking leave of any of their kinsmen or friends, that they went forth into homelessness, like a noble elephant in rut breaking through its iron fetters and solid bonds.
He wandered on tour for four months because his knowledge had not yet reached full maturity.
But when his knowledge had reached maturity, he spoke the words beginning with "Now this," showing that state.
His intention was: "All these renunciants will know of my departure, and knowing it, they will follow after me. "When they were seated" means...
"While they were sitting together. "It was as if it were whispering" means it made a sound as if it were whispering.

"To those who delight in non-seclusion" means to those who find no pleasure in solitude. "This is the time" means this is the time for me to go while those renunciants do not yet know of my departure.
"Having gone out" means having emerged from the leaf-hut; however, the Great Renunciation had already taken place long before.

He had departed. By the power of the perfections (pāramitā), although the seat was already well-prepared above with celestial coverings by the deities, it is said that "having prepared the throne" because it appeared as if prepared by him, since its accomplishment was due to the power of the Great Being’s merit.
The fourfold energy (caturaṅga-vīriya) proceeding according to the method beginning with, "Let skin, sinew, and bone remain," [was exerted].
Having made his resolution, he dwells in seclusion, living in solitude.
"By another way" means by a different direction from where the Great Being was dwelling at that time.
Granted that the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the central navel of Jambudīpa, nevertheless, at that time it was a vast forest, secluded and suitable for the retreat of yogins.
"Having sacrificed, he remains. Furthermore, another region of Jambudīpa was for the most part crowded with many people, prosperous and flourishing.
Therefore, those who went toward various districts and regions are said to have "set out on a wandering journey facing within Jambudīpa";
the meaning is that they were facing within Jambudīpa, not facing toward mountains such as the Himavat.
Commentary on the Bodhisatta’s Resolve (57):

Granted that the Blessed One, having become a Buddha, dwelt right there for seven weeks, the phrase "having entered upon a single night's stay" is said with reference to the very first full moon of the month of Visākha.
"Having gone into seclusion" means having gone to a place secluded from people.
By the phrase "having approached," he describes the Great Being’s physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) through his absence of social entanglement with a crowd.
By the phrase "secluded" (*paṭisallīnassa*), he describes his preliminary mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) through the absence of mental entanglement;

that is, by the withdrawal of the mind from wandering among various objects, it is properly settled (*pati*), and thus the mind is not scattered therein. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to that rooted in birth and so forth.
It is suffering. Granted, passing away and rebirth are indeed just birth and death;

however, having stated "is born and dies" (*jāyati mīyati*), the statement "passes away and reappears" (*cavati upapajjati*) is not intended to include those [states] contained within a single existence (*ekabhava*).
Rather, it shows that they are taken together as belonging to different existences (*nānābhava*). Thus he said: "This dyad... was spoken."
But why, when reflecting on the world’s attainment of suffering, is the restriction made by way of aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) as "of aging-and-death"?
He says "because," and so forth. The intention is that aging-and-death alone presents itself at the beginning.
"Of what has been undertaken" means of what has been commenced. When insight is begun by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), its undertaking begins from aging-and-death.
"Descending from the summit to the base," he said, meaning "as if descending from the peak of existence.
"Skillful attention" means because one attends by way of a skillful means, and because it is the occurrence of attention through such a means.

Now, in order to show that method of skillful attention—which is itself wise attention—in its essential nature and in the manner of its occurrence, the passage beginning with "Impermanence, etc. was stated.

"Right attention (yonisomanasikāra) occurs" means by way of the state of attending to things as they truly are. "Impermanence, etc."—by the word "etc.," suffering, non-self, foulness, and so forth are included. "This" refers to the attention described as "this occurred to him," which proceeds in the manner beginning with "When what exists? and so on.
"One of these" means one among those various forms of attention to impermanence and the rest. But which one is it?
"Attention to impermanence" is precisely what is meant here; the reason for this is stated as "because it proceeds by way of the contemplation of arising and passing away.

For that which both arises and falls away is impermanent; having regarded it as unstable because it is delimited by arising and passing away, the seeing of its true nature is "appropriate attention" (yonisomanasikāra) due to its being attention according to reality. Thus, from appropriate attention...
The word *nissakkavacana* (ablative) is used for the cause; by this instrumental expression “by means of this appropriate attention,” he states the meaning regarding the cause.
“There was a meeting” means there was a coming together through the mode of penetrating [the truth] as it really is.
But what is that? He says, “birth,” meaning: “But what is that cause of aging and death? Regarding the passage beginning with “Indeed, from birth,” this is the summarized meaning:
While the Bodhisatta was investigating the cause of aging and death, thinking, "When what exists does aging and death come to be?
With what as condition does aging and death arise?", he grasped the unerring cause in this way: "When X exists, Y comes to be; when X is absent, Y does not come to be;
therefore, X is the cause of Y. Thus, [he realized]: "When birth exists, aging and death come to be."
Regarding the phrase "with birth as condition, aging-and-death": when wisdom arises that grasps the cause of aging-and-death, there was a coming together with that arising wisdom.
"All the terms" refers to the nine terms beginning with birth and ending with consciousness, which have been presented in the sequence starting with, "When what exists is there birth? and so forth.

Regarding the twelvefold dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), having asked for the reason why two factors were not included here, and desiring to provide the answer, [the author] first shows the manner in which they should be included by saying, "But here... and so forth.
Having first taken the present existence, which is directly perceived, as the "first," he then refers to the future [existence] immediately following it as the "second."
"The third is past in its grasping," he said; thus, "Ignorance and volitional formations are indeed past existence. [Objection:
But surely here, even the grasping of future existence is not possible, since the insistence is shown by way of the present? [Reply: This is true;
however, it should be understood that when the cause is grasped, the fruit is necessarily grasped as well, and thus it was stated in that manner. Moreover, in this context:

The future period as well is indeed included by way of its meaning, since the teaching that includes the future period begins from that point onward with the words, "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," and so forth.
"By those" means by ignorance and volitional formations which have become the object. It does not connect; it does not link up.
For the Great Man is intent upon the present; thus, because there is no connection [with the past], [the future is not linked].
He states the reason: "By means of the unseen" (*adiṭṭhehi*) means by means of those not yet understood; this instrumental case is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark of a state of being.
Since there must be penetration once there is awakening, he says, "it is impossible to be a Buddha [without it].

"By this one" refers to the Mahāsatta. "Those" refers to ignorance and volitional formations. "Precisely by way of existence, clinging, and craving" means precisely by way of the vision of existence, clinging, and craving.
Because they possess the same capability for application (*yogakkhema*) as those [factors] included within their own respective natures, they have already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, the intention is that they need not be explained here.

(58) "By way of condition" means by way of cause; the meaning is "by way of volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*). [This is based on the passage: "When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? and so forth.

Indeed, when the succession of results is being explained by way of the succession of causes, in the investigation—"When what exists does consciousness come to be?"—if the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), which are the specific cause of consciousness, were not grasped as "when volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be," then consciousness would simply turn back from that [point];
it does not turn back from every condition. For this very reason, he said: "In name-and-form..."

“With existence as condition, consciousness comes to be. Here too, name (*nāma*) is intended as a condition by way of being co-nascent and so forth, and not by way of kamma or decisive support (*upanissaya*), because it is manifested through its adherence to the present.
“By way of object (*ārammaṇato*): by way of the objects known as ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), or by way of the object known as past existence;
for ignorance and volitional formations are included within the past half [of the cycle]. From which [point], turning back...
Consciousness is said to turn back even from past existence. "Both" refers to both the rebirth-linking consciousness and the insight-consciousness.
"It does not transcend name-and-form" means it does not go beyond name-and-form as a condition and name-and-form as an object, because it cannot proceed without them.
Therefore he said: "It does not go beyond name-and-form."
"When consciousness is a condition for name-and-form" means that consciousness is a condition for name, for form, and for name-and-form.
"And when name-and-form is a condition for consciousness"— likewise, it should be understood that name, form,
and name-and-form are conditions for consciousness according to the appropriate application in terms of fourfold, fivefold, or sixfold existence (*bhava*).
"But when both are present as mutual conditions" refers specifically to the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).
"By this much" means by way of the occurrence of consciousness and name-and-form through their mutual support of one another. "One would be born...
or would arise" is a conventional designation (*samaññā*) for "a being is born... or arises," [applied] to that which is distinct from consciousness and name-and-form.
Because there is no phenomenon that serves as the fuel for the designation of a "being. Therefore he said, "For from this," and so forth. "This very thing" refers to consciousness;
these two, namely consciousness and name-and-form, are the same.
