"Five phrases" refers to the five phrases beginning with "or would be born. Now, [one might ask: are not the fourth and fifth [phrases] included within the first and third?
He said, "They are non-different in meaning," by stating, "together with repeated deaths and rebirths.

Then, having stated again what was previously expressed by the phrase "to this extent" (*ettāvatā*)—that is, presenting and demonstrating that very meaning already explained by means of the words "namely" (*yadidaṃ*) and so forth—he spoke once more.
[The phrase] "by way of the mode of conditions in forward order" (*anulomapaccayākāravasena*) refers to that which is preceded by the demonstration of the phenomena that serve as conditions.

By way of seeing the phenomena that have arisen through conditions. For the state of being a condition for one's own effect among the conditioning phenomena is "specific conditionality" (idappaccayatā), which is the mode of conditionality (paccayākāra);

and this has been stated as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth. Because it conforms to the forward progression of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), it is the "forward mode of conditionality.
All the suffering of the round, beginning with birth, is brought about by the mind when it is directed toward it.
Having taken the term as a collective whole, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "of the mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandhassa*); thus he said, "of the heap of suffering" (*dukkharāsissa*).
Because consciousness proceeds by way of seeing the origin of the mass of suffering on many occasions, he spoke the reduplicated expression "origin, origin.
Alternatively, this [statement] "thus there is an origin" is not merely...

This is a phrase indicating origination; however, whereas the term *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination) refers to the process of arising, here the term *samudaya* (origination) expresses the state of being a condition by way of its result of production.
The factors such as consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and so forth are indicated here as the conditioned phenomena (*paccayadhammā*).
Taking them in their general form according to the desire for detailed exposition, he said, "Origination, origination."
And having established this, what will be said—that "the statement 'When this exists, that comes to be' expresses merely the recognition of conditions"—is thereby supported.
If this is so, how is it that "the wisdom of seeing arising is insight"?
This is not a fault, because by way of seeing arising from conditions, there occurs the seeing of the characteristic of production. In the sense of seeing...
“Eye” (*cakkhu*): It is called an eye because it is like an eye in its quality of seeing the arising [of suffering] directly.
“In the sense of making known”: in the sense of making [the arising] known, just as the arising is correctly known and understood. “In the sense of understanding”:
by way of the mode [of understanding], namely, “With consciousness as condition, through the arising of this and that, there is the arising of this aggregate of suffering.”
In the sense of knowing. "In the sense of having emerged and having penetrated" means:

having not previously emerged [from ignorance], and having emerged from the opposing states by means of the wisdom that sees arising (*udayadassanapaññā*), and having penetrated them by way of their conditions, by way of moments, and by way of their specific nature, thinking "this is the origin"—it is said to be *vijjā* (clear vision) in the sense of emerging and in the sense of penetrating. "In the sense of radiance" means...
It is by way of its illuminating function, through the dispelling of the darkness of delusion and the darkness of the defilements, which conceal the true nature of the origin [of suffering].
Now, in order to clarify the meaning just stated in sequence, it is said, "As it has been said," and so forth. Therein, "the eye arose" is the extraction of the phrase from the Pāḷi.
To the question, "In what sense did it arise? he says, "in the sense of seeing. [Regarding] "of the origin..."
The meaning of "by way of seeing through direct perception" has been stated. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well.
"Eye-factor" (*cakkhudhamma*) means that "eye" is a factor in the Canon. "Seeing-meaning" (*dassanaṭṭha*) means the essential nature of seeing;
it is the meaning that is to be manifested by that [nature]. The same method applies to the others as well. "By these many terms" means by these five terms. "What is stated? [is the question.]

He asks for the sake of a summary. "Mere recognition of conditions" means that what is described is merely the recognition of the specific nature of the conditions—such as consciousness and so forth—and of the conditioned states—such as name-and-form and so forth—without distinction, because it illuminates the discernment of the specific nature of conditions.
And it is said, "The young insight that has entered the path is described," because it illuminates the correct observation of the arising of formations.
61. It is called "this" because it has been personally attained and is thus immediate and direct experience; it is called the "path" (magga) in the sense of searching for the Noble Path and so forth.
For this is preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā). Therefore he said, "for the sake of enlightenment" (bodhāya).

With reference to the noun-derivation (*bhāvasādhana*) of the word "enlightenment," he said, "for the purpose of awakening to the Four Truths. The clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of full understanding, abandoning, and development are solely for the purpose of the clear realization of actualization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).
Because the purpose of living the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is the attainment of *nibbāna*, it is said: "or for the sake of awakening to *nibbāna*.
For it has been stated: "*Nibbāna* is the supreme happiness. It "awakens" (*bujjhati*) in the sense that one penetrates the Four Noble Truths through a single penetration;
thus, he states that the word *bodha* functions as an agentive noun (*kattusādhana*). "By means of the nominative cases" refers to those indicating the first grammatical case (*paṭhamāvibhatti*).
By these terms. It is precisely Nibbāna that is spoken of, because consciousness and the rest cease therein.
"Non-arising cessation" means the cessation of non-origination through the total cessation of conditions; it is absolute cessation. 62.
"By all these terms" refers to the five terms beginning with "the eye. "Merely the perception of cessation" means...
By the passage beginning with “‘Cessation, cessation,’ indeed,” only the mere perception of cessation is spoken of because it was previously undertaken;
it is not a direct vision through penetration, since the Noble Path has not yet been attained.
The correct vision of the cessation of formations is intended to occur by way of insight (vipassanā) that has reached its culmination; thus, [it is called] “leading to emergence.”
And it is said: “Powerful insight has been explained. 63.

“Having understood” means having known by means of preliminary knowledge (*pubbabhāgiya-ñāṇa*). “Thereafter” means after the subsequent stage of knowing the cessation of conditions according to the method already stated.
“In those things which are the conditions for clinging” means [in those things] that serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and so forth for all four kinds of clinging (*upādāna*).
"Among those things that have become conditions" means "among those things subject to clinging. "Carrying" means "causing to proceed. "This" refers to the statement beginning with "at a later time.

Why was it said? It was said by way of the desire to explain: "By whatever practice all Great Bodhisattas proceed toward enlightenment in their final existence, in that very same way did the Great Bodhisattva practice through insight (vipassanā)."

This is the statement of the question. Therefore he said, “Indeed, all [of them],” and so forth. Therein, the Great Renunciation and the application to ascetic striving on the day of the son’s birth are to be understood as occurring by way of natural law (*dhammatā*);
the other [events] are to be understood by way of what ought to be done (*itikattabbatā*).

Even therein, because his mind was impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) acquired through long-term cultivation and habitual practice, [he thought]: “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship,” and so forth.

The contemplation of the mode of conditions, beginning with aging and death, by way of demonstrating the attainment of hardship for the world of beings who desire to be liberated from the suffering of *saṃsāra*, is likewise the very nature of things (*dhammatā*).

Likewise, the practice of the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*) is the nature of things because it is independent of self, because it cannot be impaired by anyone, because it is an abiding in unsullied happiness, and because it belongs to the fourth jhāna. Regarding the five [aggregates]...

"Having adhered to the aggregates" means: having adhered by way of insight-adherence to the five aggregates of clinging—which are grasped through such designations as consciousness and name-and-form—and having commenced the practice.
"Successive order" (anukkama) is a name given to the gradual practice because it must be followed step by step and practiced in sequence. "Having done" means: having practiced.
In the phrase *iti rūpaṃ*, the second word *iti* has the sense of indication (*nidassana*).

By means of that [second *iti*], the first *iti* is understood to signify both the essential nature (*sarūpa*) and the measure (*parimāṇa*), because particles have multiple meanings; or rather, this meaning should be understood through the method of repetition (*āvutti*) and so forth.
And showing the sentence with an internal restriction (*antogadhāvadhāraṇa*), [it says]: "This is form (*rūpa*); such is the extent of form (*ettakaṃ rūpaṃ*); beyond this there is no further form."
He said, beginning with “there is not,” and so forth. Therein, by the phrase “the nature of being affected,” the general characteristic of matter (*rūpa*) is shown;
by the phrase “divided into primary elements and derived matter,” and so forth, its specific characteristics are shown. By both of these, the meaning of the term “this is matter” is demonstrated.

In this context, a “characteristic” (*lakkhaṇa*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of each particular kind of matter that is not shared by anything else. Its “function” (*rasa*) is that of the same [matter].
The state of being a condition with respect to its own fruit; the manifestation is its being the objective range for knowledge as it truly is, because of its existence in the ultimate sense;
the proximate cause is the immediate reason, by which its dependence on conditions is shown.

Furthermore, by the phrase "the complete discernment of material form," it is indicated that there is no material form beyond this extent, such that one might think, "This much is material form; beyond this, there is none."
The meaning of both these terms has been demonstrated by way of the complete exhaustion of form through its determination.
Regarding the phrase "Thus is the origin of form," the word *iti* here signifies a manner, as in such passages as "Thus indeed, monks, the fool is full of fear";
thus he said, "‘Iti’ means ‘thus’."

“From the arising of ignorance” (*avijjāsamudayā*) means from the emergence, that is, the state of existence, of ignorance. For "arising" (*uppāda*) is also a term for the state of existence (*atthibhāva*), as it is the very cessation of cessation.
Therefore, when ignorance established in a previous existence exists, there is the arising of form in this present existence; the meaning is that there is the emergence of form.

This same method applies to the phrases “from the arising of craving” (*taṇhāsamudayā*) and so forth. However, regarding the phrase “from the arising of nutriment” (*āhārasamudayā*): [the explanation follows].
Among the conditions for the process of existence (*pavatti-paccaya*), edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) alone is taken because of its preponderance.

When that is taken, temperature and consciousness are already included by virtue of their commonality as conditions for the process of existence; thus, it should be understood that the demonstration of the arising of matter produced from the four [other] origins has already been clarified through its conditionality.
By the phrase "the characteristic of production" (*nibbatti-lakkhaṇa*), etc., he speaks of the demonstration of arising by way of time. Therein, "the characteristic of production" means:

The conditioned characteristic of form is its arising. "Even while seeing" means not only seeing the arising through the collection of conditions, but also seeing the arising from the perspective of moments (*khaṇa*).
For, having first seen the arising by way of the time-periods (*addhā*), one stands firm;
then, having seen it again by way of the continuity (*santati*), one gradually sees it by way of moments. "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form."

Through the non-arising and cessation of ignorance by means of the highest path, there is the non-arising and cessation of future form, because in the absence of conditions, there is an absence [of the effect].
The same principle applies here in the statement: "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of karma.

"With the cessation of nutriment" means through the absence of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which is a condition for the process of existence. "Cessation of form" means the absence of the materiality originated by that [nutriment]. The rest...
It is exactly as stated. Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of change," this is a vision of decay by way of the time of dissolution;
therefore, having first seen it by way of the [three] periods of time, and then having seen it again by way of the continuity of moments, one subsequently sees it by way of the moment.
And this method is stated according to the perspective of an ordinary practitioner of insight; however, for Bodhisattvas, this [gradual progression] does not exist.
This same method applies to the contemplation of arising (*udayadassana*).
In such passages as “Thus is feeling,” the meaning should be understood according to the method explained previously for form (*rūpa*). Therefore, it was said:
“This is feeling; this much is feeling,” and so forth. Therein, regarding the phrase “the nature of what is felt” (*vedayitasabhāva*), etc., [it refers to] “the nature of what is felt,” and so on.

The word *sabhāva* (intrinsic nature) should be applied to each term as "having the intrinsic nature of cognizing. "Having the intrinsic nature of being felt" means having the intrinsic nature of experiencing.

"Having the intrinsic nature of perceiving" means having the intrinsic nature of discerning an object as "blue," "yellow," and so forth. "Having the intrinsic nature of volitional formation" means having the intrinsic nature of accumulation.
"Having the intrinsic nature of cognizing" means having the intrinsic nature of apprehending an object. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "pleasure and so forth,"...
The inclusion of painful, joyful, sorrowful, and equanimous feelings; the inclusion of form-perception and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), sound-perception and the rest are included;
the inclusion of contact and so forth—by the word "and so forth," volition, applied thought, and the rest are included;

and the inclusion of eye-consciousness and so forth—by the word "and so forth," all mundane consciousnesses are included. And just as it is with consciousness, this same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. "Of these" refers to [the aggregates] as "the origin."
Of the dhammas already mentioned. "In the three aggregates" means in the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-saññā-saṅkhārakkhandhesu*).
Because of the statement, "Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one intends," it should be said that [these three] have contact as their origin (*phassasamudayā*).

Because of the statement, "Consciousness has name-and-form as its condition (*nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ*)," it should be said that the consciousness aggregate has name-and-form as its origin (*nāmarūpasamudayā*). "Of those very same... [refers to] those very ones.
Regarding the three aggregates, the phrase for the "subsidence" (*atthaṅgama*) should also be applied specifically to contact and name-and-form, as in: "of contact, in the consciousness aggregate;
of name-and-form... The intention is that ignorance and the other factors are exactly as described under the heading of "form.
Regarding the phrase "by way of fifty-six characteristics": there are twenty-five characteristics of arising—twenty by way of conditions and five by way of moments.
By way of twenty characteristics of rise from the perspective of conditions and five from the perspective of moments—thus, by way of fifty-five characteristics of rise and fall (udaya-vaya-lakkhaṇa).

In this context, they are called "characteristics" (lakkhaṇāni) because the arising of the five aggregates is characterized by these, namely, the origination through ignorance and so forth; likewise, their non-arising and cessation are characterized.
"By these" refers to what are called the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), namely the absolute cessation of ignorance and the rest.

However, the characteristics of arising and change are simply the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*). Thus, these fifty-five characteristics should be understood according to their own nature.
"Increased in due order" means that the aforementioned knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) proceeds having become sharp, keen, and clear.

Beyond that, it refers to insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that has reached the peak of intellectual attainment through the sequence of the arising of the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*),

which are to be discussed hereafter. For even more so, it refers to that [insight] which is grasping a "womb" (i.e., taking on a potentiality) and reaching maturity through the power accumulated by the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*)—

which is designated as the "Great Vajra Knowledge" (*mahāvajira-ñāṇa*) because it proceeds by way of three million six hundred thousand modes and is commensurate with omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
As the knowledge of purification by practice proceeds, having gradually attained the highest perfection through the power of the perfection of wisdom accumulated over immeasurable time,
and having reached the state of leading to emergence, when it is joined with the noble path,
then the noble path-consciousness is liberated from all defilements according to the sequence of the paths; and as it is being liberated, [it liberates].

He is liberated in such a way that there is the abandonment of all obstructions to the knowable. That which is called the "abandonment of defilements along with their latent tendencies" (savāsanappahāna) is, in its actual meaning, the cessation through non-arising; thus he says, "by the cessation through non-arising.

[The phrase] "by the defilements known as the taints" (āsava-saṅkhātehi kilesehi) refers to those designated as taints in terms of existence from the realm of becoming up to the peak of existence, in terms of phenomena up to the stage of lineage (gotrabhū), and in terms of hearing and occurrence.
By these defilements—namely, lust, views, and delusion. This expression "by the taints" in the Canon is a statement of their defining characteristic;
however, because they are associated with them, the mind is liberated from all defilements and all evil states.
"Without grasping" means without grasping even a mere trace of those defilements.
At the moment of the path, it is said to "be liberated" from those defilements to be abandoned by that particular path; at the moment of the fruit, it is said to be "liberated.

Or, "it is both liberated and being liberated at the moment of the path" means that at the moment of a higher path, it is both already liberated from what was to be abandoned by the lower paths and is being liberated from its own respective objects of abandonment. At the moment of the fruit, it is "already liberated" alone; this applies to every moment of the fruit.
It is indeed liberated; it is not called "being liberated" [in the sense of a process].
"From all fetters" means from every bond of existence (*bhava-saññojana*) included within the lower and higher fetters (*orambhāgiya-uddhambhāgiya*);

"completely released" means released in a distinguished and manifold way. "With a mental continuum well-expanded" means through the contact of the rays of knowledge (*ñāṇa-rasmi*) to an exceeding degree.
“With his mental continuum fully and perfectly blossomed”: this is a partial description of those knowledges by which his mental continuum is well-flowered, such as the “four knowledges of the path.
A complete description will follow later; therefore, we shall analyze them in that very place.
“And all the Buddha-qualities”: this refers to all the qualities of a Buddha, beginning with the unimpeded knowledge regarding the past.
For when the Lord of the World attains the supreme path, he is said to have placed all virtues within the palm of his hand.
Thenceforth, he is called "one who stands with [all virtues] held in the palm of his hand.
Having stated "one whose intention is fulfilled," the following Udāna beginning with "Through many births in saṃsāra... is shown to illustrate the fulfillment of that intention.
It has been stated. Therein, the meaning of the first two verses has already been explained below in the commentary on the introduction to the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
As for the subsequent portion: "Of that which is struck by an iron hammer"—an iron hammer (*ayoghana*) is so called because iron is struck with it;
it refers to the iron sledgehammer and the iron mallet of smiths. It is "struck" or beaten by that iron hammer. Here, the word *eva* is merely a particle. Of that which is burning...
"Jātavedaso" refers to fire that is being extinguished; or this is a term of address used in a sense of disregard.
"Anupubbūpasantassa" means of that which has been gradually calmed, suppressed, and ceased. "Yathā na ñāyate gati" means in such a way that its destination is not known.
This is what is meant: [it is like] iron struck by an iron hammer because it was beaten with an iron fist, a spike, or the like.

When a fire that has been struck by a hammer, or a fire occurring within a bronze vessel or similar object, is gradually extinguished, no destination for it is discerned in any of the ten directions; for, due to the cessation of its conditions, it has ceased without reconnection (*appaṭisandhika*).
Thus, "of those who are rightly liberated" means: by means of the right cause, the method, preceded by liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
Because they are well-liberated through the noble path of liberation-by-eradication, being freed from both the four kinds of clinging and the taints;

and because, for that very reason, they have crossed over and stand firm having traversed the remaining floods—namely, the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha) and the flood of existence (bhavogha), which comprise the bond of sensual desire;
and because all the agitation of the defilements has been thoroughly stilled, they are not [moved] by the winds of the formations of the defilements.

For those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), who have attained and reached the bliss known as Nibbāna—the subsiding of all conditioned formations (saṅkhārūpasama) and the immovable state due to its unshakability—there is no way to designate their destination among the various realms such as those of gods or humans by saying, "It is this one.
Because there is an absence of anything to be designated, they cannot be pointed out; like the aforementioned fire, they exist in a state of non-designation (apaññatti).

The meaning is "they go. "Thus attending to" means that while attending to his own accomplishment of the task through the passage beginning with "Thus through the saṃsāra of many births," he shone forth even as he sat upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka); such is the construction.
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Brahmā’s Entreaty: 64.
*Yannūna* is a particle used in the sense of reflection. He said, "If, however, I," because the Blessed One was referring to himself with the word *aham*.
The passage beginning with "In the eighth week" explains how our Blessed One, having attained full enlightenment, [spent that time] by way of experiencing the bliss of liberation and so forth.
He practiced for seven weeks; thereafter, he did so by way of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma and so forth.

In this very same way, all perfectly enlightened Buddhas practiced at the time of their full enlightenment, and those seven weeks and other periods are defined in exactly the same manner—this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) common to all Buddhas. Therefore, the Blessed One Vipassī...
This [passage] was begun to show how he practiced in that manner at the time of his full enlightenment.
Therein, the phrase "on the eighth week" is stated with reference to the practice occurring after the seventh week and during the preceding week;
it is not because a specific eighth week, as distinct from the seven days of the *pallaṅka* (cross-legged sitting), is actually obtainable.
“Immediately after” (*anantara*) refers to the thought, “This Dhamma has been attained by me,” and so forth.
“Penetrated” (*paṭividdha*) means that it has proceeded by way of direct penetration toward [the truth] as “this is suffering,” and so on, through the knowledge of self-enlightenment;
the meaning is that it has been understood as it really is. “Dhamma” refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, [as there is no other Dhamma to be penetrated apart from that].

"Because of its non-existence. "Profound" means that, like the great ocean, it cannot find a footing for the knowledge of others—except for those who have accumulated and matured the equipment of knowledge—with even the needle-like tip of a gnat's proboscis. Therefore he said:
"This is a statement negating superficiality. Because it is impossible to fathom, one is unable to see it in its true nature or its specific details.
He said: "Because it is profound, it is difficult to see. It is to be seen with difficulty; that is, it can only be seen by someone at some time with great effort.
As for that which cannot even be seen, there is no talk of entering into it and understanding it step by step;
thus he said: "Because it is difficult to see, it is difficult to penetrate. It is to be understood with difficulty because the act of understanding it is hard to accomplish.
At this point, the following passage from the Sutta should be cited: "What do you think, monks, which is more difficult to perform or more difficult to achieve?
It is "peaceful" (santo) because its object is peaceful. It is "extinguished" (nibbuto) because all feverish distress has been extinguished.
Or, it is "sublime" (paṇīto) because it has been brought to a state of excellence. It is "satisfying" (atappako) in the sense of providing no further craving, like a meal of exquisite flavor.
And here, the truth of cessation is a peaceful object; the truth of the path is both peaceful and has a peaceful object.
It is "peaceful" because of the absence of defilements and formations whose nature is not calmed, and it is "quenched" because all feverish distress has been extinguished.
By virtue of its very state of being peaceful and sublime, it should be understood as "unsatiating" and "satisfying" because it is so refreshing for that purpose. Thus he said:
“This was said with reference only to that which is supramundane. Because it is the object of supreme knowledge, it cannot be fathomed by mere reasoning;

for that very reason, because it is the domain of subtle knowledge and because its intrinsic nature is delicate and refined, it is "subtle" (*nipuṇa*). Because it is not the domain of fools, it is to be known only by the wise;
thus, it is "to be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*). They adhere to it in the sense of taking delight in it.
They are called *ālaya* because they are served; that is, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). They are called *ālaya* because they are resorted to and served for the sake of delight;
that is, the modes of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*). "Delighting in the *ālaya*" means being devoted to the *ālaya*. "Well-rejoiced" means exceedingly rejoiced due to the absence of longing.
"Rejoices" means he finds delight, plays, and sports. Just as these beings [rejoice] in the strands of sensual pleasure, so too do they relish and take delight in passion (*rāga*).
The phrase "both kinds" and so forth was stated [in the commentary] as "ye va.
Regarding the term *ṭhāna*: it refers to the word *ṭhāna*. In terms of meaning (*atthato*), however, by "ṭhāna," dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) itself is intended.
It is called *ṭhāna* because the fruit stands therein, owing to its dependence on that; thus, it is the condition for the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) and the rest.
Ignorance and the rest. These are the conditions for these [factors] such as volitional formations; thus they are "this-condition" (idappaccaya), namely ignorance and the rest.
"This-conditionality" (idappaccayatā) is simply the state of being this-condition, just as "deity" (devatā) is simply a "god" (deva).

Alternatively, this-conditionality is the state of being a condition, or the capacity to produce, which belongs to ignorance and the rest—the "this-conditions"—in dependence upon their own fruit. Therefore, it has the characteristic of a condition in the ultimate sense.
Dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) has been shown. It is called "dependent origination" because the fruit arises dependently upon this.
By both these words, the meaning of conditionality among phenomena is clarified. Therefore he said: "This is a designation for ignorance and the other conditions, such as volitional formations.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*): "all" (*sabba*) refers to everything denoted by the phrase "the stilling of all formations" and so forth; in its actual meaning (*atthato*), it is Nibbāna alone.
Now, in order to demonstrate its nature as Nibbāna, the words beginning with "for because" (*yasmā hi*) were spoken. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to Nibbāna.

"Having come to" (*āgamma*) means depending upon it, by way of the noble path’s object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). "They are stilled" (*sammanti*) means by way of subsiding without rebirth (*appaṭisandhika*).
They become stilled. And being thus stilled, they are said to be "especially calmed"; hence he says, "they are completely pacified" (*vūpasammanti*).
By this, he shows that Nibbāna is the "stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*), because all formations are stilled therein.

For when Nibbāna is dissociated from all formations, the designation "the complete pacification of all formations" is indeed logically established. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
“Basis” (*upadhi*) refers to the aggregates and so forth, because suffering is built up (*upadhīyati*) upon them.
“Relinquished” means they have been abandoned by way of complete eradication. “All craving” refers to all craving, including its eight hundred varieties.

“All defilement-passions” refers to all passions that are defilements, such as the passion for sense-pleasures, the passion for form, and so forth; or alternatively, all defilements here are termed “defilement-passions.”
They are to be understood as such because they cause the mind to fall into a state of perversion, not merely because of specific instances of greed. As it is said: "The lustful mind is perverted;
the hateful mind is perverted; the deluded mind is perverted. "Becoming dispassionate" means they abandon their own inherent nature.
"All suffering" refers to the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), comprising the divisions of aging, death, and so forth.

By means of becoming, one becomes; through this or that becoming, one goes to another becoming. It is "bound" by way of the state of craving for becoming (*bhavanikanti*), or else by way of the fruit, because for one who possesses craving, karma leads to renewed existence in the future.

Or it is "withdrawn from that" because of the total absence of that [craving] therein. Due to sitting for long periods and speaking for long periods, there occurs stiffness of the back and dryness of the palate and throat, and so forth.
Physical exhaustion and physical distress are to be understood; however, these apply only to those who do not understand the meaning of the teaching and do not practice it.
But for those who understand and practice, even the bodily fatigue resulting from the teaching does not cause distress to the Teacher.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "And the matter of the Dhamma did not distress me. Likewise...
For it has been said: “That which is called teaching those who do not know would be weariness for me.
Both—namely, weariness of mind and vexation of mind—these two do not exist in the Buddhas, because they were utterly eradicated even at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
65. *Anubrūhanaṃ* means compounding. *So* is the particle “apissu. *Vipassiṃ* [is used] in connection with the prefix *pati-*.

He said, "Vipassissa," because it is a term used for the subject matter (*sāmī-attha*) of application. Or, they are "wonderful" (*acchariya*) because they have reached growth, or they are "not wonderful" (*anacchariya*).
For the vowel *a* also has the sense of growth, as in the phrase "the qualities of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*).

Having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and a hundred thousand [eons] solely for the purpose of sharing the Dhamma with the world including its devas...

Now, it should be understood that this [verse] demonstrates the King of Dhamma’s attainment of non-concern (*appossukkatā*) therein, the wonderful nature of the meaning of the verses, and his subsequent progress.
For the verses are not "wonderful" by way of their mere literal sense; rather, they became "objects of range" (*gocara*), meaning they presented themselves.
And since "presenting themselves" means being fit for reflection, he said, "they reached the state of being fit for thorough reflection" (*parivitakkayitabbatam pāpuṇiṃsu*).
If it is indeed an easy practice (*sukhāpaṭipadā*), how can there be difficulty? To this he says: "At the time of fulfilling the perfections," and so forth.
This refers to one who gives such things as are difficult to renounce. The particle *ha* is a mere expletive (*nipāta*) in the sense of "it is well known" (*byatta*);

some say it is used in the sense of "certainly" (*ekamsattha*). Thus the construction is: "It is well known, or certainly, that it is useless (*alaṃ nippayojanaṃ*) to teach the Dhamma thus acquired with such difficulty."
The term *halanti* has the same meaning as *alanti*, as seen in expressions such as *halanti vadāmīti*.

By those "touched by lust and hatred" (*rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi*) means by those overwhelmed and assailed by lust and hatred, just as by a snake with its venomous bite. By those "followed by lust and hatred" (*rāgadosānugatehi*) means by those pursued by lust and hatred.
“Of the [notions] such as permanence,” etc., means of the grasping at permanence and so forth. “Thus gone” means thus proceeded; that is, proceeded in the manner of impermanence and so forth.
The phrase “the Dhamma of the Four Truths” should be understood here according to what is applicable both among the [characteristics] such as impermanence and among the Truths.
Alternatively, “thus gone” means it has been gone to—having been adhered to in this way as “impermanent,” etc.—by me and by other Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

The meaning is: "known" and "penetrated. Those who are stained by sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), and whose minds are shrouded by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), do not see this Dhamma as it truly is because they are stained by the lust for views (*diṭṭhirāga*) and their adherence is perverted; they will not penetrate it.

"To cause them to grasp thus" means to make them know the Dhamma as it truly is according to its own nature through [terms such as] "impermanent," and so forth. Furthermore, there is the state of being overcome by lust and hatred.
He said, "They are shrouded by a mass of darkness," precisely because of their state of delusion.
To clarify the reason for his falling into indifference toward teaching the Dhamma, he himself raises the objection beginning with, "But why?
In this context, this present falling into indifference toward teaching the Dhamma is common to all Buddhas.

By way of the nature of habitual practice, it is said "What to me? and so forth, because the initial exhortation of one's own mind during the Great Resolve—beginning with "What is the use to me of living in disguise? and so on—is the very nature of habitual practice for all Bodhisattvas.
Therein, "in disguise" (*aññātavesena*) means not having become a Buddha while making the world, including the devas, resound [with his fame], but rather [living] merely as a Buddha...
[He did so] in an unknown form by way of entering the state of a disciple. There are three reasons for his falling into a state of indifference:
the strength of the adversaries, the supreme profundity of the Dhamma, and the Blessed One’s extraordinary reverence for it.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “For him indeed” (*tassa hi*) was commenced. In that context, the "adversaries" are the defilements such as lust (*rāga*), which [stand in opposition] to right practice.

Because they create obstacles. Due to their powerful nature, their long-term cultivation, and the difficulty of purifying them from the mental continuum of beings, they overwhelm those beings—just as a rutting elephant overpowers a weak man—leading them to ruin and disaster;
they even occupy well-constructed, densely settled areas spanning many hundreds of yojanas in length and breadth, as well as thorny wildernesses.
However, in order to demonstrate its state of being difficult to purify due to its distant penetration and its difficulty to sever, the passage beginning with “Then of it” was spoken.

In that context, because it has been internally touched, it is like a gourd filled with sour gruel; because it has been left to ferment for a long time, it is like a trough filled with buttermilk; because of its weakness from being soaked in oiliness, it is like a rag saturated with fat and oil;
and because of its being mixed with oil, it is said to be like hands smeared with collyrium, which are difficult to clean.
These are inferior similes because of the continuity of their forms and because of the brevity of the time of their defilement;
however, the defilement by the *kilesas* (defilements) is even more difficult to purify because it is beginningless and because it lies latent (*anusayita*). Therefore he said, "extremely defiled.
And just as they are inferior similes due to being difficult to purify, so too are the similes for what is profound, hard to see, and difficult to penetrate.
Even a profound teaching may become clearly manifest through the destruction of its opposites;
yet that destruction of opposites is dependent upon right practice, which in turn depends upon hearing the true Dhamma. That [hearing] is contingent upon confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma.
Furthermore, for beings in this world, it is caused by the desire for what is particularly worthy of esteem and honor in the world. Thus [it is said].
Showing that the sign for the Brahma-invitation consists in the correct practice of the Dhamma, he said, "Furthermore," and so forth.
Although it was stated as if "a certain one" were unknown, in order to show that he is actually well-known and famous, it is said:
"the chief Great Brahmā in this world-system. He is the chief Great Brahmā in the realm of the Great Brahmās.
For he is indeed well-known and renowned like Sakka in the world of the gods of sensual pleasure and in the Brahma-world.

"Apparaja" means that which has very little (*appa*) dust (*raja*) such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth as its defilement (*upakkilesa*). Those whose eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) is such—that is, having that nature—are called "of a nature with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*).
To show this meaning, he said "consisting of wisdom" (*paññāmaye*), and so forth. Very little dust such as passion...
"For those who are of that nature, of a lineage with little dust [in their eyes]"—thus the meaning should be understood here.

Regarding "through not hearing," he says "through not hearing" (*assavanatāya*) because it is used in the instrumental case, as in the expression "by means of direct higher knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā*).

"By way of the ten bases for meritorious action" refers to the ten bases for meritorious action that ripen liberation, beginning with giving. Therefore, he said "those who have performed the service" (*katādhikārā*), and so forth.

In the *Papañcasūdanī*, however, it is stated: "By way of the twelve types of meritorious action. This is said by including within giving and the other [perfections] both the going for refuge and the dedication for the welfare of others. 69.
A request (*ajjhesanā*) is an aspiration characterized by reverence toward those worthy of respect; in terms of its meaning, it is also simply an aspiration.

Thus it is said, "the eye of requesting. Because this twofold knowledge functions as the vision of knowledge regarding specific objects and constitutes a unique quality (āveṇika) belonging exclusively to the Buddhas, it is called the "Buddha-eye" (buddhacakkhu); thus he says, "for these two knowledges have the name 'Buddha-eye.
Regarding "of the three path-knowledges," it refers to the lower three path-knowledges as the "Dhamma-eye" (dhammacakkhu).

It is called "name" because it consists in the mere act of seeing, having been made into the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Since those [other] knowledges are described by way of the simile of lightning, they are merely "seeing.

However, the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*) is not merely "seeing," because it has reached the pinnacle of the function of knowledge; therefore, it is not called "the eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*).

This is because it is described by way of the simile of the thunderbolt (*vajira*). "In the manner already stated" refers to the phrase "those who have little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātika*).

In this context, it is according to the method already stated. Since those with dull defilements are called "those with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhā*), therefore those with abundant defilements should be understood as "those with much dust in their eyes" (*mahārajakkhā*). Because they are capable of destroying opposing factors, they are sharp, keen, and clear;
by way of the opposite of what was stated, they are dull. "Modes such as faith" refers to the various aspects of believing and so forth. "Beautiful" means...
“Excellent. In the *Sammohavinodanī*, however, it is stated: “Those for whom the factors such as disposition (*āsaya*) and so forth are beautiful are ‘of good character’ (*svākāra*);
this should be understood as being entirely consistent with and in agreement with the present commentary on the meaning.
For, by way of the perfection of faith and so forth, there is beauty of disposition, and by its opposite, there is ugliness. This is the reason.
The term "the other world" (*paraloka*) refers either to the modes of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) or to the Truths (*sacca*).
It is said that "one views both the other world and fault as fear" because that [other world] brings about suffering and must be viewed with fear like a fault (*vajja*).
Alternatively, the state of misfortune (*vipattibhava*) is called "the other world" because it is distinct from the state of success (*sampattibhava*); thus it is said, "viewing the other world...".

“This, however, is the text here” means that this is the scriptural passage establishing the nature of those [terms] such as “those with little dust in their eyes” (*apparajakkhā*) when explaining their meaning.
For the strength of the qualities that ripen liberation—such as faith and the rest—occurs precisely through the weakness of the unwholesome states that are their opposites;
and the strength of those [unwholesome states] occurs through the weakness of faith and the rest. Thus, regarding the qualities that ripen liberation...

In detail, according to the distinction between those who possess [the faculties] and those who do not, such types as "those with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkha*) and "those with much dust in their eyes" (*mahārajakkha*) are shown in the Pāḷi after being analyzed.

Thus, there are five types of those with little dust in their eyes by way of faith (*saddhā*) and so forth, and five types of those with much dust in their eyes by way of lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) and so forth.

In this way, fifty individuals have been elucidated, including those with sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*), those with dull faculties (*mudindriya*), and others. Furthermore, through internal subdivisions of faith and the rest—
These should be understood as having many divisions. The aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth are themselves the "world" (*loka*) in the sense of breaking apart and disintegrating.

The world consisting of the state of success (*sampattibhava*) is the "world of success"; this refers to the state of rebirth known as a happy destination (*sugati*). That by which success comes into being is the "world of the origin of success," namely, the kamma-process existence that leads to a happy destination.
The state of rebirth known as a miserable destination (*duggati*) and the kamma-process existence that leads to a miserable destination are likewise [the world of the origin of failure].
The worlds of misfortune and the worlds arising from misfortune.
Furthermore, having analyzed and shown the world by way of single and dual categories and so forth, it is said: "One world," and so on.
For nutriment and the rest are called "world" (loka) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. In that context, regarding the statement: "One world: all beings subsist on nutriment"—this...
In this discourse, which is addressed to persons (puggalādhiṭṭhānā), it is stated that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) exist in dependence upon conditions.

By this, the entire world of formations is said to be one and of a single kind, because there is no other mode of existence. The meaning should be understood in this same manner even in such passages as "two worlds" and so forth.
Furthermore, in this context, Nibbāna is not included by the mention of "names" (nāma), because its intrinsic nature is not that of the world (aloka).
But would it not follow that even the paths and fruits are worldly (*loka*) because they exist in dependence on conditions, as in the phrase "subsisting by nutriment"?
It does not follow, because here the term "world" is intended to refer to those phenomena belonging to the truth of suffering which are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
Alternatively, that which is defined as "not crumbling, not disintegrating"—that which does not become otherwise—is the world; [the paths and fruits] are excluded from that definition.
For supramundane states, there is no "worldliness. The aggregates that have become objects of clinging are the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*).

The eight worldly conditions, such as gain and so forth, are the basis for attachment and other such defilements. Regarding "the ten bases," this refers to the ten sense-bases of form, because the intention here is directed toward the meditative absorption of turning away (*vivaṭṭajjhāsaya*).
And for such a person, all karma of the three planes appears as something to be censured and to be abandoned; thus it is said.
“All volitional formations are blameworthy; all kamma leading to existence is blameworthy.

Those individuals whose faith and other faculties are dull are described here by such terms as “lacking faith” and so forth. This does not mean, however, that they are entirely devoid of faith and the rest;
rather, in each of the five dyads beginning with the “Dustless Dyad,” ten factors are taken from each, thus making fifty aspects.

It is said: "He knows these five faculties. Alternatively, it is stated thus because he knows the relative degrees of the faculties—faith and the rest—by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*).
Furthermore, when the Blessed One adverts [to beings] by way of those with little dust in their eyes and so forth, those beings appear to him as clusters of individuals, not as single units.

"Uppalinī" means "that in which there are blue lotuses (*uppala*)," referring either to a grove or a body of water; however, since it is a body of water that is intended here, he says "in a blue-lotus grove.
Those which grow and flourish while remaining submerged within the water are "those nourished while submerged" (*antonimuggaposīnī*).
They are "illustrated" (*dīpitāni*) in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, or else right here by the words "and others as well," and so forth.

They have been illuminated. "One who understands through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*): "condensed statement" (*ugghaṭana*) means the condensing of knowledge; the meaning is that one knows as soon as [the matter] is condensed within knowledge.

"One who understands through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*): one who knows the meaning through such an elaboration and expansion. "One who is led" (*neyyo*): one who is to be guided by means of summaries and so forth.

"Simultaneously with the time of being uttered" (*saha udāhaṭavelāya*): at the very moment the Dhamma is uttered, at the summary of the Dhamma, as soon as it has been spoken. "The penetration of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhisamayo*).
“Realization together with knowledge of the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Regarding the phrase “this one is called”:

when the summary matrix (mātikā) is being shown by way of the method beginning with “the four foundations of mindfulness,” one who is capable of attaining Arahatship by directing knowledge according to the teaching is called a “person who understands through a condensed statement” (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
Regarding the phrase “this one is called”: this [refers to] the matrix in brief...
Setting aside the detailed exposition, when the meaning is analyzed, one capable of attaining *arahatta* is called a "person who understands through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*).
"From the perspective of recitation" means by way of recitation; the sense is: for one who is being recited to, or for one who is causing [another] to be recited to.
"From questioning" means for one who is questioning the meaning. "The realization of the Dhamma occurs in successive order" means that one attains *arahatta* step by step.

There is no realization of the Dhamma through that birth; thus, by means of that personal existence (attabhāva), one is unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit, or at least meditative absorption (jhāna) or insight (vipassanā).
This person is called "one for whom the word is the limit" (padaparamo); this person is so called because the mere word or syllable is his highest attainment.
However, this was said in the *Vibhaṅga* with reference to two kinds of persons: "by the obstruction of kamma" refers to the fivefold kamma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*).

"By the obstruction of result" refers to rebirth without roots (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*). Since even those with two roots lack penetration of the Noble Path, rebirth with two roots should also be understood as "an obstruction of result.
"By the obstruction of defilement" refers to fixed wrong view (*niyata-micchā-diṭṭhi*).
"Lacking faith" (*assaddhā*) means devoid of faith toward the Buddha and the others. "Lacking desire" (*acchandikā*) means devoid of the wholesome desire for the wish to act;

this refers to those who have entered the state of being "lacking desire," such as the humans of Uttarakuru. "Lacking wisdom" (*duppaññā*) means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*);
however, even for one whose life-continuum wisdom is complete, if that life-continuum does not serve as a condition for the supramundane (*lokuttara*), [they are likewise considered lacking].

He too is indeed called one of little wisdom. "Incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states" means they are incapable of entering—that is, of attaining—the Noble Path, which is designated as the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
The phrases beginning with "not by obstruction of karma" are to be understood as the opposite of what was stated previously.

Regarding what should be said concerning the passage beginning with “*rāgacaritā*,” it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*: “Because it is the repository of ultimate meanings (*paramatthānaṃ*) in their respective places as appropriate, it is by name called the ‘Casket of Ultimate Meanings’ (*Paramatthamañjūsā*).
(This is because it was stated by the author himself in the conclusion of the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*. It is to be known according to the manner set forth in that commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
70. *Ārabbhā* means "having undertaken" or "with reference to," in the sense of making known to the Blessed One the meaning intended by oneself. *Uddissa* has the same meaning.
He said, "as on the summit of a rocky mountain," because a rock mountain (*selo pabbato*) is high and firm, unlike a mountain of sand or a mixed mountain.
By "the palace made of Dhamma," he refers to the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*), for that indeed resembles a mountain.
And it is like a palace in the sense of having risen above all phenomena by way of its loftiness; or, here the word *dhamma* refers to wisdom (*paññā*).
For that [wisdom] is defined in the Abhidhamma as a "palace" in the sense of being elevated. And thus it is said:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the sorrowless one looks down upon the sorrowing folk."
“As one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground, so does the wise man look upon fools.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Just as,” it is like a man who, standing on a mountain at night in the darkness, looks down below;
for him, the field boundaries, the small huts in the fields, and the people sleeping there are not perceived because they lack brightness. Within the huts—
However, because of its very nature of blazing, a mass of fire is visible;

likewise, for the Blessed One who has ascended the palace of the Dhamma and is surveying the world of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of his knowledge, because they lack the brilliance of the fire of knowledge and because of their lack of excellence, appearing like arrows shot into the night. But those fortunate individuals who have performed wholesome deeds remain far away [from such darkness].

The construction should be understood as follows: even though they remain [distant], they come within the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge because of its blazing state through the fire of mature wisdom, and because of the loftiness of his mental continuum, like the Himavat mountain.
"Arise" means: arise from the state of weariness resulting from the contraction known as indolence regarding the teaching of the Dhamma.
"By virtue of being possessed of energy" means by virtue of possessing the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna) in an eminent degree.

For "energy" (vīriya) is either the state or the action of one who is heroic (vīra). The phrase "the Māras of death and defilement" is used because, like the Māra of defilements, the Māra of death will no longer exist in the future.
The reason the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāramāra) is not mentioned is that its conquest is already implied by the conquest of the Māra of defilements.
“By the capacity for conveyance” means by the capacity for bringing one across the great wilderness of *saṃsāra* to the secure region known as *nibbāna*. 71.
Some read: “The door to the Deathless has been flung open for them.

This is because the door to *nibbāna*—the path of entry—has been set open and established through the self-arisen knowledge attained by means of the necessary condition of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). “Let them release their faith.”
"Let them proclaim their faith" means: let them manifest the manner of their own conviction. "Well-functioning" means:
because it can proceed with ease and without difficulty. He thought: "I have not spoken [of this], nor shall I speak.
—The Description of the Pair of Chief Disciples.

73. "Having conversed" means having engaged in talk and conversation such as, "Friend, your faculties are serene," and so forth. This became the condition for his approaching the presence of the Teacher at a later time.
75–6. "Graduated discourse" means the discourse that ought to be spoken in a gradual sequence. What is that? It is the discourse on giving and the rest.

Among these, first, the discourse on giving is [taught] because it is common to all people, being prevalent among ordinary folk, and because it is easy to practice; [it serves as a basis] for establishing oneself in virtue (*sīla*).

And they were taught first as being the means [to the subsequent ones]. For a person whose nature is generosity, because of their state of non-attachment toward objects of possession, easily undertakes the precepts and becomes well-established in them.
Having spoken of benefiting others through the purification of both giver and recipient by means of virtue, there follows the statement regarding the cessation of harming others;
having spoken of the phenomenon of action (*kiriyadhamma*), there follows the statement regarding the phenomenon of non-action (*akiriyadhamma*).

Having explained the cause for the attainment of enjoyments, the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā) was spoken immediately after the discourse on giving (dānakathā) in order to explain the cause for the attainment of existence (bhava).
This is for the purpose of showing that if that giving and virtue are dependent upon the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), this attainment of existence is their fruit.

And by means of these bases of meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue—which are distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior—one [is reborn] among the Cātumahārājika devas and so forth.

After explaining the discourse on heaven (*saggakathā*) immediately following that [discourse on generosity], for the purpose of showing that there are immeasurable attainments of divine enjoyments and existence, distinguished by various grades such as superior and more superior;

and then, for the purpose of showing that this heaven is defiled by lust and the other [defilements], whereas the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is forever undefiled, the discourse on the Path (*maggakathā*) should be delivered after the discourse on heaven. And while delivering the discourse on the Path...

In order to show the means for attaining that [Nibbāna], it is stated that all sensual pleasures—even those included within the heavenly realms, let alone others—are fraught with many dangers, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change;
such is the danger (*ādīnava*) of sensual pleasures. Furthermore, they are base, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
such is their degradation and worthlessness (*okāra*). Moreover, all states of existence (*bhava*) serve as the basis for the defilements (*kilesa*); thus, regarding these...
The defilement [of the world] and Nibbāna, which is entirely free from defilement—thus the benefit of renunciation should also be explained.
This meaning should be understood as being indicated here by the word *iti*, which signifies "and so forth," in the phrase "seeking this.
"The source of happiness" refers to [happiness] pertaining to the present life, to the future life, and to that connected with Nibbāna.
It is the cause of all happiness. For whatever is called the happiness of wealth in the world, it is evident that all of that has giving as its source.

Furthermore, even for that happiness associated with meditative absorption (*jhāna*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), the fruit (*phala*), and Nibbāna, giving is indeed a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
It is the root of all attainments—those such as regional sovereignty in this world...
Human success (*mānusikā sampatti*) is of such divisions as the sovereignty of a glorious universal monarch (*cakravartin*), resplendent with the seven treasures;
celestial success (*dibbasampatti*) includes the realms of the Four Great Kings and others; and there are also other kinds of success.

Of all these, this thing called giving (*dāna*) is the root and the cause. Regarding the word "possessions" (*bhogānaṃ*): it is called "possession" (*bhoga*) in the sense of being something to be enjoyed.
It is the refuge in the sense of being a support for those things acquired by name—such as pleasing forms and so forth—and for the pleasures of enjoyment that depend upon them.
"For one who has gone astray" means for one who has fallen into misfortune. "Shelter" (tāṇa) means protection, because of guarding one from that [misfortune].
"Lodge" (leṇa) means a place of retreat for one who is being overwhelmed by misfortunes. "Destination" (gati) means a place to be reached. "Ultimate resort" (parāyaṇa) means a refuge.
"Support" (*avassaya*) means a support that prevents one from falling into ruin. "Object" (*ārammaṇa*) means an object that is clung to.
It is "like a lion-throne made of jewels" because, being like a great seven-limbed lion-throne made of all kinds of jewels, it is of great value and prevents one from falling into ruin in every way.
It is "like the great earth" because it remains stable in whatever place one goes.

Because it causes [beings] to obtain [benefits]. "Like a supporting rope for an object" means that just as a supporting rope is a prop for a weak man when he is rising up or standing still, so too is giving a condition for the arising and the persistence of beings in a state of prosperity.
"In the sense of crossing over suffering" means in the sense of crossing over the suffering of the miserable destinies (*duggati*). "In the sense of providing consolation" means...
In the sense of providing proper consolation from the danger posed by enemies such as greed and stinginess.

"In the sense of protection from fear" means in the sense of guarding against the fear of poverty. "By the stains of stinginess, etc. means by the mental stains such as stinginess, greed, hatred, envy, doubt, and wrong views.
"In the sense of being unsullied" means by way of being undefiled. "Of these" refers to the refuse of the stains of stinginess and so forth.
By these very [qualities], in the sense of being difficult to assail. "In the sense of not causing fear" means by way of being unconquerable and the absence of terror.
For a donor, a master of giving, does not fear anyone even in the present, much less in the future.

By means of the term "Dhamma," the person is spoken of. "In the sense of being powerful" means by way of great strength. For a donor, a master of giving, possesses power through his own faction in the present...
It is powerful, both now and in the future through bodily strength and so forth.

"In the sense of being regarded as a supreme auspicious sign" means by way of its being universally recognized as a cause of prosperity. The sense of "reaching the ground of security" consists in leading one from an existence of misfortune to an existence of success, and in bringing about the security from bondage (yogakkhema) by reaching the ground of security.

Now, in order to show the qualities of giving by way of its nature as the practice for enlightenment—that giving accomplishes not only the perfections pertaining to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭagata*) that have reached their highest excellence, but also those pertaining to the transcendence of the cycle (*vivaṭṭagata*)—the passage beginning with "For giving...

was stated. Therein, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are for one's own benefit alone, whereas the attainment of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) is both for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others; thus, it was said: "Of these... [to demonstrate this].

Those previously mentioned were mundane; however, in order to show that these are supramundane, the passage beginning with "the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection" (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) was stated thereafter.
Within that too, the threefold knowledge was taught in sequence to demonstrate the degrees of excellence—superior, more superior, and most superior.

Furthermore, the fact that generosity serves as a condition for these has already been explained below. By this very same principle, it should be understood that its status as a condition for the attainment of the Brahma-world is also illustrated.

What is called giving (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of one’s own possessions to those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), whether with the intention of their welfare or with the intention of honoring them;
therefore, a person who is a donor is an individual whose intention is solely for the welfare of beings.
Thus, it is said that it is impossible for such a person to "harm others" or "take what belongs to others," and so he says: "While giving a gift, one should undertake moral discipline (*sīla*)."
“There is no ornament equal to virtue,” because it is not artificial and brings about a distinction of beauty at all times.
“There is no flower like the flower of virtue”—the same principle applies here as well. Regarding “there is no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue,” there are verses such as:
“Sandalwood or tagara... [and] ‘The fragrance of the seers who have long been disciplined, from their bodies... [continues].
And such passages as, "Having passed away, one goes by means of the wind," should be cited.

For virtue is indeed the ornament, the decoration, and the fragrant unguent of beings, bringing about a state that is pleasing to others to behold. Therefore he said, "By the ornament of virtue," and so forth.
When it is said, "This heaven is obtained," this refers to virtue undertaken through medium levels of zeal and the other factors. Therefore Sakka, the king of the gods, said:
“By an inferior holy life one is reborn as a khattiya;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one becomes purified.
“Desirable” means pleasant; “lovely” means desirable; “agreeable” means increasing mental delight. Furthermore, its state of being desirable and so forth—
To demonstrate this, it was said: “Here, play is eternal,” and so forth. “Eternal” means that at all times there is play; these are pleasant abidings associated with sensual desire (*kāma*).
“Prosperities” refers to prosperities of wealth. “Divine” means belonging to divine existence, which is included within the heavenly worlds (*devaloka*).
“Happiness” refers to both bodily and mental happiness. “Divine prosperity” refers to divine existence, specifically the prosperity of longevity.

The excellence of wealth and sovereignty, as well as the excellence of physical form and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*evamādi*), he refers to the celestial prosperity to be experienced by the Yāma gods and others.
"Little gratification" (*appassāda*) means devoid of gratification, because there is an absence of anything to be relished therein by the wise who see things as they truly are.
"Great suffering" (*bahudukkha*) means great suffering in the present and a continuity of extensive suffering in the future. "Many perils" (*bahupāyāsa*) refers to manifold dangers.

"In this" (*ettha*) means among sensual pleasures. "More" (*bhiyyo*) means much. "Fault" (*dosa*) is the state of being corrupted by impermanence and so forth, and by having little gratification and so forth, because of which they do not please the minds of the wise.
Alternatively, it is called a "disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) because it proceeds as the foremost wretchedness.
And thus, sensual pleasures present themselves to those who contemplate them as they truly are.

"Baseness" means a state of inferiority, because they are to be cultivated by the lowly and not cultivated by the noble. "Corruption" means the state of being afflicted and the state of being tormented.
"The advantage in renunciation" refers here to the fact that whatever dangers there are in sensual pleasures, renunciation is their opposite.
Such are the benefits in renunciation. Furthermore, he proclaimed the benefits of renunciation in such a manner as: "This renunciation is unconfined and undefiled;

it has emerged from sensual desires, emerged from perceptions of sensuality, emerged from thoughts of sensuality, emerged from the fevers of sensuality, and emerged from ill will," and so forth, [extending] to the going-forth, the meditative absorptions (jhāna), and the rest.
And you have analyzed and praised its qualities.
Regarding the phrase "in the manner stated": here, as for the unstated method beginning with "with a ready mind" (*kallacitte*), "with a ready mind" means with a mind that is pliant (*kammaniya*).

This is because, due to the removal of mental defects such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) through the teaching that proceeded previously, [the mind] has become a fit vessel for the subsequent teaching.
The meaning is "a mind capable of action. Since lack of faith and other such states are like diseases of the mind, and since those have now departed, the meaning is "a healthy mind.
It is a "supple mind" through the departure of defilements such as wrong view and conceit. It is a "mind free from hindrances" through the departure of sensual desire and the rest.
It is an "exultant mind" through its association with sublime rapture and gladness in right practice. In that regard, by the perfection of faith...
"In one with a serene mind": the connection is "when the Blessed One knew. Alternatively, "with a ready mind" means a mind free from disease through the departure of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
"With a malleable mind" means a mind that is not rigid due to loving-kindness (*mettā*), through the departure of ill-will (*byāpāda*).

"With a mind free from hindrances" means a mind that is not obstructed because distraction has departed through the departure of restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*). "With an uplifted mind" means [a mind] through the departure of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

"In a mind that is not dejected" means by way of being uplifted; "with a confident mind" means with a mind resolved upon right practice through the removal of doubt—thus should the meaning here be understood.
With the words "Just as if," etc., he shows, by means of a simile, their abandonment of defilement and the arising of the Noble Path.
"Free from blackness" (*apagatakāḷaka*) means devoid of blackness. "Properly indeed" (*sammadeva*) means well indeed. "Dye" (*rajana*) refers to the various colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
"Would take up" (*paṭiggaṇheyya*) means it would take them up and become bright. "In that very seat" (*tasmiṃyeva āsane*) means in that very sitting;

by this, their state of being quick in insight (*lahuvipassaka*), their possession of sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññatā*), and their state of having a pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge (*sukhapaṭipadā-khippābhiññatā*) are demonstrated.
It exists. It is "dustless" (*viraja*) because of the disappearance of the dust of passion (*rāga*) and other defilements that lead to rebirth in the woeful states.

It is "stainless" (*vītamala*) because of the removal of the stains of views and doubt without remainder; or alternatively, it is "dustless" due to the absence of the dust of defilements to be abandoned by the first path, and "stainless" due to the removal of the stains of the fivefold misconduct.
Regarding the term "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*), the three lower paths are mentioned in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*, while [the fourth] is mentioned in the *Cūḷarāhulovāda*.
The destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*); however, in this context, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is intended.

The statement, "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation," is a demonstration of the mode of its arising. But is it not the case that knowledge of the path has the unconditioned dhamma as its object, and not the conditioned dhamma?
This is true. However, because it takes cessation as its object, by way of its function...
It arises penetrating all that is conditioned; therefore it is so stated.
Regarding the illustrative simile "a clean cloth," this is the application of the simile: the mind is like the cloth;
the state of the cloth being defiled by adventitious stains is like the state of the mind being thoroughly defiled by the stains of lust and so forth.
The gradual discourse is like the washing stone; faith is like the water.

Just as the process of washing a cloth involves soaking it in water and then removing stains from dark spots by applying loads of ash, cow dung, and chaff, so too, having soaked the mind repeatedly with the moisture of faith, one relaxes the defilements through mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and exerts energy in purifying the mind according to the method of hearing and so forth.
By that application, just as the removal of various black stains from a cloth occurs, so too does the suppression of defilements through the exertion of energy;
the Noble Path is like the dye. Just as a clean cloth attains a state of brilliance, so too is there the purification by means of the Path of the mind whose defilements have been suppressed.
Having said "those who have seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammā*), [it follows that] "seeing" (*dassana*) refers to the vision of knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*).
To exclude others who might also have attained [merely], it is said "those who have attained the Dhamma" (*pattadhammā*).

Since there is also another kind of attainment distinct from the attainment of knowledge (*ñāṇasampatti*), it is said "those who have understood the Dhamma" (*viditadhammā*) in order to show the distinction from that.

However, since that state of having understood the Dhamma may exist even with respect to only a portion of the teachings, it is said "those who have thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma" (*pariyogāḷhadhammā*) to demonstrate the state of having understood them without exception.
By this it is shown that their realization of the Truths (saccābhisambodhi) alone is being elucidated.

For path-knowledge, by means of a single simultaneous comprehension (ekābhisamaya), accomplishes the functions of full understanding and so forth; it penetrates the phenomena of the Four Truths without exception, plunging into them from every side.
The rest is exactly as explained below.

77. "The giving of robes, etc. is said with reference to the giving of requisites such as robes. For whoever, having given the eight requisites beginning with robes—or even just the bowl and robe—to a noble one such as a stream-enterer, or even to an ordinary person endowed with virtue, makes the aspiration:
"May this gift of requisites be a condition for [my own] becoming an 'Come, monk' (ehibhikkhu) in the future," [attains that result].
And it should be understood that when there is fulfillment of the requisite conditions, this leads to the acquisition of supernormal-material requisites in the presence of the Buddhas;
the intention is that they are "endowed with proper deportment" like the Elder of a hundred years' standing.

"He showed clearly" means he demonstrated it by making it well evident before the eyes. "The welfare pertaining to this world" refers to the welfare consisting of this world, namely, the matter comprised of the five aggregates.

“Benefit for the other world”: here too the method is the same. “He showed” means he showed them according to their general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) and their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*).
Therefore he said, “impermanent,” and so forth. Therein, he showed them as impermanent because of their non-existence after having existed.

He showed them as suffering because of being oppressed by arising and passing away. He showed them as non-self because of the lack of mastery over them. These five aggregates have the characteristics of being afflicted (*ruppana*), and so on.

He showed that, in the sense of being a collection (*rāsa*), there are the aggregates (*khandha*). He showed that these, by way of their specific nature as the eye and so forth, and in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul, are the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
He showed that these very same things, which have the nature of the eye and so forth, when serving as doors and objects, are the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
He showed that these twelve causal phenomena, beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) and ending with aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), constitute dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
By way of condition, there are four [characteristics] according to the method explained below for the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and by way of moment, there is one;
thus he showed these five characteristics. By the word "tathā" (thus), he draws forward the phrase "five characteristics.
The word "iti" in "dassento" has the sense of illustration; the meaning is "in this way. "Niraya" refers to the division consisting of the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary (ussada) hells.

He showed the hell entirely. "The animal realm" (*tiracchānayoni*) refers to the various kinds of the animal world, divided into those without feet, with two feet, four feet, many feet, and so forth, including the distinctions of wild animals, beasts, birds, reptiles, and the like.

"The sphere of hungry ghosts" (*pettivisaya*) refers to the various kinds of the world of ghost-beings, distinguished by such types as those who suffer from hunger and thirst, those with sword-blades for mouths, those who live on what is given by others, those who burn with craving, and so forth.
"The host of asuras" (*asurakāya*) refers to the assembly of the *Kālakañjika* asuras. Thus, first, that which constitutes the states of miserable rebirth (*duggati*)—
