Having spoken of the welfare of the other world, he now says "the result of the three wholesome [karmas]" and so forth in order to speak of that which has become a happy destination (*sugati*).

Having included [the realms] of Vehapphala and Subhakiṇṇa within those very [heavens], he speaks specifically of "the nine Brahma-worlds" because there is no manifestation of attainment among the non-percipient beings (*asaññī*) and the formless beings (*arūpī*), and thus [those states] would be difficult to discern.
"Caused to take up" means he caused them to undertake those qualities.
"Encouragement" (samuttejana) means the production of enthusiasm in them so that those qualities already undertaken do not decline or disappear as non-beneficial factors might,
but rather so that beneficial factors increase and become purified.
He said, "He encouraged them. To show how that encouragement comes about, it was stated, "For the sake of the welfare of this world," and so forth.
"Having terrified them again and again" means having intimidated them by bringing their state into clear manifestation.
"Having made it as if already attained" means having made that matter as if it were being directly experienced by those to whom he speaks. For [the Buddha]... of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
When the meaning is being proclaimed by the Buddhas, it becomes even more manifest than if it were directly perceived before one’s eyes. For it is said in praise of the Blessed One:
“Though this world is ablaze with eleven fires, It does not experience such urgency When shrouded in delusion.”
"Having heard the words of the Great Sage as they are connected with the perception of danger, even though it is directly from the Buddhas, their word is very clear.
Therefore he said: "Indeed, consisting of the thirty-two grounds for legal action and the twenty-five great fears," and so forth. The thirty-two grounds for legal action (*kammakāraṇa*).
"They cut even the hand," and so forth, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Dukkha-khandha Sutta*.
The twenty-five great fears—beginning with "fear of birth, fear of aging, fear of illness, fear of death," and so forth—should be understood according to the method set forth in various suttas.
An executioner's block is a wooden post for striking, which is also called an *accādhāna*.
"He reproached him by means of the qualities he had attained" means that, pointing out directly through the acquisition of various specific qualities, "This too has been attained by you;
this too is a benefit," he spoke as if reproaching him by asking, "Was there anything like this before?
Therefore, it is said: "He spoke after having brought about great benefit."
"And weariness due to that" refers to the fatigue, distress, and vexation arising within the various continuums of sentient beings, caused by the occurrence of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"Here" refers to the preceding discourse for the sake of attaining the first path. It is "peaceful" because of the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena.
It is "sublime" because it is the supreme bliss that brings no satiety. It is a "refuge" in the sense of protecting from all the calamities of *saṃsāra*.

Because it is a place where those whose hearts are weary of the world may take refuge, it is called a "sanctuary" (*leṇa*). By the word "etcetera," there is an inclusion of such terms as "the destination," "the resort," and "the supreme consolation.
80. Regarding the description of the great multitude going forth:
it is said, "because the Saṅgha was incomplete," because there were no monks sufficient to constitute a formal Saṅgha. At that time, there were only the two Chief Disciples.
Commentary on the Allowance for Wandering (Cārikā-anujānanavaṇṇanā):
Regarding the question, "When did it arise?", the answer is given briefly as "From the time of his full enlightenment" (*sambodhito*) and so forth;

then, in order to demonstrate that same matter in detail, the passage beginning with "The Blessed One, it is said... (*bhagavā kirā*) was spoken. While providing support for his father, he dwelt [there] from the time of his full enlightenment.
The connection is made by bringing forward the phrase “seven years, seven months, and seven days,” yet this was because there were no disciples to be converted at that time.

Having had it roofed over with palm-leaf mats on the outside, lined with cloth on the inside, and covered above with cloth, he had a golden canopy... [etc. ...made beneath it. “With garlands” means with flower garlands.
“Wrapped in the shape of a calf. “In the midst of perfumes” means in the middle of a vessel filled with fragrances.
“Flowers” refers both to water-born flowers such as those in a vessel and to land-born flowers such as *caṅkotaka* and others.

Granted that this king was the father of the Buddha, nevertheless, the Buddhas are honored by the world; they cannot be brought under the control of anyone else, but rather they bring others under their own control. Therefore, the king said, “I do not give the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.”

“Door of giving” (*dānamukha*) means the means for performing a gift; the meaning is “the practice of giving. “Now it is not permitted for me” means that now my gift is not permitted, nor is it the case that they do not permit it.
“A life of agitation” means a miserable livelihood, that is, poverty.
“You have the power for all the bhikkhus” refers to the portion for the Blessed One and the six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.
He was able to give, but not because he possessed everything. Therefore it is said: "The general also gave his own gifts.
At the place of the senior queen means at the station of the senior queen.
Having done so likewise means having stationed secret agents. *Sucim* means pure. *Paṇītam* means sublime; this is a neuter noun used adverbially.
As in the case of [the expressions] "to one side" (*ekamanta*) and so forth. "Having broken" (*bhañjitvā*) means having crushed; the meaning is "having pressed.

"Only with the ghee, milk, and so forth produced therein" (*jātisappikhīrādīhiyeva*) means only with the ghee, milk, and so forth produced within [the cow], that is, only with the ghee and so forth taken from our own cows and such; this is the meaning. 90.
One who forgives, endures, and patiently accepts the censure of others, the injury done by others, and the defects of qualities such as cold, heat, and so forth—[he is called a *khantivādin*].
Patience (*khanti*). Because it especially heats, burns, and dispels the states that are the opposites of virtue (*sīla*) and the other perfections, it is the supreme, highest austerity (*tapo*).
Therefore he said: "The patience of endurance is indeed the supreme austerity.

By the term "the patience of endurance," he distinguishes it from the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*). Enduring, bearing with, is "endurance" (*titikkhā*).—Thus say the etymologists.
For they describe the word *titikkhā* (forbearance) as synonymous with *khama* (patience). Therefore he said, "It is a synonym for patience," and so forth.

"In every way" means in all its aspects, such as being peaceful, sublime, subtle, auspicious, secure, and so on. He is not called a "renunciant" (*pabbajita*) because he has not renounced that which ought to be renounced.
This is a synonym for that very third term, as there is no difference in meaning.

He explains that same point with the words beginning “No indeed. It is called *parama* in the sense of being supreme (*uttama*), because the word *para* denotes excellence, as in such phrases as “one who knows the higher and lower persons” (*puggalaparoparaññū*).

*Para* means "other. Now, taking the word *para* specifically in the sense of "other," he states “Alternatively,” etc., in order to show the meaning. *Malassa* means of the stain of evil (*pāpamala*).
"Because they have not been cast out" means because they have not been removed or rejected. "Because they have been stilled" means because those evil qualities have been ceased.
For it is said: "One is called a *samaṇa* (ascetic) because of the stilling of evils.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One recites the *Pātimokkha* for the monks, it is because the discourse on the *Pātimokkha* has virtue as its primary focus.
Since hatred is specifically the opposite of virtue (*sīla*), in order to show the method for its suppression, he said at the outset, "Patience is the supreme austerity.
By this, the means for warding off what is undesirable is stated; however, by the inclusion of the term "endurance" (*titikkhā*), the means for dealing with what is desirable is indicated.
Thus, by both together, the meaning is shown that one dwells having overcome the pleasure that arises [from either].
The Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is supreme because it is the complete pacification of craving.
In this context, by the mention of "patience" (khanti), the absence of failure in application is shown; by the mention of "forbearance" (titikkhā), the absence of failure in disposition is shown.
Likewise, by the mention of patience, the endurance of others' offenses is shown; by the mention of forbearance, the non-offending toward others is shown. Thus, by way of the cause—
Having shown the Pātimokkha by way of positive concomitance (anvaya), it is now stated with the words “Not indeed,” etc., in order to show it by way of negative exclusion (vyatireka).
By this it is meant that just as the taking of the lives of beings and the harming of them with hands, clods, sticks, and so forth,
is called “injuring others” and “afflicting others,” so too is the seizing of their primary property, the violating of their wives, and the act of deceiving [them].
It shows that by performing any unwholesome course of action or deed— whether it be mutual dissension, striking at the vital points with harsh speech,
idle chatter, coveting what belongs to others, finding fault through nihilism, or wrong adherence—
one causes injury and harassment, and thus one is neither a renunciant nor a recluse.
“Of all that is unwholesome” (sabbākusalassa) means of every blameworthy state (sāvajjadhamma) comprised within the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.
“Doing” (karaṇa) refers to its production within one’s own continuum; therefore, by way of its negation, “non-doing” (akaraṇa) is said to be “non-production” (anuppādana).
As for the phrase “of the wholesome” (kusalassa), since it will later be stated that “this is the teaching of the Buddhas,” it refers here to the states of the Noble Path (ariyamagga-dhamma).
And because it awakens those wholesome states belonging to the three planes which serve as the equipment for them, he says, "of the wholesome [states] of the four planes.
"Attainment" (upasampadā) means the act of attaining; since that is its acquisition, he says, "acquisition" (paṭilābha).
"Illumination of the mind" means making the mind luminous, its complete purification. Because the mind of one who possesses the supreme path—
It is said to be "completely purified" (*pariyodapīyati*); however, at the moment of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*), it is already "purified" because there is no further need for purification.
Thus, with reference to this state where purification is finalized, he says: "That, moreover, occurs through Arahatship.

The intention is that all evil is abandoned precisely by means of the "abandonment through substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-pahāna*) and so forth. For by the phrase "by restraint of virtue" (*sīlasaṃvarena*), even that which belongs to the three planes...
"In the inclusion, there is also the inclusion of the abandoning of the others"; by doing so, the inclusion of "all" is justified.
"By means of serenity and insight" refers to mundane and supramundane serenity and insight. "Having accomplished" means having brought to completion.
And here, the accomplishment [of the fruit] should be understood as being achieved by means of the causes—whether they are co-nascent or, even more so, already established beforehand.
"Of anyone" (*kassaci*) means of any being among those who are inferior and so forth, or of any slander;
by this, he rejects even slander uttered out of a desire for sport. "Not causing injury" (*upaghātassa akaraṇaṃ*): here too, the connection is made by bringing in the word "of anyone.
And "by body" (*kāyena*) is merely an illustration, for [injury] may also be caused by mind through such means as thinking of harm toward others.

Because it is to be avoided. Or rather, in this context, the term "body" (*kāya*) should be understood as including even the immaterial body (*arūpakāya*), and not merely the physical body and the mental body. Regarding *pātimokkha*:
it is that which is preeminent (*pati*) among the virtues (*sīla*) in the sense of being foremost (*mukhya*). He states the same word as *atipamokkha* by means of a variation in prefixes.
Having thus provided an analysis of the words according to their divisions, he speaks of its true nature as "supreme virtue" (*uttama-sīla*).

By the phrase beginning with “*Pāti vā*,” it shows that it is called *pātimokkha* because of protecting (*pālanato*), guarding (*rakkhaṇato*), being an excellent liberation (*ativiya mokkhanato*), and being an excellent means of liberation (*ativiya mocanato*).
Alternatively, it is called *atimokkha* because it “liberates [one] from evils (*pāpā*)”; this is to be understood through the metaphorical attribution of agency to the instrument.
Or else, “he who protects” refers to the person who, having undertaken that *pātimokkha-saṃvara-śīla*, maintains it without violating it.
It protects; it liberates one who stands firm in the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha—which has received the name "Pāti"—therefore it is called *pātimokkha*.
This is the summary here; however, the detailed meaning of the term *pātimokkha* should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Knowing the proper measure” (*mattaññutā*) refers to knowing the measure regarding food; however, that should be understood specifically by way of the virtue dependent on the requisites.

Thus he said: “Knowing the measure by way of receiving and consuming. Even if it were understood by way of the virtue of purity of livelihood, it could also be stated as “by way of seeking and relinquishing. “Free from jostling” means free from the jostling of crowds of people.

“Secluded” means free from the bustle of people. Contentment with the four requisites is illustrated by the general term “contentment with requisites,” because the other two [types of contentment] are also manifested through the method of characteristic extraction (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*).

By the phrase “for the sake of mastery over the eight attainments,” the purpose for which the resorting to a secluded dwelling is desired is shown; that is, the application to higher consciousness (*adhicittānuyoga*).
It has been said. Here, the eight attainments intended are those that serve as the foundation for insight (vipassanā), not just any [attainments];
thus, it should be understood that the entire application to higher consciousness (adhicittānuyoga) is illuminated.
The Exposition of the Declaration to the Devas.
91. *Ettāvatā* means "by this much" of the Sutta passage. Furthermore, the construction is: "and there too, having manifested the state of being well-penetrated by this...
discourse. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of contrast (*byatireka*); by it, he sets aside the meaning that is about to be stated.
*Ekamidāham* means "one day I. The word *idaṃ* is a mere particle. By the word *ādi* ("etcetera"), [the phrase] "O monks, at one time" is included.
Readings such as these are included. Regarding the phrase, "At one time, monks," the construction of the words is as follows:
"Subhagavana" means "fortunate" because of its fortune; the meaning is that it possesses beautiful glory (*sundara-sirika*) or beautiful desire (*sundara-kāma*).
For it is fortunate by virtue of its attainment of glory, and therein people long for beautiful desires. It is also [called so] because it is dear to many people.
*Subhagaṃ*: It is called *vana* because it causes one to desire (*vanayati*); the meaning is that through its own excellence, it produces affection within oneself.
Or, it is called *vana* because it desires (*vanute*); the meaning is that through its own excellence, it is as if it entreats beings, saying, "Enjoy me.
That which is both fortunate (*subhaga*) and a forest (*vana*) is *subhagavana*; [it means] "in that Subhagavana. Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, what...?
“By this elaboration,” it is said, “in a forest of such a name.

Granted that even a *sāla* tree is called “*sāla*”—whether it be any kind of tree or the lord of the forest (*vanappati*)—here, however, the latter alone is intended; thus he says, “at the foot of the lord of the forest.
“By way of uprooting the root” means by way of completely cutting off the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
“They do not depart” means they do not abandon [their state] due to their unshakable nature.
The statement, “They do not torment any being, thus they are ‘Atappa’ (Untormenting),” is said because that designation has become established among them;

otherwise, all the Suddhāvāsa deities would also be called “Atappa,” as they too do not torment any being. The same principle applies to the etymological explanations beginning with “they do not depart.”
"Sundaradassanā" means "beautiful to behold"; this is the meaning he expressed with the words "abhirūpā" and so forth. "Sundaram etesaṃ dassanaṃ" means their seeing is beautiful;
that is, their seeing by the eye is lovely, as is their seeing by consciousness—this is the meaning. "All indeed... [etc.
...are the eldest in the five-aggregate existence because there are none more distinguished than them.
“By way of seven Buddhas” means by way of the legends (apadāna) of the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Because it was requested by the Aviha deities, it was spoken by one Aviha Brahmā; since it was spoken by all of them, it is said, “likewise by the Avihas.
This same method applies to the others as well. Therefore the Blessed One said, “The deities spoke this to me. As for that which is in the Pāḷi: “Many...”
It was said, "the deities were satisfied"; all of that was spoken with reference to those who later attained distinction within his own teaching and arose therein.

"The two connections" refers to the two kinds of connection: the connection of the words on the element of Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*) and the connection of the words announcing [it to] the deities. "Concluding" means bringing to a close. Furthermore, whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta.
2. The Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta:
The Exposition of the Introduction.
95. "Janapadin" means those who possess a country (*janapada*), or the princes who are the lords and masters of a country;
by way of their clan, they are called the Kurus. If their residence is a single country, how is there a plural form? He says: "By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi-sadda*).
For grammarians desire such genders and numbers in such instances as if they were appropriate. This is the point here.
The conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) is seen elsewhere as well, such as "he dwells among the Aṅgas" and "he dwells among the Mallans.

Even when referring to the specific [plural] names of those countries or the generic term for the people, the singular number alone is used. Now, regarding the phrase "but the teachers of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*)," the word *pana* indicates a distinction;
by it, the distinction that will be stated later—beginning with "but in many cases"—is shown, namely: "this plural form is used because its scope consists of various meanings (*puthuattha*)."
"He illuminates. "Having heard" means having heard the traditional account handed down in succession, following the demonstration of the majesty of the Great King Mandhātu.
"Wandering along" means traveling through. "The place of these" refers to the realm of the Four Great Kings, beginning with the moon and the sun.
Therefore he said, "He went there," and so forth. "He" refers to the Great King Mandhātu. "That" refers to the sovereignty over the realm of the Four Great Kings.
“Having taken” means having accepted. He questioned the Counsellor-treasure again.
They stood on the ground of the gatekeepers because they had attained the protection of the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods and of the four gates of the city of the gods.
The phrase “adorned with a thousand celestial trees” should also be applied to the passages beginning with “the Cittalatā grove.”
"Having said, 'It has settled upon the earth,' it stood in a place near the ground. For the Wheel-Treasure does not actually fall to the earth;
and having stood there, it soon vanished because [the king] lacked the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch in that particular existence.
Others say, "It remained for a longer period of time. The king went alone by his own power.
“Human state” (*manussabhāva*) refers to the human condition, such as the human scent, physical form, and other natural manifestations.

“Appeared” (*pāturahosi*) means that because he had created the opportunity for karma to be experienced in a subsequent life—which yields its result through the process of rebirth within the world of the gods—the divine nature, characterized by always appearing sixteen years old and the fading of his garlands, manifested.
At that time, because humans possessed an incalculable lifespan, [the Buddha] ruled with the Sakka-kingship. “What... [text continues].
“With this half-kingdom for me,” he said, yet he remained unsatisfied due to his lack of contentment.
In the human world, his body, struck by the harshness of the season and by wind and heat, passed away.
Since a distinction established in the individual parts serves as the qualifier for the whole, even a single kingdom is expressed using the plural number.
They explain the meaning by means of the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) through the letter *da*.

"Kammāsa" refers to Kammāsapāda by the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*) is called simply "form" (*rūpa*). But how is he called "Kammāsapāda"? To this he says:
"It is said that of him... and so forth. Regarding the word "tamed" (*damita*), what kind of taming is intended here? He says: "He was restrained from the state of being a man-eater."
"However, some say that 'these elders' refers to the Majjhima-bhāṇakas; others, on the other hand, say they are the Aṭṭhakathācariyas or the Dīgha-bhāṇakas.
In both cases, they speak thus with reference to Cūḷakammāsadamma. For Kammāsapāda, the son of a yakkhinī, was tamed there by the Bodhisatta during his time as Prince Alīnasattu.
But during the time of Sutasoma, he was the King of Bārāṇasī, who, by preventing [the king] from becoming a man-eater..."
Where he was tamed, that place is named Mahākammāsadamma. Having said "son," the word "kinsman" (atraja) is used for the purpose of showing his status as a legitimate son from the breast.
Those people by whom the region where they dwelt received the name "Kuru-raṭṭha" were men who had come from Uttarakuru;
there, they observed the five precepts according to the very system they had protected [there]. Following their example, the later generation did likewise.
Thus, proceeding without interruption by way of the laws of the country, it was known as the "customary law of the Kurus" (*kuruvattadhamma*).
And this matter can be illustrated by the *Kuru-dhamma-jātaka*.
Later on, in order to show where he was first born defiled, the words beginning with "of the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru" were spoken. [The place] where [the Blessed One] resided—some...
Since there is no monastery [mentioned], the mere mention of the village of his alms-round is the natural way of introducing the narrative, as in the case of the Sakyas:
"He dwelt among the Sakyas at the town of the Sakyas named Devadaha. To show this meaning, he said, "from the place of residence," and so forth.
Furthermore, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*), "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānaṃ piyā*), or "Worthy One" (*tatra bhavaṃ*) are all terms of endearment; thus he said, "Venerable."
“This is a word of endearment. Since this word of endearment is spoken by way of profound respect, he said, “This is a word of reverence.
By excluding what is too far or too near, that which is called “neither too far nor too near” is included;
however, that should be understood at its minimum as the point where the hands of the two, when extended, touch one another. One must look with eye meeting eye.
By that too, a lack of respect is indeed shown. "Having turned his neck" means having extended his neck by way of turning it.

"For the sake of gathering families" means for the purpose of favoring families out of compassion for them, by generating a great influx of merit for them through the acceptance of alms, as if depositing a bundle of a thousand coins. "Having swept back" means...
The disciples, having thoroughly swept the place of sweeping with diligent care, swept it again.
"Three times" refers to three rounds accompanied by the four modes described as "starting from the beginning to the end," etc.; thus, he indicates that it was swept twelve times.
Because it was spoken by our Blessed One precisely because of its profound nature, it was spoken in the same way by the other Buddhas as well; this is the sequence of the Dhamma (*dhammanvaya*).

Having stood [there], it was said: “It was spoken by all the Buddhas... [etc. ...and declared. “With a terrace” means together with its surrounding platform (*paribhaṇḍa*). By the phrase “as if lifting up Mount Sineru,” he expresses the extreme difficulty of such a teaching.
He calls the sutta itself “the discourse on the sutta” because it constitutes a division of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).
Just as there is the discernment of the various grounds of the Vinaya-paññatti and of different times, [so too here].

This is the domain of omniscience alone, not shared by others. Thus, in order to show the analysis of the mode of conditions—which is free from the two extremes and devoid of an agent or an experiencer—the passage beginning with "For the Buddhas... is commenced.
In that context, "grounds" (*ṭhānāni*) means causes. "The thundering is great" is said because of the manifold nature of what is to be taught and because it is difficult to comprehend.
And the thundering roar of the teaching, proceeding by various methods, becomes great, vast, and manifold.
"It enters into knowledge" means that from that very [teaching], the knowledge of the teaching enters into each respective category of the phenomena to be taught as it analyzes them;
the meaning is that by entering thus, it is as if it stands [within them]. Thus, the greatness of the Buddha-knowledge is made manifest.
Thus, the sublime nature of the Buddhas’ knowledge of teaching and their knowledge of penetration becomes manifest in one who teaches such a Dhamma and one who has penetrated it.
And here, although it is said that "all verbal action of the Buddha, the Blessed One,
is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge," so that all the Blessed One’s teachings are not devoid of knowledge—
There is no uniformity of application everywhere due to the lion-like consistency of his conduct;
however, it should be understood that when applied by way of what is to be taught, the teaching becomes distinguished by knowledge and becomes even more profound.

But how is it that, upon reaching the formulation of the Vinaya, the teaching is struck by the three characteristics and becomes associated with emptiness? Even there, within the assembly seated together...

The teaching, proceeding in accordance with their inclinations, brings about the discernment of the impermanence and other characteristics of conditioned phenomena, as well as the illumination of the absence of selfhood and what belongs to a self in all phenomena.
For this very reason, it is said: "Having given a discourse on the Dhamma in many ways," and so forth.
*Āpajja* means having reached; that is, having attained [the state] in such a way that he emits the cry of the lion's roar of knowledge.

“Exceeding measure” (*pamāṇātikkama*) means in the sense of being immeasurable, as in such passages as “To this extent indeed by that Blessed One... and so forth. For this word *yāva* indicates an immeasurable state.
Therefore he said, “The meaning is exceedingly profound. “It shines forth” (*avabhāsati*) means it is known or appears.
For it is with reference to its appearing in such a way to knowledge that it is said, “it is seen. Is this not dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)?
Since it is exclusively profound, why is its "appearance as profound" (gambhīrāvabhāsatā) highlighted there? This is true;

however, the mention of its appearance as profound is solely for the purpose of demonstrating its absolute profundity. Therefore, having first pointed out—by way of contrast—the fourfold alternative (catukoṭika) found elsewhere, the passage beginning with "For one...
was stated in order to clarify its absolute profundity. [The phrase] "This does not exist" means:

There is no such pair as "not deep" and "appearing not deep"; therefore, he shows that among the four alternatives (catukoṭika) as they have been presented, only the last single alternative is applicable. Thus he says, "For this... and so forth.
Indicating by means of four similes those qualities of profundity by which dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is called "deep":
He said, “For the sake of grasping the peak of existence,” and so forth.

Just as it is impossible to grasp the peak of existence by stretching out one's hand because of its extreme distance, so too the meaning of the formations and other factors—arisen and brought about through conditions such as ignorance—cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge.
Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to split Mount Sineru and extract the marrow, the essence of the mountain...

It is not possible; it is not possible to know by breaking down and analytically penetrating the principles of phenomena and so forth contained within dependent origination through ordinary knowledge.

Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to hold up the great ocean with both arms, so too is it impossible to [grasp] dependent origination—which, in its vastness, is like the great ocean—by means of ordinary knowledge.
It is impossible to grasp [this] by means of mere exposition.

Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to grasp the potency of the earth after having turned over the great earth, so too it is impossible to extract and grasp the conditionality of those factors—namely, that "in this way ignorance and the rest are conditions for volitional formations and the rest"—by means of ordinary knowledge. Thus, by way of the fourfold profundity...

The four similes should be applied. This application of the meaning has been made by way of ordinary knowledge (*pākatika-ñāṇa*), because that is the nature of the penetration for those who have seen the Truths;

nevertheless, since the knowledge of disciples and paccekabuddhas regarding this matter is only partial, whereas for Buddhas alone it is complete, it is therefore said: "a question within the domain of the Buddhas," and so forth.

"Ussādeti" means uplifting by means of wisdom; the meaning is "causing them to grasp. "Apasādeti" means reproaching; the meaning is "restraining. Regarding the commentary on "ussādana": "By that" means by virtue of his great wisdom.
"Therein" refers to the Elder’s state of being clear [in understanding], yet [the fact] that dependent origination is [difficult for] others...
Regarding the state of profundity: "One nourished by the essence of excellent food" means one sustained by the taste of fine food.

"One who has performed the practice" means one who has cultivated familiarity through constant application. "A wrestler’s stone" refers to a stone that can only be lifted by wrestlers of great strength.
"Wherein lies its heavy point? means: on which side is this stone’s heaviest part? To him...
He speaks thus while demonstrating its state of lightness.
They illuminate it as if with a smoky-brown [light] because of its great expansiveness; therefore he says, "It is said of that," and so forth.
"It boils" means it turns over as if boiling, rolling about on all sides; for this is a description of its characteristic. On the back is the surface of the entire hoof-print.
“Of one reborn with a body” means being endowed with a great body; the meaning is “one of large body.
“A bundle of feathers” means a cluster of feathers. “The wind of the supaṇṇas” refers to the wind that arises from the flapping of wings during the seizing of nāgas and so forth.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Previous Adequate Support*

In order to explain in detail the causes enumerated by the phrase “by the fulfillment of prior strong support” (*pubbūpanissayasampatti*), the passage beginning with “It is said that from here” (*ito kira*) was spoken.
Therein, “from here” (*ito*) means from this *kappa*. “A hundred thousand” (*satasahassime*) means a hundred thousand [eons]. There was a city named Haṃsāvatī, which was his birthplace.
“Outer feathers” (*dhurapattāni*) refers to the outer feathers, which are the longest.
"Younger brother" (*kaniṭṭhabhātā*) refers to a half-brother who is younger, such as our Blessed One’s Elder Nanda. For Buddhas, there are no brothers born of the same womb.
How so? First, elder brothers do not arise [simultaneously]; furthermore, it is simply impossible for younger brothers to exist [at the same time].
"Wealth" (*bhoga*) means prosperity. "Tranquil" (*upasanta*) means a country that has become peaceful through the subsiding of disturbances caused by thieves.
"Having put on two sarongs" means having made only those two sarongs for the purpose of covering his body and having freed himself from all other belongings.
"For the purpose of holding the bowl" means for the purpose of holding the bowl while turning it back and forth in his hands because of the hot food placed inside.
"An upper sarong" means his own upper sarong. "These are public places" means these...
The places where the Elder performed meritorious deeds, as previously described, were well known through the Blessed One’s teaching.
"Having taken rebirth" means having taken rebirth on the very day our Great Bodhisatta took rebirth.
[End of] the commentary on the dwelling at the ford, etc.
"Grasping" is the grasping of the text. "Hearing" is hearing the meaning. "Interrogation" is the interrogation of the meaning at points where there are difficulties.
"Retention" is the fixing in the mind both of the text and of the meaning of the text. All this should be understood here by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
And for stream-enterers... [and so on]... by the destruction of delusion regarding what has been established, [one understands]: "Whatever is subject to arising..."
"all that is subject to cessation"—this is because it appears by way of one's own direct experience.
"Discernment of mind-and-body" (nāmarūpapariccheda) is the distinct comprehension of mind-and-body together with its conditions.
*Commentary on the Profundity of Dependent Origination* (Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratāvaṇṇanā)
The passage beginning with “By way of its profundity of meaning” and so forth was commenced with the words “Therein,” etc., in order to explain in detail the meaning stated briefly.

“The state of having arisen and come about through birth as a condition” means that, having arisen from the condition of birth, there is the state of successive occurrence (*uddham uddham āgatabhāvo*) of aging-and-death which is conjoined with it and conforms to its own conditions; the meaning is “the sense of continuous rolling on.”
Alternatively, the meaning of "arisen" (*sambhūta*) and the meaning of "come together" (*samudāgata*) constitute the meaning of "arisen and come together" (*sambhūtasamudāgata*).
For it is said that aging and death do not exist without birth, nor do they arise from anything else apart from birth; thus, the meaning of being "arisen through the condition of birth" is stated.

Furthermore, since it comes together (*samudāgacchati*) from birth in this way, the meaning of "come together through the condition of birth" applies to whatever birth serves as the respective condition.

The meaning is that there is the manifestation corresponding to that. It is "deep" in the sense of being unfathomable because knowledge does not find a footing therein for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
Regarding "the conditionality of volitional formations through ignorance": it refers to the manner and the state in which ignorance serves as the condition for volitional formations.
It exists. For ignorance is the condition for those various formations in whatever mode of occurrence and in whatever state it persists;
since both of these are difficult to comprehend, the meaning of ignorance as the condition for formations is [understood] through nine aspects:
by way of its being unfathomable because knowledge does not find a footing therein for those who have not accumulated a store of wholesome merit.
It is profound. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
In some instances it is taught in direct order (*anuloma*), and in others in reverse order (*paṭiloma*);

here, however, what is intended is the direct order, which consists in the arising of conditions leading to the arising of the conditionally arisen, and the reverse order, which consists in the cessation of conditions leading to the cessation of the conditionally arisen. From the beginning...
However, from the beginning to the end is intended as the direct order (*anuloma*), and from the end to the beginning as the reverse order (*paṭiloma*).
Thus, there is the three-junction, four-division [formula] through the teaching in direct order starting from the beginning and the teaching in reverse order starting from the end.
And there is the reverse-order teaching starting from the middle, such as: “Bhikkhus, what is the source of these four nutriments? and so forth.
In the forward teaching beginning with, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;
with contact as condition, feeling arises,” there is a double junction and a triple compendium.
And in such passages as, “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that can fetter, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises.”
It has one connection and two summaries. For dependent origination is taught as having a single factor. Indeed, it is found thus:
"In this regard, monks, the well-taught noble disciple attends thoroughly and wisely to dependent origination itself:
'When this exists, that comes to be... [etc] ...it ceases. Monks, in dependence on a contact to be experienced as pleasant..."
This should be understood by way of this sutta: “...a pleasant feeling arises.

Thus, because it must be set forth in such and such a manner according to each respective cause, dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is profound in its teaching. Therefore he said: “This is profundity of teaching.
For therein no knowledge other than omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa) finds a footing.
In the passage beginning with “But as for ignorance (avijjā),” the meaning of ignorance is non-knowing (*aññāṇattha*), which is the opposite of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) characterized by knowing.
It is the meaning of non-seeing (*adassanattha*), which is the opposite of seeing that consists in making the object directly present.
By concealing and enveloping [the truth], it does not allow this [ignorance] to penetrate the true nature of suffering and so forth according to reality through its own inherent nature.
It persists; this is its sense as the penetration of truth. *Abhisaṅkharaṇa* means preparation, the sense being "arranging.
*Āyūhana* means accumulation, the sense being the gathering together of associated states according to their respective functions.
A portion of non-meritorious volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) is accompanied by lust; the other is free from lust. Or, it is because lust is not an antidote [to itself].
Every formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) that increases lust and serves as a condition for the arising of lust is "with lust" (*sarāga*).

The other is "without lust" (*virāga*) because it is far removed from that. For it has been said: "For a long time, monks, this has been clung to, cherished, and grasped by the uninstructed worldling, [thinking]:
'This is mine, this am I, this is my self. Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is especially characterized by this misapprehension of a self (*attaparāmāsa*).

The basis has been stated; thus, the meaning of emptiness regarding consciousness is profound. Because of the strength of the adherence to the notions of "the self cognizes" and "the self transmigrates"—which imply agency and transmigration—the manifestation of rebirth-linking as being without agency and without transmigration is also profound.
Regarding name-and-form, their simultaneous arising at the moment of rebirth-linking is "arising together";
during the course of existence, their arising together is according to their respective suitability, with the name arising together with the form.

Because of the non-association of matter with name, there is a separation between name and name; however, because of the non-separation of matter from matter—of one part from another part—the non-separation of name from name should be applied [as stated in the *Vibhaṅga-mūlaṭīkā* 242].

When non-separation is intended by way of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation, that [non-separation] is obtained for matter in its coexistence within a single material group (*ekakalāpa*). Alternatively, ...
In the one- and four-aggregate existences, the separation of name-and-form should be understood from their not functioning together;
in the five-aggregate existence, their non-separation should be understood from their functioning together.
The meaning of "name" (nāma) is the bending (namana) of the mind toward the object. The meaning of "form" (rūpa) is its arising in a different state when brought together with opposing conditions.
The sense of being subject to deformation (*ruppanaṭṭha*). The sense of being the dominant condition for the faculties (*indriyapaccayabhāva*) is the sense of predominance (*adhipatiṭṭha*).

These meanings—“this is the world,” “these are the doors,” and “this is the field”—as stated [in the Sutta], are to be applied to the five beginning with the eye. However, for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), these meanings are to be understood from its being subject to dissolution (*lujjana*) and from its being the door and field for mind-contact and so forth.
The characteristic of the eye and the rest is their fitness for manifesting visible forms and other objects that have come into range.
Illumination is the state of being an object for the eye and the other [senses]; for the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is the act of cognizing.

The sense of "striking together" (*saṅghaṭṭana*) applies specifically to the five beginning with eye-contact (*cakkhusamphassa*), while the others should be applied to all six. Furthermore, touching (*phusana*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of contact (*phassa*).

Striking together is its function (*rasa*); the others are its modes of manifestation (*upaṭṭhānākāra*). It is described by way of its function as having the sense of experiencing the flavor of the object.
The meaning of "being felt" (*vedayita*) is according to its characteristic. The internal state of pleasure and pain is stated according to the individual nature of the three feelings respectively.
Because the strong adherence to the notion that "the self feels," the meaning of "being devoid of a soul" (*nijjīva*) is profound for feeling.
Alternatively, the being-felt by a soulless feeling is "soulless-being-felt" (*nijjīvavedayita*); that itself is the meaning, hence it is the "meaning of soulless-being-felt."

The sense of "rejoicing" (*abhinandita*) refers to being delighted by craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). The sense of "cleaving" (*ajjhosāna*) refers to swallowing and thoroughly finishing off [the object] with more powerful craving.

The remaining senses, however, are to be understood respectively as: the state of being the eldest, the state of being drawn back, the state of being difficult to cross over like a sea-monster, and the state of not reaching the further shore.

The senses of "grasping," "seizing," and "insistence" are common to all four types of clinging (*upādāna*). The sense of "misapprehension" (*parāmāsa*) applies specifically to the clinging to views and so forth; likewise does the sense of "being difficult to cross over."

For from the statement, “The wilderness of views,” the difficulty of transcending views is indicated. Alternatively, because they are firmly grasped, the sense of being difficult to transcend should be applied to all four [nutriments].
Regarding the compound “throwing into the womb, destinies, stations, and abodes,” the elision of the locative case-ending should be understood;
for in this way, there is a compound of the words *āyūhana* (accumulation) and *abhisaṅkharaṇa* (volitional formation). In whatever manner...

"Arising" (*jāyana*) has the sense of birth (*jāti*). Furthermore, arising from a combination [of conditions] has the sense of "origination" (*sañjāti*). Arising after having entered the mother's womb has the sense of "descent" (*okkanti*).
That production from birth has the sense of "generation" (*nibbatti*). Mere manifestation has the sense of "appearance" (*pātubhāva*).
Since the factor of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is dominated by death, its meanings of destruction and so forth are shown to be profound precisely in the sense of death.

For when each newly arisen state is successively destroyed, its progression toward the state of being fully ripened through the stages of brokenness and so forth is designated as "aging" (jarā) in the world.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the meaning of "destruction" (khaya) is what is expressed by aging.

Since the departure from a new state is appropriately called "destruction," the meaning of transformation (vipariṇāma) should be applied to both [aging and destruction] according to their respective functions; or else, aging may be considered in terms of the continuity of the stream (santati).

The meaning of "dissolution" (*khaya*) and "passing away" (*vaya*) should be applied here to death in the sense of breaking up and transformation, according to the conventional and momentary perspectives.
"Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) refers to the fact that the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of ignorance and the other factors is directly realized. For this has been stated in the *Nidānakathā*:
"Penetration is the unerring intrinsic nature, characterized by its own specific mark (*salakkhaṇa*), which is to be penetrated among those various phenomena taught in their respective contexts."

For that intrinsic nature of ignorance and the rest is profound in the sense of being bottomless, because it cannot be established by ignorance since it must be penetrated through non-delusive penetration by the knowledge of the path alone.
"All that" refers to all the profundity of dependent origination, which, as previously stated, is fourfold in brief and manifold in detail.
It appeared as clear as day to the Elder because he was endowed with four factors. [The question arises:
"Does it appear clearly to others as well? [One might think: "To me, at least, this dependent origination appears clearly;
but does it appear so clearly to others too? Do not speak thus. For one must stand within the method for the meditation subject of the Four Truths according to the system given by me alone.
Commentary on the Refutation:
"Coarse" (*oḷārika*) means gross (*thūla*) by way of its capacity to transgress against the object.

Although, in actual fact, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill will (*paṭigha*) are themselves the fetters of sensual desire and ill will (*kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojana*), as well as the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill will (*kāmarāgapaṭighānusaya*), nevertheless, the meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) is indeed distinct [from those].

Because its nature is that of a bond, the meaning of *anusaya* (latent tendency) is distinct from that [of the fetters], being defined as the state of becoming firmly established in the continuum through the fact of not having been abandoned.
Thus, by taking these as distinct based on their specific functions (*kicca*), it is said: "the four defilements" (*kilesa*). This same method applies to the others as well.

In the phrase *aṇusahagatā*, it means having attained the state of being atomic (*aṇu-sabhāva*). For this word *sahagata* has the sense of "being in the state of that," as in such expressions as *nandirāgasahagatā* ("accompanied by joy and lust").

Just as the penetration of the truths occurs by way of the attainment of the higher paths and by way of the penetration of the mode of conditions, so too the penetration of the truths by way of the attainment of disciple-enlightenment, solitary-enlightenment, and perfect enlightenment occurs precisely by way of the penetration of the mode of conditions;
it is to show this that the passage beginning with "And why" was stated. "In every way" means in every single manner, without leaving out even a single aspect.

The meaning is as follows: In order to show the divisions of time desired for the accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment by Great Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution, according to whether their energy is superior, medium, or mild, he said, "four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons" (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
This matter should be understood from the commentary on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*. As for the disciple, regarding partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*)...

"Established" means that, having become a disciple, one is established even there in partial knowledge due to being a trainee (*sekkha*). This constitutes an opposition to the discourse of the Buddhas,
such as "The Tathāgata fully realizes that," for the lion’s roar of the Buddhas is by virtue of what is not shared with others, not of what is shared with others.

“‘For one who exerts effort itself’—by this, he speaks specifically of the accumulation of the equipment of knowledge and the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramitā). And all merit is its proximate cause (upanissaya).
‘This is the treasure that grants all desires for gods and humans;
whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by means of this.’”

Thus it has been said. Therefore, since the entire equipment of merit (*puññasambhāra*) of all Great Bodhisattvas serves solely for the sake of the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*), as it enables the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), he said: "The mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) ... there is none.

Now, by way of demonstrating the great majesty of the very penetration of the mode of conditions, he shows the supreme profundity of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) itself with the words beginning "Ignorance" (*avijjā*).
It has been said. "By way of nine aspects" means by way of the nine aspects beginning with arising (*uppāda*).

For ignorance (*avijjā*) is a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) by being their arising, by being their occurrence (*pavatta*), their accumulation (*āyūhana*), their conjunction (*saṃyoga*), their impediment (*palibodha*), their origin (*samudaya*), their cause (*hetu*), and their condition (*paccaya*).
In the same way, volitional formations and the other factors are conditions for consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and the rest. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
“How is it that wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena?

Ignorance is the arising-stability, the occurrence-stability, the sign-stability, the accumulation-stability, the fetter-stability, the impediment-stability, the origination-stability, the cause-stability, and the condition-stability of volitional formations; in these nine ways, with ignorance as condition...”
“Volitional formations arise dependently,” and so forth.
In that context, “by way of nine modes” means by way of nine modes of functioning as conditions. It is called “arising” (*uppāda*) because the fruit arises from it;
it is the state of being the cause for the arising of the fruit. When ignorance exists, volitional formations arise, and not when it does not exist.
Therefore, ignorance, having become the arising of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), serves as their condition. Likewise, when ignorance exists, volitional formations proceed and are led forth.
And just as they are cast into the various states of existence (*bhava*) and so on, in that same way ignorance is their condition.
Likewise, they exert themselves, strive for the production of fruit, and become conjoined with their own fruit—within whichever continuum (*santāna*).
Arising by themselves, they become a bond. They emerge and arise when there is a convergence of other conditions.

They "go" (*hinoti*) in the sense that they enter into the state of being the cause for the formative forces (*saṅkhārā*). Because the formative forces "go forth" and proceed depending on ignorance, the specific ways in which ignorance enters into the state of being the cause for the formative forces—such as their arising and so forth—should be understood in this manner. In that regard:
Likewise, [the same applies] to the arising, presence, and so forth of formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the rest in relation to consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and the rest.
"It stands by means of this" is *ṭhiti*; it is the cause. Arising itself is the presence; thus it is "arising-presence" (*uppādaṭṭhiti*). This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"There is a condition"—this was said here by the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*) to show that at that time the discernment of conditions had been undertaken. And that undertaking was established in accordance with the right method (*ñāya*), as [stated]: "And how..."
"It was set in motion at the foot of the Bodhi tree by previous Great Beings, and it was set in motion in exactly the same way.
To show that the ten-thousandfold world system trembled and shook violently, overcome by the force of its wonder, he said, "At the mere sight of it," and so forth.
"Of this Dhamma" means of this Dhamma known as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, as for its meaning:

It is the cause of those things that arise from a cause. Therefore he said, "of this conditioned phenomenon," meaning that birth and the rest possess the state of being conditions for aging, death, and so forth.
The discernment of name-and-form and the discernment of its conditions do not occur merely by way of the first application of attention;
rather, they occur through a successive awakening known as the arising of knowledge again and again regarding them, [and through] the absence of both of those [previously mentioned errors].
But showing this, he said: "Non-comprehension by way of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).

Insight (*vipassanā*), which proceeds by way of abandoning perceptions of permanence and so forth, is indeed called "penetrating" (*paṭivijjhantī*) the phenomena (*dhammā*) because it attains a state of sharpness and intensity through the suppression of their opposites;

and there is also the "full understanding by way of investigation" (*tīraṇapariññā*) which is its basis, as well as the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) by way of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of full understanding and abandonment.

By saying "the non-penetration... of scrutinizing... abandonment," he shows the absence of penetration into both [the full understanding of suffering and the full understanding of its origin], namely, the inclusion of the full understanding of scrutiny and the full understanding of abandonment regarding the process of occurrence (*pavatti*).
It is called "warp" (*tanta*) because it is stretched out by weavers after they have fixed the threads upon the loom for the purpose of weaving cloth;
it is so designated because it is that which is being extended. Furthermore, it is used as an illustration due to the state of being entangled with the continuous strands of thread.
"Taken up in a state of confusion" means that it has become entangled like a thread; thus he said, "become like a tangled thread.

To show in detail the meaning stated in brief, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. "To bring together" (samānetuṃ) means to bring the latter into equality with the former, that is, to make it even and straight.
Alternatively, "tantākula" means a confused thread (ākulaṃ tantaṃ), and [the phrase] means "become like a tangled thread."
They have become entangled in various ways. Without having entered upon the Middle Way, they stumble regarding the mode of conditions due to falling into the two extremes;

thus, being entangled and utterly confused, they wander about by means of various graspings at views because of that very falling into the two extremes, and do not know how to proceed directly toward the discourse on the stability of phenomena.
Therefore he said: "They are unable to [understand] that mode of conditions..."
"To make straight. "Two types of bodhisattvas" refers to the *paccekabodhisatta* (solitary enlightened being) and the *mahābodhisatta* (greatly enlightened being).
"By his own nature" means by his own inherent character; the meaning is that it occurs without instruction from another.
"A ball formed here and there" means a ball produced in various places. "A knot" (*gaṇṭhī*) means a thread-knot. For that very reason, it is "bound with knots," meaning it has tied knots.

"Having stumbled over the conditions" means having stumbled by way of grasping at permanence and so forth regarding the conditioned phenomena whose intrinsic nature is impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

"Being unable to straighten out the conditions" means being unable to straighten out one's own vision of the sign of conditioned phenomena because of not relinquishing that very grasping at permanence and so forth; this is due to the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence to the view that "this alone is the truth."
"They have become knotted," he said, [expressed as] "sixty-two... knotted together. For whatever ascetics or brahmins are dependent upon and attached to views such as eternalism and so forth.
From the act of weaving, the term "kula" refers to the "knot" (gaṇṭhika) of a weaver—who has received that name by way of the feminine gender—due to its state of being entangled.
"Whether from the top or from the bottom, it is indeed difficult to discern whether the thread has slipped," he said;
thus, "a *kulāgaṇṭhika* is called the dyed thread of a weaver. *Sakuṇikā* refers to a bird that makes a nest; for she hangs her nest upon the branches of trees.
She brings grass, fibers, and so forth from here and there and weaves them together in such a way that their...
Just as in the case of the *kañjiya-sutta* (a length of cloth) woven by a weaver, it is impossible to bring the tip to the tip or the base to the base, or to separate them.
Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. Both of these refer to the *kañjiya-sutta* mentioned as "the knot of the cloth" and the "nest.
"In the same manner as before" means precisely by the method previously stated in the passage beginning with, "In the very same way, beings..."
Granted that muñja grass and pabbaja reeds, even as they grow, fall down due to their length and remain in the forest region entangled with one another in a state of utter confusion;
yet, they are not so difficult to disentangle as when they have been made into ropes.
To show this, it was said, "Just as those," and so forth. The rest here follows the same method explained below.
"Apāya" means non-prosperity; the meaning is that they are deprived of happiness or the causes of happiness.

"Because it is the destination of suffering" means because it is the place where the suffering of those destined for the states of loss (apāya) occurs. "From the ruin of happiness" means from its decline.

"Because of being fallen into misfortune" means because of having fallen into an ugly state, such that in that particular existence there is no prosperity of happiness; thus it is because of having fallen [into such a state].
"Thus indeed is saṃsāra. But is it not the case that what was described by the passage beginning with "the states of loss" (apāya) is also saṃsāra? This is true;
however, the mention of the states of loss and so forth is for the purpose of showing that hell and the other realms are characterized by excessive suffering.

This meaning should be understood according to the maxim of "the cow and the calf. And as for the succession of the aggregates: it is the continuous sequence of the five aggregates by way of cause and fruit.

“Proceeding” (*pavatti*). “Continuing without interruption” means proceeding without cessation. “All that” refers to all the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*) and the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), as described by the phrase beginning with “the states of woe.
“Like a ship tossed by the wind in the great ocean” is said both to show the vastness of the place where one wanders and to show the instability of that wandering.

“By way of a simile: ‘Like a yoked ox among those being led’—this, moreover, should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the state of not being a bull, and for the purpose of showing the state of being difficult to release.
Regarding the commentary on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*):
in the phrase “by this much first,” the word *tāva* indicates sequence; by it, the connection to the phrase “born like a tangled skein” is established.
He illuminates that [the condition] will become manifest from another. Regarding the phrase "there is this specific condition" (*idappaccaya*):
here, "this condition" is *idappaccaya*; therefore, "from this specific condition" (*idappaccayā*), meaning "from this particular condition.
This is what is meant: "Is there indeed a condition for aging-and-death?"—it must be stated thus: "From such-and-such a condition, aging-and-death [arises]. Therefore he said: "There is..."

“...would it not be so?...”. For here, because the word *idappaccaya* is shown to be in grammatical apposition with the word *idaṃ* (this) by means of the word *kiṃ* (what), which is in apposition with the words *jāti* (birth) and *paccaya* (condition) in the subsequent passage—namely, “With what as condition is there aging and death?

With birth as condition is there aging and death”—it is appropriate that *idappaccaya* be understood as a *kammadhāraya* compound. It is not the case here that “the conditions for this are *idappaccaya*.”

An inquiry into the origination of aging-and-death—or of anything else—arises from its being something that must be known, both in terms of its possibility of arising from conditions and its impossibility [otherwise]; furthermore, an inquiry into the conditions for aging-and-death arises.
And because the word *idam* (this) shares the same grammatical referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word *paccaya* (condition), the inquiry into the condition, "from this condition," is appropriate.

Furthermore, although that state of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) can also occur in a compound where the meaning is other than the constituent members (*aññapadatthasamāsa*), here it should be understood as a *kammadhāraya* compound because there is no desire to express the meaning of the other member. In the case of a genitive compound (*sāmivacanasamāsa*), however, the possibility of a common substratum does not exist at all.
But is it not the case that in the expression “dependent origination is conditionality by way of this” (*idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo*), the term *idappaccaya* is a genitive compound?

"Is it desired?"—Truly, it is desired; for there, having made the expression "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) the very object of inquiry, the word "this" (idaṃ) functions as a qualification of dependent origination.
But here, only the investigation of the conditions for aging and death is intended.

Therefore, just as in that case the word "this" serves as a qualification of dependent origination, so too here its function as the object of inquiry regarding the conditions is possible. Thus, in that case...
And here, a collective formation (*samāsakappanā*) is to be understood. But why is a *kammadhāraya* compound not desired there?
Because the meaning of "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)—namely, that it is the cause of those things that arise from a cause—is impossible within a *kammadhāraya* compound;
and because the meaning of "this-conditionality" (*idappaccaya*)—namely, that it is a corresponding condition for what is itself corresponding to its own condition—is likewise impossible.

Because it is intended [to be understood]. Now, the meaning grasped here by the word *idaṃ* (this) is already grasped by the mention of "aging-and-death" in the phrase, "There is aging-and-death with this as its condition.
Thus, because the word *idaṃ* cannot possibly refer to anything other than what is excluded from dependent origination, it stands for the condition;
therefore, a *kammadhāraya* compound is used here. In that case, however, of the word *idaṃ*...
Therefore, since there is no reason for [the word] to be relinquished, only a genitive compound (*sāmivacana-samāsa*) is intended. Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*,

because this exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) was begun by way of a question regarding the conditions for aging, death, and so forth— and because "dependent origination" is said to mean,
in terms of its actual meaning, the causes from which things arise— therefore, [it refers to] "of this aging and death..."
Thus was the commentary on the meaning made.
"By the wise" means by one endowed with the wisdom capable of discerning the specific distinctions among questions such as those to be answered categorically (*ekamsa-vyākaraṇīya*).

Indeed, in order to demonstrate that very wisdom of his, the words beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) were spoken. For one who holds a particular view regarding the living being (*jīva*), [the question is: "How... and so forth.
He asks about non-difference from the body with the question, "Is that life-principle the same as that body? However, such a thing is not found in the ultimate sense;
how then could its being long or short, or its difference or non-difference from the body, be explained—any more than one could explain the height or length of the son of a barren woman?
Therefore, it should be understood that this question is to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*). This silence, moreover, is not a sign of disregard for the questioner.
“It is like an affliction” means he stated another perspective by saying, “this is undeclared. This must be explained to one who wishes to understand the reason for its non-declaration;

and once it has been explained, even negligence might occur on the part of one who understands it. However, the method of explanation has already been shown by the passage beginning with “of such a person as...”.
“Without proceeding in this way” means without resorting to silence or similar tactics, as would be done in the case of a question to be set aside.
Thus it is. The expression “without having practiced” is merely an illustration. When asked, “Is everything impermanent? one should answer after counter-questioning:
“Are you asking with reference to the conditioned, or rather the unconditioned?
Similarly, when asked, “What is to be fully understood regarding the five aggregates? one should answer: “Some among them are to be fully understood, while others are not.”
It is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajja-byākātabba*), and it is this—namely, "not proceeding in such a manner"—that is intended as the meaning here.
Previously, the mere existence of a condition was urged; thus, the mere existence was answered. For an answer is generally in accordance with the question.
Now, a direct question regarding that very same point is being made; hence it is said, "Furthermore, what? Here too:
The entire passage beginning with “yathā” (just as) should be cited here.

Having made an effort by way of extended application (*atidesa*) stating, “This method applies to all instances,” the exception (*apavāda*) beginning with “conditioned by name-and-form” (*nāmarūpapaccayā*) is introduced therein.
Since he wishes to demonstrate this, the connection is that this was stated for that purpose. [This refers] specifically to the six kinds of resultant contact (*vipākasamphassa*).
The inclusion [of these factors] is because the process of ripening (vipākavidhi) begins with consciousness and ends with feeling;
for this is established in numerous scriptural passages and is generally used in the Abhidhamma to refer to those very factors. "Here" means in this sutta.

The word *ca* has the sense of distinction (*byatirekattha*); by it, the specific qualification being stated here—namely, "even though they have been included"—is illuminated. The state of being a condition (*paccayabhāva*)...
The name [“contact”] depends on that which has arisen by way of condition, because it cannot exist without it. Therefore, the construction is:

“with the sixfold base as condition” means “by this phrase, ‘with the sixfold base as condition, contact arises’. Alternatively, this term “with the sixfold base as condition” is a designation for the whole by means of a part;
therefore, what is meant is: “by this phrase, ‘with the sixfold base as condition, contact arises.’”
"Even when included" refers to the sixfold resultant contact (*vipākaphassa*). "Even when not included" refers to non-resultant contact, as well as wholesome, unwholesome, and functional contact.

The construction is: "desiring to show the specific distinction of what has arisen by way of conditions. And here, it is not only that which has arisen from conditions that is intended as "clung-to" (*upādinnam*);

rather, the condition itself is also intended as "clung-to. Thus, there is the inclusion of the internal sense base (*ajjhattikāyatana*) alone by means of the mention of the "sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*).
Having stated this, it was said: “Desiring to show [the condition] from the sixfold sense base... pe ...”. For contact does not have only the sixfold sense base, such as the eye, as its condition;

rather, according to such statements as, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,” both the form of the visible-object base (rūpāyatana) and so forth, and the name of eye-consciousness and so forth, are conditions. Therefore, this—

The construction is as follows: because it is not common—unlike advertence (*āvajjana*) and so forth, which are common to more than the six bases beginning with the eye—and because it is common to each respective contact, the Blessed One, wishing to show another specific condition by means of the word "also" (*pi*), indicated a common condition [by saying], "With name-and-form as condition, contact. This very same [point] is also [stated] in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*.
With reference to this condition, it was stated: "Contact has name-and-form as its condition.

Regarding this, the commentary on that passage provides the following explanation of the meaning: "It is for the purpose of showing the specific nature of the conditions and for the purpose of including [this] within the teaching of the Mahānidāna Sutta.

"Of the conditions" refers to birth and so forth, which are the phenomena that serve as conditions. "The source (nidāna) has been told" means that the state of being a condition has been declared categorically as the source of aging, death, and the rest.
Indeed, the subsequent teaching beginning with “Thus, moreover, this... was delivered in order to show that these [factors] are unfailing in their status as conditions.
“Nijjaṭe” means free from thorns; “niggumbe” means free from bushes. By both these terms, he shows the absence of confusion;
therefore, because a great causal source—unconfused and undisturbed—is explained herein, it is called the Mahānidāna Sutta (The Great Causality Discourse).
Because there is no state of being otherwise. 98. "Of those respective conditions" means of the respective conditions for birth and so forth.

Since the state of being a condition consists in the arising of this or that fruit from those respective conditions exactly as they are—neither deficient nor excessive—it is thus (tatho) and real (taccho).
It is "true" (*tatha*) because, even for a moment, there is no impossibility of the arising of such phenomena when the requisite conditions for concordance are present.
It is "not untrue" (*avitatha*) and non-deceptive because it is devoid of the mode of deception, since one phenomenon does not arise from conditions for a different phenomenon.
It is called "not otherwise" (*anaññathā*) because of the absence of any state of being otherwise. Therefore, it is "true, not untrue, and not otherwise."
It is said, "in order to show the state of being a condition. It is called a *pariyāya* because it proceeds (*pariyāyati*) by encompassing its own fruit;
thus he says, "by way of a *pariyāya*, that is, by way of a cause. "In every way, entirely" means all births in their entirety as gods and so forth.
"In every manner, entirely" means even therein, in every mode such as the Cātumahārājika realm and so on. These two are particles.
A particle (*nipāta*) is an indeclinable (*abyaya*), and it remains uniform in form across all genders, cases, and numbers;

thus, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "entirely, in every way, in all respects, all. However, in the explanatory commentary (*atthavacana*), the phrase "in every manner, all" and so forth is stated to demonstrate its feminine application in view of its status as a generic term (*jātisadda*). By this very method... [imena]... by this.

By the same method as stated under the section on birth (*jāti*). Regarding the phrase "among gods, etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes the gandhabbas, yakkhas, and so forth mentioned in the Pāḷi, as well as their various subdivisions.
"For the purpose of analyzing the meaning set forth here" means:
in this [text], by way of a general enumeration (*uddesa*) without specific restriction, such as "for someone, anywhere."

A particle (*nipāta*) is that which illuminates what is to be illuminated for the purpose of explaining the meaning already stated; the meaning is that a "particle-word" (*nipātapada*) is the illumination of that meaning.
"Of that" (*tassa*) means of that word. "Those" (*te*) refers to the Elder who is the recipient (*sampadāna*) of the teaching of the Dhamma.

Alternatively, "seyyathidaṃ" has the meaning "what are those? or "which ones? For the meaning that was stated without specification as "of anyone" (*kassaci*) and "in anything" (*kimhici*), [is now specified].
“What are they? This is a question arising from a desire to explain. “For the state of a deva” means for the purpose of the state of a deva.
“The birth of the aggregates” means the manifestation of the aggregates; the meaning is that their arising is such that when the aggregates have arisen, there is the conventional designation “devas.
Therefore he said, “by which. “In all instances” refers to all [phrases] such as “for the gandhabbas, for the sake of the gandhabba-state,” and so forth.
Regarding the sections on the exposition of birth (*jāti*) and the sections on existence (*bhava*), etc.:

by whatever method this application of meaning as "birth" (*jāti*) has been made, that same method should also be applied to the sections on existence, etc., such as "existence" (*bhava*) and so forth, within the sections on the exposition of birth. As for "gods" (*deva*):

these are the gods of rebirth, from the Cātumahārājika realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*); they "shine" (*dibbanti*), meaning they sport, play, and dwell amidst the strands of sensual pleasure and the like.
They are called *gandhabbas* because they "inhale" (*abbanti*) fragrance (*gandha*), that is, they consume it; they are the retinue of the Great King Dhatarattha.

They are called *yakkhas* because they "sacrifice" (*yajanti*), that is, they worship Vessavaṇa, Sakka, and others; or alternatively, they are called *yakkhas* because they are to be sacrificed to or worshipped through various acts of aspiration and so forth;
they are the retinue of the Great King Vessavaṇa. [Thus it is stated] in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
However, it is stated without distinction as "non-human beings" (*amanussā*). "Bhūtas" refers to *kumbhaṇḍas*, who are the retinue of the Great King Virūḷhaka.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated without distinction as "whatever beings have been born. Those with bone-wings include bees, beetles, and so forth; those with skin-wings include bats, jackals, and so forth;
those with feather-wings include swans, peacocks, and so forth; and reptiles include snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and so forth.
The phrase "of this and that" is not a statement intended to include what has not been mentioned, as in the case of a *yevāpanaka* (inclusive) definition;
rather, like a *nayevāpanaka* (exclusive) definition, it is intended to include what has already been mentioned. Furthermore, since the sense of repetition (*āmeḍita*) is included by the word "etc.

(*ādi*) itself, he says: "of this and that [group], such as the gods, gandhabbas, and so forth. "For the sake of that" (*tadattāya*) means for the state of being that; [referring to] within such aggregates (*khandhas*).

When [beings] are existing, there is a worldly convention of "gods" and "gandhabbas"; the meaning is "by virtue of having such a nature. Therefore he said, "for the state of being gods, gandhabbas, and so forth.

Furthermore, while "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "disappearance" (*vigama*) refer to the state of having already attained what was previously unobtained, here, however, absolute non-existence is intended.
This is why, instead of saying "when birth is entirely absent," it says "with the cessation of birth" (*jātinirodhā*).
Because it has been so stated, he says: "The meaning is 'non-existence'.
"It goes for the sake of the fruit" means that it proceeds in such a way that the fruit is produced from it;
the meaning is that it enters into the state of being its cause. "Take this! means it applies itself [to the object] in this manner: "This is my fruit; take it!"

It is as if one hands it over. Having extended the general rule without distinction by saying "This is the method," the phrase beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) was stated in order to show the meaning of the specific detail.
