One might object: "Is this birth not itself fully accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*), and since it is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), does it not lack the status of being a modification (*vikāra*)?
Likewise for aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). How then can it be the cause of that? Addressing this objection, he says: "Of aging-and-death..."

"‘Hī’ and so forth. The presence [of birth] when that [craving] is present, and the absence [of birth] when that is absent, is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) condition for aging-and-death in relation to birth.

99. ‘Determination of the sphere’ means the determination of the place of occurrence. This applies to the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*), because the aggregates of rebirth do not arise elsewhere than in the aforementioned place.
But here, however, in this sutta, by the words ‘sense-sphere existence’ (*kāmabhava*) and so forth..."

It has arrived at this point. The designation of "kamma-bhava" (existence as kamma) specifically as the "kāmabhava" (sensuous existence) and so forth is appropriate because it serves as the condition for that birth (*jāti*).
Therefore, he said: "For that [kamma] is a condition for birth by way of the extreme limit of decisive support (*upanissaya-koṭi*).
But is not "rebirth-existence" (*upapatti-bhava*) also a condition for birth by way of decisive support? True, it is; however, it is not so predominant [as the kamma], whereas kamma-existence is.
But the condition that is predominant is called the "productive state. Thus it was said: "For that [is the cause] of birth," and so forth;

the karma that leads to rebirth in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is itself "sense-sphere existence. This same method applies to fine-material (*rūpa*) and immaterial (*arūpa*) existences as well. By the phrase "for what indeed," only the delimitation of the *okāsa* (space/receptacle) is established, since the delimitation of the sentient being (*satta*) has already been performed.
"Of all three types of kamma-existence" means of all three types of kamma-existence, beginning with sensual kamma-existence.
"And of all three types of rebirth-existence" means of all three types of rebirth-existence, beginning with sensual rebirth-existence.
"Likewise the rest" means that the remaining clingings, such as clinging to views and so forth, [are causes] of all three types of kamma-existence and all three types of rebirth-existence.
"Condition" (*paccaya*) is the meaning. "Thus" (*iti*) means in the manner already stated.
Twelve kamma-becoming (*kammabhava*) and twelve rebirth-becoming (*upapattibhava*) should be understood as twenty-four existences (*bhava*).

Since clinging (*upādāna*) is called a condition for rebirth-becoming only by way of being a condition for kamma-becoming, and not otherwise, therefore clinging is the direct condition for kamma-becoming.

He said: "In this context, twelve types of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) are found in a non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*). "Of these" refers to those kamma-existences. By way of the "co-nascent limit" (*sahajātakoṭi*):
for an unwholesome kamma-existence, clinging (*upādāna*) is a condition by way of the co-nascent limit;

the other [wholesome clinging] is a condition by way of the "supportive limit" (*upanissayakoṭi*) through such modes as the immediate (*anantara*) and decisive-support (*upanissaya*). However, for a wholesome kamma-existence, it is a condition only by way of the supportive limit. Herein...

And just as it was stated "by way of the category of co-nascence" (*sahajātakoṭiyā*) in order to show that conditions such as mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance are included within the single category of co-nascence,

so too it should be understood that it was stated "by way of the category of decisive support" (*upanissayakoṭiyā*) by way of taking together the object-decisive-support, proximity-decisive-support, and natural-decisive-support.

101. Regarding the phrase "of clinging" (*upādānassa*): here, craving is a condition for the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). For the remaining types of clinging, it is a condition both by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of decisive support. This is because consciousness and the rest, ending with feeling, constitute the process of resultant (*vipāka*). 102. Regarding the phrase "that which is feeling" (*yadidaṃ vedanā*):

here, resultant feeling is a condition for that very same [clinging] solely by way of decisive support, since it is impossible for it to be so by way of any other mode. "Other" refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and functional feelings. "In another way" means also by way of co-nascence.
103. "To this extent" means by way of this much teaching which proceeds by showing the succession of conditions for aging, death, and so forth.
"Craving of the previous existence" means the craving established in a prior becoming.
Having stated, "This is the condition for craving, namely, feeling," he immediately thereafter said, "Thus it has been said: 'Feeling has contact as its condition,'" and so on.
The extraction of contact, which serves as the condition for feeling, follows the method of teaching dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) as it appears in other suttas;

however, without entering into that [method], he teaches the phenomena rooted in craving by way of demonstrating the manifestation of craving itself, as if descending from his habitual mode of teaching.
And for one who sees that teaching, [craving] ceases, having been forcibly suppressed.
And because it is as if he were teaching by force, he said, “Now,” and so forth. “Two kinds of craving”:
this refers to the craving intended here itself, which he speaks of by dividing into two types. “Craving as seeking” is the craving that occurs by way of the pursuit of enjoyments.
“Craving for what has been sought” is the craving that arises toward enjoyments already pursued. “By way of active craving” means by way of craving occurring as an obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

This craving, which arises dependent on feeling, is twofold: it consists in the search for the acquisition of enjoyments not yet obtained, and in the guarding, protecting, and so forth, of those already obtained.
It is called "search" (*pariyesanā*) because one searches by means of this [craving] through the state of agitation (*paritassanā*).
Search is thus defined both by its underlying tendency (*āsaya*) and by its practical application (*payoga*).
Thus proceeds the arising of consciousness. Therefore it was said: "When craving exists, there is [acquisition].
"The acquisition of objects such as visible forms" refers to the seeking out of objects such as visible forms together with their bases;

however, in the course of its actual occurrence, what has not yet been sought is obtained, and even that is, in terms of its meaning, simply what has been obtained through seeking because of the prior performance of corresponding karma.
Because it is obtained in this way. Therefore he said: "For that exists when there is seeking.
"The discernment of pleasure" (*sukhavinicchaya*): it is called the discernment of pleasure because it specifically discerns pleasure;

it is the knowledge that occurs having understood pleasure as it truly is—in terms of its intrinsic nature, its origin, its passing away, and the escape from it. "One should know" (*jaññā*) means one should understand.
“Discernment” (*vinicchaya*) means that one determines and ascribes various unreal aspects to an object—such as “it is beautiful and pleasant”—by way of a particular inclination.
It should be understood that the nature of discernment is exactly the same for craving and views when they observe gratification.
However, the application here is that in this sutta, only applied thought (*vitakka*) is mentioned. “In this sutta” refers to the *Sakkapañha Sutta*. Therein:
For it has been stated: "Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in applied thought (*vitakka*).

Here, in this *Mahānidāna Sutta*, by the phrase "one decides by means of applied thought itself," he explains the term *vinicchaya* as having an instrumental derivation: "that by which one decides is a decision (*vinicchaya*).
The passage beginning with "to such an extent" is a demonstration of the manner of deciding.
In the sense of coloring, it is *chanda*; likewise, in the sense of delighting, it is *rāga*.

Since this [rāga] occurs as something weak when there is no repeated practice (*anāsevanatā*), it is intended here; thus he says, "it is a designation for weak lust. *Ajjhosāna* is the clinging by way of craving and views.
For the grasping of craving, "This is mine," is for the most part dependent upon the grasping of a self.
Therefore he said, "I" and "mine," and by the phrase "strong conviction," he spoke of the attainment of stability in those graspings.

Grasping by way of craving and views means: having grasped the object of the clinging to self and what belongs to self—which has been adhered to by way of strong conviction as "I" and "mine"—and having treated it as if it were not shared with others, one stands [therein]; thus it proceeds.

It is an arising of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobhasahagata-cittuppāda*). That phenomenon by virtue of which a person, regarding an object possessed by oneself, is unable to tolerate its being shared with others is "intolerance" (*asahanatā*).
Thus they explain the meaning of the word according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*).

However, according to the definition of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*), it is that phenomenon by virtue of which a person is called "miserly" (*macchara*) due to being joined with miserliness (*macchariya*).
It is a state (*bhāva*) or an action (*kamma*); *macchariya* is a phenomenon (*dhamma*). Because of the powerful nature of stinginess, its guarding with care is called "guarding" (*ārakkha*);
thus he said, "the doors... well-guarded. It produces its own fruit, hence it is a "cause" (*karaṇa*);
any reason whatsoever is a cause, and a superior cause is a "special cause" (*adhikaraṇa*), that is, a specific cause. And as for the specific cause:
Regarding the phrase "the source of the arising of evils such as the taking up of weapons for the sake of guarding possessions," it is said: "on account of guarding" and so forth.
"For the purpose of harming others" means for the purpose of afflicting others by means of killing and the like. It is called *ādāna* because one takes (*ādīyati*) by means of it;

the taking up of a staff is *daṇḍādāna*, which is the arising of a state of mind that intends to oppress others after having overcome them. The same method applies to the taking up of a weapon (*satthādāna*).

A "bodily quarrel" (*kāyakalaha*) is a quarrel to be carried out by means of the body, such as by seizing with the hands and so forth. A "verbal quarrel" (*vācākalaha*) is a quarrel to be carried out by means of speech, such as by striking at vital points and so forth.
It is called a "dispute" (*viggaha*) because one takes up an ugly position (*virūpaṃ gaṇhāti*) by way of conflict (*virujjhanavasena*).

It is called a "contention" (*vivāda*) because one speaks what is contradictory (*viruddhaṃ vadati*) by means of it. The term *tuvaṃ tuvaṃ* [is used] because it is accompanied by disrespectful speech such as "you, you. All these [terms refer to the same thing].
In the same way, the arising of states of consciousness accompanied by hatred (*dosa*) should be understood. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Many evil, unwholesome states come into being. 112.
He brought the teaching to a conclusion: that which had proceeded by way of the direct order (*anulomanaya*), beginning with "With craving as condition, there is seeking," and so forth.
Returning once more by way of reverse order, he began with "guarding as the basis" (*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*) and turned back [the exposition].

"By way of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena*): that which has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object is "possessing the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇika*);
the lust that proceeds therein by way of coloring and by way of delighting—by way of that [lust], craving arises through the mode of coloring and through the mode of yearning.

Craving for form and so forth that occurs with respect to sense-pleasures is *kāmatanha* (craving for sense-pleasures). That which exists, is present, and persists at all times is "becoming" (*bhava*);

this refers to the view of becoming (*bhavaditthi*) that occurs [in such a way], where the latter member of the compound is elided. Craving associated with that is *bhavatanha* (craving for existence). That which ceases, perishes, and is annihilated is "non-becoming" (*vibhava*); this refers to the view of non-becoming (*vibhavaditthi*) that occurs [in such a way], where the latter member of the compound is elided. Craving associated with that is...
“Craving for non-existence” refers to craving as “the eternalist view,” and so forth. These two phenomena are:

first, the craving that is the root of the round of existence, spoken of thus, “This is the condition for clinging, namely, craving”; and second, the craving in its active manifestation, spoken of thus, “Dependent on craving, there is pursuit.
These are the two phenomena. “By way of the root of the round and by way of its manifestation” means: by way of the root of the round.
And by way of manifestation. "By two portions" means by two parts.
"Convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) means that they come together and proceed equally by way of arising; thus it is a condition. Those which have this single convergence are "single-convergent.
To the question "In what do they have a single convergence? he says: "in feeling. For both types of craving have feeling as their condition.

Thus it is said. Therefore he says: “By way of feeling as condition, there is one condition. Having flowed out from here and there and come together, the place of convergence is the *osaraṇa-samosaraṇa*.
Feeling that flows together and occurs simultaneously with other feelings upon a single object is called “convergence”;
thus he says: “This is what is known as ‘convergence by co-nascence’ (*sahajāta-samosaraṇa*).”

113. "All" (sabbā) refers specifically to resultant contacts (*savipāka-phassa*) when analyzed according to the doors of their arising; this is because the resultant cognitive process (*vipākavīthi*), beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, is what constitutes the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kathā*), which is to say, the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
Thus he says, "excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts.
"In many ways" (*bahudhā*) means in many modes. For in the five sense-doors, [the process occurs] based on the physical bases such as the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhu-pasāda*) and so forth.

Contact, such as eye-contact and so forth, is a condition for the five kinds of feeling in eight ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

Furthermore, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that arise at each of the remaining doors by way of reception, investigation, and registration, contact such as eye-contact and so forth is a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

It is a condition in eight ways. In the mind-door as well, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that arise by way of the "object-attaining" (tadārammaṇa) process, the co-nascent mind-contact is likewise a condition in eight ways; the same applies to the three-plane resultant feelings that arise by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
As for those [feelings] which arise in the mind-door by way of the "object-attaining" process...

Sensations pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-vedanā*): the mental contact associated with the adverting of the mind-door (*manodvārāvajjana*) is a condition for these [sensations] in one way by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Thus, it should be understood that contact is a condition for sensation in many ways.

114. "Of sensation and the rest" means of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). "Dissimilar natures" refers to their respective states of experiencing (*anubhavana*), perceiving (*sañjānana*), volitionally constructing (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*), and cognizing (*vijānana*).
For they are called "modes" (*ākāra*) because they are scattered about and made known in the form of feeling and so forth, which are mutually distinct.
"Those very same" means those very modes of feeling and so forth belonging to feeling and the rest. "Being clearly shown" means being manifested with care, as if directly before the eyes.
"They lead to their respective subtle meanings" refers to [the definitions]: "The meaning of 'formless' (*arūpa*) is the meaning of bending toward the object."

These are called *liṅga* (signs) because they lead to and make known various such hidden meanings that have not yet been clarified. They are the causes for the recognition of this or that [object], such as the state of being formless (*arūpa*) and so forth, because they serve as the grounds for its observation.
They are called *nimitta* (marks) because by means of them things are "measured" (*nimīyanti*), that is, inferred.
This is because they are to be pointed out in such and such ways—namely, in the manner of being formless in nature and so forth, and in the manner of being felt (*vedayita*) and so forth.

These are the summaries (uddesa) because they are to be explained. Therefore, by the words "because of their dissimilar nature" and so forth, he refers back to the very same meaning already stated by way of its causal basis.

Since the mutual dissimilar natures of feeling and the other [mental factors] are the "modes" (ākāra) and so forth in the sense already described, therefore this is now the meaning of the scriptural passage (pāḷipada) that is being stated here.

“Of the collection of names” means: of the heap of immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) consisting of the four aggregates beginning with feeling, which has received the conventional designation “name” (nāma) in the sense of bending toward the object.
“Designation” (paññatti) refers to the act of making known, such as: “the name-body, the immaterial group, the immaterial aggregates,” and so forth.
Because volition is predominant among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), it is stated: “in the mode of volition of the formations,” and so on.

For in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, within the analysis of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), volition alone is specified as: "That which is volition, intention, and the state of having intended.
The term "non-existent" (*asati*) refers to those things that do not exist; it is stated thus by means of a grammatical inversion.

"Making the four aggregates the basis" refers to feeling, perception, consciousness, and volition—these being designated as the four aggregates that serve as the supporting condition (*nissayapaccaya*).
Having made the mental object (dhamma) the basis. And since this method is possible even in the case of the five doors, it is specified as "in the mind-door" (manodvāre).
It is called "designation-contact" (adhivacana-samphassa) because it is to be grasped by way of designation (adhivacana), that is, by way of conceptual description (paññatti).
"It" refers to mind-contact (manosamphassa). And in the five-aggregate plane, because it is obtained in dependence upon the heart-basis (hadayavatthu), [it exists] in the material body.
It is indeed discerned; however, this method is not intended here, because it illustrates a way in which [mental contact] is impossible by means of the negation of feeling and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning stated is: "it might arise having made the fivefold clarity its basis.
For there is no possibility of mental contact occurring by making the fivefold clarity its basis without dependence upon feeling. This is because, in the absence of a place of arising...

Showing this meaning by way of illustrating the point already established—that the arising of a fruit from a non-arising place never occurs at any time—he said, "In the case of the mango tree," and so forth. "From the material body" means solely from the material body.
"Of that" refers to mental contact.

When opposing conditions assemble, there is a more distinct arising of dissimilarity; or, when those conditions are present, the state of being the cause for the arising of dissimilarity within one's own continuity is the mode of "being affected" (*ruppanākāra*).

That very mode of being affected is the "mark" (*liṅga*), because it leads to various specific objects that are otherwise latent, such as the resistance of the physical basis. It is the "sign" (*nimitta*) because it is the cause for the recognition of each respective object. Likewise...
Likewise, it is called "enumeration" (*uddesa*) because it is to be enumerated; in this way, the factors such as the *ākāra* (aspects) are to be understood here according to their meaning.

"Resistance" (*paṭigha*) is the mutual striking of bases and objects; "contact born of resistance" (*paṭighasamphassa*) is that which arises from that resistance. Therefore he said, "with resistance," and so forth.
"From the mental body" (*nāmakāyata*) means solely from the mental body. "Of that" refers to contact born of resistance. The rest is exactly according to the method stated in the first question.

"By way of both" means: by way of both the contact of designation (*adhivacana-saṃphassa*) and the contact of resistance (*paṭigha-saṃphassa*), which depend upon both—the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
"Having shown the condition separately for each" means: having shown the respective conditions designated as the mental body and the physical body by way of contrast (*byatirekamukhena*).
"Of these" refers to the contacts. "Without distinction" means: without making a distinction, but in a general sense. "To show" means...
It is stated [in this way] in order to show [the cause] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

"This very same cause" means that this cause, consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which operates through all six doors, is the respective cause for both types of contact. Now, in order to demonstrate that respective occurrence by analyzing it, the passage beginning with "In the eye-door, etc. was spoken.

“Associated aggregates” refers to the aggregates beginning with feeling that are associated with contact. Here, the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) should also be understood as included by the very mention of the associated aggregates, because it is inseparable from them.
The same principle applies subsequently to mental contact as well.
“Fivefold” means fivefold by way of eye-contact and so forth. “That contact” refers to impingement-contact (paṭigha-samphassa). “In many ways” means in many modes.

For thus, that which is called resultant name is a condition in seven ways for the manifold kinds of resultant mind-contact, by way of being its conascent, mutuality, support, resultant, associated, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
Furthermore, whatever function of nutriment is present here, it is a condition by way of the nutriment condition;
whatever function of faculty is present, it is a condition by way of the faculty condition. However, non-resultant name [is a condition] for non-resultant mind-contact...

Excluding the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*), it acts as a condition for the others. Furthermore, matter—divided into the eye-base and so forth—is a condition in six ways for the fivefold contact beginning with eye-contact:
by way of support (*nissaya*), prenascence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
Matter—divided into the visible-object-base and so forth—is [a condition] for that same fivefold [contact] by way of object (*ārammaṇa*), prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.

It is a condition in four ways. However, for mind-contact (*manosamphassa*), those bases such as the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dhammārammaṇa*) are conditions solely by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
But the physical heart-base (*vatthurūpa*) is a condition for mind-contact in five ways:
by way of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). Thus is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It should be understood that this contact has many conditions.
To demonstrate through the method of negation (*vyatireka*) the point that consciousness is a specific condition for name-and-form at the moment of its first arising, the text states:
"If you had not descended into the mother’s womb," and so forth. This refers to rebirth-linking in the womb-dwelling state.

For indeed, from the outside, although it is as if one is entering the mother’s womb, in actual fact it is simply the first arising of the aggregates there according to their respective conditions. Therefore he said: “Having entered... you will not exist.
“Pure” means solely unmixed with, or devoid of, consciousness. “The remainder” refers to name; therefore, “the remainder is name-and-form.”

The meaning is: setting aside this consciousness, the remainder is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). "Descended by way of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhivasena okkanta*) means by way of grasping rebirth-linking;
or it refers to that which has entered [the womb] as the first stage of development for one descending into the mother's womb.
"You will turn back" (*vokkamissatha*) means you will undergo destruction, which is the severance of the continuity of existence; and that, indeed, is called death.
He said: "By way of death. "Its" refers to consciousness; and this is stated by way of the generality of consciousness. Therefore he said:
"by the cessation of that very mind," meaning by the cessation of the rebirth-linking mind itself. "From that" means from the rebirth-linking mind.

The meaning already stated—that there is no death through the cessation of the rebirth-linking mind, or through the cessation of the second or third moments of consciousness after it—is [here] reaffirmed.
In order to clarify this through reasoning, it was said: “By the rebirth-linking consciousness,” and so forth. “In this interval” means during this period of sixteen mind-moments.
Regarding the statement “there is no obstacle”: first, let there be no obstacle to the child’s death at that time, because a death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) is impossible then;
but how is it that for the mother there is likewise no obstacle to death at that time? Because [the life-span] does not exceed its respective duration.

Because in that very interval there is the nature of passing away, and because conception itself is impossible; therefore he said, "For this is called 'no opportunity,'" the intention being "at the moment of death.
"Material phenomena arisen together with the rebirth-linking consciousness" refers to the kamma-born material phenomena that arise at the moment of descent into the womb.

For those [material phenomena] are, in the direct sense, called "matter arisen together with the rebirth-linking consciousness," and not "temperature-born" (utu-samutthāna), because they arise after the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness's arising.
Furthermore, at that time, there is simply no possibility of matter born of consciousness (citta-ja) or matter born of nutriment (āhāra-ja).
Those material phenomena that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness are of three kinds at its moment of arising.
[They are] arisen at the moment of arising, arisen at the moment of presence, and arisen at the moment of dissolution.
Among these, those arisen at the moment of arising cease at the moment of arising of the seventeenth life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
those arisen at the moment of presence cease at the moment of presence; and those arisen at the moment of dissolution cease at the moment of dissolution. In that regard:
It cannot be said that "a decaying phenomenon is a condition for a decaying phenomenon," yet it can be said regarding arising and duration; thus it was stated:
"Because they exist during the moment of arising and the moment of duration of the seventeenth bhavaṅga, they are unable to give it a condition.
[This applies] only to one whose material body has been supported.
For indeed, the name-body (nāmakāya) functions in the five-aggregate plane. With reference to that consciousness being more powerful than those material phenomena, he said:
"Of the seventeenth... [etc.]... its occurrence occurs. "The lineage is maintained" means that the lineage of the forty-eight types of kamma-born matter proceeds in an uninterrupted connection.
For first there is the rebirth-linking consciousness, and from there up to the sixteenth [moment]...
The life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) has three moments each—arising, presence, and dissolution—for each of those [sixteen types].
In that regard, thirty-two kamma-born material phenomena arise during each of the three moments of every single consciousness.
Thus, there are forty-eight for the sixteenfold [set]. This same method applies to the subsequent sets as well. With reference to this, it was said: "Of the forty-eight kamma-born..."

"Having become connected, the stream of material form proceeds. However, "if they are not able" means if the material forms arisen together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) are not able to provide a condition for the seventeenth life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

For if the death-consciousness (cuticitta) were to occur as the seventeenth moment from the rebirth-linking consciousness, [it would follow that] even during the moments of the rebirth-linking consciousness's presence and dissolution...
Kamma-born materiality would not arise, let alone during the moments of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
That being the case, since that consciousness would find no supporting condition, its occurrence would not proceed; the continuity would not be joined, but would instead be utterly severed.
Therefore he said: "It is called 'emerging' (*vokkamati*)," and so forth.
"Itthattāya" means "in this state of being. This was said with reference to the personal existence (attabhāva) of one lying in the womb;
since for such a being the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) are indeed complete, he says, "for the sake of having the five aggregates thus fulfilled.
"Upacchijjissatha" means it would be cut off by the cessation of the continuity (santāna). "Suddhaṃ nāmarūpameva" means merely name-and-form (nāmarūpa) devoid of consciousness (viññāṇa).
It is merely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Completion" is the fullness of its parts; "growth" is the attainment of stability; "increase" is the attainment of maturity;

and "expansion" is the attainment of vastness. These occur respectively according to the stages of life, beginning with the first stage; thus it is said, "by way of the first stage," and so forth. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of non-restriction;
by it, the inclusion of two thousand years and other such durations should be understood.

“Consciousness alone” is a restrictive statement; it is a phrase for the purpose of negating a self as conceived by outsiders, as well as Īśvara and other such [deities], but it is not a phrase for the purpose of negating ignorance, contact, and so forth, because the restriction functions as a term that excludes its opposite. Therefore, he said:
“This very [consciousness] is the cause,” and so on. And this method should be applied accordingly to all preceding passages as well. Now, consciousness alone...
In order to clarify, by means of a simile, the meaning that name-and-form is the primary cause [of rebirth], it was said, "Just as... and so forth.

To show that name-and-form—both individually and when combined—is incapable of performing its own function without consciousness, there is the collective mention of them together as "you, name-and-form.
"Preceding" (*purecārika*) means simply "going before. For consciousness [is the precursor] of co-nascent phenomena...
It is the forerunner. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Phenomena are preceded by mind. "In many ways" means it acts as a condition in numerous modes.

How so? For consciousness—whether it be the rebirth-linking consciousness or another—is a ninefold condition for resultant-named matter at the moment of rebirth-linking, by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

It is a sevenfold condition for the physical base (vatthurūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking, by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

It is a condition in nine ways. However, with the exception of the physical basis (vatthurūpa), the remaining material phenomena serve as conditions for other material phenomena through eight of these nine conditions, excluding the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya).

Furthermore, kamma-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) serves as a condition for the materiality of non-percipient beings, or for kamma-born materiality in the five-aggregate plane, in only one way—namely, by way of decisive support (upanissaya) according to the Suttanta method.

It exists. For it should be understood that all remaining consciousness, from the first bhavaṅga onwards, serves as a condition for that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) according to its respective suitability.

This is the summary here; however, if the method of conditions were to be shown in detail, the entire discourse of the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa) would have to be cited, and thus it has not been elaborated upon. But how is this to be understood?
“Is it by way of the suttas and by way of reasoning that rebirth-linking mentality-materiality has consciousness as its condition? It is so both from the suttas and from reasoning.

For in the Pāḷi, the fact that feeling and the other [mental aggregates] have consciousness as their condition is presented in many ways, such as in the passage beginning, “states that follow upon consciousness.
As for reasoning, it is understood here that even though materiality born of consciousness is visible, consciousness is a condition for materiality that is not visible.
When forms corresponding to a clear or unclear mind arise, they are seen; and from what is seen, there is inference of what is not seen.
By this, it should be understood here that "consciousness is a condition for the rebirth-form (paṭisandhirūpa), even though it is not seen, by means of the visible form born of mind.
For this is also true of matter originated by kamma, as it is of matter originated by mind.
Just as [the relationship of] consciousness-conditionality is taught in the *Paṭṭhāna*, so too is it here.
Here, the word *samudaya* (arising) is used as a synonym for a collection (*samūha*), like the word *samudāya* (assemblage); thus he says, "the origin of a mass of suffering.
"Solitary" means without a companion, devoid of a retinue of kings; the intention is: "We would see your status as a king only when apart from us."

For one who delights an assembly according to what is appropriate is called a "king" (rājā). "From the perspective of purpose" means that because the purpose is accomplished, it is as if one speaks even when not speaking.
By the term "heart-base" (*hadayavatthu*) itself, it should be understood that its support is also included.

Because of its state of being immediate (*ānantariya*), both the supported and the support are called simply "support" (*nissaya*). [If you say] it might be the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), this is not so.
The meaning is that "it is possible. Therefore he said, "we might see," and so forth. "In many ways" means it is a condition in various manners. How so?
First, name (nāma) is a condition for consciousness in seven ways during rebirth-linking:

by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, association, presence, and non-disappearance. Furthermore, some among these act as a root-condition (hetu-paccaya), while others act as a nutriment-condition (āhāra-paccaya).

In this way, there are other ways in which it acts as a condition. However, non-resultant mind, setting aside the resultant condition among those conditions already mentioned, acts as a condition by means of the remaining six conditions. Furthermore, some of these act as a condition by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and some by way of the nutriment-condition (*āhārapaccaya*);
thus there are other ways in which it acts as a condition, and that occurs only during the course of existence (*pavatti*), not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
As for materiality, however, the heart-base is a condition for consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking in six ways:
by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

During the course of existence, it is a condition in five ways—excluding the conditions of conascence and mutuality—and by those same conditions together with the condition of prenascence. [This applies to] the divisions beginning with the eye-base.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the fivefold materiality is a condition for consciousness—distinguished as eye-consciousness and so forth—in its respective order, by way of the conditions of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
Thus, name-and-form is a condition for consciousness in many ways.
This refers to the successive manner in which name-and-form is a condition for consciousness, and how consciousness is a condition for rebirth-linking name-and-form.

Showing that this [process]—whether it be predominant over consciousness at one time, predominant over name-and-form (nāmarūpa) at another, or equal to both at yet another—is thus threefold and is nevertheless grasped together as a single unit by the phrase "to this extent" (ettāvatā), he says: "While consciousness...
is proceeding," and further: "And this consciousness, by way of mutual dependence upon the five aggregates termed name-and-form..."
Showing that by this much alone all the processes of the round of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*) proceed, he said: "By this much...

[etc. ...rebirths. Therein, "by this much" means by this much alone, and not by anything other than this—neither by a self characterized as an agent or an experiencer, nor by a Lord (*issara*), and so forth;
for this word contains an internal restriction (*antogadha-avadhāraṇa*).

“With reference to mere words” means that, because [the referent] is not actually so—as in the case of the word *Sirivaḍḍhaka* applied to slaves and the like—it occurs having made mere words its object.
Therefore he said, “without seeing the actual meaning. “Of conventional usage” means of mere verbal designation.
“Path” means the course, the way, the domain of occurrence. Because a person is called “virtuous” by way of the act of taking refuge...
It is called "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*) by way of the activity of clear comprehension; therefore it is said, "by way of a designation for the cause.
*Utti* is etymology (*nirutti*) after having determined the cause.

They call it "description" (*paññatti*) because it makes known a single meaning through various modes, such as "wise" (*paṇḍita*) and so forth. For that very same person is described (*paññāpiyati*) as "wise," "clever," and "intelligent."
Furthermore, one is designated as "wise" (*paṇḍita*) by way of the mode of wisdom (*paṇḍicca*), and as "clever" (*byatta*) by way of the mode of proficiency (*veyyattiya*);
thus, it is a "designation" (*paññatti*) because of being designated in such modes.

Since, in this context, the terms *adhivacana*, *nirutti*, and *paññatti* have the same meaning, and every word partakes of the nature of a designation and so forth, therefore, [the term is applied] specifically to certain particular words that function in a specific manner.

It should be understood that this interpretation of the meaning has been made with the following intention: by means of terms such as *adhivacana* (designation), all verbal expressions are stated because they share the common characteristic of illuminating the meaning of a designation (*paññatti*).
Alternatively, the prefix *adhi* signifies "above" or "over"; thus, a statement that stands above [others] is a *adhivacana*. Above what? Above that which is to be illuminated.
"Of the meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to that meaning which is manifest. Alternatively, "designation" (*adhivacana*) is speech that is dependent; on what is it dependent? On the meaning.

Likewise, "language" (*nirutti*) is speech determined or fixed by the elucidation of this or that particular meaning. "Description" (*paññatti*) is so called because it makes known things such as the earth-element or a person in their respective modes.
In this way, the application of the terms "designation" and the others to all words should be understood; otherwise, [it would not be so].
It would follow that terms such as *sirivaḍḍhaka*, *dhanavaḍḍhaka*, and *kappakāra* would themselves be etymologies (*nirutti*), and terms such as *paṇḍita* and *viyatta*—
which indicate the same single meaning through their various modes of expression— would themselves be designations (*paññatti*). Thus,
even the course of activity of the conventional usage expressed by these three names, together with consciousness, must be accepted as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) to this extent.
Therefore he said “iti,” and so forth. “To be traversed by wisdom” means it should be set in motion by wisdom; the sense is that it is to be known. Therefore he said “to be understood.
“The round” (vaṭṭa) refers to the threefold round: the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), and the round of result (vipākavaṭṭa).
“It turns” (vattati) means it proceeds. This [is the meaning] of the sense expressed by the five phrases beginning with “might one be born,” etc.
This is stated by way of conclusion. By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of terms such as "woman" and "man" should also be understood.

"For the purpose of making known the designation of names" means for the purpose of making known the designations of names such as aggregates (khandha), contact (phassa), beings (satta), woman, and so forth. The basis (vatthu) is also included within this much. Therefore he said:
"Even the pentad of aggregates is made known by this much alone. "By this much" means by this extent; the meaning is: with consciousness, there is the occurrence of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Commentary on the Designation of Self (Attapaññatti) 117.
It is called *anusandhi* because one is connected by means of it; that is, the subsequent teaching which proceeds by way of connecting with the teaching that has come down previously.
That [connection] was shown for the first term; now, it is to be shown for the second term—this is the meaning.
Demonstrating this, he said, "Thus the Blessed One," and so forth. "Rūpin" means possessing form. "Paritta" means not extensive;

the sense is that it is limited. Since there is no such thing as a "self" in the ultimate sense, but it is merely a conceptual construct of those who hold wrong views, he therefore demonstrates where their perception of a self occurs and how their conceptualization of its state as having form and so forth takes place.

He says, “*Yo*,” and so forth. “Possessing form and limited” (*rūpiṃ parittaṃ*): he possesses form by way of the form of the *kasiṇa* that has appeared to himself; it is limited because of its non-expanded state. “He describes” (*paññapeti*): one who has attained various *kasiṇas* by way of the blue *kasiṇa* and others. “That” (*taṃ*): the self. “Infinite” (*anantaṃ*): because the sign of the *kasiṇa* is immeasurable, the boundary does not appear, and thus it is devoid of limits. “Having removed” (*ugghāṭetvā*): *Yo rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapeti, taṃ anantaṃ uggahetvā rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapeti.* “He who describes the self as possessing form and limited, having grasped that [self] as infinite, describes the self as possessing form and infinite. “Having grasped” (*uggahetvā*): having taken hold of. “Possessing form” (*rūpiṃ*): possessing form by way of the form of the *kasiṇa* that has appeared to oneself. “Infinite” (*anantaṃ*): because the sign of the (*attā
Having removed [the perception] by means of meditation. "The space touched by the sign" (*nimittaphuṭṭhokāsa*) refers to the area pervaded by that *kasiṇa* sign.
"Among those" (*tesu*) refers to the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*). "Merely consciousness" (*viññāṇamattameva*) refers to one who holds the doctrine:

"The self consists of consciousness" (*viññāṇamayo attā*). 118. The word "now" (*etarahi*) is used here with a restrictive sense; showing its meaning, he says "only now" (*idāneva*), thereby applying the restriction.
He stated that the matter has been concluded with the words, “not beyond this. In that context, one who asserts that beings are annihilated right there and then is an annihilationist (ucchedavādī);
therefore he said, “this was spoken by way of annihilation. That which exists eternally and is indestructible is “ever-existent” (bhāvin);
therefore he said, “this was spoken by way of eternalism” (sassata). “Not having such an intrinsic nature” means that its nature is not as the opponent claims it to be.

“Tathābhāvāya” means for the state of annihilation (ucchedabhāva) or for the state of eternalism (sassatabhāva). This is stated as an indefinite expression by way of a general indication. “Sampādessāmi” means:
having made his suchness (tathābhāva) accomplished, I shall demonstrate it; the sense is that I shall establish it. For he will say later:
“Having made him understand the doctrine of eternalism,” and so forth. “Iminā” refers to the passage beginning with “Or else, that which is not such,” etc.

By the word "vacanena" (by means of a statement), the intention is that although it is of a nature that is not subject to annihilation, it is [so described] according to the perspective of those who hold the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavādin*).
"Upakappessāmi" means I shall approach and empower.

"Evaṃ samānaṃ" means being such as it has become. "Rūpakasiṇajjhānaṃ" (the jhāna of the material kasiṇa) refers to "rūpa" by the elision of the latter member of the compound, in the sense of attainment.

Because he possesses that [form], he is called "possessing form" (*rūpī*); thus it says: "One possessing form is one who has attained the kasiṇa of form. Regarding the phrase "the view of limited self," here too the word "possessing form" should be supplied according to the method of ellipsis and so forth;
for that proponent of a wrong view stands adhering to his own state of possessing form just as he does to its limited nature.
The same method applies here to the term "formless" (*arūpī*). [The text continues: "By way of the summary of a grove abounding in *pattapalāsa* trees..."
They say that a *vallī* is a creeper with a mass of thick, tangled roots and not very long shoots, whereas a *latā* is the opposite of that.

"In the sense of being unabandoned" means by way of not having been eradicated by the Path. The sense of "underlying tendency" (*anusaya*) is the state of being ready to arise when the necessary conditions are obtained.
What is called an "immaterial kasiṇa" (*arūpakasiṇa*) is space as the removal of the kasiṇa-object, not the limited-space kasiṇa. "Both are indeed immaterial kasiṇas."

Some [say]: "Having the immaterial aggregates as its domain" (*arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ*): the immaterial aggregates, such as feeling and so forth, are the domain (*gocara*) for the dogmatic insistence (*abhinivesa*) that they are "self";

thus it is one whose domain consists of the immaterial aggregates, namely, a holder of a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*). The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative already mentioned. As for the grammatical construction (*saddayojanā*):

"one who possesses the immaterial" (*arūpī*) is so called because he possesses the immaterial—the immaterial aggregates—which have become his domain; thus, "him, the one possessing the immaterial" (*taṃ arūpiṃ*).
"The four who are 'possessors' (lābhino)" refers to the four types of speculative theorists (*diṭṭhigatika*) who, by way of attaining various meditation subjects such as the *kasiṇas*,
themselves imagine and then adopt and take up those respective views and establish them. "Their pupils" (*antevāsika*) refers to those who,
having learned those proponents' doctrines both directly and through tradition, accept and approve of them exactly as they are and establish them.

The four theorists: these are the four who, not having attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna) based on the kasiṇas, stand having themselves adhered to and taken up the aforementioned four views merely by means of speculative reasoning.
Their pupils are to be understood in the manner previously described.
Commentary on the Designation of Persons (Naṭṭhapaññatti-vaṇṇanā) 119. "One who has begun insight" means one who practices insight for the sake of future lives;
by this, he shows a person established in powerful insight. "Even one who is not learned does not designate [the self]"—this is the intended meaning. For such is the power of insight.
Even one belonging to the Dispensation who has attained jhāna and direct knowledge (abhiññā) cannot be said not to "conceptualize" (paññapeti); therefore, he is not mentioned here.
Now, the reason for their non-conceptualization is shown by the words beginning with "For these... and so forth.

"Thus indeed is the knowledge," meaning there is no erroneous grasping because that cause [of error] has been cast far away. The construction is: "There is the knowledge that 'these are merely the formless aggregates'."
Commentary on the Contemplation of Self (Attasamanupassanā) 121.
This is contemplating by way of views, not by way of knowledge. And that contemplation, in terms of its meaning, consists in the seeing of views.
The phrase “he contemplates feeling as self” refers to the personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) based on the aggregate of feeling, as it has been handed down.
"Because one does not experience an object distinguished as desirable and so forth, it is called 'non-experiencing' (*appaṭisaṃvedano*).

By way of negating the state of being an experiencer, the states of perceiving and so on are also negated, since they are inseparable from that; thus he says, "By this, the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) based on the aggregate of form is explained.
With the phrase "my self experiences," he negates the state of non-experiencing.
Therefore he said, "nor is it without experiencing. By the phrase "subject to feeling" (*vedanādhamma*), however, he rejects the claim, "Feeling is my self.
For one who possesses a phenomenon (*dhamma*) consisting of feeling is called "subject to feeling";
thus, he acknowledges that the state of being endowed with feeling belongs to that [self]. Therefore he said, "And for this [self], the nature of being subject to feeling is inseparable."

The connection is established by bringing in the statement: "The view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is said to have the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness as its basis.

Regarding the phrase "because it is associated with feeling, it feels," this expresses that [the self] performs that function through association with it, just as a person is called "intentional" due to connection with volition (cetanā).
The experience of the object is indeed obtainable for all those phenomena that possess an object; however, that occurs merely through partial contact.
Feeling (vedanā), however, is the experiencing of the flavor of the object by way of its own mastery when it has become relaxed.
By virtue of that [feeling], perception and the other [mental factors] are also said to "feel" because they are associated with it. For thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
"Having reached the state of experiencing the flavor of the object, the remaining associated states experience only a mere portion," using the illustration of the king’s cook.

This meaning has already been explained there. "Of this" refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with perception (*saññā*). By the phrase "having a nature inseparable [from them]," he indicates a specific state produced by non-separation (*avisaṃyoga*).
122. "Therein" means among those sections. "Among the three types of speculative theorists" refers to those who hold the views: "Feeling is my self," and "The one without feeling..."
Regarding those three types of speculative views who assert: “My self is feeling,” or “My self is subject to the nature of feeling”:
because the three feelings have distinct natures, for one who regards pleasant feeling as “self,” it is not logical to regard painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as “self.
Thus he said in the remaining two cases: “Whichever [feeling] whichever [person]...”
“He regards feeling as self.
By the phrase “because of having been and then not being,” he shows that [feeling] is impermanent due to its possession of arising and passing away;
by the phrase “by this and that,” etc., he shows it is conditioned because it is constructed by various causes. “That respective condition” refers to the faculty, the object, and consciousness.

“Contact to be experienced as pleasant,” and so forth—these have arisen by way of their respective causes, depending upon and relying on those very causes, through the method (ñāya) of being free from the states of eternalism and the like, as well as the states of annihilationism and the like; that is, by way of an equal cause, a corresponding cause, and a suitable cause.
“Of the nature of destruction” means subject to destruction; “of the nature of decay” means subject to decay; “of the nature of fading away” means...
“Having the nature of dispassion” means having the nature of cessation; by all four terms, he demonstrates precisely the state of dissolution of feeling.
Therefore he said: “‘Destruction’... ‘having the nature of destruction,’ and so forth.
“Passed away” means passed away through the departure of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). “Of one alone” means of one particular theorist (*diṭṭhigatika*). “In all three times” means...

"During the times of the occurrence of the three feelings. He asks with the underlying intention: "What indeed could it mean to say 'this is my self'—that 'this nature of pleasant feeling, this nature of painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, is my self'?
How can one who is not insane accept that a single thing possesses such diverse natures?
The other replies, "But will it not be so? and so forth, showing that even for him [the opponent], this is certainly not the case.
"By distinction" means by way of the classification into pleasure and so forth. In the phrase "pleasure and pain," the word "and" includes neutral feeling (*adukkhamasukha*);
or rather, it is included under pleasure because of its state of being peaceful and subtle. "Without distinction" means without classification, by way of the commonality of feeling.
"Intermingled" means mixed with the divisions of pleasure and so forth. This [feeling] is that threefold feeling.
The one who holds to a wrong view (diṭṭhigatika), having grasped [the aggregates] together as a single unit, regards them as "self.
Furthermore, it would follow that many feelings arise simultaneously, because there is no distinction in the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of feelings.

For if that were the case, since the self would always involve the occurrence of all feelings, the holder of the wrong view would have to admit—even in a single moment—the arising of many feelings through that mistaken path. Thus, for him...
By not allowing for an opportunity [to refute him], he says, "There is no arising of many feelings at one moment";
the intention is that this is contradicted by direct perception (*paccakkha*).

By this, it is meant that this view is not acceptable to the wise—both because of this proof of contradiction and because of its total non-existence; the meaning is that the steadfast do not accept this doctrine.
124. Even in a continuity of material form bound up with the sense-faculties, some kind of activity is obtained by way of the diffusion of the air-element.
Thus, taking as an illustration precisely that pure aggregate of material form where the diffusion of the air-element is sometimes found, he says:
"in a palm-leaf fan or at a window. In the phrase "among things possessing the nature of feeling" (vedanādhammesu), it means among those possessing the nature of feeling.
By the phrase “I am,” the manner in which the conceit of “I” arises by grasping the three aggregates together as one is stated.
By the phrase “This I am,” however, the manner in which the conceit of “I” arises by grasping them individually is stated.
Therefore he said, “Even a single dhamma,” and so forth. “That” refers to the arising of the conceit of “I” as “I am”; for that [conceit] ceases through the cessation of the four aggregates.
“Since no basis for them is perceived, they would not exist, just as the sharpness of a rabbit’s horn [does not exist]. By this much— that is,
by this extent of the teaching delivered through the demonstration of the connection for the phrase “born like a tangled skein,” beginning with “And to what extent,
Ānanda”— although the discussion of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) was indeed already spoken below, here however...

The discourse has been presented as an exposition demonstrating how wrong view is a great offense by way of revealing its inability to lift one’s head from the round of existence for one who holds such views;

showing this, he said, “the discourse on the round has been told. One might ask: since ignorance and craving are the roots of the round, why was the discourse on the round told here in a manner other than by addressing those two? To answer this, he said, “For the Blessed One,” and so forth.
"By making ignorance the head" means making ignorance the foremost limb; the meaning is "by way of ignorance.

"The limit is not discerned" means that the beginning or boundary of ignorance—such as "ignorance arose at the time of such-and-such a Perfectly Enlightened One or a Wheel-turning Monarch, but it did not exist before that"—is not discerned even by my unimpeded knowledge of omniscience.
The meaning is: "because it does not exist. This condition is *idappaccaya* (this-condition); therefore, from this condition (*idappaccayā*), meaning from this cause such as the taints (*āsava*).
"Of craving for existence" means of craving that constitutes the fetter of existence. "Of views regarding existence" means of the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*).
By the phrase "arising here and there," [the text indicates] the boundless succession of rebirths in this manner: "from here to there, and from there to here."
He shows this. Therefore he said, “In the great ocean,” and so forth.

(126) “Of one who is confused about the mode of conditions” (*paccayākāramūḷhassa*) is a statement of fact (*bhūtakathana*), not a qualification; for every follower of a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*) is indeed confused about the mode of conditions.
“When speaking of the turning away” (*vivaṭṭaṃ kathento*): it is called “turning away” (*vivaṭṭa*) because it is liberated from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); it is liberation (*vimokkha*).

While explaining that: "Of the doer" means of one who acts upon the Teacher’s instruction; the meaning is, of one who practices rightly. Therefore he said, "of one who dwells in the foundations of mindfulness.

For such a person, through the right practice of the contemplation of feelings and the contemplation of mental phenomena, is worthy of being described by such statements as, "he does not regard feeling as self," and so forth. Therefore he said, "one of such a kind..."
"‘No,’ and so forth. ‘In all phenomena’ means in all phenomena belonging to the three planes; for these are what are to be comprehended.

‘Nothing other than that’ means he does not regard any phenomenon other than feeling—such as perception and so on—as a self. ‘The world of the aggregates, etc. refers specifically to phenomena such as form;
in order to show that it is their collection, it is said ‘in phenomena such as form. He does not cling."

“By way of the seizing of views and craving. Since the conceit that occurs as “I am superior,” and so forth, is likewise of the nature of agitation—just like the conceits of craving and views—he said:
“Also by way of the agitation of craving, views, and conceit. If one were to say, “That is a view of such a kind for the Arahant,” that would be improper; it is not tenable.

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "such is his view" (*evamassa diṭṭhī*), it should also be construed here by beginning with: "Such a kind of view belongs to this Arahant," and so forth.
For if that were the case, the meaning would be: "If one were to say, 'The Tathāgata exists after death;
such is his view,' and if that statement of his were indeed so [true], then it would be said that 'the Arahant knows nothing' because of having such a view."
Because of their non-existence. "By that very reason" means precisely because it is improper to speak in such a manner.
Regarding "of all four positions," this refers to the four sections presented as "Does the Tathāgata exist [after death]?

and so forth. It is said, "At the end he spoke 'And why is that? etc.," because [the teaching] was condensed in the first three sections and expanded upon in the final section. "In the first three sections, the teaching proceeded in exactly that same way..."
Some say: "As in the concluding section, the text (pāḷi) has been abbreviated.

Conventional expression (*vohāra*) refers to the expressions to be used, such as "a being," "woman," "man," and so forth; "aggregates" and "bases," and so forth; and "contact," "feeling," and so forth.
Briefly stated, these alone are the bases for the occurrence of that conventional expression.

He said: "The aggregates, the bases, and the elements. Since Nibbāna is made known in the preliminary stage precisely as the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), it follows that it too can be approached by way of the aggregates; thus it is said: "The pentad of aggregates is to be approached by wisdom.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception..."
“...I proclaim the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.
Alternatively, the term “sphere of wisdom” (*paññāvacara*) refers to the grasping of phenomena belonging to the three planes; thus it is called simply the “five aggregates.

Therefore, even in the phrase “to the extent of wisdom,” it should be understood that only mundane wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*) is being referred to, for this is a discourse concerning the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
For it is said: "To whatever extent the round rolls on. Therefore he said: "The connection has been shown just like that of the words in a tangled skein.

Because the Blessed One, having here spoken the discourse on the round from the standpoint of views, also spoke the discourse on the round by way of the sequential connection, therefore the statement "the connection has been shown just like that of the words in a tangled skein" is emphatic.

This has been stated. However, it should be understood that the discussion on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) here has been elaborated solely for the purpose of elucidating its profound nature;
likewise, although the discussion on the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭakathā*) is similar, it is not included here.
The Explanation of the Seven Stations of Consciousness (*sattaviññāṇaṭṭhiti-vaṇṇanā*).
127. "Going, going": having become well-established in the practice of serenity (*samatha*), one goes by means of the progress of insight (*vipassanā*) and the progress of the path (*magga*).
Because he is liberated from both sides, he is called "one liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).
He is described as "not viewing thus" because he is considered a follower of insight (*vipassanā-yānika*); thus it is said: "And he who does not view..."

"He is called such because, as he goes along and goes along, he becomes one liberated by wisdom"—thus it was said. "Of those spoken of above" refers to the two passages that appeared earlier in the Canon:
"In what way, Ānanda, does one not describe a self, nor cause a self to be described?
and so forth, and "When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu no longer regards feeling as self," and so forth.
"Of ordinary bhikkhus. "Exit" means deliverance (*nissaraṇa*). "Name" refers to names such as "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*).

"Stated by way of rebirth-linking" means that the seven stations of consciousness are stated by way of rebirth-linking distinguished by the specific qualities of diversity of body and diversity of perception.
For it is by way of dependence upon each respective group of beings (*sattanikāya*) that there is diversity of body and so forth.
It should be understood as "arisen from the rebirth-linking included therein" because the kamma-existence that produces it has been accumulated in such a way.
"Four will come" means that the four stations of consciousness—by way of the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and formations—will arrive, according to such passages as:
"Or, friends, consciousness, finding a support in form, persists. "Of the establishment of consciousness... [The remainder of the sentence follows].
Regarding the cause for the present establishment of rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*):

in terms of its actual meaning, one should understand that these are the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations in the five-aggregate realm, and the three aggregates beginning with feeling in the four-aggregate realm—distinguished by the specific qualities mentioned.

With reference to their status as abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*), it is said, "two bases" (*dve ca āyatanāni*), meaning two places of dwelling. This is also a figurative expression for a place of dwelling.
The word *āyatana* (base) occurs here as in the expression "the two divine bases" (*devāyatanadvaya*). "All" refers to the entirety of the stations of consciousness and the two bases;
thus, the intention is that nothing therein has been left ungrasped. [One might ask: "Does this not fail to achieve a complete inclusion?
It does not, because the rounds of existence (*vaṭṭa*), the stations of consciousness, and the two bases are mutually inclusive of one another.
The particle [“seyyathāpi”] has the sense of illustration; therefore, “seyyathāpi manussā” means “just as humans.
There is indeed a distinction because, although there is no difference in the external agent, there is a difference in the internal one.

They are called “diverse-bodied” (nānattakāyā) because there is diversity in their bodies, or because their bodies are diverse; in this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well.
They are called "beings" (*nesanti*) among humans. Because they possess various perceptions, they are "those with diverse perceptions" (*nānattasaññino*).

Because there is for them a falling away (*vinipāta*) from the mass of happiness, they are "those who have fallen away" (*vinipātikā*); this is because, despite being gods, they lack divine prosperity, or because there is no non-falling (*anipāta*) for them once they have gone to the states of misery. Therefore he said: "freed from the four states of misery. [The term] *dhammapada*.

The section on the factors of the Dhamma beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "Having understood" means having first understood by means of knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).
Following that, by cultivating appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), may we also practice the right way of conduct beginning with purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
And that practice would be for our benefit—namely, for all benefits pertaining to the present life and so forth. Now, regarding the practice of virtue therein:
Showing this through a classification, he spoke the verse beginning with “And among living beings.
They are called *brahmakāyikā* because they exist within the *brahmakāya*—the assembly of Brahmas produced by the first jhāna—or within the *brahmanikāya*.
They are called *brahmapārisajjā* because they exist within the retinue (*parisā*) of Mahābrahmā, standing in the position of his attendants (*paricāraka*). Of Mahābrahmā...

They are called *Brahmapurohitas* because they stand in the position of chaplains (*purohita*) to Brahmā. They are called *Mahābrahmās* because they are great Brahmās by virtue of their long life, beauty, and other such qualities.

Although all three of these types are produced by the first *jhāna*, the following was stated—beginning with "But the *Brahmapārisajjas*"—to show that there is this distinction based on the specific mode of the *jhāna*'s occurrence. "By the limited" means by the inferior; that...
Its inferiority is to be understood from the inferiority of zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors, or it is inferior because it is merely acquired.
"Of an aeon" (*kappassa*) means of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*). It is called "middling" because it exists between the inferior and the superior;

its middling nature is to be understood from the middling nature of zeal and the other factors, or it is middling because, having been acquired, it has not been well-cultivated. "Half an aeon" (*upaḍḍhakappa*)—
It is half a *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*. "More extensive" means it is larger in measure than the *brahmapārisajja* gods and more sublime in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For it is indeed more sublime even by way of its intrinsic nature; however, that [nature] is immeasurable here.

Thus, although there is a difference in intrinsic nature between the bodies of the *parittābha* and so forth, and the *parittasubha* and so forth, they are nevertheless described by way of their unity.
Because they are determined as such, they are called "of a single body. "Exalted" means superior;

and this superiority should be understood as the superiority of zeal and the other [factors]. Alternatively, it is called "exalted" because it has been well-developed, brought to mastery, and led to a state of excellence.
Here too, a "kalpa" should be understood in the sense of an incalculable kalpa (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*) for one who is complete.
Because of the impossibility of a great eon (*mahākappa*). "Thus" (*iti*) means in the manner just described.

"They" (*te*) refers to the three types of Brahmās mentioned as "the Brahmakāyika gods. "Due to the unity of perception" (*saññāya ekattā*) means because perception has a single nature due to the state of being endowed with three roots;
for there is no other distinction in that perception apart from its associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
Thus, by this [phrase], he shows that they are "those with diversity of body and unity of perception.
*Daṇḍaukkāya* means by means of a staff-torch. *Saratīti* means it runs as it were. *Vissaratīti* means it runs as if scattered about.
*Dve kappā* means two great aeons (*mahākappa*). The same method applies to those following this. *Idha* means in this sutta. By way of the highest limit...
By the mention of the Ābhassara (Radiant) realm alone, both the Parittābhā (Limited Radiance) and Appamāṇābhā (Immeasurable Radiance) realms are included.

"Subhā" means beautiful radiance; what is strewn with such radiance is "subhakiṇṇa. While it would have been called "subhakiṇṇā," the vowel *ā* was shortened and the final letter *ṇa* was changed to *ha*, thus it is stated as "subhakiṇhā.
Furthermore, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is explained as being due to a radiance that is steady and of a single mass.

“*Subha* is a term used figuratively (*pariyāya-vacana*); its meaning is stated as ‘strewn and scattered with beauty. Here too, it should be understood that the final letter *ṇa* is intended to be changed to *ha*.
It does not proceed by breaking up into fragments because of its solid, unified nature.

They belong specifically to the fourth station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) because of the body’s and perception’s uniformity. This is due to the fruit of abundant, peaceful happiness, long life, beauty, and so forth.”
"Those of great fruit. "In this" means in the station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

They are established on the side of turning away (*vivaṭṭapakkha*) because they do not return [to saṃsāra]. Having said, "not for all time," in order to clarify that very state of not being for all time, it was stated:
"even for a hundred thousand eons," and so forth. This refers to those who have arisen after the passing of sixteen thousand eons.

Because the Brahmas of the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) attain final Nibbāna and because others do not arise there, that place becomes empty when the world is empty of a Buddha; therefore, the Pure Abodes are not permanent, and the planes of the Pure Abodes are like a military encampment.
By this very Sutta, through the indication that the Pure Abodes are among the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), their status as stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) is established.

It has been explained; therefore, even the Suddhāvāsa deities belong to the fourth station of consciousness among the seven stations of consciousness, and to the fourth abode of beings among the nine abodes of beings.
"Subtlety" means having reached a state of subtlety where only a residue of formations remains. Because there is an absence of the manifest function of consciousness, they are neither...

"Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) does not mean "non-consciousness" (*aviññāṇa*), because there is no such thing as total non-consciousness; therefore, it is not spoken of in relation to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) that possess the function of manifest consciousness.
"And that station of consciousness" refers to the first station of consciousness, according to the method explained above in its specific form.
One understands it through the classification of humans and so forth, by way of summary, and by way of its division into "name and form.
"And its origin": one understands the twenty-fivefold origin of that first station of consciousness.

The same method applies to its passing away. "Its gratification": from the fact that it is to be relished, one understands the gratification as gratification. This state of impermanence and so forth is the danger. Craving and lust [are the escape].
By means of this one is disciplined, or one goes toward this; thus, the "discipline of desire and lust" (chandarāgavinaya) refers to Nibbāna together with the Path.
The same principle applies here to the "abandonment of desire and lust" as well.

Alternatively, delighting in the thought "I am" by way of conceit and views, or "mine" by way of craving, should be regarded as a form of agitation similar to that of conceit. "In all cases" means in all the remaining eight sections.
"Therein" refers to the second bases among the three stations of consciousness mentioned above; for there, material form does not exist.
Again, "therein" refers to the first base; for there, there is only the single aggregate of material form. And the word "here" is also said with reference to that very same [first base];
for since material form there is produced by kamma, its connection by way of nutriment is not possible.

Regarding the phrase "Yato kho" (when indeed): here the word *to* expresses time, just like the word *dā*, as in such passages as "Yato kho, Sāriputta, bhikkhusaṅgho" ("When indeed, Sāriputta, the community of monks...").
Thus it is said, "yadā kho" (when indeed). "Without grasping" means without grasping any conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) by way of [the notions] "this is mine," and so forth.
"Liberated through wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) is because the eight liberations have not been attained and because there is an absence of the extraordinary power of concentration (*samādhi*).
He is liberated by the power of wisdom alone. Therefore, it was said: "Without having realized the eight liberations, but by the power of wisdom alone," and so forth.
Having brought about non-occurrence in the future, he is one who understands and is thus "liberated through wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*).

Or, one who understands and penetrates the four truths through modes such as full comprehension, even without the contact of the first jhāna, and reaches the culmination of those functions, is liberated through wisdom.
He is "liberated" (vimutta) because he is specifically freed from the state of having duties yet to be fulfilled. He is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta).
He is a "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkhavipassaka) because his insight is dry, coarse, or unsmeared due to the absence of the moisture of serenity meditation (samatha-bhāvanā);

thus he is a "dry-insight practitioner. "Having stood" means having stood by way of making it a foundation. "In one or another" (aññatarasmiṃ) means in this or that, that is, in each one. For in this way, his fivefold nature [is established].
It might be so. By the phrase, “He does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with the body,” the absence of an especially eminent power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is indicated.
By the phrase, “And having seen with wisdom,” etc., the presence of an especially eminent power of wisdom (*paññā-bala*) is indicated.

Regarding the statement, “Having seen with wisdom, his taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed”: it is not that the taints see with wisdom; rather, because of the act of seeing, the taints are destroyed.
They are said to be "exhausted, having seen them exhausted" because their exhaustion is dependent upon vision;
for vision is the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
Commentary on the Eight Liberations (*vimokkha*).
129. "Of one bhikkhu" refers to one among the seven noble persons (ariyapuggala).

The name "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) arises from the mastery of the way of practice consisting in full understanding and so forth through the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) and other factors. "Of the other" refers to the one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
Indeed, it was with reference to these two that it was previously stated, "of two bhikkhus. "In what sense" means in what intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
Indeed, the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is called "the goal" (*attha*) because it is to be known as it truly is by means of knowledge;
