that very same [nature], by changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, is spoken of as "the aim" (*aṭṭha*). "In the sense of resolute confidence" (*adhimuccanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of releasing (*muccana*) more than usual (*adhika*), with distinction (*savisesa*);
by this [phrase], although all fine-material-sphere jhāna is likewise liberated from its opposites by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), [it is distinguished].
That specific mode of development by which that jhāna proceeds, having been exceptionally liberated from its opposites, is illustrated here.

For indeed, even among those belonging to the same class, there is a distinction in the mode of manifestation due to a difference in development, just as is the case with one who has attained through view compared to one liberated through faith.
Likewise, it is because of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states that it is thus...
It is also called "liberation" (vimokkha) in the sense of being well-resolved through the state of non-restraint, through fearlessness, and through delight.
Therefore he said, "And in the object," and so forth. But this meaning—namely, this sense of being resolved—is absent in cessation, the last liberation;
there only the sense of being liberated is found. He will explain that himself later on.
"Material" (*rūpī*) means that by means of the material form included within one's own continuity, there is a distinguished material form which serves as the cause for that jhāna;
and because the word "material" (*rūpī*) indicates an intensification of meaning, it is by means of that distinguished material form that one is called "material.
Thus, the very jhāna obtained through the material form included within one's own continuity is what establishes the state of being "material" here in the ultimate sense.
It should be understood as such. Therefore he said, "internal," and so forth. "Rūpajjhāna" means "form-meditation," by the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
However, in the case of "rūpāni," the elision of the former member (*purimapadalopa*) should be understood.

Thus it was said: "forms such as the blue kasiṇa. Perception of the kasiṇa-forms is "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*); one who possesses that is "one possessing perception of form" (*rūpasaññī*). He refers to the jhāna by way of its constituent perception (*saññā*). By way of its negation—
“He has no perception of form. Therefore he said, “internally he has no perception of form,” and so forth.

By the statement, “In internal absorption there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) toward ‘the beautiful’ (*subha*),” he shows that such a resolution (*adhimutti*) may arise by way of prior mental application.
In this way, the objection regarding the possibility of being described in that manner here is effectively countered. Because [the object] is well-purified...
In the case of the color-kasinas such as blue and so forth, for those who have practiced them there, the sense of "resolute determination" (adhimuccana) arises through the power of delight;
therefore, the third liberation is described in that manner in the Commentary.
However, because meditation proceeding by way of loving-kindness perceives beings as not repulsive, it proceeds only after having become resolutely determined toward them.
Therefore, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is stated that "the development of the divine abodes is a sublime liberation.
One should understand that these two [statements] do not contradict each other, as they are expressed through their respective methods.
"In all" means without remainder; for not even a single portion of the four formless aggregates remains there.

"Because of its purity" means because it has been ceased at the time previously delimited. It is called "the supreme liberation" because it must be attained by noble ones (ariya) alone, because it culminates in the fruit of the noble ones, and because it is the state of attaining Nibbāna in this very life (diṭṭheva dhamme).
"From the beginning" means from the first attainment onwards. "As far as the final attainment" means up to that point.
"Not having stood" means not having stood in any attainment whatsoever; the meaning is that one enters [the attainments] continuously, both in direct order and in reverse order.
Therefore he said: "It is stated by way of moving here and there. "Wishes to enter" means he desires to attain.
In that context, "he attains" or "he enters" refers to the person possessing the attainment who has entered each respective state.
It is stated thus because it is considered to be "as if" [liberated].
"Liberated by two parts" means: by two parts of liberation—namely, by the liberation of suppression through the formless jhāna, and by the liberation of eradication through the Path;
and by two parts of that which is to be liberated—namely, from the material body by means of the formless attainment, and from the mental body by means of the Path.
And he is liberated. Therefore, it says, “by the attainment of the formless,” and so forth. For “liberated” means liberated from the defilements;
and while being liberated, one is liberated from the two bodies by means of the suppression and eradication of the defilements—this is the meaning here.
And in the verse, for the brahmin Upasīva, who had attained the base of nothingness, the Blessed One said, “He is liberated from the mental body,” referring to him as one liberated in both ways.
“The sage has declared. In this context, “he goes to his end” means he reaches his final destination.
“He does not enter into reckoning” means he does not enter into conventional usage such as “he has gone to such-and-such a direction. Thus, “the sage is released from the body of name”:
thus, having been reborn in the formless realm, the training sage (sekkha-muni), who was already by nature released from the body of form, further attains the fourth path therein.
Because the mental body has been fully understood, he is further liberated from the mental body as well.

Having become one liberated in both ways and being an arahant whose taints are destroyed, he attains the goal known as final Nibbāna without clinging; he does not enter into any reckoning, meaning he no longer receives such designations as "a khattiya" or "a brahmin," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “having emerged from one [of them]”: does this refer to one who has attained any one of the base of infinite space and so forth, or does it refer to one who has attained all the formless attainments?
Let it be as you wish. If it is said with reference to one who has attained all the formless attainments, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
But if it is said there with reference to one who has attained only one of them, then: “From the time, Ānanda...”
Would this not contradict such statements as, "A bhikkhu enters these eight liberations in forward order," and so forth?

Because one who has attained even a single one among the immaterial-sphere jhānas is called "an attainer of the eight liberations," since it is possible for even a single part of the eight liberations to be capable of receiving that name.
For this designation "eight liberations" applies to the collection [as a whole].
Just as a conventional designation (*samaññā*) is established for a part even when it applies to the whole, so too here. Therefore it was said:
“having emerged from one or another of the base of infinite space, etc. Having stated that [the emergence] is fivefold, some also imagine it to be sixfold;
however, that is merely their own opinion. To show that this question has been definitively settled by the ancient teachers, the passage beginning with “some, however” was stated.

In this context, "some" refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra and the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. For they, having stated that "one liberated in both ways is one liberated from both sides by means of concentration and insight," maintain that there is liberation even from the obstacles to concentration by means of fine-material-sphere concentration (*rūpāvacara-samādhi*).
Thus, he is "liberated from both sides" by way of the fine-material jhāna factor and the immaterial jhāna factor.

“Comparing”: by the phrase “just like that,” he refers to the fact that the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) possesses the same capacity for suppressing defilements as the immaterial-sphere jhāna (arūpāvacara);
this is the point being exceeded [by the comparison]. Therefore, he says “therefore,” and so forth.
“The question regarding one liberated in both ways” means a question arising based on the sixfold nature of one liberated in both ways.
"Relying on the commentary" means relying on the explanation of the meaning of that word.

"After a long time" means after a long period of time following the Elder's passing. "He reached a decision" means he attained a resolution that cuts through doubt. "That question" refers to that matter;
for a matter desired to be known is called a "question. "Never heard by anyone before" means that nothing of this kind had ever been heard by anyone.

The intended meaning is: "this class of purpose. Although it is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), and although it suppresses the defilements (*kilesa*), the word "although" (*kiñcāpi*) should be applied to each clause.
"Manifests" (*samudācarati*) means it occurs. He states the reason for this with the words "For these," and so forth;
therefore, compared to the development of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-bhāvanā*), the development of the formless sphere (*ārūpya-bhāvanā*) suppresses the defilements more specifically.
This shows that [the attainment of the formless] occurs due to the absence of the cultivation of dispassion toward form, and due to the absence of further cultivation [of the form realm].

And by doing so, the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* in the exposition of the cultivation of the formless—“As he thus repeatedly directs his mind toward that sign, the hindrances are suppressed and mindfulness becomes established,” and so forth—is thereby justified. This is the Sutta.

He states the passage on the description of persons (*puggalapaññatti*). For all the Buddha’s word is called a "discourse" (*sutta*) in the sense of indicating the meaning and so forth; this point has already been explained below.
Because the mental continuum is exceptionally refined through the attainment of the eight liberations in forward order and so forth, and because the eighth is supreme—
It should be understood that this twofold liberation (ubhatobhāgavimutti) is to be regarded as the most excellent of all because, by taking liberation as its foundation and developing insight,
one is liberated in both ways through the attainment of the supreme path.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahānidāna Sutta*.
3. Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta 131.

It is called the *Mahāparinibbāna* because it is great (*mahantam*) and it is a *parinibbāna*; that is, it occurs by setting aside the state of being worthy of veneration and the perfection of Buddhahood.

Alternatively, it is the *parinibbāna* that occurs based on the great destruction of defilements (*kilesakkhaya*), which is great because it involves the abandonment of even the latent tendencies (*savāsanappahāna*).
The Great Parinibbāna: it is called the Great Parinibbāna because it was accomplished over a long period of time or by means of a great mass of virtues;

it is called the Great Parinibbāna because it is a Parinibbāna for the sake of greatness and for the multiplicity of the relics; it is called the Great Parinibbāna because it is a Parinibbāna that has emerged from the great world;
and because of the qualities such as virtue belonging to the Buddhas, which are not shared by the entire world.

The *Mahāparinibbāna* is so called because it is the final passing away (*parinibbāna*) of the Great Buddha, the Blessed One; or alternatively, it is the *Mahāparinibbāna* because it is the final passing away when the Great Teaching (*sāsana*) is firmly established. Thus, the final passing away of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is called the *Mahāparinibbāna*, and the discourse connected with that is the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*.
It is called *Gijjhakūṭa* because vultures (*gijjhā*) dwell there; it is the peak (*kūṭa*) of this [hill] that belongs to the vultures.
*Gijjhakūṭa*: it is like a vulture (*gijjha*), or it is a peak (*kūṭa*) resembling a vulture; because this [mountain] has that [peak], it is *Gijjhakūṭa*, the mountain.

On that *Gijjhakūṭa*. Therefore he said, “Vultures,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “desiring to go up”: here the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of overcoming, as in “he understands thoroughly” (*abhivijānāti*) and similar expressions;
thus he said, “desiring to go for the purpose of overcoming. “The Vajjian kings”: those who are to be avoided...

Based on the words spoken at the beginning, "these," the kings who received the name "Vajjīs"—or the kings of the Vajjī country, the *vajjirājāno*—should be understood as having the designation "Vajjī" for the Vajjī country because of the princes dwelling therein.
"By royal power" (*rājiddhiyā*) means by their inherent nature (*sabhāva*) which conforms to the state of being a king. And that inherent nature belongs to these republican kings (*gaṇarājūnaṃ*).
Because he became renowned in the world through mutual harmony and was long-enduring, it is said that "he spoke of the state of being united.
That which develops and increases the qualities of those possessing them, step by step, is *anubhāva*; *anubhāva* itself is *ānubhāva*, meaning majesty or splendor.
Furthermore, their splendor consisted in the excellence of their vehicles such as elephants and horses, and in their state of being well-trained therein, [which was] in the world...
“Became manifest” means that it was said: “… by this he spoke. “Through the keyhole” means through the opening for the key. “A dart” means an arrow.
“They will strike down” means they will cause to pass beyond. “Arrow after arrow” (poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ) means following the arrow-feather (poṅkha) of one after the other;
the meaning is that they make the next arrow follow the feather-mark of the preceding arrow. “Unerring” means unfailing. “I shall cut off” means—
"I shall cut off the lineage of the clan by uprooting it. *Aya* means increase; its opposite is *anaya*, hence he said, "for non-increase, this is the name.
"He casts away" (*vikkhipati*) means he throws far away; the meaning is that he removes. "At the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyaṃ*) means near the Ganges.
"A port-village" (*paṭṭanagāmaṃ*) means a village with a cart-port. "The command prevails" (*āṇā vattati*). "Half a *yojana*" (*aḍḍhayojanaṃ*).
And this was said with reference to those residing within a distance of half a *yojana* from that city. "There" means in that city.
"One in whom a powerful resentment has arisen" means one in whom intense anger has been produced.
"Me" means for me. "By going" means by the act of departing.
Commentary on the Factors Leading to the Decline of a King: 134.
"Neither cold nor heat exists"—at that time, by the power of their merit, the Buddhas always experience a temperature that is perfectly balanced between cold and heat;
it is with reference to this that it was so stated. "Frequent assemblies" means constant assemblies.
To demonstrate that state of constant assembly, the words "of the day" and so forth were spoken. "Abounding in assemblies" means having many gatherings. "Cessation" means contraction.
"As long as" (*yāvakīvaṃ*) is a single word expressing an indefinite measure; since time is intended here, he said, "for as long as a period.
The meaning stated by the passage beginning with "only growth" (*vuddhiyeva*) is [now] explained by way of its opposite (*byatirekamukhena*).
To show this, it was said: "Because they do not assemble frequently," and so forth. "Agitated" means disturbed, not serene.
"Having split" means having divided by forming factions, becoming separate from one another.
"By the assembly drum" means by the drum that announces the assembly. "Or half-eaten" means partially consumed. "Sinking" means declining.

"Previously unmade" means not previously produced. "Toll" is the portion to be given to royal officials by those carrying goods when passing through mountain passes, river fords, town gates, and so forth.
"Tax" is the share obtained from the harvested crop, such as a sixth part, a seventh part, and so on.
"Fine" refers to ten, twenty, or more *kahāpaṇa* coins, according to the nature of the offense.
The punishment to be imposed is the fine. "Vajjidhamma" means the royal law of the Vajjis.

Now, in order to show in detail the dangers and benefits regarding the promulgation of what has not yet been promulgated and so forth, as well as their rejection, it was said: "Of those, what has not been promulgated," etc.
"Capable of service" means capable of attending upon [others].
"Mahāmattā" means those who possess great measure (*matta*) or magnitude (*pamāṇa*) by virtue of their lineage, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth;
"vinicchayamahāmattā" refers to those high officials appointed to judicial decisions established according to the treatises on statecraft (*nītisattha*). "Dentī" means they hand over.

"Sace coroti evaṃsaññino sace honti" means if they are indeed conscious that he is a thief. Out of fear of evil, without saying anything themselves, [they hand him over] to what is known as the system of punishment (*daṇḍanīti*).

Those engaged in legal affairs are "judges" (*vohārika*), who are called "upholders of the Dhamma. Those who uphold the suttas are "experts in the suttas of policy," appointed and established for such judicial decisions.

Those born into the eight clans inherited through tradition, who refrain from following wrong paths, are "the eight elders" (*aṭṭhamahallakapurisa*). Those born into these eight clans are "of the eight clans" (*aṭṭhakulika*).

"Honoring" means providing assistance. "Having established a sense of respect" means having established a sense of respect toward them individually, thinking, "These are our venerables. "Honoring" means paying respect;
and since that respect is preceded by a state of mental gladness toward them, he says, "they love them with their minds. "Showing humble service" means showing prostration. "They show" means...
“By saying ‘these are our grandfathers,’ ‘our grandmothers,’ and so forth, they show an attitude of reverence while maintaining a humble mind.
To “sustain” means to connect [the parts] and join them so that the continuity is not broken.
Regarding the phrase “of the forceful manner,” it refers to compulsion. Granted, because of their growth and worthiness of honor, they are called “growth and decline”; yet—

The meaning, however, should be applied according to the sequence already stated; or rather, since it is said in the Pāḷi, “Only growth is to be expected, not decline,” therefore, following that sequence, “growth and decline” is stated.
When evil kamma has found no opportunity to ripen, or when there is no occasion for the ripening of that kamma, an attack by a deity finds no entry.
But since there might be an opportunity for a divine calamity once that space had been gained, he said: "They increase unarisen [wholesome states]... etc.
By this very same principle, the meaning here in the phrase "unarisen happiness" should also be understood.

The assistance of the deities at the head of the battle should be understood through such expressions as "the showing of the army being doubled or tripled in strength" and "the showing of the state of being formidable."
“Unwanted” means undesirable. “From obstruction” means from prohibition. That which does not depart from the Dhamma is called “Dhammic” here.
Hunting wild animals by dragging dogs and the like for the sake of killing deer, pigs, and so forth, is *vāja* or *migavā*;
those engaged in that are *vājikā*, or hunters who kill deer. [The following refers to] the movement of the mind...
He asks. For by means of bodily and vocal application, she is well-known and manifest in the world.
(135) It became a *cetiya* because it was honored (*citatta*) as a shrine for the gods, and because it was a place where the world paid homage.

"Nothing is to be done" (*akaraṇīya*) means that nothing whatsoever should be performed by way of desire (*kāmaṅkāra*). However, "desire" (*kāmaṅkāra*) here refers to the manner of performing something that has already come into one's hand.
He said: "The meaning is 'not to be seized. "By fighting face-to-face" means by engaging in battle directly and straightforwardly.
To show "enticement and giving oneself," the words beginning with "enough" were spoken. Since even sowing dissension is a means in this context, it was stated:
"except for the breaking of friendship. Furthermore, that fighting is not a [proper] means has already been made clear. "This" refers to...
“And ‘except for deception, except for causing a schism in the Saṅgha’—this is the statement.
Having grasped the method of the discourse means having grasped the method, the strategy, of this discourse by the Blessed One beginning with “As long as... [and so on] ... there is no decline.
Out of compassion means out of favor toward the Vajjī kings. “His” refers to the Blessed One.

"How shall war be waged with the Vajjis?"—this is the discourse on the matter of war. "I will make it straight," he said; having brought the rival kings together, I will make them straight by altering the nature of their walls and moats.
"The quality of being established" means the quality of established conduct. "Let the lords assemble; we are not lords.
Having gone there, what shall we do?"—this is how the Licchavis did not assemble; such is the construction of the sentence. "Let the brave ones assemble"—here too, the same principle applies.
*Balabheri*: the war drum for the mobilization of the army. 136.
Commentary on the Factors of Non-Decay (*Aparihāniyadhamma*):

“Conducive to non-decline” means they are beneficial for the sake of non-decline; or, alternatively, they are called “factors of non-decline” because one does not decline by means of them. Furthermore, these...
Because they are indeed "makers of non-decline," it is said: "causing non-decline. Furthermore, because they are the direct opposites of those things that cause decline, it is said:

"becoming causes for growth. Because the Blessed One’s teaching, spreading the light of knowledge further and further, dispels the darkness in the hearts of beings and illuminates that which is to be made manifest...
And having made the meaning even more clearly manifest, as if showing an *āmalaka* fruit upon the palm of one's hand, he therefore said:
"I shall speak... [as if] a thousand moons...
Since the Blessed One was speaking of the practice of the Vajjis—such as their frequent assemblies—and so forth, right in the presence of that brahmin, [he spoke thus].
"This discourse on non-decline is not conducive to liberation; it is dependent upon the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).

But in my teaching, such a discourse as should be delivered must be one that is conducive to liberation and dependent upon the turning away from the cycle (vivaṭṭa), by which my teaching would endure for a long time and remain stable even after my final Nibbāna.
Having thus reflected, he had the monks assembled and, regarding them [with the discourse] on non-decline...
While teaching the Dhamma, he taught according to that very same method. Therefore it was said: “This is exactly like what was stated in the *Vajjisattaka*.
Thus, showing in detail the matter already stated in brief, he said: “And here too,” and so forth.

In that context, the phrase beginning with “from there” refers to the statement made regarding the message received from the various directions. Because the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*) was crowded, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies were suspended.
"Olīyamāna-koti" means perishing from both the text and the meaning. "Ukkhipāpenta" means encouraging by means of making [the text] familiar and by commenting on its meaning.
"The monks in Sāvatthī should be made to confess a *pācittiya* offense" refers to those like the Vajjiputtakas who clarify the ten points.
They say, "Gihigatānīti means connected with householders. They have gone among householders; known by them, they are "gihigata."
*Dhūmakālikaṃ* means "belonging to the time of smoke," because it does not continue after the smoke from the funeral pyre has subsided.

*Thirabhāvappattā* means having attained a state of stability, that is, having reached a state of firmness and non-retrogression within the Teaching. *Therakārakehi* means by those qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, which establish the status of an elder (*thera*), namely the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha-dhamma*).
*Bahū rattiyō* means they have known [this] for many nights since going forth into homelessness.
Establishing others in virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) is what constitutes being a leader in the Dispensation; thus it is said, "causing them to proceed in the three trainings.

They do not give instruction because [the recipients] are not fit vessels. "Lineage discourse" (*paveṇīkathā*) refers to a Dhamma talk handed down through the succession of teachers that illustrates right practice.

"The essential method of the Dhamma" (*sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ*) refers to that which leads to the attainment of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), and the fruit (*phala*).

The essential core is the lineage of Dhamma consisting of the suttas on the skill in the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), the unsurpassed state of coolness (*sītībhāva*), and the higher mind (*adhicitta*).

"Rebirth-giving" refers to rebirth through the elision of the latter member of the compound. "The others" refers to those who are not subject to conditions and do not have the eye of worldly gain; they do not fall under the power of craving.
"In forest-dwelling places" means in parts of the forest included within the forest designation. Is it not the case that craving is blameworthy wherever it occurs?
Having in mind such an objection, he says, "In regard to lodgings within a village," and so forth. By this,
he shows that attachment to forest lodgings— just like the affection and so on mentioned in the passage "one who establishes a longing for the unsurpassed liberations"—
belongs to the side of what is to be cultivated.

"By themselves" (*attanāva*) means by their own accord; this shows that they desire the arrival of well-behaved monks who have not yet come—without being urged by others—and the comfortable dwelling of those who have already arrived.
"By this method" (*iminā nīhārena*) means by this practice.

"The grasping of the Dhamma not yet grasped" (*aggahitadhammaggahaṇaṃ*) means the learning of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) which has not been learned. "The recitation of what has been grasped" (*gahitasajjhāyakaraṇaṃ*)...
The thorough reflection on the meaning of what has been learned; for the word *sajjhāya* (recitation) has the sense of reflecting.
"They go" means they approach. "They sit" by way of preparing seats and so forth. 137.

In the sense of that which is to be resorted to, it is a "pleasure" (*ārāma*). Those who delight in work (*kamma*), rather than in the burden of study or the burden of residence, are "delighting in work" (*kammaratā*).

*Anuyuttā* means repeatedly devoted through the state of being intent upon that. "Work to be done" refers to various tasks to be performed by the monks, such as the distribution of robes and so forth;

hence he said, "namely," and so on. *Upatthambhana* (support) refers to the making of double or triple layers [of cloth] and the like, for it is so called because it serves as a support for the first layer and the others.
If this is so, how is it that this delight in work (*kammarāmatā*) is rejected? To answer this, he says:
"A certain person," and so forth. "Even while doing" means even while speaking the aforementioned frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
Although it is not frivolous talk [in itself], the restrictive term is used to show that for him, that [talk] is his primary concern. "One who makes a limit" means having made a definite boundary.
He is a speaker; for it is said, "One who speaks words that have a limit. He is one of few words, meaning he speaks only in moderation, speaking solely on what ought to be spoken.
Noble silence is the attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
"He simply sleeps" means that when sleep comes, seeing no danger in it, he simply sleeps; he does not dispel it by changing his posture or other such means.
"Thus he dwells associated" means that, according to the method already stated, he dwells indeed associated with the socializing of groups.

"Those of immoral conduct and evil desires" means they themselves lack virtue; they are called "evil-desired" (pāpiccha) because they possess the desire for the esteem of qualities they do not actually have, and their desires are wicked and base.

They are "evil friends" (pāpamitta) because they cultivate friendship with wicked persons. They are "evil companions" (pāpasahāya) because they always act together with them. They are "inclined toward evil" (pāpasampavaṅka) because they are intent upon that [evil] through such things as being directed toward it.

138. "Those who possess faith (saddhā) are called 'faithful' (saddhā); thus he said, 'endowed with faith. Faith that has arrived by way of the path leading thereto is "faith that is to be arrived at" (āgamanīyasaddhā).
This is preeminent in Great Bodhisattvas because, without instruction from another, they resolve upon the object of faith after having plunged into it without error;
therefore, he said, "it belongs to omniscient Bodhisattvas. [This arises] from the penetration of truth.
Faith through arrival (*āgata-saddhā*) is faith through attainment (*adhigama-saddhā*), such as that of the *surabandha* and others.

Confidence arising toward the Buddha and the rest, expressed as “The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One,” etc., is faith through clarity (*pasāda-saddhā*), such as that of King Mahākappina and others.

*Okappanā* is the act of settling or fixing by way of believing after having entered into and leaped into [the object] with the thought, “This is exactly so. “Both kinds” refers to both faith through clarity and [faith through attainment].

There is also faith as conviction (*okappana-saddhā*). Among these, faith as serene confidence (*pasāda-saddhā*) is of a nature not to be led by others, because one gains confidence through mere hearing.
Faith as conviction, however, proceeds as if it were making the object of faith directly manifest, having plunged into and entered it, thinking, "It is exactly so.
Therefore he said: "One who is resolved upon faith is like the Elder Vakkali. For his—[that is,] for one with faith as conviction—...

“Of one who is endowed [with these qualities]. Because he possesses *hiri* (moral shame), he is *hiri*; because they possess *hiri* as their mental state (*mano*), they are called *hirimanā*. Thus it is said: “of those whose minds are... [afraid] of evil.
They shrink back from evil, are terrified of it, and fear it; thus they are *ottappī* (those possessed of moral dread).

He has heard much of the discourses, verses, and so forth; thus he is *bahussuto* (one of great learning). And here, the mention of “learning” (*suta*) is merely illustrative, for it includes retention, mastery, interrogation, reflection, and contemplation through insight.
Because they are desired here; or rather, since hearing is the root of those [qualities] as well, their inclusion should be understood by the very mention of that [hearing].

The "teaching" (*pariyatti*) consists of the three Piṭakas, because it is to be mastered by one desiring welfare, and because it constitutes the "learning" (*pariyatti*) for the accomplishment of human goals such as those pertaining to the present life.
The "penetration of the truths" (*saccappaṭivedha*) is the piercing through of the truths. That too is "great learning."

It is because of the accomplishment of the duties of learning (*bāhusacca*) as previously described. By "learning" (*pariyatti*), the mastery of the scriptures is intended here, since it is this state of being well-versed through learning that brings about the penetration of the Truths (*sacca-paṭivedha*).
"He" refers to one who is well-versed in the scriptures. He is of four kinds, because there is no fifth category.

"One who is well-versed everywhere" (*sabbatthaka-bahussuta*) is so called because he is not limited to a specific portion, unlike those who are well-versed only in their own *nissaya* or *muccanaka*, and so forth.

Because he possesses great learning (*bāhusacca*) regarding all three Pitakas without exception, he is "one who has heard much concerning all matters" (*sabbatthaka-bahussuta*), since he knows and can explain the meaning of everything.
These [teachers] are intended here because they are well-established in the True Dharma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma*),
which serves as the root for the True Dharma of practice and realization (*paṭipatti-paṭivedha*).

“Exerted” (*āraddha*) means applied. To show that twofold exertion through the analysis of the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambha*), the passage beginning with “therein” (*tatthā*) was stated. Therein, “singles” (*ekakā*) means those who dwell alone;

the sense is “those dwelling in seclusion. “Having asked” means having asked subsequently. “To cause them to accept” means having said, “You are so-and-so,” to cause them to acknowledge it by saying, “Yes.
Thus, for those possessing mindfulness capable of recollecting what was done long ago and so forth, [the task] is accomplished without difficulty.
It was said, "with reference to such bhikkhus," for the purpose of showing that they reach the fulfillment of the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
For this very reason, he said, "Moreover," and so forth.
139. It is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) because one awakens by means of it; thus, it is a factor (*aṅga*) of the harmony of qualities beginning with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
A factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) that is praised or beautiful is a "factor of full enlightenment" (*sambojjhaṅga*).

It has the characteristic of establishing (*upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇa*): it is called "having the characteristic of establishing" because its characteristic is the establishment of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena upon their objects, which consists in clearly perceiving their nature as foul, painful, impermanent, and non-self.
Investigation (*vicaya*)—that is, examination—of the four noble truths by way of their aspects such as oppression, and so forth, is its characteristic.

"Of this" means it has investigation as its characteristic. "Of exertion as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of uplifting or grasping the mind by way of the non-arising of unarisen wholesome states and so forth.
"Of pervasion as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of expansion or diffusiveness.
"Of tranquility as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of the subsiding of the feverish distress of body and mind. "Non-distraction" [is the characteristic of concentration].
It has non-distraction as its characteristic because its characteristic is the destruction of distraction; thus it is "characterized by non-distraction" (*avikkhepalakkhaṇo*).

It has reflective discernment as its characteristic because its characteristic is the act of reflecting while the higher mind (*adhicitta*), free from lethargy and restlessness, is proceeding, since it is not occupied with exertion, restraint, or encouragement;
thus it is "characterized by reflective discernment" (*paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇo*).

"By four reasons" means by these four reasons: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and being intent upon that. "By six reasons" means:
being inquisitive, making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons lacking wisdom, associating with persons possessing wisdom, and being intent upon that.
By these six reasons. However, in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*, it will say "by seven reasons";
that should be understood by adding this reason: "reflection on the practice of profound knowledge. By nine reasons:
reflection on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), reflection on the path of travel, and the honoring of almsfood.

By these nine causes: reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates, avoidance of persons who are indolent, association with persons who have aroused energy, and devotion thereto.
However, in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*, it is stated: "seeing the benefits" and "reflection on the greatness of one's birth."

Together with these, he will say "eleven. By ten reasons: namely, by the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dhamma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, the deities, and peace;
and by avoiding persons who are harsh, associating with persons who are gentle, and being intent upon that—these are the ten.
However, in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*, it is stated [that there are eleven] by means of reflecting on the Suttantas that inspire confidence (*pasādaniya-suttanta*).
Together with this, he will say, "eleven. By seven reasons:

namely, the practice of excellent food, the practice of a comfortable climate, the practice of a comfortable posture, the state of mental equanimity, the avoidance of persons with agitated bodies, the cultivation of persons with tranquil bodies, and being intent upon that—by these seven.
By ten reasons: namely, the purification of the physical basis and the balancing of the faculties.
Skillfulness regarding signs; exerting the mind at the proper time; restraining the mind at the proper time; gladdening the mind at the proper time;
looking on with equanimity at the proper time; avoiding persons who are unconcentrated; associating with persons who are concentrated;
and being intent upon that—by these ten reasons. However, in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*, it is stated as "reviewing of jhāna and liberation."

Together with this, he will say, "by eleven. "By five reasons" means by these five reasons: neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, avoidance of persons who cherish beings and formations, association with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, and being intent upon that [neutrality].
Whatever else needs to be said here will be found in the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
Granted that, in the ultimate sense, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are associated only with the Noble Path because they possess the quality of leading to liberation;

nevertheless, the teaching of the Suttas is a discourse given in a figurative or conventional sense (*pariyāya-kathā*), as it is said: "By means of this, he taught insight... [and so on]... he spoke. 140.

It is called "contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā*) because one contemplates the formations belonging to the three planes as "impermanent" by means of this [meditation]; it occurs in such a manner.

Vipassanā; for it is said that this [insight] is indeed "the perception arisen together with the contemplation of impermanence" because it is manifested only when the perception co-arising with itself has been cultivated. Or rather, this is a designation for insight itself by way of its aspect as perception.
The same method applies to the perception of non-self and so forth. They are also mundane insights, because they [arise] through such [contemplations] as "impermanent," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "they occur": by means of the word *pi* (also), mundane insight-joy (*lokīyavipassanā-pīti*) is included here;
having extracted the meaning established through implication (*atthāpatti-siddha*), the words beginning with "dispassion" (*virāgo*) were stated to show it in its own form.
Therein, "by way of what has come down" means by way of the textual tradition as it has thus come down; for in that [tradition], Nibbāna is described as "dispassion and cessation."
Here, the perceptions mentioned as "perception of dispassion" (*virāga-saññā*) and "perception of cessation" (*nirodha-saññā*) may also have Nibbāna as their object. Therefore it is said:
"Two are also supramundane. 141.
That which possesses loving-kindness (*mettā*) is "loving," namely, the mind. The bodily action originating from that is "loving bodily action."

This same method applies to the other two [types of action] as well. These instances of loving bodily action and so forth are presented here with reference to monks because they constitute the most excellent assembly among them.
However, since these qualities are common to all four assemblies, just as they are found among monks, they are likewise found among laypeople;
showing this, he said, "For among monks," and so on. Granted, loving bodily actions may also arise through hearing the Dhamma that is fundamental to the holy life.
However, showing that from the non-figurative standpoint (*nippariyāyato*) this purpose is intended through the practice of the Dhamma and listening to it, he said:

"the fulfillment of the Dhamma of higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārikadhammapūraṇa*). Even the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, when set forth by way of interrogation and exposition of meaning, must be practiced with an inclination toward welfare (*hitajjhāsaya*).
“Face-to-face” (*sammukhā*) means manifest; here, it refers to the state of being in the presence of that person for whose sake the bodily action is performed.
“In private” (*parammukhā*) means unmanifest; and this lack of manifestation refers to the state of not being in the sight of that person for whose sake the bodily action is performed.
“Going before them” means going into their presence as a companion. “By both” means—
"By those who are new and by those who are senior.
"Having lifted up" means having raised [the eyes] high.
Granted, the opening of eyes that are moistened with the oil of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and looking with a serene face is indeed loving-kindness.

It is indeed bodily action; however, with reference to that state of mind by whose power the eyes are moistened with the oiliness of loving-kindness and the face is serene, it is said: "loving-kindness is called mental action.

The word *lābha* functions as a noun (kamma-sādhana), as in such expressions as "one possessed of gains" (*lābhāvatā*) or "a gain has been obtained" (*lābho laddho*); and here, it refers to those who have "obtained [it] in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammaladdhā*).
Because it pertains to the past in terms of verbal expression, he said, "robes and so forth obtained as requisites. They are *dhammika* (righteous) because they have come according to the Dhamma;
therefore he said, "righteously obtained. Indeed, to demonstrate this very meaning, the passage beginning with "by means of hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and so forth" was stated.
"Dividing by body preceded by dividing by mind"—this was said to show the very root [of the offense]. Thus: "dividing by mind."
It is said; by this, he shows that no distinction should be made even on account of a single arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*).
"Indivisible" (*appaṭivibhatta*) is a description in the neuter past participle, or it is simply a description of the object (*kamma*), meaning "he consumes the gain without dividing it.
He does not give this or that to householders for the sake of purifying his own livelihood. "He does not consume it himself" means by himself...
He does not consume it [thinking], "May there not be for me the state of consuming what is not shared. By the phrase, "And while receiving...

[and] he sees," the establishing of that gain as common to all at three times is shown. By the phrase, "And while receiving, may it be common to the Saṅgha," the time of receiving is shown; and by the phrase, "Having taken... [and] he sees," [the other two times are shown].
This is the time of acceptance; however, since both of these do not occur without a corresponding prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*), the preceding time is established by implication.
This [prior time] occurs before the acceptance: "I shall accept it so that it may be shared with the Saṅgha.
While accepting, [the thought] occurs: "I accept it so that it may be shared with the Saṅgha. Having accepted, [the thought occurs]:...

"Having accepted it with the thought, 'Let it be shared with the Saṅgha,' one who uses the gains obtained after having thus endowed them with the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), without violating the characteristic of the final conclusion, is a sharer of common property and one whose enjoyments are not partitioned.
This, moreover, is the fourth quality worthy of being remembered. For [they] do not... pe... take hold of it.
Therefore, since even the mere undertaking [of the practice] is impossible for one who is immoral because they lack the quality of sharing enjoyments with others, how much less its fulfillment?
This is the intended meaning. By the phrase "one of pure virtue," he shows that the gain is righteous (*dhammika*).
By the phrase "not breaking the observances," he shows both the non-exclusive enjoyment of gains and the quality of sharing them with others. But when...
He says "he fulfills" because both of these fulfill the duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīyadhamma*).

By the phrase "having made it specific," it is shown that for one who gives without making it specific—whether to his father, or to teachers, preceptors, and so forth, starting from the seat of the elders—it is indeed the duty of courtesy.
However, it does not become the duty of courtesy for him [in this case] because it was given specifically at the place of attendance.

Therefore he said, “It is called ‘the maintenance of impediments,’” and so forth. If this is so, does it mean that directed giving (*odissaka-dāna*) is entirely improper for one who fulfills the qualities conducive to social integration (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*)?
No, it is not improper; rather, he said “But by that [means],” etc., to show that it is appropriate in certain instances.
Giving while making a distinction for those who are ill and so forth belongs to the side of non-sharing (*appaṭivibhāga*), as in the thought, “I will not give to such-and-such a person.”
Because there is no prohibition. For a distinction (*paṭivibhāga*) consists primarily in exclusion (*byatireka*). Therefore he said, "the remainder," and so forth.
By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even not to give," he shows that it is also permissible to give; however, this is by way of compassion, not for the sake of fulfilling one's duty.
"Well-trained" means well-trained in the method of fulfilling the duties of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*); the sense is "one who is very skillful."

Now, in order to demonstrate her skill, the passage beginning with “by one who is well-trained” was spoken. By the statement, “It is fulfilled in twelve years, not before that,” he shows its difficulty to fulfill.
For it is of great fruit and great benefit, and is accompanied by fruits and benefits even more weighty than those pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmika*). And the person who possesses it—
Like a noble person who has attained distinction, he is endowed with wonderful and marvelous qualities in the world.

For, having suppressed far away the opposing states to the merit consisting of giving and the merit consisting of virtue—which are otherwise difficult to abandon—he dwells renowned and well-known in the world with a perfectly purified mind. Regarding this matter, [the following is] by way of contrast:
The passage beginning with “If indeed... was stated in order to clarify [the matter] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
that is easily understood. Now, the passage beginning with “Thus... was stated to show the benefits pertaining both to future lives (*samparāyika*) and to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
There is neither envy nor stinginess, because these states have been shaken off through long-term cultivation. One becomes dear to human beings.
Because of its purity through the virtue of renunciation. Therefore it was said: “Giving, one becomes beloved; many resort to one,” and so forth.
One finds requisites easily, because the acquisition of requisites by those with noble aspirations is the specific benefit (*ānisansa*) of giving in this context.
What has come into the bowl does not fail him when it is being given away, because of the continuity of the great bowl that has been his for twelve years.
Because it has been fulfilled. He receives the finest goods daily because he has given gifts starting from the foremost among those worthy of offerings.

Or out of fear... [and so on] ...they incur [the offense], because their minds have long been gladdened by the fulfillment of giving with a mind free from attachment to themselves, without making distinctions between the giver and the recipient.
"In that regard" (*tatra*) means among those benefits (*ānisamsa*) that are to be clarified. "These" refers to the illustrative instances (*vatthu*) or reasons (*kāraṇa*) for that.

"Even though they do not obtain" means even though they are not recipients due to a lack of great merit (*mahāpuñña*). "They know the alms-round path to be similar" means they know the alms-round path to be similar (*sabhāga*), that is, belonging to that same category (*tabbhāgiya*).

Because it was a state beyond human condition (*anuttarimanussadhamma*) and in order to dispel the elders' doubt, he said, "Venerable sir, I have fulfilled the qualities conducive to endearment (*sāraṇīyadhamma*).
For likewise, in the second case as well, the Elder revealed himself. This very case [is cited] because of being beloved by humans and because of the ease with which requisites were obtained.
However, [the other cases] are for the purpose of elucidating the specific distinction of one who is free from fear regarding what has been received in the bowl.
“This, first of all... [as before] ...is the basis here,” it is said.

Regarding the “Great Offering of Mountain Goods”: this refers to the great offering performed with island-flowers, perfumes, and so forth, on Mount Cetiyagiri throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, as well as across the sea for the distance of a *yojana*, having set out fleets of ships and other such vessels.
“Even by way of succession” (*pariyāyena*) means even by way of a sequence. “Appropriate” (*anucchavikaṃ*).
The meaning is that this proclamation of things as they truly are is also worthy of you because it fulfills the qualities conducive to remembrance (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).
They fled without having reported [the matter], out of fear of robbers; some also say it was "because of their own difficult livelihood.

"It will suffice" means it will be sufficient. The Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to remembrance, but the deity applied herself with zeal solely through the power of the Elder’s virtue.
They are "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍāni*) because there is no break (*khaṇḍa*) in them. To demonstrate that break for them, the passage beginning with "Of which... was stated.

Therein, for those possessing the virtue of one fully ordained (*upasampanna*), the beginning and end should be understood according to the sequence of recitation. Therefore he said, "In the seven," and so forth.

However, for those possessing the virtue of one not fully ordained, the beginning and end are also obtainable according to the sequence of undertaking [the precepts]. Like a garment torn at its hem...
It is like a cloth torn at the edge or at the hem; this is a dissimilar example because it has been understood that [the precepts] are "unbroken.
The same method applies to the remaining examples as well. That which is broken or split is a *khaṇḍa*; since one possesses such a thing, it is called *khaṇḍa-sīla* (broken virtue).
The same principle applies to terms such as "with holes" (*chidda*). It is broken in the middle by way of piercing through.
The connection is: "like a cow by way of a dissimilar color. Those that are free from speckles are "unspotted" (*asabala*). Likewise, they are "uncorrupted" (*akammāsa*).

The liberation of virtue from the slavery of craving is the bringing about of its status as a necessary condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). And because a person endowed with it is called "self-governing," "independent," and "free," for that reason too they are "freed" (*bhujissa*). For this very reason, he said: "Because they are the cause of the state of being freed..."
"May I be free. Because they are praised for their state of extreme purity, they are "commended by the wise.

By means of this virtue, one might think, "I shall become a deva or some other kind of deva," and therein, because it is not clung to by craving or views such as "it is permanent, stable, eternal" or "purity comes through virtue," [it is faultless].
"This is the fault in your virtues"—[this refers] to all four types of failure.

By means of whatever misfortune, one is unable to see [it] or to disparage it. "Conducive to concentration" (*samādhisaṃvattanika*) refers to those things whose purpose is to lead toward concentration.

"Virtues that have attained a state of equality" (*samānabhāvūpagata-sīla*) means virtues that have attained a state of equality through the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*); they function in common. Certainly...
There would be no difference in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) among worldlings (puthujjana), yet that [virtue] is not absolute;
this [path-virtue], however, is absolute because its nature is fixed. Therefore it was said: "There is no difference in path-virtue. This was said with reference to that;
namely, with reference to path-virtue, it was stated: "Those virtues which... and so forth.

"Those which are" refers to those views that are directly evident both to me and to you. "View" (*diṭṭhi*) here means right view of the Path (*magga-sammā-diṭṭhi*). "Flawless" (*niddosa*) means having removed flaws;

the meaning is that it has utterly eradicated unwholesome states such as lust and so forth. "Leads out" (*niyyāti*) means it issues forth from or goes beyond the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).
For it is precisely while one is being led out oneself that it is said: "It leads the person possessing it out from the suffering of the round of existence."
It is said: "One who acts according to the Teacher's instruction is a *takkara*"; the meaning is: one who practices exactly as instructed.
"The state of having a common view" means the state of having a similar view, a state of non-differentiated view through the full penetration of truth.
"Only growth" means that in the discipline of the Noble Ones there is only growth in terms of qualities, not decline; this is the teaching on the factors that prevent decline.
This was taught here by the Blessed One, who desired that both himself and the Dispensation should endure for a long time.
(142) "Because his Parinibbāna is near" means it was said with the understanding that his Parinibbāna would take place in no more than a year plus a few months.
"This very same" refers to the passage beginning with "Thus, virtue. Here, in the phrase "thus virtue," the word *iti* has the sense of "manner" or "kind."
And because the sense of measure was taken by grouping [the factors] together, he said: "Thus, this much is virtue.
"Thus virtue" means virtue with such divisions. "This much" means this is the limit; there is nothing beyond this.
"The fourfold purification of virtue" refers to mundane virtue of the fourfold purification that serves as a requisite for the Path. Regarding "one-pointedness of mind is concentration," here too—

The same method applies here. "Standing upon which virtue" means standing firm in that virtue described as, "But first, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are perfectly pure," which serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for supramundane wholesome states.
"This" refers to the concentration of the path and fruit. "Cultivated" means fully developed and perfected by means of that virtue. It is of great fruit.

"It has great benefit" means that path-concentration (*maggasamādhi*) is of great fruit by way of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*), and it has great benefit by way of the subsiding of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

The other [concentrations] are of great fruit by way of the abandoning through subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*), and they have great benefit by way of the arising of the bliss of extinction (*nibbāna*).

"Standing in which concentration" means standing in that foundational meditative absorption (*pādakajjhānasamādhi*) which serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for supramundane wholesome states.
And by abiding in both [the concentration of the path] and the concentration leading to emergence—this is the wisdom of the path and its fruit.
"Cultivated by that" means fully developed and thoroughly cultivated by that aforementioned concentration.

Its state of great fruitfulness and great benefit is to be understood in the manner explained regarding concentration. Furthermore, it is of great fruit because it is the cause for the various classifications of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the factors of the path (maggaṅga), and the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga).
It should be understood that this is of great benefit because it serves as the cause for the classification of the seven persons worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-puggala*).

"Standing by means of which wisdom" means standing by means of either insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) or the wisdom associated with concentration (*samādhi-vipassanā-paññā*). For one whose vehicle is serenity (*samatha-yānika*), even wisdom accompanied by concentration is indeed a specific condition for the attainment of the path. "In the right way alone" (*sammadeva*) means "properly indeed."
Just as not even a trace of the taints (*āsava*) remains, so one is liberated from all taints whatsoever. This was said with reference to the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
143. The derivation of the word *abhiranta* should be understood in the same way as that of worldly nouns and verbs.
For *abhiranta*, *abhirata*, and *abhirati* are identical in meaning. Furthermore, this word *abhiranta* is a synonym for delight (*abhiruci*), not a synonym for gratification (*assāda*).
For one dwelling in some place due to the presence of gratification might, upon the disappearance of that object of gratification, experience dissatisfaction there;
however, this does not occur for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), let alone for the Buddhas. Thus he said: "For the Buddhas... there is none.

Because they lack such [gratification], there is no such thing as Buddhas leaving one place to go elsewhere after having dwelt somewhere out of a sense of attachment. [They do so] only for the purpose of training those who are to be trained.
However, having stayed in some places and accomplished their purpose there, they go elsewhere from that point solely for the sake of training those who are to be trained;
this is the case here according to their preference. Regarding the word *āyāma*, the particle *ā* has the same meaning as in the phrase *āgaccha* ("come"), which is why he says, "Come, Yāma.
But in the reading *ayāma*, the letter *a* is merely a particle. He addresses the Elder because of his close proximity.
But it was not because there were no monks living in the presence of the Teacher at that time;
for the Saṅgha of monks in the Blessed One’s presence was then of unlimited number. Therefore he said, "together with a great Saṅgha of monks.
By "the journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā," he refers to the text connected with the journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā. Regarding "the journey to Pāṭali," here too—
The same method applies. This is self-evident, as it has already been explained both immediately above and below.
Regarding the commentary on the "Sāriputta-Sīhanāda":

the passage beginning with "Venerable Sāriputta" is the textual source. It was explained in detail in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Sampasādanīya-sutta*; therefore, our intention is that we too shall explain it there in detail according to its meaning.
The Exposition of the Disadvantages of Immorality 148.
An *āvasatha* is so called because guests (*āgantuka*) come and dwell there; that very thing is a house, hence it is said:
"An *āvasathāgāra* is a guest-house for visitors. "Of the two kings" refers to the Licchavi king and the Magadha king. "Friends" means...
*Sevakā*: servants. *Kulāni*: members of a household. *Santhatan*: a spreader; one who spreads everything is a "spreader-of-all" (*sabbasanthari*);
this refers to him, the "spreader-of-all. This is a neuter abstract noun formation. Therefore he said: "in such a way that everything is spread. (149) *Dussīlo*:
here the prefix *du-* has the sense of absence, as in *duppañño* and so forth, not the sense of reproach.
He said: "One who is unvirtuous is devoid of virtue. Regarding the term "one whose restraint is broken":
first, one who has undertaken the precepts but, for some reason, has reached a breach of those precepts is indeed one whose restraint is broken.

But how can one who has not undertaken the precepts at all and is devoid of proper conduct be called "one whose restraint is broken"? He too is so called because of the breaking of good conduct, which is conducive to decline.
It is indeed called "broken restraint. By this, it is meant that one whose restraint has been abandoned is devoid of restraint.

"Various crafts" refers to those respective fields of skill. "At the time of the slaughter" means on the day the proclamation is made, such as "Do not kill living beings," during the festival of non-slaughter (*māghāta*).
"A wicked report of ill repute spreads abroad."
He becomes dejected in his underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) precisely because of the state of remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).
"Of him" means of the immoral one. "The place where he proceeded after undertaking [the precepts]" refers to the reasons for what was done as he rose up again and again.
"It comes into the range of vision" means it presents itself to the mind. "Opening [his eyes] to this world" means by way of seeing his own children, wife, and so forth at the time of opening them.

Here one sees this world. Having closed [the eyes], one sees the other world; that is, at the time of closing [the eyes], one sees the other world by way of the appearance of the sign of the destination (gatinimitta).
Therefore he said, “The four states of misery,” and so forth. The fifth phrase is the fifth section of disadvantages, stated as “With the breakup of the body,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Benefits of Virtue (Sīlavantānisaṃsavaṇṇanā) 150.
"By way of the opposite of what was stated" means by way of the opposite of the discourse on the dangers [of non-virtue].

[The phrase] beginning with "Being diligent, he is able to accomplish various tasks such as farming and trade at the proper time," and so forth, [shows that] because he possesses virtue, he is praised. Thus: "He has virtue."
“Virtuous,” “endowed with virtue,” “possessed of virtue,” and so forth—such explanatory terms are easy to understand and have not been specifically discussed [here].
151. “Dhamma-talk outside the Canon” means talk on the Dhamma that has not been included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti). “Right there” means right in the rest-house itself.
The Description of the Entry into the City of Pāṭaliputta: 152.
*Issariyamattāya* means "by the measure of his sovereignty"; or rather, the meaning should be understood as "by means of both his sovereignty and his wealth and requisites.
For even the articles of enjoyment are called "measure" (*mattā*) in the world. [He entered] the village of Pāṭali.
"Having made it a city" means that the place which was previously known by the name "Pāṭaligāma" has now been made into a city.
"Building" means establishing it. "For the purpose of cutting off the source of income" means for the purpose of interrupting the entrances to revenue.
Alternatively, the reading is "sahassasevā," meaning in thousands. Therefore he said: "in groups of one thousand each. "House sites" means...

"Places for establishing a household. "The minds incline" means that by the power of various deities, the minds of those who recite the science of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*) incline toward this or that very spot wherever the sites have been taken possession of by them.
"By the power of the craft" means by the power of the knowledge associated with that craft. "The seizing of the *nāgas*" refers to the taking possession of the dwelling places of the *nāgas*.
The same method applies to both pairs [of terms]. “A stone” means a stone lacking auspicious marks. “A stump” means any kind of stump whatsoever.

Having performed incantations (*jappita*) and avoided such sites involving construction, they build various houses in places free from such activity, as if consulting with the deities who preside over the site by way of giving instructions. “Of these”— *Note:
This passage appears to be a commentary on the *Sārattha-ppakāsinī* or similar sub-commentary discussing the building of dwellings and the role of protective deities.*
“Of those who recite the science of sites (vatthuvijjā), and of all deities. “They will increase the auspiciousness” means they will cultivate the auspiciousness.
For seeing the wise and so forth are the supreme auspicious signs. Therefore he said, “Then we,” and so on.
The sound rises up because the whole may be designated by way of its constituent parts, just as one says, “Devadatta is adorned.”
“Ariyakamanussānan” means “of people dwelling in noble lands. “Rāsivasen’eva” means “only by way of a heap,” as in “a thousand, a hundred-thousand,” and so forth;
however, since the buying and selling of small amounts of goods is found elsewhere as well, it is said “only by way of a heap.
In the first alternative, the meaning of “vaṇippatho” is “the path of traders” or “place of activity”; in the second alternative—
Showing that "vaṇippatha" means "the place where the path of merchants proceeds," he said, "the dwelling place of merchants.
Regarding "puṭabhedana," he said, "it is called 'puṭabhedana' because they break open or release the bags of merchandise there";
this is the meaning here. Thus it is stated: "The bags of merchandise... and so forth.
The word *vā* has the sense of the letter *ca*, meaning "and" or "also.

153. "Black-eared beings" (*kāḷakaṇṇī sattā*) refers to those lowly beings who cause misfortune to others and are called "black-eared" because they themselves abound in dark qualities and are the cause for producing undesirable dark results for others. *Taṃ* refers to the Blessed One. *Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ* means...
At one time in the morning. "In the manner of entering a village" means by way of the act of entering a village and putting on [robes].
"Having made it connected with the body" means having put on the robe (*cīvara*), that is to say, having taken the alms-bowl (*patta*) in the hand.
"Therein" means in that very place where he had prepared himself. "Restrained" means perfectly restrained, with body, speech, and mind well-controlled.
“May he give a portion” means that he should bestow upon those deities the merit he himself has generated.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “honored,” that very giving of a portion is the “honor”; providing protection against future calamities is the “counter-honor.
“Generally, relatives honor and revere deceased relatives by means of the giving of portions and so forth; but these [deities] are strangers.”

Having thus exhorted one another, saying, “They act in this way; therefore, their protection must be carefully provided,” he spoke the words beginning with “These” to show that the deities apply themselves with diligence there.
He said the words beginning with “These” to show that making offerings is *mānana* (honoring), while removing present dangers is *paṭimāna* (counter-honoring).
"He sees what is beautiful" means he sees only what is desirable and pleasing, not what is undesirable.
"Having carved pegs" means having taken thin wooden rods and carved pegs to join them together like door-panels.
A raft made by way of a boat is one constructed by gathering together bamboo, reeds, and so forth, and binding them with creepers and the like.
A raft is to be constructed by binding together bundles of materials.
"Water-place" is a designation for any water-place as previously described; the intention is that this term "ocean" (aṇṇava) applies specifically to the sea.
Here, "river" (sara) is intended; it is called *sara* because it flows (*sarati*) or runs (*sandati*).
Having made [this]. "Deep and vast" means deep in the sense of being bottomless, and vast because it pervades the entire threefold world (*tiloka*).
"Without clinging" means without adhering to or reaching [the other side]. "Quagmires" because they cannot be crossed by them.

"Even without a raft" means that wise people have crossed such water even without a raft of this kind; however, the lake of craving is [crossed] by means of what is called the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
The construction is: "having made a bridge, they have crossed over.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Truths.
155. Of King Mahāpanāda. "The village built at the pinnacle of the palace" means a village settled at the place where the fallen spire of the palace stood.
"Of those that produce the state of noble ones" is said by way of metaphorical attribution of agency to the sign for those who penetrate it.
"Of the truths" refers to their state of being undistorted and non-perverted. "Awakening" refers to that which pertains to the prior stage.

Knowledge is penetration; realization occurs through path-knowledge. In this context, since penetration is preceded by understanding and does not exist without it, and certain types of understanding are connected with penetration, and because the wandering in saṃsāra is caused by the absence of both, it is said in the Pāḷi:
"Through non-understanding... [and so on]... and for you. This is stated by way of taking rebirth-linking.

"Running" (*sandhāvana*) refers to the transition from one state of existence to another; "wandering" (*saṃsaraṇa*) refers to the process of moving about by way of passing away and being reborn from one state to another.

Thus he said, "from existence," and so forth. Regarding the first alternative, he said, "by me and by you," intending that the words "run" and "wandered" function as nouns denoting the object (*kamma-sādhana*).
In the second alternative, however, he kept in mind their function as nouns denoting the action or state (*bhāva-sādhana*).
Having said this, it was stated according to the literal sense as "both mine and yours. "Capable of leading" means capable of bringing [one] to;

just as a man with a rope in his hand leads a bird bound by a long cord to another place, so too does volitional formation lead the continuum of beings—bound by the rope of craving—to another existence.
Thus, it is "craving for existence" (*bhavanetti*); that [craving] is [cut] by the sword of the Noble Path.
“Completely struck down, cut off”: this refers to the total eradication of the fetters of existence (*bhavanetti*).
Commentary on the State of Non-return and the Goal of Enlightenment (156):
The two villages known by the name “Nādikā” are here expressed with the letter *na* as a substitute for the letter *ña*.
“As in such passages as ‘the signless ones do not frequent,’ etc. Therefore he said, “in the village of Ñātika. *Giñjakā* refers to bricks;

a dwelling built with bricks alone is a *giñjakāvasatha*. It is said that this residence was constructed by piling up and covering [with bricks] in such a way that there was no need for plastering work. Hence it is said: “in one made of brick.”
“In the dwelling. However, the balance-beam, door-frames, and door-panels are made entirely of wood.

157. *Ora* refers to the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*). Because they partake of that sense-sphere by way of being its conditions, they are called *orambhāgiyāni*; or, because they are beneficial to the lower portion, they are called *orambhāgiyāni*.
Therefore he said, “of the lower-fettering [fetters],” and so forth. “By means of three paths” refers to the three lower paths.
By means of three paths. For it is because they are to be abandoned by those [paths] that these fetters are called "belonging to the lower realm" (*orambhāgiya*).

Alternatively, they are called "lower-realm-bound" (*orambhañjiya*) or "belonging to the lower realm" (*orambhāgiya*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*). Now, in order to clarify their status as belonging to the lower realm by way of contrast, the passage beginning with "Therein...
is stated. They are suppressed among worldlings by the obstruction of their capacity [to arise].
Because they have been completely cut off by way of their non-existence, they do not act as obstructions for the noble ones’ rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial realms;
thus it is said, “unobstructed and uncut. “By way of production” means by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

They do not allow one to go because they constitute a bond that prevents the accumulation of kamma leading to the sublime states. [This refers to] the three beginning with personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
The fetters, such as sensual desire and ill will, although they do not act as a direct obstruction to rebirth in the sublime realms,

serve as specific conditions for rebirth in the realm of sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*). Consequently, even when one is born into that sublime realm, once the karma that caused that birth is exhausted, these fetters—

acting as conditions for rebirth in the realm of sense-sphere existence— bring one back from the sublime realm and cause one to be reborn right here again in this very realm of sense-sphere existence.
Therefore, all five fetters are indeed lower-fettering (*orambhāgiya*). Because they possess the nature of not returning by way of rebirth-linking—
that is, because they possess the nature of not coming here from that world by way of taking rebirth-linking— his coming for the purpose of seeing the Buddha,
seeing the Elder, or hearing the Dhamma is not obstructed.
The state of being thin is twofold: first, due to their arising only occasionally, they have a sparse form;
second, due to the weakness of their obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), they are not thick. "Frequently" means many times. "Thick and thick" means extremely intense.

Wherever they arise, they arise crushing that continuum (*santāna*), pervading it, accomplishing [their work], and creating darkness; however, because they have been abandoned by two paths, [they do not arise].
They arise as slight and very slight. The statement, "They become sons and daughters," is not the reason;
for they arise even by the mere touch of a limb or a minor part. This refers to the statement, "Because of the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion.
"By way of the attenuation of existence" means by way of a diminished state of existence. That [statement]—the word of the Elder Mahāsiva—is thus rejected.
Regarding the connection: those states that are obtained by the Noble Ones are indeed states where the characteristics are complete.

As for those that are not obtained, what kind of "attenuation of existence" (bhavatanuka) could there be therein? Therefore, it is said "of the stream-enterer" (*sotāpannassa*) and so forth, in order to show that in both cases there is simply no possibility of attenuation of existence;
for in the eighth existence, there is no attenuation of existence, precisely because it is the eighth.
Because of the total non-existence of all becoming (bhava). This same method applies to the remaining [types of existence] as well.
This was stated with reference to the sense-sphere world (kāmāvacara-loka), because it is impossible to speak in that way by way of the other worlds.
For even one who is a once-returner (sakadāgāmī) and is reborn among gods and humans in a mixed manner, he too [is so classified] precisely by way of the sense-sphere becoming (kāmabhava).
It must be delimited. And by the Blessed One, while standing in the world of sense-desire (*kāmaloka*), it was said: "having come to this world only once.
By the phrase "having come to this world," one among the five types of *sakadāgāmins* is selected, excluding the other four.
For one [type] attains the fruit of *sakadāgāmin* here and attains final nibbāna right here; another, having attained it here, [attains it] in the world of the devas.
One attains final nibbāna; another, having reached the world of the devas, attains final nibbāna right there;
another, having reached the world of the devas, is reborn here and attains final nibbāna—these four are not found here.

However, one who, having reached this world, dwells in the world of the devas for the full span of their lifespan, and then is reborn here again and attains final nibbāna—this is what is intended here. [In] the Commentary...
However, in order to clarify that by "this world" (imaṃ lokaṃ) it is specifically sensual existence (kāmabhava) that is intended, another tetrad is shown beginning with "If indeed... and so forth.

The meaning of "the nature of the four" is the state of being [fixed] because of the total abandonment of those evil qualities leading to the states of misery (apāya). "By the fixedness of the Dhamma" means by the fixedness of the path-dhamma.
It is "fixed" because the attainment of the higher paths is certain to occur. Therefore he said, "destined for full enlightenment" (sambodhiparāyaṇo).
Commentary on the Dhammādāsa Sutta (The Mirror of Dhamma), 158.

"The range of their various kinds of knowledge" means the attainment of this or that specific knowledge by various beings, such as, "This one is a stream-enterer; this one is a once-returner," and so forth.
"The arising of knowledge" and "the future destiny of knowledge" refer to what follows thereafter: "He is fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his final goal."
"Having come to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering"—by such statements [the Buddha] shows that [his coming] is a condition for arising accompanied by knowledge.
For one who surveys with the eye of knowledge, there is only physical fatigue; the intention is that no purpose of those to be trained is accomplished by that [fatigue].
"Mental vexation" means mental exhaustion; because it is associated with the defilements, that does not exist for Buddhas. It is taken up...
It is called a mirror (*ādāsa*) because one’s self is reflected (*ālokīyati*) in it; a mirror of the Dhamma is a "Dhamma-mirror.
