This is a designation for the knowledge of the Noble Path. By means of that, noble disciples—having dispelled their delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths and having known themselves as they truly are—may declare [the truth] as it truly is.
Furthermore, this discourse on the Dhamma is a "Dhamma-mirror" because it illuminates that very state.
It should be understood. Regarding the phrase "by means of the vision of the Dhamma," it refers here specifically to the Dhamma of the Path.

Having known it thoroughly and according to reality (*avecca yāthāvato*), the confidence that arises because of that is "confidence through penetration" (*aveccapasāda*); it is the confidence produced by the attainment of the Path.
Furthermore, because it is as immovable as a mountain of rock and does not disappear due to any cause whatsoever, therefore—
It is said: “By the immovable and the undecaying.

The phrase “the five precepts” is stated here with reference to householders, because they must avoid them absolutely. For noble ones (*ariya*), however, all precepts are indeed agreeable. Therefore he said: “But here, every kind of restraint (*saṃvara*) is indeed obtained. “Of all” means of all noble ones.
“Without contradicting the training rules” means in such a way that there is no offense regarding the disclosure of the truth. “In a suitable place” means in a place appropriate for doing so.
Commentary on the Story of the Courtesan Ambapālī 161.
At that time, it is said, Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, endowed with all things, and had reached a state of great abundance; with reference to this, it is said:
"The excellence of Vesālī is to be understood according to the method stated in the Khandhaka. Regarding that community of bhikkhus...
There were about five hundred bhikkhus who were new, having recently gone forth, and whose energy was slack. For it will be said:
"In that regard, it seems some bhikkhus were slack in their energy," and so forth. "For the purpose of establishing mindfulness" means for the purpose of establishing mindfulness in them.
"He remembers" means he recollects and bears in mind the body and so forth according to their true nature by means of mindfulness associated with knowledge. "He is clearly comprehending" means...

He knows and understands it equally through its modes. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, will follow later in the commentary on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"Comprehensive" means a statement that encompasses all states of blueness, both those pertaining to the body and those pertaining to clothing and ornaments.
"Of that very same" refers to the meaning already stated by way of being comprehensive, namely, "blue. "Showing the distinction" means...

This is the demonstration of the distinction. Just as those Licchavi kings, though naturally yellow and so forth in color, appeared yellow and so forth due to the application of ointments, so too some who were not blue and so forth in color appeared blue and so forth due to the application of ointments; thus it is said, "Their natural color was not blue," and so on.
"Blue-jewel" (*nīlamaṇi*) means those [robes] which have blue gems—such as sapphires (*indanīla*) and great sapphires (*mahānīla*)—strung upon them.
Adornments. These, it is said, being fashioned of gold yet shimmering with the luster of jewels, appear as if they were entirely blue.
"Inlaid with blue gems" means encircled by blue jewels. "Encircled by blue cloth" means surrounded by blue garments and blue cloths. "By blue mounds" means surrounded by blue jars.
"In all instances" refers to all such phrases as "they become yellow," and so forth. "She turned over" means—
"Paṭighaṭṭesi" means he struck. "Āhāro" refers to the food brought by these royal men; thus he said, "along with the people who provide that food," meaning "together with the district.
"Aṅguliphoṭo" also occurs simply through the movement of a finger; therefore it is said, "he moved his finger. "Ambakāya" means by a woman.
This is a conventional term for women, namely: "ambakā, mātugāma, jananikā."
“Look! means: look by turning [your gaze] away. Furthermore, since that looking away is a seeing again and again, he said, “See repeatedly. “Compare! means:
make a comparison such as, “Just as this assembly of Licchavi kings is endowed with a preeminent beauty, so too is the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Therefore he said, “By the Tāvatiṃsa [gods].”
"Having made them equal, look!
"Monks, compare the assembly of Licchavis to the Tāvatiṃsa devas. This is not an instruction to grasp at signs;
rather, it is a gradual discourse intended to show that the sovereign prosperity of these kings is like the celestial splendor of the gods.
This should be regarded as being like the description of the attainment of heaven. Among those monks, however, some might have grasped the sign (nimitta) there;
with reference to them, it is said, "he urges them toward the grasping of the sign.

Out of a desire for their welfare—just as the display of the attainment of heaven was [shown] out of a desire for the welfare of the Venerable Nanda—it is therefore said, "There, it is said," and so forth.
"Those whose energy has slackened" (*ossannavīriyā*) means those whose energy has become lax regarding right practice; the sense is "those who have abandoned energy.

"For the purpose of manifesting the characteristic of impermanence" (*aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of making the characteristic of impermanence manifest to the monks by way of those kings.
The Commentary on the Visit to the Rainy-Season Retreat at Veḷuva Village.

163. "Near the village of Veḷuva" means a surrounding village situated in a nearby place suitable for returning after having gone there either in the forenoon or in the evening. "Having approached" means having gone together.

"Of him" refers to the Blessed One. 164. "Harsh" means hard; the meaning is that it was more severe. "A discordant illness" means a more intense disease arising from a disharmony of the elements (*dhātu*), not merely a slight ailment.
"Having delimited with knowledge" means [having delimited] the momentariness and the painfulness of the feelings.
Having delimited and weighed the emptiness of self (*attasuññatā*) exactly as it is through knowledge, he "endured" them;
that is, overcoming them, he endured them by attributing to himself the manner in which they were crushed through the act of examination, rather than being overcome by them.
Therefore he said, "without being distressed," and so forth. "Without suffering" means without suffering on account of mental pain (*ceto-dukkha*); [as for] bodily pain...
However, it cannot be said that "it does not exist," for if that were absent, forbearance itself would be impossible. "Without having addressed" means without having spoken to.
"Without having taken leave" means without having given permission. Therefore he said: "It means 'without having given instruction and admonition.

"By means of preliminary effort" refers to the preparatory effort for the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti). "By means of the effort of the attainment of the fruit" [refers to the actual attainment].
By means of the energy associated with the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Having suppressed" means having dispelled.
Just as, for example, when a wedge is driven into a *campaka* or other tree at the time of its flowering, its capacity to flower is suppressed and dispelled for as long as that wedge is not removed;
even so, by the application of the wedge of the aforementioned energy, those feelings [of the Teacher]—
In the body, they were suppressed and dispelled for as long as [the lifespan] was delimited. Therefore it is said: “Having suppressed means having dispelled.
Life itself—the life-formative force—is so called because it is formed by karma.
When it is being severed, it is joined through the perfection of application and maintained by the conjunction of opposing conditions. “Having resolved” means resolution.
Having done so, he said: "He entered the attainment [thinking], 'May it not arise for ten months.
Furthermore, since that [attainment] deserves to be called both "resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and "proceeding" (*pavattana*), it is stated: "having resolved and having proceeded.
Momentary attainment (*khaṇika-samāpatti*) is an attainment that can be entered instantaneously without having performed such prior volitional preparation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*).
Again, the body is overwhelmed by feeling because no specific prior volitional formation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) has been made.

The sevenfold sets of form and the sevenfold sets of the formless should be understood according to the method explained in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*. It suppresses [feeling] thoroughly because the prior volitional formation is particularly intense.
Now, in order to clarify this meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as if" was spoken. "Apabyūḷho" means...

"Removed. "Having moistened in fourteen ways" means that by means of those very same sevenfold sets of material and immaterial qualities, he moistened his mind of insight—or indeed his entire personal existence—in fourteen modes, in order to eliminate the state of dryness produced by a discordant disease;
yet it did not arise at all because it had been thoroughly suppressed by the extraordinary force of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"Having been ill and having recovered again" means that he was previously ill and has since recovered from that state of illness.
"Sweetness" refers to a stiffening of the body; however, because that is preceded by a sense of heaviness, it is said: "heaviness having arisen, stiffness having arisen.
By the phrase "they do not appear in various ways," it is indicated that I also experienced confusion regarding the directions.

He shows [this] by the phrase "by the power of sorrow. Although the phenomena such as the foundations of mindfulness—the phenomena of contemplation beginning with the contemplation of the body—had previously appeared clearly and remained present, they are now no longer manifest to me. 165.
"He makes it internal" means placing it within himself alone. "He makes the person internal" means the same.
By way of impartiality, because he had previously supported him in accordance with the Dhamma. "In his youth" means during his own youth.
"Without telling anyone" means without telling any of his own pupils, keeping it hidden like a secret text.
"Having made a fist" means having kept it as a secret, as if it were held within a closed fist. Or, when that [text] is lost, everything rooted in it is lost.
*Dhammo vinassati*: that *dhamma* which was originally the root; because the *dhamma* is forgotten and lost through this [loss], it is called a *muṭṭhi*.
By saying "having made such a fist and carried it about," he shows that there is nothing at all deposited therein.
The restriction "I alone" is for the purpose of showing that the maintenance of the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus is not shared with others. By means of this restriction...

However, it should be understood that the passage beginning with "I, the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus" demonstrates the absence of the notions of "I-making" (ahaṅkāra) and "mine-making" (mamaṅkāra) in the act of maintaining the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. "In the sense of being designated as 'Teacher'" means in the sense of being designated as "the Teacher.
Or rather, the intention is "may there not be Bhikkhus"; or the reading is "mā vā ahosi. "Thus it does not exist" refers to [the thought] "I shall maintain the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus," and so forth.
The occurrence of consciousness does not take place by way of a [fixed] mode.
By the statement, "It is said for the purpose of indicating the attainment of the final passing away," it is shown that, just like the passing away itself, the Buddha-work is also a completed task.

The "axle-fastening" (bāhabandha) is the binding with a strap for the sake of strengthening the portion of the cart's axle. The "wheel-fastening" (cakkabandha) is the binding with a strap for the sake of strengthening the joints of the wheel-rim.

"That is the meaning" refers to what was stated as "he conceives by means of a combination of entanglements. Because visible forms and so forth appear as if they were a composite whole, they are called "signs of form" and so on;
[the phrase] "of those signs of form and so on" refers to these. Regarding "of mundane feelings":

when those feelings through the cessation of which the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is to be entered, their cessation brings ease, and likewise it brings ease even for one whose body is struck by intense pain.
"For that purpose" means for the purpose of dwelling in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). An island (*dīpa*) is a portion of land surrounded by water and not submerged by it;
here, however, the "island" intended is the self (*attā*), which is not submerged by any of the four floods (*ogha*), or indeed by the great flood of *saṃsāra*.
Therefore he said, "gone to the great ocean," and so forth. "Taking refuge in oneself": [the rest follows].

“Having themselves as refuge” means having themselves as their destination—that is, having themselves as their ultimate resort. “Do not seek another destination” means do not think of any other destination, refuge, or ultimate resort. Why? Because here, in the ultimate sense, the self is the Dhamma by virtue of its internal nature;
when this is accomplished, it alone is your island, your shelter, your destination, and your ultimate resort. Therefore it was said: “With the Dhamma as their island,” and so forth.
And so it has been said: “The self is indeed its own protector; for who else could be the protector? For dependence on another is merely a matter of instruction;
all other success belongs to a person solely through their own self-reliance. Therefore the Blessed One said: “You yourselves must exert effort;
the Tathāgatas are only teachers. *Tamaggē* means at the head of the connection with darkness (*tama*), because there is no state beyond that.
For this very reason, he said, "These are the foremost," and so forth. "In my" means in my teaching (*sāsana*).

"All of them have the four foundations of mindfulness as their domain" means that by developing and cultivating the fourfold foundation of mindfulness, and making that alone their domain—that is, their own sphere of activity—these bhikkhus will stand at the pinnacle.
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Radiance of the Sign (Nimittobhāsakathā): 166.
Since the Blessed One dwelt at Vesālī on many occasions, this entry into Vesālī is specified [as follows].
In order to show this, he asked, "When did you enter? and then, demonstrating [the sequence] starting from his arrival, he said, "The Blessed One, it is said," and so forth.
"By the very path by which he had come" means returning by the same path as before, up to the village of Veḷuva. "According to the established limit" means according to the time previously delimited.
"From that" means from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "This" refers to the manner now being described: the surveying of the daytime resting place, and so on.

This is a demonstration of the absolute certainty of his final *parinibbāna*. "Relaxed" (*ossaṭṭha*) means that the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) has been relinquished [with the thought], "I have only seven days more to live.
"Of the elder and younger brothers" refers to all his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*).
"I shall cause them to enter upon the path" means I shall direct them toward the practice of the path. "On a jeweled slab" means on a board placed in front [of him] inlaid with jewels.
"Regarding 'that first seeing': the seeing accomplished when [the Buddha] came to Veḷuvana in the guise of a wanderer—that was the first seeing.

Or, the seeing of you [the Bodhisattvas] which was accomplished at the time of the formal aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), as if it were directly perceived by one who places faith in the words of the Blessed One Anomadassi—that was the first seeing. Regarding 'the journey of the return'..."
The journey was for the purpose of returning.
"For seven days" is used in the accusative case to express duration. It is said that the Elder’s birth-chamber was secluded from other houses and had an open courtyard;
therefore, it was suitable for the approach of devas and brahmās, [thinking] "the birth-chamber..."
"Take care of it," he said. "He" refers to Uparevata. "That activity" refers to what was said out of a desire to dwell there.
Following the principle that "Tathāgatas ask even though they already know," the Elder asked, "Who are you?
When asked, "Are you greater than the Four Great Kings? he, attributing his own greatness to the Teacher, replied:
"These female lay disciples of our Teacher are like park-keepers," he said. For even the praise of the excellence of the disciples, in its true sense, reveals the excellence of the Teacher himself.

"Having established themselves in the fruit of stream-entry" means that, through the power of the Elder’s teaching and by virtue of the ripening of their own knowledge due to the perfection of their own supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), they became established in the fruit of stream-entry.

"They come" means as previously stated. "Therein" refers to this entry into Vesālī, namely, "he entered Vesālī for alms. "Successive discourse" (*anupubbīkathā*) is a discourse that illustrates a sequence.
"At the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena" means at the place honored by the great multitude, which had been built with bricks in the capacity of a dwelling for the yakkha named Udena.
"A monastery was built" means a monastery constructed in honor of the Blessed One. It is said.
By way of ancient convention, it is called the “Udena Cetiya. “In the case of Gotamaka and so forth” means in such cases as the “Gotamaka Cetiya” and others.
“The same method applies” refers by extension to the fact that these are monasteries (vihāra) built on sites where there were originally shrines (cetiya).

“Cultivated” means brought to full growth by way of the completion of meditative development (bhāvanā). “Repeatedly performed” means set in motion again and again through the frequent practice of meditative development. “A yoked vehicle.”

"Made like [a chariot]" means that just as a noble steed's vehicle, when directed by a skilled charioteer, proceeds according to his wish, so too has it been brought to a state where it proceeds according to one’s wish.
"In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of a basis.

"Made like a site" means that because it serves as a place for the manifestation of supernormal power through the complete purification of all defilements, it is like a well-cleansed site free from dangers.

"Made as it were": they have been established because, through being well-developed, they have been placed in a state of fitness for their respective foundations due to the removal of opposing factors.
"Heaped up on all sides": they have been brought to the accumulation of development in every respect. Therefore he said, "well-increased. "Well undertaken":
they have been properly cultivated until the peak of the development of supernormal power (*iddhi*) has been reached.
"Indeterminately" means by the indeterminate expression "of anyone whatsoever. "Having determined" means having determined it by showing the specific form as "of the Tathāgata.

By "measure of life," he refers to the maximum measure of life; the reason for taking that specifically should be understood in the same manner as explained in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
However, the Elder Mahāsiva says: "[It refers to] the one who bestows rebirth-linking upon Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence..."

"Having kept in mind the capacity of karma to bring about an incalculable lifespan, it is stated in the Canon that the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) of the Buddhas possesses the power to suppress dangers; therefore, [the Buddha] said, 'May this auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*) itself endure.
By the phrase "it is overcome by brokenness and so forth," it is shown that there is no warding off of old age through the power of psychic potency (*iddhibala*).
Thus, it follows by implication that there is no resistance even toward death.
It should be understood that even when the Elder’s statement was presented differently—as "Where was the arrow shot? And where did it fall?"—the words of the Commentary were nonetheless supported.
Therefore, he said: "That is not pleasing... [etc. ...it is restricted."
“With a mind obsessed” means that his mind was so overwhelmed that he was unable to discern what was beneficial or harmful.
That overwhelming, however, was like a small amount of water being completely submerged by a great flood;
thus it is said, “with a mind overwhelmed. “Another person as well” refers to anyone other than the Elder—that is, any worldling (puthujjana) other than the Noble Ones (ariya).

And here, the mention of the "worldling" (puthujjana) is for the purpose of showing that just as one whose inversions (vipallāsa) are entirely unabandoned and whose mind is obsessed by Māra is unable to discern any meaning, so too the Elder did not discern the manifestation of signs performed by the Blessed One at all.
Therefore he said, "Māra indeed," and so forth. The four inversions [are] regarding the foul...

“Beautiful” (*subha*) is a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*) and a perversion of mind (*citta-vipallāsa*); “pleasure” (*sukha*) in what is suffering (*dukkha*) is a perversion of perception and a perversion of mind—these are the four perversions.
“By that” means: even though the other eight perversions have been abandoned, nevertheless, by virtue of the fact that these aforementioned four perversions have not been abandoned.
“Of him” refers to the Elder. “Crushes” means by the mere act of touching.
He is like one who crushes; otherwise, if he were to crush them in that way, it would result only in the death of the beings.
The intention is: "Will he be able [to digest it]? Will he not be able? Why will he not be able? Is it not the case that he has entered the womb of the Chief Disciple?
True, he has entered, but that was for the purpose of displaying his own power, not with the intention of causing harm.
However, it is said here with the intention of challenging him, "Will he be able? because [the Buddha] has attained the crushing of the heart. Regarding the "appearance of signs" (*nimittobhāsa*):

by means of the request for him to remain for an entire eon, saying, "May the Blessed One stay for a kappa," and by means of the indirect statement, "Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of psychic power... and so forth, [he refers] to the power of his own development of the four bases of psychic power.
The sign (*nimitta*) is the production of a perception by way of its capacity to remain for an eon (*kappa*);
whereas the radiance (*obhāsa*) is the direct manifestation of one’s own intention, having abandoned such figurative expression.

"Knowing indeed" means knowing that he was possessed by Māra. He said, "By the attribution of fault, the sorrow of beings becomes slight rather than intense," because their grief arises from the cause of their own transgression.
"For the purpose of alleviating grief. But did the Elder later come to know his state of mind at the time he was overwhelmed by Māra?
He did not know it by means of his own natural power, but he understood it through the majesty of the Buddha.
Commentary on the Discourse Requested by Māra.
168. By engaging beings in what is harmful, he kills them by destroying their virtues;
or, by obstructing dispassion (*virāga*), he is as if killing each being as they are born here and there due to the causal sign of birth. Thus it is said: "He is Māra because he kills.

Because of his extreme wickedness, he is the Evil One (*pāpimā*). Because he is possessed of dark qualities (*kaṇha-dhamma*), he is Black (*kaṇha*). Because he brings about the end of virtues such as dispassion, he is the Ender (*antaka*). Of beings...

He is called *Namuci* because he does not release one from a course of conduct that brings about what is harmful. He binds the heedless with his own snare of Māra, or those who are heedless are his bonds;
thus he is the "Kinsman of the Heedless. He says, "in the eighth week," referring to the seven days following the seventh week;
however, this is not because the eighth week has a specific name for a fixed duty, as is the case with the "week of the cross-legged posture" (*pallaṅka-sattāha*) and others.

After the seventh week, having learned that the Blessed One had promised to teach the Dhamma to Mahābrahmā and Sakka, the king of the gods, at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, Māra became despondent, thinking, "Now he will lead beings beyond my domain by means of his teaching of the Dhamma.
Standing there, he thought: "Well now, I shall use a stratagem against him..."
"I shall cause [him] to attain final Nibbāna; thus his desire will be frustrated, and my own desire will be fulfilled.
Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and, standing at one side, requested final Nibbāna with the words, "Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna," and so forth.
It is with reference to this that it was said, "In the eighth week," and so on. Therein:
"Today" refers to the day of relinquishing the life-force (*āyu-saṅkhāra*). Although the Blessed One knew his underlying intention, he did not reveal it;
rather, rejecting the request, he made clear that it was the wrong time for his final *parinibbāna*. Therefore he said, "Not yet," and so forth.
"Distinguished by way of the path" means distinguished by proficiency in the penetration of the Truths. Likewise, "disciplined" means by way of the path.

They are disciplined by the complete eradication and removal of the defilements. Likewise, they are "confident" (visāradā) because, through the very attainment of the Noble Path, they have reached intrepidity within the Teacher’s dispensation;
the meaning is that they have attained a state of confidence through the disappearance of evil states such as wrong views and doubt, which cause timidity.
It is by means of that learning (suta) that escape from the suffering of the round of existence becomes possible.
Regarding that, he says "by way of the Tripiṭaka" because, according to the highest description, it is intended here as "heard.
The collection of the three Piṭakas is the Tripiṭaka; or, the three Piṭakas themselves are the Tripiṭaka, and the term "Tripiṭaka" is used in the sense of being precisely that.
"That very same" refers to that which was called "heard" by virtue of its being something to be heard, namely the Tripiṭaka. "Dhamma" means...

The *pariyatti-dhamma*. "They bear it" means they bear it by placing it in their hearts, ensuring it does not perish—just like lion's meat placed in a golden vessel—and by means of its being well-mastered and well-recited.

Thus, having shown the state of being one who has heard much and who bears the Dhamma by way of the *pariyatti-dhamma*, he now shows that same state by way of the *paṭivedha-dhamma* as well: "Then..."
The passage beginning with “or” has been stated. “Of the noble Dhamma” means of the Dhamma of the Path and Fruition, or of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
“Conforming to the Dhamma” (anudhamma) means being a Dhamma suitable for its realization.

By “conformable practice” (anucchavika-paṭipadā), he refers to that very same Dhamma of insight (vipassanā), or else to the sixfold purification (visuddhi). “Conforming Dhamma” (anudhamma) refers to that aforementioned practice.

"Conformable" means the practice of the qualities such as fewness of desires (*appicchatā*), which is conducive to self-effacement. "Those whose conduct is according to the Dhamma" means those whose conduct proceeds from having undertaken [the training].

Alternatively, it is "conformable" (*anudhammā*) because the Dhamma of the Path and its Fruit follows after this; that is, insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*). Those whose conduct is according to that are "those whose conduct is according to the Dhamma.
"His own teacher’s doctrine" means the doctrine of his own teacher, the Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). Of the world with its devas...
The Blessed One is a teacher by way of training others in conduct (*ācāra*). His teaching is the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
"They will proclaim" means they will speak from the beginning; the sense is that they will cause others to learn according to the system they themselves have mastered.
"They will teach" means they will instruct; the sense is that they will correctly awaken [others] to the textual tradition (*pāḷi*). "They will describe" means...
"They will cause [others] to understand" means they will cause them to have conviction. "They will establish" means they will set it forth in various ways;
the sense is that they will make it manifest. "They will disclose" means they will make it open. "They will analyze" means they will make it divided.
"They will make plain" means they will make what is not plain—that which is deep—plain and evident. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the Dhamma": here...

The word *dhamma* is a term for a cause, as in such passages as "knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); thus he says, "by speech that possesses a cause and possesses a reason.
"With its demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) means with its escape (*sanissaraṇa*);
just as one's own doctrine is established after having refuted the opposing doctrine, so too, by means of reasons and examples, one establishes the matter as it has been realized.
They will preach the Dhamma. Therefore he said, "Having made it leading-out, they will teach the Dhamma"; the meaning is that they will awaken the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
And here, by the six phrases beginning with "they will make known," six meaning-terms are shown;
but by the first two phrases, six phrasing-terms are shown. Up to this point, the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas [has been explained].
It has been shown by way of a method of commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanānaya*). For this was said in the *Netti*: "The discourse (*sutta*) consists of twelve terms;
all of that is both the phrasing (*byañjana*) and the meaning (*attha*).

"Comprised within the three trainings" means being included within the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). "The entire holy life of the Dispensation" (*sakalaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ*).
The supreme conduct, which constitutes the Teacher’s entire instruction without exception. "Samiddhaṃ" means perfectly increased.
"By way of the bliss of jhāna" means by way of the jhāna-happiness attained by those various bhikkhus.

"Reached full growth" means having attained complete increase through the attainment of a state that is sublime and excellent. By way of the perfection of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), it is like a tree in full bloom.
“From reaching the pinnacle of the growth of the Dispensation. “By way of being established” means by way of a foundation; the meaning is “by way of attaining establishment.
“Beneficial to many people” (bāhujañña) means it is for the welfare of a great multitude of people. Therefore he said: “By way of the realization of many people.
“Puthubhūta” means that which has become wide or extensive, or that which has reached a state of being wide or manifold (puthutta). Therefore he said:
“...in all aspects... attained. It is well-expounded (*supakāsita*), meaning it has been correctly proclaimed (*sammadeva*) as being excellent in its beginning and so forth.
169. Commentary on the Relinquishing of the Life-Force (*āyu-saṅkhāra-ossajjana*):
“Having established mindfulness firmly (*satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā*): this division of the body and so forth, designated as the personal existence (*attabhāva*), is a burden of suffering by me...”
For so long a time it was carried along, but now it must no longer be carried; for the sake of not carrying it further,

the equipment for the Noble Path has been accumulated over a very long period, and this Noble Path has been penetrated, whereby these things such as the body have been thoroughly understood through their foulness and so forth,
and the fourfold right mindfulness has been well established in its object according to reality.

"Having determined by means of knowledge" means: because the purpose for carrying this burden of suffering known as the personal existence (*attabhāva*)—namely, one's own welfare (*attahita*)—has already been fully accomplished at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree;

whereas the welfare of others (*parahita*), which consists in the disciplining of those to be guided by a Buddha, still remains to be accomplished, and that will now reach completion in just three months; therefore, he spoke.
“I shall attain final Nibbāna on the full moon of Visākha”—having thus delimited [the time] with Buddha-knowledge and made a firm resolve through every aspect.

He relinquished the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*); that is, he relinquished the dharma of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which conditions the life-span (*āyu*), thinking, “I will not enter into this attainment.
By that very act of relinquishing it, he relinquished the life-force conditioned by that [attainment].

“I shall not let it proceed,” he replied. Therefore, he said, “Therein,” and so forth. The earthquake was great both by reason of the vastness of its location and the vastness of the manner of its occurrence.
Therein, in order to show the magnitude of the earth-trembling through the vastness of its location, it is said:
“At that time, indeed... [the earth] trembled. That [location], moreover, is precisely the ten-thousandfold world-system, which serves as the field of birth.
It did not shake at any other time, even during such events as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) or the Great Birth (*mahājāti*). Why, then, did it shake at that very moment?
It was because he had, from the very beginning, formally demarcated that specific birth-field (*jātikkhetta*) for himself.
This act of demarcation should be understood as occurring by way of the natural law (*dhammatā*). For indeed, the birth-fields of previous Buddhas were also exactly that much in extent.
It was so; for it is said: “The ten-thousandfold world system became silent and untroubled... the great ocean rolled back, and the ten-thousandfold world system quaked,” and so forth.
It is called *bhiṃsana* because it terrifies those who are not yet free from lust by means of its sixfold quaking as far as the limits of the waters;
thus he says, “it produces fear,” and that very thing is the *bhiṃsanaka*. “Divine kettledrums” means:
This is merely a figurative expression for the sound of the "divine drum" (*devadundubhi*). No actual drum is intended here by the term "divine drum";
rather, it refers to the sound of a resonance occurring in the sky, which is obtained through its nature as a portent. Therefore, he said "the god," and so forth.
"The god" means a cloud; for, due to its clarity, [it is called a god] because of the sound resembling dry thundering that arises from the sky’s state of raining.
The designation "divine drum" is applied because it resounds like one. Therefore he said: "The god roared a dry thunder.
"Released by the force of joy" means that the Blessed One, having become joyful at the thought, "This burden of suffering called 'individual existence' has been carried for so very long;
now it shall soon be laid down," [uttered this] by his very nature, released by the force of joy.
He uttered an inspired utterance (*udāna*). However, in order to show that by uttering this inspired utterance this meaning was also established, the *Aṭṭhakathā* says "Why?

and so forth. To demonstrate that the word *tula* is a noun formed through the passive construction (*kamma-sādhana*) in the sense of "that which is weighed" (*tuliyati*), it says "weighed" (*tulita*). Due to its lack of power...
It is limited. For it is called "limited" (*paritta*) because it is cut off on all sides by way of its fragmented nature.
Because it suppresses opposing states, possesses a long continuity, and yields abundant fruit, it is immeasurable (*atula*) and not limited.

Those reasons by which the sublime (*mahaggata*) was previously described as "immeasurable" without distinction apply to the formless realm (*ārūpya*) even more preeminently than to the fine-material realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Regarding the term "existent" (*vijjamāna*): it is said that "the formless-sphere [kamma] is 'incomparable' (*atula*)," while the other is "comparable" (*tula*).

Among the three types of kamma, that which has little ripening—being slight, inferior, and of weak result—is "comparable. That which has much ripening—being great, excellent, and of strong result—is "incomparable.
Furthermore, that which is intermediate here is divided into two as "inferior" and "superior," and [these are assigned] to the two [remaining categories].

It should be inserted among the portions. Having determined the relative magnitude of the result (*vipāka*) precisely according to the method stated in the commentary on the "Low Triad" (*hīnattika*), the state of being balanced or unbalanced should be understood by way of that.
He said, "the cause of arising," because it arises from this; thus, "arising" (*sambhava*) means that from which something comes into being.

"Delighting in one's own internal states" (*niyakajjhattarato*) means, by way of insight (*vipassanā*) into the phenomena within one’s own continuum, through the cultivation of the field of experience.
And he was devoted to it. That karma which, being accompanied by fruition, gives rise solely to the process of existence (pavatti), is called "origination" (sambhava) in the sense of having fruition.

Yet, since that [karma] does not itself constitute the formative activity for existence such as sensual existence (kāmabhava) and so forth, the term "originating existence" (bhavasaṅkhāra) was stated after first saying "origination" in order to distinguish it from that.
"He cast off" means he relinquished it by means of the Noble Path. Having enveloped the personal existence (attabhāva) like a suit of armor...

Because it is established within himself, he has arisen from himself; thus, showing the entrusting of the action that occurs simultaneously with the breaking of the defilements, he stated the cause for both [the breaking of defilements and the establishment of the mind] as:
"Delighting within, concentrated. "Investigating" means examining [it] by way of such [considerations] as:
"Arising is danger, non-arising is security," and so forth. This is according to the passage beginning: "Weighing, investigating... and so on.

In order to show in detail the meaning that was stated in brief, he spoke the words beginning with “the five aggregates,” thereby demonstrating the manner of relinquishing the formative forces of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) according to its true nature.
Furthermore, by means of the words beginning with “thus,” he demonstrated, by way of conclusion, the meaning stated at the outset of the commentary on the *udāna*.
171. Regarding the commentary on the great earthquake:

the phrase "at which time" (*yaṃ samayaṃ*) is stated with the intention that it may be used either as an instrumental or a locative case in the nominative sense; thus he says, "by which occasion, or at which occasion.
"Lifting-up winds" (*ukkhepakavātā*) refers to winds that, having severed the wind that supports water, [arise] from the place where it stands.
The lifting winds. The statement, “Sixty... [etc. ... thick,” is said by taking only the height-measure of that wind;
however, in terms of length and breadth, it indeed cuts off even the water-supporting wind, which is ten thousand world-systems in extent.
“In the sky” means in the space previously established by the wind. “Again, the wind” refers to the lifting wind.
Having done so, once the wind that holds up the water has subsided, he binds it again and takes hold of it so that the water does not spill;
thus, by means of binding and spreading it out as a canopy while propping it up, he takes hold of it. Then the water rises up:
from that point of having bound and taken hold of it, the water, propped up by that wind, rises upward.
"It goes upward. "It indeed remains so" means that it indeed remains so from time to time. "By way of its thickness" means by way of the vastness of the great earth.
For at that time, the entire great earth sinks down and rises up; therefore, no shaking is perceived. "Of success" means of the accomplishment of the desired goal.
[This refers to] the attainment of sovereignty and so forth that is to be experienced. "Limited" means...
"Merely acquired" means not well-cultivated; and because such cultivation is not powerful, he says "weak. For here, cultivation is spoken of by way of perception (*saññā*).
"Immeasurable" means familiar and well-cultivated; for that is firm and more stable, thus he says "powerful.
The statement, "The perception of earth is limited, the perception of water is immeasurable," is merely a teaching device.
However, when the perception of water is well-developed, the shaking of the earth succeeds with ease; this is the intended meaning here that should be understood.

[The Buddha] was either stirring Sakka, the king of the gods, who was negligent due to his divine success, or testing the power of his own psychic potency which he had just attained. The shaking of the Great Elder Moggallāna’s palace is well known.
Without mentioning him, in order to demonstrate the shaking of the palace by the novice Saṅgharakkhita, it was said, beginning with, “It is said that this venerable one...”.
One whose scent is mixed with putridity is “putrid-scented” (*pūtigandha*);
by means of that very putrid scent, as if having attained birth from a mother’s womb through scent alone, he is “exceedingly like a child”—this is the meaning.
"Teacher" means the instruction of a teacher. "Supernormal power" (iddhābhisaṅkhāra) refers to that which is intended through the manifestation of various kinds of supernormal powers;
yet, because he had not properly mastered the skill in means himself, he had not yet trained in it, and thus [the Buddha] said, "You entered the battle without having trained.
By the word "overflowing," [he meant] that he turned the entire site of the palace into water.
This shows that it flows there like a palace that has been resolved upon. Then, illustrating the sequence of resolution by means of a simile, he said:
"Dear son... know thus. In this context, *kapallakapūva* refers to a poured cake;
those baking it first place a small amount of dough in a pan, gradually expanding it until they define the cake by its outer edge.

They place it having delimited it on all sides; thus, by way of the water-kasina, when one resolves, "Let the place where the palace stands be water," he points this out by means of a simile: "It should be resolved so that there is water everywhere around the palace, right up to its boundaries."
It is exactly as stated in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*: having said, "Bhikkhus, it is the natural law that when the Bodhisatta descends from the Tusita realm into his mother’s womb,
this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes, and quakes," and likewise, "Bhikkhus,
it is the natural law that when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb..."
Having stated, "And this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes, and quakes," since it is taught that at the Great Being’s descent into the womb and at his birth,
an earthquake occurs as a matter of natural law (*dhammatā*) during these great events,
the intention is that at the other four stages as well, the earthquake occurs solely by way of natural law; thus it is effectively stated in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*.
Now, in order to show the analysis of their earthquake according to its cause and the manner of its occurrence, the passage beginning with “Thus, among these” was spoken.
“By the disturbance of the elements” means by the agitation of the air element, which is reckoned as the uplifting element.

“By the power of psychic success” (iddhānubhāvena) means by the majesty of either knowledge-based psychic power (ñāṇiddhi) or the psychic power born of the ripening of karma; the meaning is “by its intensity” (tejasā). “By the intensity of merit” (puññatejasā) means by the majesty of merit.
The meaning is: "by the power of the merit of the Great Bodhisatta. "By the splendor of knowledge" means by the majesty of the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).

"By way of giving a cry of approval" means that just as the great earth shook at the moment of full enlightenment when struck by the majesty of the knowledge of penetration—which is not shared by others—so too did the great earth shake when struck by the majesty of the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*), which is likewise not shared by others.
But since that [expression] was like giving a cry of approval (*sādhukāra*) to her, it is said: "by way of giving a cry of approval. By whom [was it spoken]?

By the Blessed One, whose physical body (*rūpakāya*) was adorned with the eighty minor marks and variegated by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and whose Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*) was enriched with the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) purified in every aspect;
[and who was the possessor of] greatness in merit, greatness in power, greatness in fame, greatness in majesty, and greatness in wisdom.
The Peerless One, the Unequaled, the Matchless, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One—

though capable of sustaining his own five aggregates known as the personal existence for an eon or the remainder of an eon— nevertheless, through a specific mode of knowledge proceeding from a state of revulsion toward conditioned phenomena,

did not regard them even as a blade of grass, and thus, without attachment, relinquished the life-force by means of the method of casting off the volitional formations of longevity. Overwhelmed by the power of that [relinquishment],...
When the life-force was relinquished, the great earth trembled; however, because it remained as if established in a nature of compassion, it is said, "by way of its compassionate nature.

Since at the time of his final Nibbāna the Blessed One entered twenty-four hundred thousand million meditative attainments (samāpatti), interspersed with the attainment of the fruition (phala-samāpatti), [this state] was preeminent in his prior stage.
He brought forth sharp and heroic insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), thinking: "For the sake of which I have for so very long accumulated this supreme,
unsurpassed equipment of knowledge— unshared by others— and attained the unsurpassed liberation, that very goal of mine, the ultimate consummation,
the element of Nirvana without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu*) as the fruit reaching its pinnacle, is indeed being realized today."

Furthermore, in the Blessed One, who had attained an exceeding measure of gladness, there arose a preeminent excellence of knowledge—a singular quality not shared by others—possessing a more vast power than even the expansion of rapture (*pītivipphāra*) and other virtues. With reference to the majesty of this preeminent knowledge, which was further augmented by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it was said:
"These two alms-offerings are equal in fruit, equal in result," and so forth; therefore, regarding that...
Struck by his majesty, the great earth shook. At that time, it was as if she were manifesting the act of weeping;
thus it is said, "The eighth [sign] was by way of weeping.
Now, expanding upon the meaning briefly stated, he says, "When descending into the mother’s womb," and so forth. This, then, is the meaning:
The meaning stated by the passage beginning with “by way of giving a cry of ‘well done’” is as follows. Regarding the phrase “by way of the earth deity”:
it is said that, just like the ocean deity, there is indeed a presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the great earth.
When such a cause exists, this great earth quakes, trembles, and shakes by the power of her mind, just as [it happens] for the wind-deities and the cloud-deities.
The winds blow by the power of the mind; cold, heat, and rain come about through the power of the minds of the cloud-deities.

For instance, on the full moon of Visākha, in order to dispel the host of Māra who had appeared to create obstacles for the Lord of the World as he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the sake of his perfect enlightenment—
“This earth is insentient; it does not perceive pleasure or pain.
Yet even it, by the power of my gift, has trembled seven times.
Immediately upon these words, the great earth split open and overturned Māra along with his retinue. “This” refers to the giving of applause and so forth.
Even if it does not exist because it lacks consciousness, one can still say that it may occur by way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*) according to the method already described.
For "the nature of things" means, in its actual sense, the intrinsic nature of phenomena; it is the essential power of either meritorious phenomena or the phenomena of knowledge.
All of this has indeed been investigated. And having established it thus—
“When these phenomena are fully understood— along with their specific natures,
essential tastes, and characteristics— the earth of the ten-thousandfold world system trembled through the power of the Dhamma.
Thus, the initial statement is established.
“Demonstration by way of what has been demonstrated” (*niddiṭṭhanidassana*) means the presentation of the meaning already demonstrated; the sense is “conclusion.
“To this extent” refers both to the production of the earthquake and so forth, and to the demonstration of the cause of the earthquake as being the Blessed One.
By the method of elimination (*pārisesañāya*), he observed: “Surely today the Blessed One has relinquished the life-force formation (*āyusaṅkhāra*). For it was thus that the Elder then [perceived].
One should investigate this matter: this earthquake is not caused by a disturbance of the elements, because no such form is apparent;
nor is there any external seer of such great power during the time of a Buddha; nor is there anyone within the Dispensation who would act in such a way without first informing the Teacher;
and as for the other five [causes], they are impossible now. Thus, this earthquake is truly terrifying.
He was one whose hair and feathers had fallen out; therefore, by way of elimination, it says: "Today he perceived that the Blessed One had relinquished the life-formations.
172. Regarding the commentary on the eight assemblies:
"Without giving him an opportunity" refers to the Elder’s [request] made in the manner beginning with, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an eon."

Without giving him an opportunity to request [the teaching], [the Blessed One] spoke the passage beginning with "These eight," showing that he has subsumed three other sets of eight—distinct from the "eight on the cause"—by way of the bases for overcoming assemblies and the liberations, while collecting those other groups of eight as well. Some say:
"In order to avoid the arising of grief in the Venerable Ānanda and to prevent distraction," for if one were to speak hastily, a powerful grief might arise.
Because they must come together, or because he comes together with them, it is a "gathering" (*samāgama*), meaning an assembly. A gathering headed by Bimbisāra is a "Bimbisāra-gathering.
The same method applies to the other two [assemblies] as well. The application of the phrase "a kṣatriya assembly similar to the gathering of Bimbisāra," etc., is as follows.
The Teacher’s approach to the kṣatriya assemblies and so forth is indeed found even in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). From the beginning, by them...
"Speaking together with the Teacher" is *ālāpa*. "Conversation consisting of speaking and replying" is *sallāpa*.
"A question connected with the Dhamma" is *paṭipucchā*, [and] *dhammasākacchā* (discussion of the Dhamma).

"Speaking in dependence on shape" (*saṇṭhāna*) is due to the word *vaṇṇa* being used as a synonym for shape, as in such expressions as "having manifested the great form of a king of elephants. The word "of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to both preceding terms.
“The Teacher’s bodily form was like the bodily form of those [beings], and only theirs was perceived.
Nor was the Blessed One one who wore jeweled earrings; such is the construction. “With broken voices” means with voices that have become split.
“With gurgling voices” means with hoarse voices. “Another language” means a language other than the speech of those beings. “Inquiry” means reflection.
“‘For what purpose... does he teach?’—was this not said with the intention that when the Dhamma is taught after making oneself known, there arises in them an especially great confidence?

For those in whom confidence arises when the Dhamma is taught without making oneself known, rather than by making oneself known—it was with reference to such as these that the Teacher acts in that way. He states the purpose therein:

“For the purpose of impressioning” means: even when heard in this way—that is, even when the teacher is not identified and the place of arrival is not identified—the Dhamma heard becomes a condition for the one hearing it in the future, precisely because of its own nature as the well-spoken Dhamma (*dhammasudhammatā*).
The passage beginning with “Ānanda,” which has not been included in the formal recitation (*saṅgīti*), is shown in that manner. This same method applies to other such instances hereafter.

Commentary on the Eight Bases of Mastery (Aṭṭha-abhibhāyatana-vaṇṇanā) 173. It "masters" (*abhibhavati*), thus it is "mastery" (*abhibhu*); this refers either to the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or to knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

That which has mastery as its base (*āyatana*) is a "base of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*), namely, a jhāna. Alternatively, that which has as its base an object (*ārammaṇa*)—so called because it is to be mastered—is a "base of mastery. This is because of the mastery over the object.

The *abhibhū* (the master) and that *āyatana* (base) are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) because they serve as the foundation for specific states of happiness for the practitioner, or because they consist of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*).
Thus, the jhāna together with its associated factors is the "base of mastery. Therefore he said: "Because they are the causes of mastery," and so forth.
"Those" refers to the jhānas designated as bases of mastery. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the person’s preeminence in knowledge," this applies to both cases.
It should be applied. How? By way of being an antidote, they overcome contrary states; by way of the person’s preeminence in knowledge, they overcome objects.
For, just as there is the overcoming of objects, so too is there the overcoming of opposites through the power of knowledge alone.
By way of preliminary work (*parikamma*), one perceives forms internally, not by way of absorption (*appanā*); for [the jhāna] does not have the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) as its object.

Absorption (appanā) occurs with an internal object; however, that kasiṇa sign obtained by means of internal preliminary work (parikamma) is not yet purified, unlike that obtained by means of external preliminary work.
"Limited" (parittāni) means they are just as they were obtained, having the size of a small water-jar's opening. Therefore he said, "not increased. "Only by way of the limited" means...
Even though there is mental application (*ābhoga*) by way of color, this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is described specifically by way of its limited nature (*paritta*).
For here, limitation is the cause of mastery. Whether there is mental application to the color or not, the cultivation of the bases of mastery occurs only for one of sharp wisdom, not for another;
thus he says, "a person who has knowledge as supreme. Having mastered...

Regarding the phrase "he attains": here, both the overcoming [of the hindrances] and the attainment consist in the arising of absorption concentration (appanā-jhāna) immediately after the acquisition of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna).
Therefore, it is said: "Right at the moment the sign arises, he reaches absorption here.

And the expression "right at the moment the sign arises" is a statement characterizing the absence of a preparatory period for absorption (appanā-parivāsa). Even more so than one who is called "of quick direct knowledge" (khippābhiñño)...

The development of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) belongs only to one who has reached the pinnacle of knowledge. "In this" means in this sign (*nimitta*). "Brings it to absorption" means he leads the development to absorption.

And here, some say: "When access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*) has arisen, those two or three occasions of impulsion (*javana*) that proceed by taking that as their object belong to the side of access concentration itself;
and immediately after that, through the subsidence into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), by the practice of access..."
And they say that absorption occurs without [the preliminary work], reaching absorption at the very moment the sign arises; but that is merely their own opinion.

For an access to absorption through the preliminary work of perfuming is not intended here, nor is reflection absolutely required in the access concentration as it is in the sublime and measureless jhānas. Therefore, after the attainment of access concentration—
Reaching absorption at the conclusion of a few bhavaṅga moments, it is said that "one attains absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
This statement, "simultaneously with the arising of the sign," is intentional (adhippāyika) rather than of direct meaning (nītattha).
The intention should be understood according to the method already stated; for within the attainment itself, there is no such mental application (ābhoga) at that time.

Because it is impossible [for such attention to exist during the attainment itself]. It should be understood that for one who has emerged from the attainment, the mental application (*ābhoga*) occurs by way of prior-stage cultivation, grasping the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of the jhāna.
However, in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "By this, his prior mental application is explained. But why is there no such mental application within the attainment?
Because it is said, “even by the perception of jhāna,” he says, “overpowering... there is.

“Increased in measure” means “vast in measure”; it does not mean they have been brought to increase by one or two finger-breadths and so forth, because such an increase is impossible in this context. Therefore he says, “great. “The bowl filled with food.”
The meaning is: the food given after the bowl used for eating has been enlarged; that is, half of the food that would have been eaten by a man sitting on a single seat.

"Perception of form" (*rūpa-saññā*) means perception of form; one who possesses that is "possessing perception of form. One who does not possess perception of form is "without perception of form" (*arūpa-saññī*); here he refers to the jhāna by way of its characteristic mark, namely perception. Here, "non-attainment" simply means the non-arising of the perception of form.
"Arising only externally" means arising only upon an external object. However, in the Abhidhamma, [it says] "internally..."
“Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited and beautiful or ugly... [and so on] ...or immeasurable and beautiful or ugly.
Because these four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are thus presented, the Abhidhamma Commentary asks:
“But why is it that, whereas in the Suttanta it is said, ‘One who perceives forms internally sees external forms that are limited,’ and so forth, [it is not stated here in the same way]?”

Having raised the objection that "in this context, even among the four bases of mastery, only the internal state of being percipient of the formless is mentioned," and having stated the reason, "because internal forms are not to be mastered," [the author replies]: "Whether there or here, it is only external forms that are to be mastered;
therefore, since they must necessarily be mentioned, they are stated both there and here."
It is said: "The phrase 'perceiving forms internally' is merely an elegant turn of expression used by the Teacher.
In this context, all limited forms—whether devoid of attention to color or accompanied by it—are described as "limited, beautiful or ugly";
likewise, the immeasurable ones are described as "immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. For there exists that method [of teaching].
Having overcome those limited [objects], if they are at times directed toward by way of color, one overcomes both beautiful and ugly colors.

For the teaching of the Suttantas is an exposition by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*). However, because the Abhidhamma is a teaching by way of the non-figurative method (*nippariyāya*), those devoid of the mental application to color are stated separately, as are those combined with it. For there is indeed a distinction in the manner of overcoming in both cases.
Likewise, because this is a teaching by way of method (*pariyāyadesanā*), there is also a mode of mastery (*abhibhavana*) regarding the liberations (*vimokkha*).
Thus, the first liberation is included among the first and second bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) by the phrase "perceiving forms internally" (*ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī*), etc.;

the second liberation is included among the third and fourth bases of mastery; and the third liberation is included among the bases of mastery over color (*vaṇṇābhibhāyatana*), because they function as mastery.

In the Abhidhamma, however, because it is a teaching according to the direct method (*nippariyāya*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are explained by omitting the liberations (*vimokkha*) in order to show them without confusion. Furthermore, all meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) that perform the function of liberation are stated in the teaching on the liberations.
Thus, regarding the two bases of mastery that appear [in the Suttas] as "perceiving forms internally," in the Abhidhamma...

It is understood that the definition [of the first two liberations] is established because they are not mentioned among the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), and because such statements as "one possessing form sees forms" are expressions common to the functions of all liberations.
As for the phrase "because internal forms are not to be mastered," this is stated everywhere as "one sees external forms," without ever saying "one sees internal forms."

This is his statement of the reason; by that, he shows that whatever is caused by another reason has been stated with that specific reason. However, as for the statement in the Abhidhamma regarding the internal state of being "percipient of the formless" (*arūpasaññitā*), which is caused by the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*), one should not seek any other reason for it.
Furthermore, the fact that internal forms are not subject to overcoming is because they do not exist in the same way as external forms.

The elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*) is to be understood by way of the aforementioned determination (*vavatthāna*), because it consists of an exposition of existing methods of expression according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

If it is argued that the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) such as blue and so forth need not be mentioned, since they are already established by the phrase "beautiful and ugly colors" alone—that is not so;
for in the case of those who have applied themselves to blue and so forth, the very state of being blue and so forth is the cause for their mastery. Indeed, it is not [the case] for them...
The cause of mastery is not the limitedness or the immeasurability of the pure and impure colors; rather, it is their very nature as blue and so forth.

And among these limited kasiṇa-forms and the rest, in order to show which of these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) succeed for which particular temperament, it is said: "But among these... and so forth.
"By way of encompassing all" means by way of being common to all blue color, blue appearance, and blue luster.

"By way of color" means by way of its intrinsic color. "By way of appearance" means by way of being visible, that is, by way of being graspable by the cognitive process of eye-consciousness and so forth.
"By way of radiance" means by way of shining with a brilliant glow. *Umāpuppha* means the flower of the *atasī* plant.
It is blue precisely because there is no admixture of other colors. "Arising in Bārāṇasī" means produced in Bārāṇasī.
For some outsider who is looking at this kasiṇa-sign, which is immeasurable and excessively expanded, fear might arise, thinking:
"What is this that, having overcome and overwhelmed the entire world, is seizing it?"
However, since the Tathāgata has no such fear or timidity, these [examples] were brought forward solely for the purpose of demonstrating his state of fearlessness.
Commentary on the Eight Liberations (Vimokkha): 174.
Their meaning is indeed clear, as they have already been analyzed according to their sense below. Even the mere mention of "the liberation of some" is enough to cause fear.

Because of his delight in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), [these states exist for others]; however, for the Tathāgata, even while he dwells having attained liberation (*vimokkha*), those [states] do not exist.
Therefore, these [passages] have been brought forward solely for the purpose of demonstrating his state of fearlessness. Commentary on the Discourse Requested by Ānanda.

178. "Bodhi" refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For that is indeed described as "the penetration of the knowledge of the four paths," since the penetration of omniscient knowledge is rooted in that.
"The state thus spoken of" refers to the state expressed in the words: "If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon.
179. Even that coarse sign was made; yet because his mind was obsessed by Māra, it was not penetrated and not noticed.

183. By "with kinsmen and so forth," [he means] with friends, ministers, and relatives. They are "dear" (piya) because they are to be loved; they are "endearing" (manāpa) because they increase one's delight.
"By birth" means by the process of proceeding in accordance with birth. "Separation" (nānābhāva) is the state of being apart, the state of being distinct, the state of being disconnected.

"Parting through death" (maraṇena vinābhāva) is the dissociation from that individual existence due to passing away, because there is no returning again to that same selfhood. "Alteration through becoming" (bhavena aññathābhāva) is...

By the phrase "grasping at another existence," there is a change of state from a previous mode to a different mode, such as "a being of the sense-sphere becomes one of the fine-material sphere," and so forth;
therein too, it should be applied as "a human becomes a deity," and so on. "Where can this be found?
means: where, in what place, or in what location—namely, within this occurrence of the aggregates—can that which is said, "What has been born... may it not perish," be found?
"It is possible. He said, "This situation does not exist," meaning that it is not possible because such a cause is absent.
The intention is: "If even the body of a Tathāgata possesses such a marvelous and wonderful quality, how much more so for others?
"It will return" (paccāvamissati)—this situation does not exist, because one has established mindfulness well and delimited [the object] with knowledge.
Because the life-formations had been relinquished and the Buddha’s task was completed;
for beyond these three months, no further beings were to be converted by the Buddha here. 184.
Regarding the long endurance of the Dispensation, it is said that it consists of the noble path-dhammas together with their requisites, and thus he said: "All..."
"It was spoken by way of both the mundane and the supramundane" because it is impossible to attain supramundane states without mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
The commentary on the third recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the "Elephant's Look-Back."
186. *Nāgāpalokitaṃ* means "looked upon like a nāga"; the meaning is that the looking is similar to the look of a noble elephant (*hatthināga*).
*Āhacca* means having touched. *Aṅkusakalaggāni viya* means as if they were hooks, remaining stuck and attached to one another.
*Ekābaddhāni* means bound together with one another. *Tasmā* [refers to] because of the neck-bones...
Because they exist as a single continuous unit, like a solid block— not only in the case of the neck bones, but indeed all of them,
with the exception of the twelve great joints such as the shoulder-joints and the finger-joints—
these remain joined together in other joints; therefore, their bodily strength is equal to the measure of a thousand million-fold power of ordinary elephants.
It was so. He turned toward the city of Kapilavatthu as if turning on a pivot, just as he had done facing the city of Vesālī.

If this is so, how did it come to be called the "elephant-look"? It was by way of his underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*). For the Blessed One intended to look back precisely in the manner of an elephant-look;
however, by the power of his merit, the place where he stood remained fixed.
Because it was turned back, it is called "the elephant’s backward glance.
The statement, "This, Ānanda, is the Tathāgata’s last look at Vesālī," is not a statement giving the reason for looking at Vesālī, because that would be non-conclusive;
rather, it is merely a statement of fact. Having shown that by way of clearing the path:
Wishing to show that the reason for seeking permission here is indeed different, he said, "But surely," and so forth.
All of that was because he had departed from each respective place in succession, having gone to Kusinārā with the desire to attain final nibbāna.
By the phrase "because it is not wonderful," he avoids the aforementioned inconclusiveness; this, however, is merely a clarification. But as for this [point] here:
The phrase beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) was spoken in order to show that the cause is not erroneous. For the Blessed One did not look back at Vesālī out of longing;

rather, under the guise of looking back, he looked upon it for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, and out of compassion for the world, thinking, "This departure of mine shall be one from which there is no returning. Therefore he said, "Moreover, the kings of Vesālī," and so forth.
He brings an end to all the suffering of saṃsāra within his own continuum and is the destroyer and the bringer of non-existence [of suffering] within the continua of others.
He is possessed of vision through the five kinds of eyes known as the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine eye, the fleshly eye, and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).
Because he has utterly eradicated the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), he is supremely *parinibbuta* through the *parinibbāna* of the defilements.
Commentary on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesavaṇṇanā) 187.

"In a great expanse" means in a vast space. These are the great bases for the establishment of the Dhamma. In these, once the Dhamma has been established, it cannot be shaken away because there is no doubt.
What, then, are they? They are the Suttas distinguished by their source, such as the Suttas of Direct Descent (Suttotaraṇa), and so forth.

In the second interpretation, "apadisanti" means "they point to"; it is the reason for determining that what has been brought forward by someone—such as, "Friend, I heard this directly from the Blessed One"—is indeed "Dhamma.
But what is that [reason]? It is precisely the fact that what was thus brought forward passes the test of the Suttas and so forth.
If this is so, how can there be four [criteria]? Because the Teacher is the witness to the Dhamma in two ways.
And there are disciples; among them, the disciples are threefold according to the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual.
Thus, there are four [ways of citing authority] by way of the distinctions of those to whom one may refer, saying: "The Dhamma which has been received by me from you. Therefore he said:
"I have heard this, friend, directly from the Blessed One," and so forth. And likewise it is stated in the *Netti*: "There are four great authorities (mahāpadese): the authority of the Buddha..."

“The reference to the Saṅgha, the reference to many elders, and the reference to a single elder—these are the four great authorities (mahāpadesa). That which has the Buddha as its authority is called “the Buddha-authority.
This same method applies to the others as well. Therefore he said: “The Buddha and so forth... are the great authorities.
“Neither to be rejoiced in” means not to be accepted. The acceptance of a discourse is what is meant by “hearing.”

He said, "It should not be heard. "Words and syllables" (*padabyañjanāni*) means both words (*padāni*) and syllables (*byañjanāni*); that is, phrases of meaning (*atthapadāni*) and phrases of expression (*byañjanapadāni*).

They are called "words" (*padāni*) because meaning is reached (*pajjati*) through them; syllables and so forth are "phrases of expression" (*byañjanapadāni*). They are called "words" (*padāni*) because they are to be reached (*pajjitabbato*);
phrases such as "manifestation" (*saṅkāsanādi*) are "phrases of meaning" (*atthapadāni*). Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "'Syllables reckoned as words'..."

Some say, "Only the phrasing-words (byañjanapada) have been spoken," but that is not so. They are called *byañjana* because they clarify (*byañjanti*) the meaning; thus there are both phrasing-words and meaning-words.

They are called *byañjana* because the meaning is to be clarified by them. This is because both are included [in the term *byañjana*]. "In this place" means in this section of the sutta brought forward by him.
"The text has been spoken" means the entire dhamma of the canonical text (*pāḷidhamma*) has been set forth. "The meaning has been spoken" means the meaning of the canonical text.
The exposition has been demonstrated. "The connection has been stated" means that the linking of the subsequent teaching with the teaching as it was commenced has been stated;

the relationship has been stated. "The sequence of before and after has been stated" means that both the non-contradiction of what precedes with what follows and the establishment of distinctions have been stated and clarified.
Thus, having correctly observed the textual dharma and so forth, its thorough grasping is "careful mastery."
He said, "Having grasped it well. "They should be compared with the Suttas" means they should be tested by plunging into the Suttas with wisdom;
that plunging and testing involves entering into them and penetrating them, which is why it is said, "they should be compared with the Suttas.
"They should be harmonized with the Vinaya" refers to showing [the meaning] by way of reconciliation; thus he said, "they should be harmonized with the Vinaya."

In order to demonstrate that matter by way of the differing opinions of the teachers regarding the investigation of what that *sutta* is and what the *vinaya* is, the passage beginning with “And here” was stated. By the term *vinaya*, he refers to the text of the *vibhaṅga*.

For that [text] deserves to be called a *sutta* because it indicates the meaning of the *mātikā* known as the *sutta*. It is so called because of its various methods (*naya*) and its distinguished method.

And the Vinaya consists of the Khandhaka and the Pāṭha. Thus, when the Sutta and Vinaya are being thus encompassed, even the Vinaya Piṭaka is not fully exhausted, because it is not included within the Parivāra text.
Alternatively, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are "Sutta" because the meaning of "sutta"—such as the indication of meaning (atthasūcana) and so forth—is possible therein.
And in this way too: "The Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are Sutta; the Vinaya Piṭaka..."
Even when the division into Sutta and Vinaya is stated thus, "the Vinaya," they are not yet exhausted; that is, they are not yet grasped in their entirety. Why?
He says: "Because there is also the word of the Buddha, such as the Jātaka and so forth, which has been recited but has not been assigned the name 'Sutta.
Therefore, according to the method already stated, the three Piṭakas are not fully comprised [by those two categories alone].

The *Suttanipāta*, *Udāna*, *Itivuttaka*, and so forth, were not included in the recitation because they had not been assigned the name "Sutta" in the same manner as the *Dīghanikāya* and the other collections;
however, it should be understood that these [texts] are included here along with the *Jātaka* and others.

As for the reason why the *Buddhavaṃsa* and the *Cariyāpiṭaka* are not included here, one must seek it out—though what is the use of such a search? This is the method of commentary regarding every means.
Thus, it is rejected by the Theravāda from the perspective of its definition.
To ask "What exists?"—it shows that there is no word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) not called a *sutta*.
For indeed, we have stated in the *Nidānakathā-vaṇṇanā*: "'Sutta' is a general designation; others are specific designations. Having rejected all of that, [the opponent argues:]...
Having set aside the method of commentary stated in the passage beginning with "Sutta means Vinaya," [the author] clarifies that "this is not the meaning intended here.

He says, "Vinaya, moreover, is the cause," because it disciplines (vineti) the defilements; thus it is "Vinaya," the means for the disciplining of defilements, and since it itself effects that [disciplining], it is the "cause" (kāraṇa).

"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). "For the sake of lust" means for the state of being lustful, for the nourishment of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*).
"For the sake of bondage" means for the fetter of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*). "For the sake of accumulation" means for the purpose of increasing the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"For the sake of great desire" means for the state of being one with great desires. "For the sake of discontent" means for the state of being discontented. "For the sake of socializing" means for dwelling in the company of the multitude of defilements (*kilesa*).

"From laziness" means from the state of being indolent. "From being difficult to support" means from the state of being hard to nourish. "For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate toward the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
