"For the sake of detachment" means for the purpose of becoming detached from sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*) and the rest. "For the sake of diminution" means for the diminution of the whole cycle of existence; the meaning is "for the sake of Nibbāna.
"From fewness of wishes" means for the complete departure from wishing by way of fewness of wishes regarding requisites and so forth.

"For contentment" means for the state of twelvefold contentment. "For seclusion" means for the state of being secluded, through the accomplishment of seclusion in its factors, such as physical seclusion and so forth.
"For the arousal of energy" means for the purpose of exerting both physical and mental energy.
"For easy maintenance" means for the purpose of being easily nourished. Thus, whatever Dhamma of the scriptures [is studied] by way of learning, memorizing, interrogation, and attention...
For one who practices methodically and avoids states such as lust, it leads to states such as dispassion;

this is the Dhamma in its absolute sense. It is the Vinaya because it holds one back from falling into the states of misery and so forth, because it disciplines the defilements, and because it constitutes the instruction and guidance of the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One; thus, it is the Teaching of the Teacher.
The meaning is: "you should bear it in mind, you should know it, you should understand it.
He says, "In the Sutta [it is] the pointing out of the Four Truths," because there is no word of the Buddha in the Three Piṭakas that is devoid of the Truths.

He says, "In the Vinaya [it is] the cause for the subduing of passion and so forth," because the Tathāgata has revealed the means for the subduing of passion and so forth through the words of the Sutta.
In this context, "inclusion in the Sutta" should be understood solely by way of being contained within the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas, and not otherwise;
thus he said, "without appearing anywhere in the sequence of the Suttas.
"Having stripped off the bark" is like the stripping away of the bark from a large, healthy, standing tree by means of a splinter or a chip.

While the healthy teaching of the Buddha (sāsanadhamma) remains, those [texts] which—merely by their phrasing—appear as if included within it, yet give rise to and manifest faults such as internal contradictions like a deceptive skin (challi), are certainly included among the *Guḷha-Vessantara* and so forth;

thus he said: "The meaning is that they are known as the *Guḷha-Vessantara... pe ...*. In the phrase "for the sake of the subduing of lust and so forth" (*rāgādivinaye*), it means for the purpose of subduing lust and the other defilements.
Because they do not appear in that form—being neither manifest nor visible—they should be discarded, avoided, and not accepted.
"In all instances" means in all sections.
"But in this place" refers to this section on the exposition of the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*), beginning with the words, "In the Sutta, there are four great authorities."
Having taken together what has been stated and what has not been stated, he recites the table of contents for the miscellaneous discourse.

A "question" (*pañha*) is a matter desired to be known; its "answers" (*pañhābyākaraṇāni*) are the explanations of those questions. A "sutta" is so called in the sense of indicating the meaning and so forth; it is the Pāḷi.
That which conforms to, or is favorable to, that sutta is "Suttānuloma," which is the Great Standard of Authority (*mahāpadesa*). The teachers speak and comment upon it.

The *aṭṭhakathā* (commentary) is so called because it explains the *pāḷi* (text) by means of this [method]; this is the teaching of the teachers (*ācariyavāda*). "Personal opinion" (*attanomati*) refers to the individual thought or intention of each respective elder (*thera*).
"When a determination of the Dhamma has been reached" means when the Dhamma to be determined has appeared before one.
"These" refers to the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*) mentioned immediately prior. It is a "measure" (*pamāṇa*) because by means of it the Dhamma is measured, delimited, and determined.
Therefore he said, "That which here accords," and so forth. "The other" refers to that which does not accord with the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
Again, "the other" is said with reference to that which conforms to what is improper while obstructing what is proper.
"To be declared categorically" means to be answered with a single, definitive response; "by way of analysis" refers to the matter asked about.
Having divided [the questions] according to the distinctions of categorical determination (*avadhāraṇa*) and so forth. "By counter-questioning" means having questioned the person who is questioning.
"To be set aside" (*ṭhapanīya*) means that because it cannot be answered in any of the three ways, it is to be set aside without providing an answer.

Regarding the question, "Is the eye impermanent?", it is stated that "it must be answered categorically" with reference to the categorical determination of the subsequent term, since there is not even a trace of permanence.

In that regard, it is because [the object] does not exist there. However, regarding the restriction of the first term, the state of being answerable by analysis (*vibhajjabyākaraṇīyatā*) arises because the specific and general meanings of "eye" and "ear" do not share a common basis.
As for the objection concerning the similarity between those two, it is to be answered by means of a counter-question;
it is to be resolved both by way of negation and by way of affirmation. Thus he said: "As the eye, so the ear... [and so forth]."
“This is a question to be answered by counter-question. The proposition that “the soul is the same as the body” is a question concerning the non-difference between the soul and the body.
Since the person to whom this non-difference is attributed cannot be found in the ultimate sense (paramattha), it is like praising filial piety toward a son of a barren woman;
thus, because it is not to be declared, it is stated to be set aside (ṭhapanīya). These four ways of answering questions are the authority for that very reason.
This is because their questions must be answered according to that method.
The Great Authority of the Vinaya (Vinayamahāpadesa) is called "conformable allowable" (anulomakappiya) in the primary sense because it prescribes what is conformable to what is allowable;

however, because it resembles it through its status as a Great Authority, the term "conformable allowable" is also used as a conventional designation in the commentaries for the Great Authorities of the Suttas (Suttantamahāpadesa).

Even though the miscellaneous teachings (pakiṇṇaka-desanā) delivered by the Blessed One here and there constitute the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), it is nevertheless called the "Teacher’s Word" (ācariyavāda) because the compilers of the Dhamma first recited the Three Piṭakas and then established the path of recitation (vācanāmaggam) in accordance with the explanation of their meaning;
for the teachers (ācariyā) speak and comment upon the Pāḷi by means of this. Therefore, he said: "The Teacher’s Word."

[This is] the *Nāma-aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, the method of exposition consisting of the commentary on the meaning of the Buddha’s word, which had already been established through the three councils, was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahinda.
Subsequently, it was set down in the Sinhalese language by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding the confusion of tenets belonging to other schools.
This is known as the "Theravāda according to our own judgment."

"By grasping the method" means by grasping the method obtainable from the discourses and so forth. "By subsequent understanding" means by an understanding that follows along with the discourses and so forth.
"One's own inspired presence" (*paṭibhāna*) means the appearance of that very meaning to oneself according to the stated method;

the meanings, as they have appeared, are stated exactly as they are. "Only that which is consistent should be accepted" means that it must accord with the discourses and likewise with the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).

This shows that [the meaning] must be extracted. Since there may occasionally be a lack of correspondence with the canonical text (pāḷi) due to a careless reading in the teacher’s exposition, he says, “Even the teacher’s exposition must be accepted only if it accords with the Sutta,” showing that such a discrepancy should not be taken as authoritative.
It is the weakest of all because it arises from the individual’s own spontaneous intuition. And thus, even that [intuition] should be accepted; what kind of thing is it?
The construction is: "only when it accords with the Sutta. Regarding the phrase "in those," it refers to the three councils (*saṅgīti*).

By the statement "only that which has come down [traditionally] is authoritative," he rejects the status of being a Sutta for anything other than what was recited by Mahākassapa and the others as "Sutta" here;
for the three councils were held precisely for that purpose. "Therein" refers to the censurable Sutta. And not in the Sutta...
It should be understood that these [rules] descend [into the Vinaya], yet they are not seen in the Vinaya because they have not been heard by him;
thus, he demonstrates this very point by way of conclusion with the statement: "One must take only that which accords with a sutta on what is allowable.
In all instances, the expression "not the other" should be seen as showing the result of the restriction applied in each respective case.
Commentary on the Story of Cunda the Smith’s Son (189):

“Sūkaramaddava” refers to the tender meat of a wild boar. Since Cunda was a noble disciple who had attained the stage of stream-entry, and because others who were preparing food for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus prepared only what was blameless, [he offered this].
Therefore it is said: “meat that has been set forth. “That, they say,” refers to the specific qualifications stated in the passage beginning with “not too young.
For it is described as being both “soft and succulent. Because of its softness of flesh and through a particular method of preparation, it is called “tender.
They added nutritive essence (*oja*) out of regard for a special merit, thinking: “This is the final meal of the Blessed One.”
However, because it had been infused with divine seed in that manner, it became very heavy.

Fearing that others, not knowing that it was difficult to digest, might criticize him by saying, "He has ruined it without giving anything to anyone," the Blessed One uttered this lion’s roar, beginning with "I did not [eat it]," in order to clear away the reproach of others.
But how is this a lion’s roar? Is it not the case that even for the Blessed One, it did not undergo proper digestion? This is not so.

It should be viewed in this way: because it is fitting to say that "it has undergone transformation in the Blessed One precisely correctly," since there is no alteration arising from that [digestive] condition, and because any alteration caused by other conditions has been brought to a state of softness.
Therefore he said, "But not on account of having eaten," and so forth. For neither the Blessed One nor other ones whose taints are exhausted...
They consume food by way of producing nine types of sensations, because they partake of food only after it has been prepared with its eight constituent factors.
If this is so, why is it said in the Canon, "A severe affliction arose in him after he had eaten," and so forth?
That was said because it arose at a time subsequent to the eating; it was not said that it arose *because* of the act of eating itself.

This is the meaning according to the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Due to the power of karma that has been performed, accumulated, and given the opportunity to ripen, even when a powerful disease arises, the suppression of the painful sensations caused by heavy and oily food occurs; therefore he said, "If indeed," and so forth.
"In the desired place" means in the wished-for location; and his desire to go there is with regard to the disciples who are to be guided.

They are to be seen. In the verse as well, by the word "heard" (*suta*), it indicates merely what was heard—this is simply the speech of others—and does not show that "the wise one was afflicted by illness on account of food.
Commentary on the Fetching of Water:
191. It should be understood that the clarity of the water is due to its state of being serene; thus he said, "With clear water" means with serene water.
Because it possesses an excellent taste, it is constant; thus he said, "with sweet water. The water is indeed thin and especially cool, not thick; thus he said, "with thin and cool water.
"Free from mud" states the cause for its white (clear) nature. [This refers to] by way of mire, sludge, and so forth...
For while there is a discoloration of the water, by its very nature it is white in color.
Commentary on the Story of the Malla Son Pukkusa (192).
*Dhuravāte* means against the wind. *Dīghapiṅgalo* means one who is tall and has tawny eyes. *Piṅgalakkhiko*.
For he was known as "Āḷāra. "Such-like" (*evarūpaṃ*) means that which one will see, do, or become; it refers to what is of this kind.
"In such cases" (*īdisesu*) refers to instances where the indeclinable particles *yattha*, *yañca*, and so forth are employed.
(193) It is said, "as they issue forth," because they are like those emerging from the interior of a cloud as they wander about.
"Moving about. "Ninefold" means of nine kinds. For among the nine types, even that single kind of thunderbolt is called "ninefold" because it is included within that category.

Such is this conventional usage, similar to the common designation for one who has attained the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*). It makes unconscious those who are overwhelmed by its sound and its heat. "One wheel" means...
It is a single circle. It is called *saterā* because it appears as if it were being scattered or divided along the shore.
"Gaggarāyamānā" means making the sound *gaggarā*; for this is a term used to describe echoing. "Kapisīsā" means having the shape of a monkey's head.
"Macchavilolikā" means having a tossing appearance like a fish quivering in water. "Kukkuṭasadisā" means having the appearance of a cock with outspread wings.
At the time of plowing with a plow, there is a ring to be grasped by the hands of the plowmen; taking that as its basis, the plow is called a "staff-ring" (*daṇḍamaṇikā*).
Therefore, those shaped like a staff-ring are "staff-rings. For this reason, it says, "resembling a plow.
Even when it rains, because it cannot be drenched by water due to its state of being ablaze, the great cloud is called a "drying-cloud" (*sukkhāsanī*).
Therefore he said, "He eradicates the place where it has fallen.

In *bhusāgārake* means in a small hut made of chaff. It is said that there, having cleared the chaff from within a large heap of straw, a place suitable for the residence of renunciants, resembling a hall, had been constructed; at that time, the Blessed One was there.
It was indeed a threshing floor, but because it resembled a hall, he said, "in the threshing-hall.
Regarding the word "here," since it is used in the locative case to express a cause, he said, "for this reason"; the meaning is: "on account of the destruction of people by the falling of lightning.
Alternatively, the reading is simply "So tvam, bhante" (Thus you, venerable sir).
194. It is said that *siṅgī* is the most excellent, exceedingly radiant gold from the world of the gods, which constitutes the luster of the Buddhas' bodily complexion.
For this very reason, he says, "the color of *siṅgī* gold. Having himself raised the question, "But why did the Elder take it?
he states the reason for it with the words beginning, "Even though... It is for that very reason...

By means of these four aforementioned reasons— reaching the pinnacle of service as an attendant, cutting off the opportunity for others to speak, honoring the Teacher with that cloth, and conforming to the Teacher’s inclinations—
the Elder immediately presented that polished, gold-colored cloth to the Blessed One, saying, “May he accept it.”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this smooth cloth; it will be for my long-term welfare and happiness.
The Blessed One accepted it, and having accepted it, he made use of it. Thus it is said: “The Blessed One took one from it as an inner robe and one as an upper robe.
It is said that at that very moment, the monks finished the tailoring by merely folding the edges.
They presented it to the Elder; the Elder presented it to the Blessed One. "As if its brilliance were struck away" means its radiance was suppressed;
the word *viya* is a mere particle. For, being overwhelmed by the radiance of the Blessed One’s body, that pair of garments no longer possessed its own brightness.
"By the very edge" means from edge to edge, that is, from within itself; thus he said.
“There is no radiance outside of it.
By the phrase “it produces a clear form,” this meaning is illustrated: that due to the condition of having consumed this nutriment, there is no such disease.
This occurs at two times, because of the occurrence of the moment of attaining the two elements of Nibbāna.
Regarding the phrase "between the twin Sāla trees at Upavattana," what is to be said here will be explained further on.

(196) Everything became exclusively golden-hued because it was completely overwhelmed by the uninterrupted radiance of the Blessed One’s body—a radiance that was exceedingly pure, luminous, and of a single solid mass.

"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). "Pavattā" means the teacher in the sense of one who causes [the teaching] to proceed. He sat right in front [of the Buddha] because he was there to receive his instruction.
197. "Gains known as the benefits of giving"—this refers to the gains designated as the benefits of giving, classified into types such as the gift of beauty, the gift of strength, and so forth;
these include both those pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to future lives, which are to be desired. "Those are losses for you"—all of those are losses for you;
they are not gains at all. "Pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*) means existing in this very selfhood (*attabhāva*), which is directly manifest in this very existence.
Because one must pass away and go to another state, it is named "the future life" (*samparāya*); that which exists in the world beyond is "pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyika*).
Those pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life are "present-life-and-future-life" (*diṭṭhadhammika-samparāyika*).
"Gains consisting of the benefits of giving" means gains that have become the benefits of giving. "In every way equally" means that their fruit is equal in its entirety, not merely in part.
“Equal in fruit. By “alms-food,” he refers to the merit consisting of giving directed toward that object.
If it is intended that they have equal fruit by way of the field, then even though they belong to a single continuum, does not the field of the Arahant differ from that of the worldling?
To show this, he says, “But is it not so…,” and so forth. “By the equality of final Nibbāna”:
“By the state of the final extinction of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) and the final extinction of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*), there is equality in final extinction.

By the phrase “having consumed [the food], he attained final extinction,” it is shown that just as the Dhamma-body—supported by the physical body which was sustained by the enjoyment of excellent alms-food—easily abandoned the defilements through the successful attainment of what was suitable for nourishment, so too did he easily abandon the aggregates. Thus it is said.

The equality of the fruit of both alms-offerings is illuminated by their being the cause for the successful attainment of the abandonment of defilements (*kilesa*) and the abandonment of the aggregates (*khandha*).
It was stated that "by means of the term 'alms-food' (*piṇḍapāta*), the gift of alms-food is illuminated. For instance, in the case of Sujātā, [it is said]:
"By depending on this food, the qualities of my deity’s beauty, happiness, strength, and so forth, have been perfectly [attained]."
At that time, there was a sublime aspiration [on the part of the Buddha] that "these [qualities] might be fully accomplished";
likewise, Cunda the smith also had a sublime aspiration that "by means of this food, the Blessed One’s qualities such as beauty, happiness, and strength might be properly accomplished.

In this way, the equality of their fruits for both of them is to be understood. This is so even though [the Buddha possessed] twenty-four million four hundred thousand meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Regarding the daily practice of attaining the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*):

just as on the day of his full enlightenment, while establishing fresh insight (*vipassanā*) by synthesizing [the mind] through fourteen modes beginning with the "sevenfold set of materiality" (*rūpasattaka*), he entered those absorptions by means of the great gateway of insight (*mahāvipassanāmukha*), so too on the day of his final nibbāna did he enter all those same absorptions.
Thus, it is by way of the equality of his attainments.
Their fruits are equal. First, let it be granted that Cunda’s act of recollection was more sublime because there was no change in his state due to having given to the Blessed One;
but how was it that Sujātā’s [act] was given by a deity? He said, “And Sujātā,” and so forth, meaning “because she perceived it as such.
“At a later time” means at a time subsequent to the full enlightenment (abhisambodhi). “Again, at a later time” means subsequent to the final nibbāna (parinibbāna).
"From another. "The head of the Dhamma" means Nibbāna, which is the summit of all phenomena (*dhamma*). "Taken by me" means taken by way of myself.
Therefore he said, "It is as if it were mine," and so forth.
"Sovereignty" (*ādhipateyya*) is the state of being dominant; thus he said, "conducive to the status of being the eldest."

"Restraint" means restraint by virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). "Enmity" refers to the fivefold enmity beginning with the taking of life. For that is called "enmity" because it is of the nature of an enmity-factor and because it is a cause of enmity.
"Skill" is said to be knowledge; one who is endowed with that is "skilled," as he said: "But the skilled one is possessed of knowledge.
"Possession of knowledge" means the full perfection of knowledge, and that occurs by way of the supreme path (*agga-magga*).
It should be understood that the supreme path abandons the defilements without remainder; thus it is said: "By means of the noble path...

he abandons. Having abandoned this evil—first abandoning evil such as greed and stinginess by means of giving, and evil such as the taking of life by means of virtue, having abandoned them through the factor of substitution (tadaṅgavasena)—and thereafter [abandoning it] by way of suppression through the states of serenity and insight, then...
Having abandoned evil entirely by means of its total eradication through the successive stages of the path;

and because they have been thus abandoned, having attained Nibbāna through the destruction of lust and the rest, and through the complete subsiding of the defilements, he is "extinguished" (nibbuto) and "fully extinguished" (parinibbuto).
Grasping the core of the teaching on the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining, [the Blessed One], considering this, uttered this inspired utterance: "Thus, regarding Cunda... and so forth.
The commentary on the fourth recitation section is finished.
198. Regarding the description of the Yamakasāla grove:
"Thus it was at Kusinārā" means that just as the Thūpārāma is to the southwest of Anurādhapura, [so was this grove situated].

Thus, that park was situated to the south-west of Kusinārā. Therefore, because those desiring to enter the city approach it from the park and proceed along it, it is called "Upavattana" (the Approaching);
that Sāla grove stands there in the form of a row of Sāla trees. "In between" means in the middle. "Of that couch," it is said, refers to the one being prepared there.
Of that couch. There too... [as before] ...there was space for only one foot; therefore it is said, "between the twin sāla trees.
"Interwoven" means as if interwoven because their branches and trunks were closely attached to one another. In the Aṭṭhakathā, it is also called "standing branches.
As for what is stated in the Pāḷi, "Prepare the couch with its head to the north,"...
This was said by way of the suitability for the deities who had come to see that final sight.
However, some say, "The meaning is: 'Arrange the couch with the northern direction as the face and the eastern direction as the head,'" but that is merely their own opinion.
"These are the best of elephants": these, by virtue of their lineage, their range, and so forth, are the most excellent among the elephant-lords in terms of strength.
However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, some elephants are mentioned differently; that difference should be understood as being merely in their names.
From the time they were consumed... [pe] ...until they reached exhaustion, [it was said]: "But it was not on account of having been consumed," as stated below.
The meaning should be understood in the manner already stated. Regarding the term *caṅgavāra*, it refers to a wave.
The word “as if” (*viyā*) is used to illustrate this point by considering how a disease, having arisen according to the force of karma for which an opportunity was created, overcomes health.
This is because, as stated previously, the Blessed One is indeed capable of remaining for an eon (*kappa*) or for the remainder of an eon, and remains for such a duration of time.
Because there was no further purpose, he relinquished his life-formations and granted scope for such a deed;
therefore, it is indeed appropriate to say "as if" when demonstrating this point.
They will think that wholesome action ought to be performed, [thinking]: "In this way, that wholesome action has great fruit, great benefit, and great power."

The cessation of the suffering of the round for even a single being appears as something even weightier to the Buddhas because of its extreme rarity; therefore, it was said, "He sees yet another," and so forth. This matter should be illustrated by the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
As for the third reason—the prevention of harm arising for beings—he spoke again, beginning with "He sees yet another," in order to demonstrate that.

"Reclining like a lion" (*sīhaseyyā*): here, "reclining" (*seyyā*) means lying down; reclining like a lion is "lion-reclining" (*sīhaseyyā*). Alternatively, "lion-reclining" means the best reclining—that is, the two meanings which will follow later.

The reclining of those who enjoy sensual pleasures is described as "lying on the left side. There is no such thing as lying on the right side, because the right hand is capable of grasping the body and so forth;
and this is stated with reference to men. They are unable to lie on one side [continuously] because it gives rise to pain.
"This is the lion’s posture" means this very posture thus described as the lion’s posture.
By the phrase "because of his being full of energy," he shows the lion’s fearlessness. For other timid animals, having entered their own lairs, lie down in whatever way they can, preceded by fear;
but the lion, because of his fearlessness, lies down only after establishing mindfulness, just like a bhikkhu who acts with circumspection.

Therefore he said, "the front foot," and so forth. Having placed both front feet in one spot by way of placing the right front foot upon the left front foot; "the hind feet" refers to the two hind feet.

In this case as well, the placement of the feet in one spot should be understood according to the method already stated, and the observation of the standing position should be done with fearlessness alone.

The lion-like action described by the passage beginning with “But lifting up his head,” and so forth, should be understood as being established through the very nature of things (*dhammatā*), just like waking up without fear.
The lion’s stretching (*sīhavijambhita*) is for the purpose of making the parts of the body, which have been held in one fixed posture for too long, fit for activities such as walking.
The roaring of the lion’s roar three times is likewise [for a specific purpose].
For the purpose of avoiding animals of little power.
It is called a *seyyā* (resting place) because one rests—that is, proceeds—there in a state of non-exertion; thus it is the fourth jhāna itself as the resting place, the "fourth-jhāna-resting-place.
But what is that fourth jhāna? It is the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*); for having emerged from that, one practices insight (*vipassanā*).
Having increased [his practice], the Blessed One gradually attained the supreme path and became a Tathāgata.

Regarding this, some say: "This is what is called the 'reclining' (seyyā); it is not the [supramundane] reclining. Nevertheless, because it will be said that 'immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One passed away into parinibbāna,' therefore the mundane attainment of the fourth jhāna alone is the reclining of the Tathāgata. This being so—
One might object that the Tathāgata’s reclining belongs only to the time of his final *parinibbāna*, yet the Blessed One did not frequently dwell in the attainment of the mundane fourth *jhāna*.
However, it should be understood that the fourth *jhāna* occurring here is that which proceeds by way of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*).

In this regard, just as the reclining of beings—characterized by falling asleep—occurs through the mind of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-citta*), and that [reclining] is due to their being endowed with the continuity of their first birth; so too is this case.
The "lion's posture" (sīhaseyyā) refers to the preeminent posture; thus he said, "the supreme posture. Because there is no rising from it, it is "non-rising" (anuṭṭhānā);
it is a posture, hence "the non-rising posture. [He does not think: "I shall rise from here."
Because of the absence of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it is not said, "having applied the perception of rising.
"In this" means in this approaching of the bed without rising. Not rising is by way of the body, not by way of the mind;
and since "not rising by way of the mind" refers to falling asleep, the phrase "by way of sleep," etc., is stated to show the absence of that [sleep]. "Of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)"—
Of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) characterized by falling into sleep.
"All in full bloom" means they are blooming everywhere in their entirety, not merely in one part.
Therefore he said: "All have blossomed on every side. "Covered all over" means that with fully bloomed flowers, it is of a single uniform appearance in every respect.
"Covered": the lotuses standing as if looking down from above. "Like a peacock's tail-feather cluster" because they are strewn with flowers of five colors.

"Born on the banks of the Nanda lotus pond" means produced on the shores of the Nanda lotus pond. "The size of a large gourd" means the measure of an *āḷhaka*. "Thrown in" means cast down. "Sprinkling over the very body" means scattering directly upon the body itself.
“Sandalwood powder for the deities” refers to sandalwood powder the color of white silk, sixty or even fifty leagues in extent.
“Divine net-like fragrant powders” refers to divine fragrances and divine powders. It should be understood that yellow orpiment, collyrium powder, and so forth are also divine and supremely fragrant;
for this very reason, it says, “all varieties of divine fragrant perfumes.”
Having assembled within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), they move through the sky as if at the time of the Great Renunciation.
"They" refers to the deities. "Weaving garlands" means those very ones who are arranging a wreath. "Or not yet finished" means those who have completed it according to their intention.
"Hand to hand" means one's own hand [reaching] another's hand. "Neck to neck" means...
"By means of seizing the neck" means having grasped the other's neck with one's own neck. "Having taken hold" means having touched.
"Great fame, great fame"—this is a form of mutual address used for emphasis.
"Seeing the great exertion" means seeing the great effort being manifested in honor and worship of the Tathāgata.

"But that very way of practice" refers specifically to the preliminary way of practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*). "Suitability" means being appropriate for the ninefold supramundane dhamma to be attained.

"Virtue" refers to the virtue of conduct (*cāritta-sīla*). "The prescription of conduct" is also the virtue of conduct. "As far as the state of change-of-lineage" means that calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) must be practiced until the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*);
this is the right way of practice. Now, that right way of practice [is explained] by way of contrast...
And in order to clarify this through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmā*) was stated.

The *Jinakālasutta* is the "Black Thread" (*kālasutta*) established by the Great Architect of the Victor (*jinamahāvaḍḍhakinā*), which demonstrates the boundary of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-mariyāda*) regarding the phenomena to be avoided and those to be adopted;

and as for the statement in the sections on laymen and laywomen, "He performs worship with perfumes and flowers," this refers to the performance [of such acts] having placed them on the side of conduct and virtue (*cāritta-sīla*).
Since it has been stated thus, it should be understood that performing [the practice] in that manner is indeed permitted for both monks and nuns.
The phrase "for this is" refers to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipadā).
—Commentary on the Elder Upavāṇa.
200. *Apanesi*: he acted in such a way that [the object] moved away from its position; however, he did not rebuke him. Therefore he said, "Ānanda," and so forth.
*Vuttasadisā vā* means exactly as stated in the discourse on the "Exposition of Even Mind" (*samacittapariyāyadesanā*). *Āvārento* means covering.

Since he was the protective deity at the stupa of the Buddha Kassapa, the Elder alone possessed the power of majesty (*tejussada*), and not other Arahants—this is how the connection should be understood.
Now, in order to demonstrate that matter in detail starting from its origin, the passage beginning with “Vipassī, it is said, was a perfectly enlightened Buddha” has been commenced.
The phrase “the deities of the Four Great Kings” should be understood according to the maxim of “the cow and the ox,” since the deities of the earth and others are also included therein.
“Of those people” refers to those humans.
*Tattha* means at the cetiya of the Blessed One Kassapa.
*Adhivāsenti* means they find it agreeable.
*Chinnapāto* is like one who has cut off his forefoot; *chinnapātaṃ* is that [term], a neuter abstract description. *Āvaṭṭanti* means they turn back.

They turn by way of moving toward [the center]. Having fallen from wherever they fell, they travel for a distance of several *ratana*s solely by way of turning, and then return by way of turning back to the very place where they originally fell. Therefore he said:
"Turning back, they come to the very place where they fell. "Turning away" means they turn back from wherever they fell. Therefore he said:

“Moving in a circle from the place where it has fallen. To show that moving forward is *āvattana* (turning back) and the other three types are *vivattana* (turning away), he said “Furthermore,” and so forth.
It is unable to support the deity because it sinks down like water. Therefore he said “Therein,” and so forth. “Therein” means on the natural earth. The deities sink down.

Because the elements possess a state of extreme subtlety and delicacy. "They fashioned earth upon the earth" means that by the power of their supernormal success (*iddhi*), they fashioned earth capable of supporting their own bodies upon the natural earth.
Granted that there may still be some lust even in the absence of mental distress (*domanassa*), yet when lust is absent, the occurrence of mental distress is impossible.

Thus, because they share that same state, he said: “Free from lust means those who have abandoned mental grief (*domanassa*). They are like stone pillars because of their lack of agitation toward the pleasant and the unpleasant.
202. Commentary on the Four Places of Arousal:
“On this side of the Ganges” means on the lower part of the Ganges. “Having taken up rubbish-sweepers’ brooms,” and so forth.
This is a demonstration of the manner in which each individual performs their duties in their own respective dwelling place.
The phrase beginning with “Thus at two times” is a reference made for the sake of illustration, as it has been explained below.

Since the word *bhāvanīya* functions as a passive noun (*kamma-sādhana*) in the sense of being honored or esteemed, he says, “when [the mind] is cultivated and esteemed by the mind. In the second alternative, however, since cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and increase occur through the abandoning of opposing factors, he says, “or those who,” and so forth.

This refers to one whose mind is confident in the three objects beginning with the Buddha, and not merely through faith in the results of kamma. That perfection of faith of his should be understood in this way;
thus, showing the cause by means of the result, he said, "of one perfected in conduct. "A sense of urgency" (saṃvega) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread;
since places such as the sites of past Buddhas are also causes for its arising, he said, "those which produce a sense of urgency."

A "cetiya-cārikā" (pilgrimage to shrines) is a journey undertaken for the purpose of worshipping a cetiya. They will indeed be established in heaven, because wholesome volition directed toward the qualities of the Buddha has the nature of leading to rebirth in heaven.
Commentary on the Discourse of Ānanda’s Question (203):
"In this regard" means among women. This is the supreme practice, namely, non-seeing, because seeing is rooted in [the defilements].

"Because of that" means because of all evils. "Greed" (*lobha*) is sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Agitation of the mind" (*cittacalanā*) is a disturbance of the mind that creates an obstacle to practice.
"Chewing it up" (*murumurāpetvā*) is a description of eating while making a grunting sound, including the bones.

"Experiencing suffering for an immeasurable time" (*aparimitaṃ kālaṃ dukkhānubhavanaṃ*) is the experiencing of suffering without limit. "Relaxation" (*vissāsa*) is a lack of attachment, an absence of friction.

"Entering" (*otāra*) means the mind's penetration into that [object]. "By a hostile man with a sword in hand, or even by a *pisāca* desiring to devour him" means one might be harmed by such means as stepping upon him.

"Of her" (*assā*) refers to the woman. "The task to be performed by those gone forth" (*pabbajitehi kattabba-kamma*) refers to the work that must be done by those who have gone forth, such as receiving alms-food (*āmisa*).
Or else, "mindfulness" (*sati*) means that mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) should be established.
204. *Atantibaddhā* means not bearing a burden. *Pesitacittā* means having their minds directed toward Nibbāna. 205.
*Vihataṃ* means struck by the comb used for carding cotton, in the sense of disentangling the matted locks. Therefore he said, "well-carded" (*supothitaṃ*);
the meaning is that it has been thoroughly beaten (*pothitaṃ*) so as not to become entangled, by describing the place as beautiful and inspiring.
And the place where he was staying has been described.
Regarding the description of the wonderful qualities of Ānanda (207):
"Not seeing the Elder, he addressed him"—there, not seeing him, he reflected and, having known the Elder’s location and his state, he addressed him.
The state of being beneficial for bodily action is due to its having proceeded from an intention for benefit; thus he said, "done with the increase of benefit.
The state of happiness is the absence of bodily suffering, and the state of mental happiness is due to its being originated by mental happiness;
thus it was said, "done with pleasure and joy alone. The meaning of "non-dual" is that it is non-dual because of the analysis of manifestation and because of the state of non-duality.

The passage beginning with "just as" was spoken in order to demonstrate this. Because that deed is devoid of measure— due to the perfection of the Teacher’s field and the perfection of the Elder’s aspiration,
such that it is impossible to grasp its extent by thinking "it is only this much"—
he said, "even a world-system," and so forth.
"By means of what has thus proceeded" means by means of what has proceeded through the cultivation of directed loving-kindness (*odissaka-mettā-bhāvanā*).

One who has "performed merit" (*katapuñña*) is so called because merit has been performed and accumulated by him; the meaning is that he has undertaken the necessary application for the attainment of Arahatship. Therefore, he said:
"He shows that 'you are endowed with a resolute aspiration' (*abhinīhārasampanno*)."
208. As if stretching out toward the great earth that stands contracted in some places;
as if expanding the space that stands withdrawn; as if lowering the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, which is six hundred and sixty-four thousand yojanas in height;
and as if lifting up Mount Sineru, which is one million six hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas in height.
“...as if grasping the trunk of a great rose-apple tree (*jambu*) a hundred *yojanas* in height and breadth and shaking it.
Indeed, these five similes have been brought forth for the purpose of demonstrating the greatness of the Elder’s virtues and for the purpose of demonstrating the wickedness of others.
By the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “And by this very [fact],” [it is meant]: “I am now an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One,” and “in the world with its devas...”
The inclusion of such statements as “In this world there is no one who is my equal” should be understood in this way.

“Expert” (byatta) means endowed with proficiency (veyyattiya) consisting of skill in the *Khandhakas* and so forth. “Wise” (medhāvī) means endowed with wisdom (paññā) that is well-cultivated and termed “insight” (medhā). 209.
“The quality of hospitality” (paṭisanthāradhamma) is said by way of natural conduct; however, for monks who have approached...
He taught the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs both by way of answering their questions and according to his own inspiration at the appropriate time,
whereas for the male and female lay followers he did so by way of discourses delivered while seated.
(Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta)
210. The word *khuddaka* (small) denotes something that is similar [to what it names], while the syllable *ka* has the sense of "slight.

Thus he says: “In ‘the small city (*khuddakanagaraka*)’ [it means] in a cramped, small city that is merely a semblance of a city. Because of its shape being narrow and extensive like incense smoke, it is called “the city of the wilderness (*ujjaṅgalanagaraka*)”;
thus he says: “in the uneven city (*visamanagaraka*). Because it possesses the dimensions of a portion of other great cities, it is like a branch.
And here, by the phrase "in a small town," its insignificance is stated; by "in a barren town," its lowliness due to the deficiency of the ground;
and by "in a branch-town," its lack of preeminence. "Attained to essence" means having attained greatness of essence through wealth and other such things.
Regarding the phrase "kahāpaṇa-cart" (kahāpaṇasakaṭa): here they say, "A cart [carrying] two kumbhas; a kumbha, moreover, is ten ambaṇas. "Two enter" means two kahāpaṇa-carts enter by way of income.
"Well-supplied with food" (subhikkhā) means that food is easily obtained and the food is excellent. Therefore he said, "abounding in hard foods and soft foods.
"Making a sound" means making a cry like a crane due to a state of joy and exultation. "Not deserted" (avivittā) means not empty; at times...
The chariot goes first, and another follows behind it; sometimes the second chariot goes first, and the other follows it—thus they follow one another. "There" means in the city of Kusāvatī.
Because of its great size and because of its supernatural power (*iddhi*), musical instruments such as drums were constantly employed there.
The word *samma* refers to the sound of mutual affectionate address, such as "Samma! Samma! The word *tāla* refers to the sound of all types of musical instruments, such as cymbals and the like;
it includes the sound of the *kūṭabherī* drum and the sound of the *kumbhathūṇa* drum.
Such sounds arise because the streets are strewn with refuse, or for the purpose of gathering roots, tubers, leaves, and so forth in the forest. In that regard:
"And because of a miserable life" should be applied respectively [to the two cases]. Here, it was not as in the world of the gods, where there is a state of complete perfection in every respect.
"A great clamor" refers to the presence of deities endowed with faith and lay followers, who were right in front [of him].
There was a great proclamation. Because there was no monastery built specifically for the Blessed One and because of the vastness of the Saṅgha of monks, they came...
[as before] ...and he sent word. And while sending it, thinking, "How indeed could the Blessed One not have informed us of his own passing at this final time?
Let there be no grief among them," he sent the message beginning with the words, "Today, Vāseṭṭhas... and so forth.
Commentary on the Homage to the Mallas (Mallānaṃ vandanāvaṇṇanā): 211.

They bring (*āventi*) and manifest (*pakāsenti*) misfortune (*agha*), which is suffering (*dukkha*); thus they are "misfortune-bringers" (*aghāvino*). By this he means "those for whom suffering has arisen.
That in which one’s family turns around by virtue of being a kinsman or blood relation is "family-turning" (*kulaparivatta*). By way of belonging to such-and-such a family...
The community of beings is said to be "arranged by family cycles" (*kulaparivatta*); thus he says, "by family cycle.

Furthermore, those Malla kings, delimited by their respective family cycles, dwell in that city according to the distribution of streets and so forth; therefore it is said, "according to the distribution of streets and according to the distribution of roads."
Commentary on the Story of the Wanderer Subhadda (212).
"Doubt itself" is the state of doubt (*kaṅkhādhamma*). "From one side" means collectively, without dividing the ground, that is, in common.
Taking the tip of the seed and preparing food, the gift is called the "gift of the seed-tip. "At the time of the womb" means after the taking up of the embryo.
At the time of milking. Therefore he said: “Having split open the womb and drawn out the milk,” and so forth.
At the time of the *puthuka* (threshing) refers to the period when the crops are not yet fully ripe, but are at a stage of fruit suitable for threshing.

Regarding *lāyanagga*: he gave a gift at the commencement of the reaping of the ripened crop. *Veṇikaraṇa* is the binding together of the reaped crop by means of bundles and setting it aside; at the commencement of that—

The first portion of the gift is the *veṇagga*. Furthermore, the gathering together and piling up of the bundles is the *kalāpa*. Among those, the first portion given from the *kalāpa* is the *kalāpagga*.

The first portion given when the grain has been removed from the *kalāpa* and threshed is the *khalagga*. The first portion given when the threshed grain has been winnowed and piled into a heap is the *khalabhaṇḍagga*.
The first portion given when the grain is being transferred from the threshing floor into the storehouse is the *koṭṭhagga*.
"Having extracted" means having extracted from the granary. By the statement,

"She gave nine foremost gifts," it is shown that because she had performed and accumulated wholesome deeds (*kusala*) serving as a supporting condition for the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*)—

specifically through the giving of the very best things with the thought, "How indeed might I be released as the foremost in the presence of the Teacher"— and because her knowledge (*ñāṇa*) had likewise reached maturity...
By the phrase "having gone," he shows that [the Buddha] was a fit vessel for the teaching of the supreme Dhamma. Therefore he said:
"I shall teach this supreme Dhamma to him," and so forth. "Having fallen behind" means having become discouraged.
(213) "Desiring to know, he did not cling to his own views. "They understood" is a statement of inquiry made by one who has conceived doubt.
"Having made [the claim], they came to know"—this is the meaning he expressed. Therefore he said in the Pāḷi: "Not all indeed knew. "Of them" refers to Pūraṇa and the others.
"That admission" means that which was admitted by such statements as, "O Great King, for one who acts and for one who causes to act," or it is simply the admission of omniscience.
"Leading out" means possessing a demonstration (sappāṭihāriya), or else their admission known as their tenet-system in the sense of being an escape from the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
"Leading to liberation. It should be understood that through the excellence of the Dispensation, one attains omniscience, and by its opposite, non-omniscience.
Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Due to the absence of a purpose" means due to the absence of a purpose to be accomplished for Subhadda.
"Due to the absence of an opportunity" means due to the absence of an occasion to teach the Dhamma after having expanded upon it in such a manner. Now, that very...
In order to show the absence of opportunity, it was said, "In the first watch," and so forth. 214.

That by which one becomes a recluse (*samaṇa*) through the accomplishment of those qualities that constitute the state of a recluse—namely, according to the highest description, the qualities of the Noble Path—is such that, due to the perfection of the four paths, four types of recluses are mentioned in the Canon; these [are not found] in external systems.
Demonstrating that [the self] does not exist in any way whatsoever, he said, "The first is the stream-enterer ascetic," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by the previous teaching": this refers to the teaching stated in the passage beginning, "But in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda...
Since the intended meaning is clarified through both negative (vyatireka) and positive (anvaya) concomitance, the first method (*naya*) is here included by the expression "by the previous teaching."
It should be understood thus. Restricting his own teaching, he said, "In this," which is the construction.

"By those who have begun insight" refers to those who practice insight as part of their work on concentration—that is, referring to those whose insight has reached its culmination—not to those who have merely established insight.
Others, however, say: "Since there is not even a book on the commencement of insight in the non-Buddhist systems, this is a statement made without distinction."
They say: "The state that has been attained" (*adhigataṭṭhāna*) means the cause for what has been attained; the meaning is the preliminary path (*pubbabhāgapaṭipadā*) for that purpose.
One by whom the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*) has been attained, but not a higher path, stands in the stream-entry path.

Because of its unshakable nature (*akuppadhammatā*), or because of being established therein, he is one who has previously stood there—having previously gone to that state—and is thus called a "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) as one standing in the stream-entry path.

The remaining noble ones do not [do so] because they arise in different planes of existence. For a stream-enterer, having explained to another the path of stream-entry—the state he himself has attained—might place that other in the position of a stream-enterer;
but one who is merely an "eighth-person" (a worldling on the path) could not, because it is impossible. This same method applies to those standing on the other paths;
here too, the meaning should be understood by this very principle. "A meditation subject well-mastered" means...
One’s own familiar meditation subject for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) is intended; by this, the claim that it is a "non-specific statement" should be understood as refuted.

What is intended is omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa). For that is called "skilled, dexterous, and subtle" in the awakening to all knowable phenomena, because it proceeds therein unattached and unimpeded. [The text] exceeds [the previous amount] by one year. They are known.
By this [term], the principle is that one penetrates the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths as it truly is; thus he says, "of the noble path-dhamma," meaning the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*).
It is called a "portion" (*padesa*) because by means of it the noble path is seen directly; thus it is said, "insight on the portion, which is the path.

Regarding the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even a recluse" (*samaṇopi*), the particle *api* should be brought over and connected here from the phrase "one who dwells in a portion" (*padesavattī*).
He said: “It is stated that it ‘exists only in part’... [etc] ...it means ‘there is none.
(215) “He” refers to the resident pupil mentioned in that way. “By him” means by the teacher. He was established in his own position because he was appointed to tasks such as expelling others.
“A witness-disciple” (*sakkhisāvaka*) means a disciple who is present before the eyes; the meaning is “a face-to-face disciple. “While the Blessed One was living” means while he was still alive.
"In the presence of the Blessed One. This same method applies to the other two as well. "All that" means all three types.
But this one has attained Arahatship; therefore, he is the final witness-disciple who has reached the pinnacle of the perfected state.
The commentary on the fifth recitation section is finished.
216. Regarding the "Commentary on the Tathāgata’s Final Words":
*Taṃ* (that) was stated by the compilers of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgāhakā*) in order to show the factor of exhortation to the Saṅgha of monks... [etc. ...the intention is as follows.
The "bestowing," "awakening," or "teaching" (*atisajjana-sambodhana-desanā*) refers to the Dhamma comprised within the Suttas and the Abhidhamma; its "mode" (*pakāra*) is—

"Making known" (*ñāpana*) means establishing [the teaching] within the mental continuum of those to be trained (*veneyya*) and making it understood (*paññāpana*); thus it is said: "The Dhamma is both taught (*desita*) and established (*paññatta*).

Likewise, "teaching" (*desanā*) is the imparting (*atisajjana*) and awakening (*sambodhana*) of that meaning which has received the designation "Discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines body and speech as comprised within the system of the Vinaya;
it is the making known of that very [meaning] according to its various modes and its establishment without confusion.
Regarding "laying down" (*paññāpana*), it is said: "The Vinaya is both taught and laid down.

Because it constitutes the foundation of the Dispensation by way of being the exposition of the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the Vinaya must be studied first; thus, showing that very summary (*uddesa*) in its own form, he says, "For I have [taught] to you," and so forth.
In that context, "by way of the seven classes of offenses" (*sattāpattikkhandhavasena*) refers to the seven classes of offenses.

By way of its being untransgressible. It will accomplish the Teacher’s task because it instructs by distinguishing between what is to be done and what is not to be done, saying: "This is for you to do; this is for you not to do.
"In that and that manner" means in a mode corresponding to the inclinations of those to be trained. "These phenomena" refers to these...

Regarding the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*): because the teaching of the Suttas has these as its primary focus, it is said that "the Suttanta Piṭaka was taught.
It will accomplish the Teacher’s task by instructing in right practice according to the various modes of conduct.

There are nine roots by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. The phrase "seven contacts," and so forth, refers to their association with the seven consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*).

It has been stated. There are six "foundations" (paṭṭhāna) beginning with the triplets in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānuloma), and likewise in opposition to the Dhamma (dhammapaccanīya), in both accordance and opposition to the Dhamma (dhammānulomapaccanīya), and in opposition and accordance to the Dhamma (dhammapaccanīyānuloma).
That which possesses these twenty-four foundations is the "twenty-fourfold foundation" (catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhāna).

Furthermore, when analyzed by way of the positive conditions (paccayānuloma) and so forth, it consists of infinite methods; thus he said, "adorned with the great foundation of infinite methods" (anantanayamahāpaṭṭhānapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ).
"Will accomplish the Teacher’s task" means that by discerning the aggregates and so forth, one will bring to completion the duty to be performed by the Teacher,
the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), because this leads to the awakening to the Four Noble Truths.
"They will exhort and instruct" means that they will fulfill the duty of providing exhortation and instruction.
"Conduct" (*cāritta*) means modes of behavior; the meaning is that it consists of endearing speech toward juniors and respectful speech toward seniors. Thus he said:
"as 'Venerable Sir' (*bhaṇte*) or as 'Worthy One' (*āyasmā*). For these—namely, "Venerable Sir" or "Worthy One"—are terms of respect;
however, in the world, "His Reverence" (*tatra bhavaṃ*) and "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānaṃ piyā*) are likewise terms of respect.
When it was said, “If he so desires, let him eradicate [it],” it was also effectively said, “If he does not desire, let him not eradicate it. Therefore, it is said:
“He established [the matter] by means of a concessive statement (*vikappavacana*) itself. “Power” (*bala*) refers to the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*).

If non-eradication were seen [by the Buddha] and that alone were intended, then why did the Blessed One say, “If he so desires, let him eradicate it”? It was because of the disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) of such a person.
For there are some who, having undertaken the minor and lesser training rules, are unwilling to practice them;
if these were not spoken by the Blessed One in such a manner, distress would arise in them, which would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
But when it is spoken thus, no distress arises in them, thinking: "This fault is our own, since..."
"Among us, some do not even desire the abolishment [of the minor rules]. Some say, "But it was said thus for the purpose of making the entirety of the Dispensation dependent upon the Saṅgha.

Whatever training rule has been laid down by the Teacher, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, accept it with their heads and protect it as they would their own life. For instance, regarding those "minor and lesser training rules":
Even when it was said, "If the Saṅgha so desires, let it root this out," they did not root it out;
rather, it should be understood that they protected it even after his passing just as they had before, both to demonstrate the greatness of the Teacher’s instruction and of the Saṅgha.
For instance, the Venerable Ānanda or other monks [asked]: "Which, then..."
"Venerable sir, what is the minor? What is the very minor?"—they did not ask this because they lacked the underlying intention (*adhiṭṭhāna*) to resolve the matter.
Their statement, "The Elder Nāgasena knows the minor and very minor rules," and so forth, should not be understood in the manner just stated, because their true intention was not understood. Now:
In order to clarify that intention, it was said: "The Elder Nāgasena," and so forth.

For the Elder Nāgasena—(the details of which are in the *Abhejjavagga* of the *Milindapañha*)—at the time of the recitation (*saṅgīti*), when the Great Elders who compiled the Dhamma had selected portions [of the teachings], he presented himself to King Milinda by taking only the final portion among those selected, for the purpose of cutting off the paths of argumentation of others. The Elder Mahākassapa...
However, because he proclaims the formal act (*kammavācā*) in that manner out of a desire not to abolish even a single training rule (*sikkhāpada*), his statement should not be accepted as such.

217. *Dveḷhaka* means a twofold apprehension; the meaning is a non-unequivocal grasp. *Vimatī* is the occurrence of doubt. Therefore, he said: "the inability to reach a decision. *Taṃ vo vadāmi*: I say this to you concerning that bhikkhu who possesses doubt.

"Knowledge that makes the state of being free from doubt manifest" means precisely the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which stands having penetrated that fact, because those bhikkhus lacked the capacity to make manifest their own state of being free from doubt regarding the Buddha and the others. "In this matter" refers to this specific point. 218.
Non-negligence is *appamāda*; in terms of its actual meaning, however, it is mindfulness (*sati*) conjoined with knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Because, in that regard, by means of mindfulness...
The activity is preeminent; therefore, it is said, "by non-separation from mindfulness.
This was stated by including it within the very term *appamāda* (heedfulness), because that [term] encompasses the entirety of the Buddha’s word.
Commentary on the Account of the Final Nirvana.

219. Regarding the jhānas and so forth, because of having attained mastery over the mind to its highest degree, one enters into meditative attainments after setting a time limit, thinking, "Having entered these many attainments for this much time, I shall attain final Nibbāna. This entering into attainment is what is intended by the term "preparation for final Nibbāna.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Anuruddha.
"This too" refers to the account of having attained the aforementioned sixty-five jhānas;
it is indeed a summary statement. Why? Because the Blessed One, even then, entered all the daily functional attainments without exception;
thus he said, "Entering the city of Nibbāna," and so forth, to demonstrate this.
These two [consciousnesses] are also immediately followed by the reviewing consciousness, because they mostly possess the quality of immediate succession due to their belonging to the side of jhāna.
Since the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) is the very last, and because one falls away from existence (*bhava*) from that point, it is called "falling away" (*cuti*).
Therefore, to show that not only this Blessed One, but indeed all sentient beings fall away by means of the life-continuum consciousness alone—
The passage beginning with “ye hi keci” has been stated.
220. “Devoid of a counterpart person” means being without a person who is similar due to the incomparability of qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth. 221.
Nibbāna is that which is known, understood, and declared as “vūpasama” because it is here that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) are stilled.
222. Because the accusative case is used in its specific sense, he said, "he who passed away.

"With a well-expanded [mind]" means with a mind that is joyful and expanded due to its association with rapture and gladness (*pīti-somanassa*). He endured the feeling because it was thoroughly understood through its complete comprehension; his liberation was unobstructed because of his state of total extinction (*nibbāna*). 223.

They are called *ākāra* (modes) because they produce their own fruits, making them similar in form; thus, they are causes. "Endowed with all excellent modes" means endowed with all the most excellent modes, that is, the supreme causes consisting of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and the rest.
225. *Kathaṃbhūtā* means "of what kind.
*Cullakaddhaṃ* means a short period of time, a duration of only two or three *nāḷikas*.
— Commentary on the Worship of the Buddha’s Body.

227. That which "performs" (avacarati) rhythmic beats such as those of the *kaṃsa* gong and the *tāḷa* cymbal is called "tāḷāvacara," referring to musical instruments such as stringed lutes (*ātata*) and so forth. Therefore, he said, "all musical instruments.

"By way of the southern direction alone" means not by any other direction, but specifically by way of the southern direction from the location of the twin *sāla* trees; having carried it even further from there, by way of the southern direction.
"In a place like Jeta’s Grove" means in a place similar to Jeta’s Grove near Sāvatthī; there is also a reading: "in a place like Jeta’s Grove."
228. "In the auspicious hall of adornment" means in the hall for auspicious decoration at the time of the consecration ceremony.
229. "Devadānī" is the name of that thief.
[End of] the commentary on the story of the Elder Mahākassapa.

231. *Pāvāya* means from the city of Pāvā. Because knowledge is dependent upon mental advertence (*āvajjana*), and since there was no such advertence, the Elder did not know of the Teacher’s final Nibbāna;
thus he thought, “I shall see the One of Ten Powers. Or rather, he thought thus while producing the perception of the Teacher with respect to the Teacher’s body.
For this very reason it says, “Then, having lifted up the Blessed One... “Surely he has attained final Nibbāna.”
"He will be," he thought by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*). Although the Elder already knew, he nevertheless questioned the Ājīvaka;
and in order to explain the reason for his questioning himself, he began with the words, "But what...
and so forth. "Seven days ago from today" means that he passed away (*parinibbuto*) on the seventh day counting back from the present day.
232. "By means of a *nāḷi* measure" means by means of both a *nāḷi* and a bag (*thavikā*).

"Gentle" means one who speaks gently, one with a sweet voice. "Eloquent" means possessing ready wit (*paṭibhāna*). "Having eaten, the gruel to be drunk" means the gruel that should be drunk after first eating.
"His" refers to Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age.
*Ārādhitasāsane* means in the well-established dispensation. *Alam* means capable. *Pāpa* refers to an evil person. *Osakkāpetum* means to cause to diminish, to cause to disappear.

*Pañhavārā* means that the answers proceed like questions, such as "At whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere has arisen," and "At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material realm," and so forth; [these constitute] one [section].
There are two other stages. "If the root is destroyed, we shall become like *pisāca*s" means:
just as a *pisāca* spirit residing in a tree, when its surrounding branches are destroyed, dwells supported by the trunk; when the trunk is destroyed, it dwells supported by the root;
but when the root is destroyed, it becomes supportless—so too shall we become. Or else, [it refers to] the root.
Regarding "lost": it is said that a *pisāca* cut the root of some tree or shrub and gave it to his son;
as long as it did not leave his hand, he wandered through that area in an invisible form.
But when it was lost—either because it had been cut by someone or due to the loss of mindfulness—[he could no longer remain there].
He wanders about among humans in a visible form; with reference to him, it was said: "If our root is lost, we shall become like *pisāca* demons.

"Making me a bodily witness" means making me one who has personally realized that path through the body; therefore, he made me a witness to that teaching. That concealment is to be illustrated by the *Kassapa-sutta*. 233.
Because there were many small boxes of sandalwood, they were called "sandalwood-pile [cremation mounds]."
"Having heard that" means having heard that intention of the deities spoken by the Venerable Elder Anuruddha.
"Even a mere thread from a hempen cloth" means even a single thread from a piece of worn-out, dyed Kāsika cloth. "Or a block of wood" means a block of wood such as sandalwood used for a funeral pyre.
Because conventional designations applied to a whole are seen to apply to its parts, the bones—which are the constituent parts of the body—are called "the body."
“Did not scatter” means they remained in their original form. Having stated, “The others scattered,” he said “Thereupon,” etc., to show how they became scattered.
By the power of the deities, streams of water issued forth and extinguished [the fire]. To the question, “For what purpose were there so many great streams of water?
he replied, “The Blessed One’s funeral pyre was large. For it was indeed large, measuring one hundred and twenty cubits. “With eight tusks” means...
Indeed, their eight teeth are like ivory (poṭṭha), and for that reason they are called "eight-toothed" (*aṭṭhadantaka*).

The discourse on the Dhamma is the measure [of its excellence] because it brings about an extraordinary degree of serene confidence in those who see and hear it—due to its state of being exceedingly wonderful and marvelous—and because it specifically illuminates the majesty of the Buddha. For, in the case of the Buddha who has attained final Nibbāna...

"The power of the Blessed One is such"—when those who preach the Dhamma speak of this occurrence, the standard here is the discourse on the Dhamma as it proceeds according to the strength of their own knowledge, because the subject matter to be described is vast in scope;
therefore, the intended meaning is that this constitutes the "ground for description.
"Having had a terrace made with four kinds of fragrant substances" means: *tagara*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), jasmine flowers (*yavana-puppha*), and *tamāla* leaves.
Having ground [the ingredients] and prepared the fragrant paste, he had the border-work (paribhaṇḍa) executed. "Inlaid" (khacita) means having arranged it by way of hanging here and there;
taking fragrant substances, he made woven garlands (ganthitamālā), fragrant wreaths (gandhadāmāni), rows of jewels (ratanāvaḷiyo), and jewel-wreaths (ratanadāmāni).
By constructing a fence of reed-mats (kilañja) on the outside and a fence of coarse cloth (sāṇi) on the inside, he had a perimeter of both coarse cloth and reed-mats made.
"Wind-catchers" (*vātappatākā*) are banners that catch the wind. A couch with antelope-shaped feet is a "deer-made couch" (*sarabhamayapallaṅka*); [he sat] upon that deer-made couch.
"Men seven cubits tall" refers to those who carry spears;
because they always go together with them, it is like saying "spears are moving about. By means of them, [they surrounded him] on all sides.
"Causing protection" means "making it fivefold," as he said: "having had them surrounded by men with swords in their hands.
The same method applies here for "with bows. Having made it like a net-work of armor by means of a protective armor standing without gaps, as if it were a goat-hair blanket (*gavacchika*).

“Sādhukīḷitaṃ” means that it is “good” (sādhu) in the sense of accomplishing the welfare of both oneself and others; their “play” (kīḷita) is so called because it flows with sublime merit. The meaning is that it is a playful dwelling that is not inconsistent with the welfare of future lives.
236. Regarding the commentary on the division of the bodily relics:
“By this very method” refers to the manner in which [the Buddha], while seated on the great terrace, made no exception for anyone and [bestowed the relics] exclusively...
In this very manner. "A dream" means a bad dream. "Having put on a pair of *dukūla* cloths" means having put on two pieces of *dukūla* cloth together;
for in this way, even when one is overcome by grief, they remain without slipping off.
"One who is sprinkled with consecration" means one who is sprinkled during the auspicious ceremony of royal consecration, because it is the most excellent of auspicious occasions. "Senseless."
He was born with affection firmly established through his remembrance of the nectar-like flavor of the Blessed One’s special qualities,
with serene confidence rooted in ordinary faith, and with a softness of heart produced by the thought of the favors he had received.
"With the color of a golden image" means resembling a well-fashioned *apassena* (a gold statue).

But why are the Pāveyyakas mentioned last here in the text? Are they nearer to Kusinārā than anyone else, such that they arose last of all? Yes; it was said, “Therein the Pāveyyakas,” and so forth, in order to show that they arose last of all.
“For the purpose of worshipping the relics” means for the sake of paying homage to the Teacher’s relics. They took their respective sides, thinking, “By right, these relics belong to them. 237.
He uttered what is called the “Donagajjita” (The Roar of Doṇa), which relates to the three stages of the Teacher. For it was for this very purpose that the Blessed One [spoke].
While walking along the path, he made a resolution, thinking, "May the brahmin Doṇa, who is coming from behind,
not miss my footprints until he has seen them," and then sat down at the foot of a certain tree. Meanwhile, the brahmin Doṇa, observing,
"These are the footprints of the Supreme Person in this world with its devas," followed the trail of the footprints toward the presence of the Teacher.
He approached, and the Teacher taught him the Dhamma; consequently, he too became established in faith toward the Blessed One.
He said this; as for what he said, he spoke thus: "Let them hear... [etc. ...he said.

Being united in body through a single gathering, and united in speech through a single utterance—be thus in harmony. As for the reason for this, he said: "Being in mutual amity. Therefore he said: "Be you also in mutual amity even in mind."
238. “Of the assembled Saṅghas from here and there” means: of those who have come together and gathered from their respective places of residence;
likewise, of the groups that have come together by virtue of having met as a multitude. “Having responded” means: having acknowledged by accepting the words.
[End of] the commentary on the worship of the relic stupa.

239. *Yakkhaggāha* is possession by a spirit; *devatāveso* is a manifestation as a deity. *Khipitaka* is the disease of convulsions, having produced a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*). *Arocaka* is the disease of loss of appetite, an inability to find pleasure in food.
"On the seventh day" means on the seventh day after seven years and seven months have passed. "According to their power" means according to the power of their wealth.
"The later compilers" refers to those who compiled the second and third councils. "Seeing an obstacle to the relics" means...
Having seen that the relics, which remained in various cetiyas precisely because they had been established there,
were subject to obstacles due to those holding wrong views; and having seen that when they were properly protected by means of the Great Relic Treasury,
they would bring welfare and happiness to the world including the devas once King Aśoka, the Dhamma-king, had in the future extracted them from there and disseminated them.
"Having seen"—this is the intended meaning. "Merely by way of service" means taking up only the relic-element that is to be served.
[He placed them] into the hands of kings, not into the reliquaries (cetiyas). For thus, later on, the Great King Asoka did not obtain relics from the reliquaries.
Having caused each subsequent one to be made in accordance with what was done by each preceding one, he had eight [reliquaries] made of yellow sandalwood and other materials.
He had caskets and stūpas constructed. The same method applies to those made of red sandalwood and other materials.
"In jewel-caskets" means in caskets variegated with various gems, setting aside those made of ruby, emerald, and crystal.
"The size of the stūpa and the monastery" refers to the size of the stūpa caused to be built by the Great King Devānampiyatissa.

"May the garlands not wither": having made this resolve, "As long as King Aśoka, the Dhamma-king, has not extracted the relics from here in order to have stūpas built outside, so long may the garlands not wither. Regarding "the pulling-rope": it is the rope for pulling the bolt.
Regarding "the key and the seal-ring": both the key and the seal-ring for the purpose of opening the door.
He joined together the terrifying-looking glowing embers (*kukkula*) so that they appeared like a mechanical device (*yaṃta*) with figures linked to one another by their movement;

thus he said, "wooden figures," and so forth. Having bound it with a single axle-pin—meaning that by his own divine power (*devānubhāva*), Vissakamma bound that mechanical device, variegated with many wooden figures, with just one axle-pin and departed for the world of the gods. "On all sides," and so forth.
However, this [passage] shows the performance of specific duties by Ajātasattu regarding that relic-cause.
When the King asked, "In which place is the relic-treasure? some say: "In that assembly, there were none who had attained distinction.
[Others say: "Concealing himself and investigating based on the words of that elder..."

Others say, "They did not speak [of this] thinking, 'He will know it. Regarding the term *yakkhadāsaka*: it refers to those who assume the guise of deities through rituals such as offerings (*upahāra*), namely, those possessed by spirits (*bhūtāviggāhaka*).

This phrase—"Thus was it in the past"—was established by the compilers of the Second Council. The compilers of the Third Council also established it, having made even the enshrinement of the Great Relics its purpose.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*.
4. Commentary on the Mahāsudassanasutta:
The Description of the Royal Capital Kusāvatī 242.
“Made of gold” means made of pure gold. “This rampart” refers to the rampart made of all kinds of jewels. “Three by three” means three within and three without—thus, three by three.

The sandalwood pillar is like a city’s main gatepost (*indakhīla*), a pillar of ornament that beautifies the city. It is called an *aṅga* because by means of it one is marked (*aṅgīyati*) or known for its breadth;
thus, it is a perimeter. That which has a three-man height as its *aṅga* is "three-man-tall" (*tiporisaṅgā*).
Therefore he said, "by that," and so forth. By that [pillar] measuring five cubits and three spans. "In the leaves and fruits" refers to the palm trees made of all kinds of jewels.
“Regarding the leaves and fruits as well: the same method applies. This means that the following points are extended by analogy: “Among the leaves, one leaf is made of gold and one is made of silver;
