among the fruits as well, one mark is made of gold and one is made of silver,” and so forth.
“Between two walls” means between two successive walls. “A row of palm trees standing one after another.”
"Chekoti paṭu suvisado": that which is sharp and well-defined is its "sharpness," and he calls it "beautiful" (*sundara*) because it is the essence of the mind.

"To delight" means to arouse passion (*rāga*). "It is indeed pleasing" means it is simply agreeable. "It does not terrify" means it does not alarm; rather, because it is pleasant to the ear, it is to be cherished.
A single-layered musical instrument is one such as the *kumbha*, *thuṇa*, or *daddarika*; a double-layered one is well known.
"A square lute covered on all sides," and "the *paṇava* drum, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes the *saṅkha* conch and so forth.
"Of one well-tuned" means of one that is properly adjusted. "In measure" means in the middle pitch of tuning, characterized by being neither too tight nor too loose.
"Having moved a hand or a foot" means having prepared the rhythmic movement of the hands and feet.
"Dancing" means those who dance on branches. 243. Regarding the description of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*):
"Uposatha" refers to the virtue endowed with eight factors that should be observed by householders on all days.

One is called *uposathika* because that [uposatha] belongs to him by virtue of his undertaking it; thus, it is "of that *uposathika*. Therefore, he said: "of one who has undertaken the factors of the uposatha.

"At that time" means at that moment. But at what time? At the time when one, having perfected the accumulation of merit consisting of the requisites of giving, virtue, and so forth conducive to the status of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), and having fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turner, is endowed with the excellence of specific qualities such as birth in a particular time, island, and place, as well as lineage, physical form, wealth, sovereignty, and the like.
And at that time, he remains in a physical form corresponding to that [state].

For it is at such a time—when a distinguished man destined to be a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin), a consecrated Khattiya king endowed with the aforementioned qualities and possessed of pure virtue, practices right conduct by giving away hundreds of thousands on every Uposatha day and so forth—that this occurs, and not only when the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) has arisen. And these are the specific distinctions:
This is stated by way of what is common to all universal monarchs (cakkavatti). Therefore he said: “At dawn... [the rest] ...this is the natural law (dhammatā).
However, for Bodhisattas, both the qualities that bring about the state of a universal monarch and the qualities of a universal monarch themselves are indeed preeminent.

“Conditioned by merit of the aforementioned kind of kamma” means having as its cause meritorious kamma such as giving, self-control, and restraint, which brings about the state of a universal monarch.
"Resembling a mass of sapphire" means equal to a heap of indanīla gems.

"Possessed of divine power" means being endowed with divine-like majesties such as visibility, having a pleasing sound, moving through the sky, emitting radiance, non-obstructiveness, and being the cause for accomplishing whatever the king desires; by this, he shows that it is "divine" because it is like the divine.
For that [wheel] is not included within the world of the devas. Or, it is called *sahassāra* because it has a thousand spokes.
"In all its aspects" means in all those desirable aspects—possessing beautiful, complete parts and endowed with the [auspicious] marks—that are required for a wheel.
"They fulfill" means they make it complete; and he will now explain that fulfillment in detail.
*Panāḷī* means a hollow. The intended meaning is that it is free from any obstruction by a row of teeth that is pure and smooth.
Furthermore, because the surface all around that hollow is made of silver, it is said to be "made of solid silver.
Since this wheel has no interior space like that of a chariot wheel, it is therefore stated: "on both outer rims."
The construction is: "the rim is surrounded by a channel. Regarding "on the bands surrounding the hub and the channel":
this refers both to the band surrounding the hub and to the band surrounding the channel of the hub.
"Of them" means of the spokes. "Vases" (*ghaṭaka*) refers to small full vases that serve as ornaments. Likewise for "jewels" (*maṇika*).
A string of pearls (*muttāvaḷikā*). A boundary-line (*paricchedalekhā*) is a demarcating line existing by way of showing the respective boundaries.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes floral designs and so forth. "Well-distributed" (*suvibhattāneva*) means they are well-apportioned because they do not overlap one another.

In the phrases beginning with "well-colored" (*surattā*), by the inclusion of "well-colored," he rejects the complexion of Mahānāma; by the inclusion of "pure" (*suddha*), [he rejects the complexion of Pukkusāti].

[He perceives] impurity through the grasping of the smooth, and coarseness through the grasping of the rough. Granted that the rim-circle of that Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) was produced without any joints at all,
yet because it shines everywhere and entirely with the color of coral,
[the artist] used circular boundary lines made of bright red gold bands and so forth at the places where the joints of an ordinary wheel would have been.
Because they appear as if they were connected when being perceived, he said, "But in its joints," and so forth.
"On the surface of the rim of the wheel" means on the surface portion of the rim of the wheel. For because it moves through the air, its coral shaft there catches the wind.
"Between each set of ten spokes" means between each set of ten spokes.
*Antare* means in a nearby place. *Chiddamaṇḍalakhacito* means variegated with holes shaped like circles.
*Sukusalasamannāhatassa* means struck by a very skilled craftsman; the meaning is "played. *Vaggu* means charming.
*Rajanīyo* means causing passion to arise in those who hear it. *Kamanīyo* means lovely. *Samosaritakusumadāmā* means adorned with hanging garlands of fragrant flowers.
“Of the rim’s circumference” means of the circumference at the edge of the rim. Regarding the phrase “of both navel-tubes,” it is said with reference to the two sides of the navel-tube;
for that tube is indeed only one. “By which” refers to the two openings.
Again, “by which” refers to the two urinary channels.
"Causing [them] to listen" means making them attentive to hear.
"The moon in front and the wheel-treasure behind" refers to their relative positions, one before and one after.
"Of the inner palace" refers to the king's inner palace in Anurādhapura. "Resembling the northern lion-lattice window" refers to that of the king at that time.
It is stated thus because such a lion-window (sīhapañjara) is available on the northern side of the palace.
"Easily able" means that one is able to worship with ease, by throwing handfuls of flowers with the hand while remaining exactly where one stands—
without having to climb up anything and without having to stretch out the body.

“Blazing with the radiance of jewels of various colors” means shining with the brilliant luster of jewels of many diverse and variegated hues. “Having ascended into the sky, it proceeds” means that from the place where it has come to rest, it rises upward into the sky and moves along.
244. “Appointed by the king” refers to men appointed to the king’s service.
“Leaving Sineru on its left side” is said because it travels keeping Sineru further to its right, having placed Sineru on its left flank.

"By piercing through" means by way of penetrating across. "Fit for encampment" means suitable for the layout of a military camp (*khandhāvāra*). "With food and requisites easily obtained" means having means of sustenance such as grain, dairy products, firewood, grass, and so forth, which are acquired with ease.
"Enemy army" refers to the military force or the command of another king.
"Delighting in their arrival" means causing joy at their coming. "Sorrowing at their departure" means grieving at their going away. "May they be of service" means...

"Arrange one above the other; prepare and bring them," is the meaning. "Having examined" means having investigated by way of cause, nature, result, and the disadvantages pertaining to the present life, the future life, and so forth.
"Discerners" (*vibhāvino*) means those who make the meaning clear through wisdom;
they are the wise ones. "Followers" (*anuyantā*) means those who act in accordance [with the teaching]; it is precisely by virtue of being followers that—
However, it should be understood that while some do not refrain from evil due to disgust because of the great power of the king, others refrain out of a sense of moral dread (*ottappa*).
"Sinking down" means subsiding. "Only a league" refers to an area measuring only a league in extent. By way of its depth...
However, it descends just as the ground is seen. Therefore he said, "the surface of the great ocean," and so forth.

At the end [of the army], the wheel-treasure [is placed] so that the army will not be overwhelmed by the water. "Having the eastern great ocean as its limit" means that which has the eastern great ocean as its boundary; the meaning is: having made the eastern great ocean its limit.
"Cāturantāya" means bounded by the four oceans, or else bounded by the four quarters beginning with the eastern direction. "Sobhayamānaṃ viya":
the word "viya" is merely a particle; for it stands as something truly resplendent through its own wonderful qualities.
Indeed, even in the Pāli text, it is stated simply as "upasobhayamānaṃ."

The Description of the Elephant Jewel (Hatthiratana-vaṇṇanā). 246. Regarding the phrase "with yellow sandalwood and so forth," the word "so forth" includes the four kinds of fragrant substances and the like.

They say, "one should contemplate its arrival" because it has become familiar through the fulfillment of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti). It possesses a pure white body due to the absence of black spots and other such blemishes.
“Seven-limbed” (*sattapatiṭṭha*) means that it is seven-limbed because it stands upon seven parts: the tail, the frontal boss, and the trunk—these three—and the four feet.
“The youngest of all” (*sabbakaniṭṭha*) means inferior to all the elephants of the Chaddanta lineage. “The eldest of the Uposatha lineage” means coming from the Uposatha lineage.
The construction there is: "the most excellent of all comes. "By the method stated" means by the method stated beginning with "having given a great gift.
It comes for the sake of the wheel-turning monarchs (*cakkavattī*) and the sons of wheel-turning monarchs who are thinking of the wheel-turning monarch.
"Having removed" means having removed it by his own power; for other elephants cannot endure its scent alone.
Like a calf belonging to a domestic cow: like a calf born and raised right there with a cow that has long been familiar to the household. "The entire earth" means the whole earth known as Jambudīpa.
Regarding the description of the horse-treasure (247): "From the Sindhu breed" means from the lineage of horses of the Sindhu stock.
Commentary on the Jewel (Maṇiratana):
248. "In circumference equal to the nave of a cart" means it is the same size as the nave of a large cart.
"At both ends" means at the two ends, namely, below and above. "Up to the edge of the pericarp" refers to the two golden lotuses.
"From the edge of the central hub. "Having placed it in a net of pearls" means having established it upon a very pure net made of pearls.
"Like at the time of sunrise" indicates by way of the first light of dawn the actual moment of the sun's rising. This concludes the description of the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratana*).
249. Having stated, "The woman-treasure (itthiratana) appears," in order to show from where its appearance arises, it was said, "From the Madda royal family," and so forth.
It is said that the Madda province is the birthplace of beautiful women in Jambudīpa.
For instance, such woman-treasures as the queen of King Siñcaya, the queen of King Vessantara, and Bhaddakāpilānī originated there.
It arose in the Madda kingdom itself. "By the power of merit" means by the majesty of the merit of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rājā*).

"By the perfection of shape" means by the well-proportioned arrangement of the bodily parts such as the hands and feet; for the perfection of the whole is established through the perfection of its parts.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the body, as in such passages as, "it goes by the designation of 'form'."
"Beautiful to behold" (*dassanīyā*) means worthy of being seen because of their excellent physical form. Therefore, he said, "being visible," and so forth.
Through joy, one gladdens the mind by means of the faith in the results of kamma for those who reflect wisely.

By the phrase "bringing about confidence" (*pasādāvahattā*), just as the perfection of complexion and luster was stated [as the cause] for being pleasing to look at (*pāsādikā*), so too the perfection of being beautiful to behold is stated [as the cause] for being pleasing to look at.
He shows the method by which the accomplishment of beauty and loveliness must be stated.

Alternatively, in reverse order, the accomplishment of attractiveness through the possession of color and complexion, the accomplishment of loveliness through attractiveness, and the accomplishment of beauty through loveliness should be applied.
Having thus shown beauty and the other qualities by way of the excellence of the body, he now [shows them] also by way of the absence of defects in the body.
To demonstrate this, it was said: “or beautiful,” and so forth. In that context, just as they are possessed of the proper proportions, they are likewise pleasing due to their height and girth;
thus, because they possess the excellence of divine form yet have not reached the full state of divinity, it is said: “not having attained divine beauty.
The excellence of height is stated because of their pleasing appearance through their stature; the excellence of girth is stated because of the absence of the defects of being too thin or too stout.
“Perfection of color” is said because of the absence of discoloration. “Physical defects” refers to flaws in the body.
“Seven times beaten” means beaten seven times; this expression “seven times beaten” is stated by way of a cotton-down (*kappāsa-picu*), for there is no beating of a tuft of *tūla* cotton.
Saffron, *tagara*, turmeric, and *yava-napuppha* flowers constitute the four kinds.
"Tamāla, tagara, and turu trees, and yavana flowers," say others. "As if burnt by fire" means as if burnt by the fire that had reached the seat.

"At the very first" means even upon seeing the king, without being preoccupied with other duties, but rather before those other duties—at the very moment of seeing him; that is the meaning. [This occurred] after the king had sat down.
She whose habit (*sīla*) is to lie down after [the king] has sat down is called *pacchānipātinī*.
She is called *kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī* because she reports back what must be done for the king, asking, "What shall I do? regarding each task he has to perform.
It is said that women are generally of a deceitful nature; however, to show that this is not the case for the Woman-Jewel (*itthiratana*), the passage beginning with "But hers... was stated.
"Qualities" refers both to qualities of physical form and qualities of conduct.
"By the power of former karma" means by the power of previously performed karma that leads to the state of being a woman-jewel;
for even the meritorious deed of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) that leads to such a perfection of retinue certainly serves as the decisive support (upanissaya) for such a specific result.
Therefore he said, "By depending upon the merit of a wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavattino puññaṃ upanissāya*).

By this, it should be understood that even in the case of the remaining sentient bases (*saviññāṇakaratanāni*), which are produced by one's own karma, the fact that those respective specific qualities depend upon that [merit] as their decisive support (*upanissaya*) has been clearly demonstrated.
The fulfillment (*pāripūrī*) that was previously obtained in part begins from the moment the king attains the status of a wheel-turning monarch.
They were born fully perfected in every aspect.
250. The Description of the Householder-Treasure (*gahapatiratana*):
"By nature" (*pakatiyā va*) means even prior to the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*), by their very essence. Such as they are for a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*)...
“Endowed with the power of the Wheel-treasure”: by relying on the power of merit, the aforementioned manifestation of the majesty of the Wheel-treasure occurs;
and by relying on such power of merit of his, the Householder-treasure brings about the divine eye born of the ripening of kamma. Thus it is said.
For such a statement is made because the cause resides within a single continuum and the result is contemporaneous with it.
The Commentary on the Counsellor-Treasure (Pariṇāyakaratana): 251.

He is "wise" (paṇḍita) because he possesses the state of wisdom characterized as the realization that one is the owner of one's own kamma, expressed in such terms as "This is dhamma; this is non-dhamma.
He is "skilled" (byatta) due to his proficiency and extensive learning. He possesses "natural intelligence" (pakatipaṇṇā), which is synonymous with innate wisdom (medhā).

A wise person (*medhāvī*) [is so called] because of their existence [as such]. One who is discerning (*vibhāvī*) is so called because of the capacity to clarify and explain to others the meaning as it has been correctly understood by oneself.
"To determine" (*vavatthapetuṃ*) means to decide with certainty. This is the commentary on being endowed with the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*catu-iddhi*).

252. *Vipaccanaṃ* means ripening; it is *vipāka* (ripening), and *vipāka* itself is *vepāka*, just as "that which is cut (*vikata*) is itself *vekata*. Because it possesses a ripening that is even—that is, not too cold nor too hot—of what has been eaten, it is called *samavepākinī* ("possessing even ripening");
[the city was built] by her, the *samavepākinī*. 253. Commentary on the Lotus Pond of the Dhamma Palace:
He did not have it built by having a multitude of people gathered and digging with that multitude of people. Why then? He said: "Of the king..."
"...panā" and so forth. The reason for this will follow later. "Lotus ponds surrounded by a single railing":
here, a *pariveṇa* refers to the bank of a lotus pond that has been cleared of obstructions on all sides;
at its boundaries, which serve as its demarcation, there are lotus ponds surrounded by a single railing. "This thought occurred to him": [end of quote].
"This was [the thought] beginning with, 'What if I were now [to plant these] in these lotus ponds.
"In all seasons" means flowering during every season. "Seeds of various-colored lotuses, etc. means seeds of lotuses that flower in various colors such as red, blue, and so forth.
"A garland of water-born and land-born [flowers]" means a garland made of water-born and land-born flowers.

254. "By way of service" means by way of momentary service; this is stated according to the sequence first established, whereas later, like vehicles and couches, even women were relinquished by those who required them. Therefore he said, "even by women," and so forth.
"By way of relinquishment" means by way of relinquishment without expectation. It is given, thus it is a gift (*dāna*); that is, the object to be given.
It is called a "gift-offering" (*dānagga*) because there food is offered and distributed therein; it is the place where the meal is served.
"There are such [things]" means that those who possess their own fine linen garments and so forth, similar to those found at the king’s gift-offering, have them.

"Having abandoned" (*ohāya*) means having left behind or set aside right there. "Those who have need" (*atthikā*) are those for whom there is a need (*attha*); in the same way, "those who have no need" (*anatthikā*) should also be understood.

255. Regarding the phrase "even the sound of quarreling," the word *pi* (even/also) includes the following meaning: it is not proper to bring back into the house that which has been taken out from the house with the intention of giving. Therefore he said, "This is indeed not fitting for us," and so forth.
257. "At the top of the pinnacle" means at the very summit of the spire. "At the top of the boundary" means at the upper limit of the palace courtyard.

258. "It takes away" (*harati*): because of its extreme brilliance, it strikes against the eyes; due to its difficulty to look upon, it is as if it "takes away" or removes one's vision. That taking away occurs through their trembling; thus he says, "it makes them quiver.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the attainment of jhāna.
260. "By great supernormal power" means by the great accomplishment of desired aims. "Of those very things desired" refers to the objects of their wishes.
By the word "to be experienced," he shows that the term *ānubhāva* (power) functions as a passive noun (*kamma-sādhana*).
Having previously prepared [the requisites], he says "of the renunciation of excellence" to show that the act of relinquishing the gift had already been performed. Himself...
It is called "self-control" (*dama*) because one tames oneself by means of it.
Regarding the "former practice of the Bodhisattva," this refers to King Mahāsudassana.
"A certain elder" refers to a particular worldling (*puthujjana*) who is not well-known by name or clan.
The Elder. "Having seen the Elder" means having seen him sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
"A mat of sticks" (*kaṭṭhattharaṇa*) means a mat made of wood; the meaning is a wooden plank.

"Utensils for use" (*paribhogabhājana*) refers to vessels suitable for use, such as those for drinking water or washing. "A thorn for piercing" (*ārakaṇṭaka*) is a thorn used for piercing with a needle. "A small knife" (*pipphalika*) is a small blade. "A water-pot" (*udakatumbaka*) is a *kuṇḍikā* (water flask).
"He turned back right at the door of the gabled chamber" means that from the moment he entered the gabled chamber, he gave no opportunity for those wrong thoughts to arise.
(261) Only the *kasiṇa* appears because the Great Man had performed his preparatory work in various places, and because those locations resemble *kasiṇas* that have been well-prepared.
(262) "The four jhānas" refers to the four *kasiṇa*-jhānas; it is specifically the *kasiṇa*-jhānas and their immeasurables (*appamaññā*) that are being spoken of.
Because they were produced at that time through the influence of respect and reverence. For Great Bodhisattvas have no need for the formless jhānas;
however, they produce them as well with a view toward their serving as the basis for the higher knowledges (abhiññā).

Therefore, whatever mundane qualities the Great Being produced during his time as an ascetic and a wanderer, he produced them all at that time as well. Thus he said, "But the Great Man," and so forth.
263. The description of the eighty-four thousand cities:
"Food to be brought forth" (*abhiharitabbabhatta*) means food that must be carried up. 264.
"The established routine" (*nibaddhavatta*) refers to the previously fixed routine for cooking.
Commentary on the Visit of Queen Subhaddā (265).
"Having enticed" means having drawn him in very deeply. He explains in detail how whatever gift-requisites or wealth-requisites the king desired were each accomplished exactly as such.
(266) But if the king should conceive a desire for life, he might remain for a long time beyond this, possessing great psychic power.
“Of great power” means that the queen, having such a vast aspiration regarding enjoyments and life, strove to make the king dependent on them.
Therefore it was said: “May the king not indeed [die],” and so forth. For this very reason it was said: “Not desiring his passing away,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “generate desire (*chandaṃ janehi*),” here the word *chanda* is a synonym for craving (*taṇhā*); thus it says, “arouse affection (*pemaṃ uppādehi*). He looks with longing.
“Expectancy” (*apekkhā*) means craving (*taṇhā*), because it does not relinquish its object. Regarding the phrase “censured”:
here, responding to the implicit objection—“By whom is it censured? and “Why is it censured?”—he says, “By the Buddhas,” and so forth.
Thus, because it is censured by the wise and because it leads to an unhappy destination, death accompanied by such expectancy is censured.
He shows that [the path] is to be avoided.
"Having gone to one side" means having departed from the range of the king's vision.
This concludes the commentary on the attainment of the Brahma-world.

269. *Soṇassa* means of Soṇa Koḷivisa. *Ekā bhattapātī* means one serving-plate of food. *Tādisaṃ bhattaṃ* means such food—weighty, sweet, and succulent. *Bhuttānaṃ* means of those who have eaten. 271.
*Dāsamanussā* means both slaves and appointed officials.

Now, in order to extract the correspondence between the king Mahāsudassana’s aforementioned perfection of wealth and his past karma, he said, "But these," and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand.

"From the beginning" means from the time of its origination. That is, starting from the third existence (*attabhāva*) prior to that in which that merit was accumulated and from which that prosperity was produced.
For the Jātaka discourse on Mahāsudassana was taught by the Blessed One at that time, starting from its origination. "Like playing with sandcastles" means, for example, as follows:
Just as children, while playing, show their houses, food, and so forth made of sand according to their fancy,
and then depart, scattering all of it upon leaving; even so, the Blessed One, having shown in detail at the time of the Mahāsudassana Sutta his own inconceivable attainment of splendor,
which was like the divine prosperity he had experienced, again [proceeded] with his teaching by way of showing the danger and the escape.
Turning [the wheel] toward the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), showing that "all that prosperity has been transformed and destroyed by impermanence," he said, "Behold, Ānanda," and so forth.

"Transformed" (*vipariṇatā*) means having undergone transformation, which is the departure from its own nature (*sabhāva*). Therefore he said, "by the abandoning of its natural state" (*pakativijahanena*), and so on.
"Natural state" (*pakati*) refers to the specific nature of phenomena—such as hardness or touch—which is delimited by their arising and passing away.
Thus, from the moment of its dissolution, it is abandoned; while being relinquished, it is entirely non-existent. Therefore he said:
"Like an extinguished lamp, it has reached a state beyond designation (*apaññattikabhāva*).
"By this much" means by this extent of the path of teaching that has proceeded from the beginning. It is indeed many hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
"Whose height is this? means whose height is many hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
"Taking up the characteristic of impermanence" means having grasped that characteristic of impermanence pertaining to that attainment through the teaching and having made it manifest.

Just as an ordinary man is unable to climb a tree as high as seven hundred cubits when a ladder has been removed, so too, by the manifestation of impermanence, that attainment— [cannot be maintained].
"No one is able to ascend once the ladder of expectation has been abandoned," thus he said: "as if abandoning the ladder after having grasped the characteristic of impermanence.

"For that very reason" means for the reason already stated; for even though at first the gratification in sensual pleasures was shown in an extraordinary way, subsequently their danger, degradation, defilement, and the benefit in renunciation were shown by the passage beginning with "see their joy" and so forth.
Because it was concluded by means of a teaching after having been analyzed. "In the past" (*pubbe*) means in a previous time. "King Vasabha" refers to the great Sinhalese king named Vasabha.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "water-bubbles and so forth," dew-drops on the tips of grass and similar things are included.

As for the phrase "but as for Mahāsudassana," the particle *pana* indicates a distinction; by this, [it is shown that] King Mahāsudassana [possessed] the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).

At that very moment he was reborn and established in the state of a perfectly pure ascetic; from then on, having shaken off the defilements of the ascetic life such as sensual thoughts and the like, he entered an empty dwelling.

Even for one who had become thus, all the prosperity of a universal monarch vanished seven days after his passing, and not beyond that. This demonstrates the distinction: "Oh, what a marvelous person! What a unique excellence of qualities, shared by no other!"
“Not included” means that he refers to the matter already stated in such passages as, “It is said that in the past the King was reborn in a householder’s family,” and “Again he addressed the Elder.
For he is not included in the recitation of this particular Sutta, though he appears elsewhere as a supplementary addition to this teaching.
As for whatever has not been analyzed here according to its meaning, that is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta.
5. The Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta:
The Explanation of the Prophecy Concerning the Nātikiyas and Others.
273–275. Regarding the word *parito*: just as it expresses the sense of "all around" (*samanta*), so too does it express the sense of "near" (*samīpa*).
Thus, the meaning "all around" and "in the vicinity" (*sāmantā*) has been stated. However, by means of repetition (*āmeḍita*), the sense of "all around" is illuminated.

Furthermore, because it is said that [the Buddha] "dwells near Nādika" (*nātike viharati*) among the surrounding districts, the meaning "of Nādika" (*nātikassa*) is understood. As for the one [who is] *parito*...

He prophesies regarding various countries; therein, the prophecy concerning those who serve [the Triple Gem] is established even without being explicitly stated, or rather, because it will be explained later as an illustration, it is simply said:
"in various countries here and there. "Those who serve" refers to lay followers (*upāsaka*). Therefore he says:
"those who serve the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. "In rebirths" means in future births. Of knowledge, destinations, and merit...

Regarding the phrase "in the [modes of] rebirth": here, "rebirth as a destination of knowledge" (*ñāṇagatūpapatti*) refers to the manifestation of the respective attainment of the knowledge of the paths.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters," and so forth.
"Rebirth through merit" (*puññūpapatti*) refers to rebirth in various classes of devas. "In all places" means in all four locations, beginning with "among the Vajjis and Mallas."
"In the former" refers to what is stated in the Pāḷi. "In those very ten" means in those same ten provinces.
He explains [them] as "attendants" because many who are to be explained are found there. "Nātikiyā" means those belonging to Nātika.
"Reached the conclusion" means they have arrived at a firm decision.
Commentary on the Discourse on Ānanda (Ānandaparikathāvaṇṇanā) 276.

Since what is called the Sangha’s excellent practice is due to the Dhamma being well-expounded, and the Dhamma’s being well-expounded is due to the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, therefore even the praise of the qualities of the Dhamma and the Sangha—expressed as "O, the Dhamma!
O, the Sangha!"—is in fact a praise of the qualities of the Buddha.
Thus it is said: the meaning of the phrase "praising the Blessed One" has also been stated by way of [exclamations] such as "O, the Dhamma!

(Aho dhammo). 278. "The course of knowledge" (*ñāṇagati*) refers to the progression of path-knowledge that occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, as it has come down in such passages as "through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters" (*pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā*). It is by virtue of this very course of knowledge that...

The specific quality of each noble person (ariyapuggala), such as their being of spontaneous birth (opapātika) and so forth, exists; therefore, with reference to such a future state (abhisamparāya) of theirs, he said, "only the future state of knowledge" (ñāṇābhisamparāyameva).

279. It is "one who sees tranquility" (upasantapatiso) because it is seen as tranquil. It means one who has the vision of tranquility, one who is abundant in tranquility. Regarding the phrase "it shines forth as it were" (bhātiriva): here the letter *ra* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*), and the word *iva* has the sense of "exceedingly"; thus he said, "it shines exceedingly" (ativiya bhātī).
The Explanation of Janavasabha: 280.
Because he was like a bull (*vṛṣabha*) among people due to his seniority, this son of the gods was named Janavasabha.
After falling from this heavenly world, he became a king seven times in the human world. After falling from the human world...

"Seven times as one who has become a deva. "Right here" means in this very existence among the Cātumahārājika devas; even here, it is by way of association with Vessavaṇa. 281. *Āsā* is longing, a wish.
And here, by the term "longing-wishing," he refers to the wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) characterized by the wish to act.
For this very reason, he says, "for the sake of the path of a once-returner," and so forth. Regarding the word "yadagge": here the word *agga* is used in the sense of "beginning"; thus he said—

“Starting from that day”: as for the passage beginning with “The former... [and so on]... no falling into states of woe,” this means that for such a length of time he was reborn only from a happy destination to a happy destination because of the wholesome kamma he had performed and accumulated.

Indeed, from the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Phussa onwards, this son of the gods had gathered the equipment of wholesome deeds that serves as the necessary support for the cosmic cycle (vivatta). It is not surprising.
It is wonderful again and again. Therefore he said, "Again and again it is truly wonderful. "In his own assembly" means in his own retinue.

"Just as they were seen by the Blessed One" means that immediately following his mental advertence (*āvajjana*), just as those approximately twenty-four hundred thousand beings were seen by the Blessed One through the range of his knowledge (*ñāṇagati*), so too were they seen exactly as you have seen them. He says, "I heard this in the presence of Vessavaṇa."
Commentary on the Assembly of the Devas (Devasabhāvaṇṇanā) 282.

"For the purpose of gathering [the monks] by means of the invitation to enter the rains-residence" means for the sake of providing protection for the monks during the rains-residence so that they may be gathered together, thinking, "The monks who have entered the rains-residence will thus perform the duty of a recluse with ease. This refers to the gathering for the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).
This was for the purpose of protecting the monks from dangers while they were on their way to the presence of the Teacher after having performed the *pavāraṇā*.
The same principle applies even when they go to a distant place for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma; he himself would also come and assemble there for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
"In this or that" means in this or that dwelling place of the venerable ones.

“Even then” means even at the time when it was said, “Venerable sir, in these previous days. “For this very reason” refers specifically to the occasion of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*).
Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi: “On that very day, on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, at the commencement of the rains retreat,” and so forth. Regarding the seat:
when the Tāvatiṃsa devas had first taken their seats in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, at its four gates—
The four Great Kings sit down; this is their conduct regarding sitting upon their seats.
"For whatever purpose" means for whatever duty or motive. "For the sake of protection" means for the purpose that serves as protection. "Those whose words have been spoken" refers to the Great Kings.
283. "Having surpassed" means having overcome.
Commentary on the Story of Sanaṅkumāra: 284.
*Anabhisambhavanīya* means impossible to fully attain or realize. Therefore, he said, "unattainable," and so forth. *Cakkhupatha*:
the eye itself is the path, the way, or the means for seeing forms; thus it is called "the range of the eye" (*cakkhupatha*). In that range of the eye...
He said, "In the visual faculty" (*cakkhupasāde*); or, because it is suitable as the range of the eye, he said "within the path of vision" (*āpāthe*).
"It does not overcome" means it does not overcome; the meaning is that it does not become its object.
"Lower, lower" means starting from the Tāvatiṃsa realm and going downward, not starting from the Cātumahārājika realm, nor starting from the Brahmapārisajja realm. [The Cātumahārājikas...]
Some say that just as those in the Thirty-three [Heavens] are able to see the births and forms of one another, so too do lower Brahmās see those above;
however, that is not correct. For lower Brahmās cannot see the fundamental rebirth-form (*mūla-paṭisandhi-rūpa*) of those above;
it should be understood that they can see only what has been manifested.

"He fell asleep while listening" means that his mind had become contracted due to the cutting off of outwardly scattered thoughts as he was reflecting on the various destinies (*gati*). "Of my grandfather" refers to the Blessed One. "Pañcasikha" means one who has five crests;
thus, saying "like the Gandhabba Pañcasikha," he says "resembling the Gandhabba Pañcasikha. "Mamāyanti" means they love him. 285.
"Well-freed" means completely freed from the faults of the autumn. Because it was obstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth, the voice was not released [clearly].
Showing that it is "unobstructed" because of the absence of such [impediments], he said "unobstructed" (*apalibuddho*). It is "to be understood" (*viññeyyo*) because it makes itself known;
since this word *viññeyya* has the sense of a cause included within it and functions as an agent-noun, he said "making the meaning known" (*atthaviññāpano*).

The sweetness of sound is called "gentleness"; thus he said "sweet and gentle" (*madhuro mudū*). It is "worth hearing" (*savanīyo*) because it is worthy of being heard. Because of its worthiness of being heard...
And because it is pleasant to the ear, he says, "pleasing to the ear. "A drop" (bindu) means condensed.
It is partless—not having many constituent parts like the sound of a struck and broken bronze vessel—but a single entity; this is the meaning. Therefore he says, "a single solid mass" (ekagghana);
by this very term, its non-dispersed nature should be understood as praised. And because its point of origin is deep, it is profound; thus he says, "from the base of the navel," and so forth.
"Thus arisen" means arisen merely from the striking of the tongue and so forth. It is not sweet because the points of origin are coarse.
It does not resound far because it lacks the quality of heroism (*vīrabhāva*). It is "especially resonant" (*ninnāda*) due to its great expansion, or it is the "resonance of praise.
Therefore he said: "Like a great cloud... endowed [with these qualities]."
"Each subsequent one" refers to the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth phrases.
"Of each preceding one" means, respectively, of the first, third, fifth, and seventh. "The meaning alone" refers specifically to the description of the meaning;
for its clarity is to be understood through its intelligibility, its sweetness through its worthiness of being heard, and its lucidity through its distinctness.
"Because it is not dispersed, there is a profound resonance. Here, the word *yathā* expresses "extent" (*parimāṇa*), not "manner" (*pakāra*) and so forth;

thus he says, "as many as the assembly," thereby showing that its sound issues forth only according to the measure of the assembly—this is its natural law (*dhammatā*). Therefore he says, "only to that extent," and so on.
The passage beginning with “Ye hi keci” is an exposition by way of stating the reason for the meaning already expressed in the passage beginning with “Yāvañca so Bhagavā.
This is because, through their constant practice of the refuges and their establishment in the precepts, they bring about the attainment of the six celestial realms of sensual bliss.
Therefore he said: “Ye hi keci…pe… vadati. “Nibbematikagahitasaraṇe” refers to the going for refuge that has been entered upon by means of the Path.
For they, having entirely eradicated doubt, are indeed endowed with unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the Three Jewels;
by means of their faith that transcends the ordinary person (*pothujjanika-saddhā*), they penetrate and know the qualities of the Buddha and the others.

Their intellects being incapable of being led astray by others, they should be understood as those who have taken refuge free from uncertainty through a methodical process. "The hosts of *gandhabba* devas" refers to the multitude of *gandhabba* deities.
*Tukā* refers to a woman who has recently given birth; she is also called *tukā*. Its powder is *tukāpiṭṭha*.
When that is ground and applied, it remains as a thick, continuous layer.
[This concludes] the commentary on the developed bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
287. "Well-proclaimed" (*supaññatta*) means well-made known or awakened by various modes, or established without confusion.
Since that awakening and establishment without confusion are, in meaning, nothing other than the teaching itself, he said "well-spoken" (*sukathita*).

"In the sense of succeeding" (*ijjhanatthena*) means in the sense of being accomplished; the meaning is: as the cause for reaching completion. "In the sense of a foundation" (*patiṭṭhānatthena*) means in the sense of a firm resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

*Iddhipāda* means a "basis for success" (*iddhipāda*); the meaning is "the means for the attainment of success. It is called a "basis" (*pāda*) because by means of it one goes to and reaches success, which is designated as successive excellence.
*Iddhi* means "it succeeds"; the meaning is that it is accomplished and brought forth.
A "basis for success" (*iddhipāda*) is simply success itself as a basis; the meaning is a "component of success. Thus, first, [regarding] "the four bases for success":

The meaning here should be understood as follows: "By way of being capable of producing psychic power" (*iddhipahonakatāya*) means by way of having the capacity for the accomplishment of psychic power.

"By way of being productive of psychic power" (*iddhivisavitāya*) means by way of having the fitness for the accomplishment of psychic power. For since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the prefix *vi-* combined with the word *su* has the sense of fitness;

or else, "productiveness" (*visavitā*) is the act of issuing forth (*visavanaṃ*) or proceeding. In this context, productiveness is the state of acting according to one's will. Therefore he said: "Again and again," and so forth.

"By means of the transformation of psychic power" (*iddhivikubbanatāya*) means by means of the transformative psychic power (*vikubbaniddhi*) for the purpose of assuming various forms. Therefore, he said: "Having made it manifold, for the sake of showing it.

According to this canonical passage: "When a bhikkhu, having made desire (*chanda*) the dominant influence, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—this is called concentration through desire (*chandhasamādhi*)," concentration dominated by desire is "concentration through desire."

It should be understood that the compound is stated here by eliding the word *adhipati*; however, it should be known that the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains it by showing the meaning of the term *adhipati*, stating:
"Concentration caused by desire, or concentration predominant in desire, is 'desire-concentration' (*chandasamādhi*).
Some say, "They are 'predominant' in the sense of being of the nature of energy (*vīriya*)," for [the term] is used to exclude conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) and so forth.
"Exertion" (*padhāna*) means grasping. Alternatively, it is called "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it constructs various specific qualities; thus, it refers to all energy (*vīriya*).

In this context, the term "exertion" is used to exclude anything other than that which accomplishes the four functions; its meaning is "that which has become primary" or "that which has become supreme.
However, because the fourfold energy is intended here, the plural number is employed. This is done by way of both individual and collective application.

The meaning of the "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) mentioned previously—which was stated here according to its application by taking the sense of being a "means" (*upāya*) and the sense of being a "constituent part" (*koṭṭhāsa*)—should be understood as follows:
it constitutes the state of being the agent (*kattā*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the acquisition of psychic powers (*iddhi*) that will be explained later;

or, in the case of the psychic power to be accomplished through the bases of psychic power such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth mentioned in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, it constitutes the state of being the agent-ic psychic power (*kattiddhibhāva*), as well as [the state of being the basis] for desire and the rest.
It should be understood that this was said with reference to the state of being the instrument (*karaṇa-iddhibhāva*).

Therefore, in the phrase "supernormal power (*iddhi*) in the sense of succeeding (*ijjhana*)," both the agentive sense (*kattuattha*) and the instrumental sense (*karaṇattha*) are taken together and stated.

To first show the agentive sense, he says, "in the sense of succeeding by way of accomplishment," and then, showing the other [the instrumental sense], he says, "by means of which they succeed," and so forth. Where was this said?
Where was it said? In the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga* discourse. "Of one who has become such" means of one who has become in that manner;

the meaning is: of one who stands having acquired those states beginning with desire (*chanda*). By the terms "the aggregate of feeling" and so forth, all four aggregates are spoken of, having included desire and the rest within them. "In the remaining ones" refers to the remaining bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

In the exposition of the basis of psychic power consisting in energy (*vīriyiddhipāda*), "endowed with energy, concentration, and the volitional formation of striving" (*vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*)—energy occurs twice.
Therein, the first is a qualification of concentration: "concentration dominated by energy is 'energy-concentration'";
the second shows the factor of being endowed [with it]. For indeed, in all cases there are only two factors of being endowed: concentration and the volitional formation of striving.
For while zeal (*chanda*) and the others are qualifiers of concentration, the formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) is qualified by the word "striving" itself and not by zeal and the rest;
thus, the predominance of energy (*vīriyādhipati*) is not stated here as a property of the formation of striving.
Furthermore, energy remains as it is after having qualified concentration, but it is mentioned by the term "formation of striving" specifically as a factor of possession (*samannāgama-aṅga*).

Nor is it said that there is an endowment with two kinds of energy. However, because concentration is distinguished by zeal (*chanda*) and the others, and because the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) and the remaining factors are associated with that very same [concentration] as thus distinguished, the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are taught by way of these qualifications of concentration.
And the state of being a qualification for zeal and the others is due to their being shown as the respective supports for that [concentration].

In the passage, “It becomes ‘the basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration due to desire’... [etc]... the basis for spiritual power,’” the word *pāda* (foot/basis) is used in the sense of a support;
thus, by way of being a means (*upāya*), desire and the others are said to be the bases for spiritual power (*iddhipāda*).

For this very reason, in the Abhidhamma, in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, it is stated that desire and the others alone are the bases for spiritual power, beginning with: “The four bases for spiritual power: the basis for spiritual power consisting of desire,” and so forth. [This is also stated] in the *Pañhapucchaka*.

Having given the summary by saying, “Here, monks, a bhikkhu [develops] the four bases for spiritual power (iddhipāda), beginning with ‘concentration through desire’ (chandasamādhi) and so forth,” the state of being wholesome and so on is again analyzed specifically for desire and the rest.
For it is precisely for the purpose of showing the basis-for-power as a means (upāya-iddhipāda) that the basis-for-power as a support (nissaya-iddhipāda) is shown;
otherwise, the fourfold nature would not exist. This is how the determination of the meaning should be understood here according to the text. Now—
The passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) was stated in order to explain and demonstrate the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) by way of their prior stages of acquisition;
that is indeed easy to understand. Since the discussion of the bases of psychic power has been presented here only in brief, he says: “But in detail... [as] stated.
“Some” refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. For among them, some say, “What is called psychic power (*iddhi*) is unproduced,” while others...
However, they say that "the basis for spiritual power (iddhipāda) is unestablished. "Unestablished" means not proven in the ultimate sense (paramattha), which is to say it does not exist.
It is "brought forth" because it was introduced from the Abhidhamma recitation into the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, since the teaching proceeds in a different manner than the previous method.
"The basis for spiritual power consisting of desire" (chandiddhipāda) is simply desire itself as the basis for spiritual power. This same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well. These...
"Paṇā" refers to the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) as they appear in this sutta. Regarding the statement, "The Elder Raṭṭhapāla...

produced the supramundane Dhamma," it is said that the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, thinking, "If there is desire, how could they not grant permission? refrained from eating for seven days, obtained his parents' consent, went forth, and by relying solely on desire, he realized the supramundane Dhamma. [This concerns] the Elder Soṇa.
Devoted to meditation and having aroused energy, Soṇa Thera did not slacken his effort even when boils broke out on his feet;
thus it is said, "Soṇa Thera made energy his primary burden. Sambhūta Thera, thinking, "What indeed cannot be accomplished by one who possesses the mind?
made the mind his precursor and attained success in meditation; thus it is said, "Sambhūta Thera made the mind his primary burden."
The Elder Mogga made investigation his primary task; therefore, the Blessed One spoke to him on the theme of emptiness, saying, "Regard the world as empty.
When questioned twice—both for the purpose of suppressing pride based on wisdom and for the purpose of encompassing it with wisdom—he explained the question.
Thus it was said: "The Venerable Moggarāja, having made investigation his primary task..."
The repeated generation of desire is like sending forth a messenger; thus, the resemblance of desire to a messenger is stated.
By the term "exertion" (*parakkama*), he speaks of the quality of courage (*sūrabhāva*); and the resemblance of energy (*vīriya*) to courage should be understood from its state of steadfastness.
Because thought (*citta*) is characterized by reflection, its resemblance to the formulation of a mantra is stated.
“Perfection of birth” means being of a distinguished lineage. In the passage, “Wisdom is the best among all things,” the similarity between investigation and perfection of birth is stated.

However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the similarity between the basis of psychic power consisting of mind and perfection of birth is applied, and the similarity between the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation and the power of spells is applied.

Because it has many kinds (*vidha*) as its constituent parts (*vihita*), it is called "of many kinds" (*anekavihita*); thus he said "of many kinds. The word *vidha* is a synonym for "division" (*koṭṭhāsa*), as in such passages as "the basis of knowledge in one way" (*ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu*); thus he said, "the mode of psychic power (*iddhividha*) means a division of psychic power (*iddhikoṭṭhāsa*).
288. Regarding the commentary on the attainment of the threefold opportunity:
"Of happiness"—this is a common term for all three types of happiness; thus he said, "of the happiness of jhāna and the happiness of the Path..."

"...of the happiness of the fruit. However, because access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are subordinate due to their not being various attainments (*appanā*), they are not included here.
Regarding the first two ways of attaining the opportunity, all three kinds of happiness are obtained; but how is it in the third?
In that case, while all three are indeed not obtained, two are certainly obtained according to what is actually attained.
This is what was said: as in the expressions “even a pebble or a stone,” “a school of fish, whether moving or stationary,” and so forth.
“Associated” (*saṃsaṭṭha*) means having entered into association, having become possessed of it;

furthermore, since he possesses those [qualities] in his mind, it is said “with a mind associated. “Noble state” (*ariyadhamma*) means the quality that produces the state of a noble one (*ariya*). “By way of means” (*upāyato*).

"By way of method" means by way of the path. "By way of cause" means by way of the reason. For that method by which the practice in accordance with the Dhamma occurs is called an *upāya* (means) because one approaches [the goal] by means of it; it is called a "path" (*patha*) because it is the state of the path for the attainment of that [goal], and it is called a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it is the instrument for that [attainment].
In order to explain in detail the meaning stated in brief as “one attends to it by way of ‘impermanent,’ etc.,” it was said: “What is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāro),” and so forth.
Therein, “skillful attention” (upāyamanasikāro) is the attention that serves as the cause for the arising of wholesome states.
“Path-attention” (pathamanasikāro) is the attention that constitutes the path to those very same states. “Impermanent” means having a beginning and an end, and not being eternal.
And the construction is: he brings to mind the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) belonging to the three planes as "impermanent" when they are impermanent.
This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. However, this is the distinction: because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, they are "suffering" in the sense of suffering;
because of the state of lacking mastery, they are "non-self" in the sense of non-selfhood; and because of the state of impurity, they are "ugly" (asubha). All of this...

Indeed, that which belongs to those planes (the fine-material and immaterial realms) is conditioned; because it drips with the impurities of the defilements, it deserves to be called "foul" (*asubha*) alone.

"In conformity with the truths" means by way of being in accordance with the realization of the truths. By the phrase "turning of the mind" and so forth, the occurrence of wholesome javanas at the mind-door, which had arisen prior to that [realization] and served as a condition for the adverting consciousness, is likewise stated by way of the designation for its fruit. Of that...

For by means of that [adverting], it becomes the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of the wholesome. Indeed, adverting is called "turning toward" (*āvaṭṭanā*) because it turns the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) back [toward the object].

It is called "repeated turning toward" (*anvāvaṭṭanā*) because it turns [the mind] back again and again. It is called "mental application" (*ābhoga*) because it bends (*ābhujati*) toward an object other than the object of the life-continuum.
It is called "attention" (*samannāhāra*) because it directs itself toward [the object]. That very same object, following after itself again and again...
It is called *manasikāra* because one attends to and establishes [the object] as it arises.
"This is said" means that this is called "wise attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*), characterized by skillful attention, by means of which a person is able to bring to mind the truths such as suffering.
"Unmixed" means not mixed with sensual desires and so forth, but secluded and separated from them. [It is the happiness] arising from the cause of being separated from sensual desires and the like.
It is called "the happiness born of seclusion" because it is the "happiness of the first jhāna.
Granted that the happiness of the first jhāna is indeed mental joy (*somanassa*), yet in the Suttas it is specifically termed "happiness" because it serves as a condition for bodily happiness;
thus, here too, the joy that constitutes the jhāna is called "happiness," while the other [ordinary] joy is not. Therefore it was said:
“‘Sukhā’ (pleasant): This is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause; thus he says, “by reason of the pleasure of jhāna.
“Successive joy” (*somanassa*) refers to the joy that arises repeatedly by way of reviewing and so forth, caused by the attainment of jhāna.

“Delighting” (*pamoda*) means one who delights; it is fresh rapture (*pīti*). From that, [it is] “delighted” (*pamuda*). In such passages as “joy (*pāmojja*) is for the purpose of rapture (*pīta*”), it is fresh rapture.
“Pāmojja” is said [to mean joy]; however, here what is intended is *pāmojja* as one who is intensely glad (*pakaṭṭha-muda*) and delighted (*pamuda*).
And since that is never found devoid of mental happiness (*somanassa*), it is stated as “powerful rapture and happiness” because of their inseparable connection.
With reference to its being the direct opposite of the jhāna, it is said, “having suppressed the five hindrances. But as for the jhāna itself...

It suppresses all defilements and all unwholesome states associated with that [state], and it remains having taken its own place because it cannot be overcome by opposing states. Therefore, "because of taking its place" means because it has obtained an opportunity;

or, it is an "opportunity" (okāsa) because it serves as the occasion for the attainment of the bliss of the Path and its Fruit. The attainment of this [bliss] is "attainment of the opportunity" (okāsādhigama).
On the other hand, "attainment of opportunity" (*okāsādhigama*) means that by means of this [breathing], one attains an opening or occasion.

By acknowledging the grossness of the applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) associated with inhalation and exhalation—due to their having the nature of form, their dependence on a single material basis, and their expansive quality—he said, "Let the bodily and verbal formations be coarse for now. This is because they are the opposites of those [subtler states].
But, not permitting the grossness of certain feelings and perceptions, he asked: "In what way are the mental formations gross?
The other stated the reason, "Because they have not been abandoned," and then explained that matter by saying, "The bodily formations... and so forth.
"Those" refers to the mental formations. Because the formations that have not been abandoned possess the characteristic of being present formations, they can be called "gross."

They are "arahants"; however, because those [fetters] have been abandoned, they are called "subtle. It is said that "having relied on what has been abandoned, those that are not yet abandoned are called 'gross'.
Because it is stated in the Pāḷi, "through the subsiding of bodily formations," it is said that "bliss" refers to the bliss of the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) of the fourth jhāna.
But because it is stated, "through the subsiding of mental formations," [it refers to the moment] "of one emerging from cessation."
It has been stated. It should be understood that the subsiding of verbal formations is established by the very subsiding of bodily formations. For this reason, it says: "The second... [etc.
...they are not mentioned separately. However, although they are established by implication in the text, the Teacher mentions them in their own form to make them clearly manifest.
For in the Noble Discipline, the exposition of the Abhidhamma does not consist merely in the elucidation of what is implied by the meaning.

Regarding the term "nature" (*pakati*): just as the suppression of the hindrances is the means for attaining the first jhāna, so too the suppression of pleasure and pain is the means for attaining the fourth jhāna;
thus it is said, "the fourth jhāna, having suppressed pleasure and pain. The rest is exactly according to the method explained below.

That which is "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) is so called because it should be avoided together with ignorance, lust, and the like; it is unwholesome (*akusala*). Because it lacks those [defilements], the wholesome (*kusala*) is "blameless" (*anavajja*).
Because it is to be practiced by one desiring one's own welfare and happiness, the wholesome is "to be cultivated" (*sevitabba*);
by contrast, the unwholesome is "not to be cultivated. That which is inferior due to its base nature is unwholesome; that which is excellent due to its superior nature is wholesome.
The three dyads beginning with "blameworthy" and so forth should be understood, as appropriate, by way of these wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
"All" refers to the entire collection of phenomena (*dhamma-jāta*) comprised by the four dyads as previously stated.
They are "dark and bright" respectively because they exist as opposites; they are "with counterpart and without counterpart" because they exist as non-duals.
Ignorance, which conceals the round of existence, is abandoned through the correct penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

From that very process, the knowledge of the path of Arahantship arises. "Happiness": thus, for one who has contemplated the phenomena of the three planes by way of the doors of kamma, has intensified insight, and is established in Arahantship according to the sequence of the paths, that which [is experienced]...

Both the bliss of the path of arahantship and the bliss of the fruit of arahantship are intended here by the term “bliss. They are indeed included [within this category] because they do not constitute an immediate obstruction (*ānantariya*).
“By way of the thirty-eight objects” means by way of the thirty-eight meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as they appear in the Canon. Having explained it in detail...
The intention is that [the suttas] are to be explained according to the first jhāna and so forth, as they have been handed down.

By the words "How" and so on, he demonstrates the method of explaining that very same subject in detail. Regarding the statements "In twenty-four places" and so forth, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the *Mahāparinibbāna-vaṇṇanā*.
By the phrase "having attained the attainment of cessation," the formless jhānas are also included therein.
Because it is impossible to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) without [the fourth jhāna], and because those [preliminary stages] have the same nature as the fourth jhāna.

"Ten access-concentrations" (*upacārajjhānāni*): excluding mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), there are the eight recollections (*anussati*) and the definition of perception (*saññāvavatthāna*);
these are the ten access-concentrations. That which is called "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) conduces to concentration; at its lowest limit, this is the first jhāna.
Regarding the "conclusion," it is said: "The training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) first attains the acquisition of the opportunity.
Higher mind (adhicitta) culminates in the fourth jhāna because the formless jhānas are included within it, and because the fruition jhānas have that as their conclusion;
thus it is said: "The second is the training in higher mind. The training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) that has reached its summit is the knowledge of the supreme path.

He said: "The training in higher wisdom is the third. Showing that when one extracts [the factors] for the attainment of the three opportunities by way of the three trainings, they should also be extracted according to the respective suttas as appropriate, he said, "In the *Sāmaññaphala* [Sutta]," and so forth.
And to the extent that the three trainings correspond respectively to the attainment of the three opportunities, to that same extent, because those [opportunities] are predominant—
In order to show that they belong to the three Piṭakas respectively, the words beginning with "But in the three" were spoken.
"Having analyzed the three Piṭakas" means: thinking, "We shall be able to explain by expanding upon the three Piṭakas in their proper sequence according to the attainment of the three opportunities.
"Having combined" means: having joined together the meaning stated therein with this sutta.
Having brought it into conformity with its actual state. Regarding the phrase "badly expounded":

one cannot say that it was "badly expounded" because of an incoherent discourse or an excessively prolix discourse, since such a mode of exposition is itself the very nature of a well-expounded teaching. Thus he said: "The Tipiṭaka... is well-expounded.
Commentary on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Catusatipaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)
289. The meaning of "wholesome" (kusala) should not be understood solely by way of the Abhidhamma method; rather, it should also be understood by way of the Bāhitika Sutta.
Thus he said, "And for one skilled in the fruit. "In the sense of security" means in the sense of being free from affliction by all four types of yokes.
"Well-composed" means well-composed both by way of serenity (samatha) and by way of insight (vipassanā). "One-pointed mind" means...
Because distraction has been cast far away, his mind has attained one-pointedness and non-distraction.

Being one whose mind is rightly concentrated within his own body by way of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), he— according to the statement, "One who is concentrated understands and sees things as they truly are"—
generates knowledge and vision therein, and [extends it] even to the bodies of others outside of himself.
He generates knowledge and vision. Therefore it was said: "He sends forth knowledge directed toward another's body.

"He becomes perfectly serene" means that, through the condition of perfect concentration and with serene confidence accompanied by knowledge, he settles his mind within upon his own body. "In all places" means in all instances.
The construction is: "mindfulness is spoken of. It is spoken of as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
Because of the commonality of both insight-knowledge (*anupassanā-ñāṇa*) and vision (*dassana*).
290. Regarding the description of the seven requisites for concentration:
"In this" refers to this discourse. Virtue is the axle of the jhānas, the wheel of energy, and the chariot of the Noble Path.
Because it is stated as being by way of its nature as an ornament, he says: "It is called an 'ornament' (alaṅkāra) and an 'accessory' (parikkhāra).

"By the seven city-accessories" means by these seven city-accessories: the moat dug around the city for protection, the rampart, the wall, the pillars, the crossbars, and the parapet on the wall. The fruit is accumulated.

By this, "equipment" (sambhāra) means the cause. For medicine is the cause for life through the subsiding of disease. "By way of equipment consisting of a retinue" means by way of equipment designated as a retinue.
For the path-factors beginning with right view are "equipment" because they equip and prepare right concentration by acting as its co-nascent and other conditions.
It is called an "accessory" (upanisā) because it is resorted to and depended upon.
"With its proximate cause" means "possessing a proximate cause" (*saupaniso*); here, the term "proximate cause" (*upanissayo*) refers to a collection of factors that act as a cooperative condition.
One whose view is rightly praised and beautiful is "one of right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*), referring to the person;
[the text says] "of that one of right view. Furthermore, because he is one in whom right view is firmly established, it is said:

“For one established in right view”: right intention arises. This means that while the right view of the Path performs its function of fully understanding suffering and so forth, it eradicates sensual thoughts and the like;
thus, right intention is capable of accomplishing its own task. To show how it proceeds in this way, he said: "right intention proceeds."

"This method applies to all instances" refers by extension to the remaining phrases, such as "Right speech arises for one with right intention," indicating that the aforementioned meaning applies there as well.
Furthermore, in this context, right view is of great benefit to the practitioner who has set out for the attainment of Nibbāna;
for it is described as "the lamp of wisdom" and "the sword of wisdom. By means of it, he dispels the darkness of ignorance.
By slaying the thieves of the defilements, one reaches the security of Nibbāna; therefore, in a discourse on the Noble Path, right view is taken first.
However, here, because the teaching is expressed by way of the individual, it is said, "of one with right view.
For the person possessing right view intends rightly through renunciation-intention and so forth, and not through wrong sensual intention and so forth.
Therefore, right intention arises for one who possesses right view. And because right intention is a prerequisite for right speech—as it has been said:

"Householder, having first thought and reflected, one subsequently utters speech"—therefore, right speech arises for one who possesses right intention. Furthermore, because [one first thinks], "I shall do this and that," first...

Having made an agreement by way of speech, those various tasks are for the most part properly undertaken; therefore, right speech is an aid to bodily action, and thus for one possessing right speech, right action arises.

Furthermore, it is only for one who abandons the fourfold misconduct of speech and the threefold misconduct of body, and fulfills both types of good conduct, that the morality consisting of the eight factors of livelihood exists.
It fulfills [the latter], but not the other; therefore, for one who possesses right speech and right action, right livelihood arises.
Because right effort arises from the application of wise attention to right livelihood—which has been perfected by purified view—right effort arises for one who possesses right livelihood.

For one who applies wise attention, mindfulness becomes well-established with respect to the four bases, namely, the body and so forth; thus, right mindfulness arises for one who possesses right effort.

Since mindfulness, when thus well-established, is able—after investigating the courses of those phenomena that are helpful or unhelpful to concentration—to settle the mind upon a single object, therefore right concentration arises for one who possesses right mindfulness.
And this method has been stated by way of the factors beginning with right view at various moments during the preliminary stage; however, at the moment of the path—

However, the meaning of such phrases as “for one of right view, right intention arises,” which are stated with respect to right view and the others by way of their mutual co-nascence and so forth, is appropriate;
and this alone is what is intended here. Therefore he says, “But this is the meaning,” and so on. Regarding “in the knowledge of the path”:
for one who stands in the knowledge included within the path—that is, for the possessor of that [knowledge]. For path-wisdom [is the wisdom] of the four truths...

In the sense of right seeing, it is called "right view of the path" (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*); that very same [view], because it knows and penetrates things as they truly are, is also called here "knowledge of the path" (*maggañāṇa*).
"Liberation by means of the path" (*maggavimutti*) refers precisely to the liberation from defilements through the path, which is their abandonment by means of eradication.

Right view of the fruit (*phalasammādiṭṭhi*) itself is called "right knowledge of the fruit" (*phalasammāñāṇa*) by way of a synonym; and this synonymous expression is to be understood according to the method already stated.
This should be understood. However, liberation through fruition (*phalavimutti*) should be seen as the abandonment consisting in subsidence (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).

"The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). That path, moreover, is "opened" because it has been well-expounded by humans—without the "teacher’s fist" (*ācariyamuṭṭhi*), without making anything subsequent or external [to the teaching]. "Disciplined in the Dhamma" means disciplined in the Noble Dhamma (*ariyadhamma*).
In this context, however, it should be understood by way of the eradication and discipline of the defilements; thus he said, "They have departed by means of the right departure.

Regarding the word *atthi*, which is an indeclinable particle referring to various objects—as in such passages as "there are head-hairs in this body"—he said, "And there are [defilements] in the non-returner.
For that very reason he said, "And there are indeed [some] in the once-returner. This refers to the external condition for the fetters.

It is called *puññabhāgā* because it possesses a portion of merit (*puññabhāga*) that serves as the cause for its arising; here, the sense of "possessing" (*atthi*) should be understood as being preeminent and distinguished.
"Possessing fear" (*ottappamānā*) means being afraid and trembling. He shows, however, that it is not non-existent, but indeed exists. (291) "Of him" (*assā*) refers to Vessavaṇa.

But he does not possess [theoretical] conviction (*laddhi*), because he has penetrated the Truths (*paṭividdhasacca*). By the phrase "there is no difference in the realization" (*abhisamaye viseso natthi*), he demonstrates that all the qualities of omniscience (*sabbaññuguṇa*) are exactly the same for all Buddhas.

292. Because the cause is of a single nature, these phrases—namely, not only the phrases beginning with “This, indeed, is the holy life” (tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ), but also the phrases beginning with “The yakkha Janavasabha [saw] this matter” (imamatthaṃ janavasabho yakkho)—are included.

This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meanings) on the commentary to the *Janavasabha Sutta*. 6. Commentary on the *Mahāgovinda Sutta* (Explanation of the Great Steward Sutta).
293. *Pañcakuṇḍaliko* means one who has five bamboo poles [as a carrying pole]. *Catumaggaṭṭhānesu* means at places where four roads intersect;
for halls and other structures built there are suitable for the use of people coming from the four directions.
By the phrase "such as these," he includes both the clearing of the foot of trees and so forth, as well as the giving of food and other gifts according to one's ability.
And he gathers merits. The reading is: “His personal existence was like a mass of gold—desirable, lovely, and pleasing.

“The measure of a thousand carts” means the measure of a thousand loads; a load (*vāha*) is twenty *khārīs*, a *khārī* is about sixteen *doṇas*, and a *doṇa* should be understood as sixteen *nāḷis*. A *kumbha* is ten *ambaṇas*. Some say it is “a thousand *nāḷis*. “A golden ear-ring of red gold.”
A crest-ornament made of red gold.
Because it is precisely during the middle watch that deities obtain the opportunity to approach the Teacher, it is said: "when one portion had passed.
*Atikkantavaṇṇo* means possessing an exceedingly beautiful form; or alternatively, *kevalakappaṃ* refers to the mind.
“Deficient” means the remainder, the slightly incomplete; for the entire Gijjhakūṭa monastery was illuminated by him, except for the area immediately surrounding the Blessed One.
Therefore he said, “Like the moon,” and so forth. This concludes the commentary on the assembly hall of the devas.
294. “By the outflow of the gift of a peak made of trees the size of a *ratana*”:
this means by the outflow of the merit from giving a peak made of trees measuring a *ratana*, or by way of the result of that merit’s outflow.

“In the hall where the assembly was convened” means in the meeting hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) that had been constructed. “Made of gems” means made of gems such as ruby (*padumarāga*). “Bolts” refers to the bolts used for fastening the lion-figures and other ornaments on the pillars, beams, joints, and so forth.
"Gandhabba king" means the king of the deities belonging to the Gandhabba realm.
Since he places before him those Cātumahārājika deities who dwell near the Tāvatiṃsa gods, it is said that "he sits having placed the deities of two divine worlds in front.
This same method applies to the other three instances as well.
“Nāgarāja” means the lord of the *nāgas*, but he is not himself of the *nāga* species.
It is called an “āsana” because one sits (*āsati*) or dwells (*nisīdati*) upon it; thus, he says “a place to sit,” meaning a place for sitting.
The word “ettha” is merely a particle, or alternatively, it refers to the reading “etasmiṃ. What should be stated according to the method of extracting the meaning has been explained previously.
It is indeed fourfold. The Tāvatiṃsa devas and certain Cātumahārājika devas, for the sake of stabilizing their attained prosperity and for purification in the future, observe the five precepts;
they perform the inclusion of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for the purpose of purifying him.
Therefore it is said: "At the Great Invitation," and so forth.
"A thousand years" means a thousand years by human reckoning.
