"With fallen leaves" means with leaves that have dropped. "Where small buds have appeared" (*khārakajāto*):
those very small buds which are deep blue in color are called "buds" (*khāraka*). "Where a network has appeared" (*jālakajāto*) refers to those same small buds.
“Jātajālako” means he has become entirely like a net; some, however, explain the meaning as “he has become like a single net.

It is said that when the Pāricchattaka tree is being pruned, it becomes covered in sprouts on every side, and those sprouts are brilliantly radiant with the color of glowing coral; thus, it shines forth completely.
It stands. "Born as a bud" means a great calyx has formed. "Born as a bud" (in the sense of a *koraka*) means the state of having just begun to open after the needle-like [petals] have emerged.
"In full bloom" means blossomed and fully opened in every respect.
"The wind that shears" refers to the wind that cuts the flowers due to the condition of the meritorious deeds of the devas. "Shears" means it cuts.
"The receiving wind" means the wind that receives the flowers as they are cut one after another.
"Dancing" means performing a dance by way of arranging various kinds of ornamentation. "Of certain deities" refers to deities who are not well-known by name or clan.
"A mass of dust" means a collection of dust. "Striking the pinnacle" means having struck the summit of the Sudhamma Hall.
"Eight days" is said with reference to the four days in a fortnight together with the fifth.

Since the hearing of the Dhamma was held regularly on those aforementioned eight days, the phrase "the non-seasonal hearing of the Dhamma was caused to be held" refers to what was arranged for other occasions.
A "canopy-railing" (*chattavedikā*) is a railing to be constructed beneath a canopy at a cetiya.
A *puṭavedikā* is a railing that should be constructed by enclosing the *cetiya* and including within it the place where circumambulation (*padakkhiṇakaraṇa*) takes place.
A *kucchivedikā* is a railing that should be constructed by enclosing the interior of the *cetiya* and being connected to it.
A *sihāsana* is a seat with lion-shaped legs. A *sīhasopāna* is a staircase provided with lion figures on both sides.
They were joyful because they were free from partiality. For this very reason, it says, “having placed those of great merit at their head,” and so forth.

It should be understood that they had assembled for the purpose of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), based on the statement: “On that very Uposatha day, the fifteenth, when the night of the full moon was complete, [they gathered] for the invitation.
(295) “By nine reasons” refers to the nine qualities beginning with Arahatship, as stated in the passage: “Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Worthy One,” and so forth.

By means of the reasons that illustrate the majesty of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "and of the Dhamma," the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
thus, showing the meaning as it is thus combined, he said: "and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha, which is distinguished by its straight practice, and so forth.
This is the exposition of the eight kinds of praise according to reality (*yathābhūta-vaṇṇanā*).

296. Just as "infinite" (ānañca) is indeed "the infinite" (ananta), and "medicine" (bhesajja) is indeed "a physician" (bhisakka), so too "as-it-is-ness" (yathābhūta) is indeed "as-it-truly-is-ness" (yathābhucca);
thus it was stated in the Pāḷi. Therefore he said: "As-it-truly-is-ness means as-it-is-ness. Because they are to be praised and extolled, they are "praises" (vaṇṇā), that is, qualities (guṇā).
"How has he practiced? refers to the state of the cause, the state of the fruit, and the state of being of benefit to sentient beings.
In all three stages, there is a request born of the desire to speak regarding the practice of the Lord of the World for the welfare of many beings.
Thus, showing it in brief from the beginning until the conclusion, he said: "At the feet of Dīpaṅkara," and so forth.
Therein, *abhinīharamāno* means making an aspiration (*abhinīhāra*). Furthermore, regarding that which is here [concerning] the Great Aspiration and the perfections (*pāramīs*)...
And that which ought to be said has already been stated in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā*; therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.

The passage beginning with "At the time of the ascetic Khantivādin" and so forth is an exposition of the practice for the welfare of many people—a practice that is extremely difficult to perform and not shared by others—precisely at the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*).
That intended benefit and happiness cannot be accomplished without such action.
To show that this [practice] also has that same purpose, it was said: "Even while remaining in the Tusita heaven for the full span of his lifespan," and so forth.
Furthermore, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma and other such acts constitute a practice for the welfare of many beings once they have been accomplished.

Even the relinquishing of the life-force constitutes a practice for the welfare of many beings, in the sense of having resolved, "I shall remain for this much time. Regarding the Nibbāna-element without residue...

The practice for the welfare of many people is by way of final *parinibbāna*. Therefore he said, “As long as she...,” and so forth. “The remaining phrases” refers to the phrases beginning with “for the happiness of many people.
“The last” refers to the triad of phrases: “for their welfare, for their benefit, for their happiness. “Of the former” refers to the triad of phrases preceding that.
“Meaning” (*attha*) refers to the description of the goal (*attha*).
Even if there were teachers endowed with past factors, they too were indeed Buddhas;
thus, in substance, our Teacher is none other. Therefore he said: "In the past, we do not see anyone other than a Buddha.
And just as it was in the past, so it will be in the future—this meaning being understood through the method of inference—it is said: "In the future, too, we do not see anyone [other than a Buddha]."
But Sakka, the king of the gods, having established that matter as a settled fact, said, "But not now.
Having raised the inquiry, "What does Sakka mean when he says this?"—that is, having initiated the investigation:

"When he says, 'I do not see even in the past,' what is Sakka saying?"—it is because there were Buddhas in the past and there will be Buddhas in the future that this [present] matter is not [the same].
“Understood by Sakka, the king of the gods” means that they were understood by our Blessed One as well, through his commonality with the Buddhas;
however, since there is now no other [Buddha] whatsoever, it is said thus to show this. The phrase “at present” (*etarahi*) and so forth was stated for that purpose. “Well-expounded, etc.
refers to the words beginning with “well-expounded” (*svākkhāta*). “Wholesome, etc. refers to the words beginning with “this is wholesome” (*idaṃ kusalaṃ*).
"Even though the waters of the Ganges and Yamunā are of different colors at the place where they have not yet met, they become of one color at the place of their confluence";
thus he said, "It blends and unites even in color. It is said that there, the water of the Yamunā is indeed identical to the water of the Ganges.
Just as Nibbāna is utterly pure because it is undefiled by any defilement, so too is the path leading to Nibbāna.
Because it is unsullied by any defilement, it must be regarded as utterly pure. Therefore he said, “Not indeed,” and so forth.
By that sense of purity which makes Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna comparable to space, he stated that they are unstained and untainted by anything, saying:
“Even space is unattached and pure. Now, regarding this meaning:
The phrase beginning with "of the moon and sun" was spoken in order to demonstrate by way of illustration what has been made clear.
It "accords" (saṃsandati) and "fits" (yujjati) because of the mutual suitability between the practice to be undertaken and the actual undertaking.

"Of those established in the practice" (paṭipadāya ṭhitānaṃ) means of those who are engaged in the practice of the path. "One who has lived it" (vusitavataṃ) refers to the dwelling in the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa).
“Of those who have lived [the holy life]” refers to these [disciples]. “Having found companions” means having found companions by way of these practices.

Regarding the duties to be performed for the Teacher by his disciples here and there, this statement beginning with “without a second,” which appears in other discourses, is spoken in the sense of being peerless compared to others, not because of an absence of companions such as those previously mentioned. “Having driven away” means having removed or avoided.

The word “driving away” (*apanujjā*) contains an implicit restriction; because that removal is absolute, it is stated as “driving away indeed” (*apanujjeva*). “Gain” (*lābha*) means that which is obtained;
however, that gain is especially distinguished by the knowledge of its superior course and is intended here specifically as being vast, hence he says, “a great gain has arisen.
“Arising from the outflow of abundant merit” means arising from the overflow of very extensive and most sublime merit accumulated during the aforementioned period.
"Reborn!"—thinking, "These have been reborn; beyond this, there is no further space for me," he arose, increasing higher and higher as if filled with enthusiasm.

For indeed, great twin-clouds having arisen in all directions, as if all the perfections (pāramīs) had gathered together like a great cloud, thinking, "We shall give our fruition in a single existence," [produced] this gain, honor, and fame for the Blessed One.

They brought forth [offerings], and then the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others, with food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, approached and sought out the Blessed One, asking:
"Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods? Where is the Bull among Men? Where is the Lion among Men?
Even after bringing provisions by the hundreds of wagons, they were unable to find space on all sides.
Even for a distance of a *gāvuta*, they stand pressing against one cart’s yoke with the yoke of another, and follow along, just like the Brahmins of Andhakavinda and others.
All of this should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Khandhaka* and in various *Suttas*.
Therefore he said: “Gain and honor are like a great flood,” and so forth.

"Successive meal" (*paṭipāṭibhatta*) refers to the meal that must be given in successive order when many people have risen up according to the sequence they brought when saying, "We shall give a gift.
It reached its peak because that gift was not shared with others. He explained a stratagem to the citizens so that they might be made to give a gift in a manner impossible for others to emulate.
The *sālakalyāṇī* trees were under royal protection and were not shared by others; therefore, [he spoke] of their footprints.
A pavilion was constructed, and since the elephants—which were royal treasures—could not be obtained by the citizens, they had a sunshade held over them;
likewise, service was performed by daughters of the kṣatriyas.
The phrase "five hundred seats" is said with reference to those arranged in the Sālakalyāṇī pavilion, but many more were arranged outside of it.
He ground the four kinds of fragrant scents for the purpose of honoring the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and also for the purpose of polishing the alms-bowl.
"Water" refers to the water used for washing the bowl. They were priceless because they were composed of priceless gems.

"His head shall split into seven pieces" means due to such causes as disrespect. "I shall look upon him black" means I shall regard him as black; the meaning is that I shall avoid the harm that would arise for him.

"Kadariyā" refers to those who are stubbornly stingy and averse to meritorious deeds; they do not go to the world of the devas because they have failed to perform merit and because their state of stinginess leads them toward evil.
"Bālā" refers to those endowed with the characteristics of fools, such as thinking ill-thought thoughts and so forth;
they do not praise giving, nor are they even able to bear praising it. "Dhīro" refers to one endowed with wisdom, possessing noble insight, and [superior] to others.

Even by merely rejoicing in a gift given—by that very act of rejoicing in the gift—one becomes happy in the next world (*paraloka*), meaning one comes to possess physical and mental happiness in the hereafter.
At that time, there was a certain kshatriya named Vararoja; [the verse] "blameless...
and so forth intends to show that [such merit] would bear fruit even for one who speaks what is not true. [This was said] with two thousand five hundred and thirty additional verses.
He spoke only of their beauty because of his attachment to physical form.
Regarding the phrase "as far as the khattiyas" (*yāva maññe khattiyā*): here, *yāva* is a word denoting a limit or boundary; *aññe* is a mere particle;
the intended meaning is "all gods and humans, taking the khattiyas as the limit. Therefore he said: "the khattiyas..."
“Brahmins,” and so forth. “Intoxicated and heedless” means being both heedless through the intoxication of gain, honor, and fame, and heedless by way of the negligence that follows from it.

“In accordance with that” means following after that very thing. “Speech... meets” means that verbal and bodily actions are not mutually contradictory; rather, they flow together in harmony. “Goats and deer” means *ajāmigā*; those are the goats and deer.
“One who has crossed beyond doubt” means one who has entirely transcended the wilderness of doubt. But are not all stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) also ones who have crossed beyond doubt?
"And free from doubt"? This is true; however, this was not said with reference to one who has merely crossed over doubt in such a limited sense.
Rather, it is said with reference to that which has been entirely eliminated by means of the decisive certainty known as the comprehension of all aspects regarding every dhamma to be known.
Demonstrating this, he said, "For just as... and so forth. "In an ever-increasing degree" means according to their relative priority.
And this meaning is also established by the Blessed One’s power of knowledge regarding the many elements and various elements.

He is free from doubt in all respects because he possesses the state of seeing everything. Because he has penetrated all ultimate phenomena by means of the realization of the Truths, it is said, "by way of conventional usage," which means by way of names, clans, and so forth.
“With his purpose fulfilled” means that his desires have been entirely brought to completion. Now, one might raise the objection:

“Is it not the case that for the Noble Ones, the state of having a fulfilled purpose consists in the accomplishment of the sixteen tasks and the performance of what was to be done, rather than in the awakening to all knowable phenomena? With reference to this challenge, he says:
“In things previously unheard,” and so forth. For, just as disciples possess the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), so too do the Pacceka-buddhas.

And just as the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment), so too the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones is preceded by the full awakening to the Four Truths.
"In what has not been heard from others" (*ananussutesu*) means not heard from others. By the two words [“not heard” and “from others”], he shows that it is without the voice of another.
"Therein" (*tattha*) is the locative case used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "as the cause for the full awakening to the Truths. Full awakening to the Truths (*saccābhisambodho*).

And it should be understood as being by way of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). Regarding "mastery over the powers" (*balesu vasībhāva*): this refers to the manifestation of the ten powers of knowledge according to one's wish.
"Because he is born, he is called 'the Born'" (*jātattā jāto*)—this is said of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).
297. Dwelling in settled residence here and there, such as in royal capitals and other places; wandering on tour through the three regions at the appropriate times.
298. *Assā* means of the fruit. *Taṃ* means the cause. There is no cause for the simultaneous arising of even two [Buddhas], much less three or four.
The passage beginning with “And here” (*ettha ca*) is commenced for the purpose of showing the measurement and boundaries of the world-system mentioned as “one world-system” (*ekissā lokadhātuyā*).
*Yāvatā* means by whatever extent of space. *Pariharanti* means they revolve while encircling Sineru. *Disā* means directions.
"In the directions": this is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative. "Shine" means they gleam. "Radiating" means shining forth;

or alternatively, the moon and sun, being radiant or beautiful, shine, and because of that, the directions also shine. "As many as a thousandfold" means a world-system of that extent consisting of a thousand worlds.

"So much" refers to ten thousand world-systems, taking this very world-system as the center along with itself. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the *Mahāpadāna-vaṇṇanā*. "It is not discerned" because it is not included within the Three Piṭakas.

Commentary on the Story of Sanaṅkumāra: 300. *Vaṇṇena* means by way of perfection of form (*rūpasampatti*). Because it is easily understood, he does not comment on that term, but rather explains the meaning of the word *yasas* (fame). *Alaṅkāraparivārena* means both by way of ornaments and by way of retinue.

*Puññasiriyā* means by the power of merit (*puññiddhi*). 301. *Sampasādana* means producing confidence (*sampasādajanane*). The root *khā*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, has the sense of "knowing," as in such passages as "having reckoned this, he partakes. Therefore, he says: "Having known, we rejoice."
The Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Govinda (304).
Regarding the phrase "for as long as a long time": this indicates an immeasurable duration; thus he said, "so much... [etc. ... for an exceedingly long time.
"That Blessed One was indeed of great wisdom"—this refers to the inquiry for consent made by that Brahmā to the devas.
Showing that it has been said [thus], he said: "How do you conceive of this: 'The Blessed One is indeed one of great wisdom'?
The connection is that, desiring to answer this question himself, he spoke the words beginning with "In the past, sir.
By answering in this way, he shows that this meaning is also expressed in substance; thus he said, "This is not surprising," and so forth. Of the three...
“Māras” refers to the Māras of defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of a deva (*devaputta*).
Having already stated that “this is not wonderful,” it is stated again as a conclusion, “What is wonderful here?
A *purohita* is one who stands before a king, providing for his welfare in both the present life and the future life, by arranging matters ahead of time.
He said: "The domestic chaplain is the one who oversees all duties. By "the consecration of Govinda" is meant the consecration for his installation in the position of Govinda;
it is said that this was a rank inherited through the lineage of that brahmin family. "Because of the brilliance of his weapons" means because of the radiance of his arms.
"By reason of his capacity to protect" means by reason of his capacity to protect the king and the immeasurable multitude of beings from harm.

"Having properly relinquished" means having thoroughly surrendered and handed over [the property] out of a sense of respect for him. "One who sees the purpose" (*atthadaso*) means one who perceives each respective purpose or duty.
"Bhava" means growth or increase; or, it is "bhava" because one grows by means of it.
The letter *m* is inserted by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), and by changing the vowel *o* to *a*, it is stated as "bhavamatthu. [He addressed] the venerable Jotipāla.
However, since the term for the genitive sense (*sāmi-attha*) is used in the accusative case, he said "of you" (*bhoto*).
"Do not reject" means do not refuse; since that refusal constitutes a reply, he said "do not speak back.
"You were capable" means you were competent in the arrangement of tasks, thus he said "having arranged. [He attained] various states of existence and wisdom.
He found and obtained it, thus he is Govinda; he is a great Govinda, thus Mahāgovinda. For "go" is a designation for wisdom (*paññā*);
it goes toward meanings and awakens to them.
Commentary on the Distribution of the Kingdom.

306. "Ekapitikā vemātukā kaniṭṭhabhātaro" means younger brothers who have the same father but different mothers. "This one has been consecrated" refers to this Prince Reṇu, who was consecrated in the kingdom upon the passing of his father. "Those who make him king" are those who establish the prince in the kingship. 307.

Regarding "madentīti madanīyā," he says "causing intoxication" (*madakarā*) while showing that the word is formed with an agentive suffix (*kattusādhanata*). Furthermore, since causing intoxication is a specific cause for negligence (*pamāda*), it is stated as "causing negligence" (*pamādakarā*).

308. Having been only about ten *gāvutas* wide near the kingdom of Reṇu, they later became three hundred *yojanas* wide; thus he established all six kingdoms in the shape of a wagon (*sakaṭamukha*). Because of their squareness, they were like canopies (*vitāna*). 310.
In the verse beginning with *saha*, it is stated for the purpose of completing the metrical line. In explaining its meaning, he said, "together with him" (*teneva saha*).
Alternatively, *saha* is a particle used in the sense of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); it should be construed as "those seven Bhāradvājas were together (*saha*) [with him]. By that...
This explains that while dwelling in different locations, they exist together in a variegated manner and are inseparable.
They are "bearers of the burden" (*bhāradhā*) because they bear, place upon themselves, and carry the burden of sovereignty.
The commentary on the first recitation section is concluded.
311. "He appointed him as the domestic chaplain" means he appointed him after making him the domestic chaplain, or he appointed him to the position of domestic chaplain.
With reference to one who listens three times, it is said: "three times a day. This refers to listening at two junctions [of the day].

Having spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), it was said: "In the evening or in the morning. "From that time onwards" means from the moment he had brought his practice of ascetic observances (*vatacariyā*) to its culmination and bathed.
312. "He rose up" means he emerged; he arose. "Without reflecting" means [without thinking], "How indeed shall I [behave] together with the Brahmā?"...
"Should speak" means without even thinking about it, without generating such a thought; thus, because there was no meeting at all, he did not address him.

"Having seen that" means having seen with the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu) that cultivation of the divine abode of compassion (karuṇā-brahmavihāra), which is the means for attaining the vision of Brahmā. 313.
"Thus" means having informed the king in this way, [the king] entered seclusion. "In all cases" means in all six [cases].
On the occasions of taking leave of the khattiyas, the seven wealthy brahmins, the seven hundred dancers, and his forty wives.
Regarding the term "of equal status," he said it means "equal in birth," as in "of the same complexion and the same caste."
317. “Santhāgāra” means a dwelling for steadying the mind by means of attention to meditation (*jhāna-manasikāra*), through the calming of discursive thoughts that have proliferated outwardly;

the meaning is a hall of meditation (*jhāna-sālā*). “Already grasped” means they were indeed grasped by the Great Being through the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā-anuyoga*) by way of their arising within the continuum of his own mind.
There is no [need for further effort] because they have already been suppressed by meditation itself. For, specifically, by means of his compassion...
Because it has been developed, there is no dissatisfaction or longing; because loving-kindness (*mettā*) has been developed, there is no fear or agitation.
"Longing" refers to the exertion toward the vision of Brahmā, while "agitation" refers to the yearning for that [vision]; thus he said, "But as for Brahmā," and so forth.
*Commentary on the Dialogue with Brahmā*

318. *Cittutrāso* means merely the frightening of the mind. In what manner? By way of the names, clans, and so forth of the dwelling places where the classes of beings reside. Therefore he said, "In what [manner]," and so on.
*So* indicates that among those Brahmās well-known and famous in the world by the names Panaka, Sanantana, Bandhu, Satana, and Sanankumāra, he is one named Sanankumāra.
*Agghaṃ* refers to the food to be given to those worthy of honor. *Madhusākā* refers to sweet food—whatever is offered to a guest.
He speaks thus because food must be given by way of hospitality. Therefore he says, "But the honey-vegetables," and so forth.
"We ask" means we ask by way of invitation. 319.
Although the Great Being remained having developed the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), [he considered] among them, "the path to companionship with Brahmā."
He said "one who is doubtful" because of his lack of certainty. However, some say:

"Because his body was exhausted by ascetic practices, and because he had fallen away from the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) that he had merely attained due to the arising of fear and other emotions during the assembly of the Brahmās, he said 'one who is doubtful' because of his unarrested state of doubt.
What is known through another's experience is "known by another"; these [states] were manifest to him.
He said, “They are manifested in what is evident to others and known by others. He stated the reason for this: “Because they are constructed by another.
Regarding “mine,” *mamaṃkāro* is the act of making something one’s own; he explained it as “possessiveness” (*mamatta*) with the words, “This is mine...
[etc. ...craving. For it is by means of this that one makes it “mine,” hence it is *mamaṃkāro*; craving functions in that same way. “Among men” (*manujesu*) is used in the sense of specification.
He said, "Whosoever among men," because it does not refer to the earth-dwelling spirits (*bhummā*).
First, showing the meaning of the word "become solitary" (*ekodibhūto*), he said "become one" (*ekībhūto*); then, explaining that further, he said, "standing alone, sitting alone.
"Such a one" means one who proceeds having become alone. "Became" (*bhūto*) means born. "Resolve upon jhāna" (*jhāne adhimutti*) refers to when that [jhāna] has been produced.
"How can there be resolve if [the jhāna] has not been produced?"—to this he says: "The meaning is 'having produced jhāna.
"Foul odor" (*vissagandha*) refers to the permeation by defilements such as anger; thus, by suppressing those, one is "devoid of foul odor.
"In these states" refers to the states of the renunciants, such as seclusion, compassion, and the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
320. "Avidvā" means one who does not know. "Āvaritā" means obstructed by the prevention of the arising of wholesome superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
"Pūtikā" means become putrid through such things as a corrupted mind; they emit a foul odor or a stench due to the defilements (*kilesa*).
Because they have the nature of being reborn in the woeful states (*apāya*) such as hell, he says "those who go to the woeful states" (*apāyūpagā*). [The text continues: "By thieves... and so forth.
For one who wishes to enter but is beset [by obstacles], just as a city is enclosed by walls, gates, and moats, the Brahma-world would be shut off and barred by anger and the like;
thus it is called "the Brahma-world shut off" (*nivuta-brahmaloka*). He asks, saying, "By what is it blocked?
False speech itself is *mosavajja* (the fault of lying), just as medicine itself is *bhesajja* (the remedy). Being angry is being corrupt. Regarding "seen," etc.:
Deceiving others by claiming to have seen what one has not seen and so forth is "deception of others.
Enticing by showing something similar or appropriate is "deceiving by showing a likeness. Betraying friends is "breaking of intimacy" (*mittabhedo*) or "treachery toward friends" (*mittadubbhanam*).
Excessive stinginess is "rigid avarice. Transcending the inferiority or even the equality that exists within oneself—
*Maññanaṃ*: conceit. *Khīyanaṃ*: intolerance of the success of others and disparagement. *Vivicchā*:
because it possesses various desires and inclinations through the concealment of one’s own success and through the inability to endure sharing with others. *Mudukaṃ macchariyaṃ*:
a mild form of stinginess due to miserliness. *Yattha katthaci*: "in whatever [place]" refers to that which belongs to oneself, that which belongs to another, and that which is inferior or similar.
"Upon some object": the grasping of an object, its seizing, and its coveting.
"Intoxication" (*majjana*) is the exhilaration and exultation by way of lying on beds and so forth. "Delusion" (*muyhana*) is the non-comprehension of the object.

"In these"—that is, in these aforementioned defilements such as anger and the rest, which are designated as *kilesas* (defilements) because they soil, afflict, and torment the continuum of sentient beings, and which are evil states.
"Joined, thoroughly joined, associated, and not separated.
Herein, this Brahmā, having been well-queried by the Great Being regarding the "stench of raw flesh," explained his own evil states as they appeared to him by analyzing them through fourteen terms;
and although these were spoken with reference to such a particular mode of occurrence, [they apply here].
Furthermore, some [faults] have been mentioned; however, although some have been mentioned in the *Āmagandha-sutta*, they are not mentioned here at all.

Nevertheless, by way of the method of applying characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*) or because they belong to the same category (*tadekaṭṭhatā*), their inclusion here should be understood. Therefore he said, "But this sutta," and so forth.
In that context, "having illustrated by means of the *Āmagandha-sutta*" refers even to those odors of raw flesh (*āmagandha*) which are not explicitly stated here in their own form.

Having explained by means of the *Āmagandha-sutta* through such factors as their having a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇatā*), it should be discussed there, because they are described there in their own specific forms (*sarūpato*).
The *Āmagandha-sutta* should also be illustrated by this [present text], because some of the "stench-conditions" (*āmagandha*) mentioned here are not mentioned there.
This is because the "stench-conditions" mentioned in the *Āmagandha-sutta*, though stated there, are included here in terms of their meaning (*atthato*).

They go to the assembly; therefore, when explaining what is stated here by way of avoidance, since some things—even though they do not have the intrinsic nature of defilements according to the Abhidhamma method—deserve to be called "defilements" in the sense of afflicting the continuum of a being, it is said: "among the fourteen defilements."
He said, "They must be stripped away and abandoned," meaning they must be withered and cast off. "The lineage of the Buddhas" (buddhatanī) refers to the succession of those destined for Buddhahood;
even those destined for Buddhahood are called "Buddhas," just as it is said, "The Buddha went to Rājagaha.
"Having performed the strengthening of the Great Being's resolve" means having strengthened the arising of the thought in the Great Being, "I shall go forth into homelessness."
Commentary on the Address to Reṇurāja: 321.
“Having captivated my mind” means having drawn away my consciousness, not allowing it to turn back under his influence.
“Having dwelt having attained a state of solitude” means having attained a state of solitude through the cultivation of physical seclusion, by means of ascetic practice.
"Of one who has emerged. "Covered with bamboo leaves" means it was strewn all around the platform with mats of bamboo leaves.
"Without a scar" means a wound, or a state of being scarred like a wound, is absent. Therefore he said, "without roughness.
The commentary on the invitation of the six khattiyas.
322. "We shall train" means we shall cause [others] to train; and since training here consists in bringing about existence [of virtue], he said, "we shall encourage.

323. Regarding those who, due to the absence of the exertion of energy and the power of patience, do not possess a complete and pure ascetic practice (samaṇadhamma) even though they have gone forth—for the sake of enjoining them to those respective instances of the exertion of energy and the power of patience, it was said, "Exert yourselves," and so forth.
“The path of the jhāna of compassion” means the path known as the jhāna of compassion. “The straight path” means the path that has become straight for the purpose of reaching the Brahma-world.
“Unsurpassed” means supreme by virtue of its nature as a sublime abode (brahmavihāra). Therefore he said, “It is called the highest path.
“Guarded by the good” means protected and preserved by the virtuous so that no decline occurs, through the removal of opposing factors.

Regarding the reading “*saddhammo sabbhi vakkhito*,” some recite it thus; for them, the meaning is that the True Dhamma was spoken and proclaimed by the virtuous ones—the Buddhas and others—by means of accomplishing the welfare of both themselves and others.
“*Taṅkhaṇaviddhaṃsanadhamman*” means that at the very moment there is a conjunction with a contrary state, at that very moment [it is destroyed].

It has the nature of perishing; or rather, it has the nature of perishing because the moment of its occurrence is exceedingly brief, being swifter even than the meeting of the sharp edges of the hooves of the sons of the gods (devaputta), who are fond of racing, as they run headlong against one another from top to bottom.
Of that life—its "course" means its end. They reflect upon it.
He said, "it should be deliberated upon," because it was stated that "they should deliberate. Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental;

thus, this locative in "mantāyaṃ" should be understood in the sense of the instrumental, as in "ñātāyaṃ. "In all impediments" means in all obstructions and hindrances to the performance of wholesome deeds.
This concludes the commentary on the invitation of the wealthy brahmins and others.
324. "Of little authority" means "of little power," as he said in the passage beginning with "from the time of his going forth.
He was held in high esteem like a universal monarch (cakkavatti-rāja).
This concludes the commentary on the Great Steward’s (Mahāgovinda) going forth.
328. "The thorough understanding of the attainments" means direct personal experience; it is realization (*sacchikiriyā*). Thus he said, "They were not able to produce them.

329. "By this" refers to the phrase "we remember. For when the Great Brahmā spoke the words "we remember," the Blessed One assented by saying "it is exactly so," and thus it became established as such.
It was not for the sake of inducing world-weariness regarding the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Because there is no discourse on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, and because in the absence of the round [of existence] there can be no possibility of disenchantment or dispassion, he said, "not for the sake of dispassion," and so forth.
This is solely for the purpose of becoming thoroughly disenchanted with the round, by way of discerning the danger in the round of manifold modes and aggregates.
By the word "for the sake of disenchantment" (*nibbidāya*), insight (*vipassanā*) is expressed. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. This is the discourse on defining.
Having defined insight, the path, and Nibbāna by means of their respective terms, this is the discussion here according to the non-figurative method (*nippariyāya*);
thus he said, "But figuratively (*pariyāyena*), however," and so forth.
330. "To fulfill" means to make complete by way of the fulfillment of development (*bhāvanā*); the sense is "to produce. "Of clansmen who have practiced the holy life (*brahmacariya*)"—
With the expression "of clansmen who have practiced the holy life," he concludes the teaching by means of the highest description, namely the pinnacle of Arahantship.
"Abhinandana" (rejoicing) means acceptance, as in such passages as "they rejoice at what has come";
here, in terms of meaning, it is the mind's gladness, thus he says, "having rejoiced by accepting with the mind. "Excellent, excellent!"...
"Rejoicing with speech" means expressing approval; thus it says, "rejoicing with speech and having expressed approval.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāgovinda-sutta*. 7.
Commentary on the *Mahāsamaya-sutta*.

**Commentary on the Introduction (Nidānavaṇṇanā)** 331. Regarding the term *udāna*: it refers to the inspired utterance (*udāna*) set forth by King Okkāka for the purpose of preventing the confusion of castes.

As for the statement that even a single province may be called "Sakka" by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*), whatever is to be said on this matter has already been explained in the commentary on the *Mahānidānasutta*.
It should be understood according to the method already stated. "Laid down" means laid down by someone.
"With a barrier" means with a bridge. "Having had it bound" means having had a rampart made firm with sand, chaff, stones, lumps of clay, and so forth.
To make clearer the point briefly stated as "they increased their quarrel by provoking a dispute," the passage beginning with "the Koliyan workmen said" was spoken.

"Three Jātakas" refers to the Phandanajātakam, the Pathavī-undriyajātakam, and the Laṭukikajātakam. "Two Jātakas" refers to the Rukkhadhammajātakam and the Vaṭṭakajātakam. "By him" means by the Blessed One.
"The state of being a cause for quarrel" means the existence of a cause for quarreling.

"In an improper place" means without a valid reason. "Having created enmity" means having generated opposition. [This is explained] by the passage beginning with, "A man with an axe in his hand... and so forth.
He related the Phandanajātaka. With the words, “The earth trembles, O Blessed One,” he related the Pathavī-undriyajātaka.
With the words, “I pay homage to you, O elephant,” he related the Laṭukikajātaka.
“It is well, O many kinsmen; even the trees born in the forest...”
"The wind carries away even a single great tree," with these words he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.
"The birds go along in harmony, taking hold of the net."
“When they begin to quarrel, then they will come under my power.
With these words, he related the *Vaṭṭaka Jātaka*:
“Fear has arisen from those who wield the rod against themselves; behold the people in their strife!”
"I shall proclaim the sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), just as it was realized by me"—with these words he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
Those various acts of seduction, exerting themselves through body and speech, send forth their message: "May they become weary [of the world]."

“By the Kuṇāla Lake” means having established himself on the shore of the Kuṇāla Lake. He answered each question as it was asked, thinking, “In due course, through the occasion of the questions of the bird-king Kuṇāla, I shall relate the Kuṇāla Jātaka.
He dispelled his lack of joy by means of seeing the faults of women and by elucidating the danger, the source, and the defilement of sensual pleasures.
Having dispelled sloth by strengthening their human effort, their minds arose with the thought: "It is fitting for us to become like the Supreme Person.

"With their monastic duties unslackened" means that from the time they began dispelling discontent, they were not lax in their ascetic tasks; the meaning is that they had not abandoned their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "The Blessed One thought it was fitting for them to sit"—this is the construction.
"In the lotus pond" means in a lotus lake. "They blossomed through the awakening of the multitude of their virtues. [He thought: "This [person]... [he] did not speak to him."

By this, he shows that all those bhikkhus, because they had arrived one after another in succession, were ashamed before one another and did not report to the Blessed One the specific distinction they had realized for themselves.
He states the reason for this with the words, “of those whose taints were exhausted,” and so forth.

“At the mere moment of sinking” means at the very moment of approaching the presence of the Blessed One. “In the circle of the Noble Ones” means in the assembly of the Noble Ones. “From the enclosure of the Eastern Yugandhara Mountains.”
"From the eastern boundary of Mount Yugandhara, not from the Sunrise Mountain (Udayapabbata) as described by outsiders.
'For the purpose of showing its loveliness' means for the purpose of showing the state of being especially delightful of the world, which is adorned by the arising of a Buddha.
'Having leaped up' means having risen. 'At such a moment, at such a time, at such an instant' refers to the aforementioned [time] of the moon's disk."
"At the moment of rising," "at the time of rising," and "in the hour of rising" are stated for the purpose of showing the progressive increase of time.
Likewise, in order to show that those bhikkhus were a suitable retinue for the Blessed One by way of their birth and other qualities, he said, "Therein...
and so forth. "Deities who had attained meditative absorption" refers to deities who had entered into jhāna-samāpatti in a nearby place. "They stirred" means they rose up.
A *kos* is the measure of a place between sounds. It is said that originally sixty-three thousand cities arose in Jambudīpa;
likewise a second [set], and likewise a third. With reference to this, it says: "three times in sixty-three thousand cities.
When these are added together, they total more than one hundred thousand, namely eighty-eight thousand and nine thousand. [This makes] ninety-nine thousand.
"In nine million nine hundred and ninety thousand *doṇamukha*s" means in nine million nine hundred and ninety thousand *doṇamukha*s, plus nine hundred thousand more.
A *doṇamukha* is called a "foot-city," which is the place where a great city originates.
"In ninety-six trillion ports" means in ninety-six trillion ports (nine hundred and sixty million plus six). [This refers to] Tambapaṇṇidīpa and so forth.

[They gathered] from fifty-five jewel-mines. However, the description by way of divisions such as cities, river-mouths, ports, and jewel-mines is for the purpose of showing the great number of deities dwelling and residing therein.
If the deities have assembled from ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), then why is it said in the *Pāḷi* [text], "from ten world-systems"? To this he says: "From ten thousand... and so forth.
“Intended. Therefore, it should be understood that here the term “one world-system” refers to a thousandfold world-system (*sahassilokadhātu*).
Regarding “the Brahma palace”: in the Brahma palace built from the beginning. Regarding “the Brahma-world”: in the lower Brahma-world.
Anticipating the objection, “If those deities were thus continuous, there would be no space at all for those who arrive later,” he says: “Just as...”
"But furthermore," and so forth. Those born in the body of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsakāya) are "Pure Abode-dwellers" (Suddhāvāsakāyika).
Since the ground of the Pure Abodes is their place of residence, it is therefore said, "of those dwelling in the Pure Abodes. They are "abodes" (āvāsa) in the sense of being places of dwelling;
however, they are called "Pure Abodes" because for them, the abode is pure through the total eradication of both the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) and the other fetters.
332. Unable to find space elsewhere, he descended upon the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*).

The same applies to the others. The "Buddha-path" (*buddhavīthi*) is the path leading directly toward the Buddhas; it is impossible to cover or traverse it all the way to the edge of the world-system.
"By the very path traversed by the Buddhas" means by that path frequented by those devas and brahmās who approach the presence of the Buddhas.
A gathering, a coming together, a meeting is a *samaya*; because it is a great *samaya*, he said "a great assembly" (*mahāsamūha*).
A forest that has grown large is a *pavana*; he said "a grove" (*vanasaṇḍa*). "Hosts of deities" (*devaghaṭā*) means groups of deities.

"They concentrated" (*samādahaṃsu*) means they made [the mind] well-composed by means of supramundane concentration (*lokuttara-samādhi*), having thoroughly fixed it according to how it was concentrated.
However, it is said that [the mind] becomes "yoked" by means of concentration; thus it is stated: "they yoked [them] with concentration.

Because all [faults] such as the "cow-urine curve" and so forth were thoroughly removed, they "all... performed [it]. They are called *nettāni* (reins) because one leads the horses by means of them; they are the traces.
Since the placing of horses that have strayed from the path back onto the path is accomplished by seizing the reins, it says: "having seized all the traces, without urging [them]."
Having said that, he stated "without urging or preventing" to show that it is indeed neither an exhortation nor a prohibition.
Just as a stake driven into a wall or the ground is difficult to extract, just as a crossbar prevents entry into a city,
and just as a city-gate pillar with deep-rimmed base is firmly fixed and difficult to remove, so too are lust and the other defilements [difficult to remove] from the continuum of a being.
Because they are difficult to remove and because they obstruct entry into the city of Nibbāna, they are called "the stake," "the crossbar," and "the threshold-stake.

Due to the absence of the sprout of craving (*taṇhā*), they are "unshakable" (*aneja*); and due to their state of supreme contentment, they wander with unimpeded movement because they face the four quarters.
"Those who have gone" means they have indeed gone; they will not go further, because their taking of refuge is fully accomplished. This is the supramundane (*lokuttara*) going for refuge.
He said, "They have gone by means of a refuge-taking that is free from doubt. For they will certainly not go to the plane of the miserable states (apāyabhūmi) and will fulfill the host of devas.
However, those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha by means of a mundane refuge-taking will not go to the plane of the miserable states;
and when other conditions come together, having left the human [state]...
"The meaning here is: 'They will fill their bodies and the host of deities.
Regarding the commentary on the assembly of deities (devatāsannipātavaṇṇanā):

'Of these' refers to the assemblies of deities. 'Now' means at this time. 'Of the Buddhas' is because there is an absence of other Buddhas. 'Malleability of mind' (cittakallatā) is the softness of the mind (cittamaddava)."
But is it possible for the Blessed One alone to state the names and clans of those [deities] in such a great assembly of devas?
Yes, it is possible—to show this, it was said: “The Buddhas are indeed great,” and so forth. In that context, “seen” refers to the sense-base of visible form;
“heard” refers to the sense-base of sound; and “sensed” refers to the sense-bases of odor, taste, and tangible objects, which are the domains of the faculties that grasp what is present.
"Apprehended" (*viññāta*) refers to everything that remains to be known after what has been said. "Attained" (*patta*) means either attained by searching or attained without searching;
"searched for" (*pariyiṭṭha*) means that which was searched for, whether it was attained or not. "Mentally explored" (*anuvicaritaṃ manasā*) means merely observed by the mind alone.
"In some cases, with respect to an object of form analyzed by way of blue and so forth" refers to the Abhidhamma [definition] beginning with "blue," "yellow," and so on.

The construction is: "Wherever a visible object has been analyzed, there is no [remaining] visible object whatsoever. The phrase "by means of the sound of a drum, etc. follows the same method here as well.
"Yaṃ" means that object; "etesaṃ" means of the Buddhas.
Now, in order to support the aforementioned meaning with the canonical text (Pāḷi), the passage beginning with "yathāha" was stated. At that time, by the act of knowing...

Having said "I know" for the purpose of showing that [his knowledge] is not incomplete, he then said "I have directly known that" because there is nothing whatsoever among all that is to be known which has not been known by the Blessed One. They do not look [at him] because there is no need.
Those who are mistaken [think], "They are not possessed of an obstruction due to karma," and so forth, according to this method.

It has been said: beginning with "For whom auspicious signs have been uprooted," and because it contains an abundance of discourse on the suppression of lust—such as "One should subdue lust for human and divine pleasures"—the *Sammā-paribbājaniya Sutta* is suitable for those of a lustful temperament (*rāga-carita*).

Furthermore, because it addresses quarrels and so forth through such passages as "From what arise quarrels and disputes regarding the beloved and the unbeloved, lamentation and sorrow, along with envy... [it is also suitable for those of a quarrelsome temperament].
[They] arise from hatred, and that hatred arises from affection; and that affection arises from desire.
Thus, because it extensively demonstrates the danger in hatred through its results and its causal succession, the *Kalahavivāda-sutta* is suitable for those of a hateful temperament.
“Indeed, this is little and not enough for peace;
I declare that there are two fruits of dispute.
Seeing even this, one should not dispute.”
“Beholding security, the ground of non-dispute”—
in this manner, because it dispels delusion and nourishes wisdom, the Mahāvyūha Sutta is suitable for those of a deluded temperament:
“If one does not approve of the Dhamma of another...”
“The fool is deluded and of inferior wisdom;
all fools are indeed of very inferior wisdom,
and all these are clinging to views.”

By way of this method, the *Cūḷabyūhasutta* is suitable for those of discursive temperament because it proceeds by means of removing adherence to views through direct experience, thereby cutting off the proliferation of thoughts regarding the grasping at views within their respective objects:
“The root of the conceptual proliferation of ‘I am’— thus said the Blessed One—
one should completely restrain all [notions] of ‘I am a thinker.’”
"Whatever craving there is within oneself—
by the removal of these, one should always train with mindfulness"—

thus, with wisdom (*mantā*), one should understand the entire root of conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhā*), which consists of the defilements such as ignorance and the occurrence of the thought "I am."

One should restrain it. Whatever craving—whether classified as internal craving for form and so forth—should arise, one should train by being constantly mindful and established in mindfulness for the sake of their removal and pacification.
Faith alone is the vessel for such instruction. For that [instruction] brings benefit to him;
thus, the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta is suitable for those of a faithful temperament.
“Free from craving before dissolution,” said the Blessed One,
“not dependent on the past,
not to be reckoned as existing in the middle.”
"He has no one placed before him."—

He who has already abandoned craving even prior to the dissolution of the body, for that very reason is not dependent upon the past portion designated as the "past stretch" by virtue of being a support for craving;
nor is he to be described as "attached," and so forth, even in the middle, the present stretch of time.
Because for that Arahant there is no future course of existence due to the absence of craving and views as precursors, there is nothing whatsoever to be placed before him;
since such profound discourse is abundant [in this sutta], the *Pūrabhedasutta* was stated as being suitable for those of intellectual temperament, as in the passage:
"Then, having determined what was suitable for them..."; he brought it to mind according to their temperament.
Having taken that [teaching] to heart, he again took it to heart according to his own fitness for delivering the instruction.
"Would he know by my own inclination? means: would he know the instruction commenced solely through my own inclination, without regard for the inclinations of others?
"By the inclination of another" means: by the inclination of someone in the assembled assembly. "By way of an occasion" (aṭṭhuppattika) means...
[This was spoken] here because of an occasion that arose. "By way of a question" means by way of the question of someone who asks. "One would know the discourse already commenced":

the phrase "if he were a Paccekabuddha" was stated for the purpose of showing that, regarding the teaching of these suttas, a question [posed] to Paccekabuddhas is both burdensome and beyond their scope. Therefore he said, "he too would not be able."

And here, since neither a question for permission nor a question out of a desire to speak is appropriate, rather a question similar to one for verifying what has been seen or one for cutting through doubt is appropriate;

such questions proceed according to the individual's inclination and not according to the nature of the Dhamma itself. In that regard, if the Blessed One had asked [the question] himself in that manner and himself...
If he were to answer, there would be confusion among the listening deities, who would wonder, "What is this? The Blessed One first said one thing, and now he says another?
They would be as if they had entered into darkness; therefore it was said, "In this way, the departed deities will not be able to penetrate [the teaching].
However, in the case of a teaching according to the Dhamma (yathādhammadesanā), by way of the desire to speak...
“Confusion arises from questioning. The host of devas said, “The sun has risen,” because of the vast and magnificent nature of the radiance due to its proximity.

Regarding the phrase “in one world-system,” according to the method stated in the Sutta, there are never two Buddhas anywhere at all, neither before nor after. For this very reason he said: “In infinite... [world-systems]... he saw.”
In this verse, "I ask" means that the manifested Buddha requested the Blessed One to grant him the opportunity to question him.
"Muni" refers to the Buddha, the Sage. "Of abundant wisdom" means one of great insight. "Crossed over" means one who has crossed over the four floods.

"Gone to the further shore" means one who has attained Nibbāna, or one who has gone to the further shore—the limit or end—of all that is to be known. "Parinibbuta" (fully extinguished) is used here in the sense of Nibbāna with residue remaining.
"Steadfast" means having a mind firmly established, due to being unshakable by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
"Having gone forth from the home, having cast off sensual desires" means having cast off the objects of desire and gone forth from domestic life.
"How would that bhikkhu rightly wander in the world?"—how would that bhikkhu rightly wander, go, and dwell, remaining unsullied by the world?
The meaning is "he would transgress. 334.
Regarding the phrase "I shall recite a *siloka*": here, a *siloka* is a collection of quarters (*pāda*); it is also called a verse (*gāthā*) spoken by the seers (*isī*).
A quarter itself is a group of words with fixed phonemes and sequence; "I shall recite that *siloka*" means "I shall set it forth."
He said, "The meaning is: 'I shall cause to proceed... the syllables... The word *yattha* is the locative case used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
He stated, "'In whichever places,' for this is a designation [of the plural] by the elision of repetition (*āmeḍita*). "Of the ground" (*bhummā*) means those whose dwelling is connected to the earth.
"Dependent on this or that" means those who have taken refuge in such-and-such a place, living in reliance upon it; the intention is: "I shall proclaim my fame together with them."
By the phrase “Those who dwell in mountain caves,” he shows their dwelling in seclusion; by the phrase “resolute and concentrated,” he shows their application to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
They are a great multitude because they number five hundred. Because they overcome opposing factors and possess a refined brilliance, they are like lions.
They are settled in seclusion. "Oneness" means a state of unity.
Having become pure with a bright mind—meaning having become pure by means of attaining the path of arahantship, with a mind cleansed, and not merely through physical purity alone—they are serene;
that is, they are especially serene through confidence in the Noble Path. They are untroubled due to the absence of those defilements that cause turbidity of the mind.
"Having known the bhikkhus" means having known that these bhikkhus, whose defilements are destroyed, "see these hosts of devas with the divine eye.
"Because they were born at the end of hearing the Dhamma" means because they were born into the noble lineage (ariyajāti) at the conclusion of the hearing of the Dhamma.
"All this" refers to all of this, beginning with the phrase "more than five hundred."
“They exerted energy for that purpose” means they applied effort and enthusiasm by way of the preliminary resolve (*abhinīhāra*) for the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
Therefore he said, “Not by them,” and so forth. “Seventy” is stated by substituting the letter *r* for the letter *t*;
the meaning is “seventy. The word “thousand” (*sahassa*) is understood to follow; because it is joined with “seventy,” it takes the plural form. Thus he said, “some [say] a thousand.”
“Some [say] seventy thousand.
“Endless” (ananta) means that which has its limits removed; however, because it is exceedingly vast, he says “extensive” (vipula).
“Having observed” (avekkhitvā) means having observed individually with the eye of knowledge; they also read it as “having defined” (vavatthitvāna). That...
This is the meaning. He says "having defined" because that contemplation is a process of making a definitive determination.
He says "the very verse previously mentioned" with reference to the second half of the third verse and the first half of the fourth verse among the verses cited earlier.
He says "see, look on" because knowing is indeed seeing. He says "I shall proclaim in proper sequence" because it proceeds by way of speech.
335. "Seven thousand reckoned" means seven thousand. "Yakkhas indeed" means those of the yakkha species.

"Endowed with power" means possessed of great influence. Or, "possessed of psychic power" means having great majesty; "radiant" means having great effulgence; "beautiful" means possessing transcendent beauty;
"glorious" means having a large retinue and a widespread reputation. He spoke thus with the intention that the word *samiti* signifies proximity.
"In the presence of the bhikkhus" means:
on the Hemavata mountain, that is, on the mountain situated near the Himavanta.
"All these" refers to all sixteen thousand as previously mentioned: seven thousand from Kapilavatthu, six thousand from Hemavata, and three thousand from Sātāgira.
"In the city of Rājagaha" means in the vicinity of the city of Rājagaha. "Him" refers to Kumbhīra. 336.

Granted that he rules over the eastern direction, nevertheless he is the elder of the Gandhabbas throughout all four directions and in all four great islands, together with their surrounding sub-islands.
How so? Because they all remain under his control. [This applies] to the Kumbhaṇḍas.
The same method applies to the terms *adhipati* (lord) and so forth.

"Of that which has grown" refers to him who has increased in stature. "Just like him" means they are similar to the son of Dhatarattha in their vast number, their names, their strength, and their specific qualities such as supernatural power (*iddhi*) and so on.
"By way of including all" means by way of encompassing all of them, since there are four Great Kings for each of the ten-thousandfold world systems. Therefore he said, "And here... and so forth.

“Four quarters” means in the four directions. “The four quarters were shining, blazing, and illuminating. If this is so, one might ask: how is it that they are situated in the Kapilavatthu forest when such a great assembly has arrived?

To answer this, he says, “But those...,” and so forth. (337) The construction is: “They are the servants of those Great Kings. They are possessed of *māyā* (illusion/deceit), therefore they are *māyāvino* (deceitful).
They possess deception within them, or they are engaged in deception, thus they are *vañcanikā* (deceptive). “By means of *kerāṭiya-sāṭheyya*” means by means of a base, fraudulent practice.

They are called *māyā* because they possess *māyā* (deceit); and to show that specific practice of deception by which they are called "illusionists" (*māyākāraka*) for the purpose of deceiving others, he said "illusionists.
"So many slaves" refers to so many [beings], beginning with Kuṭeṇḍu and ending with Nighaṇḍu, who are the slaves of the eight great kings.

“Devarājāno” means kings of various divine hosts after having become devas. As for the three sons of devas—Citta, Sena, and Cittasena—they are mentioned in the Pāḷi by way of the grammatical principle of *ekasesa* (the retention of one from a group);
thus he says, “Citta and...,” and so forth. “Bhikkhusaṅghasamiti” refers to this forest where the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) has gathered and assembled.

338. “Nāgasadaha-vāsikā” means those dwelling in the Nāgasadaha [Lake]. It is said that there was a certain king of nāgas there, and because he had lived there for a long time, he possessed a vast retinue descended through generations; with reference to him, he says, “of the retinue of the Tacchaka nāga.”
“Dwellers of the Yamunā” means the nāgas who live in the Yamunā River. “By way of the term ‘nāga’” means by way of the term ‘elephant-nāga.
“Of the kind described” refers to those other nāgas of the aforementioned type, excluding Kambala and Assatara.
“Overcome by greed” means overcome by greed for food. “Because of divine power” means because of divine power; or, they are called “divine” because of their divine power. “Variegated supaṇṇas.”
“By name” means because of possessing various beautiful wings.

“Calling out to one another” means approaching and speaking. Just as crows, owls, snakes, mongooses, and so forth, though possessing natural enmity arising from their respective species, [behave] like friends...
[omission] ...the intention is that with hearts joyful and delighted, they [act] toward one another. They [saw] only the Buddha.
They went for refuge [thinking], “It is solely through the power of the Buddha that we have obtained mutual friendship.
(339) “Brothers” means brothers by marriage. Therefore he said, “on account of Sujā, the daughter of the asuras.

“Among them” means among the asuras. “Kālakañca” is his name. “Mahābhismā” means those with terrifying, massive bodies. “Incapable” means they are not capable of entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), because of their lack of desire, due to the absence of such a disposition.

Because the great asura Bali had passed away, the Blessed One, speaking of his sons, said: "And of the hundred sons of Bali," and so forth. It is said that he approached having fashioned a subtle physical form. 340.
"Having performed the work" means having performed the preliminary practice (*parikamma*). "Produced" means produced by access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).

Those produced by absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*), however, are *brahmās*; the Blessed One will speak of them later with the words "Subrahmā," etc., while this [subject] is a deity belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Thus it is said. For this very reason he says: “Those belonging to the bodies of loving-kindness and compassion are the deities produced by having performed the preliminary work for the jhāna of loving-kindness and the jhāna of compassion.

In the phrase “in the jhāna of loving-kindness and the jhāna of compassion,” the meaning is: the sign of the jhāna of loving-kindness and the sign of the jhāna of compassion; that is, for the sake of those [jhānas].

Those deities of water and so forth are established in ten groups because they abide according to their respective classes. This extends up to the ten divine bodies belonging to the body of compassion. “Of diverse appearance” means possessing appearance (color) and individual nature (character) that are manifold.
“Veṇḍu-devatā” means a deity named Veṇḍu; likewise for Sahali-devatā.
Regarding Asama-devatā and Yamaka-devatā, they say these are “two paths,” meaning two classes of deities headed by those [names].
The deities who are the attendants of the moon are those existing in dependence upon the moon, the deities who run before, behind, and beside it. Therefore he said:
“Devas dependent on sandalwood. The same principle applies here for those “dependent on the sun” and those “dependent on the constellations.

Alternatively, those deities whose sole cause is the blowing of wind are the wind-clouds (*vātavalāhakā*). Likewise, those whose sole cause is the movement of cloud-masses are the cloud-clouds (*abbhavalāhakā*).
Those whose cause is the production of heat are the heat-clouds (*uṇhavalāhakā*). As for the rain-clouds (*vassavalāhakā*), they are similar to Pajjunna.
These are not mentioned here. There is a class of deities called the Vasudevas; because he is their leader, Vāsava is [called] Sakka.
"Ten" refers to these ten classes of deities, beginning with the Veṇḍu-devas and ending with the Vāsavas.
"These" refers to these names of theirs: "Jalamaggi" and "Sikhārivā. However, some say that the letter *m* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
They say that "Jalas," "Aggis," and "Sikhāris" are their names. Among these very deities mentioned as "Ariṭṭhakas" and "Rojas," some are "like the umā flower" (umāpupphanibhāsino) in color;
this is how the meaning should be understood, for otherwise there would be eleven classes of deities.

“Ten”: these ten classes of deities, beginning with the *samāna* and ending with the *vāsava-nesi*, constitute ten groups of gods. For that very reason, they appear as tenfold according to the division of their respective classes (*nikāya*).
“*Samānā*,” etc., is the name applied to the collective assembly of those deities. The same applies to the rest. “Ten”:

these ten classes of deities, beginning with the *samāna* and ending with the *mahāpāraga*, constitute ten groups of gods. For that very reason, they appear as tenfold according to the division of their respective classes.
The three classes of deities beginning with the Sukka; "foremost deities" means deities who are pre-eminent or principal.

"In the quarters" means in the various directions. "Deity" means a cloud. "Ten" refers to these ten classes of deities beginning with the Sukka and ending with the Pajjunna, which appear as tenfold according to the divisions of the divine hosts.
"Ten" [again] refers to these ten classes of deities beginning with the Khemiya and ending with the Paranimmita, which [also appear] according to the divisions of the divine hosts.
They have come from ten directions. Regarding this, they say: "The Khemiyas, the Kaṭṭhakas, and so forth—these five classes, together with the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

"By way of name" means by following the names, that is, by way of their commonality of names such as "water-deities" and so on. For this very reason he says: "by way of a portion of the name, by way of a division of the name.
"All deities" means all the deities throughout the ten-thousandfold world-systems. He explains [this].

Having grouped together those various names according to their similarity, [the author] says "gone away" (*vigatā*) to mean they have departed as if having gone on a journey (*pavutthā*). Alternatively, "gone away" (*pavutthā*) means gone forth (*pakārato vutthā*) or dwelt (*vusitā*);
thus, birth (*jāti*) would be that which is to be dwelt through—that is, *pavuṭṭhajāti*. The phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhammā*) are of a black nature; entirely...
Because of the absence of that [darkness], the One Possessed of Ten Powers has transcended the state of blackness. Or, by virtue of being free from blemish, he has surpassed the dark;
like the moon, which has surpassed the dark through its splendor, he shines with such splendor like that very moon.
341. "The one Brahmā" refers to the son of the Subrahma deity mentioned in the Sagāthaka-vagga, who was reborn in the Brahma-world.
The noble Brahmas are established in the lower [realms], not in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Brahmas.
Tissa Mahābrahmā was an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who, having been reborn among humans at a later time, became the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
Regarding the phrase "a thousand Brahma-worlds": those who have these Brahma-worlds are "Brahma-worlds," that is, the Brahmas; [the term refers] to those Brahma-worlds.
Since the word *loka* here refers to the system of the seven worlds, he says, “a thousand great Brahmās have come.
In the following verse, he explains by way of meaning the very term “have come” (*āgatā*) that was stated [in the previous verse]. “Where” (*yattha*) means in which thousand of Brahmās.
“Other Brahmās” (*aññe brahme*) means other Brahmās besides him. He stands surpassing them in beauty, in fame, and in lifespan.
"Lord" means the sovereign over the other Brahmās by virtue of that very exercise of power. 342.
"Possessed of dark qualities": behold the foolishness of the evil Māra, the Dark One, who strives to exert himself fruitlessly in a sphere that is not his own.

By creating an obstacle to the hearing of the Dhamma—which brings about the state of being free from lust—those who are not yet free from lust become truly bound by lust; thus it is said, "let him be bound by lust."
"Making it terrifying and resonant" means having produced a formidable and great sound.
Now, showing that sound by way of a simile, he said "Just as," and so forth.
"Any one" (kañci) refers to any deity or human being present in that assembly whom [the speaker] was unable to bring under his own control; being himself not under his own control...
He remained standing as if in a jar. Therefore he said, "One who has no mastery over himself," and so forth.
(343) "By those free from lust" is merely a conventional designation for the teaching. For the entire assembly gathered there had already fled from the army of Māra;
not even a single hair on their bodies was stirred—that is, not even the mere tip of a hair was moved—so how could they have created an obstacle?
Thus, the meaning should be explained as referring to all those who attained whatever specific distinction therein by way of creating no obstacles;
or alternatively, it should be understood that by the mention of "those free from lust," both those still possessed of lust and those free from lust who discerned [the truth] therein are included.
Māra uttered this verse, having conceived a sense of wonder and amazement. For how indeed could it be...?
"Even though I am creating a most terrible, great, and terrifying [display], all these remain without change, simply composed.
Why? Because these are supreme persons who have conquered [the defilements]. Therefore he said, "All," and so forth. Such is the joy of the Noble Ones (ariya) based on the Dhamma;
such a joy never occurs among the ignoble (anariya). Thus it was said: "by the Noble Ones who exist within the Dispensation."
Even the word *suta* alone, without the prefix *vi-*, has the meaning of "renowned," as in expressions such as *sutadhammassa*;
thus he said, "renowned among people.
*Dūre* means "in a distant place. Avoiding an obstacle for the youth, she said, "It is not possible, venerable sir, to show my entire body."
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta.
8. Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta:
Explanation of the Introduction.
344. Because it was not far from Ambasaṇḍā, even that single brahmin village is referred to by the plural term “Ambasaṇḍā,” just as one says “the city of Varaṇā.
*Vedi* itself is *vediko*; *vediko* itself becomes *vediyo* by changing the letter *k* to *y*, [meaning] “in that *vediyaka* (altar-like place).
Therefore he said, “resembling a jeweled altar (*maṇivedikā*),” and so forth; that is, resembling an altar made of jewels such as sapphire (*indanīla*) and the like.

The meaning is as follows: "Even before" means prior to the construction of the shelter; it stood in the form of a cave, and because its entrance was possessed by the Indasāla tree, it was called "Indasāla Cave" according to its former designation.
"Ussukka" refers to zeal (abhiruci); that zeal, moreover, arises from the desire to see the Buddha, as well as through the exertion [to do so].
And regarding its occurrence, it is said: "righteous exertion. [It is said: "There is no one equal to Sakka... and so forth. As it is said:

"By means of heedfulness, Maghavā attained preeminence among the gods. By "a trifling amount" is meant by a mere small amount of meritorious action, without performing much meritorious karma again and again.
Sakka, too, was indeed a refuge for those terrified by great merit;

however, he became agitated, being struck by the fear of death, which was doubled by the grief arising from the loss of his extraordinary divine prosperity. Therefore it is said: "But Sakka was overcome by the fear of death.
Seeing the deities with the divine eye is like penetrating a secret; thus it is said: "He penetrated [the matter]. It is distinct.
"Vohāra" means a unique, affectionate mode of address. "Marisaniyasampattikā" means "O venerable ones" (mārisā).
For their attainments—due to their great majesty—are "endured" (sahanti), that is, they manifest; whereas others, due to their improper attention and lack of fortune, do not endure them at all.
And that state of theirs being "endurable by the venerable ones" is because they are free from suffering; thus it is said.
“It is also said: ‘free from suffering. The phrase “all alone” is said because he had come without the assembly of devas;

however, Mātali and others such as him were indeed his companions even then. For it will be said: “Moreover, this venerable one was awakened from that meditative absorption by the sound of the wheel-rims.
He did not grant an opportunity for Sakka’s knowledge to reach maturity, nor for others.
“Investigating the realization of the Dhamma by many deities”—the word *so* refers to Sakka.
*Evaṃ* is a particle used for accepting a statement; thus he said, “Let it be so,” and so forth. However, the address “Venerable Sir” was spoken by them with reference to Sakka.

345. The meaning of “the beloved... listens to the Dhamma” is to be illustrated by the *Govinda-sutta* and other such texts. “In this place made ready by him” means in the Blessed One who had been prepared by this Pañcasikha.

“Anucariyā” means the state of following; as for that following of his, it is indeed going together, thus he said: “Sahacaraṇaṃ ekato gamanaṃ” (going together, walking as one). “Sovaṇṇamayaṃ” means made of gold.
“Pokkharaṃ” refers to the hollow body of the lute. “Daṇḍo” is the neck of the lute.
“Veṭhakā” are the leather straps to be tightened for the purpose of binding and pressing the strings. “Pattakaṃ” is the hollow body (the *pokkhara*).
"Having tuned the fifty even frets" means having prepared it in such a way that it is possible to perform the tuning there in the proper sequence; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, the phrase "having tuned the fifty even frets" is stated with reference to the fixed method of playing the lute in the world of the gods; however, in the human world, there are twenty-one frets.
For this very reason, it is said in the commentary on the Vīṇopama Sutta:
“Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one finger-stops,
and forty-nine strings— such are the circles of notes.”
In that regard, there are these seven notes (*sara*): *chañja*, *usabha*, *gandhāra*, *majjhima*, *pañcama*, *dhevatā*, and *nisāda*.
There are three scales (*gāma*), meaning groups of notes: the *chañja-gāma*, the *majjhima-gāma*, and the *sādhāraṇa-gāma*.
By applying the method of instrumental performance in the human world, three modes of intonation (*mucchanā*) are made for each individual note, resulting in twenty-one modes of intonation.
And for each individual vowel (*sara*), there are seven types of *tāna* variations, from which the slower determination of the vowel occurs;
these are the forty-nine specific *tāna* distinctions. Twenty-two types of *suti* (smooth articulation) are intended—namely, three, two, four;
four, three, two, four—but according to each individual vowel, there are seven modulations (*mucchanā*), including that of the intermediate vowel (*antarasarassa*).
And he played the lute by means of its fifty strings being properly tuned. Therefore it is said: “having tuned the fifty strings. The construction is:
“at the time of Sakka’s departure,” making known [this] to the other devas.

(346) *Atiriva*: the letter *ra* is used for euphonic junction (*padasandhi*); it means “exceedingly” (*ativiya*). He went... [omitted] ...in a hurried manner because his heart was terrified by the fear of death. For this very reason he says: “Was it not indeed,” and so forth.
347. Buddhas are indeed great compassionate ones who have arisen solely for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the world including its devas;
how then could they be difficult to approach by those seeking their aid? To this he said, "I am possessed of lust," and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, "having retired into seclusion" means that at whatever interval or moment one might approach, she was at that very interval retired into seclusion, having attained meditative absorption (jhāna).
Alternatively, the word *tadantara* has the same meaning as “at this time” (*etarahi*); thus he said, “or [those who] have just now retired into seclusion.
348. Commentary on the Verses Sung by Pañcasikha:
“She announced” means that, having begun the intended singing while playing the lute, she [sang] according to the requirements of each particular passage.

Displaying the stage where dullness has become manifest, he— whose voice imitated the song of a honey-bee intoxicated by drinking very sweet and tender honey— spoke with clear speech and intoned a melody like that of a lute:
