“Like the Son of the Sakyas, through jhāna, one-pointed, wise, and mindful;”
“The Sage, seeking to attain the Deathless… just as the Sage would rejoice having attained supreme enlightenment.
And thus it is associated with the Buddha. Furthermore, that which is associated with the Buddha takes as its object the Dhamma-body of the Buddhas, serving as its support.
Having established this, he said, "The Dhamma is like that of the Arahants. It should be understood as being connected with the Dhamma and connected with Arahantship.
"Possessing a body equal to the sun" means possessing a body with a radiance equal to the sun. Therefore he said, "It is said of her...
and so forth. Since she was born on the lap of Timbaru, the king of the Gandhabba devas, he therefore said, "Timbaru, the king of the devas..."
“You were born depending on her. Because she possesses beautiful limbs, she is called “Kalyāṇī” (the Beautiful One); thus he says, “beautiful in all her limbs.
The verses previously spoken by way of the influence of passion are now spoken again concerning her alone, as if addressing her while she stands before him.
Regarding “breast and belly,” both the breasts (*payodhara*) and the belly (*udara*) are intended; thus he says, “the space between the breasts and the belly.”
“Some cause” means some affliction.
It stands having abandoned its natural state due to its state of being intensely attached.
“Vāmūrū” means beautiful thighs. Therefore he said, “in a lovely manner,” and so forth. The words *vāma*, *vikasita*, *rucira*, *sundara*, *abhirūpa*, and *cāru* [all denote beauty].
Indeed, these should be understood as having the same meaning. "Not sharp" means not keen, not harsh, and not rough. "Gentle" means soft and smooth.

"Of manifold nature" (*anekabhāvo*) means of manifold character; since that is indeed called "of many kinds," he said, "it has become manifold" (*anekavidho jāto*). "Of manifold parts" (*anekabhāgo*) means consisting of many sections. "May it ripen together with you" means:
"may that karma of mine ripen only in conjunction with you; may it ripen together with you alone."
The intention is: "May [I] experience the fruit of that karma. "Together with you alone" means:

just as the karma conducive to the appearance of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) yields its result together with the Woman-treasure (itthiratana), which is its outflow-result (nissandaphala), so too may that karma of mine yield its result for me together with you alone.
*Ekodī* means having reached a state of oneness; the meaning is "concentrated. *Jigīsāno* means "desiring to conquer.

Thus, the first alternative is stated as: "one who has become such is indeed called 'desiring to conquer'. In the second alternative, however, the meaning is stated by introducing the verb "he wanders" (*vicarati*).
"Nandeyyuṃ" (they would rejoice) means he speaks while longing for a gathering [of people] because of their exceedingly beautiful physical splendor.

"Saṃsandati" (it blends) means it accords; the meaning is that the song-voice proceeds in the very same manner as the string-sound—that is, without exceeding the modulation by which and the manner in which the string-sound proceeds. By whatever intention...
The Blessed One spoke in praise of Pañcasikha the Gandhabba. To clarify everything for which he spoke, [the author] said, "Why," and so forth.
[It was because] at the foot of the Bodhi tree, [ignorance] had been utterly eradicated. The Blessed One was equanimous because he was undefiled.
The Blessed One was well-liberated in mind from desire and lust, and from all defilements. If this is so, why [did he speak thus] to Pañcasikha?
"He spoke of the Gandhabbas' appearance" refers to the passage beginning with "But if... and so forth.

"Connected" (*ganthitā*) means linked together; however, since they are being described continuously, they appear as if gathered into a mass, which is why he said "compacted" (*piṇḍitā*). "Conventional expression" (*vohāravacana*) is a figurative term to be employed in the presence of the Blessed One and the monks.
"Of one dancing nearby" (*upanaccantiyā*) means of one who has approached and is dancing.
350. By saying, “When were you gathered?
and so forth, he exchanges greetings. “He might even show a performance” means that he might even dance by way of mimicking the act of weaving cloth. 351.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Sakka, lord of the devas, was greeted,” it is to be understood in the same manner as the passage beginning with “Now at that time.”

There is no doubt regarding the status of the words of the compiler; however, since there might be a doubt here concerning the phrase “And thus indeed the Tathāgatas,” it was stated, “These are the words established by the Elders of the Dhamma-Compilation.
Then, in order to show that the other [phrase] is likewise of that same nature, the passage beginning with “All this” was spoken.
It is said to have been uttered with a word of blessing: “May Pañcasikha be happy, may Sakka, lord of the gods...”

"Indo" is spoken as a benediction (*āsīsavāda*). One who says, "He pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet," is said to "pay homage" (*abhivādeti*) because he causes the benediction, "May you be well," to be uttered.
Likewise, one who utters such a benediction is said to "express approval" (*abhivadati*), because he remains in that very state at all times.

"Uruṃ" means "vast" or "extensive"; it is [derived from] *dassati* (he will show) or *dakkhati* (he will see), with the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti*). "Vivaṭā" means an open courtyard or space.

The darkness that was naturally present within the cave has vanished; that is to say, this ordinary darkness which existed all around the Teacher within that cave, extending for eighty cubits, has vanished due to the radiance of the deities' garments, ornaments, and bodies, and light has appeared.
He attained full awakening. However, by the very light of the Buddha, the darkness vanished; and the radiance of the devas was not able to surpass that of the Buddhas.

352. "For a long time" means I have been so for a long duration. There is no "matter of legal action" (*aḍḍakaraṇa*) because it arises in a place where there is no dispute (*avivādādhikaraṇa*). "Play and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," he includes listening to the Dhamma and other such activities.
"In the sandalwood-scented gabled chamber" means in the fragrant chamber built by King Pasenadi out of *sāla* trees.
"Because of that" means because of the attainment of those two fruits, due to the abandonment of coarse sensual desire, she has no delight even in the world of the gods.
Regarding the phrase "by the sound of the wheel-rims he emerged from that concentration," those who do not understand the underlying intention [claim] that [it refers to] the object...
Thinking that "emergence from attainment occurs due to its intensity," one might [misconceive this]; therefore, rejecting that, he said:

"Indeed, you should not say, 'One who has attained [jhāna] hears a sound. And with the intention that if there is a collision with an object, there must also be grasping, he used the word "hears"; the other [responds]: "For one who has attained the first jhāna..."

Relying merely on the statement, "Sound is a thorn," and unable to accept the rejection [of sound] based on the intention that sound is a thorn for all meditative absorption (jhāna), he cited this very passage from the Sutta:
"But did not the Blessed One...? Therein, because the perceptions of repulsion have been thoroughly abandoned through the cultivation of their opposites—the vision of faults—even by a great sound...

There is no emergence from the formless attainments; likewise, because all mundane perceptions—such as "arising is fear" and "non-arising is security"—have been completely transcended by the highest path through the cultivation of their antidote, the right vision of defects, there is never any emergence from the attainment of fruition due to the mastery of the object.
However, this is not because they have been abandoned with ease.
Emergence from all form-spheres occurs through the perception of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*);
however, since even the first jhāna cannot tolerate even a slight sound, it is said that for one attained to that state, "sound is a thorn.

But if, due to the suppression of the perceptions of resistance, there is no emergence from the formless attainments even by a great sound, how much less so from the attainment of the path or the fruit?

Therefore he said, “With the sound of the wheel-rim,” and so forth. The phrase “with the sound of the wheel-rim” is not used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*), but rather in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
To demonstrate this very meaning, it was stated, “But the Blessed One,” and so on.
Commentary on the Gopaka-vatthu.

353. *Paripūrakārinī* means she who, having made them complete and pure, has guarded them. The passage beginning with “*Itthittaṃ*” (*femininity*) and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of dispassion toward that [state].
The meaning is: the state of being a woman is a cause for contempt for the state of femininity.
*Alaṃ* is a word of rejection; the meaning is that there is no purpose [in it]. *Virājeti* means she feels disgust. “*Etā sampattiyo*” means these are [merely] attainments.
These are the aforementioned attainments, beginning with the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti). Therefore, it is by way of the inclination that has arisen through former familiarity.
"The assembly hall" refers to the Sudhamma council hall of the devas.

"He" refers to the deva-son Gopaka. "Turning it over and over again" means repeatedly revolving the words of admonition, as if one were whirling a javelin or similar weapon. "It should be pierced firmly" means it should be struck more forcefully.

“From what [source]? means from what source of knowledge that has arisen. Therefore he said, “engaged in something else. “Those who have performed merit” refers to those who have properly performed meritorious deeds (*dhamma*).
“Gift” (*dāya*) means gain (*lābha*). For it is called a “gift” because it is given by them, and it is called “gain” because it is obtained by those to whom it is given.
“In formations” … [they] became established because they had performed their duties. Therein, for those very ones staying in the Tāvatiṃsa realm—
He was reborn with a Sakka-body just like that of Sakka himself while standing in the Indasāla Cave.
Unable to sever his attachment and clinging to that gandhabba-body, [he remained there].
"To be known by oneself" means it is to be realized and known by oneself alone, not through dependence on another. "Being spoken of by you" means merely being spoken of by you.
"Viyāyāma" means we should exert unremitting energy within our mental continuum. "Pakatiyā" means by way of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); alternatively, the reading is "anussara.
Sensual lust itself is called "kāmarāga-saṃyojanāni" (fetters of sensual lust) in the sense of being a fetter due to its various modes of manifestation, such as "desire, lust, and sensual lust";
and it is called "kāmabandhanāni" (bonds of sensuality) due to the different ways it functions as a bond, tie, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "pāpimayogāni" (the yokes of the Evil One): here...
Furthermore, the meaning should also be understood by way of the remaining bonds of yoga (*yoga-gantha*).
"Of two kinds" means of two kinds by way of sensual desire for objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and sensual desire as defilement (*kilesa-kāma*).
In the two phrases "What here? What there?", the word *kiṃ* is a mere particle. "In the state of being open on four sides" refers to those [monasteries].
Regarding the three jewels beginning with the Buddha, it refers to their state of being suitable for the four quarters and their state of being unimpeded.
For the Buddha-jewel, by virtue of his great compassion, his unobstructed knowledge, and his supreme contentment, is [suitable] for the four quarters; the Dhamma-jewel, because it is well-expounded;
and the Saṅgha-jewel, because they have practiced rightly. Therefore, he said: "unattached in all directions."
Because he had attained the first jhāna of the middle grade, he immediately reached the level of the Brahmapurohita deities;
having regained his former mindfulness of jhāna and making that jhāna the foundation, he developed insight and,
by severing the lower fetters, attained the distinguished state of the path and fruit known as the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

They attained; they reached. However, some say: "With the intention that they had reached the paths and fruits by means of a body belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), they did not arise in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) because they had not attained the fifth jhāna;
rather, having attained the first jhāna, they were reborn among the Ministers of Brahmā (*brahmapurohita*)."
Commentary on the Story of the Young Brahmin Magha 355.
"Pure" means one whose underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*) is pure; the intended sense is that he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).
"The place for performing village duties" refers to the place where the villagers assemble. "By that much alone" means by the very spot cleared by himself for another.

"Having arrived, by means of standing still. "Having regained mindfulness" means having aroused a wise reflection (*yoniso manasikāra*) in his mind, thinking: "Oh, the deed I have performed has become fruitful!

"On the rock" means on a rock situated at a higher elevation in the middle of the road. "Having lifted up" means having raised it. "The path leading to this heaven" means the meritorious deed that is the path for going to this heaven, which is the place of origin for the moon and other celestial bodies.
That which is to be obtained by way of suggestion is called "kahāpaṇa" (a coin); that which is to be obtained by way of punishment is "daṇḍabali" (punishment-tax).
[The King asks: "What will the householders do? [The reply is: "Householders" refers to those who, like forest-dwellers, rely on rugged terrain; they will not cause any harm.
"Even though you knew this previously, why did you not tell me, even though you were aware of it? Thus he spoke.
"It was not said before; however, it is said now out of fear that you might find fault with me.
From the moment it was reported, there is no fault on my part," he says.
"Nibaddha" means certain or absolute.
"Pisuṇesī" means she committed the act of backbiting; the sense is that she brings slander against me into your midst.
Furthermore, having made the royal gift (brahmadeyya) something not to be taken back, [she says]: "Mayhampīti" means "for my sake as well"—perform meritorious deeds dedicated to me.
As for the blue lotus called *nīluppala*, it blooms only after rising up from the water; it does not bloom while remaining within the water.

Like a blooming blue lotus. The construction is as follows: "But this meritorious deed of ours yields its fruit in this very existence, without the need for rebirth in another life. "Even a mere thought" means even a mere thought arising from dejection.

"Long before" means at an early hour; the sense is "very early in the morning. "Worthy of the central knob" means suitable for the central knob. Having cut it and polished it smooth, he completed everything that was to be done for the central knob. For indeed, she had placed it there wrapped in a cloth.

The tying of the rafters was the preparation for the structural foundation of the hall. The binding of the central pillar and the bed refers to the act of ascending and remaining fixed upon the central pillar at the time of its installation.
The construction "on whose plank" and "whose plank was spread" should be joined accordingly.
"Not far away" means not far from the hall and not far from the *koviḷāra* tree. "The eldest of all" refers to Sujātā, the eldest among all of his wives.
“Tasseva” means “of Sakka himself. “In his presence” (santike) means having been born as one who dwells in his proximity. The palace was one thousand yojanas in size, together with its banner.
“Like a piercing needle for a crab” means like a needle used to pierce the edge of a crab’s burrow in order to catch it.
“In the form of a dead fish” means in the form of a dead fish. “It drifts away” means it moves along, floating. Of that female crane as well...
The lifespan was five hundred years, as it was indeterminate for humans, ghosts, and animals, much like that of the gods and denizens of hell.
"He raised a shout" means he made a loud noise.
"By former association" means by long-term association in previous births; for in this way, affection arises even from merely seeing someone. Thus the Blessed One said:
“Whether through former association or through present benefit,
affection arises in this way, like a lotus in water.
Regarding the phrase “in the remaining ones,” he speaks with reference to the gods in two deva-worlds, excluding the Asuras and Sakka.
"Dependent on welfare" means dependent solely on the welfare and benefit of oneself and others. Since that benefit is the cause of happiness, it is said to be "dependent on a cause.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Questions (Pañhaveyyākaraṇavaṇṇanā) 357: "What fetters" means of what kind of fetters. They are called "fetters" because they fetter and bind sentient beings to what is disadvantageous.
He asked: "By what bond? Bound by what bond? "Puthukāyā" means many bodies of beings; thus he said, "many people. "Vera" is called hatred (*dosa*);
thus he said, "free from enmity (*avera*), free from resentment (*appaṭighā*). "A weapon-staff" (*āvudhadaṇḍa*) is a staff [used] on the body with a weapon.
A "fine-staff" (*dhanadaṇḍa*) is a staff for the purpose of making one pay wealth. One who is free from both of those, by not performing either, is "staff-free" (*adaṇḍa*).

One is an enemy (*sapatta*) because of seizing what has been acquired and because of the simultaneous arising of harm; thus he said, "without enemies" (*asapattā*) means "without adversaries" (*apaccatthikā*).
"Ill-will" (*byāpajjha*) refers to mental suffering; being free from that is "without ill-will" (*abyāpajjhā*), as he said, "free from grief" (*vigatadomanassā*).
Previously, by the term "without enmity" (*averā*), the absence of malice was stated. Therefore he said, "without resentment" (*appaṭighā*). "Without enmity" (*averino*)...
But by this [verse], even the non-arising of mere anger is indicated. Therefore he said: "Without giving rise to anger toward anyone.
And the phrase "may they dwell" should also be connected with the preceding phrases, as in "may they dwell free from enmity," and so forth.

To show that this state of being free from enmity and the rest becomes manifest through sharing, he spoke the words beginning with "at the snap of a finger," and then said: "If such is their thought."
It has been said. To show that the arising of consciousness proceeds with even greater firmness, it was said: "Having given a gift and having performed an act of worship, they make an aspiration.
Regarding the phrase "iti ce," the word *ce* implies a hypothetical assumption through its connection [to the preceding]; thus he said, "and so for them.

That which has the characteristic of disparaging, envying, or being unable to endure any kind of success belonging to others is called "that which has the characteristic of disparaging the success of others" (*parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā*).

Insofar as it has the characteristic of not tolerating others sharing in one’s own excellence, it should also be said to have the characteristic of concealment. For this reason, the ancients state its etymology:
“Miserliness (*macchariya*) is that which thinks, ‘May this marvel not belong to others; let it belong to me alone.
In the *Abhidhamma*, [it is defined as] “that which, regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, salutations, and worship of others...”

These are indeed already stated in the Section on Definitions (Nikkhepakaṇḍa) by such passages as “envy, envying,” and so forth, and in their respective commentaries by such passages as “that which [thinks] regarding the gains and so forth of others:
‘What has this to do with them? and so forth; therefore, the intention is that they should be understood according to the method explained therein.
However, since envy and avarice possess many disadvantages, and the elucidation of these is of great benefit to the world, therefore—

In order to show the disadvantages—both pertaining to the present life and to future lives—even of those [faults] already explained in the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā*, he said, “But by means of stinginess regarding one’s dwelling,” and so forth.

“Therein” (*ettha*) means in these instances of envy and stinginess, or in these five kinds of stinginess beginning with stinginess regarding one’s dwelling. He wanders about as if carrying a heap of refuse on his head.
Because of the mind being attached there and because of a low inclination. "Mamā" means "by me"; or rather, this is the reading "mayā.
Even blood gushes from the mouth due to the heart being scorched by mental distress. There is even purging from the stomach for one who has consumed excessive liquor.
Another dhamma that penetrates non-existence belongs only to the Noble Ones (ariyas), and they do not harbor stinginess toward it.
Because it has been entirely abandoned. He said, "and by stinginess regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures," because stinginess regarding the Dhamma of penetration is simply impossible.
Through stinginess regarding physical beauty one becomes ugly; through stinginess regarding the Dhamma one becomes dull-witted, mute, and witless.
The phrase beginning with "Moreover" shows the result corresponding to the action (kamma-sarikkhaka-vipāka) in terms of the five kinds of stinginess. [Through] stinginess regarding one's dwelling...
One is cooked in an iron house because one obstructs the welfare, support, and happiness of others' dwellings.
Through stinginess regarding families, there is little gain, because one obstructs the gains that others might obtain from those families; "little gain" here has the meaning of "lack of gain.
Through stinginess regarding gains, one is reborn in the Excrement Hell, because for the sake of gain, one obstructs the enjoyment of what others might receive. In every respect—
For the hell of excrement is devoid of enjoyment. "There is no beauty" means there is neither the beauty of the physical body nor the beauty of virtue;
even by name alone, both kinds of beauty are absent, and wherever one is reborn, one is indeed deformed.

In a continuum disfigured by stinginess—which has the nature of concealing one's attainments—virtues for the most part find no foothold at all; and even those virtues that might otherwise take root, [fail to do so].
On account of those [defilements] as well, his complexion would not be bright; for they are not apparent in the world, like arrows shot in the night.

Through stinginess regarding the Dhamma (*dhammamacchariya*), one falls into the Kukkuḷa hell. This is abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) because it leads to states of deprivation.
One is certainly not liberated from enmity and the like, because the desire for liberation from them is unattainable due to the phenomena of birth and so forth.
[It is] like [the removal of suffering] for beings through birth and so forth.
In the phrase "I have crossed over doubt here" (*tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā*), the letter *m* serves as a phonetic euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).

"In this question" (*etasmiṃ pañhe*) means in this matter desired to be known, namely, "What are their fetters? Having heard your words, [it was said]: "They are fettered by envy and avarice. (*issāmacchariyasaṃyojanā*)

Having heard this response spoken by you thus, [he says: "Doubts have been crossed" means that the uncertainty regarding the matter asked about has been traversed and removed merely by the recollection of the teaching, not by way of its total eradication; thus he says, "not by way of the Path," and so forth.
This "wavering" has also vanished because of the very disappearance of doubt; it is a specific mode of occurrence belonging to that [doubt].
“‘What is this? What is this?’—this state of doubt (*kaṅkhā*) has also been removed and gone away.
358. The *nidāna* and so forth have their meanings already explained in the commentary on the *Mahānidāna-sutta*.
Because it proceeds by way of concealing and by way of the inability to endure the sharing with others of those dear conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) that have become one’s own possessions.”

Avarice has its source in disagreeable beings and formations; envy has its source in disagreeable beings and formations because it arises by way of intolerance toward those beings who have become one's possessions and toward formations.
For whatever is connected with the disagreeable—even if it be auspicious—is indeed disagreeable to one who is prone to anger. "Both" refers to both avarice and envy.
"Both as a cause" means both the cause of what is dear and the cause of what is not dear. "Dear" means desired. "Keḷāyita" means cherished.
"Mamāyita" means that which has been made one's own and grasped through the sense of "mine.

"He envies" means he is envious (*ussūyati*) by way of being unable to endure another’s acquisition of a dear being, thinking, "What has he gained with this?"—having requested that very same dear being [for himself]. "Oh, may it be for me! means "May it be well for me."
"May this person not have such a dear object"—thus one feels envy and gives rise to jealousy. "Possessing as their own" means cherishing them.
"In regard to what is disliked" means toward beings who are disliked because they cause them distress. "Of him" refers to the person by whom those [objects] were obtained.
"Those" refers to the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) consisting of sentient beings; even if they are unpleasant, they are so because they have arisen from those who are disliked.
"By way of perverse conduct" means by way of grasping things incorrectly. Thinking, "Who else is a recipient of such [gain]? one feels envy while esteeming oneself.
Or, even when such a thing arises for another, one feels envy thinking, "Oh, may they not have such a thing.
This method has not been included here because it follows the method already stated above.
The desire that proceeds by way of seeking sense-objects is the desire for seeking.
The desire conditioned by acquisition is the desire for acquisition. The desire that proceeds by way of enjoyment is the desire for enjoyment.
The desire that proceeds by way of storing up and guarding what has been acquired is the desire for storage. That which pertains only to the present life...
The desire that proceeds by way of answering after having reflected upon the purpose is "desire for answering. Therefore he said, "Which one? and so forth.
Since this fivefold [desire] is in meaning merely the act of craving (*taṇhāyana*), he said, "merely craving" (*taṇhāmattam eva*).
Thus, what was spoken of as "discrimination dependent on gain" refers to the thought of discrimination (*vinicchaya-vitakka*) mentioned in the Mahānidāna Sutta.

"Vitakka" (thought) does not refer to just any kind of thought. Now, in order to demonstrate the aforementioned "discernment-thought" (*vinicchaya-vitakka*) by extracting it according to the method of enumerating meanings, the passage beginning with "Discernment" (*vinicchayo*) was stated.

"One hundred and eight" means one hundred plus eight; and to show that this refers specifically to the hundred modes of craving's wandering (*taṇhā-vicarita*) and not to anything else, the term "craving's wandering" (*taṇhā-vicarita*) was stated.
The "determination of craving" (taṇhā-vinicchaya) is so called because, by means of craving, one determines the object according to the method that will be explained.
The "determination of views" (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya) is so called because, by means of the seeing of views, one determines: "This alone is the truth; all else is vain.

That which is desirable and excellent is "pleasant" (iṭṭha); that which is undesirable and not excellent is "unpleasant" (aniṭṭha). That which is to be loved is "dear" (piya); that which is not to be loved is "not dear" (appiya).
Their determination does not occur by way of craving (*taṇhā*). For by way of craving, one person considers some object to be excellent, another considers it inferior;
one cherishes it, while another does not cherish it. Therefore he said, "That very same [object]," and so forth.

"I shall give"—this should be understood both according to the method already stated regarding the desire for giving, and by way of providing the necessary support for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For that [craving] too has desire as its cause.
They are called "papañcas" because they cause the continuum—in which they themselves arise—to proliferate and expand within saṃsāra.
And when they have arisen in someone, they cause that person to proliferate [conceptually] as "one who is lustful," or "one who is attached," or "one who is wrongly obsessed."

They are called *papañcā* because they embellish [experience]. Since craving and views, when occurring in an excessive degree, cause the person possessing them to fall into a state of negligence (*pamatta*), whereas conceit causes one to fall even into a state of intoxication (*matta*) through such things as pride in birth, it is therefore said: "in the sense of causing a state of intoxication and negligence.
*Saṅkhā* is said to mean a portion; it is so called because it is reckoned or presented as a part. This is because the perception of *papañca*...
By way of their respective doors and by way of their objects, they serve as conditions for thought (vitakka) in their various parts, not in isolation;
therefore, thought is said to have its source in the "proliferating perceptions and formations" (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā).

Alternatively, because proliferating perceptions are divided into many different types, their collection is called "proliferating perceptions and formations. And by the inclusion of the term "proliferating perceptions and formations," [all factors] without exception—
The origin of suffering has been stated because it is the respective cause of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).
"Cessation is peace" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*).

"Appropriate for that" means appropriate and suitable for the attainment of that cessation and peace which is the stilling of the conceptual proliferations of perception (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*); by this, he speaks of insight (*vipassanā*).
In this context, it "goes" or proceeds by way of making the aforementioned cessation its object; thus, it is "going-there" (tatthagāminī).
By this, he refers to the path. Therefore he said: "He asks about the path together with insight.
*Commentary on the Meditation Subject of Feeling* (Vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)

359. Only what was asked was explained. Since Sakka, the lord of the gods, had indeed asked for the practice leading to the cessation of the perception and conceptualization of proliferation (*papañca*), the Blessed One—teaching him the formless meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) as the means for its attainment according to his inclination through the gateway of feeling (*vedanā*)—began with the three feelings.
Thus, by explaining only what was asked, it follows the sequence of the question and is therefore coherent.
And this has been stated. For there is no such thing as a discourse without a logical connection among the Buddhas.
Now, in order to show the reason for teaching the formless meditation subject specifically by way of feeling, it was said: "For of the deities," and so forth.

It should be understood that by the very mention of the subtle nature of the kamma-born body, its state of being exceedingly soft, delicate, and smooth is also already expressed. [The term] *kammaja* means...
The "kamma-born fire" (kammajateja). Its strength arises from its being produced by a sublime meritorious deed and from the digestion of food that is exceedingly heavy, sweet, oily, and pure.

"Even for a single meal" means even for a single meal-period. By the word "melting away," it is shown that due to the weakness of the body born of karma, the strength of the kamma-born fire, and the passing of the proper time for eating, powerful painful sensations arise, which become clearly manifest.

This shows that [feeling] occurs. This is merely an illustration; however, even pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā) becomes clearly manifest to them as it proceeds by way of non-restraint toward increasingly sublime and exquisite objects.

Equanimity (upekkhā) also arises for them only occasionally, and its nature is peaceful and sublime because it occurs only toward desirable-neutral objects. For this very reason, he said, "Therefore," and so forth.
“Form as a meditation subject” (rūpakammaṭṭhāna) means the discernment of form; the meaning is the application of insight by way of form.

“Non-form as a meditation subject” (arūpakammaṭṭhāna)—here too the method is the same. In that regard, although the application of serenity is also included under form as a meditation subject, he shows that what is intended here is the application of insight, saying:
“This very thing is called both ‘discernment of form’ and ‘discernment of non-form.’”

He said: Regarding the "Analysis of the Four Elements," the intention here is that, for the most part, one explains the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by expanding upon the analysis of the four elements.

One speaks only after first showing the meditation subject of materiality [thinking], "In this way, when the meditation subject of materiality is being explained, it will appear clearly and become well-manifested. "By this, even here [in this context], the meditation subject of materiality is [present] in part..."
"...it has indeed been analyzed," they say.
Although here the immaterial meditation subject (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) has come down by way of feeling (vedanā), the immaterial meditation subject is also obtainable by way of other states;
therefore, in order to show it through its divisions, the passage beginning with "It is threefold" was stated. Therein, "adherence" (abhinivesa) means entry.
The meaning is "beginning. For this distinction applies only to the beginning; however, comprehension (*sammasana*) proceeds by grasping all phenomena without exception.
The phrase "when the meditation subject of material form has been grasped" is said with reference to the application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) by way of the material form;
but the application of insight by way of the immaterial is generally for one whose vehicle is serenity (*samathayānika*).
That [object] should be desired; and having first discerned the factors of the first jhāna, one subsequently discerns the remaining phenomena.

Regarding "the first impact": since all mental concomitants are dependent on the mind and are said to be the activity of the mind, contact is called "the mind's first impact. "That object" refers to the meditation subject consisting of form as it has been discerned.

The object. A person in whom contact has arisen, or the aggregate of consciousness and mental factors, having been touched by the object, experiences it at that very same time through the feeling co-nascent with the contact;

yet, because contact is the specific condition for feeling and the rest—just as a lamp is for illumination—it is spoken of as being in the "prior time," which is what is meant by its characteristic of directing [the mind] toward the object. "Touching" means...

[It is so] by way of the mode of contacting the object. For this [consciousness], although it does not adhere to a single part because it is a non-material phenomenon (arūpadhamma), proceeds as if it were contacting and impinging upon the mind and the object—just as the eye contacts visible form and the ear contacts sound.
Thus, it is said to have "impingement as its essence" (saṅghaṭṭanarasa).
"It experiences the object" means that by way of its sovereignty, its lordship, and its status as master, it makes known the flavor of the object.
For while the associated states such as contact function toward the object only partially— since they consist merely of touching and so forth—
feeling functions toward the object without remainder, because it functions by way of the enjoyment of the desirable aspect and so on.
For grasping an object by way of contact and so forth is a partial experience, whereas grasping it by way of being felt is an experience of the whole according to one's desire;

since these modes of grasping possess such natures, one should not urge that, as in the case of feeling, contact and the others must also experience their own lordship through the performance of their respective functions. "Discerning" means by way of delimitation.

It knows specifically. For consciousness functions by delimiting and analyzing the object—just as a man measuring a substance with a nāḷi measure—rather than merely perceiving it like perception (saññā).
Thus, through this [consciousness], there may even occur the discernment of the three characteristics; moreover, among these factors beginning with contact, each respective one becomes manifest.
This should be understood by way of the preliminary stage established through specific conditions.

Thus, even though each [dhamma] is individually manifest, one must comprehend all dhammas that come within the range of comprehension, according to such statements as: "Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known" and "And all things, bhikkhus, are to be fully understood."

Demonstrating this, he said, "In that regard, of whichever... and so forth. Therein, the restriction "only in those consisting of contact as the fifth" applies to the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*), because they are included within that [category] and are thus grasped by the mention of it.
For the mention of "contact as the fifth" is common to all that [belongs to the aggregate of formations] and to every arising of consciousness.
And therein, by the mention of contact and volition (*cetanā*), there is an inclusion of all phenomena belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).

Because volition is predominant among them. For thus, in the *Suttantabhājanīya* of the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), only volition is analyzed by way of "volition born of eye-contact" and so forth, whereas the other aggregates are included by their own specific names.

Regarding the phrase "based on the physical basis" (*vatthunissitā*), here the word "basis" (*vatthu*) refers to the body composed of the four primary elements (*karajakāya*), not to the six bases (*chabbatthu*). How is this so?
"It is understood," he said, "referring to what was stated. But where was it stated? In the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
"That" refers to the body born of karma (*karajakāya*). The statement, "There is no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) apart from the five aggregates," is made by way of the specific context (*adhikāra*).
Otherwise, there certainly exists name that is even apart from the aggregates. "Having ignorance and so forth as their cause" means having ignorance, craving, clinging, and so forth as their causes.

Having stated that strong insight (*balavavipassanā*) consists in "wandering about while comprehending through the sequence of insight that 'it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,'" he then spoke the passage beginning with "He" in order to show the further intensification of that insight and its attainment of distinction. "Here" refers to this *Sakkapañha Sutta*.
And the reason for explaining the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*) here by way of feeling (*vedanā*) is as follows:

This is exactly according to the method explained below. And among the three ways of focusing on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānābhinivesa*) as previously mentioned, the focus on the meditation subject by way of feeling (*vedanā*) is the easiest;
thus, in order to show that feelings are clearly manifest, it is said: "By way of contact," and so forth.
The phrase "it does not become evident" refers to how those deities, headed by Sakka, perceive feelings once they have become clearly manifest.
It was not said by making the other two [feeling-aggregates] likewise;
rather, it is because of the manifestation of these [two] specifically through feeling that the Blessed One’s teaching here commenced by way of feeling.

The phrase "due to the manifestness of the arising of feelings" is stated with reference to pleasant and painful feelings, for their occurrence is gross, whereas that of the other [neutral feeling] is not. Or else, they are to be understood by way of the inclusion of both of them.
The specification of the distinction [between pleasure and pain] should be understood as follows: "For even the occurrence of the other [pain] is evident to the wise;
thus, regarding pleasant and painful feelings... The passage beginning with "When pleasure arises" is an elucidation of the manifest nature of pleasant feeling;
this, however, should be understood by way of the non-concentrated plane. In that context, [the statement] beginning with "The whole body, venerable sir," indeed...

This pleasure is shown to exist with an unappeased nature due to its coarse mode of occurrence; however, because it has the characteristic of gratification (*sāta*), it functions only by supporting both the associated mental states and their physical basis.
The meaning should be understood through the reverse of what was stated in the passage beginning, "When suffering arises," and so forth.
"Difficult to illuminate" (duddīpanā) means they cannot be illuminated by knowledge; the sense is that they are difficult to discern. Therefore he said, "overcome by darkness.
"Darkness" (andhakāra) means like one who has entered into darkness, and it causes blindness for those desiring to know.

Just as the track of a deer on a stone surface is easily marked when the preceding and succeeding parts are level, so too, through the experiences of pleasure and pain regarding desirable and undesirable objects, [the path of kamma] is easily distinguished.
Because it must be inferred among neutral objects, it is said: "That [feeling] becomes manifest as the result of pleasure and pain... and so forth.
Therefore he says, "Just as," etc. Regarding the phrase "for one who grasps by way of method," this is the method:

because there is an experience of the apprehension of an object that is desirable or undesirable, and also an apprehension of an object that is neutral or intermediate, therefore it is not by that [apprehension alone].
It must be without experiencing; that which is experienced therein is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Thus, while form and so forth—which are not being apprehended—are seen to be experienced, when there is the occurrence of consciousness directed toward an object that is neutral, it follows that there can be no experiencing by means of that [consciousness] which is itself not being experienced. For it can indeed be said:
The apprehension of neutral objects is "experience" because it has the nature of apprehension.
However, that which lacks experience regarding desirable or undesirable objects is seen to have the very nature of non-apprehension; that is what is meant by "of such a kind.

"Having excluded" means having set aside, distinguishing it even from those of the same class by saying, "I call it joy," and so forth, [distinguishing it] from other immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
"Having analyzed, one should make it unassociated"—this is the meaning.

And showing that this teaching—which, after explaining the meditation subject of form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), turns back toward the meditation subject of the formless (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of feeling—is found in other suttas as well, depending on the individuals to be trained accordingly, he said "not only... and so forth.

In this regard, the manner in which the teaching is presented in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta will be clarified immediately hereafter; the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness in the Majjhima Nikāya is likewise the same.
In the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta: "Thus, Lord of Devas, when it has been heard by a bhikkhu that 'all phenomena are not worth adhering to,' he directly knows all phenomena; all..."
It is stated thus: "Having directly known the Dhamma, he fully understands all phenomena;

having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, contemplating dispassion...
and so forth. Therefore it was said: "Having established the formless meditation subject by way of feeling..."
...he demonstrated. But regarding the great destruction of craving (*mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya*), [it is said]:

“He who has thus abandoned both attraction and aversion, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
As he does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it...”
It is stated in such passages as, "Whatever delight there is in feelings, that ceases. It is stated in the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* in such passages as, "But how many kinds of feeling are there, lady?
It is stated in the *Mahāvedalla Sutta* in such passages as, "Friend, 'feeling' is said; in what way, friend, is it said to be 'feeling'?
Thus, these are the places where the meditation subject of feeling (*vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) appears in the *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* and others.
It should be stated after extracting [the relevant portion].
It was said, "Having first explained the meditation subject of form (rūpakammaṭṭhāna)," so he says "the meditation subject of form," etc., to show how that is explained here.
It is abbreviated; in what way is it abbreviated? It is merely the object of feeling, for feeling is for the most part directed toward material phenomena as its object.

Because it proceeds by way of the five doors. And for one who says that feeling has its object already established by that [materiality], the phenomena that are its objects have in fact already been grasped beforehand in their actual sense;
thus, by this implication, it is shown that the meditation subject of materiality is what is grasped first here, not because it is grasped as a distinct form. Therefore he said:
"Therefore, it will not have been included in the Canon.
(360) "In two portions" means by way of the categories of what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated.

"Of such a kind" refers to that which leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states; because it is associated with sensual desire, that is called "dependent on the household life."
It is said: "the joy of dwelling at home. "Of desirable things" means of dear things. "Of lovely things" means of things that are desirable.

"Of agreeable things" means of things that increase the mind's delight; for that very reason, they are called "mind-pleasing" (*manorama*) because they delight the mind. "Connected with worldly baits" means dependent on craving and associated with sensual desire.
"Regard[ing them] from the perspective of acquisition" means: "Oh, these have been acquired by me!"...
"Having obtained" refers to one who relishes the objects of form and so forth as they have been obtained. "Past" means that which has passed by. "Ceased" means that which has reached cessation.
"Altered" means departed through the disappearance of its own nature. "Recalling" means reflecting upon them by way of relishing.
"Worldly" means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure; for the strands of sensual pleasure are like a house to the lust of sensual desire.
Here, "home" is intended.
"Of such a kind" refers to that which leads to the decline of unwholesome states and to the increase of wholesome states;
and because it occurs by way of renunciation and so forth, it is associated with renunciation (nekkhamma). Therefore, he said: "joy based on renunciation."
Now, in order to demonstrate that by way of the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself, it was said: "In this regard, what are they? and so forth.
Therein, when renunciation (*nekkhamma*) characterized by insight (*vipassanā*) has been shown, the others are necessarily shown by way of its cause, its fruit, and its purpose;
thus, demonstrating that very characteristic of insight, he said: "In the very nature of forms... and so forth. [He speaks of] "change, fading away, and cessation."
The construction is: "having understood both the state of being subject to transformation through aging, as well as the crumbling and ceasing [of formations] due to aging and death.

"Joy arises" means that after the joy, rapture, and tranquility that have arisen in sequence during the course of the progress of insight (vipassanā), a considerable measure of joy arises thereafter; with reference to this, it was said:
“For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is at peace,
there is a superhuman delight as he correctly discerns the Dhamma.
To whatever extent he comprehends with wisdom the arising and passing away of the aggregates,”
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless. Regarding "by way of renunciation":

this refers to the state of going forth and so on. For one who goes into the presence of the bhikkhus to go forth with the thought, "I shall escape from the suffering of the round of existence," for one who is going forth, for one who is observing the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), and for one who is purifying it—[rapture and gladness are attained].

The practice of one who has undertaken and is living according to the ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa), as well as that of one performing the preliminary exercises for the kasiṇas and so forth—all this is intended here by the term "renunciation" (nekkhamma).
Since access concentration (upacārajjhāna) is generally completed through the recollections (anussati), the phrase "by way of the recollections" was stated;
however, it is further specified as being "by way of the first jhāna and so forth. And herein, just as with the going-forth (pabbajjā)...

Renunciation (nekkhamma) is so called in the sense of going forth from the bondage of the household; likewise, insight and the other [wholesome states] are also renunciation by virtue of being its opposite. Therefore it was said:
“Going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight— All wholesome states whatsoever Are called ‘renunciation.’”
Regarding the word *ca* here, it is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*), since joy (*somanassa*) is what is intended.
It has been stated that "the exposition of the jhānas in the Suttantas proceeds by way of the fourfold method," and thus [the phrase] "by way of the second and third jhānas" is used.

"In two" refers to the two types of joy mentioned as "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*) and "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*).
"In joy with applied thought and sustained thought" refers to the joy belonging to the limited plane or to the joy in the first jhāna.

"In those who are intent upon joy" means in those who have established insight (vipassanā) in joy. By the word "pi" (also), he shows this meaning: that rapture exists even in those whose joy is well-established. "From insight into joyful [states]" means from insight into the occurrence of joy accompanied by applied and sustained thought.

Insight (vipassanā) without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakkāvicārā*) is more excellent, because a distinction in insight is established by way of the phenomena being comprehended (*sammasita-dhamma*), since such specific distinctions are also achieved on the path (*magga*).
This point, however, is to be illustrated by the statement of the Venerable Mahā Datta Thera of Moravāpī, which occurs thus:
"The aggregates that have become the object of insight determine the specific factors of the Noble Path, such as the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*)."

361. "Grief and sorrow rooted in the household life" refers to the grief that arises on account of not obtaining the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), and also that which arises from their loss.
"By contemplating non-attainment" means by way of agitation, thinking "I alone do not obtain them," due to the failure to attain them.
"By recollecting" means by way of recollection, reflecting through such thoughts as, "Alas, that was mine; alas, it is no more."
Therefore he said, "Thus in the six doors," and so forth.
"In the unsurpassed liberations" means in the noble fruit-liberations, such as the fruit of emptiness (*suññatā-phala*). "They long for" (*pihanti*) means they have a longing;
the meaning is that they hope for them. But how can hope arise with reference to supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*)? This, however, should not be viewed in that way.
“‘Because longing occurs there by way of making it an object’—this is because [the person] is not an object [of consciousness], and because the person has not yet been attained.
However, when one establishes longing directed toward the unsurpassed liberation obtained through hearsay, one is said to ‘establish longing for that.
Therefore he said, ‘When indeed shall I... and so forth. When a desirable object has come into range at the six doors, [one contemplates it] by way of impermanence and so on...”

The construction is: “having established insight. By the phrase “on a desirable object,” he shows that this mental grief (*domanassa*) does not arise by its very nature only with reference to undesirable phenomena;
rather, it arises with respect to any object whatsoever through the impact of desire, being caused by the non-attainment of what is wished for.
Thus, in the manner expressed as “When indeed shall I...? [the meaning is shown].

The construction is: "Having established a longing (*piha*), they are unable [to practice] even during this fortnight... [and so on]... they do not grieve after [death]. The phrase "by way of renunciation" (*nekkhammavasena*) is stated with reference to the occurrence [of thought] such as:
"I did not get the opportunity to go forth in this fortnight, in this month, or in this year;
I did not get the opportunity to perform the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*," and so forth. This also applies to the phrases "by way of insight" (*vipassanāvasena*) and the rest.
The application [of the rule] should be understood according to this method.
Since the particle *eva* (only) occurs, it is understood that the restriction applies elsewhere; thus it is said: “In that too... only the grief associated with the household life.

For here, the state of being grief associated with the household life is not restricted to the state of having applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*); rather, it is restricted to the grief associated with the household life itself.

The state of being with initial application and sustained application (*savitakkasavicāratā*) is fixed [for household-based grief] because the particle *eva* serves the purpose of excluding its opposite.
"Household-based mental grief is exclusively with initial application and sustained application; it is not without initial application and sustained application.

However, renunciation-based mental grief may be with initial application and sustained application, or it may be without initial application and sustained application. Mental grief that serves as the cause for that which is with initial application and sustained application...
[It is] sorrow accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra-domanassa*). What is that? It is the sorrow based on the household life;
however, that which arises by way of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth is the cause for sorrow without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra-domanassa*).

And since this method was stated figuratively (*pariyāyavasena*), he said: "But in the direct sense (*nippariyāyena*), however," and so forth. If this is so, why [does the text say]: "And whatever..."?

He says, "But of this," and so forth, because it is stated in the Pāḷi as "without applied thought and without sustained thought. "By way of conceiving" means by way of imagining. It is stated in the Pāḷi. "Therein" refers to that conceiving.
This is the method now being explained. "Being a condition for mental distress" means being a condition for *domanassa*.
For one who wishes to produce the paths and fruits by making access concentration or the first jhāna, etc., the basis, [this applies].
When sorrow arises due to their non-attainment, those [conditions] are called its "conditions"; thus, by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), those phenomena are called "sorrow.

However, one who, having such sorrow arise, does not cast off the burden but gradually intensifies insight (*vipassanā*) and brings forth the states of the Path and Fruition, [those conditions] are called "sorrow" by way of metaphorical designation for the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*).
Showing this meaning, he said, "Here, monks," and so forth. [An objection is raised: "But at that time, only dejection (*domanassa*) arose for him;
the states of insight, the path, and the fruit caused by dejection did not arise.
How then can one speak by applying the conventional designation 'dejection' to that? To this he replied: "By taking it as 'dejection' in order to show the practice of others," and so forth.

"With applied thought and sustained thought, with mental distress" means: with mental distress characterized by applied and sustained thought. "Three-monthly" (*temāsikā*) means that which is to be accomplished in three months; it refers to that which lasts for three months.

These practice paths, beginning with the three-monthly, are to be understood according to whether one's faculties are superior, medium, or dull as they proceed in such a manner, or alternatively, according to whether one's exertion is superior, medium, or dull. "He tends" means he devotes himself to wakefulness (*jāgarika*).
The commentary on the story of the Elder Mahāsiva:
"In great assemblies numbering two thousand or three thousand" refers to the number of people.

"Commentary Elders" (*aṭṭhakathātherā*) means those elders who inquire about the meaning of the commentaries. "On the way back" means on the path returning from the village to the monastery after receiving almsfood. "Having had them take three or four hot drinks" refers to three or four types of warm beverages.
"With some elaboration" means with some elaboration consisting of bodily activity. He formed a perception because he did not notice someone walking behind him at night.
But why did the Elder go without informing his pupils? To this he said, "The Elder, it is said," and so forth. When he asks, "What is called Arahantship?
he speaks with reference to the fact that its attainment is not difficult. "With the four postures" means with all four.
For one who is engaged in the modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), the intention is: "Therefore, until the attainment of Arahatship, I shall renounce lying down.

"Is this suitable for you?"—having become stirred with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thus encouraging his energy, he resolved upon Arahatship because his insight had been well-practiced over such a long time and his knowledge had reached maturity.

"He rubbed" (*parimajji*) means he wiped. Some, however, explain the meaning as: "'He rubbed' means that after turning it over, he took hold of it while it was being washed by the Elder and washed it himself."
The object of insight (vipassanā) refers to access concentration, the first jhāna, and so forth.

Regarding the phrases "with applied thought and sustained thought, with mental distress," and so on, it should be understood according to the method already explained for the case of mental joy (somanassa).
362. "Of such a kind" means that which leads to the overcoming of unwholesome states and to the decline of wholesome states—of such a kind.

Furthermore, because it is associated with sensual desire, it is called "domestic" (*gehasita*); thus he says, "equanimity based on the domestic" (*gehasitaupekkhā*). Regarding the terms "of the fool" (*bālassa*) and so forth:
one is a "fool" (*bāla*) due to being joined with the qualities that characterize a fool; one is "deluded" (*mūḷha*) due to being confused regarding one's own welfare and the welfare of others;

one is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*) due to causes such as generating the many defilements and so forth; and one is "not victorious over the flood" (*anodhijina*) because one has not conquered the floods of defilement by means of the paths that conquer the floods.
Because he has conquered the floods (*oghajina*) by conquering the defilements (*kilesa*) in their entirety, this excludes his being a trainee (*sekkha*).
Because he has not yet conquered the resultant [kamma] that would arise beyond the seventh existence, he is "one who has not conquered the result" (*avipākajina*);

alternatively, because the Arahants are "conquerors of the result" (*vipākajina*) due to their state of non-relinking (*appaṭisandhika*), this excludes his being one beyond training (*asekkha*). [This applies] to all [beings] regarding the many dangers...

Because they do not see the danger [in things], due to their habit of not seeing the danger in delusion—the root of evil states—they are "unlearned" (assutavato) because they lack both scriptural tradition (āgama) and realization (adhigama).
Such a person is, in one sense, called an "ordinary worldling" (andhaputhujjana);

thus, to demonstrate his status as an ordinary worldling, it is stated again: "of the worldling" (puthujjanassa). "Of such a kind" means characterized by the aforementioned manner, preceded by delusion.
"It does not transcend form" means it is not a cause for the surmounting of forms; the intention is that it does not transcend the defilements regarding the object of form.

Since the equanimity associated with greed—which occurs by way of indifference toward the object due to the lack of clear manifestation of knowledge—is what is intended here, [the author], showing an object suitable for that greed, says:
He said, "In regard to a desirable object. Because they do not transcend it due to a failure to see its danger, they become stuck right there by observing its gratification.
Through the power of attachment—that is, greed—and because it is difficult to release from, they arise as if bound by that [attachment].
"Of such a kind" means that which leads to the abandoning of unwholesome states and to the increase of wholesome states; such is it.
However, because it proceeds by way of renunciation such as going forth (pabbajjā), he said, "based on renunciation" (*nekkhammasitā*).

Now, in order to show that by means of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the passage beginning with "In this regard, what is... was stated; its meaning should be understood according to the method explained above.
She transcends form (*rūpa*) because she correctly perceives the danger (*ādīnava*) in form. From the destruction of form...
Because it cannot be overcome by defilements. "Desirable" means a desirable object, both by its intrinsic nature and by way of intention.

"Of one who is not lustful" means of one who does not lust, who does not arouse lust. "Of one who is not hateful toward the undesirable"—the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated previously.
"Not viewing with equanimity" (*asamapekkhanam*) means not viewing evenly, rightly, and thoroughly; that [lack of equanimity] occurs toward the desirable, the undesirable, and the neutral.

Since the fool experiences [craving] toward both the desirable and the undesirable as if they were equal, the text does not say "toward the desirable, the undesirable, and the neutral," but rather says "not being deluded by non-equanimity.
The meaning is: for one who is deluded by way of non-equanimity toward all three kinds of objects.

This refers to equanimity associated with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Equanimity based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is similar in nature to feeling; it functions in the mode of neutrality (*udāsīna*).
It is similar to the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā) in its occurrence.

Here, by the phrase "upekkhā vā," it is precisely that which is taken as "upekkhā" in this description of equanimity. Therefore, because even the equanimity of mental neutrality (tatramajjhattupekkhā) is included here by the term "upekkhā," it is said with reference to that: "the equanimity arising by way of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas."

“In that equanimity based on renunciation” (*tāyapi nekkhammasitaupekkhāya*) is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). The passage beginning with “That which by way of renunciation” is already clear, as it follows the method explained below.

If at that time Sakka possessed only the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), then why did the Blessed One extend his teaching all the way to Arahantship? To this he says: “For Buddhas,” and so forth. “Young Sakka” (*taruṇasakko*) means one who is new or recent.
Sakka has appeared. For it is with reference to his recent appearance that he is called "the young Sakka"; he possesses neither childhood nor old age.
"The place gone to and come from" refers to the cause of going and coming. It is not discerned; it is not apprehended.
For when those dwelling in the womb pass away, the material form born of kamma vanishes, and immediately thereafter, so too do the forms born of mind and born of nutriment.
Because of the absence of conditions, however, that which is born of the primary elements (utuja) continues its lineage for a very long time, becoming either broken, withered, scorched, or worn away;

but it is not so for the devas. For because they are of apparitional birth (opapātika), when the materiality born of kamma disappears, the remaining materiality of the continuity of the sixfold base also disappears along with it. Therefore he said: "The going out of the lamp’s flame..."
“It was as if [he were] so. The other deities did not know [this], because he had been reborn in that very same place once again in the form of Sakka’s own body.
“In three places” means at the points where joy, grief, and equanimity are relinquished.
“Only the fruit already produced” means precisely the supramundane path and fruit, which constitute the fruit produced by the path of approach, just as cream is produced from ghee.
It has been explained. Like a bird, having seized something graspable, having flown up and soared aloft—of this noble Dhamma known as the path and its fruition.
This concludes the commentary on the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

“*Pātimokkhasaṃvarāya* means *for the restraint of virtue that consists of the Pātimokkha*; this is the meaning here,” he said, [explaining] “*for the restraint of virtue that is supreme and foremost*.
Regarding this, the Elder Suma, who dwelt in the Dīghavāpi Monastery, says: “The Pātimokkha virtue is the foremost virtue among all virtues.
However, his pupil, the Elder Cūḷanāga, who was versed in the Three Piṭakas, says: “The Pātimokkha restraint itself is the virtue; as for the others...”
Not admitting that there is such a thing as the meaning of "virtue" as it has been described, [he holds that] what is called restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors;
purity of livelihood is merely the procuring of requisites in a righteous and equitable manner;
and dependence on requisites is merely the use of requisites already obtained after reflecting, "This is for my benefit. In the ultimate sense, however, it is only the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
It is virtue (sīla). For one whose [precept] is broken is incapable of guarding the others and thus becomes non-virtuous;
whereas one who is entirely healthy is capable of guarding the rest and is therefore "endowed with virtue" (sampannasīla).
Thus, because the others are its attendants, and because they are entirely or partially included within it, that alone is the primary virtue.
He said, "It is for the sake of the restraint of the highest, foremost virtue.

In this regard, just as previously—when asked by Sakka for the practice leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*)—the Blessed One analyzed feeling, which is the root of both conceptual proliferations and that practice, and taught the practice by way of abandoning the phenomena of defilement in accordance with Sakka's inclination; so too [is it here].
"Completion of the qualities of purification": thus, when the Blessed One was asked about the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), which is the very root of that same practice,

he spoke the passage beginning with "bodily conduct as well" in order to show— by way of abandoning the factors of defilement— the completion of the qualities of purification, both *how* and *from what* that [virtue] is purified, according to the inclination of Sakka.

Having done so. Regarding the discourse on virtue (*sīla*), the reason for explaining the types of bodily conduct that are not to be practiced has already been stated; therefore, "by way of courses of action" (*kammapatha-vasena*) means by way of the wholesome and unwholesome courses of action.

Furthermore, "by way of courses of action" means by way of the analysis of those courses of action; for even those forms of bodily misconduct and so forth that have not yet attained the status of a full course of action [are included].
Here, it is stated that the state of being an improper bodily conduct and so forth belongs to those things that are not to be cultivated, such as the "things not to be cultivated" (asevitabba).

"By way of designation" (paṇṇattivasena) means by way of the designation of the training rules (sikkhāpada). For whenever there is a particular abstention (veramaṇī), explaining both of these by way of designation is what is called "speaking by way of designation.
Therefore he said, "In the door of the body," and so forth. "Transgression of the training rule" (sikkhāpadavītikkama) is that by which one transgresses a training rule.
The unwholesome state that arises in the manner of transgressing a training rule (sikkhāpada) is what constitutes the state of having an improper bodily conduct and so forth.
Non-transgression (avītikkama) is the opposite of transgression; it is called non-transgression because one does not transgress by means of it—that is, virtue (sīla).
Livelihood (ājīva) is that by which one seeks [sustenance] wrongly or rightly; in its essential meaning, it is the activity of searching for the requisites of life.
It is the gatekeeper of body and speech. If this is so, why is it mentioned separately? He says, "Because," and so forth.
Noble seeking (*ariyapariyesanā*) is seeking that is faultless; it is noble seeking because it is to be sought after by the noble ones (*ariya*), meaning by the virtuous.
By the reverse of what has been stated, ignoble seeking (*anariyapariyesanā*) is to be understood.
"Subject to birth" means having the nature of being born, having the characteristic of arising. "Subject to aging" means having the nature of aging.

"Subject to illness" means having the nature of illness. "Subject to death" means having the nature of dying. "Subject to sorrow" means having the nature of grieving. "Subject to defilement" means having the nature of becoming defiled.
"Son and wife" means both son and wife. This method applies everywhere. Their designation is made as a single unit by way of a dvanda compound.
Regarding "gold and silver": here, because it does not undergo alteration and remains entirely as gold, "gold" (*jātarūpa*) means refined gold.
Because it possesses a white nature, it is called "silver" (*rajata*), that is, *rūpiya*. Here...
However, setting aside gold, whatever is fit for use or enjoyment— such as coins used in commerce— is included under the term "silver.
With the words, "These acquisitions, monks, are subject to birth," he shows that these so-called acquisitions of the strands of sensual pleasure are all indeed subject to birth.
In the section on the nature of disease (*byādhidhammavāra*) and others, gold and silver are not included. For this [form], there are no diseases such as headaches;
nor is there death, reckoned as passing away, as there is for sentient beings; nor does sorrow arise.
"Death, reckoned as passing away," refers to the cessation of the aggregates included within a single existence; that does not exist for it, though momentary cessation does.
It is indeed obtained at every moment. However, because it is defiled by the corruptions such as lust (*rāga*), gold is included in the section on "states subject to corruption" (*saṅkilesadhamma*);

likewise, because it is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*), it is included in the section on "states subject to birth" (*jātidhamma*); and because it decays after taking up impurities, it is included in the section on "states subject to aging" (*jarādhamma*).
It is not to be sought after by the Noble Ones (*ariya*); thus, it is also called the "un-Noble search" (*anariyapariyesanā*).

Now, in order to show that [unwholesome state] by way of improper search (*esanā*) as well, the passage beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) was stated. In this same manner, the meaning should also be understood for the bright side (*sukkapakkha*).

"Seeking the requisites" refers to searching for weapons, poison, and so forth; "performance by way of application" refers to the undertaking of the means, the generation of the corresponding effort, and the production of such an approach;
"going for the sake of killing living beings, etc."—the word *kāla* (time/occasion) should be applied to each of these individually.
“From the time of seeking the requisites, from the time of making the effort, and from the time of setting out.
The other refers to the bodily conduct and so forth described as “to be cultivated. One must also arouse the mind.
For when the mind has been thus aroused, if the necessary conditions are present, one who performs such effort and exertion reaches the pinnacle of practice.
He grasps it. Therefore he said: “Monks, I say that even the mere arising of a thought is of great benefit regarding wholesome states.
Now, in order to show what has reached its culmination—namely, what is not to be cultivated and what is to be cultivated—he said “Furthermore,” and so forth.

By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “schism in the Saṅgha, etc.,” he includes such things as shedding blood [from a Buddha]. Only by means of attending upon the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṅgha...
"Success in attending upon the jewel of the Dhamma" refers to the statement: "by way of going to attend upon the Three Jewels two or three times a day.
"Dispatching archers" means sending out men who are archers. By the word "etcetera," he includes such things as requesting the five boons.
"Having won over Ajātasattu, [it refers to] making a request among families for one whose gain and honor have declined by way of producing profit."
For those pursuing such ignoble quests as these. "For the sake of fulfillment" means for the purpose of fulfillment.
For it is by way of the supreme path and its fruit that there is fulfillment of all things to be cultivated; therefore, all the preliminary practices are for that purpose.
Furthermore, even the restraint of the Pātimokkha becomes complete only through the supreme path; thus, it is for that purpose [that the training is undertaken].
Having explained the preliminary practice, he concludes by saying: "The Pātimokkha...

[is] the restraint of the sense faculties. 365. Regarding the commentary on the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*): "For the closing of the sense faculties" means for the purpose of covering the sense faculties. And the sense faculties are the doors, such as the eye and so forth.
"Guarding the doors of the sense faculties" means that their covering and restraint is a protection against the arising of unwholesome states; thus he said, "by way of guarding the doors.

Non-restraint consists in the lack of guarding the doors of the sense faculties through the pursuit of forms and so forth that should not be cultivated, whereas purity of cleansing states consists in the abandoning of defiled states.
Granted, forms and so forth that should not be cultivated are also shown in the Canon, yet by Sakka, the practice for the sake of sense-faculty restraint was [emphasized].

Regarding the word "asked": in order to show that very point by way of exclusion, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The passage beginning with 'visible forms cognizable by the eye' was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating restraint of the faculties by way of forms, etc., that are to be cultivated.

Having said, "He remained silent," the phrase beginning with "even though he wished to speak" was spoken to clarify the reason for his silence by way of contrast (*vyatireka*). "He" refers to Sakka, the lord of the gods.
"Form" refers to the form base (*rūpāyatana*); its "non-habituation" means simply not seeing it, which is why he said, "it should not be cultivated and should not be seen.

However, when one sees the form belonging to the continuum of a living being, either the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) becomes established by way of attention to repulsiveness, or else confidence (*pasāda*) arises by way of the unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariya*), or else through the conviction in the result of kamma.
Having been sacrificed [in the fire of analysis], there is either the attainment of the perception of impermanence through the discernment of the mode of non-existence.

It is called a "syllable" (*akkhara*) because it is articulated (*akkharana*). That very thing, when elevated by its uninterrupted arising into what is termed a "phrase" or "sentence," manifests the intended meaning;
thus it is called "expression" (*byañjana*). This occurs by way of synonyms found in poetry, drama, and so forth, as well as by way of vocal utterance.
And with reference to that which stands by way of the state of being variegated through the mental diversity arising from conceptualization based on the arrangement of various [sounds], he said:
"When one hears a sound that is a syllable of mind (*cittakkhara*) or a phoneme of mind (*cittabyañjana*), lust and so forth arise.
"Dependent on meaning" means dependent on the welfare pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*). "Dependent on the Dhamma" means dependent on the Dhamma of turning away (*vivaṭṭadhamma*).
Or it is based on the Dhamma of the supramundane Triple Gem. *Pasāda* means faith in the Triple Gem, as well as faith in the results of kamma.
*Nibbidā vā* means weariness with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of the perception of impermanence and so forth.
