That which is practiced by way of obstructing the [proper] scent and flavor and so forth is called "not to be practiced" because it is a practice undertaken through improper method (*ayoniso*). [By contrast,] through proper method (*yoniso*)...
That which is practiced after having been reflected upon is called "to be cultivated" because it is grasped by means of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). Therefore it is said:
"The odor which one smells," and so forth.

But "that which one touches" refers to that tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*) which is to be cultivated, even though one touches it while it is still unmanifested (*anipphanna*). [Through this] comes the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).
And there is the reaching of the summit of the practice of wakefulness. And energy is well-exerted through the exalting of the fourth noble lineage.
And the subsequent [instruction]... is assisted by being directed toward right practice.
Those mental phenomena, classified as desirable and so forth, which come into the range of one who is attending to and adverting to them.
The analysis of the phrase "mental phenomena cognizable by the mind" (*manoviññeyyā dhammā*) should be understood as follows:

for one who attends [to the object] by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, those mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that come into the range of perception—such as these are to be cultivated; this is the construction.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the rest, as well as impermanence (*anicca*) and the rest, is to be seen. "The Dhamma of the three elders" refers to the practices that will now be described.

The three elders had mental objects cognizable by the mind. Thinking, "They did not allow [the mind] to run outside," [it is understood that] during these three months, whenever their minds arose free from the meditation subject, they did so only with reference to forms and so forth that had already come within the inner courtyard;
and since dissimilar forms and so forth could not possibly exist within the inner courtyard, their minds [remained] through the suppression of wandering thoughts.

This shows that they will not allow [the mind] to run outward. From the dwelling-house—that is, from the inner chamber where one dwells; from the five internal aggregates belonging to oneself, which are the objective field of insight (vipassanā).
It is said that the Elder performs every task he must do by way of the primary focus on his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). 366.
Because of its undivided state through non-delusive clear comprehension (asammoha-sampajañña), it is "one-sided" (ekanta) because it has only one end; or, it is a "one-sided doctrine" (ekantavāda).
These are their absolute doctrines. Therefore he said, "They speak only one [thing]," meaning they have non-different doctrines. "Of one conduct" means having identical conduct.
"Of one conviction" means having identical convictions. "Of one conclusion" means having identical final goals.
Thus, Sakka [summarized] what he had previously heard regarding the various doctrines, conducts, convictions, and conclusions of the many recluses and brahmins.

Now, having stood firm after knowing [the world] to be essence-less through the penetration of the Truths, he wishes to know the reason for that and therefore asks him by way of contrast with the words, "Are all phenomena indeed...?
Here, "elements" (*dhātu*) is said by eliding the latter member of the compound *ajjhāsayadhātu*; and in meaning, *ajjhāsayadhātu* is simply *ajjhāsaya* (inclination).

Thus he said: "They have diverse inclinations, they have manifold inclinations. The statement, "When one wishes to go, another wishes to stand," was spoken by way of illustration in order to show that even regarding modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), beings with a single inclination are rare, let alone regarding their acquired views (*laddhi*).
"Whatever inclination they have" means whatever inclination they have, such as eternalism and so forth.
"They adhere" means that, through the dogmatic adherence to their respective views, they turn toward them and settle upon them with an inability to relinquish, grasping them with a firm hold.
"By means of strength and misapprehension" means by the strength of their view and by the misapprehension of their view.
"Grasping firmly" means taking up an exceedingly tight hold. "They express" means according to what they have adhered to.
They proclaim their own views, cause others to grasp them, and establish them. Therefore he said, “they speak of, illuminate, and praise it,” meaning they shout it out.
Having gone beyond the extremes, they are *accanta*; those for whom the ultimate goal (*niṭṭhā*) is absolute are *accantaniṭṭhā*. “Of all” means of all recluses and brahmins.

Nibbāna is also called “the security from bondage” (*yogakkhema*) because it is not afflicted by any of the four bonds (*yoga*). Although one should say “those who have reached the absolute security from bondage” (*accantayogakkhemā*), [the text uses the form *accantaniṭṭhā*].
By the designation with the vowel *i*, it is said: "one who has attained ultimate security from bondage" (*accantayogakkhemī*);
or, because they possess ultimate security from bondage, they are called "those who have attained ultimate security from bondage. They "move" (*caranti*) means they approach or attain [the goal].

It is also a name for Nibbāna because one reaches the end of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), whereby one exhausts and completely wears away [that suffering]—thus it is "the end" (*pariyosāna*).

“Sankhināti” means he exhausts by means of complete eradication. “Vināseti” means he brings about its total disappearance from that very point. “Vimuttā” means liberated through a specific release consisting of an absolute departure from the suffering of saṃsāra.
Regarding the statement, “Envy and avarice are one question,” one might ask: is not envy and avarice the answer? This is true;
however, that which is intended to be known is the question, and that very thing is what is answered. Therefore, there is no fault here; otherwise, [the distinction would be lost].
It might be like answering a question about a *labuja* fruit when one has been asked about a *amba* fruit; thus, he explains the answer by means of the heading of the question.
For in this way, only the words of the answer—beginning with "the dear and the not dear"—are taken up, and the same method applies to such passages as "one [sees] the dear and the not dear.

By the phrase "proliferation-perception" (*papañca-saññā*), it is said that "proliferations" (*papañcā*) themselves are expressed by means of the heading "perception"; hence he says, "proliferation is one. Herein...

And just as three questions arose because the inquiry into *pātimokkha-saṃvara* was answered by way of the classification of bodily conduct and so forth, so too there would be six questions because the inquiry into *indriya-saṃvara* was answered by way of the classification of visible forms and so forth.
That being the case, there would be nineteen questions; however, since the question was made as one by virtue of the commonality of "restraint of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvaratā*), thus...

If it were because of the commonality of being inquiries regarding the restraint of the Pātimokkha, then those three [questions] would also be just one question, and thus all twelve questions would become one; this is not so.
For when the bodily conduct and so forth are explained in detail, an immeasurable analysis is possible to provide due to their vast scope. The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is the exposition of that.
However, when form and the other [aggregates] are explained in detail, such a detailed classification cannot be provided because their scope is narrow.

Thus, due to its vast scope, the inquiry into the restraint of the Pātimokkha was formulated as three questions, whereas the inquiry into the restraint of the sense faculties, being of narrow scope, was formulated as only one question.
Therefore it is said: "There are fourteen great questions."

367. "In the sense of moving" means in the sense of shaking. For craving itself moves because it lacks stability in its occurrence through the modes of sensual lust, lust for form, lust for the formless, and so forth;
and it causes that very continuum in which it arises to move by dragging it along into states of existence and the like.
Therefore, in the sense of moving, craving is called *ejā* (the mover). "In the sense of oppressing" means in the sense of afflicting each respective [being].
By way of being the cause of suffering. In the sense of corrupting (*padussana*):

it is a "boil" (*gaṇḍa*) in the sense of being a manifold corruption through the nature of unrighteous passion (*adhamma-rāga*) and so forth, by way of being face-to-face or behind one's back, and by the trickling out of the impurity of the defilements (*kilesa*). In the sense of having entered:
in the sense of entering because the underlying tendency (*āsaya*) is difficult to extract. It "draws" means it leads [one] according to its own inclination. "High and low" (*uccāvaca*)...

The state of being sublime and the state of being inferior. Regarding those ascetics and brahmins: there is also a Pāli reading, “yesāhaṃ,” for which some explain the meaning as “yesaṃ ahaṃ” (of whom I am).
“Evaṃ” means in accordance with what was heard and in accordance with what was learned.

“But as for me, venerable sir, although I am a teacher of the Dhamma to other ascetics and brahmins, I am a disciple of the Blessed One... [and so on] ...one whose destiny is toward full enlightenment.”
In this way, he makes known his own state of being a stream-enterer.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Joy (Somanassapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā): 368.
"He has entered" (*samāpanno*) means he has plunged in, like a battle-array that has spread out. "They conquered" (*jiniṃsu*) means as [the gods did] so that the asuras would not [return].
They were unable to lift up their heads; thus, showing that the gods had indeed been victorious, he said: "The gods defeated the asuras so that they would not return again.
For such a victory resulted in the attainment of an extraordinary sense of well-being (*vedanā*). Regarding the "two kinds of nutritive essence" (*ojā*):
it refers to the two types, celestial and asuran. Only the gods shall enjoy it, because there is no entry for the asuras.
“*Daṇḍāvacara*” means that which is within the range of punishment or an obstruction; “*sadaṇḍāvacara*” means together with that which is within the range of punishment.
The meaning is: it is to be accomplished either by striking with a staff or by obstructing.

“In this very place” means in this very Indasāla Cave. “Of me who was formerly a deva” means of me, Sakka, who was formerly a deva. “Being [still] so” means even now, being Sakka, my life has been regained once more.
“Divine bodies” means celestial; he says “divine personal existences” (attabhāvā) because they are bodies comprised of the five aggregates.

By the phrase “I shall enter the womb unconfused,” he shows that for noble disciples (ariyasāvakā), unlike the blind worldlings (andhaputhujjana), there is neither death in delusion nor entry into the womb without full awareness;
rather, there is both death without delusion and entry into the womb with full awareness. Noble disciples...
Because their destiny is fixed, they arise only in the happy realms; even there, when arising among humans, they will take rebirth in noble families.
Sakka’s own aspiration was likewise. Therefore it is said in the Pāḷi: “Where my mind delights”;
referring to that, he said, “Wherever for me,” and so forth. Moreover, Sakka, by means of his own divine power...
One is indeed able to know such a person.
"By reason" means by a fitting reason, one that is appropriate for the state of a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). Therefore he said, "by an equal [reason].
He speaks with reference to the path of the once-returner (sakadāgāmimagga), because the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga) will be explained under the sixth purpose.
“Desirous of knowing” means desirous of penetrating a distinction not yet attained. “Will be within the human world” is because there will be no further rebirth as a human.
“Once again” means having arisen among humans and passed away from there, once again. “In this Tāvatiṃsa heaven. To the question “What kind of supreme one? he says: “Sakka,” and so forth.
"In my final existence" means in my last existence, at the very end of all existences. By the word "by life-span," he includes all qualities such as beauty and so forth that coexist with it.
And by the word "by wisdom," he includes all qualities such as faith, mindfulness, energy, and so forth.
"In that personal identity" means in that final Sakyan identity. "Having become one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm" refers to the state of one who attains parinibbāna in the interval and so forth.
Without proceeding to [any other stage], being one who goes upstream exclusively toward the Akanittha realm, he is reborn successively in Aviha and the other heavens.

He says, "That shall be my dwelling," thus saying this. To explain the meaning stated in brief—"He will be reborn in Aviha and so forth"—the passage beginning with "It is said that he... was spoken. And this method is not only...
He spoke the words beginning with "Sakka, the king of the gods" in order to show that this [state] belongs not only to Sakka, but indeed also to great merchants and great female lay disciples.

370. Because his underlying aspiration was not yet fulfilled—due to the attainment of worldly existence and the attainment of Nibbāna—he remained with his desires unaccomplished, standing as one who merely wished to attain various [states]. "And those recluses" means those who have gone forth. "Dwelling in seclusion" means...
"I think they dwell having cultivated the threefold seclusion.
"Attainment" (*sampādanā*) means the attainment of the Path, its bringing about, its being brought to perfection.
"Failure" (*virādhanā*) means non-fulfillment, practice by an improper means. "They do not succeed" (*na sambhonti*) means they do not achieve it. Regarding the meaning as asked:
"Inability" means simply the lack of capacity to speak correctly; thus he said, "being unable to speak after having mastered [the subject].
"Therefore" means because of having the same lineage as the Sun (Ādicca). For this very reason he said, "by name Ādicca by lineage," therefore.
He whose kinsman is the Sun is Ādiccabandhu; or alternatively, he who is the kinsman of the Sun is Ādiccabandhu—the Blessed One.
To him, the Kinsman of the Sun. For the Blessed One is the legitimate son of the Buddha by virtue of his being a stream-enterer. Therefore it was said:
"He who makes light in the midst of darkness, Vairocana, the radiant one of blazing splendor;"
"Do not swallow me, Rāhu, as you move through the sky;
release my progeny, O Rāhu, the Sun! Thus, regarding "Sāma," it refers to the application of oneself;
for the application of oneself by a disciple to the Teacher is indeed what is called "Sāmaññapayoga" (the meeting/application). Therefore, he said, "We pay homage."
"Having touched the earth" means having touched the earth while filled with joy, thinking, "While sitting upon this very earth,
I have attained this marvelous Dhamma," and while filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, thinking, "Upon this very earth has arisen such a marvelous and wonderful Jewel of the Buddha.
"Questions long desired" means for the sake of uprooting doubts that had lain dormant for a long time.
"Perhaps I might be able to question the Blessed One?"—thus was his question formulated through such a longing.
Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Points) on the commentary to the *Sakkapañha Sutta*.
9. Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta: Explanation of the Section on the Summary (Uddesavāra). 373.
"Why did the Blessed One speak this sutta?"—with these words, he asks about the uncommon origin (*asādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna*), as well as the common [origin].
However, without specifying it as "manifest," it was stated as "of the inhabitants of the Kurū kingdom" and so forth. For the "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is the source of the teaching;
that is twofold, by way of the distinction between common and uncommon. The common [origin] is also twofold, by way of the distinction between internal and external.
Therein, the internal common origin is the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Blessed One. For, being impelled by that—
The Blessed One’s mind was inclined toward teaching the Dhamma to those who were ready to be trained. As it is said:
“Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,” and so forth.
However, the external, common cause is known as the entreaty of the Great Brahmā Sahampati, who was accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand Great Brahmās. And thus it has been said:
“Having understood Brahmā’s entreaty”: for after that entreaty, having allayed the state of indolence born from reflecting on the Dhamma, the Blessed One became intent on teaching the Dhamma.
And just as with Great Compassion, so too the knowledge of the Ten Powers and other such qualities should be mentioned as being internal origins for the teaching. For everything...

Having understood, as they truly are, the phenomena to be known, the manner in which they are to be taught, and the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings, the Blessed One—through his skill regarding what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna) and so forth—set forth a diverse method of teaching in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained.
Furthermore, that which is unique [to the Buddha] is twofold, distinguished as internal and external. Therein, the internal is that great compassion by which...
One should understand both that by which this discourse was set forth—the knowledge of teaching—and the external circumstances;
to show the latter, he said, "of the inhabitants of the Kururaṭṭha country," and so forth. Therefore it was said, "He asks about the uncommon origin";
by this, among the four ways of presenting a discourse—those arising from one's own inclination and so on—it is the specific presentation of the discourse (*suttanikkhepa*) that is asked about.

The other [commentator] says, "It happens," and by means of the passage beginning with "of the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kuru," he shows that "the presentation of this sutta is due to the inclinations of others.

It is said that at that time, the kingdom of Kuru was indeed endowed with the excellence of climate and so forth, because for the most part the beings dwelling there were well-practiced through their possession of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the power of merit performed in the past. Therefore it is stated: "because of the perfection of the conditions of climate and so forth."
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), he includes the excellence of food and other such things. Some, however, say:

"Due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of having previously performed the duties and religious observances of Kuru, that kingdom—while being for the most part endowed with a favorable climate and so on, much like Uttarakuru—became during the time of the Blessed One exceptionally possessed of suitable weather and other conditions.
"Cittasarīrakallatāya" means by way of the health of both the mind and the body.
"Those whose power of wisdom has been assisted" means those who have obtained the supportive efficacy of knowledge, or those in whom the fire of wisdom has been repeatedly cultivated.

"In twenty-one places" refers to fourteen places by way of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), one place by way of contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*), likewise one place by way of contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*), and five places by way of contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*); thus, in twenty-one [places].

Regarding the "stages": "Having included the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) within Arahantship" means that, by way of the teaching, he has included it within Arahantship in such a way that the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths leads to the attainment of Arahantship.

Just as various flowers such as jasmine and champak, or the seven treasures such as gems and pearls, when placed within golden boxes or golden caskets, [shine] according to the excellence of the receptacle;...

They shine with distinction and perform their functions because of their pleasant nature; likewise, this teaching of the Blessed One, given to the assembly dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru—which has become a distinguished vessel through its perfection in virtue, vision, and so forth—shines even more brightly and performs its function.
By the words beginning with "Just as a man," he shows this meaning. "Therein" means in the kingdom of Kuru.

"By nature" means both by their own inherent disposition and even prior to this teaching of the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*; this is the intended meaning. "They dwell devotedly" means they apply themselves to the practice of meditation in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction.

"With a neglected selfhood" means that it is not fitting to live with a mind that is negligent—that is, a mind that does not direct itself toward any appropriate mental attention (such as regarding things as impermanent) due to its lack of restraint, but instead remains attached to objects such as forms; [this constitutes] dwelling in negligence.
The intention is that, having abandoned [these], one should become heedful.

Regarding the term *ekāyano*: here the word *ayana* is a synonym for "path. To show that it is not merely a synonym for "going" (*ayana*), but rather that there are many other synonyms for "path" as well, he provides the citation of the words beginning with "of the path," provided that it is indeed a synonym for "path."
Regarding the objection, "Why is the word *ayana* (way) further called 'path' (*magga*)?", he says "Therefore," and so forth.
Therein, "one path" means it is indeed one single path; for there is no other path leading to Nibbāna. [Objection:

Is it not the case that the establishment of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is intended here as the path, while there are many other path-factors (*maggadhamma*) besides it? [Response: True, they exist; however, those...
By the very mention of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), [the other factors] are included because they are inseparable from them.

For while knowledge, energy, and so forth are mentioned in the detailed exposition (niddesa), it should be understood that their inclusion under mindfulness alone in the summary (uddesa) is due to the inclinations of those to be trained.
By the phrase "not being a forked path," he shows that this path, like its lack of multiple routes, likewise lacks the quality of not leading to Nibbāna.

"By one" means by one who is without a companion. This state of being without a companion is twofold: either by the absence of a second person, which is called "physical seclusion" (*vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā*);
or by the absence of craving as a second [mental associate], which is called "mental seclusion" (*pavivittacittatā*). Therefore he said, "by one who is physically secluded and mentally secluded.
Even a superior person in the world is called "one," as in such expressions as, "I will do your work alone for a single day."

He said: “‘Of one’ means ‘of the best. If the meaning of *ayana* (going) is the sense of escape from *saṃsāra*, then since this is common to others as well who possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), how can it be [the path] of the Blessed One alone?
To this he replied with the words beginning “Even though,” and so forth. In the phrase “In this very...,” the particle *kho* is used for emphasis;
therefore, the meaning is “in this very [path]. For this is merely a distinction in teaching, namely, that it is called either “the path” or...
Or it is called "the way" (*ayana*). The word *ayana* refers to the classification of actions, such as those to be done and so forth. Therefore he said: "But in meaning, however, it is one.

"Proceeding by way of various doors and methods of development" means that it proceeds by way of the doors of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and so on, and even therein, by way of the doors of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and so on, through the method of development.
"The single way" (*ekāyana*) means going to one [goal]; the meaning is that it goes to Nibbāna. For Nibbāna, because of its state of being without a second, is...
And because it is the supreme state, it is called "one. As it is said: "For there is one truth; there is no second. And:
"To whatever extent, monks, there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared to be their foremost.
"Destruction itself is the end" is *khayanta*; one who has seen the end of destruction regarding birth is *jātikhayantadassī*. Without distinction, all [phenomena]...

"One who feels compassion for beings with a desire for their welfare" is *hitānukampī*. "They crossed over" (*atarinsu*) means they have crossed over. "In the past" (*pubbe*) refers to former Buddhas, or to the past time. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to their speech;
however, it is not appropriate for that [word] to denote the expression of an action.

For there is no denotation of an action-expression in the word *eka* when it signifies a being, due to its primary function of counting. This is as seen in such phrases as "even once he might go upwards."

It must be [interpreted] with the phrasing "it goes once" (*sakid-ayana*). Having thus joined the meaning: "having joined the meaning of the compound word as 'that which has a single going' (*ekaṃ ayanaṃ assā*).
"In both ways" means according to the former method and the latter method.
It is not tenable here because the path intended in this context does indeed proceed on many occasions. Therefore he said, "Why? and so forth.
“‘It goes in many ways’” shows the unsuitability of the former method; “‘and its going is manifold’” [shows the unsuitability] of the latter method.

In this phrase—either in the sentence “This, monks, is the one-way path,” or in the classificatory statement “the preliminary path and the supramundane path”—it is called the “mixed path,” meaning the supramundane path mixed with the mundane. Of purification and so forth...
The Elder Teacher, including that which is caused by a non-figurative reason (*nippariyāyahetuka*), said, "the mixed path.
The other [teacher], however, saying that what is intended here is a figurative cause (*pariyāyahetu*), said, "the preliminary path.
"Having heard the sound" means having directly perceived the sound announcing the time, namely, "It is time, venerable sir, for hearing the Dhamma," or [having heard it] through tradition.

And having heard [this]. "Having thus lifted up" means: they do not wander about as if carrying a load of sugarcane, failing to discard this speech which is "beautiful and heart-stealing," but rather they hold it fast.
"Is agitated" (āluḷeti) means that it becomes stirred up and confused.

By the phrase "the path of the single way" (ekāyanamaggo), the path of the preliminary foundations of mindfulness (pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamagga) is meant; by this much, the intended meaning here is established.
Furthermore, for the sake of its ornamentation, in order to show the preliminary path (pubbabhāgamagga) for that [Noble Eightfold Path], the verses beginning with "Of paths, the eightfold...
were also brought from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* and placed here.
In the sense of going to Nibbāna: it is "going to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagamana*) because one goes to, that is, attains, Nibbāna by means of it; that very thing...

The meaning is "having the nature of being non-perverted"; by that, it means "in the sense of going to Nibbāna" or "being the means for attaining Nibbāna. "In the sense of being to be traversed" means "because it is to be sought.
Alternatively, the reading is "in the sense of being to be approached," which means "because it is to be reached.
By the phrase "by lust and so forth," only lust, hatred, and delusion are included: "Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion..."
This is because of the statement, "It is a stain. However, by the phrase "by covetousness, improper greed, and so forth," these are mentioned separately for the purpose of including all defilements.
In order to show the definiteness of the meaning stated as "for the purification of beings," he says "For thus," and so on.
Granted that "for purification" is a general designation, yet it refers specifically to the mind.
In order to show that "purity" is intended here [in this specific sense], it was said: "But by way of the stain of form," and so forth.
To demonstrate that this is not merely a statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but rather something spoken here with direct reference to the subject, he said: "For thus," and so on.
Furthermore, since this purification of mind, when accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and the rest, therefore...
It is said: “For the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,” and so forth. Therein, *soka* (sorrow) is the mental distress and inward brooding caused by the loss of relatives and the like.

*Parideva* (lamentation) is the verbal outburst resulting from the state of being overwhelmed by sorrow due to the very same causes—the loss of relatives and so on—expressed through such cries as, “Where is my only son? Where is my only son? and the like.
"Transcending here" means the non-arising [of defilements] in the future; thus he said, "for the sake of abandoning.
However, showing that this leads to such transcending by way of illustration, he said, "For this," and so forth.
In that context, "purify what was before" refers to the purification of the defilement of craving regarding past aggregates.
*Pacchā* means later. *Te* means "for you. *Māhu* means "let there not be. *Kiñcanaṃ* refers to the defilements such as lust;
by this, the purification from defilement regarding future aggregates is stated. *Majjhe* means in the middle between those two. *No ce gahessasi* means if you do not grasp;
by this, the occurrence of clinging toward the continuity of present aggregates is stated. *Upasanto*.
"You will wander"—thus, when there is purification from the defilements pertaining to the three periods of time, you will dwell having become peaceful through the extinction of all feverish distress;
with this in mind, he concluded the verse with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Therefore he said, "This verse," and so forth.

"Sons" means those born of one's own breast, or others such as those given away (*dinnaka*), those adopted (*kittima*), and so on. "Father" means the biological progenitor, or others who occupy the position of a father.

“Relatives” means kinsmen. This is the meaning here: whether they be sons, fathers, or other relatives, they do not provide protection from death—that is, from being overcome and seized by the Ender, Māra—for one who has been attacked. Why? Because there is no refuge in kinsmen.
Indeed, there is no protection from death by virtue of kinsmen; therefore, in the case of Paṭācārā, [the Buddha spoke] beginning with, “Both your sons have passed away,” and so forth.
"Do not lament fruitlessly; rather, see the Dhamma as it truly is"—this is the intended meaning.

"Established in the fruit of stream-entry" means that at the conclusion of the sublime teaching on the Dhamma, which had been delivered in accordance with the truth, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry adorned with the thousandfold method.
But how did she [attain] this fruit of stream-entry by way of the path of the foundations of mindfulness?

He said, “But because...,” and so forth, [meaning] he established [the point]. For there is no attainment of the Noble Path by disciples without the discourse on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.

As for the phrase, “Having heard this verse,” this was stated because this verse—which functions to dispel sorrow—was heard first; for even that discourse on impermanence is merely an adjunct to the teaching of the Truths.

[This] having been done. In the other verse, however, there is nothing further to be said. "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means the cultivation of wisdom (*paññā-bhāvanā*), for that is what is intended here.

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because the contemplation (*anupassanā*) of form and so forth as impermanent and so on is indeed the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā*);
therefore. "They too" (*tepi*) refers to the ministers Santati and Paṭācāra.
He sent five robbers, each accompanied by a retinue of one hundred robbers, in succession.
Having entered the forest and searching for the Elder, they eventually came into his presence. Therefore he said:
"Having gone there, they surrounded the Elder and sat down. "Having suppressed the feeling" means the painful feeling caused by the breaking of the thigh bone.
Having dispelled [the pain] through non-attention, joy and gladness arose because even the stain of remorse was impossible.

Therefore he said, "By relying on purified virtue. For as the Elder was reviewing his virtue, the sublime joy and gladness arising by relying on that purified virtue suppressed the painful sensation produced by the breaking of his thigh bone.

“*Tiyāmarattiṃ*”: this is the accusative case used to express continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). By this, he shows his heedfulness (*appamāda*) regarding insight (*vipassanā*) and his exertion in practice (*paṭipatti*).
“*Pādāni*”: on the feet. “*Saṃyamessāmi*”: I shall restrain; the meaning is that I shall bring them under control (*saññattiṃ karissāmi*).
“*Aṭṭiyāmi*”: I am disgusted. “*Harāyāmi*”: I am ashamed. “*Vipassissam*” means I saw clearly (*sampassim*).
"Pacalāyantānaṃ" means of those who are drowsy, having fallen into sleep. "Agatiṃ" means a non-domain (of conduct).
"Vatasampanno" means endowed with the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*). He says "pamādaṃ" (negligence) with reference to drowsiness.
"Oruddhamānaso" means one whose mind is restrained. "Pañjarasmiṃ" means in the body; for here, the body is called a "cage" because it is a collection of bones bound together by sinews.
Because he used to carry his body under a yellow-colored banner and because he was skilled in wrestling, he was known as "Pītamalla" (the Yellow Wrestler);
having gone forth into homelessness, he became known as the Elder Pītamallatthera. Regarding the phrase "in the three kingdoms": this refers to the kingdoms of Paṇḍu, Coḷa, and Goḷa.
Thinking, "All the wrestlers receive honor and respect in the island of Siṃhala," he came to Tambapaṇṇidīpa. That very...

"Making a hook" means: having made a hook for the elephant of one's own mind with regard to the meaning revealed in the *Natumhāka-vagga*—namely, that "form and so forth should not be grasped as 'mine'"—he walks with his knees when his feet are failing him, being unable to walk further due to excessive pacing, thinking, "If I sit down, there will be an opportunity for sleep. "Having explained" means...

Having explained his own realization (aññaṃ byākaritvā) by way of making known the fruitfulness of his own exertion of energy, he thereby inspired his fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārīnaṃ) toward that same goal.
"Bhāsitaṃ" means speech; as to whose it was, he says: "Of the Best of Buddhas, the Proclaimer Supreme over the Whole World.
The passage beginning with "Not yours" is a demonstration of the manner of its occurrence. And this [speech] is the cause for the absolute pacification of my mental formations (saṅkhārānaṃ).
Declaring this, he recited the verse beginning with “Impermanent indeed...”;
by this, he shows that I am now healthy—being free from the disease known as momentary dissolution—and have attained final nibbāna.
“Assa” means Sakka’s. “Upapatti” means rebirth as a deva. It became exactly as it was before because he was reborn precisely in his capacity as Sakka.

Subrahmā is his name. Having seen the rebirth of the celestial nymphs (accharā) in hell, he spoke the words beginning with “This mind is constantly terrified,” referring to the perpetual state of mental trepidation that had arisen in him from that time onward.
In this context, *utrasta* means agitated or frightened; *ubbigga* means stirred with awe. Alternatively, *utrasta* means stirred with awe, while *ubbigga* refers to being [overcome] by fear.

It moved together with its support. "In regard to those that have not arisen" means in regard to those yet to come. "In regard to duties" (*kiccesu*) means in regard to various things that ought to be done.

Alternatively, the reading is "in regard to difficulties" (*kicchesu*), which means "in regard to sufferings"; this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), meaning "a sign of future suffering.
The construction is: "when duties have arisen" means when they have appeared. At that time, [it refers to] what had arisen for his own retinue.
He speaks with reference to suffering (*dukkha*).
"From awakening" (*bojjhā*) means from the noble path (*ariyamagga*). The word "except for" (*aññatra*) is used in the ablative case in view of this [word];

the meaning is "setting aside awakening. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "From austerity" (*tapasā*) means from the practice of austerity; by that, [there is] the attainment of the path.
It shows the practice of effacement as a means. "Restraint of the faculties" refers to the restraining of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth;

by this heading of "restraint through mindfulness," it shows all virtue of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*), or else, according to the method of the "extracting the characteristic" (*lakkhaṇahāra-naya*), it shows all fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhi-sīla*). "Relinquishment of everything" is so called because of the relinquishing of everything and the abandoning of all defilements (*kilesa*).
For when the defilements have been relinquished, the round of kamma and the round of its result are likewise relinquished.
"Safety" means security, the state of being free from calamity.
It is called *ñāya* because one definitely goes (*kamati*) toward Nibbāna by it; or, that [Nibbāna] is realized (*ñāyati*) or penetrated by means of this, thus it is *ñāya*, namely, the Noble Path.
He said: "The 'method' (ñāya) is called the Noble Eightfold Path. Regarding the phrase "due to being devoid of the net of craving" (taṇhāvānavirahitattā):

it means because of being secluded from the net (vāna) designated as craving. For craving is called a "net" (vāna) because it weaves (vinati) and binds together the aggregates with the aggregates, the fruit with karma, and suffering with sentient beings.
Now, this net does not exist here; or rather, when this [Path] has been attained, there is no net for the person.

They call it Nibbāna, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). Since realization (sacchikiriyā) means making [the truth] directly manifest for oneself without depending on another, he says "by way of being personally witnessed" (attapaccakkhatāya). One might object:
since "for the sake of purification" (visuddhiyā) intends the purification of the mind (cittavisuddhi), do not the overcoming of sorrow and so forth follow from the very mention of "purification"?
They have already been grasped; with reference to the inquiry as to why they are grasped again, it is said, "In this regard, although...
and so forth. "Skilled in the logic of the Dispensation" means one who is proficient in the principles of the Dhamma, such as the characteristics of the Truths and Dependent Origination.
"He makes known each respective meaning" means that whichever individuals are to be enlightened, he makes them understand according to their needs, whether by way of summary or detailed exposition.
They are to be awakened; the Blessed One, awakening each of them in such and such a way through the excellence of his own teaching, makes known that respective meaning.
"Showing by making it manifest" means showing that respective meaning by making it clear, without taking into account any offense regarding the meaning.
For the Fully Enlightened One does not possess speech that must be established through the pointing out of offenses regarding the meaning and so forth. "Conduces to" (saṃvattati) means...

It arises; the meaning is that it exists. Because there is never any purification of the mind for one who has not transcended sorrow and lamentation—since the purification of the mind is accomplished only by means of the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation—it is therefore said:
"It exists through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation. Furthermore, because an ordinary person (puthujjana) is touched by painful phenomena conditioned by mental distress...
Sorrow and the rest overcome [the mind], but when these have been fully understood, they no longer exist; therefore it is said:
"The surmounting of sorrow and lamentation is by means of the subsiding of pain and dejection. "Of the method" (ñāyassa) refers to the supreme path and the third path.
For through the attainment of those, there is, respectively, the subsiding of pain and dejection. It is also concomitant with the realization of direct knowledge (sacchikiriyābhisamaya).
The realization of the other [truths] is spoken of as being caused by the realization through direct experience, because of its inseparable connection with that [realization].
Or, the phrase "the attainment of the method for the direct experience of Nibbāna" is said with reference to making it manifest by means of the knowledge of the fruit;
furthermore, this term "for the direct experience of Nibbāna" (*nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya*) should be understood as a dative case.
“Vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ” means words of praise. Showing that this was not only practiced here but was indeed the Teacher’s habit elsewhere as well, he said, “For just as...,” and so forth.
In that context, it is “beautiful in the beginning” (ādikalyāṇa) because it is beautiful at the start, or because its beginning is beautiful.
The same method applies to the other two phrases. It is “possessing the meaning” (sāttha) due to the perfection of its meaning. Due to the perfection of its phrasing (byañjana)...
It is "with its phrasing. It is "entirely complete" because it is fulfilled by the five aggregates of dhamma beginning with virtue, and because there is nothing further to be added.

It is "pure" because it is free from defilements and because there is nothing to be removed. It is the "holy life of the Dispensation" (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) because it consists of the most excellent conduct, and the "holy life of the Path" (*maggabrahmacariya*).
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is in the *Visuddhimagga*.
It should be understood in the manner already stated. "Noble lineages" (*ariyavaṃsā*) means the lineages or traditions of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others.
"Foremost" (*aggaññā*) means they should be known as the foremost because of their preeminence over all other lineages. "Ancient" (*rattaññā*) means they should be known as long-standing.

"Traditional" (*vaṃsaññā*) means they should be known as the traditions of the Buddhas and others. "Time-honored" (*porāṇā*) means ancient, not being of recent origin. "Untainted" (*asaṅkiṇṇā*) means unmixed.
“Not removed”: they have not been removed by the Noble Ones (ariya) in the past with the thought, “What is the use of these? They are not being censured:
even now they are not being removed by them. They will not be censured: in the future as well, they will not be removed by them. “Unreproached by the wise...”:
by those in the world who are wise—monks and brahmins—they are not perceived [as faults], nor are they blamed or criticized.

"Meaning" (*attha*). "By means of [the words] beginning with 'for the sake of purification' (*visuddhiyā')" means by means of those words that illuminate purification and so forth. "By means of phrases" (*padehi*) means by means of sentences, or by means of portions of the Dhamma distinguished by such categories as the meaning of purification and so on.
"Calamity" (*upaddava*) means misfortune (*anattha*). "Purification" (*visuddhi*) means the act of purifying, the abandoning of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
"Memorization" (*uggaha*) is the bringing [of the text] to the lips. "Mastery" (*pariyāpuṇana*) is thorough familiarity. "Retention" (*dhāraṇa*) is the fixing of the meaning in the heart.
*Parivattanaṃ* means reciting.

*Gandhārako* means one born in the country of Gandhāra. *Pahonti* means they are able. *Aniyyānikamaggā* refers to wrong paths, or alternatively, to paths that are either fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) or not so fixed.
*Suvaṇṇaṃ* is said to refer even to counterfeit gold. *Maṇī* refers even to glass gems (*kācamaṇi*).
"Gold" (*mutta*) refers even to bamboo, and "coral" (*pavāḷa*) is said to refer even to a sprout; therefore, these are specified by such terms as "red Jāmbūnada gold.

"Not below that" is because the body and so forth intended here lack the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of feeling and the rest, and because in the lower instances of inclusion, the dhammas of the three planes—body, feeling, mind, and liberation—are already grasped separately as distinct objects of perversion (*vipallāsa-vatthu*).
This was said with reference to the undesirable objects of the perversions; however, because there is no fifth object of perversion, he said, "not above.
For here, the classification of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is according to the classification of their objects.
"Three foundations of mindfulness" is a demonstration of the range of meanings for the term *satipaṭṭhāna*, but it does not refer to the specific term *satipaṭṭhāna* as used here in the text.

Regarding the phrase "seeing the meaning" (*atthadassana*): in the passage beginning with "the domain of mindfulness" (*satigocara*), the word "beginning" (*ādi*) includes those sections of the Suttas that clarify the domains of mindfulness, such as: "With the arising of contact comes the arising of feelings; with the arising of name-and-form comes the arising of consciousness;

with the arising of attention comes the arising of mental phenomena," as well as those passages where the "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are taught. Likewise, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*...

The word "beginning" (ādi) should be understood as indicating that other portions of the Pāḷi remain to be shown. "The foundation for mindfulness" (satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ) means the place where mindfulness is to be established.
Since forms and so forth become the objects of mindfulness for one performing acts such as giving, he says "the foundation for exertion" (padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ) in order to preclude that [ordinary sense].
The intention is that the prefix *pa-* here indicates the sense of "exertion" (*padhāna*), as it does in expressions such as "sublime states" (*paṇītā dhammā*).

"Ariya" refers to the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is the best among all beings. "In this" means in this *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta*. He indicates the sutta by means of a portion of it; for therein it is said:
"There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One... deserves... Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion, seeking their welfare, out of compassion..."
"Having taken it upon himself [to teach], he says: 'This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness. Yet his disciples do not wish to listen; they do not lend an ear;
they do not apply their minds to understanding; and they proceed in opposition to the Teacher’s instruction.
In such a case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased, nor does he experience displeasure."
He dwells untainted, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which the Noble One cultivates … [as before] … he is worthy of it.
Furthermore, monks, the Teacher … [as before] … “This will lead to your welfare.
Yet some of his disciples do not wish to listen … [as before] … nor do they act in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is not displeased.
He is not displeased, yet he does not experience displeasure; he is not pleased, yet he does not experience pleasure.
Having avoided both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is called the second [jhāna].
"Furthermore, monks... [as before] ... 'It is pleasant,' and his disciples listen... [as before] ... they conduct themselves accordingly.
In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure;
he dwells untainted, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is called the third [ground]."

Thus, the state of being undrenched by aversion and attraction, and the state of transcending both through constant mindfulness, is called "the establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). For it is only Buddhas who possess constant mindfulness due to its being an exclusive quality (*āveṇika-dhamma*), and not Paccekabuddhas and others.
The prefix *pa-* signifies "commencement," and since commencement implies "proceeding," he says: "because it is to be brought forth."
"Meaning. Since *sati* functions as the instrument, that which is established by means of it is "the establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
For the word *ana* frequently has the sense of the object (*kamma*) through its verbal usage; likewise, the sense of the agent (*kartr*) is also obtained for it. Thus it is said:

"It establishes itself, therefore it is an 'establishment' (*paṭṭhāna*). In the phrase "it establishes itself," the prefix *pa-* indicates a leaping forward (*pakkhandana*) characterized by intensity.

“Having descended, having leaped in, having spread out, it proceeds”—this is the meaning, he said. Again, while explaining the meaning of the term *bhāva*, as well as the words *sati* and *paṭṭhāna*, he says “or else,” and so forth;
by this, when the former alternative [of *bhāva*] is present, it is understood that the word *sati* and the word *paṭṭhāna* have the sense of the agent (*kattuattha*).
In the sense of remembering (*saraṇaṭṭhena*) refers to what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
And in the sense of recollecting. "This" refers to that which was stated as "mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness";
this is what is intended here in this passage of the sutta.
"If it is thus": if mindfulness alone is the foundation of mindfulness, and mindfulness is indeed a single dhamma, then being so, why...
“*Satipaṭṭhānā*” is a plural form; thus he says, “because of the multiplicity of mindfulness,” and so forth.

If those mindfullnesses are many, then for what reason is the term “path” (*magga*) used in the singular? This is the construction. “In the sense of a path” means in the sense of leading out (*niyyāna*). For the dhamma of the path is that which leads out;
by virtue of that very quality of leading out, having attained unity, it goes exclusively toward Nibbāna, and it is sought after by those who desire that goal.
"It is being sought" (maggīyati); thus he says, "For this has been said," thereby citing what he himself had previously stated.

Therein, "these four kinds of mindfulness" means these fourfold applications of mindfulness by way of the contemplation of the body, and so forth. "At a later time" means at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga).
"Accomplishing their function" means that, in the prior stage, they individually [accomplish their function] by way of dispelling perceptions of beauty and so forth regarding the body and the rest.
Having proceeded thus, at the moment of the path, mindfulness itself accomplishes the task of abandoning by means of the total eradication of all four kinds of perversion;
it then proceeds toward Nibbāna by way of making that its object. Here, the plural number is used precisely because of the accomplishment of these four tasks.
And "when this is so" (*evaṃ sati*) means that, by taking their unity from the standpoint of the path, they are called "the path."
Because it can be called "fourfold" by means of the singular number and by way of the diversity of objects, [the term] exists;
thus, with the connection of the words, the teaching beginning with "This is the one-way path" is indeed possessed of a sequence, not without a sequence—this is the intended meaning.
To establish this very point by means of an illustration, the Sutta passage "The crusher of Māra’s army" is cited.
Having brought [the examples] forward, the illustration beginning with "Just as" is correlated. The section beginning with "Therefore" is the conclusion.

Specifically, since the body and feeling are the causes of gratification, for the purpose of abandoning them, the demonstrations of their foulness and suffering-nature regarding those gross and subtle objects of craving are easy to perform for those of dull and sharp wisdom who follow the temperament of craving; thus, these [demonstrations] are for them.

Thus it is said: "The Path of Purification. Likewise, regarding those mental states—which are the specific causes for the view that takes "the permanent self" as its object—there are the visions of impermanence and non-self.
These are presented through the categories of "with lust" and so forth, "perception-contact" and so forth, and "hindrance" and so forth;

and because these states range from being not too diverse to being excessively diverse, they are taught for the purpose of abandoning them in those of dull or sharp wisdom who are of a speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*).
These [factors] are easily understood; thus they are called the "Path of Purification" (*Visuddhimagga*).
And here, just as it is possible for both mind and mental states to serve as the objective basis (*vatthu*) for craving, so too can body and feeling serve as the objective basis for views.

Therefore, although all four [aggregates] serve as the objective basis for both craving and views, the specific designation is employed in order to show which one is the predominant condition for which.
“*Kata*” should be understood [as follows]: one who is a practitioner of sharp wisdom and serenity, while grasping a coarse object, does not remain fixed upon it;
rather, having entered into jhāna and emerged from it, he grasps the feeling. Thus it is said: “because of not being stuck on a coarse object.
However, for one whose vehicle is insight (vipassanā-yānika), the mind leaps into the subtle mind and into mental phenomena (dhammas).

The state of being the path to purification for those whose vehicles are insight (vipassanā-yānika) with either dull or sharp wisdom through the contemplations of mind and mental objects has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "for them there" (*tesaṃ tattha*), here the word *tattha* is to be construed with the term "for the purpose of abandoning" (*pahānatthaṃ*).

The same principle applies to the subsequent instance, "for them there" (*tesaṃ tattha*). Since the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) are found especially in the body, the body is specifically [the basis] for the flood of sensuality (*kāmogha*).
Feeling is the basis for the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), because through the grasping of pleasure within the various states of existence, there arises a craving for existence (*bhavassāda*).
Consciousness is the basis for the flood of views (*diṭṭhi-ogha*), because through the grasping of a solid continuity, there especially arises the adherence to a self in consciousness.

Ignorance is the basis for the flood of ignorance (*avijjā-ogha*), because confusion arises due to the difficulty of discerning phenomena (*dhamma*) and the difficulty of penetrating that phenomena are merely phenomena.
Phenomena (*dhammā*) are the bases; therefore, four [foundations] alone have been taught for the purpose of abandoning them.

Thus, by the very statement that the body and so forth are the bases for the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the rest, it is also illustrated that they are the bases for the yoke of sensual desire (*kāma-yoga*), the taint of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), and so on, because in meaning they are not different from the floods.
And to the extent that the body is the basis for the flood of sensual desire and the rest, [so too are the other aggregates].
That is the basis for the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*). “The underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) underlies painful feeling”:

feelings consisting of the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) are specifically the basis for the bodily tie of ill will (*byāpādakāyagantha*).
Grasping at the mind as permanent, and the misapprehension that “the self is purified through virtue” and so forth, [is the basis for the bodily tie of views].

The mind is the basis for the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*). For one who does not see what has come to be as it truly is due to a lack of discernment regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there arises the dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth," which consists of the views of eternalism or annihilationism (*bhavavibhavadiṭṭhi*); thus, mental phenomena (*dhammā*) are its basis.

The body’s status as the basis for the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is exactly as previously stated; for to the same extent that the body is the basis for the flood of sensual pleasure, it is likewise the basis for the clinging to sensual pleasure.

Because the basis (*vatthu*) is non-different in meaning. Feeling (*vedanā*) is the basis for the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), because through the relish of pleasant feeling, one becomes indifferent to the next world and gives rise to the misapprehension that "there is no giving," and so forth.

The fact that mental states (*citta-dhamma*) serve as the basis for the other types of clinging is exactly as stated in the method of the third and fourth fetters (*gantha*). That body and feeling are the basis for desire, hatred, and wrong course of conduct is likewise established.
The application regarding the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), ill will (*byāpāda*), and the bodily tie (*kāya-gantha*) is exactly as described by the method already stated.

Because delusion arises regarding a mind possessed of lust and so forth through the grasping of a solid continuity (*santatighana*), the mind is the basis for the "approach of delusion" (*mohāgati*). Because fear arises when there is no comprehension of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), phenomena (*dhammā*) are the basis for the "approach of fear" (*bhayāgati*).
From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; from the arising of contact comes the arising of feelings; [and] with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) as condition...

Because of the statement, "consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form," the nutriments of physical food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which constitute the origin of the body and so forth—become fully understood through the thorough knowledge of the body and so on;
thus he said, "for the sake of the full understanding of the fourfold nutriment.
"The method of the treatise" refers to the method of commentary on the Suttas according to the *Nettippakaraṇa*.
"By way of remembering" means by way of supporting (upadhāraṇa) the body and so forth, as well as wholesome states and so forth.

In the sense that "they go toward Nibbāna by means of this," it is called *sati* (mindfulness). In this context, "convergence in unity" (*ekattasamosaraṇa*) refers to the coming together and meeting in Nibbāna, which is a single state and of a single nature.
It is precisely to demonstrate this that the passage beginning with "Just as... was stated.

Alternatively, because they are identical in being the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is "oneness" (ekatta). The convergence upon that is "convergence in oneness" (ekattasamosaraṇa);
it is simply their sharing in that same nature. However, in order to demonstrate their status as the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, he said "just as" and so forth.
In this sense, the refuge, the oneness, and the convergence are stated together as the reasons for the single state of the foundations of mindfulness.

They are to be seen separately in the former case. Alternatively, when the meanings are "by way of remembering" (*saraṇavasena*) or "by way of going" (*gamanavasena*), that very going is the convergence (*samosaraṇa*);

or, when the meaning of the word *sati* is not being expressed as "convergence," then since there is no other meaning for the word *sati* than the state of remembering (*dhāraṇatā*), the former [meaning] is the cause for the existence of mindfulness (*satibhāva*), while the latter is the cause for its singleness (*ekabhāva*).
Even though they converge upon Nibbāna, these foundations of mindfulness are said to be conjoined as the causes for their becoming one.

The statement, "in fourteen ways, in nine ways, in sixteen ways, and in five ways," is made with reference to the sections on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānapabba*) and so forth that appear later in the text;
however, it is also stated by way of their immediate subdivisions and the subdivisions following from them.

Furthermore, manifoldness is indeed obtained through cultivation; the resemblance to goods set out for sale in the four directions should be seen as the power of the cultivation of the various foundations of mindfulness, beginning with body-contemplation.

The question "desiring to speak" (kathetukamyatā) is asked because other types of questions are impossible here, and because it is stated thus due to the desire to teach by way of exposition and so forth. The phrase "here" (*idha*) indicates the support for the bhikkhu who is practicing the path being described.
Since there is no support for this other than the Teaching (*sāsana*), it is said: "Herein means in this Teaching. The passage beginning with "Dhamma...
and ending with "this is their chatter" is intended to bring them face-to-face with oneself, and that is for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma with due care.
Because of such statements as, "Monks, move within your own range, in your ancestral domain," these teachings constitute the range of the monks.

That is to say, the contemplation of the body and so forth. In this context, because a monk exists by means of the practice of the contemplation of the body and so forth, he shows the monk by saying, "He dwells contemplating the body," etc.; for that [practice] is restricted to the monk, he says:
"Because it demonstrates the state of being a monk through the practice. This is because [the monk] conforms to the conduct of the Teacher and because he is the receiver of the entire dispensation.
And [he is] a fit vessel for every kind of instruction. "When he has been taken" means when the monk has been taken.

Because the assembly of monks holds the position of seniority, the other assemblies are also effectively included by way of meaning—just as when a king goes out, his retinue follows—hence he said, "the rest," and so forth.
Having thus analyzed the first reason, he spoke the words beginning with "and whoever this... in order to analyze the other [reason] as well.

"One should walk evenly" means that, having abandoned uneven conduct of body and so forth, one should walk with body and so forth in a balanced manner. Being peaceful through the subsiding of lust and other defilements,
tamed by the restraint of the sense faculties, certain through the guidance of the four paths, a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārī*) due to his excellent conduct,

and having laid down the rod by refraining from physical violence and the like in all respects— he who stands thus in the state of a Noble One (*ariya*) is characterized by the expulsion of evil, the calming of evil, and the breaking of the afflictions (*kilesa*).
One should understand [the term "body"] as referring to a brahmin, a recluse, or a monk;
and in such passages as "this body and external name-and-form," it refers to the pentad of aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*);
likewise in such passages as "he experiences pleasure with the body," and "at that time, there is tranquility and complete subsiding of the body."
Since the mental aggregates, such as feeling and the rest, are also called "body" (kāya), he said "in the body" (kāye) meaning "in the material body" (rūpakāye) in order to distinguish it from those.
And "of the phenomena beginning with hair" means of the primary elements and derived matter designated as hair and so forth.

Thus, having shown the word *kāya* according to the method of etymology (*saddanaya*) as "the sense of accumulation," "the sense of a physical frame," and "the sense of a mass," he now [shows it] also by the method of philological derivation (*niruttinaya*).
The phrase beginning with "and how" was stated in order to show this. "Arising" means they come into being.

"Because of non-confusion" means that although there is a possibility of lapsing into the contemplation of feelings and so forth within the body—since feelings and the rest are also dependent upon it and bound to it—the meaning is "because of [the practice] not being confused with those [other factors].
Furthermore, because the word *kāya* (body) has a collective scope and functions as a designation for a composite whole...
And the singular form "in the body" (*kāye*) is used for the aspect of foulness (*asubhākāra*);

likewise, although the mind (*citta*) is divided into many distinctions by way of its objects and so forth, it is taken collectively as a single unit through the commonality of its nature as consciousness, and thus the singular form "in the mind" (*citte*) is used.

However, because feeling (*vedanā*) is to be contemplated individually as it is divided into pleasure and so forth, it is expressed with the plural form "in feelings" (*vedanāsu*), and in the same way...

The exposition has been set forth; and since the phenomena (*dhammā*) are of more than fifty divisions, and the modes of contemplation are likewise manifold, they too are expressed in the plural number.

For the purpose of preventing the grasping of a whole, the wandering after a conventional designation, the seizing of a core, and the adherence [to a self], [the text speaks of] the body by way of its limbs and members.

And by separating those [parts] from the hair and so forth, as well as the hair and so forth from the primary and derived material phenomena (*bhūta-upādāya-rūpa*), he said, "Thus, not in the body," and so on.
Even those who maintain the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) do not grasp a whole with respect to a collection of parts such as the components of a palace or a city;

however, some might still pursue a conventional designation (*samaññā*) thinking, "There is something called a 'city' that exists. This is similar to the pursuit of conventional designations such as "woman" or "man."

The illustration of the city has been stated. There is no such thing as a "body" apart from the aforementioned collections—the collection of limbs and members, the collection of hair of the head and body and so forth, and the collection of primary elements and derived matter; how much less so for things like "woman" and so on. Thus he said:
"Is a body, or a woman, or a man, or some other phenomenon perceived? By the phrase "some phenomenon," [he implies...]
He rejects the concepts of a "being," a "life-principle," and so forth; however, the "whole" (the possessor of parts) is rejected by the very rejection of the body.

If this is so, how can there be the pursuit of conventional designations such as "body" and so on? To this he says: "They perform [their functions] with respect to the phenomena... as already described. "In such and such a way" means in the manner of the body and so forth.
"Whom he sees" refers to whichever woman or man he sees. But is it not the case that there is no seeing of women or men with the eye?

This is true: however, that which is said to be "seen" by way of the perception occurring as "I see a woman" or "I see a man," or that which is seen through wrong vision or false view—that is not truly seen;
the meaning is that it is not the visible base (*rūpāyatana*), because its nature as form is falsely imagined through the grasping of a perversion.
Alternatively, that [which is seen] is a collection of the primary and derived elements consisting of hair and so forth.
"It is not seen" means that it is not seen because it is not cognizable by eye-consciousness; or, "it is not seen" means that which is seen is not [truly] seen.

"That which is seen, he does not see" means that the visible object-base (*rūpāyatana*), which consists of the collection of the primary elements and their derivatives such as hair and so forth, he does not see according to reality with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).
"Not seeing, he is bound" means that this personal existence (*attabhāva*) is not seen as it truly is with the eye of wisdom.
Not seeing [this], one is bound by the fetter of defilements, thinking: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
"Not contemplating other phenomena" means not contemplating other natures; the meaning is that one does not contemplate any aspect other than the foul (asubha) and so forth.
With the words "What is meant? and so on, he makes this very meaning clear. "The earth-body" refers to the portion consisting of hair and the rest.
He calls the earth element "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of phenomena;

or rather, he calls "body" the characteristic earth element itself—which exists in many divisions throughout the entire physical frame—taking it as a collective whole in its occurrence from beginning to end. The same method applies to the "water-body" (*āpokāya*) and so forth.
"Of what is thus grasped" means: of that which is grasped by the blind and foolish as being "I" and "mine," in the sense of a self and what belongs to a self.
Now, in order to show body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) by way of the seven modes of contemplation as well, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) is commenced.
Therein, “he contemplates as impermanent” means he contemplates the body, which arises from the four [nutriments], as “impermanent.
When he sees it thus, it is said that he “contemplates its mode of impermanence” as well. And for one who has become such, there is the grasping at permanence...
It is said, "not as permanent," because it has been stated that "even this does not exist. For it is described thus: "He abandons the perception of permanence.
And here, in the phrase "he contemplates only as impermanent," the particle *eva* is indicated by elision;
therefore, to show the meaning excluded by it, it is said, "not as permanent. Nor should one suspect here an exclusion of contemplation as suffering and so forth.

Because the particle *eva* has the function of excluding the opposite, and because those [qualities] have already been dealt with in the preceding teaching, the same method applies in such passages as "he contemplates as suffering" (*dukkhato anupassati*).
However, this is the distinction: since what is impermanent is suffering, he contemplates that very body as suffering;
and since what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates it as non-self. Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self—[is not...]
That which is to be rejoiced in and that which is not to be rejoiced in—one should not be stained by either; therefore it is said:
“He becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not impassioned.
The meaning is that, being thus unstained, he causes passion to cease rather than its arising, and does not produce its origination. Practicing in this way, he relinquishes rather than grasps.

For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth is called "the relinquishment of abandonment and the relinquishment of leaping forward," because by means of the factor of substitution (tadaṅga), it abandons the defilements along with the body and the volitional formations that support it; and because, through seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps forward into Nibbāna, which is its opposite, by inclining toward it. Therefore, one who is endowed with it—
The bhikkhu abandons the defilements in the manner described and leaps into Nibbāna;
being thus established, he does not take up the defilements by way of rebirth, nor does he take up the conditioned object by way of seeing it as faultless. Therefore it is said:
"He relinquishes, he does not take up. Now, in order to show which phenomena are abandoned through these contemplations:

It has been said: “Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence,” and so forth. In this context, “perception of permanence” refers to the distorted perception (viparīta-saññā) that occurs in the form, “conditioned phenomena are permanent.
The mention of “perception” is intended to show that the abandoning of the distortions of view and mind occurs precisely through the abandoning of the distortion of perception;
alternatively, it should be understood that those [distortions] are included under the heading of perception. “Delight” (nandi) refers to craving accompanied by rapture (sappītika-taṇhā).
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.

By the word "dwells" (*viharati*), the dwelling in the postures of one who possesses the practice of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) is expressed; thus he says "he conducts himself" (*iriyati*), meaning he carries out the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
Because it pervades [the mind] by way of making it its object, [it is said to exist] "in the three realms of existence" (*tisu bhavesu*).
It has been stated that, in terms of their arising, the defilements belong only to the limited plane (*parittabhūmaka*).

Although the abandoning of defilements is "exertion" (*ātāpa*), and this applies to right view and the other factors as well, the word *ātāpa*—just like the word *ātappa*—is conventionally established specifically for energy (*vīriya*);
thus it is said, "this is a name for energy. Alternatively, regarding the abandonment of opposing factors, [it refers to] the associated states...

Because it is the exertion of energy (*vīriya*) proceeding by way of intense striving that constitutes its preeminent ardor (*ātāpana*), it is energy alone that is so described, and not other phenomena.
Furthermore, the vowel *ī* in the term *ātāpī* indicates either praise or excellence;

thus, by the inclusion of the word "ardent" (*ātāpī*), he demonstrates possession of the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*). Being "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means knowing correctly, thoroughly, and personally, without confusion.
The meaning is: by way of discerning other phenomena [as they arise], it is "right" (sammā) because it is non-erroneous; it is "all-around" (samantato) because it understands in every aspect;

and it is "personally understanding" (sāmaṃ pajānanto) because its occurrence brings about successive distinctions. If one contemplates by means of wisdom, how is it the "establishment of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna)?
To this he says: "For it is not," and so forth. "Universal" (sabbatthika) means existing everywhere (sabbattha).

Because they must be cultivated when the mind is sluggish (*līna*) or excited (*uddhata*). Or else, all the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) that are to be developed are "all-beneficial" (*sabbatthika*) because one who desires them requires these [factors] whether [the mind] is sluggish or excited.

It is precisely by means of wisdom (*paññā*) which has received assistance from mindfulness (*sati*) that the monk, here engaged in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) regarding the body, dwells contemplating the body. "Internal contraction" (*anto-saṅkhepa*) is internal sluggishness; it is indolence (*kosajja*).

The meaning [of the compound] is as follows. Regarding "accompanied by means" (*upāyapariggaha*): here, the purification of virtue and so forth, counting and so forth, and skill in learning and so forth constitute the "means" (*upāya*);
conversely, the opposite of these should be understood as the "non-means" (*anupāya*).
And because one whose mindfulness is established does not abandon the aforementioned means nor grasp at the non-means, it is said: "one who is muddled in mindfulness... is incapable."
"Ten" refers to the state of being incapable of discerning and avoiding the appropriate means and non-means, as well as of relinquishing and not relinquishing.

For this yogi, since mindfulness itself is stated here as the *satipaṭṭhāna*, he says "having shown its associated factor" because its associated states, such as energy (*vīriya*) and so forth, are its constituent factors (*aṅga*).
And here, the word "factor" (*aṅga*) should be understood in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).
And here, by the mention of mindfulness alone, concentration should also be understood as included, since it is comprised within the aggregate of concentration.

Alternatively, this teaching is headed by mindfulness; for the abandoning of defilements or the attainment of Nibbāna is not possible through mindfulness alone, nor does mindfulness occur in isolation.
Therefore, in this teaching on jhāna, [mindfulness] is mentioned just as the terms "with applied thought" and so forth are used.
Regarding the phrase "the demonstration of the factors of association" (*sampayogaṅgadassana*), the word *aṅga* should be understood as having the sense of a constituent part.
The term "factor of abandonment" (*pahānaṅga*) is used to indicate the factor to be abandoned, as in the passage beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*).

Since it is the mundane path (*lokiyamagga*) that is intended here, rather than the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*), he demonstrates only the preliminary purification (*pubbabhāgiyavinaya*) by means of "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or "suppression" (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
He said, "Or. "Of those phenomena" means of phenomena such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. For since those [other phenomena] are not intended there, it is said:
"This was stated by way of extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāra-naya*). "Therein" means in the *Vibhaṅga*. "Herein" refers to this word "in the world" (*loke*).
Since the abandoning of the two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) has been stated without distinction, the specific mode of abandoning is stated again for each one individually.

He said "by way of distinction" (visesena) in order to show this. Alternatively, he said "by way of distinction" and so forth, demonstrating the purpose of the statement regarding the removal of covetousness and dejection instead of saying simply "having removed the hindrances.
