For the purpose of this [statement] is to show the abandoning of favoring and opposing, and so on, which are the direct opposites of the cultivation of the contemplation of the body.
"Based on bodily excellence" means based on the perfection of the physical body, such as beauty, strength, youth, health, and so forth.

By way of the reverse of what has been stated, opposition rooted in bodily failure should be understood. "Development of the body" means the development of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*);

for it is this that is intended here by the term "development of the body. Regarding the phrase "of the states of beauty, pleasure, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be seen as including such things as attractiveness and permanence.
Regarding the phrase "of the states of foulness, pain, and so forth," the word "and so forth" here includes such things as unattractiveness and impermanence.
"Tenā" means by the statement regarding the abandonment of attachment and so forth. "For it is the power of yoga," etc., is an elucidation of the very meaning already stated.
"The power of yoga" (yogānubhāvo) indeed means the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanānubhāvo). "Capable of yoga" (yogasamattho) means capable of applying oneself to yoga.
For by the preceding statement, "free from attachment and aversion," etc., the benefit for one devoted to meditative cultivation was stated.
The second [verse] refers to the practice of one devoted to meditation (*bhāvanā*). For meditation does not succeed for one who is oppressed by attachment, aversion, and so forth.

Regarding the word "contemplating" (*anupassī*): it should be understood that the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is stated here as the illumination of contemplation—that is, the contemplation obtainable within this term "contemplating. Otherwise, there would be the instrumental case ending "by means of contemplation" (*anupassanāya*).
It would not be appropriate. For here it is contemplation itself that is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); the object is not intended here, or rather, it does not apply.
The connection is: "the maintenance of the body has been stated.

And because the maintenance of the meditation subject is accomplished by this, it is specifically called "maintenance of the body. For for one who possesses a meditation subject, the maintenance of the body is only for the sake of the meditation subject.

"Pariharaṇatthaṃ" means for the purpose of maintaining. Since it is by means of the phrase "ardent," etc., that the maintenance of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is expressed, it is stated specifically as "maintenance of the body" (kāyapariharaṇaṃ).
Alternatively, by the mention of "body" (kāya), there is the inclusion of the mental body (nāmakāya) as well, not merely the physical body (rūpakāya);

thus, the maintenance of the meditation subject is also included. And having done so, the inclusion [of the term "body"] in the phrase "by the abiding mentioned here in 'he dwells' (viharatī)" is justified.
It is established that [the phrase] "he dwells contemplating the body" is stated in order to specify the particular dwelling.

However, the passage beginning with "ardent" (*ātāpī*) is an expanded explanation, together with its means of accomplishment, of the brief statement regarding the maintenance of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

By the inclusion of the term "ardency" (*ātāpena*), this same method applies to the phrases "with mindfulness and clear comprehension" (*satisampajaññena*) and so forth as well. This is the "all-pervading meditation subject" (*sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).
Recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and meditation on the foul.
This tetrad, when maintained by a practitioner, is called the "all-purpose meditation subject" (*sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).

Because it serves as a protection for the practice of the meditation subject in all circumstances, and because it must be maintained without interruption through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, it is included under the heading of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
"Stated" means it has been spoken. Alternatively, "calm" (samatha) is stated by way of mindfulness, because it is included within the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).

However, the construction is: "but the meaning was stated in the Vibhaṅga. "Together with that" means together with the text of the Vibhaṅga, which proceeds by way of analyzing the essential meaning (bhāvattha) alone, without taking the literal meaning of the words (saddattha).
"The method of the Commentary" (aṭṭhakathānaya) refers to the manner of explaining according to what is appropriate, by way of clarifying even the literal meaning of the words.

The method of commenting on the meaning has been stated. "How it accords" should be understood as follows: in what way it accords and conforms, not contradicting [the meaning] either in terms of its literal sense (*atthato*) or its underlying intention (*adhippāyato*).

Regarding the phrase "the restatement of feeling and so forth," here it is because mental states (*cittadhammā*)—by virtue of their status as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*)—are dependent upon feeling.

In the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*), because immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) exist in dependence upon material form (*rūpa*), there might arise the confusion of regarding feeling (*vedanā*) as the contemplation of the body and so forth;

therefore, the second mention of "feeling" is for the purpose of showing its distinctness from those [other aggregates] and for the purpose of demonstrating the analysis of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*).
Thus, one is not a contemplator of the body in regard to feeling, nor a contemplator of mind or mental states; rather—

By the phrase "he is one who contemplates feelings," the definition of the mode of contemplating feelings is shown as being unmixed, by way of seeing it only within the objective basis known as feeling. Likewise:
"At whatever time there is pleasant feeling, at that time there is neither painful nor neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; or at whatever time there is painful [feeling]... and so forth.

By not merely stating the general property of the absence of feeling—“at that time there is no other feeling”—but by demonstrating each specific feeling through its separation [from others], the resolution of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) is shown, which is the discernment of the state of permanence.
Through this demonstration of their existence for only a single moment, there is the vision of impermanence; from that very fact, the vision of suffering and non-self.
It has been clearly discerned. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "resolution of the compact, etc.," this further meaning is to be understood:
for he is one who contemplates feeling in feeling alone, not one who contemplates other phenomena. What is meant?

Just as a fool might contemplate a water bubble—which lacks the nature of a gem—as having the appearance of a gem, so too this [contemplator] does not [view] the feeling, even though it is pleasant in its persistence, let alone...

In the case of the other [the unattractive], one contemplates the aspect of its pleasant appearance; however, because of its momentary perishability, its lack of mastery over itself, and its leaking of the impurities of the defilements, one contemplates it as having the aspects of impermanence, non-self, and foulness;
and because of its suffering due to change and its suffering inherent in formations, one especially contemplates it as suffering alone.
Thus, regarding mental states as well, the purpose for repeating [the contemplation] as appropriate should be stated.

This is because only mundane [states] are intended for the practice of comprehension. By the words "But this alone," etc., he shows the limit of what is to be known, namely, "only this much is to be understood here.

By the phrase "this is the method," he indicates that just as the mind and mental objects are to be contemplated, so too one who contemplates them is "one who contemplates the mind in the mind" and "one who contemplates mental objects in mental objects."

"Should be known" refers to this meaning by way of extension (*atidisa*). "As suffering" means because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is suffering; the sense is that it should be contemplated as "suffering.
The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.
"Whoever sees pleasure as suffering" refers to a bhikkhu who, due to the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāma-dukkhatā*), views a pleasant feeling as "suffering."

He saw with the eye of wisdom. He saw suffering as a dart: he saw, that is, he perceived, the feeling of suffering as a dart because it produces oppression, because it pierces inwardly, and because it is difficult to extract. "Neither-suffering-nor-happiness" refers to the feeling of equanimity.
"Peaceful" means that, unlike pleasure and pain, it is not coarse and its nature is calmed by way of its conditions.

"Calm. He who has seen that which is calm as "impermanent"—because it does not exist after having been, because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is temporary, and because it is the opposite of the permanent—he is indeed a bhikkhu of right vision; the meaning is that he is one who clearly sees feeling with absolute certainty.

"Also as painful" means that they are painful by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*). "That [feeling] is in suffering" means that I declare all that which is felt to be included within and encompassed by suffering, because it does not transcend the suffering inherent in formations.

"And also from pleasure and pain" refers to the fact that pleasure and so forth are pleasant through the knowledge of their stability and change, and are painful through the ignorance of their change and stability.
The meaning is that because they have been so stated, the three [types of feeling] should be contemplated as pleasant, and the three [types of feeling] should also be contemplated as painful.

The seven contemplations have already been explained above. "The rest" refers to what remains from the aforementioned classification into pleasant and so forth; that is to say, the distinctions such as "with material gain" (*sāmisa*) and "without material gain" (*nirāmisa*), which are to be discussed in the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*).

“Of objects... up to... of distinctions”: this refers to the distinction of the diversity of objects such as visible forms, which is further divided into blue and so forth; the distinction of the diversity of predominance such as desire and so forth, which is further divided into inferior and so forth;
the distinction of the diversity of conascent factors such as knowledge and jhāna, which is further divided into prompted, unprompted, with applied thought, and so forth;

the distinction of the diversity of planes such as the sense-sphere and so forth, which is further divided into superior, middling, and so forth; and the distinction of the diversity of kamma such as wholesome and so forth.

The construction is as follows: it should be contemplated by way of the diversity of the destinies leading to the divine realms and so forth; by way of the diversity of dark and bright kamma-results and their divisions such as being experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth;
and by way of the diversity of functional kamma belonging to the limited plane (*parittabhūmika*) and so forth, and its divisions such as being three-rooted (*tihetuka*) and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the diversity of [kamma] with and without a physical basis (*savatthuka-avatthuka*), and the division of those common to the three types of persons (*puggalattaya*).
The inclusion is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "of the specific and general characteristics," the construction is:

by way of both their respective specific characteristics, such as contact and so forth, and their general characteristics, such as impermanence and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the phenomenon of emptiness," this refers to that which has the intrinsic nature of emptiness, namely selflessness (*anattatā*).
To clarify this, it is stated in the Abhidhamma: "At that time, there are phenomena (*dhammā*); there are aggregates (*khandhā*)," and so on.

The teaching on the discourse of emptiness has already occurred; since that [defilement] was already abandoned previously because of its prior abandonment, it need not be said to be abandoned again for each respective instance.
For defilements, when being abandoned, are not abandoned according to the distinction of their objects, because only those yet to come and ready to arise are to be abandoned.
Therefore, having stated the abandonment of covetousness and so forth in one place, [it need not be repeated] in another.
He shows this point—that it should not be said [that they are abandoned separately]—with the words, “But even here,” and so forth.

Alternatively, since what is abandoned at one place during a single moment of the path-consciousness is indeed abandoned everywhere, it should not be said that there is a separate abandonment for each.
For they deserve to be called “abandoned by the path. In that regard, the first objection is answered by the exclusion of different persons; it is not...

For what has been abandoned by one person is not necessarily said to have been abandoned by another. The final [point] is the exemption based on different moments of consciousness (*nānācittakkhaṇika*).
By "different moments of consciousness," the intention is "moments of mundane path-consciousness" (*lokiamaggacittakkhaṇa*), for it is the preliminary path (*pubbabhāgamagga*) that is intended here.

Furthermore, in mundane cultivation, what is abandoned in the body is not suppressed (*vikkhambhita*) in regard to feeling and so forth. Even if it were not to manifest, [it would still be abandoned].
Because it has been thoroughly abandoned through the cultivation of its opposite, it cannot be said that "there is a non-arising of covetousness and grief" in that case;
therefore, its abandonment must indeed be stated once again. What is abandoned in one instance is abandoned in all others;
thus, there is either the cultivation of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness, or, by way of mundane cultivation, the mere non-arising [of those states] everywhere.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). For in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated in four places: "The five aggregates are the aggregates of clinging; they are the world.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Explanation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the section of the summary.
Mindfulness of the Body (*kāyānupassanā*).
Commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness of Breathing (Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā) 374. "By way of object" means by way of the objects to be contemplated, such as the body and so forth.

"Dividing into fourfold" means dividing into fourfold according to the enumeration. Then, taking each individual foundation of mindfulness from among those four foundations of mindfulness, [one contemplates] the body...
"Vibhajanto" (analyzing) is the remainder of the sentence.
Regarding "Kathañca" (and how): here, "kathaṃ" is an interrogative concerning the manner; thus, he asks about the specific modes of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) that are being demonstrated.

The word "ca" (and) indicates a distinction; by it, he refers to the specific quality that was not made manifest in the section on the summary (*uddesavāra*), but is now being clarified in the section on the detailed exposition (*niddesavāra*).

He illuminates [this]. Since even among outsiders some portion of this exists, the phrase "of one who produces all modes of contemplation of the body" (*sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa*) is employed to include every variety.

By this, it refers to the fourteen modes that have come down in the *Ānāpānapabba* (the Chapter on Mindfulness of Breathing) and so forth, as well as the modes of internal and other contemplations included therein;
likewise, it includes the modes of the four jhānas based on the objects of the kasiṇas, hair, and so forth, described in the *Kāyagatāsati Sutta*, which consist of color, shape, and so on.
It includes all these various types, such as the mundane and so forth, without exception.
And these types exist only within this very teaching, not outside of it; thus it is said: "in every way... and the negator.
In that context, "the negation of being otherwise" means the negation of any other teaching serving as a support for a person who has produced the contemplation of the body in all its aspects.
By this [statement], "In this world, monks," he shows that here the word *idha* (in this world) includes the sense of *eva* (only/alone).
For there are even single words used as exclusives, such as "subsisting on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*). Therefore he said: "In this world alone, monks, is one a recluse," and so forth.
For that person is one whose qualities constituting the category of a recluse are complete, who has produced every mode of contemplation of the body.
"Parappavādā" refers to the various doctrines and sectarian positions of others, namely those of the followers of other religions.
The phrase beginning with "imassahi" was stated to show that forest dwellings and the like are suitable lodgings for meditation.
A "duddama" is a stubborn ox that has not been tamed; it is a rogue bull. Just as at the time of milking, [one ensures] that no milk remains in the udders...
It flows; thus is a counterfeit cow that prevents milking. The relish arising in dependence on visible forms, sounds, and so forth, is the flavor of the object such as the visible form.
"An object previously practiced" means an object familiarized with prior to going forth, or throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"One should bind" means one should fasten. "By mindfulness" means by way of correctly discerning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Of mindfulness that has proceeded": regarding the "object," it means the object of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Firmly" means steadily;
the meaning is that one should make it stable so that the concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—of one who practices with mindfulness may be accomplished.
It is the proximate cause for the attainment of distinctions and for dwelling in happiness in this very life for all Buddhas and for some Paccekabuddhas.
And for the disciples of the Buddha who have attained distinction through other meditation subjects, it serves as the foundation for their dwelling in happiness in this very life.
Like a teacher of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*), the Blessed One points out suitable places of residence for yogis.
Like a leopard, the bhikkhu dwells alone in the forest and accomplishes his desired goal by crushing opposing forces; thus, it is the supreme fruit.
He speaks with reference to the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). "A ground suitable for the speed of exertion" means a ground that serves as the basis for the speed of energy in meditation.

The construction is: "breathing long by way of the breaths and exhalations occurring over a duration, or breathing short by way of the breaths and exhalations occurring for a brief moment. "Training thus" refers to this.

For one training in meditation by way of perceiving the length and shortness of the in-breaths and out-breaths, experiencing the whole body [of breath], and the gradual subsiding of the gross and subtle [breaths];
or for one who, having become such, practices the three trainings;

[the phrase] "in the sign of the in-breaths and out-breaths" refers to the counterpart sign established in dependence upon the in-breaths and out-breaths. One comprehends the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of the physical form (rūpa).

One who is intent upon insight (vipassanā) is called "one who practices mindfulness of breathing" (assāsapassāsakammika). One who is intent upon insight by way of the formless (arūpa) comprehends the factors of jhāna.
The "basis" (vatthu) is the physical body (karajakāya), because it serves as the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors.
There is no other being or person; this is the view of purity: "This is merely phenomena (dhammamatta); it is not without cause."
Nor is it caused by an unequal cause such as a Supreme Deity (Issara), but rather it is caused by ignorance (avijjā) and so forth;

thus, having crossed over doubt through the overcoming of uncertainty regarding the three periods of time, he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) by means of the comprehension of aggregates (kalāpasammasana) according to the method beginning with "Whatever form, O bhikkhu," and so on.
Increasing insight (vipassanā) by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbaya-anupassanā) and so forth, he proceeds gradually through the sequence of the paths (magga).
“Or in another’s body of inhalation and exhalation”: this statement was made on the grounds that this passage occurs in the context of the section on comprehension (*sammasana*);
however, from the perspective of serenity (*samatha*), there is no arising of the sign of absorption (*appanā-nimitta*) in another’s body of inhalation and exhalation.
“Without omitting” means without skipping over at intervals. “At the time of moving back and forth” refers even to internal and external phenomena.
The time when [the mind] proceeds through uninterrupted cultivation has been explained. However, since these two cannot be obtained simultaneously, it is said:
"internally" and "externally. The meaning is that these two factors joined together cannot be obtained as a single object at one time; they cannot be taken as an object all at once.
It is called "origination" (*samudaya*) because it arises from this; that very thing, in the sense of being a cause, is a "dhamma," thus it is the "dhamma of origination.
The cause for the arising of inhalation and exhalation is the body born of karma (*karajakāya*), and so forth. One whose nature is to contemplate that is "contemplating the dhamma of origination.
Showing that dhamma of origination by means of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. Therein, *bhasta* means a bellows. *Gaggaranāḷi* means a pipe for blowing a fire.

Regarding the "body born of karma" (karajakāya) and so forth: just as the body of inhalation and exhalation is related to the body born of karma and so forth because it has that as its cause, so too the body born of karma and so forth are related to the body of inhalation and exhalation by being its cause. Thus, they receive the designation "phenomena subject to origination in the body.
This is why it is said: "Origination... is spoken of. Alternatively, [the term] refers to the primary nature (pakati).
The word *dhamma* here—as in such expressions as "subject to birth" (*jātidhammā*)—refers to the natural tendency that arises when the body's conditions come together;
thus, one who contemplates the body is called "one who contemplates the nature of arising" (*samudayadhammānupassī*). Therefore, he says: "And the body born of kamma," and so forth.
And by taking it in this way, the locative case in the phrase "in the body" (*kāyasmiṃ*) becomes even more appropriately justified.

Regarding the phrase "contemplating the nature of vanishing" (*vayadhammānupassī*): although destruction is causeless, when certain causal factors are absent, the absence of that which would have arisen is conventionally treated as if it were the cause of that non-arising.

Thus, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the absence of the physical body (*karajakāya*) and so forth is stated to be the cause for the vanishing of the body of inhalation and exhalation (*assāsapassāsakāya*).
Therefore he said, "Just as with the bellows," and so on. This, then, is the explanation here.
The exposition of the meaning is according to the first alternative. According to the second alternative, the meaning should be understood as being without even access concentration.

Since the contemplation of the characteristics of arising and passing away—like the contemplation of the internal and external—does not occur at one and the same time because their objective bases are distinct, it is said:
"Contemplating arising at one time and passing away at another time. "There is the body..."

The word *eva* is indicated as being elided (*luttaniddiṭṭha*). Having stated "the body itself is what exists," he says "not a being" and so forth to show that which is excluded by way of this restriction.

Its meaning is as follows: that which is imagined by others as a "being" (*satta*)—either because it is attached (*visatta*) to form and the other aggregates, or because it causes others to become attached (*sajjāpana*), or because it possesses the quality of a being (*satva*)—is [denied] because it merely fills out that collection of beings (*sattanikāya*).

It is called a "person" (*puggala*) because of its nature of passing away and being reborn, and because it "wastes away" (*galana*). It is called a "woman" (*itthī*) because the womb is that wherein one is fixed (*thīyati*) and congealed (*saṃhaññati*).

It is called a "man" (*purisa*) because he lies (*seti*) or exists (*pavattati*) in the former (*puri*) part [of the body]. It is called a "self" (*attā*) because the conceit "I" (*ahaṃ-māna*) is placed (*āhita*) therein.

It is called "belonging to self" (*attaniya*) by way of being one's own property. It is called "I" (*ahaṃ*) by taking the view that there is no other; and "mine" (*mama*) by way of what belongs to me.
Having considered [the body] as "mine," and having considered it as "someone else" distinct from the aforementioned categories, one considers it as "belonging to someone.
There is no one whatsoever to be conceptualized in this way; there is only "the body itself that exists.
Thus, by means of these ten phrases, he clarifies the emptiness of self and what belongs to self regarding the body. "In this way" means in the manner stated, beginning with "only the body exists."
"For the sake of making knowledge the measure" means for the sake of bringing the knowledge of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā-ñāṇa*) to the ultimate limit.
"For the sake of making mindfulness the measure" means for the sake of bringing the mindfulness that grasps the body and the mindfulness of occurrence (*pavattana-sati*) to the ultimate limit.

For, by the method already stated, the mindfulness that has been established through the successive arising [of thoughts] as "there is a body" brings about an even greater degree of knowledge regarding that object.
And it serves for the strengthening of mindfulness. Therefore he said: "for the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Because this cultivation is the direct antidote to the grasping of craving and views, it is said: "craving... [omitted] ...he dwells.
Being thus, he does not perceive anything in the world as "I" or "mine"; how could he grasp at it? Thus he said:

“*Na ca kiñci*,” etc. Regarding the phrase *evampi*: here the word *pi* (also/even) indicates a collective sense for what has not been explicitly stated, because such a meaning as was indicated below is absent;
thus he said, “taking the subsequent meaning,” just as in the case of:
“even down to one who is an animal, this too becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. However, *evaṃ* is a reference back to the manner already indicated.
He says, "But by this... it is shown," because it was formulated by way of a conclusion.
Since the preliminary stage of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is intended here, it is stated that "mindfulness is the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, that mindfulness is the very originator of the craving for whatever personal existence (attabhāva) it arises in, and it is indeed the originator of that [craving] as well.
Because it is absent when that [craving] is absent, he says: "The prior craving is its originator," just as in the case of "with volitional formations as condition.

According to the method of the Suttas, the entire mundane continuity of consciousness—arising from the seed of that consciousness within the continuum—is called simply "consciousness with volitional formations as condition. "Cessation" means the cause of cessation; it refers to the non-arising of both.
The meaning is "having become the sign. Or, it is "non-occurrence" (appavatti) because nothing occurs therein.
The passage beginning with "the full understanding of suffering" was stated to show that the noble path proceeds solely by way of accomplishing its four functions;

for its penetration through cultivation is established even without being explicitly stated. "By way of the Four Truths" means by way of the meditation subject of the Four Truths. "Having ascended" means...

"Having ascended by way of a succession of purifications, one leads the meditation further"—this is the meaning. "The gateway to deliverance" means the means for escaping from the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The commentary on the section on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section on the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
375. Regarding "by way of the modes of deportment" (*iriyāpatha*): *Iriyā* means moving or activity; here, however, it should be understood as bodily application.
The path (*patha*) of such movement—that is, the course of its occurrence—is the "mode of deportment" (*iriyāpatha*), which refers to the physical postures occurring by way of walking and so forth.
For when a being is walking, he performs the action to be done with the body, whether standing, sitting, or lying down; these are [the modes].
"By way of the postures" means by way of the classification of the postures. "Furthermore" (*puna caparaṃ*) means again and further; the intention is:

"I shall speak of another meditation subject for the contemplation of the body that is even more [extensive] than the aforementioned meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*);
listen. The phrase "while walking," and so forth, refers both to one who knows merely the act of walking and to one who knows the specific details involved in walking and the like.
And that is a general statement; therein, the mere knowledge of going and so forth is not intended here, but rather the knowledge of the specific details of the going and so forth is intended.
To show this by way of analysis, it is said: "Therein, 'sensual pleasure'... and so on.
"The perception of a being" means the perception that "a being exists," the grasping at a being. One does not abandon, one does not relinquish [the thought]: "I am going."

Because of the presence of the thought "let me go," one does not remove or dispel the perception of self—the distorted perception occurring in the form "there is a self, an agent, an experiencer"—because it lacks an opposing factor, or because it is not counteracted.

For one who is thus [distracted], how could there be the state of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and so forth? Therefore he said: "The meditation subject or the development of the foundations of mindfulness..."

“Or does it not exist? As for the passage beginning with “But of this,” etc., it refers to the bright side (sukkapa-kkha); its meaning should be understood as the reverse of what was stated [in the previous section].
Indeed, in order to explain that very same meaning, the passage beginning with “For this,” etc., was spoken.
Therein, “Who goes? is the inquiry regarding the agent of the act of going, having treated the instrument (the goer) and the action as inseparable.
That [negation] has the sense of negating a self characterized by agency and existence, because it demonstrates the establishment of going as belonging to the mere phenomenon (dhammamatta) alone.

"Whose going?"—this expresses that same meaning through a different turn of phrase (*pariyāyantara*), by distinguishing between the instrument (*sādhana*) and the action (*kiriya*), thereby clarifying the state of the action of going being unrelated to an agent. For, having internalized the sense of negation, [it shows this].
The word *kiṃ* (what) is employed in both senses. However, "What is the reason? is a question regarding the unerring cause of the action of going, which has a negated agent.

For this so-called "going" is a specific mode of occurrence of phenomena, caused by appropriate conditions free from false causes, such as: the self is conjoined with the mind, the mind with the sense-faculties, and the sense-faculties with their respective objects.
Therefore he said, "Therein," and so forth.
No being (satta) or person (puggala) goes, because it is established that there is only the movement of phenomena (dhamma), and because nothing exists apart from those phenomena.
Now, in order to demonstrate that it is only phenomena that move, he says: "By the expansion of the air-element produced by the activity of consciousness," and so forth.

It has been stated. In that context, "the diffusion and vibration of the air-element as a mental action" (*cittakiriyāvāyodhātuvipphāro*) means: it is both a mental action and a diffusion and vibration of the air-element; [it is] by that [term].
And here, by the inclusion of "mental action," one excludes the diffusion of the air-element not bound to the faculties;

by the inclusion of "diffusion of the air-element," one excludes the mental action consisting of the differentiation of volitional verbal intimation (*cetanā-vaci-viññatti*); by both [terms together],...

However, it clarifies bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). Having said "he goes," the phrase beginning with "therefore" (*tasmā*) was stated to show how the conventional expression "he goes" occurs when the body is in motion. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the consciousness that has arisen by way of the desire to go.

"It generates wind" (*vāyaṃ janeti*) means it produces a material aggregate (*rūpakalāpa*) in which the wind element (*vāyodhātu*) is predominant; and here, its predominance is due to its functional capacity (*sāmatthiyato*).

Not by measure. With reference to the air element—which arises from consciousness associated with movement and which functions through a specific mode as the condition for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body—it is said: "Air produces intimation.
For intimation is a modification concomitant with intention. And it is precisely because of this aforementioned predominance that there is the mention of "air."

It is not solely because of the air element’s status as a producer [that it is called motion]; otherwise, it would be difficult to establish the status of intimation (*viññatti*) as derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
"Leading forward" (*purato abhinīhāro*) is the movement of the body toward the front, which is termed "advancing" (*abhikkama*).

Having stated this briefly by means of the extended application (*atidesa*)—"The same method applies"—the text says "In that case too... and so forth, in order to explain that meaning. "Starting from the limit" means starting from the lower limit, that is, from the soles of the feet. "The state of being elevated" (*ussitabhāvo*) means the state of being raised up.
"Knowing thus" means knowing that walking and so forth occur solely through the expansion of the air-element, which is the activity of the mind.

For one who knows thus, the investigation "it occurs in this way" is spoken of by those who do not know things as they truly are—either through the influence of false adherence or by way of worldly convention—for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion through such knowledge. However, "there is, moreover," refers to one's own mode of inquiry.
This is the statement of the question. "There is not" is a word of negation regarding a being by way of a definitive conclusion.
The phrase beginning with "Just as," however, is an elucidation of that very meaning through a simile; it is indeed easy to understand.
"A ship by the force of the wind" means: just as an insentient ship goes to another place by the force of the wind, and just as an insentient...
Just as an arrow reaches another place by the force of the bowstring, so too the insentient body, struck by the wind, goes to another place led by the aforementioned air;

in this way, the application of the simile is to be understood. However, if someone were to say, "Just as the boat and the arrow go to another place by means of the person who pushes them, so it is with the body," let it be so.

Thus, this intended meaning is as follows: just as the movement of a boat depends on a person whose characteristic is to be compacted—that is, who is joined together—and not on one whose characteristic is not so compacted, so too it is with the body.

What loss is there for us? Rather, even more so, the mere nature of phenomena (dhammamattatā) gains its footing, and not the notion of a "person. Therefore he said: "By way of the yarn-thread," and so forth.
In this context, "impelled" (*payutta*) means set in motion by conditions through the activity of going and so forth, according to the method explained below.

"Stands" (*ṭhāti*) means it remains. "Here" (*ettha*) means in this world. "Without causes and conditions" (*vinā hetupaccaya*) means without the causes and conditions such as the air element (*vāyodhātu*) originated from the mental state of the desire to go.
"It stands" (*tiṭṭhe*) means it would remain. "Who indeed could go? (*vajeyya ko nāma*)—this is the connection [to the verb *vajati*, meaning "goes"]. The sense is one of negation (*paṭikkhepattha*).

And here, by the word "what" (kiṃ), through the denial of standing or moving due to the absence of a causal condition, it should be understood that just as self-emptiness is revealed, so too impermanence and suffering are revealed by demonstrating that the entire occurrence of phenomena exists in dependence upon conditions.
"Directed" (paṇihito) means established or placed in whatever manner by various conditions. This is an inclusive statement.
This is a term that encompasses all four postures together; since the postures were previously described individually, the meaning here is that they are spoken of by taking them collectively.

Alternatively, in the previous method, the posture was the primary factor and the body was secondary and merely produced [by it]; here, however, the body is the primary factor and the posture is secondary.
The second method was stated in order to show [the process] after having produced the subsequent result; thus, in this way, the distinction between these two methods should be understood.
"Established" means occurring.
Even the grasping of the postures is the grasping of the body itself which possesses the postures, because that [posture] is a particular state of it.
It is said: “By grasping the postures, he dwells contemplating the body in the body.
For this very reason, here the arising and so forth are set forth solely by way of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

Regarding the word “and so forth” (*ādīnaṃ*), by the word “and so forth” here, one who sees the characteristic of production—such as “through the arising of craving, through the arising of karma, through the arising of nutriment”—[sees] the arising of the aggregate of form.
"Sees" comprises these four aspects; likewise, it should be understood that "with the cessation of ignorance," and so forth, comprise five aspects.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on the postures is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension (Catusampajaññapabba): 376.

Regarding "by way of the fourfold clear comprehension" (*catusampajaññavasena*): it is called *sampajāna* because one knows thoroughly (*samantato*) or in every manner (*pakārehi*), or because one knows clearly and specifically (*pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ*).
The state of being *sampajāna* is *sampajañña*, which is knowledge proceeding in such a manner. It is divided into various types, such as the movement of the hands and so forth.

The four kinds of clear comprehension combined constitute the "fourfold clear comprehension. By means of this, the phrases beginning with "in going forward" have already been explained in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and need not be explained again;
therefore, the clarification of the meaning of those specific passages should also be understood according to the method established therein.
Thus: "In going forward and in returning, he acts with clear comprehension," and so forth.

Since, according to the word of the Buddha, the contemplation of the nature of arising and so forth is intended here specifically for the material body (rūpakāya) by means of grasping the fourfold clear comprehension regarding advancing and so forth, he said:
"The arising and passing away of the aggregate of form alone must be drawn out.
For advancing and so forth are indeed specific modes of occurrence belonging only to material phenomena. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension is finished.
Commentary on the Section on Attention to Repulsiveness (Paṭikkūlamanasikārapabba): 377.
"By way of attention to repulsiveness": that which is repulsive because it is to be loathed is simply "repulsive" (*paṭikkūla*); its intrinsic nature is that of the repulsive.

The aspect of repulsiveness, by way of attending to it. For even without a word expressing the state (*bhāva*), the meaning of the state is understood, as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth.
Since this was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, the meaning of the passage beginning with "this very body" should be understood according to the method explained therein and in its commentary.
A *pūtoḷi* is a covering made by binding materials such as cloth into the shape of a sack.
"Mixed in one place in various ways" means that, to this extent, the various colors and the hair and so forth are the objects of comparison (*upameyya*).

"The time when it has become manifest" refers to the time when, having transcended conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*), the unattractive aspect of the hair and so forth becomes established. Demonstrating that the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (or "aspect"):
Having said “thus,” he spoke the words beginning with “by the counting of the head-hairs, etc. to show that mode of appearance in its specific form.

For here, body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*) is the contemplation of the arising of the foul states known as head-hairs and so forth, which possess an extremely malodorous, loathsome, and repulsive aspect.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the section on contemplation of repulsiveness is finished.
378. Commentary on the Section on Contemplation of Elements:
"By way of contemplation of elements" means by way of the development and mental attention directed toward the four elements beginning with the earth element.

The meaning is: "by way of the analysis of the four elements. For *dhātumanasikāra* (attention to the elements), *dhātukammaṭṭhāna* (the meditation subject of the elements), and *catudhātuvavatthāna* (the analysis of the four elements) are one and the same in meaning.
A "cow-slayer" is one who kills cows for the sake of a livelihood.
An "apprentice" is one who lives near him by way of performing work and depends upon him for his livelihood. "Having pierced through" means having pierced each other at a single point.
"Designated as the middle point of the great crossroads" means that because it is the very place where the four great roads intersect, it is designated as the "middle.
Since those four great roads, having come from the four directions, seem to converge there, that place is called a "great crossroads" (*catumahāpatha*);
[the phrase refers to] at that great crossroads. Regarding the word *ṭhita*, "standing... [and so forth].

In passages such as "or," the term refers to being endowed with the postures (iriyāpatha) designated as "standing" (*ṭhāna*), or—since the word *ṭhā* has the sense of "ceasing from movement"—it indicates being endowed with the remaining postures by setting aside the posture of walking;
however, here it is intended to indicate the mode of occurrence of the material body in whatever way it may be, which is why he said: "by whichever of the four postures..."
"Because it is established by way of its mode, it is 'as it stands'. Therein, "by way of its mode" means by way of the mode of occurrence of the material body, such as standing and so forth.
For standing and the rest are called "postures" (*iriyāpatha*) because they are the path (*patha*)—that is, the course of occurrence—for the activity designated as "posture";
this is the intended meaning. "As it stands" means as it occurs, as it has been described; here, the very posture [already] mentioned is the object of the aspiration.

He said, "As it is situated and as it is directed," to clarify what was intended. Alternatively, "situated" (*ṭhita*) is an illustration of the body's association with the postures (*iriyāpatha*) known as standing;
"directed" (*paṇihita*) is an illustration of its association with the other postures.

Alternatively, "situated" is an illustration of the persistence (*avaṭṭhāna*) at each respective moment of the material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) comprised by the body according to their own functions; "directed" is...
"Established" (*paṇihita*) means placed in various ways by way of those respective conditions; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
"He reviews" (*paccavekkhati*) means he looks back again and again; having analyzed [the object] with the eye of knowledge, he sees it individually and distinctly.
Now, in order to demonstrate the meaning already stated by way of explaining its essential significance, [the text says]: "Just as for a cow-slaughterer," and so forth.

It has been said. Therein, "of one who is rearing" means of one who is causing it to grow by increasing the accumulation of flesh through the use of rice-scum, boiled rice, cotton seeds, and so forth.
"Killed and dead" means having been harmed, it is dead; and "dead" means merely dead. For this very reason he said, "at that very moment.
"The perception 'cow' does not disappear" means that those various limbs and members, as they were previously situated...
The designation "cow" (*gāvī*) is applied even to a cow that is merely dead because its particular configuration has not yet perished.
They are called *bīlā* because they dissolve, break apart, and fall asunder; the *va* in *bhāgā* becomes *ba*, and the *i* becomes *ī*.
Thus, *bīlaso* means having made them into individual parts (*bīlaṃ bīlaṃ*). "Having divided" means having separated the flesh from the collection of bones, or [having separated it] from there.
“Dissected” means having divided the flesh into its constituent parts. For this very reason, it is said: “The perception of flesh occurs.

This applies even to one who has gone forth but whose meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is not yet mastered. “Resolution of the compact” means the dissection and analysis of what is compacted by way of continuity, mass, function, and substance.
“Contemplating by way of elements” means, through the process of resolving the compact, contemplating each element—such as the earth-element and so forth—individually.

For one who reflects by separating [the aggregates] one by one: "The perception of a being" (sattasaññā) refers, they say, to the perception of a being that occurs by way of the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi);
however, it is entirely appropriate that even the conventional perception of a being should then disappear, because of the accomplishment of the analysis of the compact mass according to reality.
For this being so, the meaning of the object of comparison (upameyyattha) is indeed nothing other than [identical to] the meaning of the simile as stated above.
It blends and comes together. For this very reason it is said: “The mind settles by way of the elements alone.

"Dakkho" means one who is clever and skilled in various conventional designations (*samaññā*), because he knows that, for example, when a cow has just been born and its tail, hooves, horns, and so forth are present as an undifferentiated collection of parts such as bone and flesh, there is the designation "cow," but not [yet] the designation for the differentiated parts such as bone and flesh;
however, once those parts are differentiated, there is the designation for the bone, flesh, and so on.

"The four postures are like a crossroads": just as a cow stands at a crossroads, the fourfold posture—which constitutes the path for the activity of the body—is explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there and in its commentary. The remainder is exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the section on the contemplation of the elements is finished.
379. The commentary on the section on the nine charnel-ground contemplations:
[this refers to] the discourses that proceed specifically regarding corpses cast away in a charnel ground, such as the bloated corpse and so forth.

Furthermore, the portions of the foulness of the bloated corpse and so forth, which are denoted by those [terms], have been given the technical designation "chapters on the charnel ground" (*sivathikapabbāni*) by the compilers of the canon.
Therefore, he said, "to analyze by means of the chapters on the charnel ground. "One day dead" means having died and passed one day.
"After the exhaustion of life" means after death, subsequent to the termination of the life-faculty. "Arising" means having emerged.
"Uddhumātatta" means being bloated, puffed up, and swollen. "Vinīla" refers to what is discolored and mixed with various other colors;
or, it is "vinīla" because it has become blue through the transformation of its previous color.
The addition of the syllable "ka" in the term "vinīlaka" does not alter the meaning, just as in the expressions "yellowish" (*pītaka*) or "reddish" (*lohitaka*). "Paṭikkūlatā" means repulsiveness.

Because it is loathsome. To show that the letter *ka* has the sense of "loathing" (*kuccha*), as in the phrase "a wicked report spreads abroad," it is said that what is loathed is "bluish-black" (*vinīla*). By crows, vultures, and so forth, from the places where [the flesh] has fallen away.
"Flowing with pus" (*vissandamānapubba*) means oozing with pus; the meaning is that it is trickling here and there. "Such a state" (*tathābhāva*).
[The corpse] with its state of oozing fluids.
"That bhikkhu" refers to the one spoken of as: "He who might see a body cast away in a charnel ground," that is the bhikkhu. He applies the similarity [to himself].

The phrase beginning with "This too" is a demonstration of the manner of application. "Life-span" (*āyu*) refers to the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) and the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*).

In this context, it follows the course of consciousness. "Heat" refers to the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*). "Thus, its very nature is putrid" means that its nature is one of extreme foul odor, loathsomeness, repulsiveness, and putrefaction;
the intention is that it is not merely a slight [change] as in the case when vitality and the other factors have not yet departed.
"It will become such" means "it will possess such a state"; thus he said, "it will become characterized by such varieties as bloatedness and so forth."

“Having plucked out, having plucked out” means having torn out, having torn out. “Possessing some remaining flesh and blood” means that because it has not been entirely consumed, it is possessed here and there by a small amount of residual flesh and blood.
By saying “the hand-bone by another,” the scattering of the hand-bones is indicated without distinction;
thus, in order to show their scattering without exception, he said, “even the sixty-four varieties,” and so forth.
“Terovassikāni” means having passed through a rain; since those [garments] have actually elapsed for a year, he said, “atikkantasaṃvaccharāni” (having exceeded a year).
Here, “putrefaction” refers to the state of being crumbled due to the loss of solidity caused by age.
To show how that occurs, he said, “in the open air,” and so forth. “Terovassikāneva” means having exceeded merely a year.
Thus it is. Because the second cemetery section and the others have been defined by way of being devoured and so forth, it is said:
"The application should be made by way of being devoured and so forth.
The commentary on the section on the nine cemeteries is finished.

By the restrictive phrase "these two alone," it is determined that the object of meditation for absorption (*appanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) is restricted to those two, because of the absence of such absorption in other sections. For wherever there is the particle *eva*, it restricts the meaning to something other than that;
thus, one should see that the status of the two sections as objects of meditation for insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) is not prohibited, since they involve the seeing of impermanence and so forth.
The sections on the charnel ground (*sivathika-pabba*) are for the purpose of discerning the danger in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
He said: "Because it was stated by way of contemplating the dangers (*ādīnavānupassanā*) of the charnel grounds.

Since the fact that the sections on the postures (*iriyāpathapabba*) and so forth lead to absorption (*appanāvahatā*) is already evident, he said: "The remaining twelve as well. Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
Commentary on the Contemplation of Feeling (Vedanānupassanā) 380.

Regarding the phrase "pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanā*): here, it is called "pleasant" (*sukhā*) because it pleases (*sukhayati*). The meaning is that it causes the associated mental states and the body to obtain satisfaction.
Alternatively, it is pleasant because it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) or carves away (*khanati*) physical and mental affliction.
Others say: "It is 'pleasant' because it is easy for her to grant space. It is called *vedanā* because it feels (*vedayati*), that is, it experiences the flavor of the object.

"While feeling" (*vedayamāno*) means while experiencing. Regarding what should be said about the terms "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*) and so forth, it is exactly according to the method already stated in the section on the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
"Feeling with full awareness" (*sampajānavediyanaṃ*) is the act of feeling by one who is fully aware.

“Basis-objects” means objects such as visible form and so forth. Here, the object consisting of visible form and so forth is intended by the term “basis” (*vatthu*) because it is the locus for the occurrence of feeling.

“*Assā*” means “it would be. Since there is no agent apart from the phenomenon (*dhamma*), he says “feeling itself feels” in order to show that the phenomenon itself possesses the status of an agent. By the phrase “it is a mere conventional expression,” [he shows that] “pleasure...”
By saying, "While experiencing a feeling, I experience a pleasant feeling," he shows that this is merely conventional usage (*vohāramatta*).
"Sighing" means sighing by way of allowing an opportunity for that [feeling] after seeing the danger in suppressing a powerful surge of sensation;
for if one holds back the surge too much, great suffering arises, which might even cause other disturbances.
Because of that, the Elder turned back and forth repeatedly. "Having yoked energy with serenity" means:

because of the excessive intensity of the energy of endurance (*adhivāsana-vīriya*), by way of reducing that [energy], he yoked energy with serenity through the production of a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) by means of concentration.

"Together with the analytical knowledges" means together with the supramundane analytical knowledges (*lokuttara-paṭisambhidā*); for at the moment of the Noble Path, the analytical knowledges function by way of non-delusion.
Furthermore, there is the realization [of the Dhamma] by way of taking the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) as its object.
Alternatively, even regarding mundane states, when they arise, he says "together with the analytical knowledges" with reference to their capacity therein.

Or, "one who attains final nibbāna level-headed" means that having become one who attains final nibbāna at the same moment [as the attainment of arahantship], he passes away in the very next moment following the moment of reviewing.
And just as it was said regarding pleasure—“Who experiences pleasure? and so forth—with reference to clear comprehension of feeling (*sampajañña-vedayita*), so too is it said regarding pain.
In that context, it is called *dukkhā* because it causes suffering (*dukkhayati*); the meaning is that it oppresses and afflicts both the associated mental states and the body.
Alternatively, it is so called because it badly devours (*duṭṭhuṃ khādati*) or it digs away (*khanati*) bodily and mental ease (*sāta*).
"It is painful. Others say: "It is painful because it requires a difficult granting of space. "Immaterial meditation subject" means the discernment of the immaterial;
the meaning is that it is an application of insight by way of immaterial phenomena. It does not become manifest because the mode of appearance of both contact and consciousness is unmanifest.
Therefore he said: "It appears as if in darkness. And this phrase, "it does not become manifest," refers to...
This was said with reference to such individuals; for them, feeling alone appears most clearly at the beginning.
Thus, what is stated in the *Sakkapañha-vaṇṇanā* and other works—namely, "contact becomes manifest" and "consciousness becomes manifest"—is not contradicted.
The construction is: "the meditation subject being explained by way of feeling becomes manifest."
And as for the phrase, “Because the arising of feelings is manifest,” this is stated with reference to pleasant and painful feelings.

For their occurrence is coarse, whereas that of the other [neutral feeling] is not. Alternatively, since it must be understood by way of grasping both of those, the occurrence of the other is likewise manifest to the wise;
thus, the unqualified mention of “feelings” (*vedanānaṃ*) should be seen [as including all]. It is according to the method stated in the *Sakkapañha* [Sutta].
It should be understood; therefore, the specific meaning to be stated therein is to be taken according to the method already explained in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*.

Previously, it was stated that "feeling itself feels by making the basis its object," which demonstrated the understanding of feeling's lack of self (*anattatā*) due to its dependence on an object for its existence;
now, showing the understanding of its impermanence (*aniccatā*) and other characteristics, [the text says]: "This..."

“There is another way of understanding,” he said. Just as two states of consciousness cannot exist simultaneously at one moment because of the absence of multiple simultaneous conditions, so too there cannot be two feelings at once because they function toward distinct objects;
thus he said, “because of the absence of painful feeling at the moment of pleasant feeling. And this is merely an illustration, for at that time neutral feeling is also absent.

Therefore, by understanding that other feelings which previously existed have ceased at the moment of a pleasant feeling, the non-existence of even that pleasant feeling is indeed known; thus, showing its very manifest nature, he said:
"Because this pleasant feeling was previously non-existent," and by this very statement, the manifest nature of those other feelings is also shown.
It should be seen. Therefore he said: “Feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change.
For by the mention of “impermanent,” the state of feeling’s disintegration is shown, because once it has been shattered by impermanence, it is easily understood.

By the mention of “unstable,” its manifest nature is shown, because it does not persist through constant cultivation and so forth. By the mention of “subject to change,” its state of suffering is shown.
Because it demonstrates changeability (*aññathatta*), by that very fact even pleasant feeling is suffering, let alone the others;

thus the suffering-nature of all three feelings is shown. Therefore, it should be understood that the comprehension of the three characteristics regarding all three feelings—namely, "whatever is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is entirely non-self" (*anattā*)—is thereby illuminated.
Hence he said: "In this way, one is clearly comprehending (*sampajāno*) therein."
Now, in order to establish this matter by means of a Sutta, he says: "And it is said also," and so forth.

Therein, "at that time one does not experience a painful feeling" means that at that time of being possessed of a pleasant feeling, one does not experience a painful feeling because it has ceased and because it has not yet arisen, respectively, for what is past and what is future. However, there is no possibility of a present [painful feeling].
This has already been stated. They are impermanent (*anicca*) because they exist for only the duration of their own functional moment.

They are conditioned (*saṅkhata*) because they are produced by causes coming together and combining. They are dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) because they have arisen in dependence upon conditions such as the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*).

They should be understood as subject to destruction (*khayadhamma*), subject to vanishing (*vayadhamma*), subject to fading away (*virāgadhamma*), and subject to cessation (*nirodhadhamma*), owing to their nature of wasting away, passing away, crumbling, and ceasing.

It is called "material" (āmisa) because it is to be touched by the defilements; the five strands of sensual pleasure are "with material" (sāmisa) because they are accompanied by material things through their function as objects. Therefore he said: "dependent on the material of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Regarding the passage following this—"There is feeling," and so forth—he says: "in the very same manner as stated in the section on contemplation of the body.
The commentary on the contemplation of feelings is finished.
Commentary on the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanā) 381.
"With lust" (*sarāga*) means together with lust as it occurs by way of association. Therefore, he said: "accompanied by greed" (*lobhasahagata*). Regarding "free from lust" (*vītarāga*):
although here one would expect the term "free from lust" to be the counterpart to the term "with lust," [this is so] for the range of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*).

However, because only those belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka) are intended here, it says "mundane wholesome and indeterminate," and then clarifies that very intention with the words "But this...
and so forth. The remaining two are rooted in hatred (dosa), and two are rooted in delusion (moha); thus, there are four unwholesome types of consciousness.

Since these lack association with greed (rāga), they possess no state of being "with-greed" (sarāga) in themselves; however, because they are caused by that [greed], they may be said to be "accompanied by it" at the time [they arise].

Since that state of being free from lust does not exist at all, only the state of being liberated from suffering is obtainable here; thus he said, "it partakes neither of the first term nor of the last term.
If this is so, does it follow that there is only a partial understanding?

It does not follow, because those [factors] are included within the intermediate category of suffering (*dukkha*). However, as for those who say, "If the state of being an opponent is not apprehended, there is an absence of association..."

If they maintain that "in this case, the measure [of the object] is like that of certain indeterminate states," then according to their opinion, the inclusion of the second term should be understood to apply to the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses as well.
The meaning in the second dyad should also be understood in the manner already stated.

Regarding the unwholesome roots, because it proceeds together with delusion (*moha*), he says "together with delusion" (*samoha*); thus he says, "accompanied by doubt and accompanied by restlessness."

And since here the restrictive emphasis on the first member of the compound—namely, that it is "with delusion together with [the other factors]" (*saha eva mohena*)—is indeed applicable, it is therefore said, "But because...

and so forth. Furthermore, because of extreme delusion and because of possessing a particularly distinguished form of delusion according to the method of individual application (*pāṭipuggalika-naya*), the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness can be called "muddled mind" (*momūha-citta*); thus, they are specifically designated as "with delusion."
It is said that the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses do not function in that way; thus, he speaks with apprehension, saying, "they indeed do function.

"Overcome by sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhānupatita*) means accompanied by, or followed by, sloth and torpor through association. The fivefold wholesome consciousness prompted by deliberation is "contracted consciousness";
it is called contracted because it proceeds by way of contraction toward its object. This is due to a specific condition.
"Accompanied by restlessness" means conjoined with restlessness born of lack of firmness; otherwise, every unwholesome consciousness would indeed be accompanied by restlessness.
"Distracted mind" is so called because it proceeds toward the object in a scattered manner through a specific kind of distraction.
It is called "lofty" (*mahaggata*) because it has attained greatness through its capacity to suppress the defilements, its vast fruitfulness, and its long continuity;

or else, because it has proceeded by means of great and sublime factors such as zeal (*chanda*). Furthermore, that [state] pertains to the planes of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpabhūmi*), since there is nothing greater than that in the world.
Therefore he said: "belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres" (*rūpārūpāvacara*). And here, its counterpart is—
"It is merely limited (paritta)" means "not exalted (amahaggata)," that is, belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

"With-surpassable" (sauttara) means together with those things capable of surpassing it; by contrast, "unsurpassable" (anuttara) is its opposite. This should be understood in relation to both of these categories, hence he said:
"With-surpassable means belonging to the sense-sphere," and so forth. By means of concentration (samādhi) capable of suppressing opposing states, [one attains] correctly...

"Placed" means concentrated. Therefore he says "of which," and so forth. "Of which" means of which consciousness. That which is not concentrated by the aforementioned concentration is "unconcentrated.
Therefore he says "devoid of both types of concentration. That which is liberated through liberation-by-its-factors is the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere;
that which is liberated through suppression-liberation is sublime consciousness. Both of these [are unconcentrated].
He spoke with intentional meaning, saying: “It is liberated by means of liberation through its factors and suppression.

If one were to understand “devoid of both kinds of liberation” as referring to any state where both types of liberation are absent, there would be the possibility of doubt even regarding supramundane consciousness;
therefore, to exclude that, he said: “There is no opportunity for... [etc. ...uprooting. And the state of being an opportunity is intended here in the sense of the range of comprehension (sammasana).
It is to be understood. As for that which has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning, it is self-evident because of the method already stated below.
The commentary on the contemplation of mind is finished.
Contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā).
The Exposition of the Section on the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā): 382.

The meaning that the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) has been demonstrated in five ways by way of showing the classification of phenomena such as those to be abandoned is understood from the text itself;
thus, indicating this meaning, [the text says]: "To explain the contemplation of phenomena in fivefold fashion."
He asked: "If this is so, why are they taught specifically by way of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth? [The answer is:

"Because of the inclinations of those to be trained (*vineyyajjhāsaya*). For those disciples for whom the hindrances must first be explained in detail among the phenomena to be abandoned, it was for their sake that the Blessed One first taught the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) regarding the hindrances here. Likewise, even the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) is preceded by serenity (*samatha*)."

After that, there is a further teaching concerning the aggregates to be fully understood, the sense bases, the factors of enlightenment to be developed, and the truths distinguished as those to be fully understood and so forth;
therefore, even the development of serenity (samatha) here is intended only for the sake of insight (vipassanā).
Since the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) has insight as its primary focus and abounds in insight, it is [distinguished] by way of this specific emphasis on insight.
Explaining the state of having been taught, he says, "Moreover," and so forth. Therein, the exposition of the summary by way of the aggregates, bases, and the truth of suffering should be understood.

By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "the inclusion of the aggregates of perception and formations," he includes the inclusion of all five aggregates of clinging, because the others are contained within them.
Because they do not exist at the time of understanding that "there is no coexistence of dark and bright phenomena," it is said, "by way of frequent occurrence.
"Existing" means being found within one's own continuum. "In what way" (yathā) refers to the manner [in which it occurs];
however, since it is stated that "the arising of sensual desire occurs," this is specifically the manner of the cause of sensual desire, which in meaning is simply the cause itself.
He said: “By which reason. The word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for the meaning that is about to be stated.
“Therein” refers to the phrase beginning with “and just as,” etc.

“Even beauty” means even sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). For that [beauty] is called “beautiful” by way of its own mode of grasping; and because it serves as the sign (*nimitta*) for other sensual desires that arise in that same mode, it is called a “sign.”
*Ca*: A beautiful object (*subhārammaṇa*) is form and so forth when it is apprehended as desirable or in a desirable manner.
"Inappropriate attention" (*anupāyamanasikāra*) is attention that is not a means for attaining the desired welfare and happiness. *Taṃ*: that inappropriate attention. *Tattha*:
therein, in those two kinds of beautiful signs which serve as both a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and an object (*ārammaṇa*). *Āhāro*: nutriment, meaning a condition for itself.
It is called "the fruit" because it brings forth the result.

"The foul" (*asubha*) refers to the foul meditative absorption (*asubha-jjhāna*), by dropping the middle term; that, moreover, should be understood as occurring with respect to the ten inanimate foul objects (*aviññāṇaka-asubha*) such as hair and so forth, and with respect to the animate foul objects (*saviññāṇaka-asubha*).
For in the *Girimānanda Sutta*, the perception regarding hair and so forth is termed "the perception of the foul" (*asubha-saññā*).

Thus it was said. And here, it should be understood that the inclusion of both the fourfold improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) is made for the purpose of showing them without exception.
Among those, however, what is intended here is the mental attention [to things] as "beautiful" regarding the unattractive (*asubha*), and as "unattractive" regarding the beautiful;
the others are included because they are conducive to those two.

The apprehension of the repulsive aspect among the eleven kinds of foulness, or practicing in such a way that the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises therein, is the apprehension of the foulness sign (*asubhanimitta*).
Devotion to the development of foulness (*asubhabhāvanānuyoga*) is the application of oneself to the development of foulness that brings about access and absorption.
[For one who is] moderate in eating and temperate in food, there is no opportunity for sloth and torpor because they are overcome.
They say that sensual desire is abandoned when one does not obtain [the object]; and this same meaning is stated in the *Niddesa* as well:

"But he who correctly understands the repulsiveness of food, its transformation, its basis, and the extreme loathsomeness of its supporting condition, as well as the fact that the body subsists on nutriment—he, in every respect, regarding food..."
One who knows the measure [of food] is called "one who knows the proper amount in eating" (*bhojanamattaññū*). For such a person, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is indeed abandoned.
The Elder Tissa, a practitioner of the meditation on the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*), was one who saw teeth-bones. "Abandoned" means abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vasena*).
This same principle applies to similar instances that follow. According to the method of the Abhidhamma, all greed (*lobha*) is the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).
He said: “By the path of arahantship.
Even resentment that has arisen previously is considered a cause for the resentment arising subsequently, by virtue of being the sign of resentment.

One who feels affection (*mejjati*) and is endearing (*siniyhati*) is a friend (*mitto*); it is a person seeking one’s welfare. That which exists toward such a friend, or that which belongs to a friend, is [called] *mitta*.
“Loving-kindness” (mettā) means the desire for the welfare of others; both absorption (appanā) and access (upacāra) are applicable here because the term is used in its general sense.
When it is said “liberation of mind” (cetovimutti), only absorption is applicable, because there is no complete liberation from the opposing states until absorption is reached.
“That” refers to wise attention (yonisomanasikāra). “Therein” means in loving-kindness. “Causing it to proceed frequently” means practicing it repeatedly (bahulīkāra).
The arousing and setting in motion of the bringing about of welfare for beings through loving-kindness is the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness.
The attention directed toward loving-kindness that first arises is itself the sign of loving-kindness, because it serves as the cause for the subsequent arising [of loving-kindness].
Those who have karma as their own are "karmically self-determined" (*kammassakā*); these are sentient beings. The state of being such is "karmic self-determination" (*kammassakatā*).
Being heirs to one’s own kamma (*kammadāyādatā*). Here, "reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) refers to the investigation of the dangers and benefits of ill will exactly as they are.
Here, "having good friends" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) refers to being possessed of good friends who abide in loving-kindness.

Regarding the "specified, unspecified, and directional pervasions" (*odissaka-anodissaka-disāpharaṇa*; cf. *Maṇisāramañjūsā*, 1.115), these are by way of oneself, those very dear, friends, neutral persons, and enemies.
There is the directed method, and when the boundaries have been merged, there is the undirected method.

The extension of the directions by means of radiating in one direction and so forth should be understood as the way of grasping loving-kindness (*mettā*). Alternatively, there is the directed extension of directions according to the monastery, the road, the village, and so on;

and there is the undirected extension of directions according to the east and other cardinal points, free from specific reference to a monastery or the like. It is with reference to this twofold way of grasping that the phrase "the directed and undirected extensions of directions" is used.
It has been said. "Grasping" (uggaha) should be understood as extending up to the stage of access (upacāra). "Cultivation" (bhāvanā) is the repeated practice of what has been grasped.
In that regard, it is fivefold by way of the categories: "all beings," "living things," "creatures," "persons," and "those included within individual existence.

Within each of these, it proceeds in four ways—thinking, "May they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves happily"—thus making twenty modes in total.

Loving-kindness (mettā) as a non-specific pervasion is sevenfold when it proceeds by way of the categories of beings—namely, all women, men, noble ones, non-noble ones, deities, humans, and those in the states of misery—or twenty-eightfold;
it is tenfold when it proceeds by way of the categories of directions across the ten directions;
or, within each direction, it is divided into four hundred and eighty types according to the distinctions of beings, women, and enemies, and so forth.
And the pervasion should be understood as specific.
That improper attention by which discontent (*arati*) and the rest arise is "improper attention regarding discontent and the rest.
This locative case is used in the sense of "that by which" something is produced. This same method applies to the following cases as well. [Discontent] with remote lodgings...
It is the state of shrinking away from the arising of wholesome states. "Bending of the body" is the bending of the karma-born body into an unsightly posture.
"A state of sluggishness" is the attainment of contraction.
This is because its nature is to establish the practice of wholesome states and its nature is to wither away their opposites.
And because it is energy that has arisen from the very beginning of the element of undertaking, he says, "the energy of the first undertaking.

Since there is neither the dispelling of sloth nor the attainment of firmness through the mere first undertaking, it is therefore said, "it is stronger than that [initial effort] due to its emergence from sloth.
However, because it brings about successive excellence through repeated practice as it arises again and again, [it is even stronger].
It becomes exceedingly firm; therefore it is said: "Because it steps from one stage to the next, it is even stronger than that.
