"Grasping the sign in overeating" means grasping the sign of sloth and torpor in overeating—the grasping of the cause and non-cause of sloth and torpor, such as:
"When this much has been eaten, that food becomes a cause for sloth and torpor; when this much has been eaten, it does not."

The meaning is "it occurs. This is stated by way of contrast; therefore, it should be understood that moderation in eating—the fact that "when one has eaten this much, that food does not become a cause for sloth and torpor"—is also shown by implication. Hence he said: "Four or five...
does not occur. "The daylight of the sun" means that even for one who attends to the sign of the sun's light perceived during the day at night.

The meaning here should be understood in this way. Because the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are dependent on energy, it is said: "Also by talk that is favorable and dependent on the ascetic practices.

As for remorse (*kukkucca*), since it occurs through the grieving over what has been done and left undone, it possesses the same characteristic as restlessness (*uddhacca*) insofar as it brings about a lack of mental tranquility; thus it is said: "Lack of tranquility means an unpeaceful state; in terms of its actual meaning, this is simply restlessness and remorse.

For one who is well-versed in the scriptures and investigates the discourses and so forth both in terms of the letter and the spirit, and who dwells frequently therein, there is the possibility of attaining the knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*) and so forth.
"There is no distraction" means that through practice according to the method and through the engagement in appropriate remedies, there is no grieving over what has been done or left undone;
thus he said, "By great learning... [and so on]... restlessness and remorse are abandoned.
To the same extent that restlessness and remorse are abandoned by great learning, they are also abandoned by being one who asks many questions and by being one who knows the training (vinaya).

This is how it should be understood. Furthermore, since service to the elders brings about the character of the elders, they are said to cause the abandoning of restlessness and remorse because they bring tranquility to the mind.
However, it should be understood that those who dispel remorse—namely, the masters of the Vinaya and virtuous friends—are mentioned here regardless of whether they are elders.
And since distraction for renunciants is for the most part caused by remorse, [the text] says, "one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is unallowable," and so forth.

By way of the method of training (*vinaya-naya*), such qualities as being one who asks questions (*paripucchakatā*) and so forth have been demonstrated. In the phrase "when restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) have been abandoned," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Because remorse is accompanied by mental distress (*domanassa*), its non-arising in the future is stated to occur through the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmi-magga*).
That wherein something stands or proceeds is called a "basis" (*ṭhānīya*); thus, "bases for doubt" (*vicikicchā-ṭhānīya*) refers to those things which are bases for doubt. Regarding doubt...
Phenomena that serve as causes are called "grounds" (*ṭhānīyā*), meaning they "stand. That which has doubt as its ground is "doubt-grounded" (*vicikicchā-ṭhānīyā*);
in terms of its actual meaning, it is simply doubt itself. For that [prior] doubt, by virtue of being a homogeneous cause for the doubt arising subsequently, is the unique cause.
"Wholesome and unwholesome": they are wholesome in the sense of being produced through skill (*kosalla*); their opposites are unwholesome.
Those that are unwholesome are blameworthy, not to be cultivated, and inferior. Those that are wholesome are blameless, to be cultivated, and superior.

Alternatively, wholesome states are inferior when initiated by inferior zeal and so forth, and superior when initiated by superior [zeal and so forth]. "Dark" means black, because they cause the mind to lose its luminosity.

"White" (*sukka*) means pure, as they produce a state of luminosity in the mind. Or, they are "black" (*kaṇha*) because they are the cause for a black lineage of rebirth, and "white" because they are the cause for a white lineage of rebirth.

These very same factors are the counterparts (*sappaṭibhāga*). For the black factors are the counterparts to the white ones by way of being their direct opposites, and likewise the white ones are the counterparts to the others.
Alternatively, they are "black-and-white-counterparts" (*kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāga*), meaning they are both black and white and possess counterparts. [The next term is] "pleasant" (*sukhā*).
For feeling is the counterpart to painful feeling, and painful feeling is the counterpart to pleasant feeling.
Granted that all doubt regarding the eight bases is abandoned through great learning and interrogation, nevertheless,
because the remaining doubts are rooted in doubt concerning the Three Jewels, he said, "concerning the Three Jewels."
Regarding the realization of the qualities of the Triple Gem, doubt—expressed in such phrases as “one who doubts the Teacher”—is impossible.
As for the phrase “one who has mastery in the Vinaya,” it is said that one effects the abandonment of the doubt described as “one who doubts the training”;
thus he says, “even for one who has attained mastery in the Vinaya. “One who abounds in resolve known as faith that inspires confidence” refers to the object of faith.

For one who is frequently intent upon resolving by means of resolution (adhimokkha) known as faith that does not enter [into doubt], it should be understood that "resolving" (adhimuccana) is simply the arising of resolution (adhimokkha).
Alternatively, resolution (adhimokkha) is the inclination, leaning, and tendency toward faith.

"Arising and passing away" refers to things subject to the nature of arising and passing away. "In the case of the sign of beauty, the sign of ugliness, and so forth" means: "in the case of the sign of beauty, etc."

In the phrase “in the sign of the foul, etc.,” the word “etc. (ādi) should be applied to each term individually. Therein, by the first “etc.,” there is the inclusion of the sign of repulsion and so forth;
by the second, there is the inclusion of the liberation of mind through loving-kindness and so forth. Whatever else remains to be said here follows the same method already explained.
The commentary on the section on the hindrances is finished.

**Commentary on the Aggregates (Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā)** 383. The aggregates are called *upādānakkhandhas* because they are to be grasped (*upādātabba*) by means of clinging (*upādāna*), either by way of being made an object or otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "thus is form" (*iti rūpaṃ*), the intention is that the word *iti* here has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*; thus he says, "this is form."
Because it includes the grasping of all forms according to their own nature, there is a complete exhaustion of everything; thus he says: "This much is form;
there is no form beyond this. Alternatively, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of manner;

therefore, by the phrase "thus far as to form," he demonstrates form exhaustively, including whatever variety of form exists by way of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya*). By way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

This is because of their nature as being subject to change (ruppana-sabhāva), and because of their respective natures as the eye and so forth, or as visible form and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the case of feeling and the rest," one should apply the explanation here as follows:
"One understands feeling by its nature, thinking: 'This is feeling; this is the extent of feeling; there is no feeling beyond this.

And regarding "by its nature," it should be applied as: "by its nature of experiencing (anubhavana-sabhāva), and by its nature of being pleasant and so forth. The remainder is easy to understand, as it follows the method already stated.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Aggregates is finished.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Bases (Āyatana-pabbavaṇṇanā): 384.
Regarding the phrase "in the six internal and external [bases]," the word "six" (*chasu*) refers to "in the six internal and in the six external."
Each [pair] should be applied separately. Why, then, are these two groups stated as exactly six each?

Because of the determination of the doors, objects, and the arising of the classes of consciousness. For, in the case of a class of consciousness included within the cognitive series of eye-consciousness, the eye-base alone is the door of its arising, and the visible-object base alone is its object;
likewise for the others in relation to their respective [bases and objects]. However, for the sixth [consciousness], that which is termed the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind—
A portion of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is the door of arising, and the uncommon object is the phenomenon-base (*dhammāyatana*).

It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; the meaning is that it enjoys visible form and makes it manifest. It is called "ear" (*sota*) because it hears. It is called "nose" (*ghāna*) because it smells.

Taste is "life" (*jīvita*) by virtue of being the cause of life; it is called "tongue" (*jivhā*) because it invites that life. It is the source (*āyo*), the place of arising, for base, tainted phenomena (*sāsavadhamma*).

The body (*kāya*). It is called "mind" (*mano*) because it cognizes and discerns an object. It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it manifests a change of color, making known its state as something internalized within the heart.
It is called "sound" (*sadda*) because it flows forth through its own conditions, being carried along and reaching the state of being cognizable by the ear-consciousness.
It is called "odor" (*gandha*) because it makes its own basis fragrant and manifest. It is called "taste" (*rasa*) because beings relish and enjoy it.
It is called *phoṭṭhabba* (the tangible) because it is touched (*phusati*). They are called *dhammā* (mental phenomena) because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Furthermore, all of them are called *āyatanāni* (bases) in the sense of extending (*tanana*) the influxes (*āya*), and so forth. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding the phrase "one understands the eye": here, "eye" refers to the sensitive eye (*pasādacakkhu*), not the physical eye consisting of its constituent parts (*sasambhāracakkhu*), nor the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) and the others.
It says, "the eye-sensitivity. This refers to what was stated: "That which is the eye, derived from the four great elements, is sensitivity.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of including the meanings that are about to be mentioned. "By way of its own unerring essential function and characteristic" means by way of both its own unerring essential function (*rasa*) and its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*):
namely, the function of drawing toward visible forms, and the characteristic of being the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by visible forms.
The meaning is: by way of the characteristic of the translucent matter (pasāda) originated by kamma, which has the desire to see as its cause.
Alternatively, "by way of the characteristic of its own true nature" means both by way of its own true nature and by way of its characteristic.
And "its own true nature" (yāthāvasarasa) should be understood as the non-perverted essence (aviparītasabhāva). For that [essence] is tasted—that is, it is relished—by way of unerring penetration.
It is called "rasa" (taste/flavor) because it is relished; therefore, what is meant is "by way of its specific characteristic.
"By way of characteristic" means by way of the general characteristics such as impermanence and so forth.
In passages such as, "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," it is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) in its collective entirety that is intended.
The plural form "and in visible forms" (*rūpe ca*) is employed to clarify the meaning that they are the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, rather than being separate [from it].

And by that same method of teaching, although it is stated here as well that "one understands visible forms," nevertheless, taking everything together under the commonality of their nature as visible form, it says: "and external matter consisting of the fourfold origination."

The meaning is according to the singular number. "By way of its own characteristic" should be construed as both by way of its function as the objective field (*visayabhāva*) for eye-consciousness and by way of its characteristic of impinging upon the eye (*cakkhupaṭihana*).

"Depending on both" means that the eye is a condition by way of being a decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*), while the forms are [conditions] by way of being an object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and an object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).

And [the term] "dependent" refers to that which has become a condition. Although this is an exposition of the Suttas, since it is based on the Abhidhamma, it is indeed a discourse in the non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense;
thus, showing the fetters according to the Abhidhamma method, he says: "The fetter of sensual lust... up to ... the fetter of ignorance.

In this context, *kāmarāga* means lust for sensual pleasures (*kāmesu rāgo*), or alternatively, it is both sensual pleasure and lust, hence *kāmarāga*. That very thing is a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) in the sense of being a bond.

For this [fetter] fetters and binds that person who possesses it to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*)—that is, it fetters and binds a being to suffering—or else to future existences such as *bhava*, or karma to its result; thus it is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).

In the same way, the meaning of the fetter of repulsion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*) and the others should be stated accordingly as appropriate. Regarding the phrase "by way of their own essential characteristic": here...

However, it should be construed by way of one’s own function, which consists in not relinquishing the round of existence for a being, and by way of the characteristic, which consists in the aforementioned bondage.

The inclusion of "delight in sensual pleasures" (kāmasāda) is for the purpose of turning away from "delight in existence" (bhavasāda) and "delight in views" (diṭṭhisāda). "Delighting" (assādayato) means for one who is taking pleasure [in them].

"Abhinandati" means for one who rejoices by way of affectionate craving (*sappītika-taṇhā*). By both these phrases, the arising of sensual lust, which serves as the condition for powerful sensual lust, is stated.

This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. Regarding "aniṭṭhārammaṇe" (unpleasant object), here the word "āpāthagataṃ" (come into the range) should be brought in and connected by changing the case ending from "āpāthagate. "Etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ" (this object)...
This object is so subtle and so difficult to discern. “Permanent,” “stable”—this is merely an illustration;
it should be understood as including [views] such as “it will be annihilated” or “it will perish,” when one grasps it in such ways.

Through the influence of attachment to the first type of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), one thinks, “Is it a being?,” and through the influence of attachment to the other, one thinks, “Of a being...”
...is one who doubts, thinking, "Is it so? For doubt, which follows from the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, is absent when views are absent.

"Of one who longs for existence" means: "Since this desirable object of form has become easily obtained for us in such a state of prosperity, may there be such a state of prosperity, or even one superior to this, in the future as well."
"Of one who desires existence. "Such a form" means a form of such a kind; this is stated by way of applying the designation of the whole to its parts.
For the designation of the whole is applied to things similar to it, as in the expressions, "That very same partridge," or "Those very same medicinal herbs.
"Being envious" means generating envy or jealousy. "Being stingy with another" means practicing stinginess by making something not common to another.
"By doing": by all nine fetters as previously described.
"And that cause" refers to the cause of each respective fetter, namely: the analysis of signs such as the sign of beauty and the sign of repulsion; objects such as desirable and undesirable forms;
and the corresponding appropriate attention. [This occurs] when it has not been suppressed, has not been eradicated, and has arisen having reached its own plane.
With reference to that, it is said: "In the sense of not having been abandoned, [it is] arisen. The state of being presently arisen is already included by the mention of "manifestation" (samudācāra).
"By which cause" means by that cause known as the cultivation of insight and serenity;

for that is the cause of its abandonment both by way of partial eradication (tadaṅga) and by way of suppression (vikkhambhana). Because envy and avarice lead to rebirth in the states of misery (apāya)...

The first path is said to be what is abandoned [by it]. If this is so, how is the Sutta passage, "By the complete destruction of three fetters, one is a stream-enterer," to be explained? That was stated by way of the Suttanta method.

For the teaching of the Suttantas follows the conventional order, whereas this commentary is according to the Abhidhamma method; thus, there is no fault here. "Of the gross" means of the coarse, since...

It is characterized by constant arising, obsession, and intensity. "Of that which has reached the state of a subtle atom" means having attained a minute or subtle state due to the absence of the aforementioned modes.
Here, it should be understood that the non-arising of the fetter of restlessness is also stated, because of its inseparable connection with the aforementioned fetters.
Due to their identity of meaning, [the sense bases] such as the ear and so forth are [defined] by way of their individual nature, essence, and characteristic.

Showing that "understanding" and the understanding of the arising, etc., of the fetters conditioned by that [ignorance] should be understood in the same manner as already stated, he extends the application by saying, "The same method applies.
Or, "in regard to one's own states" means in regard to one's own internal sense-base states, or in regard to both types of one's own states. In this...
"By means of grasping the internal bases within one's own side" means by way of grasping the internal bases;
thus, the grasping of the bases in their entirety, both within one's own continuum and that of others, is established.

The same method applies here as well to the phrase "or to the phenomena of another. "Of the base of visible form" refers to the base whose intrinsic nature is form, which is divided into eleven types (including the half).
Having brought forward the phrase, “It should be extracted according to the method stated for the aggregate of form,” it should be connected [to the following].

Regarding “the remaining aggregates”: this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations. By the expression “according to the method stated,” through this extended application (*atidesa*), one should understand the specific distinctions:

that for the aggregate of form it is “from the arising of nutriment,” for the aggregate of consciousness it is “from the arising of name-and-form,” and for the remaining aggregates it is “from the arising of contact.”

One should cause [the former] to be resolved; however, since the other is the same in all instances—as in the section on the aggregates—there is no exclusion of the supramundane in the section on the bases (āyatana) as there is in the text for the aggregates.
Therefore, it is stated: "Supramundane states are not to be included. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the section on the bases is finished.

Commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgapabba) 385. "Of the being awakening" means of the being awakening from the sleep of the defilements, or of the being penetrating the Noble Truths.
"In the factors" means in the causes, or in the constituent parts. From the moment the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayavayañāṇa) has arisen...
He said, "One is called 'standing on the path to full enlightenment' from the moment one has begun insight; thus, 'the practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara) is [on the way] to full enlightenment.
The teaching of the Suttas is indeed an exposition by way of a figurative method (pariyāya), and this teaching on the foundations of mindfulness proceeds by way of the mundane path;
therefore it was said, "'the practitioner of yoga is [on the way] to full enlightenment,' for otherwise he would have been called 'a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka).'"

The meaning of the phrase “conducive to the enlightenment factor of mindfulness” (*satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā*) should be understood according to the method explained here for the phrase “conducive to doubt” (*vicicchāṭṭhānīyā*). “That” refers to wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to mindfulness; this is a locative case used in the sense of what is to be accomplished.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension together constitute “mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension” (*satisampajañña*). Alternatively, mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension is the knowledge that takes hold of the purposeful nature of things such as the “excellent” (*abhikkanta*) and so forth, with mindfulness as its primary factor.
Because it brings about the state of acting with mindfulness in all circumstances, it leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.

It is as follows: just as the abandoning of contrary states and the cultivation of corresponding states lead to the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, so too does avoiding persons devoid of mindfulness, associating with persons who practice with mindfulness, and applying oneself appropriately therein lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*). This is the meaning he demonstrates.

“Mindfulness and clear comprehension,” and so forth. There was a certain Elder named Tissadatta, who, having taken a golden needle at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), challenged the assembly, asking, “In which of the eighteen languages shall I preach the Dhamma?
By “Elder Abhaya,” he refers to the Elder Dattābhaya.
Investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*) is the investigation of phenomena, or the investigation among phenomena; that itself is the enlightenment factor.

Regarding that enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, what is to be said concerning such passages as “wholesome and unwholesome phenomena” has already been stated according to the method explained below.

In that context, “frequent practice of wise attention” refers to that which arises by way of understanding, as it truly is, the respective individual essences, intrinsic natures, characteristics, and so forth, of the wholesome and other phenomena.
It is an arising of consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-cittuppāda*). For that is called "appropriate attention" (*yoniso-manasikāra*) because it is non-erroneous attention;
and since it involves the turning toward that [object], even the act of adverting (*āvajjanā*) belongs to that same category. Its frequent occurrence is its cultivation (*bahulīkāra*).

"For the sake of further increase" means for the sake of repeated development. "For the sake of expansion" means for the sake of vastness. "For the sake of fulfillment" means for the sake of complete nourishment.
"Being inquisitive" means the state of one who asks after having investigated thoroughly.
Having attended upon a teacher and investigated the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, when one asks about whatever therein constitutes a knotty point—asking, "Venerable sir, how is this?
What is the meaning of this? regarding the meaning of the aggregates, bases, and so forth—the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) arises.
It arises. Therefore he said: “The abundance of the aggregates, elements... [and so forth]...”. Regarding the phrase “making the bases clear”:
here, because it is the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors, the body and the robes connected with it are intended by the term “bases.
Making them such that they bring happiness to the mind is what is meant by “making the bases clear.”
Therefore it was said: “Of internal and external,” and so forth. “With aggravated humors” means with aggravated humors such as wind (vāta) and the rest.
“Smeared with sweat and filth” means smeared both with sweat and with the bodily filth known as *jallikā*.

By the word “and” (*ca*), other things that bring affliction to the body and the mind are also included. Regarding the phrase “or a lodging,” by the word “or” (*vā*), the inclusion of alms-bowls and so forth should be understood.
"When there is an object" means when it has become an object. How are these objects for one intent on meditation? This is stated by way of the mental states that arise from time to time;
for those mental states lead to a lack of purity in one-pointedness of mind. "Among the mind and mental factors" refers to those that serve as the support-condition and so forth.
The word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "knowledge also" (*ñāṇampi*) has the sense of inclusion.
Therefore, it shows that not only is the object itself impure, but when that object is impure, knowledge regarding it is also impure; thus,
by means of the impurity of the support, it demonstrates the impurity of the supported, just as the impurity of the object results in the impurity of the subject.
“Making them equal” means, in terms of function, making them neither deficient nor excessive.

Because the function of resolution (*adhimokkha*) is more prominent due to the presence of a credible object, while wisdom (*paññā*) is not yet clear and energy (*vīriya*) and the other faculties are lax, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes strong.
Therefore he said, “the others are weak. “From that” means from that [state] of the faculty of faith.

Due to its powerful nature and the feebleness of the others, it does not allow them to fall into the side of indolence. "Exertion" (*paggaha*) is the grasping and providing of support for the associated mental states;
"the function of exertion" (*paggahakicca*) is simply exertion as a function. This should be connected by supplying the words "is unable to perform.
"Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the act of approaching and remaining upon the object, or non-abandonment. It is the rejection of distraction.

Non-distraction is that by which [the mind], being associated [with it], becomes undistracted. The function of seeing is that by which one perceives the true nature of the object as it really is, just as the eye perceives visible form;
however, because it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), it is unable to perform this function.
For among co-nascent phenomena (*sahajātadhamma*) that arise together while exercising the lordship of a faculty, [one predominates].

The accomplishment of the goal occurs solely through the state of single flavor (ekarasatā), and not otherwise. Therefore, the phrase "tasmā" (therefore) refers back to that very meaning by way of its causal status.
"Taṃ" (that) refers to the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). "By means of reflecting on the individual essence of phenomena" (dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena) means:

when the faculty of faith has become powerful due to the exceptional occurrence of resolute confidence (adhimuccana) in the qualities—such as sublimity—of the object to be believed, [one reflects] upon the distinction between conditions and the arisen-from-conditions, and so forth, of that object.

By investigating things as they truly are. For when things are grasped according to their own-nature and essential character by way of this principle of the nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*), there is no expansive resolve (*adhimokkha*);
this is because the activity of wisdom (*paññā*) is predominant through the thorough understanding that "this is the own-nature of these phenomena.
Indeed, among the factors that bear the burden [of the path], just as when faith is powerful, wisdom becomes weak; [so it is here].

Thus, when wisdom is strong, faith becomes weak. Therefore it was said: "By reflecting on the specific nature of that phenomenon, or by not attending to it in the same way as it became strong while one was attending to it, it should be diminished. "By not attending to it in that way" means:
by that mode of attending through which the faculty of faith became strong for one who is devoted to meditation, [one should not attend to it].
This means "by not devoting oneself to cultivation. Here, the state of the faculty of faith being powerful is twofold:

either because it exceeds its function due to a particular condition of one's own, or because the functions of energy and the other [faculties] are weak. Regarding these, the method for diminishing [the others] is shown in the first alternative.
In the second alternative, however, as one attends to [the object], because the functions of energy and the others are weak—

The faculty of faith has become strong; thus, by means of non-attention, and by means of attention that brings about the efficient functioning of energy and the other faculties, one should diminish the faculty of faith by making it of equal flavor with them.
By this method, the procedure for diminishing the remaining faculties should also be understood.
The Story of the Elder Vakkali. For that venerable one, being devoted to faith and having performed his duties, lived constantly intent on beholding the physical body of the Teacher.
Although the Teacher admonished him with the words, "What is the use to you, Vakkali, of seeing this foul body?
He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me," and directed him toward a meditation subject, he did not apply himself to it.
Having cast himself down, he climbed onto the precipice to end his life. Then the Teacher, while remaining seated as he was, revealed himself by emitting a radiance and said:
“A bhikkhu full of gladness, with faith in the Buddha’s teaching...”
"Attain the state of peace, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.

Having spoken this verse, he said, "Come, Vakkali! Being sprinkled as if with the Deathless itself by those words, Vakkali became joyful and glad, and he applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
However, because his faith was so powerful, it did not allow the path of insight to enter; perceiving this, [the Buddha]—
The Blessed One, having purified a meditation subject for him so that his faculties might reach equilibrium, gave it to him.
Standing by the method given by the Teacher, he intensified his insight and attained Arahantship through the successive stages of the paths.
Therefore, this was said: "The story of the Elder Vakkali is the illustration here. "Here" means in the case of the predominance of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
Regarding the failure of the other faculties to perform their respective functions:

"the distinction of other functions" refers to specific functions such as establishing [mindfulness], and so forth. In the phrase "tranquility and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood as including the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity.
"Should be diminished" means that, for example, the strength of the faculty of faith is diminished by reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva).

It diminishes; thus, the preponderance of the energy faculty (*vīriyindriya*) diminishes through the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the rest, because that [cultivation] belongs to the side of concentration (*samādhi*).

For just as the cultivation of energy and the other faculties protects the preponderance of the concentration faculty from falling into indolence, so too does it—protecting the preponderance of the energy faculty from falling into agitation—certainly cause it to diminish. Therefore...
It is said: "That which is to be abandoned through the cultivation of tranquility and so forth. This is the story of the Elder Soṇa; that is, the story of the Elder Sukumāra-Soṇa.
For that venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the presence of the Teacher and dwelling in the Cool Grove (Sītavana), thought:
"My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness merely by means of ease; even by undergoing hardship, the duty of a recluse..."
"must be done," he resolved upon that very standing-walking meditation and applied himself to striving.
Although blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he disregarded the pain and exerted firm energy; yet, due to his excessive energy, he was unable to produce any distinction.
The Teacher went there, exhorted him with the "Lute Simile" instruction, and [taught] the path of yoking energy with equanimity.
Having bestowed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), [the Teacher] went to Gijjhakūṭa after purifying it.
The Elder, too, applying effort with equanimity according to the method given by the Teacher, developed insight and established himself in Arahantship. Therefore it is said:
"The story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown. "In the others as well" means in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
"Balance" (*samatā*) refers to the state where faith and wisdom are neither deficient nor excessive in relation to one another, as it is with concentration and energy.

For just as it is especially desirable that faith and wisdom—which serve as the two separate "yoke-animals" (*dhuriya-dhamma*)—do not overstep one another in their respective functions, such that absorption (*appanā*) is achieved through their equal balance; so too it is with concentration and energy.

When there is a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) between those factors belonging to the side of laziness (*kosajja*) and those belonging to the side of restlessness (*uddhacca*), because they mutually support one another, the absorption (*appanā*) of the associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) succeeds perfectly through the absence of falling into either of the two extremes.

The passage beginning with “one who possesses strong faith” (*balavasaddho*) is an exposition of the very same meaning already stated by way of contrast (*byatireka*). Its meaning is as follows: one who is endowed with powerful faith but whose knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is not clear...
Thus he is one whose faith is foolish, not one rooted in verified confidence. For he places his trust in what is groundless, just like the disciples of the sectarians.
He sides with the "crow faction," that is, the faction of deceit. Running ahead with a wisdom devoid of faith, he imagines such things as:
"Merit consisting in giving arises even by the mere arising of the thought, without the actual relinquishing of the object to be given."

Deceived by things that merely resemble the true causes, one who has become thus—his mind parched and ruined by dry speculation—does not accept the words of the wise and does not respond to their exhortation.
Therefore it was said: "Like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable.
And just as in this case an imbalance between faith and wisdom brings no benefit but only harm, so too...

The mutual imbalance of concentration (*samādhi*) and energy (*vīriya*) does not bring about benefit; it brings about only harm. Likewise, it does not bring about non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), but rather brings about distraction (*vikkhepa*).
The intention is that it overcomes indolence (*kosajja*), and by means of that, one does not reach absorption (*appanā*).

The same principle applies here to the statement that it overcomes restlessness (*uddhacca*). "Both of those" refers to the pair of faith (*saddhā*) and wisdom (*paññā*), as well as the pair of concentration and energy.
"It should be made even" means it should be made of equal flavor.
"For one whose work is concentration" means for one whose meditation subject is serenity (*samatha*). "Thus" means this being so; the meaning is: when faith possesses a slight degree of strength.
"Believing" refers to the thought: "How can the arising of jhāna occur merely by attending to 'earth, earth'?"
Without reflecting, thinking, "Surely the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed," he has faith and generates confidence.
"Okappento" means resolving by way of conviction as if entering into the object, and leaping forward into it.
Strong one-pointedness is required because meditation (jhāna) has concentration as its primary factor. "Of both" refers to concentration and wisdom.

Since one who performs the task of concentration must also possess a high degree of wisdom due to the preeminence of their concentration, he says, "by way of evenness" (*samatāyapi*), which means "by way of balance" (*samabhāvena*). This refers to mundane absorption (*appanā*), for he speaks with apprehension, saying, "it certainly occurs.
However, supramundane absorption is desired by them precisely through such balance. As it is said: "tranquility and insight..."
“He develops the union.
If, specifically, the equality of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, is desired, why does he say, “But mindfulness is required to be strong in all cases”?
“In all cases” means in the five factors belonging to the side of lethargy and agitation.
Regarding the faculties: taking only a portion belonging to the side of restlessness, he says, "faith, energy, and wisdom.
Otherwise, joy (*pīti*) would also have to be included. For it is said, "by concentration belonging to the side of laziness," but not "by serenity, concentration, and equanimity.
"That" refers to mindfulness (*sati*). One who is appointed to all royal duties is a "general officer" (*sabbakammika*).
"By that" means by that reason which is desired in all instances; this is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
They are "universal" (sabbatthika) because they are applicable everywhere, and because they are desired when the mind is either sluggish or agitated;

or else, they are "universal" because all the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) to be developed in a sluggish or agitated mind have need of them. "Mind" refers to wholesome consciousness (kusala-citta).
For when that exists, it is a refuge and a resort for one who has not yet attained, for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, and for the sake of reaching what has not been reached.
Therefore he said, "manifested as protection," and so forth.

"Those whose wisdom has not penetrated the divisions of the aggregates and so on" means those whose intellects are not established in the aggregates, sense bases, and other categories, even by way of extensive learning in the scriptures.

For service to those of great learning brings about knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). Even one possessing nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassanā*) is indeed unilaterally called "wise" because he stands in knowledge consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*);
thus it is said: "service to a person endowed with the wisdom of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-paññā*) that grasps the fifty characteristics.
This refers to the knowledge that delimits that [insight] by way of the profundity of the phenomena to be known (*ñeyyadhamma*).
“Grasping at the profound state” means: “by means of profound wisdom that occurs regarding the profound aggregates and so forth.
For that object of knowledge is called the “course of profound knowledge” because one must proceed toward it by means of such wisdom;
or, the course of profound knowledge is the occurrence of that wisdom there in its various modes. Thus he said, “by means of profound wisdom,” referring to the reviewing of that [wisdom].
“...contemplation of analysis. Just as one who has attained fullness of mindfulness is indeed an Arahant, so too is one who has attained fullness of wisdom;
thus it is said: “The completion of development occurs through the path of Arahantship. This same method applies to energy and the other [faculties] as well.
Regarding the fivefold tortures of binding in hell, which are described in the passage beginning with “They thrust a red-hot iron stake through the hand,” etc.:

Because they generally perform [these tasks] first for a being who has been reborn, and because they are mentioned at the beginning in such discourses as the *Devadūta Sutta*, he says: "starting from the time of the fivefold binding and penalization.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the time of carrying carts, etc.," he includes the times when one is oppressed by other humans and by animals. "One..."
“Between Buddhas” (*buddhantara*) is said here with reference to beings who are reborn among the *petas* again and again;
or it is stated thus because some *petas*, like certain animals, may possess such long lifespans.
For instance, Kāla the Nāga King, having lived in the presence of four Buddhas, will remain until the time of Metteyya as well.
They say that he will obtain the presence of the Blessed One; this refers to what was stated regarding his lifespan of an eon (*kappāyukatā*).
"One who sees the benefits" means one whose nature is to see the advantages in energy (*vīriya*), thinking: "All supramundane and mundane attainment of distinction depends solely upon energy.
"The path of travel" means the way leading to Nibbāna together with its preliminary stages.
It is the sequence of the Noble Path together with insight, or the succession of the seven purifications.

For, considering it as the path to be traversed by a bhikkhu for the sake of escaping from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is called the "path of going. "Abounding in bodily fortitude" means being intent on strengthening the body in whatever way possible.
"Alms-food" refers to the alms of the country. [It is] one's own deed toward the donors of requisites.
"Piṇḍāpacāyana" is the honoring of the alms-food by making right practice bear great fruit. "Taking it out" means taking it out from the bowl-bag.

"Hearing that sound" means hearing those words of the female lay follower with the divine ear through the power of the five super-knowledges while standing at the door of his own leaf-hut. Human prosperity...
“Divine attainment and the attainment of Nibbāna—these are the three attainments. ‘Will you be able to give?

means: ‘By means of the meritorious deeds consisting of giving and service performed by you, through the attainment of the status of an excellent field [of merit], will you be able to bestow successively the attainments of gods and humans, and ultimately the attainment of Nibbāna? Thus the Elder addressed himself.”
He asks. "Smiling" means smiling out of the joy that arises at the conclusion of the reflection, thinking: "I have indeed transcended the suffering of the round (saṃsāra) without difficulty.
"One who has practiced wrongly" means one who has not practiced rightly by transgressing the laws of birth, family, and so forth. Thus, just as one who has practiced wrongly...

Just as a son, by that very same improper conduct, becomes an outsider from the family lineage and does not share in the inheritance from his father, so too the lazy person, through that state of laziness, is one who has practiced improperly and thus does not share in the noble wealth—the inheritance to be obtained from the Teacher.
Only one who has aroused energy obtains it, because of practicing rightly. Thus, the energy factor of enlightenment arises.
The construction [of the commentary] is thus throughout.

"Great" means great and vast in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), unique and not shared by others. Showing that this greatness of his qualities became manifest in the world through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*), he said, "Of the Teacher," and so forth.

Since the state of being a son of the Śākyas arises for one who has gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation through the act of going forth, he said, "With unconfused... and so forth, in order to show his status as a son of the Buddha.
Avoiding from afar those individuals who are indolent— those who do not know even the mere name of meditation, who are preoccupied with physical strength, who eat as much as they please,
who devote themselves to the pleasures of lying down and so forth, and who engage in frivolous talk— is the avoidance of lazy persons.

[This is contrasted with] those who have initiated energy through the commencement of meditation according to such instructions as "by walking and sitting during the day," and who possess firm persistence.
Approaching from time to time is the cultivation of persons who have initiated energy. Therefore he said, "Having filled the belly," and so forth.

In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, these two—reflection on the greatness of one's birth and reflection on the greatness of one's fellow-celibates—are not included; rather, [the four factors] are: the dispelling of sloth and torpor, and reflection on the right exertions.

It has been included. Therein, the reflection on the right efforts is included precisely because of the vision of their benefits, since it demonstrates that the attainment of mundane and supramundane distinctions depends upon energy (*vīriya*).
The dispelling of sloth and torpor is included precisely because of being intent upon that;

for one who is devotedly engaged in the production of energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is already accomplished as a matter of course. Therein, [the following are included]: avoiding persons who are lazy due to sloth and torpor, and associating with persons who have initiated energy.

Through the application of conditions that dispel the opposites of that inclination, such as reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), the factors for arousing the energy enlightenment factor (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) should be seen as acting by way of encouragement.
The joy (*pīti*) previously arisen is itself [the cause] of the joy arising later, because it serves as a specific cause and a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). Thus, it is "joy indeed."
"States that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture" is what was said; however, the plural designation is used because of its multiplicity due to its frequent occurrence.
The practice by which it arises is the attention that produces it.
What should be said regarding "recollection of the Buddha" and so forth is to be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Because access concentration is the culmination of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), it is said, "as far as access [concentration].
"Pervading the entire body" means pervading the entire body with sublime forms produced by rapture (*pīti*). The construction is:

for one who is recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma, too, the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) arises, pervading the entire body as far as access [concentration]. The same applies to the remaining recollections.
And this should also be applied to the reflection on the *Pasādanīya Sutta*, because that too belongs to the same category by virtue of being a "basis for liberation.

Even when there is only a partial pacification of formations, the attention of development proceeding through wisdom in such a way—just as in the case of complete pacification—becomes capable of suppressing the defilements;
it brings about access concentration and is endowed with such joy and mental happiness.
He said, "It leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture," adding, "also for one who reviews the attainment...
and so forth. In that context, the reading is "the defilements have been suppressed. For they do not manifest. The word *iti* has the sense of a reason;
thus the construction is: "because they do not manifest, therefore it is for one who reviews their non-manifestation."
Indeed, the arising of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) is not appropriate for one who is reviewing defilements.

Regarding the state of being like chaff and coarseness due to the absence of confidence and affection toward things that inspire confidence, this is understood from the failure to show respect and reverence; thus he said, "in the case of coarseness indicated by lack of careful performance."

The enlightenment factor of tranquility (*passaddhisambojjhaṅga*)—which is characterized by the subsiding of agitation of body and mind—is indeed tranquility itself as one of the factors of enlightenment mentioned above; the construction of the sentence is: "In this way, there is the arising of that very enlightenment factor of tranquility.
"The practice of refined food" means the practice of refined and suitable food.
By the mention of "the happiness of the postures," the inclusion of suitable postures should be understood. For when those three kinds of suitability are practiced, they [conduce] to the body...
By way of producing pliancy, it brings about mental pliancy and serves as the cause for both kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*).
"Pleasure and pain found among beings are without cause"—this is one extreme; "they have an unequal cause such as a Creator God (*issara*) and so forth"—this is the second.
Not approaching either of these two extremes, [the view that] they arise through their respective karma—this is the Middle Way.
Practice. One whose application is neutral is "one of neutral application"; the state of being such is "neutrality of application.
For this [neutral application], by serving as the cause for the body to become tranquil after having abandoned its agitation, brings about the two kinds of tranquility.
By this very fact, it is shown that avoiding persons with agitated bodies and associating with persons whose bodies are tranquil bring about those same results.
It should be understood as "commended.
When grasped by way of observing the mode of being composed, serenity (*samatha*) itself, having arisen previously, is the sign of serenity (*samathanimitta*).
That which has various peaks (*agga*) due to wandering among diverse objects is "diverse-peak" (*byagga*), meaning distraction (*vikkhepa*); for it is thus.
It is said that its essence is instability and its manifestation is agitation;

because it lacks one-pointedness, it is the opposite of non-distraction, thus it is "non-distraction," which is concentration (*samādhi*). That very thing should be called the "sign" (*nimitta*), as before. Therefore he said:
"And in the sense of non-distraction, it is the sign of non-agitation."

The purification of the basis and the balancing of the faculties are said to bring about wisdom; they also bring about concentration, and because they bring about concentration, they bring about wisdom as well. Thus it is said: "The purification of the basis... [etc.]... should be understood.
Because skill in the development of the causal factors is inseparable from skill in protection, and because skill in protection is rooted in that, it is said:
"Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa-sign. And the phrase "of the kasiṇa-sign" is merely an illustration.

It should be observed. For skill in apprehending any sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) or any sign for the arising of jhāna is indeed "skill in signs" (*nimittakusalatā*). By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "excessive laxity of energy, etc.," one includes dullness in the application of wisdom (*paññāpayogamandatā*) and a deficiency in gladness (*pāmujja*).
"Its uplifting" means the raising up of that sluggish mind by means of arousing the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) and the others.
The extraction from a lapse into sloth. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"But at whatever time, monks, the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the cultivation of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, the time for the cultivation of the energy enlightenment factor, and the time for the cultivation of the rapture enlightenment factor."
For what reason? Because, monks, a sluggish mind is easily stirred up by these qualities.
Just as if, monks, a man should wish to kindle a small fire and were to throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, and throw dry wood into it—
"And if one were to blow upon it with the breath from the mouth and not sprinkle it with dust, would that man be capable of rekindling the small fire?"—
"Yes, venerable sir. And herein,
the arousing of the development of the factors of enlightenment, such as the investigation-of-phenomena factor, occurs by means of their respective nutriment.
That [state] is to be understood, and it has just been explained immediately above. By the phrase "through the arousal of energy, etc.," the word "etc.

includes possession of the power of wisdom-application and both joy and dejection. "Its suppression" is the prevention of that agitated mind from falling into the offense of agitation by means of arousing the enlightenment factor of concentration and so forth. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Monks, on whatever occasion the mind is agitated, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, monks, an agitated mind is easily pacified by these states.”
“Just as if, monks, a man were desirous of extinguishing a great mass of fire, and he were to scatter wet grass there...
[and so on] ...and sprinkle it with dust—would that man be capable of extinguishing the great mass of fire?
“He would not, venerable sir.”
Here too, it should be understood that the development and arousal of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga) occurs by way of their respective nutriment;

therein, the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor has already been explained. That of the concentration enlightenment factor (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) he will explain immediately after this.
"Due to the weakness of the application of wisdom" means due to the paucity of the activity of wisdom. For just as giving has non-greed as its primary constituent, [so too is the case here].
Virtue has non-hatred as its primary constituent; likewise, meditation has non-delusion as its primary constituent.
In that regard, when wisdom is not strong, then meditation does not bring about progressive distinction between what precedes and what follows;
like unprepared food, it does not produce delight in the mind of the practitioner. Therefore, that [meditation] becomes tasteless. Likewise, through the correct practice of meditation...

One who follows a path that is not the true way does not find the bliss of tranquility; for that reason as well, the mind becomes disenchanted. Therefore it was said: "The application of wisdom... [the mind] becomes disenchanted.
To show the remedy for that—the arousal of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and the arousal of confidence (*pasāda*)—he said:
"The eight bases for spiritual urgency," and so forth. Therein, birth, aging, sickness, and death are to be applied as appropriate.
Regarding the statement "they exist in a happy destination (sugati) and a miserable destination (duggati)":

the suffering of the woeful states (apāya-dukkha) should be understood as something distinct from those [previously mentioned], consisting of the fivefold bondages, hunger, thirst, and so forth, caused by mutual affliction.

Since all of that has been taken as pertaining to the present existence of various beings, the sufferings rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa-mūlaka-dukkha) for past and future times have been taken separately. As for those beings...

It should be understood that the eighth ground for spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*) has been taken here as the suffering of livelihood—which is not shared with others—experienced by those who subsist on food and who subsist on the fruits of their exertion.
This is called "encouraging at the proper time" (*samaye sampahaṃsanā*);
this refers to the method of generating spiritual urgency and producing confidence in the mind during the occasion when it ought to be encouraged, according to the manner already described.
And "properly gladdening" means satisfying by first generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and then producing serenity (*pasāda*).

"By resorting to right practice" means by resorting to the practice of meditation that is right—that is, non-uneven—through the absence of lethargy (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*), and by way of the path of calm (*samatha*).
Regarding the terms "not lethargic" and so forth, [it refers to] those states belonging to the side of indolence (*kosajja*).

It is not sluggish due to the absence of excessive dullness; it is not restless due to the absence of excessive factors of restlessness; it is not dissatisfied due to the perfection of application of wisdom and the attainment of the bliss of tranquility;
and for that very reason, it proceeds evenly upon the object, having entered the path of serenity (*samatha*).

In this regard, there is no need for further effort in exertion because of its lack of sluggishness, in restraint because of its lack of restlessness, or in encouragement because of its lack of dissatisfaction.
It attains [this state]. For "neither sluggish nor restless" means that it proceeds evenly toward the object; because of the absence of relishing, it has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*).
Alternatively, because it proceeds evenly, it is neither sluggish nor restless. It should be understood as not relishing the entry into the path of serenity.
This is called "equanimity at the appropriate time"; this refers to the mind of cultivation at the time when it ought to be viewed with equanimity.
It is called "looking on" (pekkhanā) after having overcome the opposing factor characterized by non-exertion regarding encouragement, restraint, and instigation.

Because it suppresses the opposing factors and because it serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā), even access-concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) accomplishes the state of being concentrated in a person through the fulfillment of the function of concentration; thus, it is said [in the commentary] that it possesses the same functional weight (samadhura-bhāva) in this regard.
“Whether access concentration or absorption.
Regarding the statement “states that are bases for the enlightenment factor of equanimity,” whatever needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already explained above.
The state of neutrality, by way of abandoning both attraction and aversion, is the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
The reason is that [tranquility] succeeds when that [equanimity] is present, and fails when it is absent.
Furthermore, since that state of equanimity is twofold according to its object, he says: "equanimity toward beings and equanimity toward formations.

And since conflict regarding both of these is removed precisely by the cultivation of the tranquility enlightenment factor, [the author] speaks in order to show the method for abandoning only that which is non-concordant.
“Equanimity toward beings” and so forth was stated. Therefore he said: “avoiding persons who dally with conditioned formations.
For equanimity is specifically the antidote to lust. And thus it is said: “Equanimity is the path of purification for one who has much lust.
“In two ways” means by these two: reflection on one’s own karma as one’s own property, and reflection on the emptiness of a self.
By these reasons. The restriction "only two" is for the purpose of showing the equality of the number.
Here, only the number is the same; the things numbered are not entirely the same in every respect. The state of being ownerless is the state of being non-self-possessed (*anattanīyatā*).
For if there were a self, the robe—or anything else—might be called "belonging to the self" by virtue of its being something owned by it; however, no such thing exists at all.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Not lasting" (*anaddhaniya*) means not enduring for a journey, not remaining for long; the sense is that it is brief and impermanent.
"Temporary" (*tāvakālika*) is a synonym for the same.
"One treats as 'mine'" (*mamāyati*) means one creates possessiveness; having grasped it with the craving "it is mine," one remains [attached].
They treat conceit as something to be subdued by thinking, "This is mine.

This teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is taught by way of the preliminary path; thus, with reference to the factors of enlightenment belonging to the preliminary stage, it is said: "Mindfulness that grasps the factors of enlightenment is the truth of suffering. The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Origin of the Four Truths: 386.
“According to their intrinsic nature” means according to their non-perverted nature. Or, whatever nature there is at the moment of affliction—that is the intrinsic nature.
The meaning is: "from being subject to deformation, etc., and having the nature of hardness, etc.
"That which produces and originates" means that which produces the suffering characterized by occurrence and originates the suffering characterized by the cause.
"Prior craving" refers to the craving established prior to the arising of the suffering as it has been grasped; for when the cause is established, there is the emergence of its fruit.
The construction is: "He understands: 'This is the origin of suffering. The same method applies here for "This is the cessation of suffering.

"The non-occurrence of both" refers to the cause for the non-occurrence of the two—namely, suffering and its origin. It is called "non-occurrence" (*appavatti*) because neither of those two occurs by means of it;
it is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). He fully understands suffering, which is the truth of suffering, by way of the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*).
"It delimits" means the Noble Path is the full comprehension of suffering; that is the full comprehension of suffering.
The meaning of the remaining two phrases should also be understood according to this method.
Commentary on the Description of the Truth of Suffering.

388. *Evaṃ vuttā* means "stated thus" by way of enumeration (*uddesa*). It is a term that encompasses all beings (*sabbasattānaṃ pariyādānavacanaṃ*) because it is expressed through repetition (*āmeḍita-niddesa*) with the intention of providing a detailed explanation (*byāpani-icchā*).
*Sattanikāye* means "in the category of beings"; the sense is "in the collection of beings," "in the assembly of beings," or "in the multitude of beings.

For within the various destinies (*gati*) distinguished as gods, humans, and so forth—such as the earth-dwelling gods, kṣatriyas, elephants, those afflicted by hunger and thirst, and so on—one is distinguished by this or that specific birth (*jāti*).

A "group of beings" (*sattasamūha*) is a "class of beings" (*sattanikāya*). From the non-figurative standpoint (*nippariyāyato*), taking the first arising of the aggregates to be "birth" (*jāti*), it is said that "birth is the act of being born. This change consisting of arising is not [substantially] established;

therefore, in order to show together with that [change] those aggregates in which it is intended, the phrase beginning with "of those with change" (*savikārānaṃ*) was stated. "Of those with change" means by way of what is termed "arising" (*uppāda*).
“By means of change, for those things subject to change. For the three characteristics, beginning with birth, are specific modifications of phenomena.
By the phrase “a synonym adorned with a prefix,” he shows that the expansion of the word is achieved solely by means of a prefix.
“In the manner of entering” means in the manner of descending into the egg-shell and the womb. “Designated as production” means designated as the complete perfection of the sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Alternatively, "birth" (*jāti*) refers to birth with incomplete sense bases; "arising" (*sañjāti*) refers to birth with complete sense bases, for complete birth is indeed "arising.

In the sense of descending, it is "descent" (*okkanti*); this refers to birth by way of the egg-born and the womb-born, for they take rebirth-linking as if they were descending into or entering an eggshell or a womb-membrane. In the sense of manifestation...

“Abhinibbatti” (rebirth) refers to birth by moisture (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), for these beings are born having already appeared [fully formed]. *Abhinibbatti* is birth that is manifest (*abhibyatta*).

The passage beginning with “jananaṃ jātī” (birth is being born) is stated in order to show birth by encompassing all sentient beings through two pairs of terms each: according to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and according to the modes of birth (*yoni*). “Of this and that being... [etc. [is said].
Because it is stated by way of the "being" (*satta*), this is a conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*). Regarding the term "manifestation" (*pātubhāva*):
here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner"; by this, the inclusion of the phrase "acquisition of the sense-bases" (*āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho*) should be understood.

For this too is an ultimate discourse (*paramattha-kathā*). "In the one-aggregate existence, etc. means in the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences (*bhava*). In that [existence], of the aggregates...
When there is manifestation: "the acquisition of the sense bases" (āyatana-paṭilābha) refers, by way of two pairs of sense bases, to the two types of fourfold and single-aggregate existences;
to the five sense bases arising at the moment of rebirth-linking in the remaining [existence], namely in the form realm;
and to seven, nine, ten, or again ten, and eleven sense bases, by way of those with deficient or non-deficient faculties in the sense realm.
The grouping should be understood by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*). They manifest right here; they do not come from anywhere else.
They are said to be "acquired" because that continuum of a being exists. Alternatively, the acquisition of the sense bases should be understood as the acquisition of their own-being.

389. "The exposition of the state" (*sabhāvaniddesa*) means an exposition of its own nature (*sarūpaniddesa*). This is its own nature by virtue of being aged—that is to say, "old age" (*jarā*) or "decline of life-force" (*vayohāni*).
The very act of aging is "the state of aging" (*jīraṇatā*); or else, the mode of that which is aging is expressed by the suffix *-tā*, hence he says: "an exposition of the mode and the state.

"Broken teeth" (*khaṇḍitadanta*) are called "broken" (*khaṇḍita*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound. It is by virtue of such a transformation (*vikāra*) that a sentient being is said to be "broken."
That which is called "brokenness" (khaṇḍicca) is so termed because he has broken teeth. Likewise, one who has grey hair is called "grey-haired" (palito); that is "greyness" (pālicca).
Or, because the skin is wrinkled, he is "wrinkled-skinned" (valittaco), meaning his skin possesses wrinkles.
"By way of the fruit's metaphor" means by way of the conventional designation of the fruit.
390. *Cavana* itself is the state of falling away (*cavanatā*), or the mode of one who is falling away is expressed by the suffix *-tā*.
"The aggregates break up" means that the aggregates which constitute the final limit of the continuum of aggregates included within a single existence break up;

through that very breaking up, they go to cessation and non-appearance. Therefore, breaking up, disappearance, and death are synonymous. "Death" (*maccumaraṇa*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence.]
Death is that which is reckoned as "death" (maccu), consisting in the severance of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) included within a single existence. Therefore, he said, "not momentary death.

By not forming the compound "maccumaraṇa," the separate connection—that which is called "death" (maccu) is disintegration, and that which is "death" (maraṇa) is the relinquishing of life—is not improper. "The passing away of time" (kālakiriyā):

The time of death is specifically called "time" because it cannot be transcended; its activity—meaning, in terms of its actual nature, the very attainment of the dissolution of the aggregates of death, or the activity of "Time" (Kāla) as the "End-maker" (Antaka)—is what is called in the world "death" (cuti), which means "passing away" (maraṇa).
All of this is merely conventional discourse, expressed in terms of "beings" (satta) by way of the phrase "of those various beings," and so forth.

Because it has been so stated. This is an exposition of the ultimate meaning (*paramatthakathā*), because there is no indication of the destruction of those phenomena (*dhamma*) which, existing in an ultimate sense, possess intrinsic natures such as being subject to transformation (*ruppana*).

"Self" (*atta*) is that wherein consciousness exists; thus it is "selfhood" (*attabhāva*), meaning the aggregate of the five constituents (*khandhasamūha*). The "deposition" (*nikkhepa*) is the laying down of that [aggregate].

“Falling” (*pātana*) means destruction (*vināsa*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is shown that “falling” is spoken of as “casting off” (*nikkhepa*) by way of figurative usage regarding the result, based on the cause of casting off, as in the passage beginning with “of one who has reached death.
The phrase “the breaking up of the aggregates” (*khandhānaṃ bhedo*) is a description of the destruction of the collection of phenomena proceeding in a continuous succession;
thus, it is a discourse on the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) from a partial perspective. [The phrase] “of the life-faculty” (*jīvitindriyassa*)...
However, since there is not even a trace of conventional usage here regarding "severance," it was said:
"But the severance of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is death in the ultimate sense (paramattha) in all its aspects.

Even though this is so, that disintegration of the aggregates (khandha) due to the occurrence of which there arises the conventional expression "Tissa has died, Phussa has died" exists because the continuity of the aggregates (khandhappabandha) has not yet been severed.
It is said, “it deserves to be called ‘conventional death’,” and thus he says, “this very thing is also called conventional death.

Therefore he says, “for it is simply the cutting off of the life-faculty,” and so forth. For the total severance of the continuity [of existence] is what constitutes death by eradication (*samucchedamaraṇa*).
391. “By misfortune” means by an undesirable thing. In expressions such as “the analytical knowledge of phenomena” (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the word *dhamma* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
He said: "By way of being a cause of suffering. "Sorrowing" (socana) has the characteristic of sorrowing because it is to be characterized as such.
The state of one who has sorrowed, or of a person who sorrows, or of the mind, is "the state of having sorrowed" (socitabhāva). "Internally" means within the personal existence (attabhāva).
It dries up by virtue of its own harsh nature; it completely parches by means of drying up on all sides through the process of becoming firmly established.
392. “*Ādevo*” means that which causes one to cry out and lament by uttering [cries] again and again;
thus, the word *ādevana* is used as the cause for those who undergo such transformations as the shedding of tears. “*Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ*” means each respective quality (*guṇa*).

“*Tassevā*” means of that very same crying and lamenting. “*Bhāvaniddesā*” means that it is a description in terms of the abstract state (*bhāva*), namely: “the state of crying out and the state of lamenting.”

393. That which has a body as its support is "bodily" (*kāyika*). Therefore he said, "having the sensitivity of the body as its basis. That which endures what is difficult to endure is "endurance of suffering" (*dukkhamana*);

that very meaning is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), hence it is "the state of endurance of suffering," and [the feeling] is so called because of that. It is "unpleasant" (*asāta*) due to its being contrary to what is pleasant (*sāta*).

394. That which exists in the mind is "mental" (*cetasika*). Furthermore, because it is associated with the mind in various ways, he therefore said, "associated with consciousness" (*cittasampayutta*).
395. *Saṃsīdana* is sinking all around by way of obstructing one’s engagement with all sense objects.
*Visīdana* is an excessive or deformed sinking, by way of making it impossible even to stand up. *Cittakilamatha* is the exhaustion of the mind through the mode of sinking.
*Upāyāsa* (despair) is not itself suffering because it is a fault (*doṣa*), owing to its being a distinct dhamma included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Furthermore, those who would say that "despair" (*upāyāsa*) is simply "mental grief" (*domanassa*) should be refuted by this canonical passage:
"Despair is associated with three aggregates, one base, and one element; it is associated with some [factors] through one aggregate, one base, and one element.
He stated, "Despair is an intensified effort," because the prefix *upa-* has the sense of intensity (*bhusattha*).
The exposition on development that illustrates the mere nature of phenomena (dhammamattatā) demonstrates that there is no agent other than the phenomenon itself;

and since there is no agent, there is likewise an absence of anything to be done by it or to be grasped by it. Thus he says: "Expositions on development that illustrate the absence of self and what belongs to self.

(398) Regarding the phrase "of things subject to birth" (jātidhammānaṃ), the word *dhamma* here is a synonym for "nature" (*pakati*); thus he says: "of those whose intrinsic nature is birth" (*jātisabhāvānaṃ*).

The meaning is that they have birth as their nature. Since the desire for the cultivation of the path is to be understood as being caused by the cultivation of the path itself, he said, "without the cultivation of the path," in order to preclude such a desire.
According to another method, "But this is not so" refers to that [thought]: "O, may we not be subject to birth; may birth not come upon us. Thus...

The state of being subject to non-arising existing in the Noble Ones who have abandoned the origin [of suffering], and the non-returning of birth existing in those who have attained final Nibbāna, are what is intended.

Since this cannot be attained without the cultivation of the path even by one who desires it, and can be attained through cultivation even by one who does not desire it, it should be understood that "what is to be attained" here does not mean "attained by means of desire. Thus is the meaning to be seen in this context.
The word *pi* has the sense of a summary of the meaning that is about to be explained; thus he says: "The syllable *pi* [is used] taking the remaining [words] from below.
The word *yaṃ* is in the instrumental case with the sense of cause; thus he says: "by whatever phenomenon (*dhammena*).
For this word *dhamma* here has the sense of cause, and the cause should be understood as the unobtainability [of the desired object]. Or, *taṃ* refers to the non-attainment of the desired thing.
Thus, in this context, the meaning is stated by means of a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) as "that which [is] pleasure" and "by which [is] pleasure.
However, when the word *yaṃ* (which) refers to the word "desire" (*iccha*), then desire qualified by non-attainment is stated.
But when it refers to the phrase "does not obtain," then non-attainment qualified by desire is stated; yet that, in its actual sense, is a distinct phenomenon (*dhamma*).

Although it does not exist [in that way], nevertheless, what is stated is simply a desire directed toward an unattainable object. "In all instances" means in all the sections that have come down, beginning with "subject to aging," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the truth of the origin (samudayasacca).

400. *Punabbhavakaraṇaṃ* (the making of renewed existence) means *punobbhavo* (renewed existence), having elided the middle word (*uttarapadalopaṃ*). This should be understood as being like the word *mano*, where the first member of the compound ends in the vowel *-o*.

Alternatively, because the meaning is conveyed by the suffix *-ika* in the sense of "habitual practice" (*sīlana*), the absence of a word expressing the action itself should be understood, just as one says "a person whose habit is eating without soup is a 'soupless eater' (*asūpiko*)" [where the act of eating is implied]. (*Sammohavinodanī*)
However, the meaning stated as “it gives renewed existence, it leads to renewed existence, it produces existence again and again,

thus it is ‘leading to renewed existence’ (ponobbhavikā)” could also be established for those [meanings] through the term *ponobbhavika*, because of the plural designation in the rule for secondary derivatives (*taddhita*),
or because of the variety of secondary derivative formations, or because secondary derivatives possess the characteristic of expressing meanings [not restricted by specific rules].

This was said having made [this distinction]. In this context, it should be understood that the [craving] co-arising with karma gives rise to renewed existence (*punabbhava*), while that which does not co-arise but acts as an assistant to karma leads to renewed existence; both types bring about birth again and again in existence.

It is "delight-and-lust" (*nandīrāga*) in the sense of delighting and in the sense of coloring. That which is delight-and-lust and that which is craving in the sense of thirsting—both of these are this [same thing].
Since there is identity of meaning and only a difference in phrasing, it is said that craving has reached identity in meaning with delight-and-lust (*nandī-rāga*).
Here, the word *saha* (together with) has the sense of being of that nature, as in the expression “phenomena with visibility” (*sanidassanā dhammā*) and so forth.
Therefore, “accompanied by delight-and-lust” means having reached the state of delight-and-lust, because it proceeds without abandoning the state of delight-and-lust in all its stages.

The meaning [of the term] is as follows. It is stated, "arisen in connection with lust.
