Since lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms is mentioned separately, it should be understood that the arising of the aspiration for existence is spoken of here specifically in relation to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).
It is said to "arise" in the sense of its initial occurrence toward various objects of affection, and in the sense of its repeated recurrence.
"Enters" (*niviṣati*): this should be connected to the entering of arising by way of both obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and underlying tendency (*anusaya*).

"In prosperity" means in human excellence and in the state of a deva. "One's own eye" refers to the eye together with its physical basis, or the mass of flesh together with its translucent sensitivity (*pasāda*).
"Very clear" means possessing the five sensitivities that are perfectly pure, well-settled, and endowed with the colors blue, yellow, red, black, and white.
Like a silver tube, it is hollow because of its whiteness within. Like a necklace-string, it is attached to the ear-lobes.
A nose that is *tuṅga*—meaning high and long—is called *tuṅganāsā*; this refers to one’s own nose which has received such a designation. Alternatively, there is the reading *laddhavohārā*;
in that case, those beings who have a high (*tuṅga*) nose are *tuṅganāsā*, and thus they are those who have received such a designation. Their own...
The construction “they conceive” (*maññanti*) should be supplied [to each]. They conceive the tongue... [etc. ...by way of its color, shape, and function. They conceive the body... [etc.
...by way of its excellence in height and girth. They conceive the mind... [etc. ...as capable of reflecting upon objects such as the past and so forth.
They conceive the internal odors of the body and so forth obtained by oneself, as well as external odors such as those of ointments and the like.

Regarding the phrase "arising, it arises": when it is in the state of arising, the act of arising (*uppādakiriyā*) is stated here as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) by way of its general sense—that "it arises here"—and it is also distinguished by its object (*visaya*) by way of that which is to be characterized (*lakkhitabba*). For there is no lack of distinct terminology based on generalities and particulars.
Alternatively, in the term "arising" (*uppajjamānā*), arising is stated as the cause (*hetu*) without being specifically intended [as the primary focus], while "it arises" (*uppajjati*)...
If it arises as the state of the fruit, it is said that "it arises here.
[End of] the commentary on the description of the Truth of Cessation. 401.
Having stated, "All [these terms] are indeed synonyms for Nibbāna," the passage beginning with "For Nibbāna... is given in order to make that meaning more evident.
It has been undertaken. In that context, "having come to" means having made it the sign. For the complete fading away and cessation of craving is rooted in Nibbāna.
It fades away by way of going to destruction; it ceases by way of going to non-occurrence.
It is relinquished by way of giving up through lack of concern, or by way of abandoning. Furthermore, it is renounced by way of casting it far away so that it does not occur again.
It is liberated by way of releasing from that which is like a bond; it does not adhere by way of non-affliction.
But why is this Nibbāna, being one and the same, spoken of by various names? Showing that it is due to the diversity of its opposites, he said, "For it is one and the same," and so forth.
Because Nibbāna is by nature devoid of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma), even its names are derived from its qualities.
It is said, "by way of being the opposite of all conditioned things," because they are indeed devoid of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*).
"Complete fading away" (*asesa-virāga*) means that craving fades away here without remainder; this same method applies to the remaining terms as well. However, this is the distinction:
it has no arising, or rather, when it is attained, there is no further arising for the person; thus it is "non-arising" (*anuppāda*), the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*).

The meaning in passages such as “non-occurrence” (*appavatta*) should also be understood according to this method. Accumulation (*āyūhana*) is the origin; its opposite, by way of being contrary to it, is non-accumulation (*anāyūhana*).
When craving has not been abandoned, it arises wherever [conditions permit]; but when it has been abandoned, its absence in those very same places is clearly demonstrated.
Thus he said, “to show its absence right there. “Non-designation” (*apaññatti*) means non-designating; [as in the example: “bitter gourd...”

Or it refers to the absence of conventional expression, such as "it exists. Just as a person desiring the non-occurrence of a bitter gourd vine would cut its roots, so too the Noble Path—having Nibbāna as its object—is the abandoning of craving for one whose mind is inclined toward that non-occurrence.
Nibbāna, which is the state of the non-occurrence of craving, should be regarded as being like the non-occurrence of that [vine].
In the second simile, Nibbāna is like the southern gate and the Path is like the executioners.

Although the thieves are executed at the southern gate, they are later said to have been "executed in the forest"; likewise, although craving has ceased by reaching Nibbāna, it is said to have "ceased in the eye and so forth" because there is no further performance of its function there. This is how it should be understood. (The previous [simile]).

The former simile was stated for the purpose of showing that what has been ceased by means of the Path may be described as "ceased with regard to things of a pleasant and agreeable nature," while the latter was stated for the purpose of showing that what has been ceased by resorting to Nibbāna may likewise be described as "ceased with regard to things of a pleasant and agreeable nature";
this is the distinction between them.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path (Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā) 402.

"For the purpose of rejecting other paths" means for the purpose of rejecting the status of being the practice leading to the cessation of suffering in the path imagined by the sectarians (titthiya), or else, the rejection of the state of being a path in something else is the "rejection of other paths"; it is for that purpose. Furthermore, "this" refers to one's own [path].

And among those monks, because it is directly perceived by some, there is the expression "directly perceived" (*paccakkha*). By the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), he states the derivation of the word *ariya* as "being far removed" (*ārakatta*).
Regarding "because they produce the state of an *ariya*": an *ariya* is one who makes [others] noble (*ariyakaraṇo*), with the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).

Alternatively, an *ariya* is so called because he makes a person noble (*ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaṃ karoti*). Or else, an *ariya* is so called because he produces the attainment of the fruit of an *ariya* (*ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā*).

One who causes [others] to obtain the fruit and generates it is "noble" (ariya). Here, it should be understood that by the former [term], the acquisition of the name "noble" is stated by way of one's own function, and by the latter, it is stated by way of the fruit.
A meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that brings about the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is a "meditation subject on the Four Noble Truths";
or, the practice of development directed toward the Four Noble Truths is the "abode" (ṭhāna) for the particular excellences of the yogin.
The meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths: the first two truths constitute the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) because they are the cause for its occurrence;

the latter two constitute the non-round (*vivaṭṭa*) because they are the means for attaining its cessation. There is a focus on the meditation subject within the round because it exists as something to be grasped in its own form;
there is none within the non-round because it is not an object [of such grasping], and even if it were an object, it would serve no purpose. "Having mastered the first two truths" means...

The connection [is as follows]: For in the text on meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna-pāḷi*), "learning" (*uggaha*) is the bringing of the words to the tongue by means of observing their meaning. Thus he said:

"repeatedly turning it over with the voice. By the terms "desirable" (*iṭṭha*) and "lovely" (*kanta*), he shows the state of being inclined toward cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*magga*), not the state of delighting in them;
and it should be understood that the performance of the function [of the faculties] therein consists precisely in that state of being inclined toward them.
“By a single penetration alone” means by the very act of penetrating with a single knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Penetration (*paṭivedha*) is the piercing through (*nibbijjhana*), characterized by moving without attachment toward an object due to the absence of resistance. Realization (*abhisamaya*) is the awakening (*avabodha*), characterized by the attainment of the object without missing it.
It is simply the knowing that arises after delimiting [the truth] thus: “This is suffering; this is the extent of suffering; there is nothing beyond this.”
"Penetration in the manner stated" refers to penetration by full understanding (*pariññā-paṭivedha*);

it is said thus because, when that knowledge is occurring, one subsequently grasps its mode of occurrence so that there is no delusion regarding the specific nature and other characteristics of suffering.
This is not, however, because path-knowledge occurs by way of the formula "this is suffering" and so forth. [This is so] because of the fact that what has been abandoned need not be abandoned again.

"Abandonment" (pahāna) means drawing away, relinquishing, and cutting off; it is "penetration by abandonment" (pahānapaṭivedha) because, according to the method already stated, it is the penetration [of the truth] itself.

This [penetration] also functions to strike down and bring about the state of non-arising for that defilement which, if not abandoned, would prevent the cultivation of the path from occurring, and which would otherwise arise even when the cultivation of the path is absent.
It is stated thus because it moves without attachment due to the absence of resistance in the such-like occurrence of knowledge. Realization (*sacchikiriyā*) means making directly manifest;
it is the taking of an object in its own form, free from hearsay, modes of expression, discursive thought, and so forth, grasping it according to its true nature as "this is that.
That very realization, by the method already described, is penetration (*paṭivedha*); thus, it is "penetration by realization" (*sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha*).
By that [means]. However, because this knowledge does not completely eradicate the obstruction, it is unable to take cessation as its object;

rather, it proceeds precisely by analyzing that [cessation] according to its true nature through the eradication of the obstruction—thus it is so described. Development (*bhāvanā*) means producing and increasing.
In this context, it is in the sense of production regarding the first path, and in the sense of increase regarding the second and subsequent paths.
Or rather, it should be understood in both ways for both cases.

For even in the first path, it can be recognized as "development" (*bhāvanā*) in the sense of "increasing," since one increases the comprehension of the process (*pavatta*) and so forth occurring in the path leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*), according to what is appropriate.

And in the second and subsequent paths, it is [development] in the sense of "arising," because of the abandoning of defilements not yet abandoned and because of the establishment of the state of being a different type of person (*puggalantara*).
Development can indeed be known; that very development, according to the method already stated, is penetration—thus it is "penetration by development.
This too has been stated by taking up its actual occurrence, so that once knowledge has proceeded, there is subsequently no delusion regarding the specific nature of the path factors.
Let alone the path-phenomena as they have been realized; even regarding the fruition-phenomena as they occur, he is free from delusion just as he was regarding the realized phenomena of the truths.
Therefore it is said: "He has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma.
Because, impelled by the true nature (dhammatā) of reality, [his consciousness] following the sequence of the path takes as its object the realized phenomena of the truths.

The reviewing of the path, the fruits, the abandoned defilements, the remaining defilements, and Nibbāna takes place; likewise, the truth of suffering includes personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth.
This explanation of the meaning should also be clarified in relation to such passages as "by the clear realization of full understanding" (*pariññābhisamaya*).

Regarding the statement "he realizes by a single clear realization," the caviller (*vitaṇḍavādī*) here says: "The knowledge of the Noble Path [realizes] the four truths by way of distinct clear realizations..."
Regarding the phrase "performing what is to be done," he should be convinced by means of a specific discussion in the Abhidhamma.
Now, in order to explain that very single realization (*ekābhisamaya*) in detail, the passage beginning with "Thus for him... was stated. As for the statement, "In the prior stage...
penetration occurs," one might ask: "Is it not the case that penetration does not belong to the prior stage? This is true from an absolute standpoint (*nippariyāyato*), but here—
However, the understanding that occurs by way of learning and so forth is called "penetration" (paṭivedha) figuratively.

Alternatively, because it is the cause of penetration, the knowledge regarding suffering and the other truths occurring in the prior stage by way of learning and so forth is called "penetration," but not because its intrinsic nature is that of penetrating.
"By way of function" means that here the function to be performed by the prior-stage knowledges of suffering and the rest is brought to completion; for this very [knowledge]...

Or, it means "by way of full understanding" (*pariññādi*), because knowledge has the function of disclosing suffering and so forth. "Penetration of the object" refers to penetration by direct realization (*sacchikiriyā*).

"That" refers to the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*). "Here" means in this context. When the [stages of] learning and so forth are being discussed, it is not mentioned because there is no occasion for it;
for only when there is actual attainment (*adhigama*) would there be an occasion for that reviewing.

Indeed, in order to show that this is not the proper occasion, the passage beginning with "And of this" was stated. "Previously, from the grasping" means prior to the grasping of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
For "grasping" refers to the thorough comprehension of the Truths by way of learning and so forth.

Thus, because those [Truths] have been thoroughly grasped, through the firmness of attention, the preliminary thorough knowledge of suffering and the other [truths] certainly come to be; hence he said, "from the grasping."
“...from the time it has been established. “At a later stage” means at the moment of the Path (magga).

They are “difficult to see” because, although they are manifest at the moment of their own occurrence, they cannot be seen by ordinary knowledge (*pakati-ñāṇa*) according to their intrinsic nature and essence.

Furthermore, they are “profound” because they must be seen as they truly are by profound developmental knowledge (*bhāvanā-ñāṇa*), and specifically by the noble path-knowledge (*ariya-magga-ñāṇa*) when it has reached its culmination. Therefore he said:
"But from the perspective of penetration of the characteristics, both are profound. The others [the aggregates, etc.

are supremely profound because they are not manifest in their mode of occurrence—due to being undefiled and non-defiling, having reached ultimate happiness, being non-arising existence (*anuppatti-bhava*), and never having arisen before—and because they can only be seen by supremely profound knowledge; they cannot be seen by ordinary knowledge.
“Impossible to accomplish” means they are difficult to see. Therefore he said, “But for others,” and so forth. “Exertion” (payoga) means action or effort.
He shows by way of similes that this [effort] must be of a greater magnitude and more difficult to perform, with the words beginning “for the sake of grasping the peak of existence” and so on.
“At the moment of penetration” means at the moment of the Noble One’s full realization of the Four Truths through the Path. That knowledge is indeed one and the same.
That single knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa) functions to accomplish the tasks of full understanding and so forth regarding suffering and the rest.
"In these three instances" refers to these three bases for sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty, which are indicated by way of what must be abstained from.
[This refers to] the threefold unwholesome intention arising separately [for each]. "By way of the analysis of the words" (padapacchedato): here, the path traversed is...
It is called a "footstep" (*pada*). That means or cause by which sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) arises is its path of travel;

thus, its cutting off and destruction is the "cutting off of the footstep" (*padapaccheda*), and [the term refers to] from that cutting off of the footstep. Bringing about the state of non-arising is the "means for non-arising";
by way of that. Fulfilling the factor of the path (*maggaṅga*) by accomplishing the function of the path, it alone accomplishes the threefold function.
Wholesome intention arises. Here, the eradication of the threefold unwholesome intention itself should be understood as the accomplishment of the threefold task.
By this method, the meaning should also be understood in such passages as "in these four instances.
Regarding "abstinence from false speech" and so forth, it should be noted that in the *Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*, abstinence is volition (*virati-cetanā*), along with all associated mental states.

Regarding the phrase "and the training rules (sikkhāpada) have been handed down," the *Sammohavinodanī* states that, by way of the primary factors—namely, the volitions of abstinence—they are both "abstinences" and "volitions.
Therefore, some [commentators] maintain: "By the word 'etc.
(ādi), there is not only an inclusion of the abstinence from malicious speech and so forth, but also an inclusion of the corresponding volitions."
They say this; that would be appropriate because it is being stated by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).

Alternatively, the abstinences (*virati*) should be associated with the moments of refraining from false speech and so forth, while the volitions (*cetanā*) should be associated with the moments of uttering well-spoken words and so forth. However, at the moment of the Path (*magga*), only the abstinences are intended, because volitions do not constitute factors of the Path.
This is just as a single knowledge (*ñāṇa*) can be the knowledge of suffering and so forth, whereas a single abstinence...

Furthermore, just as there is the state of abstaining from false speech and so forth, right speech and the rest cannot be established as states [of virtue] because a single volition lacks the nature to accomplish the three functions of right speech and so on; and because, were those [functions] accomplished, the status of being the three factors would not be established.
For a bhikkhu, bodily and verbal misconduct caused by livelihood is indeed caused solely by unwise seeking of food.

He said, "It may be: 'edible food... [and so on] ... misconduct. And the inclusion of bodily and verbal misconduct is for the purpose of showing that the corruption of livelihood occurs only through the doors of body and speech, not through the door of the mind. Therefore he said, "in these very seven instances.
Regarding the phrase "of those that have not arisen": they are "not arisen" either by way of non-occurrence or by way of having an unexperienced object. Otherwise...
Indeed, in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, there are no evil, unwholesome states that have not arisen. Therefore he said, "In one existence," and so forth.
"In one existence" means in whichever existence this person exerts this energy.
"He generates" means he produces. By forming such a desire, he is said to generate desire in this way. "He makes effort" means he applies the practice.
He exerts effort. "He sets forth energy" means he causes bodily and mental energy to proceed in various ways.
"He makes the mind uplifted by energy" means that by means of that very co-nascent energy, he makes the mind uplifted by preventing it from falling into indolence as he raises it up.
"He sets forth striving" means he performs the striving of energy. In successive order...
These four terms should be applied by way of repeated practice (*āsevana*), development (*bhāvanā*), frequent exercise (*bahulīkamman*), steadfastness (*sātaccakiriyā*), and performance (*kiriyā*).
The phrase "previously arisen" is stated using a figurative expression based on similarity; for such an expression is used for things that are similar, as in the cases:
"That is the very same partridge," or "Those are the very same medicinal herbs. Therefore he said, "now, those of that kind. Regarding "arisen," [the opposite is] "un-arisen."
[This refers to] those who have fallen into a state where they ought not to speak [thus]. "For the sake of abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing.

Regarding the phrase "of unarisen wholesome states," here "wholesome" refers to superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*); their "arising" means attainment or acquisition, and by contrast, their non-arising is non-attainment.
Thus he says: "of the unobtained first jhānas and so forth. "Viriya for stability..."
When it is said, "He exerts," momentary stability is not intended, because there would be no purpose in exerting energy for that sake;
rather, continuous stability is intended. Thus he says: "In the sense of being established by way of a continuity of repeated arising.
Forgetting is the failure to see due to the influence of opposing states; non-forgetting is its opposite.
He said, “Non-confusion means for the sake of non-destruction. “Further increase” is repeated arising;
since that is an occurrence higher and higher, he said, “for further development. “Fullness” is the attainment of a state of proficiency and strength through constant occurrence;
thus it is said, “for fullness, meaning for a vast state,” which is to say, for greatness. It is for the purpose of bringing cultivation to completion.
For the purpose of strengthening the development of the jhānas and so forth.

"In four instances" means in the four instances beginning with the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. "By way of accomplishing the function" means by way of effecting all four kinds of functions together.

Although the jhānas are diverse both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path, [they are nevertheless unified] by means of the factors that assist concentration—namely, those characterized by directing, smoothing, gladdening, intensifying, and the nature of sublime happiness.

Right concentration is analyzed by way of the four jhānas, which arise through the excellence of meditation and are distinguished by their association with applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors;

nevertheless, this single concentration possesses the fourfold function of effort— namely, the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and so forth— just as effort does, and it possesses the fourfold function of abandoning perceptions of beauty and so on regarding the body and other objects that are actually foul, painful, impermanent, and non-self, just as mindfulness does.

The meaning is this: because it does not accomplish the function of the concentration of the four jhānas, the first-jhāna concentration itself [is present] both in the prior stage and at the moment of the Path;
likewise, the fourth-jhāna concentration itself [is present] both in the prior stage and at the moment of the Path.

"By way of various Paths" means that the jhānas are various by way of the various Paths, such as the first Path and so forth. The second and subsequent Paths are also [the causes] for the second and subsequent jhānas.
Regarding the phrase "But this for him": here, having taken all four kinds [of paths] as a unity by way of their nature as the path, it is said "for him" (*assa*);
the meaning is "for this path. However, "this" (*ayaṃ*) refers to the distinction consisting of being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar by way of the jhāna.
"It occurs according to the rule of the foundational jhāna" is stated here making the rule of the foundational jhāna the primary factor; and as it is here:
The same applies to the *Sammohavinodanī*. However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, a fixed rule for insight (*vipassanā*) is stated because it is not in conflict with any [other] doctrines;

here, on the other hand, a fixed rule for the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) is stated because it serves to exclude the doctrines concerning the person who has attained comprehension (*sammasita-jjhāna-puggala-jjhāsaya-vāda*).
It should be understood that the fixed rule for insight is not rejected here either, as it is common [to all]. Furthermore, there are other doctrines of the teachers (*ācariya-vāda*).
"Those to be explained later should be analyzed. Thus, first analyzing the aforementioned rule regarding the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), he says:

"First, by way of the rule of the foundational jhāna. One becomes possessed of the first jhāna because the attainment (*samāpatti*) that has emerged in the proximate location makes the Path conform to its own nature, just as the color of the ground [conforms] to the color of the lizard. They are indeed complete.
“They exist” means that there are eight or seven; they are seven because of the absence of right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).

They are six because of the absence of the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*). He extends the principle of their being seven or eight to the path factors and enlightenment factors by saying, “this is the method.
The intention is that this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* regarding the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the formless realm (*arūpa*).
But is it not stated there that "in the formless realm, the threefold and fourfold jhāna arises," and not "the fourfold and fivefold jhāna"?

True, this is so; however, for those who have doubts, by demonstrating its arising, it should be understood that he spoke thus because, in effect, it was already stated that "the fourfold and fivefold jhāna arises. And having regard for the whole [set], "And that..."
He said, "The transcendental (lokuttara), not the mundane (lokiya)," meaning that "the unity of a part is the differentiator of the aggregate of characteristics.
For in that case, only the fourth jhāna arises as mundane, not the set of four or the set of five.
Here, "how" means how it is to be understood in the absence of a foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna). "Taṃjhānikāvassa tattha" [means] that for him, there is the attainment of that jhāna therein.
The intention is that three paths arise by taking as a basis the first fruit and so forth belonging to those jhānas,
through the cultivation of the higher paths. However, having cultivated a path belonging to the third or fourth jhāna,
and taking as a basis the immaterial fourth jhāna arisen therein and the fruit belonging to that jhāna, the cultivation of the higher paths occurs such that other jhānas also arise.

That which determines the factors of jhāna and so forth, and which serves as the basis for the preliminary volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) leading to attainment, is not itself to be comprehended; thus, it should be understood that even the fruit [of the path] has such a basis.
"But some," however, says this with reference to the Elder Mahādatta of Moravāpi. Again, "some" refers to the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya.
In the third instance, "some" refers to both the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga and others who maintain the view that "it determines only the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*)."
Immediately after that was said, he speaks with reference to the other elders, excluding two elders.

Since cessation, when grasped as the non-occurrence of suffering and its origin included within one's own continuum, appears as if it were itself included within one's own continuum, it is therefore stated:
"or the four truths of oneself. [This refers to] another.
The same method applies here as well. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world, I proclaim the origin of the world, I proclaim the cessation of the world, and I proclaim the practice leading to the cessation of the world.
But how [does one] who is a beginner [perceive] the truths of cessation and the path?

"Grasps" means it grasps a mode established through hearsay and so forth. And by doing so, even when referring to the supramundane factors of enlightenment (lokuttara-bojjhaṅga), the act of grasping is not contradicted.

"According to what is possible" means in accordance with what is possible; the meaning is that, setting aside the truth of cessation, arising and passing away should be understood by way of the remaining truths.
The commentary on the Origin of the Four Truths is finished.
The commentary on the Contemplation of Mental Objects is finished.
404. The seven charnel-ground meditations, beginning with "a skeleton with flesh," constitute the meditation subject of bones (*aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhāna*).

The fact that the other [subjects], such as the bloated corpse and so forth, are by their very nature [suitable] for the nine cemetery meditations (*śivathika*) is why they are stated to be subjects for absorption (*appanā-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Only two" refers to mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*); these two alone [are meant].

"Adherence" (*abhinivesa*) is adherence through insight (*vipassanā-abhinivesa*), which is the discernment of the phenomena to be comprehended (*sammasaniya-dhamma-pariggaha*). As for postures (*iriyāpatha*) and looking forward and so forth, because they are merely specific states of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*), [they are not included].
They do not come within the range of comprehension, unlike intimation and so forth. It was said that the hindrances and the factors of enlightenment are not to be grasped from the very beginning;

thus it is stated: "The postures... [and so on]... does not arise. By means of the designation "hair" and so forth, the material phenomena that constitute their basis are grasped, just as the phenomena derived from them are grasped by the designation "hair" and so forth;
and by way of the hindrances and so forth, the states associated with them and the states supported by them are likewise grasped.
And with this underlying intention, the Elder Mahāsiva stated that "adherence arises even regarding postures and so forth. However, the passage beginning with "Does it exist for me?
demonstrates that for a beginner, there is no desire for postures and so forth by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) is preceded by non-thorough knowledge (*apariññā*).

Granted that the term "bhikkhu" is used here and there in the summaries and detailed explanations in such passages as, "In this case, monks, the bhikkhus..."—that is done for the purpose of showing that one attains the status of a bhikkhu through such practice;
however, in order to show that the teaching itself is common to all, it was stated simply as, "Whosoever, monks," rather than "only a bhikkhu. Thus, he says: "Whosoever, monks, is a bhikkhu..."

He said, "Or... and so forth. "Aññā" (full knowledge) is the wisdom of the supreme path that has reached its peak, knowing without transgressing the boundary of what is known through the path of seeing;
because it is the fruit of that [path], he said, "Aññā is Arahantship," referring to the "fruit of the summit" (aggaphala).
The construction is: "showing the liberating nature of the Dispensation even in a shorter period of time. "Niyyātentī" means leading out.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
10. Commentary on the Pāyāsi-rājañña Sutta. 406. The construction is:

"Because he was given this name by the Blessed One himself. Since princes are designated as "kumāras" (princes) in the world, and this one was the king’s biological son, therefore it says: "They recognized him as... the king’s... and so forth.

"Assa" refers to the Elder. While performing meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand aeons, he was unable to attain distinction by being reborn among gods and humans because his faculties were not yet matured.
"On the third day" means on the third day after the day he ascended the mountain.

Because they were destined for the enlightenment of disciples (sāvakabodhi) and because their accumulation of merit was preeminent, they did not go to the lower realms; rather, for one interval between Buddhas... [they remained] experiencing [the results]. "The deity" refers to the deity of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), who had previously been his companion in the practice of the Dhamma.
Having said, "Born from the womb of a noble maiden," the passage beginning with "And she... was spoken in order to demonstrate, from its very origin, the manner in which he was conceived.
Therein, "she" refers to the noble maiden. The word "and" (*ca*) has a distributive sense; it illuminates the specific distinction that is about to be stated.
"Family home" (*kulaghara*) means the house of her husband's family. "Signs of pregnancy" (*gabbhanimitta*) refers to the signs of conception.

The sign of the stabilized development. Although Visākhā was also included among the families residing in Sāvatthī, she is mentioned specifically as "Visākhā" in order to show her preeminence there, just as one might say, "The brahmins have arrived, and Vāsiṭṭha has also arrived.
As for "the deity," here too it is that same deity from the Suddhāvāsa heaven. "Five times" refers to [the Buddha's address] beginning with, "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu, this is an anthill... and so forth.
When the fifteenth question had arrived:
*Setavyā* is the name of that city by way of its feminine gender. As for *uttarena*, due to its connection with the particle *ena*, the accusative form “*Setabyan*” is stated in the Pāḷi;
however, in accordance with the meaning, it is understood as *setabyato* when referring to the word *uttara*.
The construction of departure (*nissakkappayoga*) has been employed. "An anointed king" (*anabhisittakarājā*) refers to one born of the Khattiya caste who has not yet received consecration.
Commentary on the Story of King Pāyāsi (407):
"View itself is a 'state of view' (*diṭṭhigata*). By the word *gata*, he indicates an extension of the phrase; or rather, it means the mere reaching (*gatamatta*) of a view.
"Wrong view" (*diṭṭhigata*) means the mere grasping of a view because it proceeds by way of grasping what is not as it truly is; the meaning is that it is simply a purely erroneous adherence.

Furthermore, that wrong view, having arisen through such factors as improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), reaches the state of active manifestation (*samudācāra*) due to the absence of opposing states and the acquisition of favorable nourishment;
thus, it is said in the Canon that "it has arisen" (*uppannaṃ hoti*).

“Citing various reasons” means citing various corresponding reasons such as “because beings are annihilated right there and then,” [or] because of citing the reason for coming here from there, and going from here to there.
408. This usage of the word *purā* (formerly) refers to a domain where the intended meaning has not yet been reached;
thus he says: “*Purā... pe... saññāpetīti yāva na saññāpetī*’—that is, ‘until he has made them understand.’”
Commentary on the Simile of the Moon and Sun (411).
Just as the moon and sun, by virtue of their magnificent and vast radiance, cannot be overcome by any other light, so too this [wisdom] cannot be overcome by any other;
demonstrating this, he said, “The moon... [cannot be overcome] by another,” and so forth. By the word “etc. (*ādīhi*), the phrase “to what extent... is included.
This also includes such challenges as: “In what places do these [rays] proceed, and how far does their radiance pervade?
To “envelop” means to bind; the meaning is to pursue. “To unravel” means to answer that.
“Therefore” means because he is unable to unravel the aforementioned challenge, therefore. Of himself...
Claiming a faction that denies the existence of the Sangha, he said, "In another world, not in this one," and so forth.
To show the reason why this nihilistic view (natthikadiṭṭhi) nevertheless claims, "He is a god," the passage beginning with "But the Blessed One...
was stated. [It means: "Even gods are annihilated precisely as divine beings; even humans are annihilated precisely as human beings."
Or his view might be: "They are being annihilated. And by taking it thus, the statement "They are gods, not humans" is not contradicted.
Likewise, "in the moon" means in the moon-palace (*candavimāna*), and not when the moon itself is being discussed.
412. They have affliction (*ābādha*), thus they are "afflicted" (*ābādhika*). Suffering has arisen in them, thus they are "suffering" (*dukkhita*). By faith...
They are to be trusted; they are the basis for the arising of faith. Therefore he said, "I [entrust] you," and so forth.
They are "trustworthy" (paccayikā) because they possess trustworthiness (paccayana) regarding these matters. This concludes the commentary on the simile of the thieves.

413. "Having pointed out" (uddisitvā) means having approached and shown [the beings]. "Among the beings who undergo karmic punishment" (kammakāraṇika-sattesu) refers to those beings in the Saṅghāta hell who are undergoing execution.
"Karma itself" (kammaṃ eva) means precisely the karma performed by each of those hell-beings.

"He inflicts karmic punishment" (kammakāraṇaṃ karoti) means he inflicts various punishments corresponding to the accumulation [of their deeds]; the meaning is that he thus produces suffering. Regarding the term "hell-wardens" (nirayapālā), here the word *iti*...
The word *ādi* (etc. has this meaning; by it, the entire commentary on the section concerning hell (*nirayakaṇḍa*) is included therein.
Having thus demonstrated the existence of hell-guardians (*nirayapāla*) through the Sutta, he now states "In the world of humans" and so forth in order to demonstrate it through reasoning as well.
In that context, they are called "hell-guardians" because they guard those in hell—that is, they protect them by not allowing them to escape from there. As for what follows here...
That which ought to be said should be taken from the *Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā*.
415. Regarding the commentary on the simile of the man in the cesspool:
"Nimmajjatha" means "plunge out," that is, cleanse it completely. Since such cleansing of each respective excrement consists in its removal, he says, "Apanetha" (remove it).
"Impure" (*asuci*) means unclean; however, because it does not increase the mind's delight and is not pleasing to the mind, he says "disagreeable" (*amanāpa*).

Because it has reached its own inherent nature, which is reckoned as impure and shares in the state of impurity, he says "reckoned as impure" (*asucisaṅkhāta*), meaning "become a portion of the impure.
"Foul-smelling" (*duggandha*) means a bad odor, an undesirable odor; moreover, it is not just any odor, but specifically a putrid odor.
He said, "The stench of a corpse. It is fit to be loathed; it is fit to be despised. It is repulsive, being a form repulsive to the sense of smell.
It "oppresses" (ubbādhati) in that it oppresses from above and on top. The scent of humans... [etc.
...oppresses because of its exceedingly impure nature, because it is born and reared in filth itself, and because the olfactory faculty of the devas is sharp and clear.
416. Far away [in the higher realms] are those such as the Paranimmitavasavatti devas and others.
419. *Sundaradhamme* means in beautiful qualities. *Sugatisukhaṃ* means both the happy destination (*sugati*) and the happiness included therein.
The commentary on the simile of the pregnant woman.
420. *Aya* means that which comes from meritorious action (*puññakamma*) and arises; it is happiness (*sukha*). Its opposite is *anaya*, which is suffering (*dukkha*).
"Not accomplished" (*apakkanta*) means not yet reached its conclusion or finality. "They do not bring to maturity" means they do not cause it to reach its final end.
"They do not sever" because of the blameworthy nature of one's own downfall. "They wait" means they look forward with expectation. But for whom does he find relief?
"Reaping the fruit of karma" means either performing [the action] while awaiting the result, or like a hired servant who awaits his wages (*nibbesa*), which is the remuneration.
Regarding "having broken through," he says "having pierced" (*bhinditvā*) to indicate that it is merely an expansion of the word by means of a prefix (*upasagga*).
This concludes the commentary on the Simile of the Dream.

422. “Whether going out or entering, there is a ‘living being’ (jīva)” — this was said according to his own inclination. For he is one whose mind is distorted by the delusion of wrong views, thinking thus:

“At the time of seeing dreams, the living being goes out from the body and, wandering here and there by way of seeing various groves, delightful places, and so forth, enters back into the body once again.”
Then, as an elder might extract a large bolt by means of a small pin, the Thera—desiring to remove the view of annihilationism under the guise of the conventional term "living soul" (jīva)—asked:
"Do they see that living soul of yours entering or exiting?
He spoke thus, employing the term "living soul" while referring to the movement of the mind, in order to demonstrate where such a conventional designation for a "living soul" applies.
423. "Having wrapped" means having wrapped by way of a wrapping-cloth (*vekha-dāna*). "At the time of passing away" means at the time when passing away—that is, death—has arrived;

it does not mean at the time of actually passing away. "Merely the aggregate of form" means merely a collection of a few material phenomena. For at that time, only a mass of material phenomena produced by temperature (*utu*) is obtained.
Alternatively, the word "merely" (*matta*) has the sense of excluding other qualifications; by this, [it excludes] the specific types of continuity-form such as those born of karma (*kamma-ja*), etc.
He causes them to cease. "They become non-occurrent" means they do not exist; this is the meaning. However, one perceives a "living being" in consciousness;
therefore, he says, "the aggregate of consciousness goes," the intention here being that it is not apprehended therein.
This is the commentary on the simile of the red-hot iron ball.
424. *Vūpasantatejo* means one whose heat has departed. 425. Regarding the word *āmata*:
here, the prefix *ā-* is a partial synonym (*upaddhapariyāya*), as in the word *āmisa*; thus he says "half-dead" (*addhamata*).
Alternatively, *āmata* means one who is dying with a slight affliction or fever; for while dying, his heat has not yet departed.
He is not as if dead and gone; therefore he said, "he has begun to die. Likewise, the shaking off of form is simply the turning back of the mind;
thus he said, "turn it back. For one who wishes to turn it back, there is the complete overturning and shaking;
that is the making of it further away, which is why he said, "make it further away. Of that which has been made facing outward...

"Turning this way and that" means shaking [the head]; thus he said, "Do it repeatedly. With the intention that the sense faculties are unimpaired, it was stated: "And he does not experience that base.
This concludes the commentary on the simile of the blowing of a conch shell.

426. One who blows a conch shell, or causes it to be blown, is a *saṅkhadhamo*. "Having made it resound" (*upalāpetvā*) means having caused it to speak by means of applying successive sounds; the meaning is "having made it endowed with sound. Since that, in actual fact, is simply blowing, he says "having blown" (*dhamitvā*).
Commentary on the Simile of the Fire-Worshipper Ascetic (428):

"One who has kindled fire" (*aggiko*) is so called because fire has been kindled within him. And his state of being a fire-worshipper (*aggikabhāvo*) arises from the performance of fire-oblations (*aggihuta*), sacrificial offerings (*māla*), and altar-constructions (*vedi*).

And because he desired to attend upon him with offerings of fuel, smoke, grass, ghee, oil, and the like, as well as with oblations such as bali-offerings, flowers, incense, and perfumes, it is therefore said, "an attendant of the fire. "May I cause him to attain long life" means:
may I cause his life to reach its final stage so that he becomes long-lived. "May I lead him to growth" refers to the limbs of his body.

And one should provide a split for the quality-parts. The two fire-sticks (*araṇī*) are the upper fire-stick (*uttarāraṇī*) and the lower fire-stick (*adharāraṇī*); thus there is a pair of fire-sticks. 429.
“In this way” means by such modes as “the foolish royal seer Pāyāsi,” and so forth. “By him” refers to the Elder.

“By the nature of smearing the stated appropriate reason” means by the essential character of smearing the stated appropriate reason. “By the characteristic of grasping the yoke” means by the characteristic of grasping an equal burden.

"By *palāsa*": it is called *palāsa* because it causes one to throw away (*palāseti*). The meaning is that, as if biting into the superior virtues of another, one discards them and makes them equal to one's own virtues;
for *palāsa* has the function of making things equal. Thus, "by that *palāsa*.
This concludes the commentary on the simile of the two caravan leaders.
430. *Haritakapattaṃ* means a green leaf; the sense is "a small leaf. Therefore he said, "at least," and so forth.
Regarding *sannaddhadhanukalāpaṃ*: here *kalāpaṃ* refers to a quiver;
and since that is fastened together with the bow and cannot be fastened without it, he said "with the bow and quiver fastened. *Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni* means roads for traveling.
Because those various water-courses and paths were thoroughly drenched by the rain, water flowed and streamed here and there.
Therefore he said: “The paths and the caves were filled with water.

*Yathābhatena* means as placed upon the carts; the meaning is that she placed them when told, “Mother, place this here,” because the word for the act of placing expresses the general nature of the action. Therefore, the meaning stated is “as they were loaded” and “as they were taken.”
Commentary on the Simile of the Dice-Player (Akkhadhuttaka-upamāvaṇṇanā):
434. "The losing die" (*parājayaguḷa*): He swallows that die by which, when a particular tally-stick (*salākā*) is placed, defeat occurs, so as to conceal it from view.

"The act of sacrificing" (*pajjohana*): This refers to the act of offering in various ways. Since this is performed by way of making offerings (*balidāna*), he says, "the ritual of offerings" (*balikamma*).
Commentary on the Simile of the Hauler of Sāṇa Cloth 436.
"A village site" means that which must be entered as a village itself, yet not inhabited due to its emptiness. Therefore he said:
"the portion of a village from which people have departed. "A village plot" (gāmapada) is like the place where a man has set his foot, with its boundaries clearly defined.
“*Pada*” is what is called [a place]; thus, a place inhabited by village-dwellers, a house reached and occupied, is called a “village site” (*gāmapada*).
Therefore he said, “this is the very meaning. “Well-equipped” (*susannaddha*) means well-prepared in the sense of being fit for travel when easily grasped.
But that preparation is specifically by way of being well-fastened; hence he said, “well-bound” (*subaddha*).

Although iron and other metals also possess the nature of metal (*loha*), the word "metal" (*loha*) is conventionally established in the Teaching (*sāsana*) specifically for copper; thus he says, "Metal means copper.
**Commentary on Going for Refuge (Saraṇagamana-vaṇṇanā)** 437.
"Abhiraddho" means one whose mind is gratified. Since this gratification of the mind toward the Teaching occurs by way of serene confidence (*pasīdana*), he says, "abhippasanno" (serenely confident).
"Pañhupaṭṭhānāni" means the "appearances of questions," that is, the appearances of knowledge (*ñāṇupaṭṭhānāni*) in you by way of answering me regarding the matters I have asked.
438. Regarding "saṅghāta":
he says "ghāta" because the sound *sam* is merely for the purpose of increasing the word. "By the fruit of ripening" means by a corresponding fruit.
It is not of great fruit because it is defiled by the killing of living beings such as cattle. "By way of the excellence of its qualities" means by way of the result of its arising.
"By way of the brilliance of its power" means by way of the natural radiance produced by the removal of opposing factors. It is not of great brilliance because it is unpurified.
"By way of the expansion of its ripening" means by way of the vastness of the fruit of ripening; "by way of its fulfillment" means...
Meaning: "In a field with defects" (*duṭṭhukhetta*) means in a field corrupted by defects such as being saline (*usabha*) and so forth;

however, because there is no sowing [of seed] there, it is without essence, hence he says "in a field without essence" (*nissārakhette*). "In bad ground" (*dubbhūme*) means in a portion of ground that is contemptible;
its state of being contemptible may be due to its lack of essence or due to defects such as being uneven (*ninnatā*). Of these, the first alternative is shown by the first phrase; the other...
To show this, he said, "on uneven ground. "Severed and split" means [damaged] by the striking of sticks and so forth.

"Putrid" means they have reached a state of decay because they were not dried properly despite being smeared with cow dung and the like. Since those [pieces of wood] do not possess heartwood, it is therefore said, "without core.
"Struck by wind and sun" means their capacity as seeds has been destroyed by wind and by the heat of the sun. Thus he said:
“*Pariyādinnatejānī*”: The capacity of a seed—such as rice that has just been harvested—to produce a sprout is the essence (*sāra*) of that rice;
its “taking up” (*ādāna*) or grasping is simply its arising in such a manner. However, these seeds are not like that, because they possess defects such as being broken or damaged.
The entry of the rain into the field is simply the raining itself; this is [stated] by way of negation.
Showing this, he said: “It would not rain properly. Here, the construction is as follows: by means of the sprouts, roots, leaves, and so forth, there is upward growth;
by means of the root-fibers and so forth, there is downward spreading; and by means of the leaves, flowers, and so forth, there is expansion on all sides.
“By the harming of others” means by the affliction of others. “From a produced requisite” means from the gift of requisites such as food and clothing that have already been brought into existence.
For even by the killing of cows and other animals, the food there is considered suspect for those who receive it.

The phrase "because they have not been killed by another" is a statement of the reason for their virtuousness. "Excellence of qualities" means an abundance of qualities; the meaning is that they are distinguished by supramundane qualities such as virtue and the rest.
"Vast" means sublime by way of the perfection of faith and so forth.
Commentary on the Story of the Young Brahmin Uttara (Uttaramāṇavavatthu): 439.
Then, because the cooked rice prepared with those husked grains remained entirely free of husks, it was called "rice with husks removed" (*uttaṇḍulabhatta*).
*Bilaṅga* refers to sour gruel (*āranāla*), so called because it is produced from fermented grain; that very same substance is also called *kañjiya*.
“Jātaṃ” means sour gruel (kañjiya); that which has this as its second component is called “bilangadutiyaṃ,” and it is also referred to as “kañjikadutiyaṃ.
“Dhorakāni” means washed [cloths]. Since even those that are thicker deserve to be called “thūlāni” (thick), therefore it is said, “and thick ones.
“Guḷadasāni” refers to the thickness of the threads and the density of the sour gruel.
And [the leaves] have their stalks joined together. Therefore he said: “In heaps... the stalks. *Anuddisati* means he speaks of them one after another.
*Asakkaccaṃ* means not respectfully, acting with disregard; and since that occurs due to the absence of faith in the fruit of kamma, he said:
“devoid of faith. *Acittīkataṃ* means not treated with honor by way of presenting it with respect.
Therefore, he said, “devoid of esteem,” and so forth. Or, “not esteemed” (*acittīkataṃ*) means that which was not made in such a way as to bring wonder to others;
it was performed without regard for excellence. Furthermore, the sublime and refined nature of the mind is impaired precisely by giving without respect (*asakkacca-dāna*).
“Cast away” (*apaviddhaṃ*) means having treated it like something to be discarded; by this, [he shows] regarding that gift—
He speaks of the cause of reverence. "Named Serīsaka" means having the name "Serīsaka. "Empty" (tuccha) means void due to being devoid of a retinue and attendants.
441. Regarding the description of the devaputta Pāyāsi:
"By its power" means by the power of that gift. "Sirīsa tree" means one endowed with a radiant trunk, branches, twigs, and foliage.
A divine sirīsa tree, pleasing to behold, stood there. It stood having manifested at the door of the celestial mansion to demonstrate the correspondence between the fruit and the action.
"By way of former habit" means by way of dwelling and familiarity there in a previous birth.
To show that it was not merely by way of former habit, but also by way of the subtlety of the season, he said: "There, indeed, for him..."
“...there is great happiness,” he said.

“He” refers to the young brahmin Uttara. [The questioner] asked: “If Pāyāsi was reborn there after giving a gift without respect, how did Pāyāsi’s female attendant, who gave her gift with respect, come to be reborn there? To this he replied: “But as for Pāyāsi’s...”
"By way of longing" means by way of having a desire for *pāyāsa* (rice-milk porridge), or because he had previously dwelt there before.

"A celestial mansion that travels through the quarters" refers to a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) that, being situated in the sky, moves about in all directions, rather than one connected to trees, mountain peaks, and so forth. "In the forest of Vaṭṭanī" means in the street of celestial mansions.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Pāyāsi-rājañña-sutta*.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Mahāvagga is completed.
The sub-commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
